Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
- Published
The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.
Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.
He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.
El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.
The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.
It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.
In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.
Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.
But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.
These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.
A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.
As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.
Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.
"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.
"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.
El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.
For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.
"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.
Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.
In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.
Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.
"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.
"The latter cannot be understood without the former."
Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.
Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".
She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.
For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important.
"It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."
El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.
For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.
However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system.
The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.
When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.
While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts.
"I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
"Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."

The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

For the popular diabetes and obesity medications known as GLP-1s, addiction medicine is one of many possible promising next acts.
Eli Lilly is investigating a new drug, brenipatide, and testing it in alcohol use disorder. A new company called Baseline Therapeutics is studying a GLP-1 receptor agonist in alcohol, cocaine, and methamphetamine use disorders; Altimmune is testing one called pemvidutide for alcohol. Addiction medicine specialists are hopeful that the Food and Drug Administration may soon approve a new medication for alcohol use disorder — the first in two decades.
But some telehealth platforms that specialize in treating addiction aren’t waiting. In the last year, a few companies have begun to market off-label prescriptions of GLP-1s, both branded and compounded, to treat alcohol use disorder and other addictions.

What cost England in ODI run-fest vs Sri Lanka as Harry Brook's 'genius' double century has 'no value whatsoever'?
Harry Brook wows Sky pundits Nasser Hussain and Mark Butcher with record-breaking ODI double ton from 114 balls but England end up on losing side after bowling too short and lack of middle-overs wickets; Sam Curran goes at 11.44 runs an over in expensive outing
Thursday 22 October 2026 20:35, UK
At the halfway stage, most people would have given Sri Lanka no chance.
The ask was a herculean 430, second only to the 438-9 South Africa peeled off versus Australia in Johannesburg in 2006 when it came to successful ODI run chases.
But on a day when South Africa beat Australia once again - this time in a one-sided Test match in Gqeberha - Sri Lanka stunned England in a Rawalpindi run-fest.

That meant Harry Brook's astonishing 202 from 116 balls, during which he reached 200 from 114 deliveries to set a new record for the fastest ODI double ton, came in vain.
So where exactly did things go wrong for England?
How did England lose that game?
Not with the batting, obviously, as Brook's sizzling knock - the highest for England in a men's ODI, eclipsing the 182 Ben Stokes scored against New Zealand in 2023 - was backed up by half-centuries from Tom Banton, Joe Root and Will Jacks.
The bowling was the issue with Sri Lanka rallying from 24-2 once Kamindu Mendis had been bowled by a beauty from Josh Tongue and captain Kusal Mendis was run out backing up without facing a ball after Gus Atkinson tipped on to the non-striker's stumps.
Sky Sports' Nasser Hussain noted how England overcompensated from bowling too full during their 87-run defeat to Pakistan at the same venue on Tuesday by dropping too short, particularly to Pavan Rathnayake, who top-scored with 130 from 106 balls.
The former England captain also lamented his country's long-standing issue of middle-overs wickets, with only one taken between Kusal's run out in the fifth over and Rathnayake holing out off the expensive Sam Curran at long-on in the 41st.
Rathnayake put on 166 with Avishka Fernando for the third wicket and then 133 with the wisely-promoted Dasun Shanaka for the fourth - both of his team-mates made 97.
Hussain: Lack of middle-order wickets a concern for England
Hussain said of the wicketless woes: "It comes from that middle period where England, historically, over the last two or three years, have struggled to take wickets.
"That is even with Adil Rashid, who did not play in this game, at his best, so that is something they need to solve, a box they need to tick. Getting back Jofra Archer, rested for this series, will help and add a bit of firepower.
"Maybe Adil has come off his best but today showed the need for Archer, and Rashid being back to his best. We all big up Adil but he has just dropped off, maybe because of injuries."
Former Sri Lanka batter and Hussain's fellow Sky Sports pundit Kumar Sangakkara said: "England needed an all-out push to take wickets when they had Sri Lanka 24-2. You have 429 on the board.
"Have set plays, try to bowl the bumpers, fielders set for catches - of if you want to restrict because conditions are not suitable for wickets, then go to death bowling early, try to cut off the boundaries.
"The only way they were going to lose the game was by the boundary count rising. If you are a fast bowler, you stop the fours with fields set and the sixes by executing the best deliveries.
"Still, England need to give credit to an incredible batting performance from Sri Lanka."
Sri Lanka get over the line after 'marathon'
That point about Sri Lanka is an important one from Sangakkara.
For as loose as England were with the ball - Curran, in just his second game since The Hundred in August due to a groin injury, struggled to land his moon balls and yorkers and was flogged for 103 runs from his nine overs - Sri Lanka were superb.
They showed grit after slipping two down early, then the ability to adapt by pushing Shanaka up the order - he smoked eight sixes in his 50-ball 97 - and when late wickets had seen Sri Lanka wobble a bit, Janith Liyanage fired under pressure with an unbeaten 61.
Liyanage crunched two fours and a six across three balls off Curran to trim the ask to 29 from 21 deliveries and then spanked the winning six with one ball to spare after Tongue has taken two wickets in two deliveries earlier in the final over.
Hussain added: "Sri Lanka had to be pretty much perfect for 50 overs and they were. There were lads in there who played pretty much the perfect innings.
"It was like running a marathon for Sri Lanka - they saw that last bit and started to stumble when they needed to be calm.
"So Liyanage in the end - that was incredibly special. You looked at his body language, it was like, 'leave it to me, lads' - he was calm, composed and belted it down the ground.
"It was a perfect, historic chase and brilliant for Sri Lanka. They are such a talented, passionate cricketing nation. They needed a day like today and they got one."
Why Brook said his double hundred 'does not matter'
Brook had spoken earlier in the week about wishing there was a match-winning column in players' stats.
If that was part of cricket, then for a long time in Rawalpindi on Thursday it looked like Brook's would have a big fat tick in it.
In the end, though, the Yorkshireman insisted that his individual heroics "didn't matter."
Brook, whose innings featured 21 fours and 10 sixes said: "I always say I want to make match-winning contributions, have a match-winning impact. Unfortunately I've got 200 and it's not been match-winning. In my eyes, it doesn't matter. It had no value whatsoever."
Still, Hussain and Sky Sports colleague Mark Butcher enthused over the England captain, with Hussain calling him the best male multi-format batter in the world and saying his presence makes the team contenders at next year's 50-over World Cup in Africa.
The pundit added: "Every shot selection he made was spot on - it had to be to score 200 that quickly. He has been touched by genius ever since we have seen him.
"The biggest area of growth for this ODI team is if Brook can convert his Test and T20 form into this format. He did that, it was magical.
Butcher said: "Sometimes your breath is taken away with Brook and you don't quite have the words to describe what you are watching.
"Such is his precision and the way he can uses the pace on the ball, he can pretty much manoeuvre it wherever he likes. Then he will fly out of the crease and hit you for six.
"He has such balance, his hands are so good, the control of the bat face is as good as anybody I have seen. He can play a shot for pretty much every delivery. He is absolutely box office."
Now, if England could just get the bowling sorted…

Thousands of protesters took to the Paris streets on Thursday (October 22, 2026) while other cities banned demonstrations following a weekend of clashes and widespread looting that marked France's most violent unrest in years.
Also Read: Clashes and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
Organisers of the Paris protest said an administrative court overturned a ban issued by police after they challenged it. The Paris prefecture previously said the ban was necessary, given the risk of street violence after groups of masked youth clashed with officers, looted shops and torched cars over the weekend.
The Paris court ruling was not immediately made public. Protesters, including many youngsters, gathered peacefully and chanted in a southeastern part of the city amid heavy police presence.
“We don't need tear gas for our future to look bleak,” read a banner they unfurled.
Organisers signed a police document stating that the protest would remain stationary due to the risk of violence.
More bans were expected in the coming days. French President Emmanuel Macron said such measures aim to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
The right to demonstrate is protected by the French Constitution, and bans on demonstrations planned for Thursday (October 22) in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were seen by some as an infringement on French people's right to protest.
High school and university student groups said they will continue to mobilise, even though the autumn school break started this week.
Mr. Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysée Palace that the strategy adopted for the coming days is to ban protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority.”
“The rules are simple, and I think they're just common sense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days," he said. “For those who still want to protest, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes."
Mr. Macron blamed the weekend's violence on “actions led by radical far-left groups who aimed to bring the Republic down," in addition to criminals who came to loot.
The turmoil in Paris and other French cities has prompted a strong security response. Night curfews have been implemented in some areas of the French capital, as well as in other cities where calm has been restored.
Authorities are bracing for another big protest day
Thursday's planned protests were seen as a prelude to Saturday's (October 23) big demonstration, when activists from the CGT labour union and the “ yellow vest ” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join.
Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier, will also be banned, local authorities said. Cities outside Paris have been hit hard by the unrest, including Limoges where a fire nearly destroyed the 19th century city hall.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled on November 5, and called on private and public sector employees to join.
From student protests to a broader social movement
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, even in smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as complex and unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before next year's presidential election to choose Macron's successor.

The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack
JAMMU: A Jammu court has imposed two life sentences and fines of Rs 2 lakh on Mohammed Sharief, a terrorist who gunned down three members of a family, including a six-month-old infant, in Ramban district’s Gool area over 21 years ago.In his order on Wednesday, principal sessions judge Ramban Ajay Kumar Gupta rejected defence arguments that the attack had taken place more than two decades ago when Sharief was young, his long incarceration and possibility of rehabilitation.Besides the life sentences, the court imposed two separate terms of 10 years on Sharief under various sections pertaining to murder and arms act offences. “All sentences shall run concurrently, while the period already spent in custody shall be set off in accordance with law,” the judge said.The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack and directed J&K State Legal Services Authority to provide compensation to heirs of the deceased and the survivors.Judge Gupta rejected defence arguments about the testimony of two injured eyewitnesses, saying they were reliable and corroborated by medical and other evidence. Defective investigations or delay in recording statements could not automatically result in acquittal when credible evidence otherwise established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the judge said.
Public prosecutor Wajid Ahmed pressed for maximum punishment under law, contending that the murder of three innocent family members, including the baby, and the use of an AK-47 rifle warranted a stringent sentence.The court considered aggravating and mitigating circumstances and held that although the crime was extremely grave, the case did not warrant the death penalty under the rarest of rare principle.

Minister giving Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts
Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs says up to 500 temporary layoffs are due to U.S. tariffs
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is giving the American parent company of Hamilton-based Stelco 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts.
In a "demand letter" sent to Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs on Thursday, Joly says the company is violating its commitments under the Investment Canada Act.
"In the event Cliffs fails to comply with this demand, the Minister may, pursuant to section 40 of the Act, make an application to a superior court," the letter, obtained by Radio-Canada, reads.
Joly indicates that if the government proceeds with legal action, it would be asking the courts to issue monetary penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially direct the company to divest from Stelco.
"I remain prepared to sit down with Cleveland-Cliffs to find a solution. But our bottom line is clear: protect Canadian jobs, defend our steel industry and ensure that commitments made to Canada are respected," Joly said in a statement.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly answers questions from reporters in Ottawa on Oct. 14. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Cleveland-Cliffs said late last month that it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles certain steel production at Stelco, a move the federal government says violates "binding commitments" made when it bought the company in 2024.
The federal government has said the company's purchase of Stelco included promises to employ "at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees" as there were in 2024 through 2029.
The company said the planned layoffs are in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs on steel squeeze its sales. But Joly has dismissed that reasoning.
"Let me be clear: no act of God or change in market conditions can relieve Cleveland-Cliffs of the commitments it made to Canada. Those commitments are not optional," she said in her statement.

Mourners killed by Kenya police at ex-PM's national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
- Published
Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found.
During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force.
BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles.
Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones.
In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.
The BBC went through more than 1,500 images and videos to establish the location of those killed in the stadium on 16 October 2025, and also spoke to some of their relatives.
Forensic analysis by the BBC suggests an elite police unit responsible for protecting the president may have fired the fatal shots.
Kenya's longest serving opposition leader and former prime minister died the previous day while receiving medical treatment in India. He was one of the country's most influential political figures.
A year on, Kenya's police watchdog, the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), is still investigating the deaths and police response and no-one has been held to account.
The interior minister defended the police by saying they had been under "so much pressure" after working for many hours non-stop and had been deployed to a new venue at the last minute.
"The investigations are being done by an independent police oversight authority, we believe that their findings will help us take appropriate legal action," Murkomen said.
Responding to questions about the conduct of police he said: "I don't think… somebody [was] sitting there and saying: 'Shoot now'. It is the judgment of the police officer at the spur of the moment."
Yvonne Akinyi, who husband was among those killed told the BBC: "The people who we look at to protect us, these are the people that cause us this pain. These are the people that make us to become young widows in this country, young orphans in this county," she said.
Odinga's death at 80 prompted an outpouring of grief across Kenya. Thousands gathered at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport as his body was flown home.
The body had originally been due to lie in state at parliament, but the scale of the crowds and fears of a security breach forced a last-minute change of venue to Kasarani Stadium. Officials say they had little time to secure the 48,000-capacity venue, and thousands spilled onto the pitch and into the stands unchecked.
After several hours of waiting to see the coffin in 30C heat with no public address system for official updates, a small section of the crowd began throwing objects, including plastic chairs, at officers guarding the VIP pavilion. Police fired live rounds as mourners pushed toward the pavilion. Footage from elsewhere in the stadium shows the crowd remained largely peaceful.
Goodbye Raila
BBC Africa Eye investigates the killing of three mourners at Raila Odinga’s national farewell
Watch on iPlayer
In total, three people were killed.
One of them was Evans Kiche, a 40 year-old-chef and father to seven children. BBC analysis shows he was around 60m from the confrontation when he was killed by a gunshot wound to the head.
The two other mourners killed, Vincent Ogutu and Jidah Burka, were at least 160m away, in the opposite stands, far removed from the pavilion.
Autopsy reports confirm that Ogutu died from a gunshot wound to the chest and 42 year-old Burka was fatally shot in the head.
Piecing together a timeline of events, BBC Africa Eye identified at least eight police officers operating together, wearing tactical clothing and military camouflage. These officers carry assault rifles, with no visible insignia and faces covered.
Their uniforms and movements are consistent with a layer of security assigned to President William Ruto and other VIPs before and after the shooting. At least three officers of this unit appear to fire their weapons.
The BBC identified three of them as part of an elite police unit responsible for presidential protection.
The BBC cannot establish which bullets killed each victim, and cannot rule out other officers firing inside the stadium.
Kenya's National Police Service told the BBC: "There are huge lessons picked from the day's events," which had "formed a fundamental learning curve for a better, more professional application in the future." The IPOA did not respond to a request for comment.
Ogutu, a 36-year-old father of three, hadn't planned to go to Kasarani, his wife told the BBC. He was in central Nairobi on the morning of 16 October with friends when they saw the crowds heading to the stadium and decided to join.
Within hours, he was dead.
His widow Yvonne Akinyi described how the killing upended their family, saying their children were now orphans.
As she prepares to mark a year since her husband's death, Akinyi is no closer to understanding why he died while paying his respects at an event organised by the government.
"I will just try to be that strong woman. Very strong. But deep inside there is a hole," she said.
"It is very painful because sometimes you just sit down and ask yourself. At Kasarani there were so many people, so many of them. Why him."

Manchester United manager Michael Carrick apologised to the club’s travelling supporters and took responsibility for his side’s 4-1 defeat to Como in the UEFA Champions League on Wednesday, describing the performance as unacceptable.
Carrick approached the away section at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia after the final whistle, repeatedly raising his hands in apology following another disappointing outing for United.
“I care an unbelievable amount about the supporters. They are the heartbeat of this football club and they always will be,” Carrick said.
The defeat extended United’s winless streak to seven matches across all competitions and marked its fifth loss of the season, increasing the scrutiny on Carrick just months after he signed a two-year contract.
MATCH REPORT | Como vs Manchester United Player Ratings — Nico Paz scores twice as Italian side thrashes Red Devils
The former United midfielder acknowledged that the team had fallen well short of expectations and accepted responsibility for its struggles.
“It was more than disappointing. I think everybody has got to take responsibility for that,” he said.
Carrick added that the manner of the defeat was particularly difficult to accept, with United unable to match Como’s intensity and attacking threat.
Nico Paz scored twice for Cesc Fabregas’ side, while Anastasios Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon were also on target. Substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored a consolation goal for United in stoppage time.
The result continued a difficult start to the campaign for Carrick, who had initially impressed during his interim spell in charge last season.
Appointed temporarily in January, he oversaw a turnaround that helped United finish third in the Premier League and qualify for the Champions League, earning him the permanent managerial position.
However, United has managed just one Premier League victory this season and has already been eliminated from the English League Cup.
With results deteriorating, Carrick’s position has come under increasing pressure, although he insisted he had not considered his future when questioned after the match.
“I’ve not given my own position any thought,” Carrick said, maintaining that his immediate concern was the club’s supporters and the team’s performance.

Period blood is the only blood that does not flow because of violence. “Still, society despises that blood the most.” Savitri Hooda, 65, speaks straight into her phone camera, standing under a neem tree in her home’s backyard. That video, shot from Rohtak’s Mungan village, 70 km north-west of Delhi, got 19,000 ‘likes’ on Instagram.
In another reel, she looks at the camera and calls her own generation “shoddy”. “Should I list their misdeeds? They killed daughters in the womb, discriminated against their own daughters, burnt their daughters-in-law for dowry, and leered at other women. They treated women as second-class citizens and now cannot stand their freedom.” That got her 4,87,000 likes and a whole lot of comments from people showering love on “Dadi”.
Welcome to @tai_savitri’s month-old Instagram account, which has just 27 posts but 3,08,000 followers. Her bio says: “Desi feminist from Haryana. Freedom and unfiltered opinions.”
The overwhelming response to her profile has been startling even for the family. Her son, Ashish, recalls receiving the first podcast invitation when Savitri had around 3,000 followers. After her video on mental health went viral last month, interview requests began pouring in.
Across the National Capital Region (NCR), women over 60 are putting their voices out on social media. They are singing, dancing, and giving out wisdom that the youth is lapping up.
The irreverent feminist
For Savitri, speaking her mind is hardly new. The rebellious streak that now finds an audience online surfaced when she was a schoolgirl. She dropped out in Class 7 after her mother, whom she describes as “very conservative”, refused to let her participate in a school play about dowry and opposed her taking up judo as well. “She thought it would disgrace the family. So I quit my studies in protest,” Savitri says.
It is a decision she still regrets.
Her formal education may have ended early, but Ashish says his mother has always been receptive to new ideas. She listens, reflects, and frequently brings her own observations into discussions, sometimes surprising the family with the connections she makes.
Her curiosity has also translated into considerable digital independence. Savitri records and uploads videos, manages her YouTube account and responds to comments herself. She uses the voice-to-text tool because it is faster than entering text manually. “If someone writes in English and I cannot understand the comment, I reply, ‘Thank you for sharing your views’,” she says.
To meet her is to meet an anti-influencer. She sits cross-legged on a bed in a dimly lit room, plaster peeling off its green-painted walls. Clothes hang shabbily on pegs. Ashish, an aspiring stand-up comic and novelist, leaning against a pillow beside her. She asks her husband to make three cups of tea. “What is the point in talking about feminism if I cannot finish patriarchy at my own house?” she says, chuckling.
Her social media journey started as a son’s sentimental plan during COVID-19. “He said it would preserve my memories. That the children could watch their grandmother singing folk songs when they grew up,” Savitri says, as her grandson sits by her. “I was fond of singing, so I agreed. That channel, ‘Yo Apna Haryana’, renamed ‘Tai Savitri’, now has 3,31,000 subscribers and 14,000 videos. But singing felt hollow after her singing partner lost her 28-year-old son in an accident. So she quit.
“When the singing stopped, we had to think about what to do next,” says Ashish, who has a postgraduate degree in Zoology. The answer emerged from conversations at home.
Ashish had developed an interest in theatre, philosophy, and psychology over the years. So, discussions about ideas and society were a regular feature of family life.
Ashish says that he does not quote philosophers word for word to his mother. Instead, he translates them into everyday language, allowing discussions to unfold at home over days or even weeks before they eventually find expression in a video.
It led to her creating videos on feminism and against social evils.
Bertrand Russell’s proposition that people should need a licence to become parents, for instance, prompted a conversation that led to one of Savitri’s most-watched videos on parenting. At other times, the starting point is something she observes in society or among people around her. “The videos are not scripted. If I get her to deliver it as a script, she won’t be able to speak with the same conviction,” says the 27-year-old.
After a mental health video went viral, the family received an anonymous call from a man who threatened to kill Savitri. “That was the first time I was genuinely frightened,” says Ashish.
Her criticism of local godmen in her videos has also drawn displeasure. The backlash has not been confined to anonymous callers. A khap leader once called on his father, Bijender Singh Hooda, to complain. “He said my father had removed the nath — the nose rope — from his wife. He was comparing a woman to an animal controlled by a nose rope,” he says.
Savitri, meanwhile, draws inspiration from watching godman-philosopher Osho and civil services exam coach Vikas Divyakirti. Her subjects have expanded from feminism to mental health and Gen Z, but Ashish says there is no deliberate strategy behind the transition. The themes emerge naturally from what they see and discuss around them. But she is not done. “Whether people throw flowers at me or slippers, I am going to debut as a stand-up comedian soon. My son is writing it for me,” she announces. And she wants a passport stamp. “I have seen enough of Haryana, now I want to go abroad. I don’t have money. If someone sponsors me, I would like to travel to Australia and the U.S.,” she says, deadpan.
The dancing dadi
More than 100 km from Savitri Hooda’s village in Rohtak, in a crowded lane of Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh, Birvati, 85, another woman is blowing up the idea of age-appropriate. Yellow tee, brown pants, two pigtails, the unlettered dadi (paternal grandmother) breaks into a Haryanvi pop number —‘Mera Balam Thanedar’— with the energy of a teenager.
She has 5,36,000 views with just that one video. Her handle on Instagram, dadi_comedy_63, has 230 posts and is less than a year old, with 1,16,000 followers already. Her son Kiranpal sells artificial jewellery, at weekly markets. These days, he says, the market comes to them. “People now recognise her. When we go to the market, people come and sit beside her and say, ‘Amma, look how well your videos are doing!’ There is so much excitement. People ask her, ‘Amma, where did you learn all this? You do it so well!’” he says, proudly.
Birvati, with white hair and wrinkled skin, plays humble, but knows her influence. “I don’t like praising myself, but there is hardly anyone who has not seen my videos. People, not just in India, but even abroad are getting to know me,” she says with a toothless grin.
“Women my age tell me, ‘Amma, you have done something remarkable at this age. You have made a name!’” she adds.
Her granddaughter Neha says people are pulled in by her energy.
“The dance moves she does are rare for people her age. Most people are fascinated by her energy,” says the 20-year-old, who is Birvati’s choreographer, costume designer, and editor. “She wears different outfits for songs, rarely a sari. She experiments with hairstyles, and even asks me, ‘Can I go out wearing jeans?’”
But this wasn’t supposed to be Birvati’s channel. It was Neha’s. She has a degree in optometry and wanted to create online content. Her parents said no, afraid of facing a problem finding groom for a girl who is popular online. So Neha brought in her grandmother, who had been the life and soul of every family wedding in her youth, to dance with her. They started in December last year, with a YouTube channel called ‘Neha Panchal’, posting dance and humorous videos, both dadi and granddaughter in frame. Their first video got a like from singer Neha Kakkar. That was enough to keep going. Instagram came a month later. And it exploded. Younger audience, more likes, more engagement. “Whenever I tell her we are shooting, she gets ready an hour in advance. She is more excited than I am. She gets dressed on her own. Sometimes she chooses the song herself. Some videos on the rooftop, some in the park outside, and some on the middle floor. I have decorated a corner for this,” Neha says.
“In the beginning, the comments were brutal. “At this age, do bhajans, not dances. Go to the temple,” people wrote. Neha’s batchmates laughed at her, saying she was unnecessarily dragging her grandmother in. She ignored them. Now the whole family is involved. Neha’s mother, Poonam, once hooked to Hindi novels, is the scriptwriter for their comedy sketches. “She reads stories, watches things, and comes up with ideas.” Older sister Riya also pops in.
Birvati wants to contribute financially. Neha says Punjabi singers have approached them for paid promotions, but the income is still small and unsteady. But Birvati wants to grow into her newfound career and make her own songs. “I want a role in a Haryanvi music video,” she says.
Dare to deadlift
Cut from a 50 sq. ft. house in Ghaziabad to a plush plotted house in South City-I, Gurugram. Amrit Kaur, 75, sits gracefully on a beige tufted sofa, hands folded neatly in her lap, composed, almost stern. Four years ago, she could barely walk. “I have always been strong. But four years ago, I became seriously ill. I was very weak, and was admitted in hospital,” she recalls. “I thought I would recover in a few days, but the weakness was considerable.” Today she does an hour of strength training at 4 a.m. every day.
She can do a dozen push-ups.
Her Instagram handle, @getfitwithdadi, has just 40 posts, 17,000 followers and a video with 80 lakh views. Her son, Aminder Singh, sits beside her. In his early 50s, Singh is the founder of Team Aminder, and has been training people for 30 years, with clients in 42 countries. “She was very weak after hospital. But I used to tell her, ‘Mummy, you are very strong,’” he says.
He made her start small. Tie a rope between door frames. Pull it. Do a squat. Again.
“At first, I could do very little. But slowly, I began to feel that I was regaining some strength,” Amrit says, who was reluctant to start.
Amrit begins her day at 3 or 3:30 a.m. with prayers. “Then I begin exercising,” she says. “I keep chanting ‘Waheguru, Satnam, Waheguru, Satnam’ as I squat. My prayers and exercise go on together. Gradually, I increased the time. Now I exercise for an hour.”
Commentaires pour in. “You have done something wonderful, Dadi! You are amazing!” says one. She reads them, but doesn’t reply. “I feel particularly happy when others imitate me. I feel the exercises I do are useful to others,” she says. At the nearby gurdwara, devotees now recognise her as: “Arre, video wali dadi (Oh, the grandmother from the video)!” Taking a cue from Amrit, Aminder’s mother-in-law Deepa Bindra has started her own handle @getfitwithnaani, with seven posts and 3,916 followers already. Amrit has a message that isn’t about protein: “Exercise is effective only if we are happy.”

Rhode Island sues Meta over its approach to scam ads
It’s the first state to sue the social media company on these allegations.
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter F. Neronha has filed a lawsuit against Meta over the company's handling of scam advertisements. The suit alleges that the social media business does not do enough to prevent fraudulent ads on its platforms. It further claims that Meta has not taken stronger action against those scams because they generate revenue for the company.
"For a company that engages so many Rhode Islanders and Americans, maintaining high standards for consumer safety should be of the utmost importance," Neronha said. "As alleged, Meta knowingly exposed vulnerable users to fraud and scams, and made enormous profits in doing so. When companies, big or small, take advantage of Rhode Island consumers, this Office will do everything within our authority to hold them to account."
In a statement to Reuters, which first reported on the state lawsuit, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the company has removed more than 159 million scam ads from its platforms. "The attorney general refused to engage with us on ways we protect Rhode Islanders from scams, and has instead hired an out-of-state private law firm to concoct a lawsuit that ignores the full range of actions we take to combat scams every day," Stone said.
The release from the AG's office says Rhode Island is the first state to take action over the alleged inaction, although it isn't the first time the social media company has been sued on this subject. The Consumer Federation of America filed a lawsuit in April and Santa Clara County in California did the same in May.
A 2025 report from Reuters found that scam advertisements across its networks could be providing billions of dollars for Meta, possibly as much as 10 percent of its revenue. The company has engaged in actions to shut down the bad actors behind some of those phony ads and sue the creators of other ones. It also added some user protections for suspicious messages earlier this year.

In September 2026, high school and university students, along with teachers, launched massive protests in France demanding reforms in the education system and increased funding for schools. Joined by ordinary citizens, farmers, and workers frustrated by the rising cost of living and an economic crisis, the demonstrations escalated into a nationwide, violent movement by the third week of October. These protests resulted in severe property damage, the burning of buildings, and thousands of arrests. As the unrest turned increasingly violent, the French government imposed partial curfews across several cities.
In this context, a video (here and here) is being shared online claiming to show protesters in France attacking security forces, who were seen defending themselves with riot shields. Let’s verify the claim made in the posts.
Claim: Video of protesters in France attacking security forces, who were seen defending themselves with riot shields in October 2026.
Fact: Although protesters in France did clash with security forces, the viral video is unrelated to those events. The video actually shows individuals throwing rocks at police during a protest in Medan, Indonesia, on 29 August 2025. Hence, the claim in the post is Misleading.
We first noted the word ‘POLISI’ written on the riot shields in the viral video and identified it as the Indonesian translation of the word ‘Police’. We then conducted a reverse image search of the video and found the same visuals had been uploaded by several media outlets (here, here & here) in August 2025.
According to the media reports, the video shows people throwing rocks and sticks at police during a protest in Medan, Indonesia, on 29 August 2025. The demonstration took place after the death of a delivery rider in clashes between riot police and students who were protesting against lawmakers’ allowances.
A comparison of the surroundings in the video with Google Streetview imagery of the parliament building’s surroundings confirms that the location is in Indonesia, not France. We previously debunked this video in September 2025 when it was linked to protests in Nepal.
To sum it up, an old video from Indonesia is being falsely shared as footage of protesters attacking security forces in France.

No jeopardy but loads of fun - Champions League sets new goals record
- Published
More teams, more games - and more goals.
Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite club competition has delivered all of the above and more.
Especially the goals part.
Already trending upwards over the past two campaigns, there has been a genuine goals boom in this year's competition.
The 187 goals scored so far have come at an average of 4.16 per game - the highest in Champions League history.
"Look how many goals have been scored, it's phenomenal," ex-Manchester United and England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "The attackers are being clinical."
Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock described the volume of goals as "incredible" - so how unusual is it?
What the stats say
Ready for lots of numbers?
Not only is the current goals-per-game percentage the highest ever in the Champions League, it is the third highest in European Cup history - behind only 1959-60 (4.19) and 1955-56 (4.38).
While 40 goals were scored across nine games on Tuesday, last week was even more spectacular.
Last Wednesday saw the third highest-scoring day in Champions League history (46 goals), bettered only by the final league-phase matchdays of 2024-25 and 2025-26, when 18 matches took place.
The 78 goals scored across Tuesday and Wednesday last week made matchday two the highest scoring in history.
That was nine more than the total scored on matchday one this season (69) - which, at the time, was the second highest-scoring matchday since the new league phase was introduced in 2024-25.
Will we see the record fall again this week? It's already halfway there.
More entertainment = more quality?
Ever since Uefa announced its plans to alter the format of the Champions League in 2021, the impact on matches has been a hot topic. Scrutiny has only increased since the changes were implemented in time for the 2024-25 season.
After beginning life as a six-team invitational tournament in 1955-56 before growing to a 32-team knockout tournament in 1967, the Champions League as we know it began in 1992.
A group stage was added, with the last 16 entering a knockout phase. There was a brief spell with two group stages, but this was reverted back to the single group-stage format for the 2003-04 tournament.
The group stage previously featured 32 teams in eight groups of four, with the top two sides from each of those groups qualifying for the last 16.
For the start of the 2024-25 season, the group stage was replaced with a 36-team league phase, with each side playing eight one-off fixtures instead of six games against three teams.
The top eight finishers qualify directly for the knockout stages, with those placed ninth to 24th entering a two-legged play-off stage.
The bottom eight are eliminated, meaning that after eight matches, 24 sides are still in the competition. Some argue that that creates a lack of jeopardy, which encourages teams to play more expansively.
But do more goals equal better quality?
"I think the entertainment has gone up, although I'm not sure the quality has gone up," The Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"If I'm looking at the games it's brilliant to watch and thrilling because the football itself is fantastic - but what do they mean?
"The lack of jeopardy, why would PSG and Barcelona play for a draw, why not go for it? If you need five wins from the eight games you know you've got some margin there. If you lose it's OK. I think the format allows all the teams to loosen up.
"The entertainment value is there but I think you come away from these matches sometimes and still think 'what does it all mean?'. The lack of jeopardy early on does deliver entertainment."

This genuine remark circulated in October 2026, though Trump said it months prior to the 2024 election. His full comments showed he was speaking about then-Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic opponent in that year's presidential election, previously indicating that she was in favor of abolishing private health insurance in favor of government-run plans.
In mid-October, two weeks ahead of the midterm elections, people claimed U.S. President Donald Trump said that if Democrats win, "You're going to be thrown into a system where everyone gets healthcare."
For example, users shared the quote or a brief video clip on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived). Some Snopes readers also searched the website for information about the alleged quote.
Trump truly said that if Democrats win, "You're going to be thrown into a system where everyone gets healthcare." He made the remark months ahead of the 2024 election while urging voters not to vote for his opponent, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Therefore we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to Trump.
Some posts wrongly showed "if Democrats win" as part of his direct quote, though the meaning was much the same. Also, he said "everybody," not "everyone" — an insignificant difference.
Users reposting the quote or a video clip omitted some context from Trump's comments, mainly that he appeared to be warning about Harris previously indicating, most notably during a June 2019 debate (at 20:14), that she supported abolishing private health insurance in favor of government-run plans. (She later walked back that comment, saying she misheard the question.)
Snopes emailed the White House to ask whether Trump still believed Democrats running in future elections might seek to abolish private health insurance. In response, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster sent a statement promoting Trump's healthcare policies, claiming his administration "has lowered costs and enabled Americans to take control of their health."
More of what Trump said
Trump made the "everybody gets healthcare" comment while delivering remarks about affordability at his Bedminster, New Jersey, golf course on Aug. 15, 2024. During his speech, tables of groceries and displays about rising prices flanked his lectern.
Trump's relevant remarks transpired as follows, with "she" referencing Harris (emphasis ours):
She cosponsored legislation to abolish very popular private health insurance, which 150 Americans rely on, dumping everyone onto inferior socialist government-run healthcare systems with rationing and deadly wait times while massively raising your taxes.
She wants to take away your private healthcare. There are many people in this country who spend a lot of money on private healthcare. It's the best healthcare in the world, by the way. But they want to do it. They worked hard to make money. And they want to do it. Under her, you're not going to have private healthcare plans anymore.
And you can be a wealthy person or a middle-income person, and you want to spend on a really good plan, better than a government plan could be, far better, and you're not going to be allowed. You're all going to be thrown into a communist system. It's a communist system. You're going to be thrown into a system where everybody gets healthcare. It's, you wait for your doctor like 10 months, 12 months, 11 months. You gotta see some of these plans, how they work in other countries, it's disgraceful. So, private healthcare is gone, she wants it out.
The above remarks begin at the 13:57 mark in this YouTube video.

Trump weighs in after his envoy calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’
President claims Russia has been barely involved in Iran war despite evidence to the contrary

President Donald Trump on Wednesday seconded his roving peace envoy’s fawning description of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” and praised the autocratic leader for having released an American his government had taken hostage after Trump waived bipartisan sanctions meant to hinder Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Earlier in the day, Witkoff, a real estate developer with no experience in diplomacy who Trump has nonetheless tasked with international negotiations normally entrusted to the secretary of state, praised Putin and credited him with saying nice things about Trump during a meeting that was recorded and released on Russian state media.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again,” Witkoff said.
Asked about the exchange and pressed on whether he agreed with Witkoff, Trump offered a qualified “yes” to the query.
“Well, I guess you could say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out. But you know, I I wouldn't say anything one way or the other,” he said.
The president then falsely claimed that Russia has “not gotten involved with Iran,” ignoring the fact that Iran and Russia have a longstanding relationship that has seen both governments assist each other in their respective efforts to undermine Western-aligned governments — and the United States itself.
Trump’s comments came hours after Putin announced the release of imprisoned US citizen Stephen Hubbard following a plea for his release from his American counterpart, who had previously suggested his decision to allow Russia to continue to sell diesel fuel despite sanctions enacted by Congress was part of a gambit to secure Hubbard’s release.
Hubbard, 74, had been held in Russian custody since April 2022 and was serving a nearly seven-year prison sentence in a penal colony for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, charges he denies.
Putin told US special envoy Steve Witkoff that the former schoolteacher was at the St. Petersburg Pulkovo airport and waiting to fly back to the U.S. with him. Witkoff thanked him for the goodwill gesture.
The US envoy flew into Russia's second city on Wednesday morning to review new ideas on ending the war in Europe, with allies anxious that president Trump appears to be turning away from Kyiv while firming up relations with Moscow.
Trump welcomed the news of Hubbard’s release on Wednesday, claiming the retired schoolteacher was released at his request in a telephone call with Putin last week.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia,” the president said.
“There was no “swap” necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin.”
Following a closed trial, a Moscow court convicted Hubbard of being a mercenary in October 2024 and sentenced him to six years and 10 months in prison.
James Reynolds and Liam Gilliver contributed reporting from London

New Delhi: In a fresh bid to curb overprescribing and irrational use of medicines, which typically drive up patients’ medical bills and fuel drug resistance, the health ministry's Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) has laid out clearer criteria for selecting medicines included in the National Formulary of India (NFI) 2026, according to two officials and an IPC document reviewed by Mint. The move aims to encourage safer, more appropriate treatments without restricting doctors’ clinical judgement. The updated guidelines cover a wide range of essential treatments, such as everyday priority medicines: antibiotics, pain relievers, government-cleared drugs, low-cost generic substitutes sold at Jan Aushadhi outlets, and vital medicines stockpiled for public health emergencies. Earlier, these guidelines mainly focused as an academic handbook for listed with basic medicine dosages and safety details drawn primarily from national drug approvals. The guidelines serve as a reference for doctors and pharmacists on the appropriate prescribing, dispensing and administration of medicines across healthcare settings. While intended to promote rational drug use, they remain advisory and do not override professional clinical judgment or existing regulations. The guidelines include monographs drawn from five broad categories: the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM); treatments under National Health Programmes (NHPs); drugs cleared by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO); formulations meeting Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) standards; and drugs recommended by an expert panel. The panel selects therapies based on clinical urgency during emergencies, approvals by state licensing authorities, and formulations under the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP) to boost affordable generic access. The IPC document noted that medicine monographs and usual formulation strengths are based on medical literature, regulatory approvals, national programmes, and expert inputs, adding that the inclusion of specific strengths does not preclude doctors from prescribing other strengths when required. “These guidelines are intended to guide physicians and pharmacists on safe dosages, standard formulations, and appropriate therapies, while curbing irrational use of medicines that can cause antimicrobial resistance, adverse drug reactions,” said one of the officials. In an attempt to control misuse of drugs, India earlier banned several irrational fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, created the Schedule H1 prescription-audit register for critical antibiotics, launched public awareness campaigns against over-the-counter (OTC) antibiotic misuse, and mandated generic prescribing across public health facilities. This assumes significance for the over 1.3 million registered modern medicine doctors in India, where the domestic pharmaceutical market size is valued at around $50-60 billion. “Healthcare professionals are expected to exercise their professional judgement and clinical expertise when prescribing medicines to their patients. Applicable statutory provisions and regulatory requirements shall prevail in the event of any inconsistency with the contents of the Formulary," the IPC document said, adding that it is periodically reviewed and updated, factoring in clinical inputs, new evidence and relevant recommendations to ensure its "continued clinical relevance”. “These guidelines promote rational prescribing. It provides healthcare professionals with updated information on medicines, their appropriate uses, precautions and adverse effects," said Dr Rajeev Jayadevan, public health expert and former president of Indian Medical Association, (Cochin). "While existing drug regulations continue to apply, rational prescribing requires doctors to choose appropriate treatments and doses based on individual patient's needs.” Queries emailed to the health ministry spokesperson on Wednesday remained unanswered until press time. Priyanka Sharma is a journalist at Mint, where she covers the Union Ministry of Health and the pharmaceutical industry. Her work focuses on explaining government policies and how they impact healthcare and the medicine market in India. With 12 years of experience in journalism, she has built a reputation for providing clear and honest news on important health topics that affect the entire country.

Her educational background includes a journalism degree from the prestigious Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC) and specialized training in public health from the Public Health Foundation of India. Before her current role at Mint, Priyanka worked with India Today, The Pioneer, and ANI. She also served as a lead consultant for the National Health Authority, which gave her firsthand knowledge of how the government manages large-scale health programmes.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has asked all medical colleges and medical institutions across the country to constitute patient safety committees/cells and designate nodal officers to strengthen patient safety practices and reduce avoidable harm in healthcare settings.
In a recent communication to the heads of medical institutions, NMC has asked institutions to share the composition and details of their patient safety committees, along with the particulars of the designated patient safety nodal officer, with the National Patient Safety Secretariat (NPSS) at the Directorate-General of Health Services (DGHS).
As per the direction, the proposed committee is to be chaired by the director, head of the institution or medical superintendent, with representation from relevant specialties and patient safety domains.
Patient safety framework
According to the NMC, the patient safety framework covers 11 domains, including medication and surgical safety, blood and medical device safety, laboratory and diagnostic safety, and infection prevention and control. Other areas include patient and family engagement, vaccine and injection safety, operational research in patient safety, facility safety covering biomedical waste management, fire safety, structural safety and environmental safety, along with safety in AYUSH services.
The Commission notes that the move places responsibility on medical institutions to establish an institutional mechanism for monitoring safety practices rather than treating patient safety as an isolated clinical responsibility.
According to the latest order, institutions should comply with the directions and communicate the required details to the NPSS.

Power department staff begins 3-day strike against private discom in Gurugram, Nuh
The Haryana Bijli Karamchari and Engineers Joint Sangharsh Morcha called for a strike after the power sector regulator granted a licence to a private firm.
Around 40,000 electricity department employees on Thursday began a three-day strike against the entry of a private power distribution company in Gurugram and Nuh, leading to disrupted supplies in several residential and industrial areas due to unattended breakdown complaints.
The Haryana Bijli Karamchari and Engineers Joint Sangharsh Morcha called for a three-day strike after the state's power sector regulator, HERC, on October 19 granted a licence to a private company to supply electricity in Gurugram and Nuh districts along with the existing state-owned discoms.
Around 40,000 electricity department employees have joined the strike, which saw a widespread impact across the state, disrupting electricity supply, water services, industrial production and several essential activities, the forum of employees' union said in a statement.
Deep Dive
Also read: ESMA: Chandigarh prohibits power firm staffers from going on strike for 6 months
The HERC, in an order dated October 19, granted a parallel electricity distribution licence to Eleven Power Private Limited for 25 years in both revenue districts under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
The Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission (HERC), a three-member statutory body, is responsible for regulation of the power sector in the state. The state government, on the recommendation of a selection committee, appoints the chairperson and members of the commission.
On Wednesday, Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini said the state government will represent the employees' case before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) against HERC's decision.
Also read: Will challenge HERC’s decision to grant licence to pvt firm: Saini
Saini said the government is ready to engage lawyers trusted by the power workers' unions to pursue the case.
Saini also held a review meeting with administrative secretaries to assess arrangements for the three-day strike.
Meanwhile, the Joint Front, representing the striking employees, said that with almost the entire workforce participating, numerous 33 kV and 11 kV feeders affected by breakdowns remained out of service.
Electricity supply was disrupted in several urban and rural residential areas. Industrial production was also affected due to the disruption of power supply to industrial feeders.
Electricity complaint centres, substations and offices at the sub-divisional, divisional and circle levels were largely deserted, the forum said.
Also read: Haryana milk strike enters second day, milk supply remains unaffected
Most constituent organisations of the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, along with Sarv Karamchari Sangh Haryana and workers' organisations, including CITU, AITUC, INTUC, extended support to the strike and organised demonstrations at various locations.
Subhash Lamba, vice president of the Electricity Employees Federation of India (EEFI), and Shailendra Dubey, Chairman of the All India Power Engineers Federation (AIPEF), also opposed the parallel distribution licence and expressed solidarity with the striking employees.
Senior leader of the Joint Front, Devender Singh Hooda emphasised that electricity employees and engineers were not striking for higher salaries or allowances. Their struggle, he said, was aimed at protecting electricity distribution from privatisation and safeguarding the interests of farmers and ordinary consumers.
Expressing regret over the hardships faced by consumers, he said the employees' struggle was intended to ensure access to affordable and reliable electricity for all.
He appealed to farmers, consumers and the public to support the movement and press the government to revoke the parallel distribution licence.
He warned that handing electricity distribution over to private companies could make power increasingly unaffordable for farmers and economically weaker sections in both rural and urban areas.
Lamba of EEFI alleged that the Haryana government was attempting to undermine the strike by bringing technical employees and supervisors from neighbouring states, including Punjab and Himachal Pradesh.
Questioning the government's position, Lamba asked: "If the chief minister and the energy minister oppose privatisation and stand with electricity employees, why is a parallel distribution licence being granted to a private company in the first place?"
He argued that if legal obstacles stood in the way of stopping the licensing arrangement, the government should explore appropriate legal and legislative measures to resolve them, noting that the BJP governs both Haryana and the Centre.
The EEFI leader said that the government must demonstrate its opposition to privatisation through concrete action rather than statements or assurances.

On Thursday, Haryana Energy Minister Anil Vij said the strike is unnecessary as it is HERC's decision to grant a parallel electricity distribution licence to a private company.
Vij said that he himself is against privatisation because so much public money and infrastructure have been invested, and employees' jobs are at stake.
Therefore, the government opposed the move firmly, but the decision went against us. The government is now appealing against that decision in APTEL and is trying to obtain a stay against the regulatory commission's order as soon as possible, he said.
He told the employees to leave the path of strike and join duties. "If you want to give any advice to our lawyer while preparing the case, give it. If you want to appoint your own lawyer, do so. Or if you want to suggest another lawyer, tell us, and we will hire that lawyer."

Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
- Published
Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.
The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.
Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.
"She's stable, she's improving," Muhammad Ali Pate said.
The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.
"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.
