  - Published15 September
None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing.
Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help.
"She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme.
Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola.
After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said.
Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements.
Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda.
It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there.
Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension.
Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts.
"We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together."
Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus.
And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak.
The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak, which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths.
Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists.
"Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said.
The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades.
In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial’s lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October.”
The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health’s offices and seized vaccines. Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected.
Of the trial’s rejection, Stabell Benn wrote: “We regret the decision because we considered the study scientifically and ethically justified, but we respect the government’s authority to decide whether research may proceed in the country.”
Trial ethics
The World Health Organization and many outside experts have sharply disagreed with Stabell Benn and her colleagues on the trial’s justifications and design. It has been widely decried as “unethical” because it would withhold the newborn dose of hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants.
With the country’s high rates of chronic hepatitis B infections, this would put thousands of babies at risk of developing a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Experts have further said that there is no scientific justification for the study, given the vaccine’s long use and strong safety record. The WHO wrote in February that the trial “posits hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence” to justify putting newborns at risk.

The US State Department has warned American citizens travelling to mainland China to exercise increased caution, citing the risk of wrongful detention, arbitrary enforcement of local laws and restrictions on leaving the country.
In a travel advisory issued on October 19, 2026, the department assigned China a Level 2 warning, advising travellers to exercise increased caution. It said China's expansive national security, counterespionage and data security laws give authorities broad discretion to detain or interrogate foreign nationals, including over routine business activities, research and public expression.
The advisory also flagged risks for Americans of Chinese heritage, businesspeople involved in disputes, academics, journalists and individuals with current or former connections to the US government.
According to the State Department, foreign nationals in China may face interrogation, detention or expulsion over alleged violations of national security laws. The advisory said authorities could classify a wide range of documents, data, statistics and other materials as state secrets, potentially even retroactively.
The department warned that activities such as conducting research or handling publicly or commercially available information could expose foreign nationals to scrutiny.
Americans with current or previous affiliations with US law enforcement, the military, intelligence agencies or other government bodies may face additional risks, the advisory said. People travelling on US government-funded programmes and those involved in business disputes with Chinese companies were also identified as potentially vulnerable.
The department said some Americans have faced criminal charges in connection with civil business disputes. In certain cases, disputes have reportedly been resolved through settlements favouring Chinese businesses.
The advisory highlighted China's use of exit bans, which prevent individuals from leaving the country.
According to the State Department, such restrictions may be imposed to compel people to participate in government or Chinese Communist Party investigations, influence civil disputes, pressure relatives or associates to return from abroad, or gain leverage over foreign governments.
Americans may discover an exit ban only when attempting to leave China, the department warned. It also said there may be no available legal process to challenge some restrictions in court.
The advisory noted that exit bans linked to civil or business disputes have remained in place for years in some cases, preventing Americans from travelling abroad for medical treatment. It also cited instances in which restrictions were imposed on US citizen children whose relatives were under investigation.
The State Department said Americans facing wrongful detention could remain imprisoned for years and may not receive consistent access to US government representatives or family members.
The advisory warned that dual US-Chinese citizens, former Chinese citizens and Americans of Chinese descent may face additional scrutiny or harassment.
China does not recognise dual nationality, according to the department. Chinese authorities may consider certain individuals Chinese nationals if they enter using Chinese-issued identity or travel documents, potentially restricting US consular assistance if they are detained or placed under an exit ban.
The State Department encouraged dual nationals and naturalised US citizens of Chinese descent to enter mainland China using a US passport and an appropriate Chinese visa.
It also cautioned that former Chinese citizens may face additional administrative requirements before being allowed to leave the country.
The department advised Americans to assume that Chinese security services could access emails, text messages and social media posts sent to or from China. It also warned that messages exchanged through Chinese applications could potentially be read even when users are outside the country.
According to the advisory, people could face detention or deportation for private electronic messages critical of the Chinese government, Hong Kong, Macau or the Chinese Communist Party.
Americans were also advised to avoid demonstrations, exercise caution near large gatherings and avoid photographing protesters or police without permission. Foreign teachers and students could face detention or deportation for expressing views contrary to the ruling party's positions, the department said.
The State Department recommended that Americans travelling to China enrol in its Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive updates and help the US embassy or consulate contact them or their emergency contacts during emergencies.
Travellers were advised to carry a valid US passport and Chinese visa, establish a regular communication plan with family or employers, purchase travel insurance and prepare for the possibility of detention or limited access to consular assistance.
The department also urged visitors to review local laws and customs, avoid illegal drugs and ensure their luggage contains no ammunition or prohibited weapons.

Deep within the intestinal wall, beyond where digestion and nutrient absorption occur, are immune outposts called solitary isolated lymphoid tissues, or SILTs. These structures host cells that govern how aggressively the gut reacts to microbes. A weak response lets pathogens take root while an overactive one causes the immune system to attack the gut — a hallmark of inflammatory disorders like Crohn’s disease.
A new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has traced this balancing act to a protein called RelB. By engineering mice lacking RelB in these cells, researchers at the National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi, uncovered a paradox: the same protein drives opposite effects depending on its cellular environment and anatomical niche.
The finding could matter for patients with inflammatory bowel disease because a drug that targets an overactive immune response may also weaken the gut’s ability to fight harmful bacteria. And understanding where RelB is helping or hurting could be important before this pathway is considered for treatment.
The gate-keeper
To execute many of its immune effects, the gut relies on IL-23, a signalling molecule that triggers inflammation to ward off threats.
IL-23 “functions as an alarm system at barrier surfaces such as the gut, skin, and lungs,” Gourishankar Ghosh, a professor of chemistry and biochemistry at University of California San Diego, U.S., said.
In the gut, it sparks a chain reaction that switches on antimicrobial defences. “However, uncontrolled production can drive chronic inflammatory diseases, including psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.”
The researchers found RelB is a gatekeeper for this system: it dictates whether the gut can even produce the sentinel dendritic cells residing in SILT outposts to make IL-23. In RelB-deficient mice, this defender population nearly vanished.
Soumen Basak, an immunologist at NII who led the study, explained that earlier research suggested RelB simply helped existing cells pump out IL-23. Faced with the missing cells, the team investigated further.
“We considered two possible explanations: either the absence of … RelB reduced the number of IL-23-producing [dendritic cells] in these mice or simply a lack of RelB impaired the ability of these dendritic cells to make IL-23,” Dr. Basak said.
The study proved the former is the primary culprit.
Known troublemaker
However, RelB does not act as a heroic shield everywhere in the gut. While it builds a protective army in the intestinal wall, it suppresses regulatory T-cells — the immune system’s peacekeepers — in the nearby lymph nodes.
Earlier work from Dr. Basak’s lab found that by shutting down these peacekeepers, RelB worsens chronic intestinal inflammation.
The answer to how a single protein pulls off this Jekyll-and-Hyde routine might lie in the dendritic cells themselves.
Devesha Kulkarni, assistant professor of medicine at University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), said dendritic cells are “not one fixed cell type” with a single job. Instead, they are shapeshifters that adopt distinct identities based on the tissue they lie in and the local chemical signals.
And now, scientists know RelB helps fix that local identity — a role Dr. Basak said he considers to be a major conceptual leap.
Flipping the switch
The researchers found RelB switches on the production of a second protein, RBP-J. This acts as a key, unlocking a completely different communication network. And only when this connection completes can immature cells develop into the gut’s specialised IL-23-producing sentinels.
The finding reveals a surprising twist: two systems long assumed to operate independently — RelB and the communication network — actually cooperate to arm the gut.
“Making a delicious dish requires the right combination of many ingredients — salt, turmeric, garlic, ginger, and spices,” Dr. Basak said. “Each ingredient contributes a unique flavour, but none can produce the desired taste on its own. Our study emphasises that signalling pathways must also work together in a coordinated manner to generate appropriate cellular and immune responses.”
That said, a deeper mystery remains: how can a single protein act as a brake in one context and an accelerator in another?
Alexander Hoffmann, professor of immunology at UCLA, said the contradiction comes down to competition. RelB, he said, is a relatively weak activator compared to its cousin, RelA, so when both proteins try to access the same gene, the weaker RelB gets in the way.
By blocking RelA’s strong signal, RelB dials down the overall effect so “it seems like a repressor,” Dr. Hoffmann explained.
But on genes that RelA cannot access — like the one that triggers the gut’s defenses — “RelB’s weak activation potential is sufficient to drive gene expression.”
“This new work is a remarkable example of how the Basak lab over many years has developed expertise in dissecting complex networks of interaction,” he added.
Delicate drug target
Drugs that block IL-23 are already frontline treatments for inflammatory bowel disease, making RelB an intriguing but delicate new drug target. Because the protein acts as both guardian and saboteur depending on its neighbourhood, safely targeting it remains a complex challenge.
Saurabh Mehandru, associate professor of Gastroenterology at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, said that because the research used mice, “the findings will need to be extended before they can be read directly into patient care.”
He also pointed to a key gap that Basak’s team has also acknowledged: because the protective cell clusters are almost entirely missing in the modified mice, it is difficult to prove whether RelB is required to build those cells in the first place or simply to keep them alive once they are formed. Future experiments tracking the lifespans of these cells will ultimately settle that debate, Dr. Mehandru added.
Dr. Basak is already looking ahead. His team wants to know if the relay operates at other vulnerable barriers, like the lungs, and whether tweaking it could yield new treatments.
Anirban Mukhopadhyay is a geneticist by training and science communicator from New Delhi.

- Snopes has long debunked claims that electronic voting machines in the United States are rigged to switch votes from one candidate to another. During the 2026 midterm elections, these claims spread again as people flocked to the polls for early voting.
- There is no evidence voting machines were switching votes one way or the other. As some officials told us, these reports were likely the result of human error or touch screen alignment problems.
- Voting machines undergo extensive testing and election administration in the United States is decentralized, meaning that local and state governments oversee the accuracy of their voting machines. Voting machines are typically closed networks that are not connected to the internet.
- Each state referenced in claims that Snopes reviewed requires public testing of voter equipment ahead of its use in elections. While each state's standards differ, they each must follow federal standards requiring that voters have "an opportunity to verify the votes selected and correct any errors before casting the ballot." Many of these states also use a paper-record system, meaning a voter will select candidates on an electronic machine and then print their ballots, allowing for further review before submission.
With fewer than two weeks until Election Day, rumors spread in late October alleging electronic voting machines across the country were switching votes for Democratic candidates to Republicans in various midterm races.
For example, on Oct. 21, users on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived), X (archived) and other social media platforms shared (archived) a copied-and-pasted post reading as follows:
There is a very disturbing trend being seen in early voting. Texas, Florida, Tennessee, Ohio are reporting difficulties getting the machines to accept democratic votes. The machines change them back to Republican unless the voter persists, pressing several times to get the correct vote to go through.
Check your machine, check to see that it accepted the correct vote. Make sure your voice counts.
Stella Parton, a sibling of the late country music star Dolly Parton, alleged in a Facebook post (archived) that one of her vote selections "kept defaulting to Marsha Blackburn," referencing the long-time Republican U.S. senator in Tennessee who is running for reelection. Parton said, "I would never vote for her for anything," adding, "Don't let them rig this election."
While our research found no shortage of posts spreading the rumor, we located only a very small number of examples of people who claimed, anecdotally, that they personally experienced a vote-switching issue.
Snopes has debunked vote-switching claims since at least 2014; our research found examples of this rumor from as early as 2008.
As with previous vote-switching claims, no evidence credibly suggested voting machines were switching votes one way or the other, whether as a software bug or some sort of election fraud scheme. Instead, all available data pointed to either human error or potentially touch screen alignment problems. As such, we have rated this claim as false.
Voting machines in the United States undergo extensive testing before use, often in public.
Importantly, we have yet to receive information from any state or territory suggesting that a sizable number of voters completely submitted a ballot with incorrect selections. From the data we reviewed, this matter appeared to largely involve people purportedly experiencing temporary issues prior to casting their correct selections.
Snopes emailed state election officials in six states at the center of these vote-switching claims to ask about the allegations. None of them shared information suggesting they uncovered proof of any such widespread activity. Some pointed to human error and touch screen calibration, saying voters can review selections and ask for help from a poll worker prior to confirming submission of a ballot.
We will update this article if we receive more information, including replies from Parton and county officials.
Contextualizing voting conspiracies
Claims about "rigged" voting machines often fail to consider the detailed standards and processes that officials, from the local to federal level, use to prepare for U.S. elections, as well as how decentralized the elections process is.
In the United States, states and local governments run their own elections and purchase their own voter equipment using their own budgets, making it highly unlikely — if not impossible — to coordinate a widespread conspiracy to "rig" or "steal" an election, especially without leaks to the public.
Research from the Bipartisan Policy Center has found that the average voting equipment in the United States is about 7.3 years old as of 2026, indicating that most equipment has been used in previous elections. These machines largely have no connectivity to the wider internet or wireless technology because federal certification requires voting systems to be "air-gapped," or entirely independent.
As we've previously said, even in the instances where ballot scanners are connected to anything, it is typically a closed network.
Furthermore, while each state may have different requirements, all voting systems must meet a set of minimum standards in the Help America Vote Act of 2002.
According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, baseline requirements include "providing voters with an opportunity to verify the votes selected and correct any errors before casting the ballot, the ability to produce a record with a manual audit capacity, and accessibility for voters with disabilities and alternative language needs." In addition, voting systems must have error rates of no more than one error per 10 million ballot positions.
Many states also use or mandate use of the federal government's voluntary voting systems standards program, which was updated in 2021.
Snopes searched news coverage and online rumors across the country for reports of vote-switching issues. Here's what we found in the states where these rumors appear to be the most popular, as of this writing:
Florida
On Oct. 21, news station WFOX in Jacksonville, Florida, wrote that "some voters have reported problems with the touch screen on ExpressVote machines."
In an email to Snopes, Duval County Elections Supervisor Jerry Holland pointed to human error. Holland said that voters should use the stylus provided.
"If they are touching the screen to select, it appears their fingernails can reach the selection above," Holland said.
During a video interview with WFOX, Holland specified that voters can check their selections on a printout before submitting the ballot:
The ExpressVote fills out your ballot for you. It does not tabulate. And what it also does is, when it fills it out and prints it, you have the opportunity to look. If you see any mistakes on that, you can get another ballot [or] use another machine.
Holland also told us that he knew of no reports of voters completely submitting a ballot with incorrect selections, saying, "No one has reported they cast a ballot with wrong selections."
Florida's election machine testing system involves public auditing for accuracy, and detailed certification memos for each election machine the state uses are available on the state's Division of Elections website.
Kansas
On Oct. 22, the Kansas City Star reported that Johnson County, Kansas, Election Commissioner Connie Schmidt acknowledged that officials recalibrated several touch-screen voting machines after receiving reports from election judges about voters raising concerns regarding their selections.
In an email, Schmidt told us that officials have heard directly from three voters reporting concerns with a ballot marking device, and that "all three reports were received after the voter had already cast their ballot and left the polling place."
She continued: "We have also received five calls from Early Voting locations where a Supervising Judge reported that a voter raised a concern while making their selections. In each instance, a technician responded, recalibrated the screen and verified the accuracy of the touchscreen."
Schmidt also sent us a graphic displaying how best to use the voting machines:
(Johnson County Election Office)
Kansas requires that voting equipment "shall never be connected to the internet." The state also tests the equipment ahead of the election in front of the public (Page 5).
Ohio
Although a popular copied-and-pasted post warned social media users about vote-switching issues in Ohio, we found no news reports from Ohio suggesting that voters have come across this problem, at least as of this writing.
In a post on Facebook, Ohio's secretary of state called the rumors about vote-switching "intentional election disinformation." The post noted that Ohio law requires voting equipment testing and a bipartisan post-election audit. Furthermore, like the other states listed here, votes in Ohio are printed from election machines onto paper ballots, which voters can then review.
South Carolina
Sydni Bain, a spokesperson for the South Carolina Election Commission, told us that her office has commonly received reports of voters having trouble making selections during past elections, especially in years with high turnout rates. She said voters can review their selections, including with a printout, prior to fully submitting their ballots.
When a selection is made, it is very apparent. The box beside the selection is checked and the block containing the selection is highlighted. Voters should pay attention to ensure these selections reflect their wishes.
Voters should also carefully review their selections on the ballot review screen before printing their ballot to confirm their choices are accurately reflected. If a selection is not correct, the voter can navigate back through the ballot at any time to change selections.
After printing the ballot, the voter should carefully review their paper ballot before putting it in the ballot scanner.
South Carolina's state election commission also has released a video showing how to use the paper-based system. State law requires voting systems to disable connection to the internet when used for elections and the preservation of all electronic records for no less than 24 months following the election. Voting machine testing is open to the public. 
Tennessee
In Tennessee, residents in Williamson and Madison counties have reported issues with ballot selections.
WSMV, an NBC affiliate, interviewed two voters who experienced issues at different Williamson County election machines with choosing their candidates. One of the voters, Jackie Herrud, said she was attempting to vote for a Democratic candidate, Jerri Green, over Blackburn — the same specific problem Parton experienced.
However, WSMV reported that the Tennessee secretary of state's office said that out of approximately 400,000 early votes cast, the office had received only one complaint related to this issue.
Williamson County Election Administrator Chad Gray said the county has found "no discrepancies in the voting equipment."
"If we are made aware of any issue reported, even related to any unintended touch on the screen, the ballot marking devices are examined by the officials representing each party to ensure they are working properly," Gray said.
Gray said he recommends that voters use a stylus if they have trouble with the touch screen and, when making selections, "to touch the middle of the center of the rectangle containing the candidate's name or desired choice."
Poll officials, Gray said, are always available to answer questions or help if voters have trouble with the equipment.
In Madison County, NBC affiliate WNBJ reported that several community organizations had received complaints about election machines "changing some votes." Madison County Administrator of Elections Lori Lott told the outlet that the machines undergo extensive testing, including by "both Republicans and Democrats" who are experienced machine techs appointed to the elections board.
Tennessee's secretary of state's office did not immediately return a request for more information. We are also awaiting responses from the counties involved.
Tennessee, like some of the other states listed, uses electronic voting machines that print a paper ballot for voters to review before casting a formal ballot.
The state's government provides instructions for voting using each kind of machine. Tennessee law requires the election commission to notify local political parties' committees and independent candidates when the machines are examined. They can then designate a representative to be present during testing to ensure the machines are "properly prepared for use in the election." The state also requires county commissioners to publicly test the machines.
Texas
Alicia Pierce, a spokesperson for the Texas secretary of state's office, said in an email that she was "not aware of anyone reporting this experience to our office." Similar to other states, Pierce said Texas election machines print paper ballots after a voter makes electronic selections. The state encourages voters to review the physical ballot before casting it.
In 2022, the Texas Tribune debunked claims that electronic voting machines had switched people's votes from Democratic to Republican candidates:
But this isn't a case of grand conspiracy, malfeasance or rigged machines. Instead, election officials, security experts and voting rights advocates say some of the touch-sensitive screens on voting machines can be tricky to use, much like miscues while trying to use a smartphone. Midland County Election Administrator Carolyn Graves likened the experience to texting with a small keypad.
"If you don't hit it just exactly right, you're gonna hit one of the letters around it," Graves said. "It's essentially the same thing. If you don't hit it with the tip of your finger or turn your finger to the side, then you could hit the other [choice]."
The Tribune also interviewed Dan Wallach, a computer science professor and election security researcher at Rice University, who reportedly said these issues have existed since electronic voting machines were introduced more than two decades ago.
"As far as we can tell, these are simply design issues with the machines," he told the Tribune.
Texas does not connect its voting systems to the internet at any point in time, and the machines undergo testing in front of the public.

A major new Lancet Commission has listed 17 interlinked catastrophic threats that could shape global health through 2100. Zooming out to take a bird’s eye view of the possible threats, the Commissioners have counted amongst them — pandemics, obesity, antimicrobial resistance, nuclear conflict, and artificial intelligence.
Driven by the motive to move away from the intense focus on certain domains, the default mode that health care governance and activism has taken so far, the Commission took upon itself the task of freeing the world from being bogged down with single issues, though the benefits of that have been aplenty, the time had come to go beyond.
Launched at the recent World Health Summit in Berlin, the report urges global leaders to stop treating these issues in isolation, and start viewing them as deeply interconnected economic, environmental, and national security challenges. The Commission, “composed of 37 experts in health, economics, security, and technology, uses a foresight-driven, health-focused approach to identify 17 priority threats to human health.” Not a crystal ball gazing exercise, it reportedly assessed threats by calculating the expected cumulative disease burden — measured as amenable disability-adjusted life-years from 2025 to 2100 — that can be reasonably altered through policy intervention. It lists two of these major catastrophic threats: nuclear conflict and malicious use of AI: as having extinction potential. Additional threats include climate change, air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, conventional conflict, declining development assistance for health, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking, and unhealthy ageing.
While the report seeks to identify the threats to human health and survival, and could been seen as doomsdayist, in principle, it is not an apocalyptic forecast of unavoidable doom. The model it uses, as described here earlier, is “amenable” Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) — meaning it measures how many years of healthy life can still be saved if take decisive policy action is launched today. It predicts that high-income nations will see dominant health losses from non communicable risks such as obesity and poor mental health. On the other hand, low-income regions will bear the brunt of childhood malnutrition and the collapse of international aid.
The Commission analysed hundreds of risks across 204 countries and territories. A threat was classified as “catastrophic” if it could account for at least 1 billion DALYs (healthy years lost to illness, disability, or premature death) by 2100. These 17 threats were then categorised into a pyramid of severity, with extinction potential right on top (nuclear conflict and malicious AI) at Category 1, and then cascading down to Category 2 (major catastrophic threats) and Category 2 (environmental, social and health risks).
Although the likelihood of Category 1 dangers remains low, the report says, the scale of harm, should they be realised, would be apocalyptical. The bulk of the threats come under category 2, and include obesity, which represents the largest single potential health loss identified in the report. Addressing high body mass index (BMI), poor diet, and physical inactivity could prevent a massive 23.1 billion DALYs, the report says.
Similarly, improving global access to education could avert 16.1 billion DALYs, it claims. The income gap between the rich and poor represents an amenable health burden equivalent to 25 COVID-19 pandemics, it avers.
The report flags poor mental health rapidly rising in the higher income countries, as also the pressures on societies from ageing populations without adequate health support systems. While smoking, high blood pressure, antimicrobial resistance, alcohol use, child malnutrition and naturally-occurring pandemics are conventionally connected with health; climate change, conventional conflict and air pollution also find a place in the list. The withdrawal of international aid has been flagged: severe cuts to health aid from wealthy nations could cause 1.5 billion DALYs, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing 70% of this blow.
A key, central argument of the report is that these threats amplify one another. For instance, climate change directly exacerbates childhood malnutrition, air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, and mental health issues. Focusing on climate mitigation alone, without strengthening local healthcare infrastructure, again, will fail to stop the downstream health fallout. It also indicates that the estimated 1.89 billion DALYs saved by meeting climate targets is a conservative underestimation, accounting for direct heat and pollution harms. It advises nations to plan for unmodeled “invisible” consequent threats such as mass displacement, geopolitical instability, and drought.
However, the primary criticism against the Commission report is that it skirts acknowledging the current geopolitical crisis, the growing rise of intolerant governments, and the collapse of international collaboration between nations. Even recently, the terse flow of information from Russia where a suspected case of pneumonic plague death was reported highlights the frigidity between nations that prevents seamless global co-operation.
Though it does have a cascade of priorities, in effect the Commission does not attempt to present “a fixed ranking of threats or policy priorities.” Instead, it makes it very clear that the analysis is a dynamic process and findings are amenable to change as and when evidence shifts. But the most important contribution that can be attributed to the Commission is how it managed to pivot the global approach to health threats — to move it from attention and focus on individual subjects to move to a larger consideration of all the complex factors impacting human health. Whether the global axis will now swivel on this pivot remains to be seen, given how complex a task this report has laid out for the world.

- Fortnite has revealed the upcoming collab with popular rapper Lil Uzi Vert in the next season.
- The eight-second teaser also offers a new look at the upcoming Chapter 7 mini-season, including skins and a returning POI.
- The update will add the Lil Uzi Vert Icon Skin, Anime Syd with a Cuddle Team Leader edit style, and a remixed version of Anvil Square.
Fresh off Fortnite’s A$AP Rocky collab, which the American rapper announced on October 21, 2026, another brand-new artist has joined the hype bandwagon, dropping another teaser for the Chapter 7 mini-season. This time, it’s none other than popular rapper Lil Uzi Vert, who shared the Fortnite teaser on his Instagram page on October 22, giving us a new look at the upcoming mini-season.
The official Fortnite Lil Uzi Vert eight-second teaser showcases various colorful frames, with the rapper’s Icon Skin bathed in pink and purple. The clip begins with Uzi’s skin posing with the Pink Tape Flag with a skull emoji, while the next moment features a small tease of the skins you can expect in the next Fortnite Chapter 7 mini-season, including the Anime Syd skin.
For those unfamiliar with who Syd is in Fortnite, she’s the person behind the Cuddle Team Leader persona, who made an appearance in one of the Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4 quests. Along with the upcoming cel-shaded Syd skin, we also see a glimpse of the anime Cuddle Team Leader edit style, which Epic will likely pair with the Anime Syd bundle.
Furthermore, we also get our first look at an iconic Fortnite Chapter 4 Season 1 landmark, the Anvil Square, remixed to fit the upcoming mini-season’s theme. Like the A$AP Rocky teaser, the new Lil Uzi Vert clip also showcases a Pirate Chest in Fortnite, similar to the ones already available in the current chapter, with a red jewel and a purple crowned skull.
The clip then ends with Lil Uzi Vert posing with his Pink Tape Flag in Fortnite in an anime-inspired art style. So, while players expect the next Chapter 7 mini-season to have a pirate and treasure hunt theme, it will also likely include anime-themed cosmetics, as seen in the new teaser.
For now, we expect the new Fortnite Chapter 7 mini-season to debut on November 1, 2026. However, this is based on speculation, and Epic has yet to confirm the final date. Expect more teasers leading up to launch.

Leh, Oct 22: The Ladakh administration has defended cancelling land allotment to Sonam Wangchuk's institute, citing the activist's "disregard for the law", and said the allotment automatically lapsed due to unpaid dues and an unexecuted lease deed.
In an affidavit filed in the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, the administration maintained that the 40-year lease allotment covering 1,076 kanals and 1 marla of land at Phyang Thang had "lapsed by operation of law" on May 5, 2019, due to the Himalayan Institute of Alternative Learning (HIAL)'s failure to execute a lease deed or deposit mandatory land premiums within the stipulated one-year period.
The affidavit running into 136 pages was filed by Leh Deputy Commissioner and CEO of LAHDC, Romil Singh Donk, in response to HIAL's writ petition challenging the August 21, 2025, cancellation order of leased land to the institute.
The affidavit said the writ petition is "misconceived, devoid of merit, and barred by delay and laches" and made it clear that the original allotment order issued on May 5, 2018, was conditional and explicitly stated that the lease would be deemed cancelled if the allottee failed to execute the deed within a year.
The administration asserted that HIAL never deposited a single rupee towards land premium or ground rent and failed to secure formal possession through the Tehsildar as mandated.
Furthermore, the Higher Education Department of UT Ladakh certified in October 2026 that HIAL is not a recognised university, nor are its courses affiliated with the University of Ladakh or other statutory bodies, violating the core objective of setting up an alternative university.
Bringing other context before the court, the affidavit highlighted the past conduct of HIAL's founder Wangchuk and his organisation, the Students' Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh (SECMOL), and said that SECMOL has occupied 124 kanals of state land at Phey for over three decades without formal allotment or payment of an assessed Rs 80 lakh premium.
The affidavit also references the violent protests in Leh in September 2025, which led to Union Home Ministry's intervention, the cancellation of SECMOL's FCRA registration, and Wangchuk's brief detention under the National Security Act prior to its revocation in March 2026, as part of a consistent pattern of public order disruptions.
When approached for comments, HIAL CEO Gitanjali Angmo denied the claims made by the Ladakh administration in its affidavit.
Citing a September 25, 2025 order by the Home Ministry cancelling SECMOL's FCRA registration, the affidavit said it was done due to multiple statutory violations which included accepting foreign funds from a Swedish donor to study the sovereignty of the nation deemed prejudicial to national interest.
It said that local residents, the Phyang Welfare Society and village Nambardars have repeatedly petitioned authorities since 2018, alleging broken promises regarding the university project, unauthorised diversion of ancient irrigation streams for "Ice Stupa" experiments, and an alleged illegal encroachment of an additional 174 kanals beyond the boundary wall.
The affidavit said the villagers complained that HIAL deceived them with false promises of a world-class university, blocked ancient pasture lands, and repeatedly diverted centuries-old natural irrigation streams for Ice Stupa projects, causing severe water shortage for local farmers.
Urging the high court to dismiss the petition, the administration highlighted the antecedents of Wangchuk and SECMOL and submitted that the organisation and the petitioner are merely vehicles through which Wangchuk has repeatedly sought to hold public land on his own terms.
The affidavit also said that HIAL had made false statements under oath in its petition by claiming it sent repeated reminders during the first year and deposited all requisite dues.
It annexed official records showing zero written communications between May 2018 and March 2020, zero payments deposited, and suppressed letters written by HIAL in June 2020 seeking a complete waiver of both premium and ground rent, a request that was never granted.
Tracing official records dating back to 2006, the affidavit pointed out a series of administrative actions and warnings issued against Wangchuk and SECMOL and recalled a October 2006 communication by the then district magistrate of Leh, which recorded that Wangchuk openly threatened the Hill Council and district administration during a council meeting, prompting officials to recommend surveillance and preventive detention.
The affidavit further detailed orders from March 2007, where the DM imposed a complete ban on public gatherings, speeches, and the circulation of provocative VCDs by SECMOL, noting that the organisation was running large-scale anti-establishment propaganda threatening public tranquillity and unauthorisedly collecting funds from the public.
Official reports from the chief education officer in April 2007 also recorded that Wangchuk had unauthorisedly occupied 200 kanals of land under the guise of educational programmes and disrupted the smooth functioning of the education department.
The administration submitted that this pattern of holding public land without paying state dues continued over the years, including at SECMOL's Phey campus, and has culminated in the present situation where 1,076 kanals of state land have been held for over six years without a valid lease or payment of premium and ground rent.
Linking these past events to broader law and order concerns, the affidavit said that agitations led and incited by Wangchuk in recent years ended with the office of the Chief Executive Councillor of the very Hill Council that originally allotted the land being set on fire.
The administration maintained that a litigant with such a record does not approach the court with clean hands and is not entitled to discretionary or equitable relief.
Dismissing the awards, guest visits, and international recognitions cited by Wangchuk in his petition, the administration said that personal eminence and accolades are wholly irrelevant to the legal question of lease compliance.
It asserted that no recognition, however distinguished, serves as a substitute for fulfilling statutory allotment conditions, stating that the activist's reliance on such honours is merely an attempt to divert attention from an admitted legal default.
Emphasising the Public Trust Doctrine, the UT administration argued that public land is held in trust for the populace and cannot be treated as private largesse and urged the court to dismiss the petition with costs and suggested that the reclaimed land be allocated to reputed national institutions such as a Sainik School, Eklavya Model Residential School, or Sindhu Central University.
The affidavit also highlighted speeches by Wangchuk inciting a mob during a hunger strike on September 24, 2025, which led to the burning of political party offices, torching of police vehicles, and injuries to over 30 security personnel.

Arignar Anna Zoological Park in Vandalur will not be allowing visitors on October 22 and 23 as a precautionary measure following confirmation of H5N1 avian influenza infection in water birds by the National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, on October 2, 2026.
According to Forest Department officials, seven water birds in the zoo had died between October 3 and 7. Of them four were painted storks, one grey pelican, one grey heron and one oriental darter. As soon as the first bird died on October 3, the zoo officials cordoned off the area.
Immediate preventive measures, including disinfection, sanitisation, and strict implementation of biosecurity protocols, were undertaken in accordance with the Government of India’s guidelines, officials said. However, the zoo remained open as no further bird mortality or sickness has been reported since October 9.
Now that the confirmation has come, the zoo management has to follow the protocols laid out by the Centre and so the zoo would remain closed on Thursday and Friday, officials said.
This temporary measure is intended to facilitate intensive sanitisation, strengthen biosecurity measures, and ensure close monitoring of the situation. The public are requested to cooperate with the precautionary measures, a press release from the zoo said.
According to the protocol, as soon H7 avian influenza is confirmed, visitors’ entry needs to be stopped forthwith.
The movement of the vets and labourers should be restricted and in no case they should move from infected pens to healthy pens. The management of the healthy sheds should be done by a separate team. Maximum possible number of birds is to be sampled, while sampling a water body, birds arriving at different locations be taken into consideration, it should be ensured that different species are proportionately represented.
In addition to sampling of birds, environment samples like water, soil are to be collected and sent for testing, the guidelines state. The control actions to be initiated are same as for domestic poultry. However, endangered and precious captive birds confirmed as non-infected could be exempted from culling, say officials.
Sampling has to be repeated every 15 days for at least four times and if consecutive two samplings from the last positive result are found negative then the opening of the zoo for public could be considered by the competent authority, according to the action plan for prevention, control and containment of avian influenza.

Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.
Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.
The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.
Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

On October 22, Vox is co-hosting a panel and reception honoring the 2o26 L’Oréal-UNESCO for Women in Science 2026 Award recipients, our second year celebrating this group of scientists.
Introducing the 2026 L’Oréal-UNESCO for Women in Science Awardees
Vox is partnering with L’Oréal UNESCO to celebrate its 2026 grant recipients.
The program, part of the global L’Oréal-UNESCO for Women in Science initiative, recognizes five women postdoctoral scientists whose research ranges from bioengineering to astronomy. Meet them below:
Dr. Danielle Stevens: Innate Immunity, Computational Biology — University of California, Berkeley
Using artificial intelligence to speed up the engineering of disease-resistant crops by targeting plant immune receptors, with the goal of cutting global pesticide use and protecting our food supply.
Dr. Anna Romanov: Bioengineering: Immunology — Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Integrating bioengineering, synthetic biology, and immunology to build molecular technologies that reveal how B-cells evolve, then applying those insights to the development of vaccines and biologic therapies.
Dr. Katherine Lagerstrom: Ecology and Evolutionary Biology — Princeton University
Studying how human-driven change — pollution, antibiotics, captivity, and human contact — reshapes animal microbiomes and the way microbes evolve, including the spread of antibiotic resistance in the gut microbiome.
Dr. Clarissa Do Ó: Astronomy & Planetary Sciences — California Institute of Technology (Caltech)
Building the tools and technologies used to photograph planets beyond our solar system, laying the groundwork for finding new Earth-like planets rotating around Sun-like stars to allow deeper understanding of where our own planet fits in the universe.
Dr. Tana Pottorf: Neuroimmunology — The Ohio State University
Investigating the role of immune cells (macrophages) after spinal cord injury, aiming to develop therapies that preserve their helpful effects while curbing chronic inflammation and improving recovery.
At the event, Vox Media Creative will premiere five short documentaries exploring these scientists’ groundbreaking work.

On Thursday, the health authorities in France shared that the Shamonda virus has been detected in a human for the first time. The rare case has been detected in a patient with severely compromised immunity levels, who died earlier in October, reported AFP. The health and agriculture ministries assured that "no health risk to the general public" has been identified in a joint statement. It added that the human infection seems to be "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient" who was hospitalised for a serious medical condition. "Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," the ministries said, quoting the agency. Shamonda virus typically affects livestock, particularly cattle. It belongs to the Orthobunyavirus group, the same group of viruses as Schmallenberg virus (SBV). While the disease has been reportedly observed mainly in cattle, it can also be found in sheep, goats, alpacas and horses across European countries. Shamonda virus is typically transmitted to animals via small biting insects. It was first detected in Europe this summer, as per the authorities. The patient reportedly contracted the virus through the bite of a midge in eastern France, where the virus was circulating in animals during the spring and summer, the ministries said. "The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death are very likely linked to infection with the Shamonda virus," as per the authorities, based on preliminary findings. But "clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are still ongoing", they added. Shamonda virus symptoms can be fever, diarrhea, fatigue and a reduction in milk production, as per UK’s Animal and Plant Health Agency. However, the virus is said to be not fatal for cattle, reported Independent citing the British Agriculture Bureau. The Shamonda virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s. Since then the virus has been detected in animals of Africa and Japan. However, it is now spreading among several European countries this year. Despite its previous circulation in Africa and Asia, the virus has now only seen in Europe over the summer. For the unversed, no human cases of the Shamonda virus had been ever documented across the world until now in France. Women are protesting around Poland for free access to legal abortions
Women are protesting in Poland for access to free and legal abortion services
WARSAW, Poland -- Women plan street demonstrations in more than 20 Polish cities and towns Thursday to protest the lack of access to free and legal abortion.
They're accusing Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to fulfill its promise to relax Poland's strict abortion laws, and protesting even though the parliament passed two bills on Tuesday aimed at easing abortion rules. The measures are likely to be vetoed by the conservative president, Karol Nawrocki.
Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.
She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki's veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women's support to win elections next year.
Since 1993, legal abortions have been allowed in Catholic Poland only in cases of severe fetal abnormality, risk to the mother’s life and health, or the pregnancy being a result of rape or incest.
Polish women have been pushing for the legalization of abortion ever since, including in a nationwide wave of demonstrations of women wearing black called “Black Protest,” which began in 2016.
Rather than being liberalized, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of fetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, an overwhelming majority of which are carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
And abortion remains a taboo subject in Poland, which now has one of Europe’s most restrictive abortion laws, with only Malta imposing stricter limits.
Tusk’s pro-European coalition won the 2023 election in part on a promise to liberalize Poland’s abortion laws. But in 2024, Tusk said his government wouldn't be able to overcome the likely veto of a conservative president. Instead, measures were introduced to prevent hospitals from refusing to perform legal abortions on religious grounds.
"The state will increasingly effectively stand on the side of the woman when she is making dramatic decisions in her life,” Tusk said in 2024 when he announced the measures.
Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared to 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the national health fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.
Activists organizing Thursday’s protests are claiming the Tusk government has betrayed Polish women — and that Tusk's claims that women's access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.
“The government's promises act as a type of disinformation,” Marcinek told the AP. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is ok, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it's very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”
Meanwhile, international donors are less interested in supporting Polish women's rights because they mistakenly believe things have improved, Marcinek said.
In 2025, the Abortion Dream Team opened an “ abortion clinic ” across from the parliament building in Warsaw where women can get information about their options, or even take their abortion pills in the company of supporting activists.
This September, the activists also launched a parcel locker dispensing abortion pills at the same location, nicknamed “Abortomat."
The dispenser is operated by the international feminist non-profit Women Help Women. It enables women needing abortions to get the pills the next day, rather than wait for up to two weeks for home delivery, Marcinek said.
“There are also people who cannot safely order such pills at their own address, for example because of an unsupportive family or abusive partner," she said. “These women can get a pin number and pick up the pills in the machine the next day.”
“In Poland, assisting with an abortion is a criminal offence. Even passing the pills from hand to hand can be considered a crime,” the Abortion Dream Team wrote in a statement. "That’s why we’re hacking the Criminal Code and bringing abortion into the 21st century.”

Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is 'entering a new phase' with Muse
He expects the agent will generate more revenue per user than the company's apps.
It's only been a few weeks since Meta introduced Muse, but the company's personal agent is already becoming central to Meta's plan to start making money off its massive investment in AI. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that the company is already working on monetizing the agent, and that he expects Muse to eventually generate more revenue per user than Facebook and Instagram.
Even though Muse is only available in the US and Canada, Meta has already seen significant adoption of the agent. Zuckerberg said that more than 10 million people have started using it since its early September rollout. "Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it," Zuckerberg said during the company's third-quarter earnings call Wednesday. "We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people."
Muse is also significantly more expensive for Meta to operate compared with its other services, and Zuckerberg said the company was already working on its plans to monetize the agent. Meta plans to build "commerce tools" that will allow it to charge businesses fees for transactions facilitated by its agent, the CEO said. He noted that shopping is currently the "most common" use case for the agent, and that people are spending an average of $200 per purchase with Muse. Meta will incorporate its AI subscriptions for people and business owners who use the agent more heavily as well.
Zuckerberg predicted that revenue from Muse could eventually surpass the money it currently makes from its apps, at least by some metrics. "The average revenue per American user for our existing family of apps users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place," Zuckerberg said.
Muse is also "central" to Meta's plans to make more money from its AI glasses, according to Zuckerberg. While the company doesn't currently "make a large profit on the hardware" it sells, adding Muse to the product will help Meta sell more AI subscriptions, Zuckerberg predicted.
Meta previewed Muse on its smart glasses last month during Connect. The company said users will be able to talk to their agent in much the same way they can currently chat with Meta AI, and will be able to check in on tasks or add items to their agent's to-do list. Meta didn't specify if Muse on its glasses would require a separate subscription, but Zuckerberg's statements suggest that at least some Muse features will be paywalled on the glasses. (The company has contemplated upcharging for other glasses features, including its upcoming hearing enhancement ability.) Muse will be available on Meta's glasses "next month," Zuckerberg said.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

BENGALURU: It has been a difficult day for cybersecurity, with critical vulnerabilities in PHP triggering an urgent global patching effort, millions of reported hacking attempts, and precautionary shutdowns of some online services. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the scale of the incident was unusual, remarking at an event in Cologne in Germany that he had not seen anything like it “in a long, long time”.
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued a critical-severity warning over two vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used open-source scripting language that powers websites and web applications. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely, disclose memory and potentially compromise affected systems.
In its advisory issued on Wednesday, CERT-In said reports had confirmed large-scale exploitation in the wild and urged organisations and individuals using affected versions to apply security updates urgently.
CERT-In Flags Vulnerabilities
Google Cloud executives Chris Betz, chief information security officer, and Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, said PHP and cybersecurity firm Wiz Research disclosed the two vulnerabilities after research that used multiple AI models to identify and help remediate them.
Google Cloud said its own infrastructure was not vulnerable, but warned that customers running PHP applications on the platform could be exposed. It urged customers to update their applications to patched PHP versions and redeploy them. Google is also rolling out updated serverless base images for supported PHP runtimes, with automatic updates available for certain services and configurations.
The scale of the response has extended beyond India. “In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. Companies and govt agencies in several countries temporarily restricted access to some online services as a precaution while they worked to secure vulnerable systems.
Cloudflare’s blog said it successfully deployed mitigations for all its customers after the PHP vulnerabilities were leaked before their official disclosure date. The company observed attack traffic targeting customers and tracked how attackers modified their payloads to try to bypass its security.

Approach African GP with humility, says Hamilton

Lewis Hamilton has addressed concerns on human rights grounds about holding an African Grand Prix in Rwanda by saying people should "approach it with humility".
Formula 1 has signed a 10-year deal with the central-east African country starting in the early 2030s.
Briton Hamilton, who has campaigned for a race in Africa for many years, said: "I don't get to choose where we go. Naturally, there are problems all over the world today, so I've seen many of the stories. But I think we really have to approach it with humility.
"There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the West intervening."
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
