Quick Answer
Apple’s HomeView is a $299 smart home hub with a 7-inch touchscreen, A18 chip, AI-powered Siri, and personalized experiences for up to six users. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, it offers smart home controls, FaceTime, and voice and face recognition, but has limitations with apps, games, and video.
It was pretty much THE product in the spotlight at Apple’s recent Welcome Home event. The HomeView marked Apple’s debut in the smart home hub segment. Of course, it does what every smart hub is supposed to do – let you control different smart devices in the house – but hey, this is an Apple product, so some distinct, different (and odd) touches have been added to the regular mix. As we wait for the HomeView to arrive in India at $299/Rs 39,900 on November 13, here are fourteen things worth noting about Apple’s most high-profile entry into the smart home segment:
Table of Contents
Totally buttonless with clean, smooth sides
Yep, Apple has finally delivered a touchscreen device with zero physical buttons. Only it is not an iPhone, as many had been predicting. The HomeView has only a single Type-C port (for power requirements) and no physical buttons or switches at all. Even the Type-C port is on the back of the wall-mounted version and in the spherical base of the regular version, so the sides of the HomeView are totally plain. Minimalism unlocked!
Comes in regular (iMac G4) and wall-mounted versions…and they both cost the same!
The HomeView is fundamentally a 7-inch touchscreen tablet that gives one access to different smart devices in the house, as well as does some very cool things (more on that later). It comes in two models: the regular version, which comes attached to a spherical, dome-like base and flexible “arm”, making it look like a small iMac G4 (the Sunflower Mac, remember?) and is meant to be used on a table, and there is a “Wall Mounted” version, which is just a tablet that can be mounted on a wall. Both need a power outlet as they have no battery of their own. Rather remarkably, both versions come at the same price: USD 299 (Rs 39,900). This is kind of odd because they both have rather different components and requirements, as we shall see.
Want more for your bucks? Get the regular HomeView; the Wall Mounted one has a few things missing (and fewer colors)
They might have the same price tag, but the regular HomeView is much more value for money than the Wall Mounted one. The HomeView comes with two full-range drivers, a down-firing woofer, and also has dual force-canceling radiators for spatial audio and better bass. The Wall Mounted variant, on the other hand, is more of a tablet. It has only the two full-range drivers, and no woofer or radiator. What’s more, the wall mount for it costs extra – USD 59.95 or USD 79.95 depending on the option you choose from Schneider Home (more options are expected to come shortly). The regular variant also comes with a 1.5 meter Type-C cable and a 30W power adapter, which the Wall Mounted variant lacks (the mounts give these options).
As if this were not enough, you even get more color options in the regular HomeView – it comes in Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Grey, while the Wall Mounted variant has just Silver and Space Grey! If money is (relatively) tight, the regular HomeView is a no-brainer. You get additional speakers, more color options, a charging cable, and a Mac-ish design for the same price! Those speakers and that Mac-ish design at the same price as the Wall Mounted option would do it for us. The presence of that base does add to the weight of the regular HomeView – it is 952 grams as compared to the 286 grams of the Wall Mounted one.
As bright as an iPad (with also the lowest nit count on an Apple product)
The HomeView is basically a 7-inch touchscreen tablet. It comes with a Liquid Retina True Tone LCD display which is totally square in shape, with a resolution of 1088 x 1088 and a pixel density of 220 ppi. Interestingly, while its other specs are inferior to those of the iPad and iPad Air range, the HomeView comes with the same level of brightness – 500 nits. This means that the HomeView will have the same exceptional brightness that the iPad and iPad Air offer. 500 nits is also the brightness level of the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air. Interestingly, the HomeView also comes with the lowest brightness of any Apple product ever – a stunning 0.3 nits.
There’s an iPhone 16/ MacBook Neo family chip inside it
The HomeView is powered by the A18 processor, which is similar to that seen on the iPhone 16, 16 Plus and 16e. In purely tablet terms, this makes the HomeView more powerful than the base iPad (11th generation), which runs on the A16 Bionic. Interestingly, even the MacBook Neo launched earlier this year was powered by a similar processor, the A18 Pro.
Runs on…anonymous (as of now) OS
Although it says that “Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI,” Apple has not yet released the name of the operating system on which HomeView runs. It is a blend of iOS and iPadOS, and is believed to have been codenamed HomeOS. What it will be finally called is anyone’s guess.
You cannot install apps on it
Rather surprisingly, given Apple’s stress on apps, the HomeView has no app store of its own at the time of writing. It comes with a number of preinstalled apps (on Built-In Apps, as Apple calls them), but there seems to be no provision for installing apps on it. The HomeView can, however, run some apps from the iPhone – Audiobooks, Classical Music, and Apple TV. Rather interestingly, there is no visible support for any maps app yet.
It can identify faces and voices too (but seemingly does not have Face ID)
The HomeView comes with face identification through a single camera, and Apple says that it also recognizes voices, and comes with special “Secure Exclaves” that process camera and microphone feeds in a secure zone where they cannot be accessed by other software on the device or even by Apple. Interestingly, there is no mention of Face ID in the tech specs of the HomeView, so we are assuming that the feature is not available on the HomeView and the face identification system on the device is a different one.
Can handle up to six users…but guests are allowed
A single HomeView can have up to six different users who can use all its features and functions. The device takes information from iPhones or iPads, such as contacts and calendar, from the iPhone or iPad of the user to customize experiences for them. However, every user’s information will be kept private and not shared with others. There can be guest users too, but they will be able to access only a limited number of functions, such as controlling smart home accessories, checking the weather, setting timers, and playing music.
The camera is only for calling, as of now – no photography!
The HomeView comes with a 12-megapixel camera with an f/2,4 aperture, but from what we can see so far, its function is limited to identifying the user and making FaceTime calls. It comes with Center Stage that keeps you in the center of the frame during FaceTime calls, but as of now, it cannot record video or take pictures.
And it can switch seamlessly and speedily between users
Perhaps the most spectacular feature of the HomeView is the fact that it literally transforms itself depending on who is in front of it. It works with the iPhone or iPad of each user and shows them the content when they use the device. Every user has their own customizations and information, which the others cannot see, and the HomeView literally presents each user with their own version every time they appear in front of it and are identified – and judging by what we have seen in the demos, it does so almost instantly, while maintaining the privacy of the previous user. That A18 chip and that 12-megapixel front-facing camera are incredibly fast!
A tab that does not do too many videos…yet
In spite of being relatively large in size, the HomeView does not come with a dedicated app for videos – as per the Apple website, it does not even come with Apple TV preinstalled. While HomeView does not have a dedicated Apple TV app preinstalled, Apple confirms support for Apple TV content and compatible third-party video apps. However, the range of supported services and how they work on HomeView remain worth checking.
No fun and games either…yet
Rather remarkably for a device that is designed to be used by the family, the HomeView does not come with any games at the time of writing. We are so hoping that changes and Apple adds some fun, turn-based, multiplayer games to the tablet. Imagine being able to play Ludo, Scrabble, Chess, or Monopoly on this!

Almost two years into President Donald Trump’s second administration and young Americans -who helped him win the White House in 2024 - are shifting their support to Democrats, polling suggests.
Just weeks ahead of the midterm elections, the number of voters aged 18 to 29 who identified as Democrat or leaned that way has jumped from 55 percent in 2024 to 70 percent, according to the latest New York Times/Siena poll of likely voters.
Across the country, young voters are more likely to cast their ballot for the Democratic candidate in their district by 44 percentage points, compared with a 10-point margin in 2024, the poll found.
While Trump made gains with young voters two years ago, only 16 percent of voters aged 18 to 29 now approve of his job performance, compared to 79 percent who disapprove. In another blow, 86 percent of those 18 to 29 disapprove of how the president has handled the economy.
Trump’s war in Iran is also proving deeply unpopular with younger voters, with 87 percent saying they disapprove.
Young male voters flocked to Trump in 2024, with more than half (55 percent) of the demographic signaling their support for him, according to the NYT/Siena poll. Now, Democrats hold a 1 percent advantage over the president with young men.
Support for Trump and Republicans among young women, who lean more liberal, has also dropped since 2024.
Still, younger voters are not massively impressed with the Democrats either. The poll found that 41 percent said the party was not focused on the right issues. Still, the Republican Party fared worse among the demographic—77 percent said the GOP had the wrong focus.
Overall, the NYT/Siena poll found that the majority of voters, aged 18 to 29, believed Democrats had a better handling of the economy, the cost of living, immigration, foreign wars, healthcare, AI, gas prices and corruption than Republicans.
The Harvard Youth Poll, released Thursday, had similar findings. Democrats lead Republicans 63 percent to 26 percent among likely voters ages 18–29, with 10 percent undecided, it found.
Half of young Democrats (50 percent) said that they will definitely vote in November, compared with 34 percent of young Republicans. Among young people who say they will definitely vote, 63 percent describe their vote as opposition to Trump and his policies, compared with 14 percent who describe it as support.
“Young voters are poised to deliver a sharp rebuke to President Trump, while the broader generation is sending a message to everyone in power,” said John Della Volpe, director of polling at the Institute of Politics.
“Young people feel economic pressure, and they’re holding the current administration responsible — making the midterms a critical referendum on Trump and his policies,” added Sophia Robertson, student chair of the Harvard Public Opinion Project.
Trump’s approval rating has languished near historic lows for months but the White House has brushed off the unfavorable polls.
“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a previous statement.
Trump himself has acknowledged that the president’s party historically tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterms.
“For whatever reason, I don't understand it, nobody does. Nobody's been able to explain it. Whoever wins the presidency, Republican or Democrat, automatically does poorly in the midterms,” he told reporters earlier this month.

US President Donald Trump took aim at NBA star LeBron James on Thursday, condemning the basketball player for conduct he deemed disrespectful while the national anthem was played at a recent game.
"While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country," Trump wrote on Truth Social alongside a video depicting James moving during the anthem. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!"
In the footage posted by Trump, James is seen lined up alongside Philadelphia 76ers players, stretching his arms in a pre-game routine and mimicking basketball shots.
Trump’s attack on James comes after the NBA legend made his competitive debut for the 76ers Tuesday night, leading his new team to a 106-100 win over defending champions the New York Knicks.
James, 41, opted to extend his hall-of-fame career in the off-season by signing a deal with Philly and scored 14 points in 34 minutes on court Tuesday.
Tyrese Maxey topped the scoring with 28 points while Jalen Brunson posted 21 for the Knicks.
Speaking to NBC after the game, James said: “I could be a lot better. Still getting my rhythm, obviously just a little bit over two weeks with the new squad.
“But I like the way we played. I think we played exceptionally well.”
This is not the first time that Trump has slammed sports stars for their behavior during the national anthem.
During his first term as president in 2017, Trump hit out at NFL players involved in the ‘Take a Knee’ protests, insisting it was “very important” that they stood for the anthem.
Prior to a game in October 2017, Trump posted on Twitter: “Very important that NFL players STAND tomorrow, and always, for the playing of our National Anthem. Respect our Flag and our Country!” before adding video of the Chicago Blackhawks and the St Louis Blues with the caption: “19,000 RESPECTING our National Anthem! #StandForOurAnthem.”
Just days earlier, Trump had also written on social media: "The NFL has all sorts of rules and regulations. The only way out for them is to set a rule that you can't kneel during our National Anthem!"

Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.
Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.
Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent.
“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.
Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.
LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed.
Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals.
Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product.

Declan Rice struck eight minutes from time to earn Arsenal a 2-2 draw against Bayern Munich in the UEFA Champions League 2026-27 league phase at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday.
Eberechi Eze opened the scoring for Mikel Arteta’s side before Alphonso Davies equalised for the host. Harry Kane then converted a second-half penalty to put Bayern ahead, only for Rice to restore parity in the closing stages.
Arsenal suffered an early setback when Bukayo Saka sustained a thigh injury in the eighth minute and was replaced by Eze.
The substitute made his presence felt in the 25th minute, latching onto Martin Odegaard’s pass behind Bayern’s defence before beating Manuel Neuer. Although the assistant referee initially flagged for offside, VAR overturned the decision and awarded the goal.
Bayern responded 10 minutes later through Davies, who timed his run to perfection to collect Kane’s through ball and finish past David Raya.
The German side, missing Michael Olise, Joshua Kimmich and Jamal Musiala, gradually gained control after the equaliser but could not find another breakthrough before half-time.
Both goalkeepers were called into action after the restart. Neuer produced an excellent save to keep out an Arsenal header, while Raya denied Dayot Upamecano at the other end.
Bayern eventually took the lead in the 61st minute when Kane’s shot struck Jurrien Timber’s arm inside the penalty area. The England captain stepped up to convert the resulting spot-kick.
The goal extended Kane’s scoring streak to 10 consecutive Champions League appearances, leaving him one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record of 11.
With Bayern seemingly heading towards victory, Arsenal found a way back through Rice in the 82nd minute.
Substitute Viktor Gyokeres played a clever pass into the midfielder’s path, and Rice finished past Neuer to ensure the visitors returned to London with a point.
The draw was only the second time Arsenal had dropped points in 12 matches across all competitions this season.
Arteta’s side moved to seven points from three Champions League fixtures, while Vincent Kompany’s Bayern reached five points after recording its second successive draw in the competition.

The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The PHP Foundation did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.
“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity.
With more than 1 million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.
Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.
Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours – but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening, the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Prime minister Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.
“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”
Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, has said publicly that she will vote to remain in Canada, but that she will not require elected members of her party to do the same.
Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold during a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.
In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, told the Guardian the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” said Farkas.
“And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together because no result will permanently put this to bed,” he added, “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

Bluesky adds iPad support in latest feature update
Profile links to third-party platforms have also arrived on the social network.
Bluesky rolled out several features in its latest update, notably beta testing support for iPads. The social network should start looking and performing better on the Apple tablets as a result of the changes. The Beta Features section of the Settings menu can be used to share feedback about any bugs or wonkiness found in the Bluesky iPad app.
Another update is aimed at self-promotion. Bluesky users can now put links to external platforms at the top of their profiles. The company framed the addition as a way for creators to get better support from their Bluesky audiences by connecting their profiles to crowdfunding platforms such as Patreon or Ko-fi or to more of their content in a website or newsletter. This might also cut down on some of the "link in bio" language that's so common in many social media posts. The Edit Profile menu now has a Links section where those external sites can be added.

Early backers Kae Capital Fund II and Kalysta Capital Fund II bagged 38.3X returns on shares sold through manufacturing company Zetwerk’s IPO, emerging among the biggest gainers in its offer for sale (OFS). At ₹151 apiece, the upper end of the IPO price band, the sale price was 38.3 times the two funds’ weighted average acquisition cost of ₹3.94 per share. Kae Capital Fund II pocketed ₹196.3 Cr by selling around 1.3 Cr shares, while Kalysta Capital Fund II received ₹63.3 Cr from the sale of 41.9 Lakh shares. Both investors retain sizeable holdings after the sale. Kae Capital Fund II holds 4.3 Cr shares valued at ₹649.3 Cr at ₹151 apiece, while Kalysta Capital Fund II holds 1.4 Cr shares worth ₹211.4 Cr. The payouts come after Zetwerk’s IPO closed with 3.06X subscription, attracting bids for 56.62 Cr shares against 18.50 Cr shares on offer. The company’s shares are scheduled to list on the exchanges tomorrow. Meanwhile, Peak XV and Lightspeed sold shares through multiple investment vehicles, with returns varying across their funds. Peak XV pocketed a combined ₹359.3 Cr through two vehicles – Peak XV Partners Investments V and Peak XV Partners Growth Investments III. Peak XV Partners Investments V sold around 1.8 Cr shares for ₹271.8 Cr, clocking a 23.9X return multiple. It retains 12.2 Cr shares valued at ₹1,842.2 Cr at the IPO price. Peak XV Partners Growth Investments III received ₹87.5 Cr from the sale of around 58 Lakh shares, realising a 3.3X return multiple. It retains 4 Cr shares worth ₹604 Cr. Together, the two funds held a 12.1% stake in Zetwerk before the OFS. Lightspeed, which invested through three vehicles, collectively pocketed around ₹440 Cr. Lightspeed Venture Partners Select IV Mauritius sold around 1.4 Cr shares for ₹211.4 Cr, while Lightspeed India Partners II, LLC sold 1.2 Cr shares for ₹181.2 Cr. Lightspeed India Partners III, LLC received ₹47.5 Cr from the sale of 31.5 Lakh shares. Lightspeed India Partners II recorded the highest return multiple among the three vehicles at around 10.9X. Among other selling investors, Accel clocked a 19.5X return. However, Creovate Innovation sold shares at 0.9X its acquisition cost, taking a loss on the stake sold. Zetwerk Cofounders Pocket ₹423 Cr Zetwerk cofounders Amrit Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan collectively pocketed around ₹423 Cr through the OFS, selling approximately 1.4 Cr shares each for ₹211.4 Cr apiece. Following the sale, Acharya retains 10.1 Cr shares worth ₹1,525.1 Cr at the IPO price, while Ramakkrushnan retains 11.4 Cr shares valued at ₹1,721.4 Cr. Cofounders Rahul Sharma, Vishal Chaudhary, and Ankit Fatehpuria also sold shares through the OFS. The RHP categorised the three under “individual selling shareholders”. Sharma and Chaudhary each pocketed around ₹26 Cr by selling approximately 17.2 Lakh shares, while Fatehpuria received ₹34.3 Cr from the sale of 22.7 Lakh shares. The shareholder payouts formed part of Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO, comprising a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end of the price band. Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories. It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation. Ahead of the issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors. Domestic mutual funds, including SBI Mutual Fund and ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, accounted for around 46% of the anchor book. Global investors, including Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, also participated. On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹2,649.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr. Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

Kenya cult leader's children still being starved weeks before trial, son says
- Published
The eldest son of Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, convicted of murdering 191 people, says his younger siblings were still being forced to fast as recently as two weeks ago.
Dan Mackenzie, 27, said he reported the case to police, who rescued eight children, including his five younger siblings from their grandmother's house, and took them to a rescue centre.
"They were basically forcibly fasted because they were denying food to them for almost three days," he tells BBC's Newsday.
His father was found guilty on Monday of murdering 190 children and one adult who starved to death in Shakahola forest, near the Kenyan coast.
He had ordered members of his doomsday cult to starve themselves and their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Twenty-eight other cult leaders were also convicted of murder.
- Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders 
  - Published21 hours ago
Dan Mackenzie, who had initially defended his father, said at first he had struggled to understand the allegations against the cult leader, but came to realise the scale of the tragedy during the court proceedings.
"When I was 12, I was forced to fast for almost a week," he says. He also remembers church members beating him for hours to make him attend a service as a child.
Now, he says he felt he had to report family members who still believe in the teachings in order to free his siblings. "I had to report my grandmother."
The cult leader's doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".
"I left school when I was seven," says Dan.
Now living in the coastal town of Malindi, Dan earns a living as a motorcycle taxi driver, supporting himself and his younger siblings.
He said some people in the town had been angry with him because of his father's crimes, but others "had accepted him because he had distanced himself from that life".
"I hope the verdict would bring some comfort to those who had lost friends and relatives," Dan tells BBC's Newsday.
On Monday, Stephen Mwiti, 48, who said he had lost all six of his children to the cult, welcomed the verdict.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court.
His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
Delivering her eight-hour judgment in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".
One of his co-accused told the court that Mackenzie had said anyone who resisted fasting must be forced to go to heaven "through kicks and blows".
Burials in the forest where the cult was based were described as "weddings", with those who died celebrated as having "wedded with Jesus", the judge said.
Mackenzie and other cult leaders also face separate cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and denying children an education.
The murder verdict is the first ruling on the most serious charges against the pastor, who was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were discovered in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, near Kenya's coast.
He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.

Srinagar, Oct 22: Jammu and Kashmir Police in Shopian have arrested a drug peddler and recovered contraband substance from his possession.
A police spokesperson said that during routine naka checking at Borihalan near Danish Resort, a police party from Police Station Heerpora intercepted an Alto vehicle bearing registration number JK03H-7227 travelling from Shopian towards Heerpora. During search, 60 grams of charas-like substance was recovered from driver’s possession. The accused have been identified as Mohd Shafeeq Lone, son of Bashir Ahmad Lone, resident of Sedow, Heerpora.
Accordingly, FIR No. 117/2026 under relevant sections of law has been registered at Police Station Heerpora and further investigation has been initiated to ascertain the source of the contraband and establish its forward and backward linkages, spokesperson said.
J&K Police reiterated its firm commitment to maintaining a drug-free society and urged the general public to cooperate with law enforcement agencies by sharing information regarding drug peddling, illegal cultivation of narcotic plants and substance abuse in their localities.

In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”
New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.
Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”
“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.
To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.
“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”
Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a $5 billion settlement the company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP News reported.
But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.
“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.
Meta will appeal
In a press release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”
“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”
A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.
The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the Verge highlighted Meta’s third-quarter earnings report, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.
The excessive penalties come as Meta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”
AGs warned to keep watch on Meta AI
Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.
In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”
The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.
Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”
Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.
Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.
“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,”Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

NEW DELHI: Kashif Minhas has captured thousands of photographs of cricketers over the years. He is also an avid birdwatcher who sometimes waits for hours to get that perfect shot. But when his sons are playing and he is busy behind the lens on the ground, the avid shutterbug finds it difficult to keep his nerves in check.
"I have thousands of photographs of international cricketers. When I am completely focused on a match, I become very attentive to every ball. Capturing a catch at the right moment is special. However, these days, when my sons are playing, I sometimes enjoy watching the cricket live more than photographing it," Kashif Minhas, who runs a car business in Multan for a living, tells TimesofIndia.com.
Earlier this year, Kashif was caught on camera by the broadcasters after his elder son, Arafat Minhas, playing only his third ODI, got out against Australia at the Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore. As Arafat was dismissed, Kashif, standing behind the boundary rope with his camera, could not hold back his emotions.
"I was clicking his photographs, and the moment he got out, I put my hand on the camera and lowered my head. The television cameras caught that reaction, and it went viral," he says.
The world doesn't know about my third son, Abdullah Minhas. He is immensely talented as well. He is a left-handed top-order batter and a right-arm leg-break bowler. He has been selected at the Under-17 level and is working hard.
Kashif Minhas
"They [the broadcasters] know I am his father, so they often keep a camera on me. I even asked the director not to focus on me because I did not want to be shown in front of everyone. People think I am an official photographer of the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), which I am not. I freelance for a local newspaper, Daily Pakistan. But they told me that the visual had helped them garner a lot of views, so I thought, 'Chalo, kisi ka toh bhala ho raha' (At least someone is benefiting from it)," he adds.
Kashif, however, was deeply hurt by the false stories that circulated after the visuals went viral.
"That story made me sad. We have been in the car business since 1980, and I have a large showroom in Multan. Some people portrayed the story as if we belonged to a poor family and I had started photographing my children because we had run out of money. That is not the case. Photography is just my hobby. I have a very good car business and import cars from Japan. I never needed money to fund my children's cricket," he says.
(L-R) Abdullah Minhas, Arafat Minhas and Sameer Minhas at a cricket academy in Multan. (Special Arrangement)
Kashif's two sons, Arafat Minhas and Sameer Minhas, have shown the world what they are capable of. Arafat has played five ODIs and seven T20Is for Pakistan. The all-rounder has already taken two five-wicket hauls, one each against Australia and England, in his brief international career. Sameer Minhas has lit up age-group cricket, and one cannot forget his 172 off 113 balls against India in the 2025 U-19 Asia Cup final.
Kashif says his third son is also getting ready.
"The world doesn't know about my third son, Abdullah Minhas. He is immensely talented as well. He is a left-handed top-order batter and a right-arm leg-break bowler. He has been selected at the Under-17 level and is working hard," says a proud father.
Pakistan's Arafat Minhas celebrates after taking the wicket of England's Jordan Cox during the tri-series one-day international cricket match between Pakistan and England, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Anjum Naveed)
Like many fathers in the subcontinent, Kashif, too, is a cricket tragic.
"I was also a cricketer. I represented my regional team in Multan. But my father asked me to quit cricket and focus on the family business. He told me to leave cricket or leave home. I left home for two or three days, but then my mother asked me to come back and give up cricket. Nothing is more important to me than my mother, so I quit," he recalls.
But one fine day, while playing with a tape ball in their car porch, Kashif's eyes lit up when he saw Arafat and Sameer, then aged nine and seven, respectively, cutting, driving and pulling.
When I saw my children playing, I immediately realised that they had something special in them. I decided that what had happened to me should not happen to them. I wanted them to have the opportunity to pursue cricket.
Kashif Minhas
"The floor was wet, and their hand-eye coordination was amazing. When I saw my children playing, I immediately realised that they had something special in them. I decided that what had happened to me should not happen to them. I wanted them to have the opportunity to pursue cricket," he says.
"I took them to a local cricket academy, and when I saw how well they were playing against pace, I began to take their cricket more seriously. Arafat performed well in the PCB Under-13 tournament, then at the Under-16 and Under-19 levels. Sameer followed in his footsteps, and soon Abdullah will do the same. We kept trying and praying, and Allah blessed us," he adds.
Sameer Minhas register Pakistan's highest Youth ODI score, takes team to 347/8 against India in U19 Asia Cup final
Kashif, who had to give up his own cricketing ambitions, acknowledges that cricket is a tough sport to succeed in and requires much more than time and money.
"It requires a lot of dedication. You have to make sacrifices. I was away with my children for their training when I heard the news of my father's death. After his demise, I had to spend a lot of time at the office. But whenever they played matches outside Multan, I would travel and sit at the ground from morning until evening," he recalls.
As his sons progressed through age-group cricket, Kashif came up with the idea of taking up photography as a way to stay close to them. He started freelancing and soon found work with a local daily. As Arafat and Sameer began making waves with their performances, Kashif, too, became a familiar face on cricket grounds across Pakistan, camera in hand.
Kashif Minhas takes a picture during the Pakistan Super League. (Screengrab)
"It was an amazing moment for me," says Kashif, recalling Arafat's ODI debut against Australia in Rawalpindi.
"I never imagined that a day would come when my children would represent Pakistan in international cricket and I would be on the ground photographing them. It felt like a blessing, and I was very happy that day. He [Arafat] performed well in the last match [against England]," he further adds.
Kashif has never been harsh on his sons regarding cricket. But he has one dream he hopes to fulfil through them: winning an ICC trophy.
"I was never harsh on them. When they were not performing well, I would tell them that it was not their day and that their time would come. I would encourage them to stay prepared for the next opportunity. I never wanted to put unnecessary pressure on them. But I will be even happier when my children win an ICC trophy for their country," he says.
Pakistan's Arafat Minhas, who took the six wickets, displays the ball on the end of the tri-series one-day international cricket match between against England, in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Anjum Naveed)
The Minhas family could have etched its name in the Guinness World Records, with members representing Pakistan at different age-group levels. But the PCB has declined a request from the over-50s team to participate in the International Masters Cricket World Cup, which is being hosted by India in January next year. 
Minhas Sr was a member of that squad. Pakistan won the previous edition of the tournament, held in Sri Lanka last year, but this time the board has informed the Pakistan Veterans Cricket Association that its team will not be permitted to travel to India and participate.
"It would have been great to represent Pakistan, but it's okay. I will get the chance later," he says.
For Kashif Minhas, cricket has come full circle. He once had to abandon his own ambitions at his father's insistence, but he made sure his sons had the freedom to pursue theirs. Today, he watches them represent Pakistan, capturing their highs and lows through his lens while carrying the hopes of a father who knows what it means to let go of a dream. An ICC trophy would be the ultimate reward, but for Kashif, seeing his sons live the dream he once had to give up is already a journey worth cherishing.

At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
- Published
At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.
Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.
In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines in the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."
More severe weather is forecast in France, with Storm Austen - a newly named weather system moving in from the Atlantic - expected to reach the country's north-west.
France's weather service, Météo-France, has issued an orange-level wind warning for five western departments from Thursday evening into Friday.
The alert covers Côtes-d'Armor, Finistère, Morbihan, Ille-et-Vilaine and Manche.
Storm Adam had already brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, where at least three people were killed.
Several towns along the Mediterranean coast were cut off by floodwaters, while helicopters were deployed to rescue people stranded on rooftops.
Members of the Military Emergencies Unit found the body of a woman in the town of Oliva, Valencia, during rescue operations on Monday.
Two other women were confirmed dead over the weekend. One woman's body was washed up on a beach in Sagunto, in the eastern region of Valencia, and another was swept away by floodwaters in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez made a promise that the national government would provide resources to help in reconstruction during a visit to the Valencia region on Tuesday.
The Valencian government approved on Tuesday an aid package of €23.5m (£20m) for those affected by Storm Adam.

The disease didn’t have a name in our house. It had descriptions: the way her hands shook or she lost her words midsentence. The way she could be fully present at breakfast then somewhere unreachable by dinner.
And it had a history. My grandmother had died at 29 of what we believed was something similar, my mother had been symptomatic before I was old enough to form the question, my older sister would be told at 26 that she had it, too. What the disease had in our house was a pronoun. “It.” As in, “it got worse over the winter.” As in, “your sister might get it.” As in, “we don’t know much about it.”
That last sentence was repeated so many times, by so many doctors, that it stopped feeling like an update and started feeling like a fact about the world. Some things were known. This wasn’t one of them. We filed it alongside questions that were genuinely unanswerable, not worth revisiting.
We were wrong about that. I just didn’t know it yet.
I grew up as the primary caregiver for my mother from roughly age 8‚ managing the household, bridging the gap between what was happening inside our walls and what we presented to the world outside them. By the time I was old enough to understand what I was doing, I had already been doing it for years, not because anyone assigned it to me explicitly but because someone had to and I was there and I was capable, and it turned out that capability was its own kind of assignment.
The disease organized my childhood the way weather organizes a farming life. You don’t fight it, you work around it, you learn its seasons. And somewhere in the years of working around it, you stop asking what it is and start managing what it does.
Three generations of women in my family — my grandmother, my mother, my sister — carried the same condition through the same blood before any of us had a clinical word for it. Fifty years of documented family history. Fifty years of doctors who shrugged with genuine sympathy and said, rare. Poorly understood. Difficult to characterize.
I believed them for a long time.
Here is something worth knowing about the category called rare disease. Rare does not mean unknown. It usually means underresearched, underfunded, and underconnected to the people living inside it. There are approximately 7,000 to 10,000 identified rare diseases, depending on what definition you use. Many of them have names, and many have researchers who have dedicated careers to a single mutation, a single protein, a single entry point into the vast underlit territory of conditions that affect small numbers of people and therefore attract small amounts of attention and money.
The work on these diseases gets done‚ slowly, in small labs, by scientists who chose a difficult corner of medicine because something drew them there. The work gets published. The knowledge accumulates.
And then, in too many cases, it stays there. There is no architecture reliably connecting what medicine knows about a rare condition to the families living inside it. Research participants from earlier decades have no right to follow-up notification. Families whose cases contributed to literature that eventually named their disease may never know the paper was written.
The loop, opened when the family first came to medical attention, can stay open indefinitely on their end. On the other end, in a database they don’t know to search, the loop may have closed years ago. This is not malice, it’s infrastructure, but the cost is real regardless.
The cost is my mother going through nearly 40 years of illness without being told that someone had looked at what she had and given it a name. The cost is my sister and her 15 years of deterioration and her death at 41, in a world where a researcher somewhere had been asking the same questions we asked in our living room, except the researcher was getting answers and we were not getting calls.
I am a research methodologist. For 23 years I have worked at an academic medical center building systematic reviews‚ assembling bodies of medical literature to answer clinical questions, following citation chains, evaluating sources, asking the next question without assuming the answer. I had the skills and the access and I had stopped looking, and that is the sentence I keep coming back to. I had stopped asking the question that mattered most to me personally‚ not because I forgot, not because I stopped caring, but because somewhere in the decades of shrugged answers, I had accepted the not-knowing as the settled state. The doctors had said rare, poorly understood, difficult to characterize for so long that I had internalized their uncertainty as my own. A research methodologist’s skill set and a grieving daughter’s resignation, and the resignation had won.
There is a specific exhaustion that comes from caring for people with unnamed conditions across many years. You ask the questions when they feel fresh. You push when pushing feels possible. And then the decades accumulate and the people you were asking on behalf of are gone, and you are left with your own life to build from whatever remains, and the unanswered questions stop feeling like questions and start feeling like the way of things.
I’ve written a memoir about all of this called “Naming It.” After finishing the memoir, I sat down with the oldest document I had, my grandmother’s death certificate, which my aunt mailed me 20 years ago. I looked at it many times without understanding it, because I had not yet learned how to read it. Going through it to check a fact I stopped on cause of death: acute coronary thrombosis. A catch all. It was not an answer. It was a placeholder. It still is. In 1954, though, differential diagnosis capabilities were limited and no one looked further.
Using Claude I typed in everything I knew about what came after my grandmother’s death and my family’s history, along with the research from the ’80s and ’90s. Within seconds it answered what decades of shrugs had not. The research had worked, comparisons were made, and “it” had a name: FENIB, an ultra-rare genetic neurodegenerative disorder with progressive dementia and seizures, found in less than 1 in 1 million people. It had been named and studied for years. My family was in the literature. We had seen doctors for years. Still, no one told us.
Learning the name did not only answer a question. It reorganized everything behind it, the way a random set of details rearranges the moment you learn the one thing connecting them. I spent my life managing what the disease did. Now I understood what it was.
My grandmother handed my mother an inheritance that nobody named. My mother did the same. I can hand my children an inheritance with a name.
So I told them. Not in front of a fireplace the way I had pictured it growing up, when I was telling children who did not yet exist how I survived. This time it was at our favorite restaurant on an ordinary Wednesday. I told them everything I discovered over the previous 72 hours. The death certificate, the research, the name: FENIB.
For decades the disease in our family had only a pronoun. My children are the first generation to grow up with its name.
Miranda Pappas is a research methodologist with more than two decades of experience evaluating clinical and scientific evidence. She holds a master’s degree in counseling psychology and is the author of the forthcoming memoir “Naming It.”

A pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the open-source programming language that powers much of the modern web, has forced governments and companies across the globe into emergency action. The vulnerabilities, identified as part of OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative and flagged separately by Google’s cybersecurity wing Wiz, could potentially give attackers a direct path to a server’s file system or database. For an internet ecosystem built largely on top of open-source components, this is a code-red scenario. The vulnerabilities were flagged by AI, and a fix was issued on Wednesday afternoon. The response has been unusually broad. Finland has shut down state internet services, while the Netherlands’ cybersecurity agency has taken its website offline. France, too, has temporarily taken certain websites down. India’s CERT-In (Computer Emergency Response Team) and the US National Security Agency (NSA) have also advised organisations using PHP to update their systems or take their affected systems offline until immediate patching is not possible. Japanese Prime Minister (PM) Sanae Takaichi, in a post on X, urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP. The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities. This led to some users experiencing issues accessing the website on Thursday. The episode is significant not only because of the severity of the flaws but also because of how they were found. OpenAI said its GPT-5.6 Sol model identified one critical flaw, while Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI described the episode as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory”, arguing that the development demonstrates both the defensive potential of AI and the growing risk that the same capabilities could help attackers develop exploits faster. For organisations running PHP-based websites, applications and APIs, the immediate priority is to identify exposure, apply vendor patches and assess whether systems may already have been compromised. The wider tech industry is also rushing to coordinate and mitigate any problems emerging from the fracas. So how did the two flaws, which affect nearly every website on the internet, suddenly come to light? More Than Half Of Internet At Stake PHP is a server-side programming language that is used to build websites and web apps. It processes user requests, connects to databases and often controls access to sensitive backend systems. Because it sits between the public internet and an organisation’s data, a flaw in PHP can have consequences far beyond a single website. The newly disclosed vulnerabilities could allow attackers to reach a server’s file system or database. In practice, that means an attacker may be able to read, modify or delete files, access stored credentials, extract customer data or move deeper into an enterprise infrastructure. At the heart of the crisis are two interconnected flaws rated 9.2 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity scale. The bugs exploit deep memory-handling mechanisms inside the PHP execution core. This allows unauthenticated external attackers to send crafted web traffic, bypass security checks, and execute arbitrary code directly on the host server. Making matters worse, these flaws aren’t restricted to modern builds. These vulnerabilities are believed to have existed in every version of PHP since version 5, which was first released in 2004. Websites running older versions face a more difficult upgrade path, as PHP 8.1 and earlier are no longer supported. The recommended fix is to move web servers to the latest version, PHP 8.5.12. While the vulnerabilities were originally discovered by a joint team involving Google and OpenAI, the planned multi-month remediation timeline had to be rushed. After proof-of-concept details leaked prematurely on technical forums like Hacker News, PHP core maintainers were forced to rush out emergency builds ahead of the schedule. “With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated. It marks an AI inflexion point,” said Google Wiz in a post. India Braces For Impact India’s exposure is likely to be substantial because PHP remains widely used across government portals, educational institutions, small businesses, ecommerce platforms and legacy enterprise systems. Many Indian organisations also rely on shared hosting providers, third-party web developers and older PHP-based content management systems. In these environments, the organisation using the website may not directly control the PHP version or patching cycle. As such, this could create a dependency on hosting providers and managed-service vendors to apply updates quickly. The government’s own digital footprint could also be impacted. Many public-facing portals and state-run services often depend on PHP-based stacks. A vulnerability that potentially allows access to databases could also raise major concerns among the general populace. The effect is already visible. As per website tracker DownDetector, websites like Airtel, Duolingo, Jio, Bank of Baroda, IRCTC, and State Bank of India, among others have been facing issues in the past few hours. As a result, CERT-In has issued an advisory for all “organisations and individuals using PHP. The agency has flagged “high risk of remote code execution and complete system compromise” due to these vulnerabilities. “These vulnerabilities exist in PHP due to memory corruption and improper resource control. A remote attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities by sending a specially crafted request to the targeted system. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code and compromise affected systems on the targeted system,” said CERT-In. Going forward, Indian startups and companies will have the job of quickly identifying every PHP-based website and API in use. They will then have to apply the official patch as soon as it is available. Where immediate patching is not possible, organisations should restrict public access, place affected systems behind a web application firewall, monitor logs for suspicious activity and consider temporary isolation. They should also review backups and recovery plans in case compromise is detected. How Bad Is It? The immediate operational impact could be disruption. Enterprises that cannot immediately patch vulnerable PHP systems could potentially have to take their systems offline until mitigation processes are complete. For businesses, this can mean suspended websites, unavailable customer portals, delayed transactions and interrupted internal tools. For public-sector bodies, the risk extends to citizen services, government communications and critical administrative systems. The government actions illustrate the scale of concern. As mentioned above, various bodies in Finland, the Netherlands and France have taken various websites down as a precautionary measure. The security consequences could be more damaging. If cyber attackers gain access to a server’s file system or database, they can potentially steal personal data, business records, authentication credentials or payment information. They could also modify website content, install persistent access tools or use compromised servers as a base for further attacks. Cyberattacks In The AI Age The PHP vulnerabilities show how quickly security has changed in the AI era. AI can now help researchers uncover flaws hidden in widely used software, giving defenders a chance to prepare fixes before attackers exploit them. At the same time, agentic AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploit development just as easily as it can support patching and threat detection. As models become more capable, the gap between a flaw being found and an attack being launched may shrink dramatically. This puts pressure on organisations to move from periodic security reviews to continuous monitoring, rapid patching and stronger default protections. For organisations, the lesson is clear. Security can no longer be treated as an annual compliance exercise. Companies will need fast patching processes, least-privilege access controls, robust backups and incident-response plans. They must also assume that attackers may use AI to find and exploit weaknesses faster than before. The PHP episode may be remembered less for the vulnerability itself than for what it signals. AI is becoming a central force in both offensive and defensive cybersecurity. The advantage will belong to organisations that use it to find, fix and prevent problems before adversaries can act.

Mumbai, Oct 22: The rupee depreciated 12 paise to 94.50 against the US dollar in early trade on Thursday, weighed down by weak domestic markets and elevated crude oil prices.
According to forex analysts, the rupee began trading on a flat-to-lower trajectory due to sluggish domestic equities and surging crude oil prices. However, the downside remained cushioned by a softer US dollar and declining US Treasury yields.
At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at 94.47, then lost ground to touch 94.50, lower by 12 paise over its previous close.
On Wednesday, the rupee surged 53 paise to close at 94.38 against the US dollar.
"We expect the rupee to trade with a slight positive bias on IPO related foreign inflows and weakness in the dollar. Softening of US treasury yields and reports that Russia is ready for new peace talks may also support the rupee," said Anuj Choudhary, Research Analyst, Mirae Asset Sharekhan.
Choudhary further added that traders may take cues from weekly unemployment claims data from the US.
The dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was trading lower by 0.21 per cent at 101.56.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading higher by 1.58 per cent at USD 110.54 per barrel in futures trade.
The rupee remains finely balanced within 94-97, said Anindya Banerjee, Head of Commodity and Currency Research, Kotak NEO.
"The RBI has bought itself time, the Jio IPO has added near-term dollar supply, and a US trade agreement could strengthen the structural inflow story. But if portfolio selling accelerates again or crude makes a decisive move towards USD 120, that balance will be tested," Banerjee added.
On the domestic equity market front, Sensex fell 642.51 points to 73,067.18 in early trade, while Nifty declined 241.35 points to 22,570.90.
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) purchased equities worth Rs 1,022.32 crore on a net basis on Wednesday, according to exchange data.

Several parts of Gurugram, Faridabad and Nuh districts are reeling from power outages, water disruptions and other problems as Haryana's electricity department employees stage a protest against the privatisation of power distribution. According to news agency PTI, more than 3,000 electricity-related complaints were received on the first day of the strike in Gurugram.
The demonstration, which will continue until October 25, began following the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission's (HERC) decision to grant private company Eleven Power a parallel licence to distribute electricity in Gurugram and Nuh for 25 years.
The strike by Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (DHBVN) workers has also affected electricity supply in Gurugram, Faridabad and Nuh districts since 10 PM on Wednesday.
In Faridabad, people in the New Industrial Township-2 area took to the streets, demanding the restoration of power supply. They said the power cuts had also affected the water supply.
Industrial establishments in Gurugram's Daulatabad, Kadipur and Sector 37 were also affected, raising concerns about the impact of the strike on manufacturing and commercial operations in Gurugram, Haryana's capital city.
Several entrepreneurs, including Maini in Gurugram, reported losses due to prolonged power cuts.
Industrial units in Kadipur and Basai were also affected by the outages.
"Power cuts at industrial units have brought machinery and production to a halt, impacting business operations. With operations suspended across hundreds of units, the risk of losses has increased," Maini was quoted as saying by PTI.
Several residential colonies in Gurugram were forced to rely on generators after their inverter backups ran out, residents said.
The prolonged power cuts also disrupted water supplies in several areas, leaving residents facing a shortage of drinking water. Residents said they were relying on water stored in tanks but warned that the reserves would last only a few more hours.
"Electricity and water are both essential services. Where is the government? Residents are held hostage by DHBVN staff. There has been no power since 10 pm yesterday. Either the government should settle employees' demands or depute the Disaster Management team to restore the supply. Officers are also showing helplessness. In such a situation, how will we come up with a solution?" said Shiv Kumar Sharma, a resident, according to PTI.
On Wednesday, Chief Minister Nayab Singh Saini said the state government would represent the employees' case before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) to challenge HERC's decision. He also offered to engage lawyers trusted by the workers' unions to pursue the matter.
Saini chaired a review meeting with administrative secretaries to assess preparations and arrangements for the three-day strike.
Several workers' and farmers' organisations have backed the protest. Most constituent organisations of the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, along with the Sarv Karamchari Sangh Haryana and trade unions such as CITU, AITUC and INTUC, expressed solidarity with the striking employees and held demonstrations at various locations.
Subhash Lamba, vice president of the Electricity Employees Federation of India (EEFI), and Shailendra Dubey, chairman of the All India Power Engineers Federation (AIPEF), also opposed the parallel distribution licence and extended their support to the agitation.
