Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.
The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant, because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.
“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.
“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.
Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.
“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”
The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.
“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”
Ahead of the updated versions of PHP becoming available, some organizations took their websites offline as a precautionary measure. Multiple sites belonging to the Finnish government, including the National Land Survey, were inaccessible, according to reports. French government websites and the Port of Rotterdam’s website were also offline, according to Reuters.
“Everybody should patch immediately, exploitation may happen very fast and at a scale,” says Olejnik. “AI makes exploiting such vulnerabilities of immediate importance. Like, indeed, a minute or so.”
Security company Wiz, which is owned by Google, claimed its researchers discovered the vulnerabilities in PHP partially using AI tools, while OpenAI and security firm Calif also say they independently discovered the issues and worked together. Dubbing an exploitation demonstration php2shell , the Wiz researchers write that in some cases the vulnerabilities can be exploited “fairly easily.”
“The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory,” Wiz writes in its research. “That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.”
Details of the upcoming vulnerabilities first appeared from the maintainers behind PHP on October 20. In a short post on the PHP website, the PHP Foundation wrote it was giving “advance notice” of the security flaws and upcoming release of the fixes. While omitting specific details about the vulnerabilities or the versions impacted, it said both flaws are considered to have a “critical” 9.2 score out of 10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” the security warning on the PHP site said ahead of Wednesday’s release. According to reports from Bleeping Computer and Ars Technica, some details about the vulnerabilities may have leaked before they were due to officially be published.
The early warning from the PHP Foundation may have given some developers, security teams, and companies enough of a heads up to start preparing to update systems using PHP. Ahead of the details being published, warnings from the EU’s Computer Emergency Response Team (EU-CERT) and Australia's cybersecurity agency said IT teams should be prepared to update their systems as soon as possible, with the potential for websites to be taken offline while fixes are applied.
Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC), published an alert saying organizations should “prepare for immediate updating of systems” using PHP. “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” the agency wrote online.
The NCSC advises that organizations and businesses should identify systems running PHP across their tech infrastructure. There should be a particular focus on systems using PHP that are connected to the internet, including monitoring them for any potential exploitation. The next step is applying PHP updates as they are available and monitoring for updates from software companies as they may use PHP within their apps or services.
“If you find signs of compromise, isolate the system, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office,” Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber assistant director posted online. “Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

At least 6 killed, 40 injured as passenger bus crashes into tree in Chhattisgarh’s MCB district
Six people were killed and 40 injured after a bus crashed into a roadside tree on the Manendragarh-Kelhari road in Chhattisgarh’s MCB district. CM Vishnu Deo Sai announced compensation.
At least six people were killed and 40 others injured after a passenger bus carrying 46 people crashed into a roadside tree in Chhattisgarh’s Manendragarh-Chirmiri-Bharatpur (MCB) district on Thursday, police said.
The accident took place shortly after noon near the Semarmathani turn on the Manendragarh-Kelhari road when the bus was travelling towards Kelhari, a police officer said, adding that four of the injured were in critical condition.
Superintendent of police (SP) Ratna Singh said passengers told her that the driver lost control of the steering, following which the bus crashed into the roadside tree.
“Six passengers, including four women, died in the accident. Around 20 people, including the driver, suffered serious injuries, while another 20 sustained minor injuries,” Singh said.
Police identified the deceased as Panchram (70), Madhu and Neha, all three residents of Rojhi village; bus owner Sipahi Lal from Kelhari; Sangeeta from Gudru village in Kelhari; and Sukaron (80) from Kelhari.
The injured were taken to hospitals in Manendragarh and Chirmiri. Two seriously injured passengers were referred to Ambikapur for better medical treatment, while two others were shifted to the district hospital in Chirmiri, police officers said.
Chief minister Vishnu Deo Sai expressed grief over the deaths and directed the district administration to ensure proper treatment of the injured. The state government will provide ₹5 lakh each to the families of the deceased and ₹50,000 each to those injured, Sai said.
Police said an FIR will be registered and action will be taken against those found responsible after the investigation.

A new subscription service promises an evolving collection of 'bold and bizarre' indie games
Publisher Pantaloon says the Playbill won't feature games that use generative AI in any way.
Curator-turned-publisher Pantaloon has unleashed a subscription service that fans of indie games might be interested in digging into. The Playbill is a take on Xbox Game Pass, albeit one that focuses on "bold and bizarre" titles.
The initial lineup features third-party games such as Buckshot Roulette, Silt, Ex Sanguis and Cabin Factory. Those sit alongside Pantaloon's own games: Sub-Verge, Occlude, It Takes a War, Boxroom, Rolla and the delightful music creation sim Offbeat.
Much like Game Pass offers first-party Xbox titles (save for new Call of Duty offerings) to subscribers on day one, the Playbill will gain all of Pantaloon's own games as soon as they're released. The service even has its own timed exclusive in the shape of Virtue: Prologue, a visual novella companion piece for Virtue and a Sledgehammer, which is out next week (and a game I'm very much looking forward to.
In addition, the Playbill offers demos, playtests and "abandoned prototypes" for you to check out in a section called the Green Room. At the outset, there are playtests for a few interesting-looking games, namely Isle Goblin, Mr Magpie's Harmless Card Game and Lemonade Apocalypse.
"We want the Playbill to be a celebration of more experimental and eccentric games," Pantaloon founder Jamin Smith said. "The nature of the model reduces that barrier to entry for players to check out genres and experiences that might not be surfaced by Steam's market-shaping algorithms. It's also worth stating that we won't feature or platform any games that use genAI in any form; the Playbill is a celebration of the craft of making games."
Pantaloon moved into publishing after building an audience of more than 50,000 newsletter subscribers, who were able to complete puzzles to receive game keys or pay for codes for its curated titles. The puzzles are free to access on the Playbill, along with the service's community features, Virtue: Prologue and a couple of ARGs. The full lineup of games is available through a Primo subscription, which costs a reasonable $5 per month or $60 per year.
It's worth noting that the service is key-based. Pantaloon will cycle games out of the Playbill when it runs out of keys and it will add new titles on a regular basis. Annual subscribers can snag all 13 games in the initial lineup, as well as each new title that's introduced.
Things are different for monthly subscribers. They'll get a guaranteed game each month, and they won't be able to pick which one. "The monthly titles are part of bespoke partnerships, so the games are defined," Smith told Engadget. "That said, some of our puzzles — like this month's — allow a choice of reward to those that can solve."
If you sign up for a monthly plan, you'll be able to access all of the games after you've been a subscriber for six consecutive months. This is "a mechanism just to prevent somebody getting all 14 titles straight away and then canceling," Smith added.

Construction on Trump’s beloved arch could start in just a few weeks, court documents reveal
The proposed monument is set to be erected in Memorial Circle, located across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial

Construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot victory arch could break ground in just two weeks, shortly after Election Day, according to court documents.
In a court filing Wednesday, the Department of Justice said that the National Capital Planning Commission is scheduled to meet November 5 to consider approving the final plans. The Department of Interior and the National Parks Service could then issue authorization.
“NPS may publish such notice as early as November 5, 2026, and construction could commence as early as November 5, 2026,” the Justice Department said. The court filing comes as a federal judge considers whether to halt construction in response to a lawsuit.
The proposed monument, which echoes the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, France, is set to be erected in Memorial Circle, located across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. Plans indicate it will include gilded statues and an observation deck, with the words “One nation under God” emblazoned across its white stone facade.
Trump said last month that the arch would also double as a “top grade Military Complex,” but plans released last week by the administration do not appear to include a national security purpose.
The president has said the towering monument is meant to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. But when asked by a journalist last year who the arch was for, he replied: “Me — it's going to be beautiful.”
At 250 feet, the arch would eclipse the U.S. Capitol Building, the Lincoln Memorial, the White House and even the Arc de Triomphe. “I'd like it to be the biggest one of all,” Trump told reporters in February. “We're the biggest, most powerful nation.”
It’s unclear how much the project will cost. The White House has said it will likely rely on both private and public funds, according to The New York Times. The National Endowment for the Humanities has set aside $15 million.
The proposed arch has sparked debate since Trump unveiled plans to build it last October. Several lawsuits have been filed to stop the monument from being erected, including one by a group of Vietnam veterans. They argue the arch lacks the required congressional approval and would obstruct views of Arlington National Cemetery, where over 400,000 people are buried.
Democrats have derided the construction effort as a vanity project, and a number of protests have been held in Memorial Circle.
According to an April Ipsos survey, 52 percent of Americans oppose the arch, while 21 percent favor it.
If built, the riverside monument would join a growing list of construction and restoration projects undertaken by Trump in Washington, D.C., including his $400 million White House ballroom and the Trump-Kennedy Center renovations.

No exact casteist slur in FIR? Allahabad HC says case need not be quashed
The Allahabad High Court has ruled that an FIR need not quote a casteist slur verbatim to sustain a case under the SC/ST Act. It said sharing a village can help presume caste awareness and dismissed the accused's appeal against summons.
The Allahabad High Court has ruled that the absence of an exact casteist slur in an FIR does not, by itself, justify quashing a case under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The court also observed that the fact that the accused and the victims belong to the same village can be considered to presume that the accused knew the victims’ caste, subject to Section 8 of the Act and the facts of the case.
Justice Santosh Rai dismissed an appeal filed by Nitesh Bind and others challenging a summons order passed by the Special Judge in Jaunpur on December 3, 2025. The case originated from an FIR registered at Machhlishahr police station in Jaunpur district.
The appellants argued that the FIR did not mention any specific caste-based slur and, therefore, failed to establish the essential ingredients of the offence. They sought the cancellation of the summons order.
Opposing the appeal, the state counsel submitted that the FIR contained specific allegations of causing injuries and using insulting language. Statements recorded during the investigation described the individual roles of the accused, while the injury reports corroborated the allegations. The prosecution also pointed out that the accused and the injured persons belonged to the same village, suggesting that the accused knew their caste.
The court noted that Nitesh Bind, Pintu and Ranjeet had been named in the FIR in connection with allegations of assaulting the victims and using insulting language. Statements recorded during the investigation attributed specific roles to Nitesh Bind and Ranjeet Bind, while the injury reports supported the allegations.
The court further observed that the FIR mentioned the accused as residents of Daudpur village in Machhlishahr, Jaunpur, and that the informant and the injured persons also belonged to the same village.
Considering these circumstances, the court said that the fact that the accused and the victims were residents of the same village could be taken into account under Section 8 of the SC/ST Act while drawing a presumption regarding the accused’s knowledge of the victims’ caste, subject to the applicability of the statutory provision and the facts of the case.
The High Court held that the specific allegations, statements of the injured persons and corroboration through injury reports justified the trial court’s decision to summon the accused. It found no illegality in the order and described it as a reasoned decision.
Dismissing the appeal for lack of merit, the court declined to interfere with the summons order.

Dear For Love & Money,
My husband and I are in our 60s, the baby boomer generation. Due to hard work over the course of our adult lives, we've been able to comfortably retire. Because my husband and I set them up for success, our two kids, now all grown up, are doing quite well. 
We paid for a considerable portion of their college costs, their health insurance, and their car insurance until they moved out. We drove them to all the extracurriculars that helped get them where they are today, and paid for a couple of decades' worth of food, clothing, and shelter. They also got to have amazing life experiences, such as a two-week European vacation when they were teenagers.
Recently, we had them and their spouses over for dinner, and a lighthearted conversation came up about inheritances. Our kids joked about who the favorite child was and who was likely to inherit our wealth. Since they were kidding, my husband and I didn't feel at the time that we needed to set the record straight. 
But now we've been talking and are now wondering if we need to say more — because we actually don't plan on leaving any inheritances for our children. We plan to use our hard-earned savings for our retirement years.
If we live the comfortable, adventurous lives we want to over the next 20 years, we don't expect there will be much left for an inheritance. We even plan to sell the house, which is paid off, to afford our final years when we need assisted living.
I don't feel like we owe our children anything, and they don't seem to need anything. However, I'm starting to wonder if telling them our plans will be a problem. How do I tell my kids there isn't going to be any inheritance after we pass?
Sincerely,
Boomer Who Wants to Spend My Own Money
Dear Boomer,
Maybe I grew up poorer than I realize, but in my experience, few middle-class people plan on receiving a financially meaningful inheritance.
We expect to go through Grandma's basement and figure out what to do with a lifetime's worth of accumulated belongings. We hope our parents have life insurance policies to cover the costs of wrapping up a life and saying goodbye.
But few of us truly envision future will readings where the black sheep laughs cynically about being cut out, the stepson throws a tantrum over not inheriting the Van Gogh collection, and the niece no one's ever met inherits it all.
However, we've all seen that movie. Thus, we joke about our parents' wills, favorite children, and who will inherit Yellowstone Dutton Ranch when they're gone.
You asked me how to tell your kids, "There isn't going to be an inheritance," but I don't think this is an announcement you need to make. For most people who hold no claim to great wealth, even if they are financially comfortable, estate planning is a family affair.
You and your husband will still have the final say over your estate, but medical bills, inflation, health concerns, and all sorts of unknowns can easily complicate money matters. Your anxiety might stem from you second-guessing a dynamic you were comfortable with back when the reality felt far away.
You might not have a fortune to bestow on your children when you pass, but you will still give them an estate to sort out and conclude. They will be the ones to carry out your end-of-life wishes and figure out memory care should the need arise. Your children are the ones who will need to present death certificates to close down your bank accounts and hold an estate sale should you stay in your house to the end, after all.
Considering the enormity of this task, looping your children in now is a good idea. There's no need for this conversation to include a dramatic confession about how little you have to leave them; instead, it invites them into your plans and lets them know what to expect.
It isn't too late to start investing a small amount and designating the returns for your children, of course. But remember that when your kids are playfully squabbling over inheritance, they are likely thinking of the possessions you will be handing down rather than money.
For instance, my dad has a large library of floor-to-ceiling bookshelves packed with hardbacks written by writers like Louis L'Amour, Dean Koontz, and Agatha Christie. Neither my siblings nor I expect to receive even a tiny cash legacy, and we know the books hold little value, but you can bet we always argue — mostly in jest — over who will inherit the collection.
Simply taking the time to thoughtfully divide your prized possessions and sentimental momentos and naming who gets what in your will is likely more of an inheritance than your kids expect, but one they will be very grateful to receive.
In your letter, you listed all the ways you've set your kids up for success, but I didn't need the list to believe you. You have built a legacy where your adult children and their partners can sit around your dinner table joking with you and one another. This is the best legacy — one full of love and laughter. You did it.
Rooting for you,
For Love & Money

South Korea seeks new ways to free a huge gray shark after it slips back into canal
A city in South Korea is again trying to free a huge dusky shark from a narrow canal
SEOUL, South Korea -- A city in South Korea was trying Thursday to come up with a new way to free a huge dusky shark out of a narrow canal. Workers in the port city of Busan had herded the shark, nicknamed Bukangi, out of the canal the day before, after weeks of trial and error — only for it to swim right back in hours later.
Now Busan authorities and the country’s Oceans and Fisheries Ministry are determined to guide Bukangi back to open water, saying it is critical for the shark’s safety and health.
The unconventional rescue effort on Wednesday involved dozens of workers maneuvering a floating platform through the canal to push the 3-meter-long (9.8-foot) female shark out. After lingering in nearby waters for hours, the shark swam beneath an outer barrier net installed on the platform that night and reentered the waterway.
According to officials, Bukangi is now stuck between that net and a second one about 50 meters (55 yards) into the mouth of the canal, with on-site inspectors and rescuers debating ways to guide it back out as the shark circles the small patch of water.
Lee Gwang-seok, an official with the Oceans and Fisheries Ministry, said Bukangi was unlikely to slip past more barriers and move farther up the canal, considering the density of the nets and the narrow waterway in that section that leaves little room for the shark to squeeze through.
There were no signs that the shark had been feeding regularly during its monthlong stay in the canal, and falling water temperatures could pose additional health risks, officials say.
The local Busan authorities did not immediately say when a new rescue effort for Bukangi would proceed.
Sharing the Korean name of Busan’s North Port, where it was first spotted in mid-September, Bukangi had become a major tourist attraction as it slowly circled the canal, its fins slicing through the water’s surface.
Busan officials, who made Bukangi a city mascot, say the shark attracted more than 1.7 million visitors to the canal, and hundreds of people lined up along the canal on Wednesday to watch the unusual rescue effort.
Marine scientists don’t have a clear answer as to why the shark entered the canal, or why it has stayed.
Its behavior may have something to do with Busan being one of Asia’s busiest ports — away from the ruckus, the narrow canal may appear to be a safe space, according to Kim Hyun-woo, a senior researcher at South Korea’s National Institute of Fisheries Science.
The North Port is a major hub for container and cruise traffic, possibly producing an intimidating environment for the shark. It’s also possible that the noise from vessels, bright lights and electric fields generated by nearby facilities and equipment have interfered with the shark’s senses, Kim said. While authorities have stressed the need to get Bukangi out to sea quickly, Kim said patience will be key, giving the shark time to adjust to the waters beyond the canal before venturing farther out.
“The shark has been staying inside the canal for an extended period, so I didn’t expect it to head straight out into the open water,” Kim said. “It would be best to give it about a week to leave on its own.”
Wednesday’s operation was the third attempt to free Bukangi, following failed efforts on Sept. 29 and Oct. 2 that involved boats spraying streams of water and nets placed across the narrow waterway.
Bukangi avoided the boats and swam over the nets. Dusky sharks can grow up to 4.2 meters (13.7 feet) long and live in tropical and temperate waters around the world, roaming long distances to find waters ranging between 18-26 degrees Celsius (64-79 degrees Fahrenheit) while feeding on fish and squid, according to Kim’s institute.
The species reproduces slowly, making it vulnerable to population declines, and is listed as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources.
Water temperatures in the Busan area were around 20 degrees Celsius (68 degrees Fahrenheit) on Thursday morning, according to official data.

Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest hits Italy’s buffalo mozzarella output
Truckers are blocking deliveries over the high cost of diesel amid the ongoing Iran war
A truckers’ protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of €3 million (US$3.37 million) in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said.
The week-long strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left fuel pumps empty in much of southern Italy.
The government approved new tax breaks for truckers on Thursday, but it was too early to tell whether they were enough to end the protest.
The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain.

In Summary
- Apple’s Welcome Home event was recently held, showcasing the launch of new products.
- The event saw Apple announce its first dedicated smart home hub device, the HomeView, and also marked the return of the HomePod mini, as well as the launch of a new Apple TV.
- We take a look at eight notable takeaways from this Apple event, which was different from the brand’s other launches.
Apple’s Welcome Home event on 13 October was anything but business as usual. The brand, known for its high-profile launches and minimalistic products, turned things around with a relatively minimalistic launch and a high-profile new product, the HomeView. The event marked Apple’s entry into a new product zone and also saw the return of an old favorite. Here are eight notable points from the event that saw Apple literally come home:
Table of Contents
What! No “real”, detailed event for a new product line?
We cannot remember the last time Apple introduced a whole new product line without a proper event – we did not even get the sort of video introduction that established Apple product lines get, let alone entirely new ones. The Welcome Home event saw Apple get into the smart home hub segment, and do so without an elaborate presentation explaining why it was doing so, what the segment needed, or even what was magical about the HomeView. We instead had a relatively quick video introducing us to not just the HomeView, but also the new HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4K.
HomeView got the views, but Home Collection might be the real star 
 As many had predicted, Apple is now looking at smart home gadgets as the next tech frontier to conquer. And although the tablet-like HomeView got most of the attention, the brand also announced the  Apple Home Collection, which was described as  “a  new lineup of smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.” This is literally an ecosystem for homes. According to Apple, what makes the devices in this collection special is that they all work through the Apple Home app and require no separate app of their own. As more devices get into the collection (and perhaps more brands too), the Home Collection could end up being the real star of Apple’s home campaign.   Interestingly, Apple’s Home initiative works better with the iPhone, iPad, and iPod touch (if you still have one), but is relatively limited on the MacBook Air and MacBook Pros. As per Apple Support, one needs an iPhone or iPad to add accessories to Home – a Mac cannot do so. Of course, this could change in the coming days, but as of now, it seems that mobile devices are more likely to drive Apple’s Home initiative than them good old Macs! Apple has been (in)famous for not giving too much publicity to products made by other brands (unless they were special editions of its own products) in its product launches, but Welcome Home saw it give due space to devices from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, which are part of the Apple Home Collection. The last time we saw Apple so comfortable with tie-ups was when it worked with Motorola for the original ROKR E1 (one of the first mobile phones that Apple actually worked on, and which was actually introduced by Steve Jobs in 2005). While that tie-up did not work out too well, it did lay the groundwork for the iPhone. How the current tie-ups work out could well decide Apple’s future in the smart home zone. We refuse to rule out an iPhone like iHome, which lets you control everything mechanical in your house, aided by AI. The original HomePod Mini was launched in 2020, almost two years after the launch of the HomePod. And many observers believed that the Mini’s success kept the HomePod and Apple’s smart speaker ambitions alive. However, after that first appearance, the Mini largely slipped out of public view and did not get a successor. Until the Welcome Home event, which finally saw the Home Pod Mini 2nd edition, almost six years after the first HomePod mini. That has got to be one of the longest sabbaticals for an Apple product in recent times. Is Apple going to be more regular with new HomePods, now that it is looking to make its presence felt more at home? We are keeping an eye.  While the HomeView was showcased as the Apple Hub, the new Apple TV 4K is actually capable of fulfilling that role too. In its release, Apple states, “As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarised notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes.” Yes, its primary strength is entertainment, but under that surface, the new Apple TV 4K is a slightly less flashy and more affordable home hub. Some observers feel that it is only a matter of time before Apple TV blends into the HomeView, but others feel that Apple will develop it as a sort of screenless home hub. We are genuinely puzzled by this. While the HomeView seems to be a tech wonder that can manage other devices in your home and handle FaceTime calls and a whole lot else, it actually has no access to the App Store or its own App Store, as some other Apple devices have. Interestingly, the Apple TV 4K has its tvOS App Store, which makes it a little more versatile.  A common thread that ran through all the products launched at Welcome Home was the prominence given to Apple Intelligence. Indeed, “an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad” is essential to drive the HomeView, Apple TV comes with “An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence,” and “Siri AI transforms the HomePod mini experience.” Apple is clearly throwing the kitchen sink at AI this time. Will Apple Intelligence rock on the Apple Home front? Time will tell.  Apple Home was supposed to be his brainchild, but where was Apple CEO John Ternus? Apple’s new CEO did not feature in the videos introducing the new products, or even in the press releases pertaining to the event. This is clearly a CEO who prefers to let his products do the talking.
Apple at Home: more about phones and tablets, less about notebooks?
Tie-ups are cool again
Welcome back Home, HomePod Mini! 
Apple TV is actually a “home hub” too
Apple TV has an App Store, but HomeView does not 
Apple Intelligence rules at this Home! 
And one more thing…

Quick Answer
The Fitbit Edge is a $179.99 fitness tracker with a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, built-in GPS, ECG, replaceable battery, and up to seven days of battery life. It also offers Google Maps navigation, Gemini-powered coaching, advanced health tracking, and a special Stephen Curry edition.
The fitness world may be in a “to screen or not to screen” state, with fitness bands without screens gaining popularity, but Google is clearly keeping its Fitbit feet in both screen and screenless fitness trackers. Days after launching its Fitbit Air screenless tracker in India, the Search giant has launched the Fitbit Edge, a fitness tracker with a display that sits right in the middle of the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, both in terms of pricing (it starts at USD 179.99, well above the USD 99.99 of the Fitbit Air but well below the USD 399.99 of the Pixel Watch 5) and display size. Only time will tell whether it will hit the golden middle ground between “lots of display” and “no display at all,” but while we wait for the Fitbit Edge to hit stores later this month (and indeed, hopefully arrive in India soon), here are twelve points worth noting about the latest Fitbit in fitness town:
Table of Contents
A big display in an increasingly no-display zone
In a fitness band world that seems to be aiming to become more and more screen-less, the Fitbit Edge comes with a big-gish display for a fitness tracker. It has a 1.34-inch AMOLED, always-on display, which is 46 percent bigger than the one on the Charge 6, its predecessor. It is also much brighter and has Gorilla Glass 3 protection. Fitbit actually claims it is the brightest and biggest display on a Fitbit fitness tracker. Should the Fitbit Air be jealous?
Wear it without Wear OS: Fitbit OS onboard
It comes from Google and also has a display on board like the Pixel Watch 5, which has led many to assume that the Fitbit Edge must be running on Wear OS, but that is not the case. The Fitbit Edge actually runs on Fitbit OS. And like all Google fitness devices, it also uses the Google Health app to keep track of your data and give you fitness inputs. While this means you get relatively less distraction and only basic notifications, it also means you do not get access to third-party apps on the device.
Bye bye Haptic, Hello real button!
One of the biggest headaches of the Fitbit Charge 6 was its pressure-sensitive, haptic touch button, which many of us struggled to use (it almost had a vibe of its own). Thankfully, the Fitbit Edge fixes that and brings a physical button on the side for controls. We couldn’t be more glad. The haptic control on the Charge 6 was a bit of a pain and messed up what was (and still is) a superb fitness tracker.
A battery that can be removed and replaced
Most modern devices have given up on the concept of a removable battery, which was sad because once the battery of a device died, it tended to render an otherwise perfectly good device useless, unless one went in for complex engineering. That, however, has been changing thanks to regulations from the EU, and the Fitbit Edge comes with a removable battery. Which means you can simply remove the battery and replace it if its health deteriorates, increasing the life of the fitness tracker.
Very Air-y battery life
In terms of battery life, the Fitbit Edge rather surprisingly has the same battery life as the display-less Fitbit Air – about a week. However, keeping the always-on-display feature on reduces this to a rather low two days.
Metal frames that can take an ECG…and save your life (in select countries)
The Fitbit Edge’s metal frame can be used to take a 30-second manual ECG. This can highlight heart rate irregularities and can also spot signs of AFib. The tracker also has an optical PPG heart rate sensor that continuously tracks one’s heart and pulse rate and alerts the user if their heart rate is unusually high or low. The catch is that the ECG is only available in select countries, but it is still great to see an ECG on a fitness tracker – a feature seen generally in premium smartwatches.
Take it swimming
Much like its screen-less sibling, the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge too is pretty sturdy. The device comes with 5 ATM water resistance, which means you can easily take it along for your swim sessions. The device also features IP68 dust and water resistance, and as we mentioned earlier, Gorilla Glass 3 protection.
Comes with GPS and is stair-worthy
The Fitbit Edge has an improved and built-in GPS, something the Air lacks, so you do not need to carry your phone along to cover outdoor workouts and activities. It has multi-constellation support, which is paired with a new antenna and chip, making the device up to 40 percent better at tracking locations than the Charge 6. The Edge has another edge over the Air – an integrated altimeter, which can detect changes in altitude, and comes in handy not only while counting stairs but also during hikes and trekking, where you can accurately measure altitude change.
Get Google Maps directions on your wrist:
The Fitbit Edge might not have Google Wear, but it works in sync with Google Maps on your phone and can show you turn-by-turn directions on your wrist. The feature requires you to have an active Bluetooth connection between your phone and the Fitbit Edge, and directions will start popping up on your tracker screen when you start walking, running, cycling, or even driving. That big display really helps!
Quick Notifications, quicker actions but no call support:
The Edge has a mixed relationship with your smartphone. It is a few steps ahead of the Air in terms of notifications, or some might say behind it in terms of a distraction-free experience. You get basic call, message, and app notifications on the tracker, and also get quick reply and navigation access on it. However, you cannot use it to handle calls because the device does not have a mic or a speaker. You can accept a call from the tracker, but it will be directed to your smartphone.
Google Health Guardian’s on your wrist
Earlier limited to the more expensive Pixel Watches, Google’s Health Guardian is available on the Fitbit Edge. This comes with cardiovascular tracking and alerts, alerts for potential breathing and pulse issues, and tracking of trends in the background to create monthly reports on blood pressure and even insulin resistance. It also unlocks premium features of the Google Health app, like personalized coaching and deeper tracking and analysis.
Gemini present, but cannot be summoned:
The Fitbit Edge comes with personalized Gemini coaching to help you meet your health and fitness goals. But complete access to all of Gemini’s features requires a subscription, and you cannot summon the AI assistant on your tracker – you have to use your phone for it.
And one more thing: There is a Stephen Curry edition:
The Google Fitbit Edge comes with a special edition, designed in collaboration with 4-time NBA champion Stephen Curry. It pairs the regular tracker with a Satin Pyrite aluminum case and also features a custom moisture-wicking, water-repellent, recycled polyester yarn band. Also on board are special basketball watchfaces. Mind you, all that extra goodness will set you back by an additional USD 40 – the Stephen Curry edition starts at USD 219.99.

Will Lindblad and Lawson be retained by Racing Bulls? F1 Q&A
- Published
Kimi Antonelli has his first opportunity to secure the 2026 drivers' championship at this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin.
Antonelli must win the race with Mercedes team-mate George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower.
Austin is the first of six races scheduled to take place between now and the end of the season in December.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the race in Texas.
Will Liam Lawson get the Racing Bulls seat for next year? - Chris
Racing Bulls are one of only two teams where the 2027 driver line-up is not finalised. The other is Haas, where Oliver Bearman has not yet been confirmed alongside new signing Rafael Camara, although that is only a matter of time.
At Racing Bulls, it's a three-don't-fit-into-two situation, with current race drivers Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad in the frame along with Red Bull junior driver Nikola Tsolov, the Bulgarian who is second in the Formula 2 championship at the moment.
This is the first time in Red Bull history that Helmut Marko is not in charge of driver choice at the junior team and it's unclear what approach they will take under the new management.
In the past, one might have expected them to drop Lawson, on the basis that he has had his chance and is not likely to be considered a long-term candidate for a full-time seat at Red Bull, and put Tsolov in alongside Lindblad.
But there is an argument that the Red Bull young driver programme has been mismanaged for 20 years by Marko and former team boss Christian Horner and they should take a more considered, patient, methodological approach.
In the past, Marko and Horner took a very ruthless approach. A driver would get a shot, and if they did not deliver pretty much immediately, they were dropped.
On one level, it made sense - they were looking for world-class drivers who could lead Red Bull. And if a driver was not that level, they felt they had no use for them.
But at the same time, it sometimes meant putting two unknown quantities together, which made it harder to judge the quality of either.
An alternative approach might be to keep a known-quality benchmark on board against which it is easier to judge the ability of a newcomer.
On that basis, it would make sense to keep Lawson and Lindblad together for 2027 and make Tsolov the reserve, put him in the simulator and give him some tests in older cars to provide him with F1 experience.
The reasoning is that while Lindblad's debut season has been impressive in patches, Lawson is consistently quicker at the moment, both in qualifying and in races.
So if Lindblad is to be considered a future candidate for Red Bull, this argument would go, he should be given an extra season to prove whether he can consistently beat Lawson. Because if he can't, the obvious conclusion is that he is not a candidate for the senior team.
If they put Tsolov in with Lindblad, they have two unknown quantities, which helps no-one in the bigger picture.
A decision has not yet been taken, and ultimately it rests with the shareholders, Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, with under them Red Bull CEO Oliver Mintzlaff, who is in overall charge of the F1 programme.
Why is F1 going to another country, Rwanda, with what can only be described as very poor human rights? Is this another case of if you have the cash we'll come to your country irrespective of significant international concern regarding the suppression of political dissent, press freedom and the country's military involvement in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo? - Paul
Formula 1's owner Liberty Media has been looking to establish a race in Africa since it took over the sport in 2017.
It was the one glaring omission from the calendar, and the race in Rwanda will give F1 a presence on every single inhabited continent, as well as access to a largely untapped market.
But finding a country that is suitable to be a host has not been easy.
Various possibilities were investigated. There was a project in Morocco near Tangier, but that didn't have the necessary finance.
At one point, F1 looked quite close to a deal to return to Kyalami in South Africa for the first time since 1993, but there were issues with the promoter.
There are currently as many as four separate projects in South Africa, including Kyalami and two in Cape Town. But they are all too far away from being realistic possibilities.
Many - if not most - grands prix are funded by governments in one way or another, so it's hardly a surprise that the one African bid to come to fruition has government backing.
It's a sensitive situation because Rwanda receives international aid, and the government and F1 have been keen to emphasise that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Then there are the accusations of 'sportswashing' - a term given to the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
DRC's Minister of Foreign Affairs Therese Kayikwamba Wagner issued a statement last week to say that while DR Congo supported the idea of a grand prix in Africa, they were opposed to Rwanda being its host.
She accused Rwanda President Paul Kagame of "fuelling a devastating war in our country", adding that wars in the DRC have claimed millions of lives, that people continue to be driven from their homes and Congolese natural resources exploited and appropriated.
The statement also pointed out that the US has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's military and senior officials because of their involvement in supporting the M23 rebel group in the DRC, undermining a peace agreement.
Kayikwamba Wagner added: "This is also an opportunity for F1 to show its audiences and supporters what the sport truly stands for. It should require credible, independent guarantees that no money used to host the race comes from conflict-linked minerals or the exploitation of Congolese resources."
An F1 spokesperson said: "We have a long track record of delivering significant economic, social and cultural value to our host nations.
"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good.
"When racing around the world we ensure the exceptional standards, values and integrity of the sport are shared and delivered by both promoters and partners.
"As we've seen, sport can be a huge driver of change and unifying force and look forward to the positive impact that the African Grand Prix will have."
If Imola is the back-up track for the last race and is being prepared for that, who's paying for the work? Surely not the track? - Joe
Imola is being readied as a potential host for the final grand prix of the season on 4-6 December if the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi cannot be held.
At the moment, F1 is pressing ahead with the Middle Eastern races, having been given what it considers suitable security guarantees and reassurances.
F1 is being advised that there have been no attacks on civilian infrastructure in Qatar or the United Arab Emirates since May.
But the sport is aware that the situation in the Middle East is unpredictable and volatile, and is bracing itself for a potential escalation after the US mid-term elections, which will be held on 3 November.
In addition to the war between the US/Israel and Iran, Saudi Arabia is currently engaged in a conflict with the Houti rebels in Yemen.
It remains the case, though, that if the Houtis can hit the Saudi Arabia capital Riyadh with a missile strike, or facilities belonging to oil company Aramco - an F1 sponsor - in Dhahran, or the country's east-west oil pipeline, then their missiles could also reach the locations of the two final grands prix of the season.
F1 is aware of the possibility that US President Donald Trump could take actions that intensify the conflict in the region after the mid-terms, and that's why Imola is being readied as a back-up.
F1 has an agreement with Imola that it will cover any costs it has incurred in setting up for the grand prix if it does not happen.

If, as seems likely, the Red Bull/Ford engine turns out to be as good as, if not better, than the Mercedes one, will customer teams want to buy it, and would Red Bull consider supplying it to them? - Mike
The F1 engine regulations contain clauses that require manufacturers to supply engines to customers if so requested, but not in their first season.
At the moment, there are two manufacturers which supply only one team - Honda (Aston Martin) and Audi - and Red Bull who supply two, both in-house.
Mercedes supply four (McLaren, Alpine and Williams, in addition to the works team), and Ferrari three (Haas and Cadillac as well as the factory outfit).
The rules state that the obligation to supply a team without an engine falls initially on the engine manufacturer with the least customers, although these things are all subject to negotiation.
At the moment, there is no team looking for an engine.
However, it is well known in F1 that Aston Martin owner Lawrence Stroll earlier this year explored the possibility of ditching Honda before deciding to stick with them following their difficult start to the season.
And while this is now hedging into the area of speculation, it's not hard to imagine Stroll coming back to that idea if Honda doesn’t make a major step forward in performance and competitiveness over the winter.
In that scenario, then, yes, it's likely that Red Bull and Mercedes would be the manufacturers he approached. And with Mercedes being full - and wanting to cut their supplies to two customers rather than three for the next engine regulations - Red Bull would definitely be an option.

In my career, one of the things I have found that has evolved tremendously, is the approach to the care of prostate cancer. The disease used to be simply diagnosed and treated. However, now there is much more attention to its aggressiveness, chances of recurrence, and most importantly, ways of controlling the disease without negatively impacting the quality of a person’s life.
This progress is especially important in the case of intermediate and high-risk localised prostate cancer, when surgery and radiation therapy have proven to be effective treatments. Hormone therapy is used in certain patients depending on their risk factors. Nevertheless, recurrence is still an issue in some cases, after treatment aimed at curing the disease.
This is why the rising interest in immunotherapy for prostate cancer attracts my attention. A recent Phase 3, double-blind clinical trial, published in The Lancet, has added to this conversation by examining whether an immune-based approach can enhance the effects of established treatment, radiotherapy, in men with localised, high-risk prostate cancer.
Harnessing the immune system
Treatment through immunotherapy has changed the scenario in a variety of cancers, and yet, it has proven to be difficult when it comes to treating prostate cancer. Traditional immune-checkpoint inhibitors, for example, cannot be used to treat localised prostate cancer.
The therapy being used in this latest Phase 3 clinical trial, however, differs from traditional therapies. Aglatimagene besadenovec is an innovative viral immunotherapy that works by delivering the therapy directly to the site of the tumour. It works by killing tumour cells and stimulating the body’s immune response against the cancerous cells.
From a clinician’s point of view, this is an intriguing direction since it goes beyond treatment of the tumor via just one pathway. Radiation can be used to control the local growth of the tumour, hormones can address the dependence of the disease on androgens, while the immune system can add yet another layer to the treatment.
A crucial point to remember here, though, is that this is what the immune system can potentially do -- it is not yet a guaranteed outcome. Oncology is a field where an interesting mechanism is just the starting point; one has to wait for more research and trials to help establish the outcome, which is what really counts.
Promising findings
Benefit in terms of disease-free survival was achieved by means of the combination strategy. Another exploratory analysis showed that 80% of patients treated with the experimental therapy were negative for tumour cells in their prostate biopsies after two years, while only 63% of the control group achieved this outcome.
While these results appear promising, it is important to note that they should not be overstated. Specifically, the prostate biopsy was an exploratory analysis for an evaluable subgroup of patients and did not represent the primary endpoint of the trial. Likewise, other outcomes mentioned in the results of the study will need further follow-up and evaluation.
This is crucial for the patient. An encouraging outcome does not guarantee that a new treatment will replace an already existing one.
Bringing immunotherapy in early
Immunotherapy for cancer is mainly used in the case of advanced and metastatic cancer. What I liked about this study is that one can see how immune therapy works at the early stages of cancer when it is localised and treatment aims at curing.
The issue with treating cancer is that despite the absence of any visible tumours in scans, there may still be a trace of the disease left. Could activation of the immune system early help eliminate those cells? This would seem like a good direction for future research.
What patients should know
For now, I think of these results as positive signs rather than a revolution in the established management of prostate cancer.
Individualised decision-making should remain a key component of treatment with attention paid to factors as PSA values, Gleason score, imaging studies, risk group, age, general condition of the patient and his personal preferences. Surgery, radiotherapy and hormonal therapy are essential, and an individual treatment modality varies from case to case.
It’s important to understand that there is continuous progress being made in prostate cancer treatment. Doctors and scientists are beginning to think about how we can combine different treatment methods rather than using only one.
If we will learn in future how to predict who can benefit from immunotherapy, how stable this effect is and if it leads to improved prognosis in the end, then such treatment might become a crucial step in localised prostate cancer treatment.
That is where, for me, the true promise exists, not in replacing something that works but in figuring out how to make it work even better for the patient.
(Dr. Ashwin Giridhar is senior consultant & lead - urology & uro-oncology, HCG Cancer Hospitals, Hebbal, Bengaluru. drashwingiridhar@gmail.com)

El Salvador deploys special forces to Haiti to help find 4 missing soldiers who came under attack
Two officials have told The Associated Press that El Salvador has deployed 100 special forces soldiers to Haiti to help recover four missing soldiers from the Central American country who recently came under attack by gangs
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador deployed 100 special forces soldiers to Haiti on Thursday to help rescue four missing soldiers from the Central American country who recently came under attack by gangs, two officials told The Associated Press.
The special forces arrived a day after Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele announced a military operation to rescue the four aviation technicians and threatened a more forceful response if they’re not released alive and unharmed.
An official with El Salvador’s government not authorized to speak on the matter said an additional 100 soldiers were going to be deployed to Haiti on Thursday night. The official said Salvadorean authorities were operating under the assumption that the four missing Salvadoreans are still alive.
Haiti’s government said Wednesday evening that the four missing soldiers were abducted, marking its first comments since the attack that occurred Sunday in Croix-des-Bouquets. Authorities have said the soldiers were traveling in an armored vehicle that came under fire from gangs that also used explosives.
It’s the first major attack since the international gang suppression force began operations, replacing a Kenyan-led force that struggled to help Haitian police quell gang violence given a lack of resources and funds.
Haitian police and the gang suppression force have been fighting armed men in the area ever since the attack occurred, and authorities have warned residents to remain indoors.
The Miami Herald first reported the deployment.
El Salvador’s presidential office did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment.
The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitel'homme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the U.N. and the U.S.
No one has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack.

It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of the EV tax credit. It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world’s embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time.
At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year.
Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you.
That sounds rather dystopian. But Anderson told Ars in an interview that once you realize what your vehicle is capable of doing (beyond the paradigm of being a car to go places), it opens up a world of convenience that might be hard to envision right now. He’s not talking about an Optimus-style robot that’ll do your laundry, but a tool that you use every day that expands to do more things.
OnStar is your new PA
GM’s newly announced OnStar AI will play a role. “Imagine you worked late, and you get in your car to go home,” he told us. “Your car might remember that you ordered takeout from a restaurant recently that you frequent and like. The car could prompt you and place a pick-up order for you, which will be ready when you arrive to pick it up.”
Trust is the key here, and Anderson reiterated that several times, suggesting that a car might be a more trusted piece of technology than a mobile phone. “People have a relationship with their cars that they don’t have with other things,” he said. “If your phone randomly suggested your favorite restaurant, it might give you pause, but if your car did so within the appropriate context you might be more willing to accept that.”
OnStar AI will do more than just learn your habits; it will be able to help you better understand and better use your vehicle, we’re told. For example: a driver hears the car beep but doesn’t know what the alert was for. In this case, they could ask OnStar and it would be able to tell them—for example, a speed limit warning. Being a specialized AI trained specifically on the details of the car, it can be integrated in a way that other models, like Google’s Gemini, cannot.

GM
Thanks to new compute on board, announced at last year’s Forward, the car will be able to handle much of that processing locally without requiring a connection to the cloud at all. But a cloud connection could improve the drive or make it safer. For some time now, automakers and suppliers have promised systems that crowdsource data to infer and predict road conditions—if you’re driving through a snowy area, and the cars in front of you have had traction control events, you could receive a warning to be extra careful as you approach.
GM also wants to keep customers within its own ecosystem. Imagine a two-car, two-GM OnStar AI household, and you’re late picking up your child from practice. Here, OnStar AI could look and see your spouse is actually closer, swap roles, and re-direct you to the takeout place to pick up dinner. OK, it’s a very specific use case.
Can you trust it?
Trust continues to be the key. Anderson knows that must be earned, and trust is difficult to get back if it’s broken.
His approach is to put that customer trust first in what he does. For example, GM’s new infotainment system will have the ability to record from the cameras as a dash cam and store that video. And it can upload that video to GM’s cloud to access anywhere. But it is end-to-end encrypted, meaning that when it hits GM’s servers it’s in a format that GM can’t read. If law enforcement wanted to view the video, GM wouldn’t be able to help because it could not decrypt the video.
That is the type of trust that is absolutely needed when dealing with this type of personal data, because there is a convenience to a lot of this. But the opportunity for that data to be misused is also there—it wasn’t too long ago that GM was found to be selling customers’ data, often without their knowledge, to insurance companies.
We’ll want to experience GM’s new attitude in practice, of course, but hearing an automotive executive directly address that concern head-on was refreshing.
Car, take the wheel

This all leads into the fully autonomous functionality that GM is working on. Ars also spoke with Rashed Haq, VP of Autonomous Vehicles at GM, about the current state of the level 4 technology, and more importantly, when it’ll be safe enough for customers to use.
“We look at two key factors, safety and roadcraft,” Haq told me.
Safety obviously includes the vehicle’s occupants, but also the general public. And that requires millions of miles of testing in the real world but also digitally. Automakers like GM will never be able to prepare for every scenario, but it will combine training data with an open vocabulary to assess what information is there and make a driving decision based on that. Haq also reiterated the company’s expectation that when the car is driven by the computer, the responsibility falls on GM and the computer if something goes wrong due to a malfunction.
The second key here is roadcraft. That means making sure that the vehicle isn’t creating a hazard or problem for other vehicles on the road. You’ve likely seen videos where Waymo vehicles are all crowded on a street blocking traffic: That’s not something GM wants its cars to do.
Eventually, all of this leads back to the idea of a car working for you for tasks that aren’t just driving places. Your car could go pick up your dry cleaning, or at least drive there and wait while someone comes out and deposits the clothes inside it. You could ride to school with a child, both sitting in the back seat, reclaiming some time together because the car is doing the mundane task of driving.
It’s an interesting idea and will only happen if consumers trust GM and their vehicle enough to do that, something we won’t know until closer to that technology maturing.

GM also announced its Gen-4 EV architecture based on LMR battery technology. As we learned last year, the new lithium manganese-rich battery chemistry promises energy densities close to nickel-manganese-cobalt but without that expensive cobalt, making their cost closer to that of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry cells.
A 30 percent cheaper battery should help GM offer a wide variety of EVs, hopefully including some affordable models, like the now-limited-run Bolt.
If GM can also deliver affordable autonomy, built on a foundation of trust and safety, it’ll be a unique offering from a US automaker and will put the company in a better position to take on the challenges from global competition.

The Logitech MX Keypad makes managing AI tools, apps, and everyday tasks easier with nine customizable LCD keys, app-specific shortcuts, and one-click automations. It’s compact, reliable, and highly flexible, but at $99.99 (INR 15,999), it’s best suited for those who regularly use AI tools and shortcuts.
AI has fundamentally changed how I interact with devices. Ever since I started using an AI dictation app and a few other AI tools to get things done, I barely type anymore. Instead, I press a button on my Mac or on Android, say what I want, let AI transcribe it into text for me, and press enter. AI agents that have full access to my computer do everything.
On smartphones, you can easily ditch the keyboard if you want to and replace it with a single mic icon, like most AI dictation apps do today. But on devices like a Mac with a physical keyboard, that is not possible. Even so, I found myself using mostly one key more than any other: the Fn button, a shortcut I use to type with voice typing and to instruct AI applications and agents on my Mac what they need to do.
All this time, I have really wished I could replace my entire Mac keyboard with just a handful of buttons that do one specific job. That’s pretty much the idea behind the Logitech MX Keypad. However, it doesn’t replace your keyboard; it sits next to it and lets you perform actions with a single click. It comes with nine customizable LCD keys. You can assign shortcuts, launch apps, and trigger specific actions with a single press, making it easy to perform the most-used actions with just a single click.
The best part about the Logitech MX Keypad is not the buttons but the idea behind this approach, and how well they executed it.
I have been using the Logitech MX Keypad for more than a week now, and I honestly love this approach and the thought process behind it. In this review, I will share my full experience with the device and how useful it is for me as a vibe coder and someone who hates remembering shortcuts.
