Logitech MX Keypad Review: The Missing Controller for AI-First Workflows
The idea of getting things done with fewer interactions is not new; we have had this for years, and we refer to it as shortcuts. And this isn’t the first time someone has created a separate device for it. In 2017, Elgato released the Stream Deck, a similar 15-key LCD controller for streamers that allowed users to switch between scenes, launch applications, and automate actions with a single button press.
And Logitech, the company behind this product, also isn’t new to this idea as well. Back in 2024, when AI was just a buzzword, the company announced the MX Creative Console, which has similar ideas of controlling apps and easy-to-access shortcuts with just a button. Fast forward to 2026, when AI usage has grown, the company recently introduced the Logitech MX Keypad, the same idea, but now as a keypad designed to sit next to your keyboard.
Logitech MX Keypad Design and Appearance: Compact and Well Built
The Logitech MX Keypad has a two-piece design. One is the keypad itself, and the other is a detachable stand; you can prop it up using the stand, or you can place the keypad itself directly on the surface, where its slightly slanted design makes it easy to access. It also comes with a slanted surface that makes it easy to interact with. It also comes in two colors; I received the Graphite color. There is also a Pale Grey variant that looks best if you have a premium desktop setup.
The base has a rubber finish so it won’t slip off smooth tables and stays firmly in one place, and the keypad itself is slim and lightweight and connects to Mac or Windows via a USB-C cable. The same cable powers the device, so you don’t need a separate power source, though I wish it had wireless connectivity and a built-in battery. But since it uses only one USB cable, you can tuck it to the back and keep the setup clean. Both are solidly built.
The Keypad comes with nine customizable keys with their own individual LCD displays, along with two left and right navigation controls in the button array, aligned to the left, and with a Logi logo to the right. On the back, the USB-C cable connects to the device and is also removable. The buttons have a glossy, smooth finish; they aren’t tactile, but I like the soft, jelly-like click when pressed.
The LCD button displays are sharp; the icons and the action text are sharp and easy to read, even in brightly lit desktop setups. They are also full-color displays, so you can choose different themes based on your needs and preferences. And at just 91.7 × 77.9 × 25.5 mm, it also doesn’t take up much space on your desk.
Logitech MX Keypad Specs and Features: Nine Keys That Do a Lot More
The Logitech MX Keypad has nine physical LCD buttons, where each button can be assigned a different action or shortcut. But you are not limited to just nine shortcuts. You can set up 15 individual pages for each app, which allows you to set up 135 shortcuts for each app and switch between them using the switch arrows below.
For most users, this setup should be enough to perform frequently used shortcuts and actions, and the Logi Options+ app also lets you create and assign multiple shortcuts for each app, so you have set up multiple shortcuts and switch between them daily.
In my testing, I didn’t notice any latency between pressing the button and seeing the action happen on your Mac. Since it’s designed for developers, it also shows live actions, including the running status of your AI model.
For instance, when using Claude, the Keypad shows the live running status of the AI model. You can also stop the task directly from the keyboard with a single press; you can also create a new chat; approve Claude to perform actions with a single click, which is the most common in AI agents where you need to manually click Allow every time the model needs your permission to perform a task if you set it to manual approval.
If you don’t want to use these controls, you can customize the buttons and assign completely different tasks that suit your workflow. In addition, the Logi Options+ app supports various system shortcuts, including clipboard shortcuts such as pasting copied text, clearing the clipboard, formatting text, and other useful actions like making text title case, and more. You can also control volume, use automation to run multiple actions with a single click, and more. Even without AI tools, you can set up automations for everyday tasks.
Logitech MX Keypad Everyday Use: The Little Things Make It Work
Devices like the Logitech MX Keypad should make your work easier rather than adding extra burden. If the team behind this hasn’t thought about these tiny interactions, using the device becomes a burden for the user.
First, it automatically switches profiles based on which app you are using. Even if you set multiple custom profiles, the app instantly switches to the app you are using without having to manually switch between different sets of shortcuts.
In my testing, it works, and the keypad instantly switches to the shortcuts I set for each app, even for the app I custom-built. It also works with other apps and software, including the latest AI applications like VS Code, Claude Code, your browser like Chrome, or the usual shortcuts you can use on the Mac’s home screen.
Another thing that I initially thought would be extra work is manually turning off the device if I shut down my Mac. Thankfully, Logitech has thought of that too: the Keypad automatically powers off when you shut down your computer and turns back on automatically when you start. Although they may seem like tiny details, these thoughtful interactions make the Logitech MX Keypad easy to use instead of adding to your workload.
Logitech MX Keypad Interface and App: Reliable and Easy to Customize
The app also offers plenty of customization options, which I cover in detail in this section, but one handy feature is the ability to adjust key brightness, which can come in handy if you are working in dark environments.
Although many people say Logitech device companion apps are buggy and unreliable, that hasn’t been my experience with the Logi Options+ app I installed on my Mac. The app worked for me without any issues throughout my testing and was surprisingly reliable.
It also has one of the cleanest UI experiences for an accessories provider. The app lets you completely customize your Logitech MX Keypad. By default, you have a general profile that appears when you turn on your Mac and are on the home screen. You can also create multiple general profiles and switch between them too.
You can also create and customize profiles for each individual app. Logitech already offers popular shortcuts for some popular and most-used apps like Google Chrome, Slack, and more. So you don’t need to set everything from scratch. If you cannot find the action you are looking for, you can create your own shortcut and add it to an app profile.
There is also a dedicated Logitech Marketplace that lets you access various shortcuts created for apps by the community. AI apps like Claude and ChatGPT aren’t available by default, but they are available in the Logi Marketplace. Even if an app isn’t available in the marketplace, you can build your own plugins and custom profiles using the Logi Actions SDK. Logitech also partnered with GitHub to offer 3 months of a GitHub Copilot Pro+ subscription for free and include all shortcuts for the VS Code app.
And since you have everything under your control, you can create custom profiles for the personal applications you have created on your device.
This level of flexibility makes the device stand out, even for power users who want to perform everyday tasks with just a button instead of constantly switching between apps, navigating menus, and repeating the same steps.
Logitech MX Keypad Compatibility: Mac and Windows Only, with Some Setup Required
And for those wondering whether it works with Android, iPhone, or even iPads, no, it doesn’t. To use it, you need the Logi Options+ app installed on the device, which is currently limited to Windows and Mac. You also need to download an additional file, such as a .crx extension, to work in Chrome and go through multiple steps to set it up for the first time. Once setup is done, it works flawlessly. But if you are a developer, you can also technically build a workaround to control an Android app or other devices.
Logitech MX Keypad Review Verdict: Worth It if It Fits Your Workflow
Overall, the Logitech MX Keypad is a well-crafted device that makes a lot of sense for people who spend much of their day with AI tools, whether they are developers, students, or creative professionals.
It is not just about triggering shortcuts with a single press but also about tiny details that make it easy to use. Also, at $99.99, it can be a neat and useful addition to your desktop that is genuinely useful. Remember that it will take a bit of time to get used to its input style, and sometimes you will even forget it’s there if you don’t make it part of your workflow. At $99.99 (INR 15,999), it’s a worthwhile addition to your desktop.

The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield on Wednesday evening.
Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. State department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”
The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.
The announcement comes as some media – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.
However in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and stressed that the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.
Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport that was the kingdom’s deadliest in years, as the war with the group escalates.
On Wednesday evening the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that one Saudi resident was killed in attacks on King Fahad international airport in Dammam, on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
Eight people were injured and the airport also suffered some material damage, according to officials. Global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.
Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east also killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.
Neither attack was immediately claimed by the Houthis, but airports and oil facilities have been a major target of the militant group in their recent wave of missile and projectile strikes on Saudi Arabia.
The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran in late February. NBC reported that the US military has been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, however a spokesperson from US central command told the US outlet that service members are regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
The withdrawal of staff from the region comes amid reports that Trump has been presented with plans for restarting strikes on Iran, after the midterm elections.
The New York Times reported that the US and Israel developed plans for a “short but intensive operation”, after defense secretary Peter Hegseth travelled to Israel earlier this week for meetings with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Last week Trump said the US was looking to knock out Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a site linked to the country’s nuclear program, however the president has publicly said that he does not intend to restart the war before the 3 November elections.

When the sun goes down, the wind picks up in central New Mexico, whipping through arid canyons with a ghostly howl that for centuries, locals have likened to the wails of the folkloric ghost La Llorona.
How the biggest renewable energy project in US history finally got built
The SunZia wind farm is a marvel. Why did it take 20 years to build?
A few hours east of Albuquerque, this June, those gusts began powering the largest wind farm this continent has ever seen, twirling over 900 colossal steel turbines. Each is as tall as the Statue of Liberty, scattered across a patch of desert roughly the size of Chicago. They plug into a 550-mile transmission line stitched across the Southwest and are now powering over one million homes — as far away as California.
The SunZia Wind and Transmission project is a rare 21st-century triumph of American infrastructure, an engineering marvel that generates more electricity than the Hoover Dam. When the turbines came online this spring, they immediately broke records for wind-generated power in California’s energy supply, where solar power may rule the day, but the winds of New Mexico increasingly fuel the night.
Key takeaways
- SunZia, the largest clean energy megaproject in US history, finally came online this June, sending New Mexico wind power to customers in Arizona and California.
- For over a decade and a half, the project was delayed by permitting issues, lawsuits, and above all, an energy market that wasn’t ready for the power it had to offer.
- With the nation’s electricity demand skyrocketing, SunZia’s collaboration with conservationists may offer a blueprint for getting more megaprojects built.
After years of stagnant power growth, the US is absolutely starving for more electricity, with demand projected to rise by 25 percent by the end of this decade, and a staggering 78 percent by 2050. Enormous as this challenge might seem, it may ultimately be the catalyst the country needs to dramatically dial up its renewable energy infrastructure, so that the years to come are powered not by gas or coal, but by clean energy sources like the sun and the wind. By next summer, the project will have prevented about 9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from entering the atmosphere, according to Pattern Energy, the project’s developer.
For decades, however, it seemed the project would remain little more than a spectral dream.
“It works!” This was the call Hunter Armistead, Pattern’s CEO, remembers getting from his head engineer when the turbines came online for the very first time. “We were creating power, and it was showing up 550 miles away in Phoenix, almost as if it was magic.” During the ribbon-cutting for the wind farm, some construction workers showed off massive new turbine tattoos. “It’s their pride that for the rest of their lives, they can drive by and tell their kid, ‘I did this,’” Armistead said.
But SunZia almost didn’t get built at all. It is not just the project’s scale that makes it remarkable, but the utter morass its developers slogged through to bring it online. The project spanned five presidential administrations, an ownership change, a major reroute, and a standoff with a US military base.
It also involved a series of lawsuits from local tribal communities and environmental advocates, some of which remain pending even as the turbines now finally whirl. Building any renewable megaproject requires vast amounts of space, and hyperspecific natural conditions, like a wind that blows at night or a reliably sun-soaked desert plain. Then getting that energy to major cities means traversing some of the most pristine, spectacular natural corridors this nation has left, and particularly in the Southwest, rubbing up against the sacred lands of local tribal communities.
The decades-long saga to settle some of these tensions has turned SunZia into a helpful lesson, and for many, deserved or not, it became the ultimate poster child for permitting reform. And for many years, the country’s need for power didn’t seem to call for such a wildly ambitious project anyway. But in the interim, as the world changed, SunZia changed too, becoming — at least in some places — a better and more collaborative project than it was when it began. And now, with a nation finally focused on building more clean energy megaprojects, it can offer a glimpse of what’s to come, even a blueprint of what could be.
The real reason(s) it took so long for SunZia to get built
When SunZia was first proposed in 2006, the same year Twitter went online, coal was still the most important electricity source in America, and the nation’s appetite for electricity had remained nearly flat year after year.
And for the next 17 years, SunZia flailed, never even breaking ground. It ping-ponged between financial and regulatory purgatories that most commentators have attributed to endless permitting delays. There were, for example, a few state-level permitting debacles, with New Mexico rejecting SunZia’s initial transmission route in 2018. Even after such interstate power lines get federal approval, they often need to wait years longer for approvals from every state in which their project passes.
Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, for one, has cited SunZia as a key impetus for his co-sponsoring the Senate’s new plan for permitting reform. This would make it easier for the federal government to coordinate approval processes for interstate transmission lines, ensuring that they happen concurrently and preventing one state from dragging its heels.
The project had faced one particularly large and sticky permitting challenge: getting the power through the White Sands Missile Range. But this, and other challenges, were eventually resolved relatively quickly. And to David Hayes, who served as deputy secretary of the Department of the Interior during the Obama administration, this suggests that financing hamstrung the project even more than red tape.
“The facts are the facts, and they got their permit,” said Hayes — all the way back in 2015, not long after the Obama administration put SunZia on a “fast-track” to approval. “So we finally got the permit done. Hooray, right? And then nothing happens. Nothing happens.”
Part of that was the fact that the two states where SunZia wanted to build its transmission lines were not entirely on board. But it was also the sheer expense involved in building the project, especially given that the federal approval required burying parts of the transmission line near the missile range. Moreover, even if everything went perfectly with the project’s permitting process, it might have been impossible to build SunZia back then, said Armistead, because “we really didn’t have the market need for it.”
The US simply wasn’t as ravenous for new electricity as it is right now, and the importance of building out the future of energy was not enticing enough for investors on its own.
But, refusing to die a slow death of a thousand permitting blockades or financial setbacks, SunZia instead evolved. Pattern Energy, initially only in charge of developing the wind farm portion of the project, took over the transmission line project in 2022. Around that time, SunZia applied for a revised federal permit, one that would circumvent the missile range, and within less than two years — a relative sprint for federal bureaucracy — they had a new approval in hand. Then came $11 billion in financing from several global financial institutions, pension funds, and clean energy investors. Then, a few years of construction time later, the Americas’ biggest wind farm was finally switched on.
And more massive projects like this will be needed because nowadays, “there is no longer the excuse” of a market unready for high volumes of clean energy, Armistead told me. “It is game time, and we’re supposed to get this done.”
What America’s biggest clean energy project got right
One of the secrets to SunZia’s ultimate success in New Mexico was the project’s ability to strike compromises, even with some of its earliest critics. In some cases, a bunch of birds.
Right about now, the earliest migratory birds, like the crimson-capped sandhill crane, have begun arriving at their Southwestern wintering grounds, not far from some of SunZia’s newly operational high-voltage transmission lines.
This crane had nearly gone extinct before, driven in part by an explosion of new hydroelectric dams in the early 20th century, whose construction dried out local wetlands. SunZia’s initial route, which was planned across one of the most congested flyways in the country, threatened them again, birders feared, alongside other migratory species who might accidentally fly into the new power lines, a threat believed to kill millions of birds nationwide each year.
While SunZia’s original developer, the Southwestern Power Group, was largely unmoved by those concerns, said Sarah Rose, vice president of climate at the National Audubon Society, the nonprofit found an unusually receptive partner to compromise when Pattern Energy took over.
“They took their role as a project developer really seriously,” she said, “and I think they engaged with us with a lot of integrity and a lot of good faith.” Under a rerouting plan, original power lines were moved north, erected next to existing infrastructure, or affixed with visual warning systems or bird diverters. Not only did the changes make the bird advocates happy, but they were enough to help convince the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission, which had rejected SunZia’s permit application a few years earlier in part due to these concerns, to unanimously approve the project in 2022.
To be clear, not everybody believed Pattern always made the appropriate compromises, especially in Arizona, where SunZia’s route remained unchanged under the new management. Peter Else, a local environmentalist, has spent years fighting SunZia in court over its intrusion into the scenic San Pedro Valley, a region that is sacred to Indigenous communities such as the Tohono O’odham Nation and San Carlos Apache Tribe. To see it marred by more power lines through the landscape has been like “mourning a death,” Else said, “like an ecological homicide.”
He would have liked to see SunZia try to run the valley’s new power lines alongside existing ones, as it managed to do in parts of New Mexico, a process that Armistead told me would not have been possible because the Arizona portion of the line “was already put to bed,” and the original federal permit had found the valley to be “the least impactful and best route.” A lawsuit from the Tohono O’odham Nation and San Carlos Apache Tribe accusing SunZia and the Department of the Interior of failing to protect the valley remains pending.
Of course, climate change threatens many of these regions more than a single power line. In the two decades it took SunZia to begin pumping clean energy across state lines, waves of extreme heat have taken tens of thousands of American lives, and the entire Southwest has continued in a megadrought unseen in the past 1,200 years.
These are some of the very concerns that SunZia seeks, in part, to combat. And if we want to avoid even more heat deaths, extreme droughts, more flash floods, and more habitat destruction, then we probably will need a lot more facilities like it, some of which will require hard tradeoffs.
But they aren’t doomed always to. It may have taken SunZia over a decade to learn that lesson, but for future megaprojects, the blueprint may already be there. The nearby 280-mile high-voltage Southline Transmission Project spanning parts of Arizona and New Mexico is set to begin construction next year, and it’s been so intentional about minimizing its ecological and cultural impact that even Else praised it as a good idea. And this approach could pave the way for even more essential large-scale projects like it. “If more folks could come to the table looking for solutions as opposed to expecting conflict,” Rose said, “I think we would be able to move a lot more quickly.” Ideally, it won’t take another 20 years.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
Meta’s new business terms could still help it justify training AI on scraped sites.
Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.
Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

El Salvador's president threatens Haitian gangs over military hostages
- Published
El Salvador's president has said he has launched a military operation to rescue four air force personnel who have been missing in Haiti since Sunday.
Threatening further action, Nayib Bukele said that Wednesday's attack was "nothing" compared with what would happen if all the hostages - who he said were not combatants - were not returned alive.
They went missing after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups," El Salvador's armed forces said. The ambush occurred in Croix-des-Bouquets, an area controlled by armed groups.
They were part of the so-called Gang Suppression Force (GSF), approved by the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, to tackle escalating gang violence in Haiti.
According to an X post from Bukele, the mission consisted of pilots and technical personnel, whose primary jobs were to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".
His post said the Salvadoran military operation's single objective was to bring the four men back home alive.
He added that if all four were returned alive, without being harmed, "everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping".
Bukele added they were kidnapped "in a cowardly manner" while returning after buying food at a market in the area.
A statement released by the Armed Forces of El Salvador on Sunday said the group was ambushed while travelling back to its camp in an armoured vehicle, which caught fire after being hit by explosives.
So far, no gang has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Salvadoran helicopters were deployed to assist, with multiple attempts to make an approach by land and air hampered by fighting and local security conditions, the armed forces said.
On Wednesday, before Bukele announced the launch of the military operation, the GSF said it was searching for the four missing personnel following the attack.
It added that it had "engaged armed gang elements, with helicopter support" and that early reports had indicated that several gang members were killed.
Earlier this week, the UN warned that Haiti's armed gangs were adapting to intensified security conditions, saying that they were "stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas".
Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and two weeks ago postponed presidential and legislative elections - scheduled for 13 December - indefinitely.
The country has been wracked by economic chaos, a political vacuum and increasingly violent gang warfare since its president was assassinated in 2021.
More than 5,500 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti in 2024. Armed gangs currently control about 85% of the capital, Port-au-Prince.

A Rajasthan youth arrested by Tamil Nadu police, for reportedly using deep fake videos of Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay to collect money from gullible people, has approached the Madras High Court seeking bail in the case booked by the Cyber Crime Cell of Crime Branch-Criminal Investigation Department (CB-CID).
The plea has been listed for hearing before Justice N. Ramesh on Friday (October 23, 2026). Petitioner J. Shyabu Khan, 28, of Boontoli village in Alwar district of Rajasthan was arrested on September 12, 2026 and brought to Tamil Nadu on a transit warrant before being lodged at a local prison here pursuant to his remand.
The charge against him was that he created Facebook accounts titled ‘All India help Vijay Thalapati’ and ‘All India help’ in which the AI-generated deep fake videos of the Chief Minister were used promising help to people in need if they get themselves registered on payment of registration fees to a particular UPI number.
The cybercrime cell had come across the deep fake videos during regular cyber patrolling, tracked down the IP addresses to Boontoli and nabbed the petitioner with the assistance of Rajasthan police. The Principal Sessions Court in Chennai had on October 14, 2026 refused to gant bail to the petitioner.
Though the petitioner claimed his friend Sakrulla had created the impersonating videos, used his Facebook ID, mobile phone number as well as bank account to commit the crime, the sessions court refused to grant bail since the investigation was yet to be completed.
In his present bail plea before the High Court too, the petitioner claimed to be innocent and said his family had been put to great prejudice because of his incarceration for the last 40 days. He agreed to abide by any condition imposed by the court for the purpose of grant of bail.
The petitioner also claimed the police had arrested him without ascertaining the true facts and said the investigation must have got almost over by now as more than a month had lapsed since his arrest.

Major US banks are tightening restrictions on third-party artificial intelligence (AI) agents after detecting instances of the technology accessing customer accounts, with some agents appearing to act independently of users’ instructions, according to a report by Axios.
Financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Citigroup, are working to contain the risks posed by AI agents as the technology advances faster than banks can adapt their security systems and policies, Axios reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The concerns centre on whether AI agents with access to banking credentials could carry out unauthorised transactions, move funds or perform other activities that affect customers’ finances. Banks are also struggling to distinguish between agents acting on a user’s instructions and those operating beyond the authority granted to them.
Here is what to know about the issue.
What are AI agents, and why are banks concerned?
AI agents are software systems designed to carry out tasks on behalf of users, potentially with limited human intervention. Depending on the permissions granted, they may be able to navigate websites, retrieve information, interact with services and complete specific tasks.
In banking, customers could use these tools to review their finances, manage budgets, make purchases or carry out other activities through their accounts.
However, access to a banking account introduces risks that go beyond those associated with ordinary AI assistants. If an agent has a customer's login credentials and permission to perform transactions, it could potentially take actions with direct financial consequences.
According to Axios, banking executives are concerned about agents accessing accounts and attempting activities that do not appear to follow users’ instructions.
Some banks have also tracked instances in which agents contacted call centres or appeared to take actions independently of the customer, people familiar with the issue told Axios.
The report does not establish that these incidents resulted in financial losses.
Several major financial institutions are taking steps to limit third-party AI agents' access to their platforms, Axios reported.
- Morgan Stanley: The bank has begun blocking third-party AI agents from accessing its platforms, according to people familiar with the decision.
- JPMorgan Chase: The bank is among the institutions restricting access by third-party agents.
- Bank of America: The bank is also restricting agents, Axios reported.
- Citigroup: Citi is among the banks taking steps to limit access.
- Wells Fargo: The bank was among the financial institutions identified in the report as confronting the risks associated with AI agents.
A Morgan Stanley spokesperson told Axios that the bank had not observed instances of “rogue AI agents accessing our platforms.”
A Chase spokesperson advised customers not to share their usernames and passwords with anyone.
The reported restrictions reflect banks' concerns about allowing external software to interact with systems that hold sensitive financial information.
According to Axios, some of the situations involve AI agents or assistants accessing customers’ accounts using login credentials provided by the account holders themselves.
Although customers may authorise an agent to access their information, this can conflict with the rules of banks that require customers to log in to their own accounts.
The distinction is important: a customer allowing an AI agent to access an account does not necessarily mean the bank permits that access under its terms of service.
The greater concern arises when agents are given permissions beyond simply viewing information. An agent with the ability to make purchases or transfer money could potentially carry out actions that users did not intend.
Banks also face a separate challenge in determining whether an agent's activity is genuinely user-directed. According to Axios, some executives have found it difficult to establish whether an agent has been authorised by a customer or has exceeded its permitted role.
Rather than allowing AI agents unrestricted access, most banks have authorised or are moving towards permitting read-only access, Axios reported.
Read-only permissions would allow an agent to view financial information without being able to initiate transactions or otherwise change an account.
This approach could let customers use AI tools to review spending, organise budgets and analyse financial information while reducing the risk of agents moving money or making purchases.
Banks already provide similar access to some third-party applications, including Quicken, which offers budgeting and personal-finance tools.
However, read-only access is not a complete solution to every security concern. Banks would still need to ensure that sensitive financial information is accessed appropriately and that account holders retain control over who can view their data.
One of the biggest challenges for financial institutions is determining whether an AI agent is operating within the boundaries set by its user.
Traditional banking security systems are designed to identify suspicious logins, transactions and other unusual behaviour. AI agents complicate that task because they may access accounts using legitimate credentials and perform activities that resemble normal customer behaviour.
An agent could have the account holder's permission to retrieve information but attempt to carry out an action outside that permission. Banks may struggle to determine whether the activity reflects the user's actual intentions.
Axios reported that banks are finding it difficult to distinguish between different agents and to establish whether an agent has been authorised by the customer or has gained access and begun operating independently.
The rapid development of AI technology adds to the challenge, as new capabilities and potential vulnerabilities can emerge before financial institutions have updated their safeguards.
Banks are working to prevent unauthorised activity while preparing contingency plans in case their safeguards fail, according to Axios.
Their response includes restricting third-party agents, reconsidering the conditions under which external software can access accounts and preparing plans to secure or restore customer access if a serious incident occurs.
The report said some institutions are also undertaking “day after” scenario planning to determine how they would respond if an AI-related security incident disrupted access to customer accounts.
Financial institutions face a difficult balancing act. They recognise that customers are likely to want AI agents to handle more financial tasks in the future, but granting these tools broad access before adequate safeguards are in place could expose customers to significant risks.
As Axios reported, banks have financial resources and experience operating critical infrastructure, but money alone may not be enough to keep pace with technology that is evolving rapidly.
For customers, the immediate concern is how much access they grant AI tools and whether that access complies with their bank's policies.
Customers should avoid sharing banking usernames, passwords or other sensitive credentials with third-party AI services unless they have verified that the arrangement is supported and permitted by their financial institution.
Where available, limited permissions, such as read-only access, may reduce the risk associated with allowing an external tool to view financial information. Customers should also review the permissions granted to connected applications and monitor their accounts for unfamiliar activity.
The developments do not mean that all AI agents are unauthorised or that every instance of agent access is malicious. They highlight a growing problem for financial institutions: ensuring that AI tools can provide useful services without compromising account security or acting beyond a customer's instructions.

A team from Haryana’s BPS Government Medical College (BPSGMC) for Women in Khanpur Kalan has won the IMU-Ron Harden Innovation in Medical Education (IMU-RHIME) Award 2026, the first time the award has been won by an Indian college. The award was for BPS Government Medical College for Women’s student leadership programme ‘Network of Student Leaders’ (NEST).
The award was presented at the 19th International Medical Education Conference, held at IMU University in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and was received by Dr. Sumita Sethi, Professor of Ophthalmology at BPSGMC. Dr. Sethi presented the winning work on behalf of the college team, which also includes Dr. Renu Garg and Dr. Ruchi Agarwal.
The award is aimed at encouraging innovations in medical education and recognising innovations by academics, “which otherwise might go unnoticed,” the official document on the award says.
“Humbled and delighted to share that our initiative on student leadership, NEST (Network of Student Leaders) received the IMU-Ron Harden Innovation in Medical Education (IMU-RHIME) Award 2026 at the 19th International Medical Education Conference at IMU University, Kuala Lumpur,” Dr. Sethi posted on social media.
“This is the first time since the award was instituted in 2008 that the rolling trophy has come to India,” she added.
The award, instituted in 2008, has previously been won by medical colleges in Hong Kong, Malaysia, the U.K., the U.S. and Pakistan.
Under the NEST programme, 278 medical students from 11 colleges across India received leadership training and went on to lead 63 projects addressing community health issues, including menstrual hygiene, cervical cancer awareness, child marriage and drug abuse.
“None of this would have been possible without the core faculty of NEST, Dr. Renu Garg and Ruchi Agarwal,” Dr. Sethi added.
The Director congratulated the team on its achievement, describing it as a matter of pride not only for Haryana but also for the Indian medical fraternity.

U.S. and Israel are planning for a possible attack on Iran, source tells NPR
TEL AVIV, Israel and ISTANBUL — The U.S. and Israel are preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran in early November, after the U.S. midterm elections, a person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning told NPR on Thursday. Iran said it is prepared.
The person, who spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity to discuss the preparations, said Israel had initially planned to strike Iran in mid-October, about two weeks before Israeli elections on Oct. 27, but President Trump objected.
According to the person briefed, the U.S. is now amassing forces in the region to be ready to attack by early November, after the U.S. midterm elections, but that these preparations could also be part of a campaign to pressure Iran to reach a diplomatic deal.
U.S. midterm elections take place on Nov. 3.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking reelection, is campaigning on a threat to topple Iran's regime.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iranian state media on Thursday, "We are just as prepared for diplomacy as we are for war."
"Any scenario is conceivable, including the possibility of an attack by the U.S. and Israel," Araghchi said.
Iranian state media also quoted a security source saying that if Iranian officials or civilian infrastructure were attacked, Iran would retaliate by targeting U.S. interests in the region, as well as the infrastructure and assets of countries participating in the war.
The U.S. and Israel launched a war on Iran on Feb. 28, killing its supreme leader and a number of senior Iranian officials. Since then, the two sides have failed to uphold a ceasefire agreement and have traded strikes over the control of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has blocked the key global waterway since the start of the war, targeting commercial vessels, and the U.S. responded by imposing a blockade on Iranian ports and its oil shipments.
The U.S. strikes have reduced Iran's military capabilities, including its air force, air defenses and its navy. But despite the inflicted damage, Iran remains a threat to the Arab countries in the Gulf, as well as Middle Eastern states farther away, including Israel. It has targeted U.S. military bases in the Gulf and Jordan.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard has threatened that if the U.S. and Israel resume attacks, data centers and underwater internet cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Deputy for Political Affairs of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Yadollah Javani said that Iran was prepared to destroy internet cables running under the Strait of Hormuz.
"The Americans must leave the region — they no longer have a place here — and they can never restore the situation to what it was before the war," he said.
Iranian state media also said that seven oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz were targeted by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps on Thursday. Four tankers caught fire and three others hit naval mines.
A new report by the International Monetary Fund says disruptions to energy production, shipping, tourism and trade this year have delivered substantial shocks to countries in the Gulf, even as higher oil prices offset some of these losses for energy exporters.
The international lender says Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar are all expected to experience contractions of around 16% to their economies this year.
The economies of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also in recession this year.
The IMF says if the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran continues and energy supply disruptions persist, the price of oil will average $130 a barrel in 2027.
Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, Ruth Sherlock from Jerusalem and Hadeel Al-Shalchi from Istanbul, Turkey. Aya Batrawy contributed to this story from Dubai, UAE.

Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
- Published
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the "horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."
He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.
Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.
Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

In this context, visuals showing crowds are being shared on social media with the claim that they show gatherings at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and outside Parliament House (here, here, here). Let’s verify these videos.
Claim: Visuals showing anti-CEC protestors gathering outside Parliament and Jantar Mantar.
Fact: These videos are AI-generated, not real visuals. No media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. Hence, the claims made in these posts are FALSE.
Video 1: 
Upon closer examination, we noticed a Gemini logo, associated with Google’s AI tool, in the bottom-right corner of the video, suggesting that it may have been AI-generated. We further analysed a keyframe from the viral video using SynthID, which also detected AI-generated content in the clip.
Video 2:
On performing a relevant keyword search, we found that no media reports mentioned the viral video or any protest by the public against the CEC inside the Parliament premises. We analysed the viral video using Hive’s AI-detection tool, which indicated that the video was AI-generated.

The inaugural Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship will be held in Ahmedabad from October 23-31, bringing together 13 countries for nine days of high-octane kabaddi action.
Organised by the Amateur Kabaddi Federation of India (AKFI), with the approval of the International Kabaddi Federation (IKF), the tournament will see more than 400 players spar across 62 matches. The men’s competition will feature 39 games while the women’s edition will feature 23 games.
The championship was formally unveiled at a curtain-raiser press conference on Wednesday, where the official jersey, team captains, anthem, logo and mascot were revealed.
India’s men’s team will be captained by Surjeet Singh, with Naveen Kumar as vice-captain. Nidhi Sharma will lead the women’s team, with Ritu serving as vice-captain.
The participating nations are India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Canada, Singapore, Malaysia, Uganda, England, Scotland and Australia.
The semifinals in both categories will take place on October 30, followed by the finals on October 31.
The tournament has the overarching ambition of breaking into the Olympic roster in mind as it seeks to push the popularity of the sport to fresh markets. The organisers hope this tournament will make a case for the sport’s inclusion in the Commonwealth Games.
With Ahmedabad set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2030, the tournament also offers an opportunity to showcase the city’s capacity to host international sporting events and introduce kabaddi to a wider global audience.
Tejasvi Gehlot, General Secretary, International Kabaddi Federation, said, “The inaugural Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship marks an important step in expanding kabaddi’s international presence. Bringing national teams from across the Commonwealth together will give athletes a new platform to showcase their abilities and introduce the sport to a wider global audience.”

Vanessa Kerry is the new WHO envoy for health resilience. What's on her to-do list?
Resilience is one of those buzzy buzzwords. But what does it mean, exactly? Bouncing back from tragedy? Conquering obstacles? Having the inner strength to follow a dream when the odds are against you?
For Dr. Vanessa Kerry, the definition is pretty straightforward. It boils down to being prepared. In the world of global health, she says, that means "strong systems, primary care and the ability to respond."
Those are the ideas that will guide her in her new job as special envoy for health resilience at the World Health Organization.
It's the latest addition to an impressive resume. Kerry was WHO's first special envoy for climate change and health, is director of global health and climate policy at Harvard School of Public Health and is the founder and CEO of Seed Global Health. That nonprofit group has been building resilience in lower-resource countries for over a decade, dispatching coaches and mentors to educate and train local healthcare students and practitioners as well as building financial and material resources.
Kerry's activism reflects seminal moments from her younger years. In grade school, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. At age 14, she traveled to Vietnam with her father, former Senator and Secretary of State John Kerry, and was deeply struck by the poverty she saw.
A high-risk delivery
Then came the crisis in Rwanda.
Between her third and fourth years in medical school, she spent time in a hospital in Rwanda. One day she was asked to "be a helping hand" with a woman's labor and delivery, working with a nurse.
Kerry said, "I'm a student." So that was the team — this medical student from the U.S. and a Rwandan nurse.
"The mother was pushing, but the baby was not advancing," Kerry remembers. "The shoulder had gotten stuck, and so we needed to do the maneuvers to help to deliver." She tried to remember everything she could from time spent in a "labor rotation a while back." There was no imaging, no specific training either she or the nurse had had for this type of situation.
"We were lucky," she says, "Because what we remembered worked." Mother and child survived.
Kerry, now 49, recalls: "I remember walking out of that room thinking, that was extremely distressing — more than that, extremely shocking and terrifying.
She could only conclude "this whole system doesn't work."
That harrowing delivery was the germ for Seed Global Health. She knew that many of her colleagues wanted to work to improve global health. But many of the opportunities involved flying in to perform certain procedures, then returning home.
"They made a contribution in that moment, but what then?"
When she returned to Boston from Rwanda to finish her residency at Massachusetts General, she began hatching the idea of working with the Peace Corps to send doctors and nurses to sub-Saharan Africa as medical educators to train health care workers who could then train others — building a country's internal health care system. Seed's collaboration with the Peace Corps lasted from 2012-2018, focusing on the development of country-led efforts at HIV/AIDS epidemic control.
Today, Seed is active in several sub-Saharan African countries for its training efforts. In Uganda, for example, Kerry says that her group has partnered with the Ministry of Health to build up emergency medicine by training 30 emergency medicine physicians. When an Ebola outbreak occurred there earlier this year, she says that these emergency physicians and other specialists were able to train over 3,000 health workers around the country in Ebola case management and infection prevention and control.
Seed, she says, has taught her that building resilience "is not a daunting task. If you train health workers, they can monitor and provide healthcare, they can provide surveillance, they can provide prevention."
Building responsive healthcare systems is what her new job is all about, she says. "We've been funding disease by disease and crisis by crisis. We can be thinking about this differently."
Her goal is not merely to jump in when a new outbreak occurs. "If a nation does not have a health system infrastructure in place, they will probably not be prepared to respond to the emergency. Resilience means building a system that will already be in place."
And it also means listening to local voices. "Countries know what their priorities are to care for their population," she says. As the resilience envoy, she wants to make sure there is ample funding so "we more effectively address the biggest burdens of disease."
Diane Cole writes for many publications, including The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She is the author of the memoir After Great Pain: A New Life Emerges. Her website is DianeJoyceCole.com

07 అక్టోబర్ 2026న లండన్లోని పార్లమెంట్ స్క్వేర్లోని గాంధీ విగ్రహం వద్ద యూట్యూబర్ ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ, భారత ఎన్నికల సంఘం ఓటర్ల జాబితా సవరణ ప్రక్రియలో అవకతవకలకు పాల్పడుతోందని ఆరోపిస్తూ ప్రధాన ఎన్నికల కమిషనర్ జ్ఞానేష్ కుమార్కు వ్యతిరేకంగా నిరసన చేపట్టారు. అంతకుముందు ఢిల్లీలో జరగాల్సిన నిరసనలో పాల్గొనకుండా ఆయనను పోలీసులు అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్న నేపథ్యంలో, ఈ సమస్యను అంతర్జాతీయ స్థాయిలో తెలియజేసేందుకే ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ ఈ నిరసనకు పిలుపునిచ్చినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పాకిస్తాన్, బంగ్లాదేశ్ కు చెందిన వ్యక్తులు ఈ నిరసనకు మద్దతు తెలుపుతూ ఆయా దేశాల జెండాలను ప్రదర్శించారంటూ ఒక వీడియో సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: లండన్లో ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ అక్టోబర్ 17న నిర్వహించిన నిరసనలో పాకిస్తాన్, బంగ్లాదేశ్ దేశాల జెండాలను ప్రదర్శిస్తున్నప్పటి దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ నిరసనకు సంబంధించినది కాదు. అది 15 ఆగస్టు 2026న లండన్లో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ స్వాతంత్ర్య దినోత్సవాల సందర్భంగా పాకిస్తాన్ గాయకుడు అమీర్ హష్మీ నిర్వహించిన వీధి ప్రదర్శన తాలూకు పాత వీడియో. అయితే, ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ నిరసనలో పాకిస్తాన్, పాక్ ఆక్రమిత జమ్మూ కాశ్మీర్, బంగ్లాదేశ్ వ్యక్తులు పాల్గొన్నట్లు, జెండాలు ప్రదర్శించినట్లు కొన్ని మీడియా సంస్థలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే కార్యక్రమాన్ని మరిన్ని కోణాల్లో చూపుతున్న ఆగస్టు 2026 నాటి వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) లభించాయి. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ కార్యక్రమాన్ని లండన్లో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ స్వాతంత్ర్య దినోత్సవాల సందర్భంగా 15 ఆగస్టు 2026న పాకిస్తానీ గాయకుడు అమీర్ హష్మీ నిర్వహించారు.
పాకిస్తానీ గాయకుడు అమీర్ హష్మీ శాంతి, ఐక్యత మరియు మానవత్వాన్ని చాటడానికి, ఇరు దేశాల స్వాతంత్ర్య దినోత్సవాలను పురస్కరించుకుని 15 ఆగస్టు 2026న లండన్లోని పిక్కడిల్లీ సర్కస్ వద్ద ఒక ప్రత్యేక వీధి ప్రదర్శనను నిర్వహించారు. ఈ కార్యక్రమంలో పాల్గొన్నవారు భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ జెండాలను ప్రదర్శించారు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్నది 17 అక్టోబర్ 2026న లండన్లోని పార్లమెంట్ స్క్వేర్ వద్ద ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ నిర్వహించిన నిరసన కాదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
అయితే, ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ నిరసనలో పాకిస్తానీ, పాక్ ఆక్రమిత జమ్మూ కాశ్మీర్ (PoJK), బంగ్లాదేశ్ వ్యక్తులు పాల్గొన్నట్లు, జెండాలను ప్రదర్శించినట్లు కొన్ని మీడియా కథనాలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. కానీ, మేము వాటిని ధ్రువీకరించలేము. అలాగే, అమీర్ హష్మీ కూడా భారత ప్రజలకు సంఘీభావంగా 17 అక్టోబర్ 2026న ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్లో ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోను పోస్ట్ చేశారు. కాగా, ఈ వీడియో 15 ఆగస్టు 2026న జరిగిన తన కార్యక్రమానికి చెందినదని, ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ నిరసనతో దీనికి ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదని అమీర్ హష్మీ పాకిస్తానీ మీడియా సంస్థ Geo News కి స్పష్టం చేశారు.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియోకి మరియు లండన్లో ధ్రువ్ రాఠీ చేపట్టిన నిరసనకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. అది ఆగస్టు 15న జరిగిన వేరొక కార్యక్రమానికి సంబంధించిన పాత వీడియో.

Lisa Blunt Rochester, a Democratic US senator from Delaware, has written to National Football League (NFL) Commissioner Roger Goodell seeking answers about the league’s protocols for detecting, preventing and treating blood clots after Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and bilateral pulmonary emboli (PE).
In a letter dated October 21, 2026, Blunt Rochester raised questions about the medical decisions that allowed Hurts to play against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London after doctors detected a blood clot in his calf. She also asked whether the NFL would review the Eagles’ handling of the case, including the decisions on his fitness to play and subsequent international air travel.
The senator said the issue was deeply personal to her, as her husband, Charles Rochester, died at the age of 52 after blood clots travelled to his heart and lungs following an Achilles tendon injury sustained while playing recreational basketball.
“I am deeply relieved that Mr. Hurts's story did not end the way my husband's did,” she wrote, calling on the NFL to use its influence to help prevent deaths caused by blood clots.
Lisa Blunt Rochester, born on February 10, 1962, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, has represented Delaware in the US Senate since January 2025. She previously served as the state's at-large representative in the House of Representatives from 2017 to 2025.
She was the first woman and the first African American elected to represent Delaware in Congress. She holds a bachelor's degree from Fairleigh Dickinson University and a master's degree from the University of Delaware.
Before entering Congress, Blunt Rochester held several public-service positions in Delaware, including state secretary of labor, deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Social Services, and state personnel director. She also served as chief executive of the Metropolitan Wilmington Urban League and later as a senior fellow at the University of Massachusetts Boston.
Blunt Rochester's October 21 letter asked the NFL to explain its medical protocols and decisions surrounding Hurts' diagnosis. She raised five key questions:
1. NFL-wide blood clot protocols: Does the league have standard procedures for detecting, preventing and treating DVT and PE, and which medical guidelines inform them?
2. Clearance to play: What standards determine whether a player can participate when a blood clot is suspected or diagnosed? Does the NFL have a league-wide return-to-participation protocol?
3. Education and awareness: What training do players, athletic trainers and coaches receive to recognise the symptoms of DVT and PE?
4. Risks associated with travel: What steps does the NFL take to reduce blood clot risks, including those linked to long-distance flights?
5. Review of the Eagles' handling of the case: Will the league conduct a thorough review of the decisions to clear Hurts to play after his diagnosis and to travel back to the US from London? She also sought a timeline for any review.
Hurts suffered a blow to his calf during Philadelphia's October 4 game against the Los Angeles Rams. According to the Eagles, an ultrasound performed in London on October 10, following the team's flight and walkthrough, detected a superficial blood clot.
The team's medical staff and doctors in London concluded that he could safely play against the Jacksonville Jaguars on October 11. The Eagles said a follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours. A subsequent scan on October 14 detected movement in the clot. Further testing revealed DVT and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning blood clots had affected both lungs.
Hurts was subsequently placed on injured reserve and is expected to miss the remainder of the season. His treatment includes blood thinners, which prevent him from participating in football activities while he is taking them.
The Eagles said they remained in communication with the NFL throughout the process. The league's chief medical officer, Dr Allen Sills, also defended the medical staff's handling of the case.
On October 21, Goodell said the NFL welcomed an investigation after the NFL Players Association called for a review of the Eagles' handling of Hurts' blood clots.
“The protocols were followed,” Goodell said, adding that the league's chief medical officer had reviewed the steps taken. He also emphasised that Hurts' health was the primary concern.

An iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199. An iPad is $449. If you want both—the iPhone as your primary device and the iPad to handle some work when you’re away from your desk—you'll be spending a total dollar amount that’s pretty close to the $1,999 price of Apple’s first folding smartphone, the iPhone Duo.
So can the Duo’s 7.6-inch screen pull double duty as a phone and a workstation? Does it make sense to shell out a few hundred more dollars for a single gadget that can theoretically handle the workload of two devices?
I wrote my entire iPhone Duo review on Apple’s new handset. I used a note-taking app called Bear, which was mercifully optimized for the Duo’s larger screen. (Read my review and you’ll hear about how most apps aren’t optimized; it could take weeks or months for everything to look right.) But surprisingly, I didn’t hate the experience.
I have run this experiment before on Android foldables and even smart glasses with virtual workspaces, but iOS has its own unique hurdles. Notably, iOS doesn’t recognize a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad by default. Instead, you have to go to the phone’s accessibility settings and enable AssistiveTouch—then you’ll get an iPad-like cursor that lets you navigate the Duo’s interface and select text without constantly reaching for the touchscreen.
Even with the cursor, small tasks like pasting hyperlinks into a written piece or quickly Googling topics for additional research are slower and more cumbersome, so I left those for the end when I moved everything into WIRED’s content management system. Even then, I had to switch over to my desktop for the final touches.
Apple also imposes arbitrary multitasking restrictions in iOS because, well, Apple likes to control how people use its devices. For example, if you open two apps in split-screen mode, you can only view them in an equal 50-50 split. Unlike most operating systems that let you adjust how much of each app you can see by dragging the border in between the windows, iOS leaves you stuck with a view that gives both apps equal screen space. If you want to use the iPhone in portrait orientation and stack two apps vertically, one on the top part of the screen and the other on the bottom, you’re out of luck. In portrait mode, you can only pin video apps to the top with another app below.
One thing Apple did get right is app pairs. You can “pin” two apps together, and they will live in your Recents, ready when you need them. Say you always want to look at your email and calendar together; you can pair them and find them in Recents whenever you need them. (Tap the bar in the middle to lock and save the pair.)
My keyboard of choice is an old Seenda folding Bluetooth keyboard that is admittedly not very good. I imagine we'll see an array of compact keyboards hitting the market soon—like Nillkin or ProtoArc keyboards already available now—to cater to workaholics who need to work everywhere. I also used one of Apple's cases, the iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand, to keep the phone propped up. You can use various MagSafe kickstands, tripods, or cases with the Duo.
I typed most of the day, but I also had to juggle between apps to respond to coworkers or hop on a Zoom call. Thankfully, the Slack iOS app updated the day before my testing to fully support the iPhone Duo's larger screen and vertical navigation, making it very easy to bounce between multiple conversations in the two-pane view. I still think Apple should add a feature like the iPad's Slide Over, where you can “hide” a floating app off to the side and bring it back in when you need it. It’d be the perfect spot for messaging apps like Slack, WhatsApp, or Messages, and it wouldn’t interrupt your split-screen experience.
Zoom wasn’t optimized for the Duo, though my editor said the video quality from the inner and outer selfie cameras was “really good.” I used the folio kickstand to Zoom on the big 7.6-inch screen until we realized my video was stuck in an awkward portrait orientation, so I laid the phone down on the table and pointed the 5.4-inch outer screen toward my face, which made it feel like a traditional laptop experience.
The app that annoyed me the most was Gmail. Even though Google updated the Google Search app to be compatible with the iPhone Duo early this week, the rest of Google's workspace apps currently look awful on the Duo. I imagine full support will come very soon, if not on Friday, when the Duo officially launches. The two-pane view in Gmail (or any email app) is a game-changer for clearing a bunch of emails when you’re on the go.
By 6 pm, battery life was sitting around 45 percent, which is very impressive. That's with around six hours of screen-on time.
You probably won’t want to replace your laptop with the iPhone Duo. And anyone accustomed to the iPad’s larger screen may feel cramped on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas. But with a kickstand and the right portable keyboard? Knocking out focused, light work on the Duo is entirely doable. Things will get even more interesting once Apple Pencil support arrives later this year.
But as I packed up my keyboard, I couldn’t shake a familiar feeling. Maybe we’ll realize a single do-it-all device isn’t as great as it’s chalked up to be. Maybe it is better to kick back with a dedicated MP3 player. Or snap photos with a camera. Or write in a notebook. Or work off a laptop.
Speaking of which, did you hear Apple’s making a touchscreen MacBook?

What to know as 6 women testify in Russell Brand rape and sexual assault trial
Actor and comedian Russell Brand is facing allegations of rape and sexual assault in a London trial
LONDON -- Six women who accuse Russell Brand of sexually assaulting and raping them in separate instances have described during a London trial their encounters with the British actor and comedian.
The women, who don't know each other, allege they were assaulted by Brand between 1999 and 2009 in locations including workplaces, a hotel room and a bathroom at a bar.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. He denies all the charges.
Prosecutors allege Brand was a “ruthless” and manipulative sexual predator who at the time had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact.
The first woman alleged that Brand raped her in a hotel room in 1999 after she met him during a performance on the fringe of the Labour Party annual conference.
A friend of Brand's testified that some weeks after the alleged rape, the actor told him he "may have gone a bit too far” with a woman.
Another woman alleged that Brand orally raped her in 2004 in the restroom of a London bar. The woman said that she had just met Brand and was chatting to him at the bar when he suddenly grabbed her breasts then dragged her into the bathroom.
A third woman, a then 21-year-old fan, said that Brand anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009.
Three other women also testified about alleged assaults in their workplaces.
One of them alleged that Brand grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into the men’s bathroom at her office in 2001. Another woman alleged that he kissed and groped her at the London radio station where she worked in 2004 or 2005. A third woman said that he pressed his face into her groin and demanded a massage while recording for a television project in 2009.
The women said they didn't report the alleged assaults at the time out of shame, and because of concern that they wouldn't be believed because of Brand's celebrity status. They individually went to police to report what happened to them after a 2023 television program broadcast anonymous accusations against Brand.
Brand, who is on bail, has appeared in the courtroom with his wife, Laura Gallacher, throughout the trial. He listened intently from the dock, and sat expressionless much of the time as his accusers told of their encounters with him.
In police interviews, he denied ever engaging in nonconsensual sexual activity.
The actor's lawyer, Ian Winter, questioned the women's accounts during the trial. He's expected to argue that sexual encounters from Brand's past have been “reimagined” when he outlines his case next week.
It's not clear if Brand himself will testify. The trial is expected to last up to 10 weeks.
Known for risque stand-up comedy routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek" and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
But in the past decade, he has largely moved away from mainstream media after he relocated to Florida and amassed millions of followers on social media with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand has come under increased scrutiny in recent years after multiple allegations of sexual assault surfaced. Last year, the BBC said that concerns about his behavior — including complaints that he had sex on the broadcaster's premises and exposed himself in the studio — weren't handled appropriately because of his status.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.
The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.
Mysteries remain
Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.
Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords.
A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5.
Tor volunteers partially outlined the initial compromise of the management server and Switzerland2 and the attempt to intercept unencrypted email. Tuesday’s report revealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic.
“If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won’t notice anything at first,” Kaba, the name of the Tor volunteer who authored the post, wrote. “Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you’re unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. Advocating for patient listening and empathy, he added, "We should try to understand them.
Emphasising the need for constructive engagement rather than outright dismissal, former chief of the Indian Army, General Manoj Mukund Naravane (Retd), on Thursday weighed in on recent statements made by Gen Z concerning "regime change," remarking that having a "different way of thinking does not mean they are wrong."
Speaking to ANI, the former Army Chief stressed that society and authorities must make a genuine effort to understand the perspective, grievances, and confusion of the younger generation through regular dialogue.
"The younger generation has a different way of thinking. However, having a different way of thinking does not mean they are wrong," Gen Naravane (retd) said.

Advocating for patient listening and empathy, he added, "We should try to understand them.
