Geneva – His Excellency Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, today signed several funding agreements totaling € 25.5 million to support critical health priorities.
The agreements include € 4.5 million of funding for the Core Voluntary Contribution Account (CVCA) of WHO; these are fully flexible funds which allow WHO to allocate resources to key priorities outlined in its General Programme of Work. An additional € 15 million will be used to deliver on specific key priorities, such as One Health, the advancement of universal health coverage, and primary health care, communicable and noncommunicable diseases, the medical countermeasure initiative, and the country readiness strengthening through WHO’s office in Lyon.
A large part of the contribution (€ 6 million) is aimed at covering the humanitarian response on several fronts: € 2 million will go towards enhancing mental health initiatives in Ukraine; € 0.35 million is to support the response to the cholera outbreak in Malawi; € 1 million will support WHO’s humanitarian response in Gaza, with an additional € 2 million dedicated to strengthening the technical and human activities of the WHO Office in the occupied Palestinian territory. Finally, € 0.65 million will go to the Contingency Fund for Emergencies, to be used as needs arise.
“As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health. France's financial contributions and agreements, signed today, provide flexibility and align well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, power and perform for health” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General.
France’s WHO Framework Agreement for the period 2020-2025 ensures sustainable funding for priority health programmes, aligned with WHO priorities.
Some of the joint 2022-2023 collaboration priorities include the work of the WHO Academy, based in Lyon, stronger health systems towards universal health coverage, health emergencies – in particular the International Health Regulations (IHR) and health emergencies preparedness – and reducing health inequalities.
These priorities align with the France Global Health Strategy 2023-2027, published in October 2023.
“Committed to global health, France supports the WHO’s action in crises and for the benefit of the most vulnerable,” said Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations.
In 2020-2021, the Republic of France contributed over US$ 143 million to WHO, (including assessed and voluntary contributions), with 76% of the contributions in flexible and thematic funds. Flexible funds allow WHO to assign resources when and where they are needed most, ensuring that key priorities are funded, and a better flow of funds, enabling a more agile delivery of WHO’s objectives as per the General Programme of Work.

A large clinical trial combining Moderna's mRNA cancer vaccine with Merck's immunotherapy reduced the risk of melanoma death or recurrence by 42%, the companies announced on Thursday, potentially opening a new era in personalized oncology.
Moderna shares closed more than 17% lower on Thursday after the trial findings leaked on an oncology website, despite having nearly quadrupled through Wednesday's close since August when the trial's success was first announced without full data. Merck stock also fell about 1.8%.
The Phase 3 trial, which tracked more than 1,100 patients, also revealed that the combination treatment reduced the risk of the cancer spreading by 38%.
The findings mark the first data demonstrating that pairing a custom vaccine based on a patient's unique tumor mutations with a drug that boosts the immune system can successfully halt the disease. The vaccine was tested alongside Merck's Keytruda, one of the world's top-selling medicines.
Keytruda functions by removing a natural brake that cancer cells rely on to hide from immune attack. Meanwhile, the vaccine instructs patient cells to produce copies of specific mutations, allowing the immune system to seek out and destroy them.
Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel stated that the findings herald a new chapter in treating cancer.
"With this ability to create new T cells that are specific to your tumor... the clinical impact is very profound, and as we saw in the Phase 2 (trial), very lasting," Bancel said in an interview.
The companies are preparing to file for US regulatory approval, expecting to launch the personalized cancer vaccine in 2027, Bancel noted.
The results, evaluating patient outcomes over the initial two years following treatment, are scheduled for presentation on Saturday at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference in Madrid.
Among subjects who received the vaccine paired with Keytruda, 82.2% remained cancer-free after two years, compared to 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is highly statistically significant. It is not by chance," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
Ahead of the meeting, several Wall Street analysts noted that investors were looking for the combination to cut the risk of recurrence by 40% or more.
"There appears to be a sell-on-the-news reaction playing out here," William Blair analyst Myles Minter wrote in a research note, pointing out that Moderna shares remained up 525% this year even with Thursday's downward move.
Minter added that the findings were "great data, in our view, but investors will continue to debate the fundamental valuation."
The trial assessed nine doses of the vaccine, known as intismeran, administered with Keytruda beginning 13 weeks after surgery to remove melanoma lesions, comparing responses against the standard single-therapy treatment of Keytruda alone.

One of the most obvious effects of U.S. President Donald Trump's presidencies has been a growing distrust in U.S. elections. Trump has claimed for more than a decade that elections are "rigged" against him and other Republicans, and though election deniers certainly existed before him, his victories gave the narrative a national platform and real support.
One type of claim of fraud that Trump and others have spread focuses on alleged noncitizen voting. Such claims vary, but we've found that they generally map to the following train of thought:
- The Democratic Party has transported a massive number of immigrants into the United States, through either legal or unauthorized channels.
- These immigrants are instructed (or bribed) to vote for Democrats, presumably as a deal for letting them into the country.
- The number of immigrants who will supposedly vote in the election is large enough to change the result of the election. Without these supposed "illegal" votes, Trump and/or another Republican candidate would win the election.
This rhetoric was especially prevalent during the 2024 presidential election — Trump made immigration a massive part of his election platform and consistently attacked former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris on the issue. Since retaking office, his administration has promoted the SAVE America Act, which analysts say would heavily restrict voting access, and attempted to find evidence suggesting his so-called problem of noncitizen voting is a real concern, sowing further distrust in the process. 
For example, a July news release from the Department of Homeland Security suggested, without providing any supporting evidence, that more than 250,000 noncitizens were registered to vote across California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania (note that three of these four states have Democratic governors). Snopes fact-checked the DHS claim, speaking to election officials from all four states. All four denied the allegations, noting that even if the figures were correct, DHS had not provided them with the information necessary to do anything about it.
Over the years, Snopes' investigations have consistently revealed that claims about noncitizen voting are contradicted by the following facts:
- The Democratic Party is not transporting a massive number of immigrants into the United States (especially not in 2026, given they are the minority party). We've also repeatedly disproved claims that the Democratic Party is "importing immigrants" and providing them with benefits.
- It is illegal for any noncitizen, whether in the country legally or not, to vote in U.S. federal elections. The punishments for doing so are severe and include deportation.
- There are many protections in place that prevent noncitizens from voting. Because of these protections, noncitizen voting rarely happens — and certainly not at the frequency required to sway the results of a presidential election.
Trump has been saying this for 12 years
Trump's history of election denialism goes back so far that it even predates his 2016 presidential bid. In an October 2014 post on Twitter (now X), he claimed there was "nothing stopping illegal immigrants from voting," which he said was "very bad (unfair) for Republicans." As will become a running theme, he did not cite any sources.
During his 2016 campaign, Trump falsely claimed that 14% of noncitizens were registered to vote, relying on a faulty and improperly collected dataset, according to PolitiFact.
In 2020, Trump infamously refused to concede the election he lost to Biden, claiming massive fraud. In this case, he did not connect the alleged fraud to immigration or noncitizens, but the claim sowed doubt in electoral security nonetheless.
In 2022, Trump supporters who believed his rigged election claim became poll watchers. Reuters reported an uptick in poll watchers, who are supposed to be nonpartisan observers, illegally intimidating voters and poll workers. The Republican National Committee also established a voter integrity program that year to ensure the results were fair.
In 2024, the Trump campaign partnered with the RNC and expanded the voter integrity program, explicitly saying its purpose was to "stop Democrat attempts to circumvent rules." The allegation that noncitizen immigrants were illegally registering to vote was just one of the ideas the Trump campaign used to justify these efforts.
What the evidence says
Noncitizens rarely vote in U.S. elections. This is not a partisan opinion. The Cato Institute, a conservative think tank, concluded this in 2020 and reiterated the same conclusion in 2026
Supposed data that concludes the opposite is often wrong. That survey Trump cited in 2016 to claim that 14% of noncitizens were registered to vote? A 2015 statistical analysis of that study found the result was simply due to human error — out of a nationally representative sample, all the "noncitizens" who marked themselves as registered to vote were almost certainly U.S. citizens who accidentally recorded themselves as noncitizens when taking the survey.
In 2016 and 2017, the Brennan Center for Justice, a liberal nonprofit organization, investigated 42 jurisdictions across 12 states to find out whether there was any truth to claims of voter fraud. Of the 10 jurisdictions across the nation with the highest population of noncitizens, the survey looked at eight of them.
According to the center's report, voters cast 23.5 million votes in these jurisdictions in the election. The institute counted 30 cases of suspected noncitizen voting that required further investigation. That's an occurrence rate of 0.0001% — similar to the odds of being struck by lightning in your life.
Under federal law, states are required to maintain and audit voter rolls regularly to ensure an election's integrity. As an example, Georgia was a focal point of the 2020 election. Trump claimed fraud and asked Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to "find 11,780 votes," essentially asking him to flip the state's results. Raffensperger ordered an audit of Georgia's voter rolls in 2022 announcing that the state found 1,634 cases in which a noncitizen attempted to register to vote between 1997 to 2022, about 65 per year. But according to that report, none of the individuals in those cases ever officially voted, thanks to the existing protections that safeguard the voter registration process.
In order to learn about the numerous protections in place to prevent noncitizens from voting in U.S. federal elections, Snopes spoke to election officials in Arizona and North Carolina, two of the swing states in the 2024 election. Based on their testimony, these are the steps any noncitizen in the country would have to take in order to cast just one ballot and have it counted. 
First, if the noncitizen encounters government officials while entering the U.S. (i.e. they enter through a legal port of entry or seek asylum), their name and other identifying information will be added to a federal database that marks them as a noncitizen.
Second, this person would need to apply to register to vote (except in North Dakota, which verifies voter eligibility at polling places with a strict voter ID law). The other 49 states require voters to attest under penalty of law that they are U.S. citizens, that they are over the age of 18 and that they are residents of the state they wish to vote in. Any noncitizen found to be misrepresenting themself as a citizen "for any purpose or benefit," including to vote, would face deportation.
These registration forms require applicants to provide a large amount of personal information. This is a problem for immigrants living in the country illegally, who may rightly be afraid the government could use that information to arrest or deport them.
During the voter registration process, according to the election officials, the individual would have to prove they are a resident of the state they live in, most commonly using a driver's license or Social Security number. 
In order to apply for that documentation, the individual would have to provide more identifying information to the government (here are the requirements for a Social Security Card, for instance) alongside immigration paperwork that confirms their status as a noncitizen. At this point in the process, multiple governmental databases would now list this person as a noncitizen.
The election officials told Snopes that each voter registration application is reviewed and cross-checked against driver's license and federal immigration databases from the Department of Homeland Security to scan for any discrepancies. If election officials have any suspicions, (for instance, if information is missing because the immigrant entered without authorization and is therefore not in a database), they can flag the application for further review. That process requires even more personal information from the voter, and election officials can always deny the application if they aren't satisfied.
A few jurisdictions in the United States, including San Francisco and Washington, D.C., allow noncitizens to vote, but only in some local elections, not federal elections. In San Francisco, for instance, noncitizens are allowed to vote in school board elections only. However, noncitizens in these jurisdictions must register to vote using a specific form in a specific way. This means that such noncitizens are added to the voter rolls with the explicit knowledge that they are noncitizen voters, and their ballots can be tracked as such.
Looking at a different case, between June 2023 and June 2024, a glitch at the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission mistakenly placed 6,600 noncitizens applying for driver's licenses and state IDs on voter rolls despite them answering "no" when asked whether they were citizens.
That might sound more concerning, and perhaps it is. But, as Gerry Cohen, a member of the Board of Elections in Wake County, North Carolina, told Snopes, "There's a big difference between registering to vote and actually voting."
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who was not governor when the glitch occurred, said in a statement that of the 6,600 noncitizens placed on voter rolls as a result of the glitch, fewer than 400 cast ballots, and they did so across both party affiliations. There was no evidence that the noncitizen voting flipped the results of any races.
Taylor Kinnerup, communications director for the Maricopa County recorder's office in Arizona, added an additional distinction in a Zoom call: "There's also a big difference between casting a vote and that vote being counted."
After arriving at a polling place, according to Kinnerup and Cohen, voters are required to provide their name (and depending on the jurisdiction, their ID). These names are then checked against registration records (again, except in North Dakota). If there's a match, a ballot is printed for the voter. The voter then signs, affirming under penalty of law that they understand the penalties of casting a fraudulent ballot.
The voter's signature is a part of the verification process. Kinnerup said Maricopa County poll workers compare the signature to the voter's other recorded signatures before the ballot is opened and counted. As with voter registration, election officials can flag the ballot for further inspection if they have any doubts about the validity of the voter's signature.
Under Section 302 of the Help America Vote Act, signed into law by President George W. Bush in 2002, voters who are not on a voter roll but attest they are an eligible voter can still cast a provisional ballot in a federal election, something that might initially seem concerning. But even in this case, there are still protections. A provisional ballot is counted only if the voter's identity, citizenship and residency can be confirmed in the days following the election. Kinnerup explained the process using an example she said Arizona regularly deals with.
"California is a deep blue state, and some Republicans in Southern California might have the idea to cast a ballot in Arizona because it's a more competitive election," she said. "So there are Republicans in Southern California who drive across the border to Yuma County, Arizona, walk into a polling place and ask for a ballot."
The Help America Vote Act requires election workers to provide such people with a ballot. However, in order for these ballots to count, these voters would need to provide identification to confirm their citizenship and residency. Their California driver's licenses would be a red flag for poll workers, indicating these would-be voters were not Arizona residents, and the ballots would not be counted after investigating the voters' credentials.
What Trump has done since 2025
Since 2025, Trump's Justice Department has filed more than 60 charges of voter fraud against noncitizens, according to Reuters, marking a significant increase from Biden's presidency (according to the right-leaning Washington Times, Biden's Justice Department charged 13 noncitizens over four years).
It's also worth noting that being charged with a crime does not imply guilt — a 2026 PBS investigation into allegations of noncitizen voting found that Trump's DOJ has announced "far more charges than [it has announced] convictions."
The administration has also attempted to create a national voter registry database to prevent noncitizen voting. In March 2025, Trump issued an executive order calling for the Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration to share data in order to make it easier for state and local governments to verify citizenship and voter status.
The League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center sued over privacy concerns, and a federal judge granted a stay, preventing the government from implementing the data consolidation. The Supreme Court overturned that decision in September, clearing the way for the Trump administration to create the combined database.
As part of that March 2025 executive order, the Trump administration also demanded all states reform their voting registration systems and send voter rolls to the administration, threatening to withhold federal funding if they do not comply. Those orders have also been tangled up in lawsuits, and the Trump administration has often lost.
On the Congressional side, Republicans have attempted to seize on the narrative through the SAVE America Act, a bill that would mandate those wishing to register to vote show documented proof of U.S. citizenship. This means that in order to register to vote, voters would have to submit an identity document such as a REAL ID or passport when registering to vote.
However, those IDs would be valid under the SAVE America Act only because obtaining them also requires providing citizenship documentation like naturalization papers or a birth certificate — a document that 9% of American citizens don't have immediate access to, according to research from the Brennan Center. Although the SAVE America Act has passed through the Republican-controlled House of Representatives several times, it has been repeatedly blocked in the Senate.
Trump has repeatedly pushed Republicans to make the bill a top priority. For instance, in September 2024, facing the threat of a government shutdown, Trump posted on his social media platform, Truth Social, calling for Republicans to reject any stopgap spending bill that did not include "absolute assurances on election security," because Democrats were supposedly attempting to "stuff" voter registrations with "illegal aliens."
(The SAVE America Act was briefly resurrected at that point, but Democrats objected to its inclusion in the spending bill. Eventually, House Speaker Mike Johnson partnered with Democrats to pass a bill that did not include the SAVE America Act in order to avoid a government shutdown).
In March, Trump threatened to not sign any bills until Congress passed the SAVE America Act. In June, Trump initially appeared to back a bipartisan bill on housing reform before backing off for the same reason. The effect of these threats is unclear, however — bills automatically become law if the president does not sign them within 10 days.
Finally, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has conducted public and sometimes violent arrests of immigrants throughout Trump's second term, including cases where migrants have been pulled out of their cars on the street or arrested at immigration hearings. Some have been sent to foreign countries and camps where they have allegedly been tortured. This has led many immigrants — authorized and unauthorized — to tread carefully.
Since 2024, according to the Brennan Center, Florida, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, New Hampshire, Ohio, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming have all passed laws establishing or tightening voter ID requirements on the pretense of blocking noncitizen voting.
T
Part of what made Trump's claims about noncitizen voting stick is that they combined two of his favorite targets: election integrity and border security. It's important to examine what exactly Trump and his allies claim when criticizing or attacking Democrats in that regard.
The following post on X is a good example:
The post claims that during a town hall with Latino voters, Democratic then-presidential nominee Kamala Harris said she wanted to allow "illegal immigrants to become citizens who will then be able to vote."
This is an explanation of the Democratic Party's immigration platform and a statement about the privileges of United States citizenship, not an admission that Harris was going to rig the election. Harris was stating a fact: that immigrants in the United States illegally do not have a direct path to citizenship. 
Although it is true that giving such immigrants a pathway to citizenship would eventually allow them, as naturalized citizens, to vote in U.S. federal elections, going through that process would likely take a long time. According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, lawful permanent residents are required to live in the United States for five years before they are eligible to apply for naturalized citizenship.

Como handed Manchester United a second successive Champions League defeat on Wednesday, winning 4-1 at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia as Nico Paz scored twice and supplied an assist for Cesc Fabregas’ side.
Michael Carrick’s team, beaten 2-0 by Atletico Madrid last week, fell behind in the second minute. Lucas da Cunha picked out Paz near the edge of the penalty area, and the Argentine created space past Harry Maguire before curling a left-footed shot beyond goalkeeper Senne Lammens.
United struggled to impose itself on the contest and went into the interval trailing 1-0. Carrick introduced Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo at half-time, but the changes did little to halt Como’s momentum.

Four minutes after the restart, Paz turned provider, threading a pass through the United defence for Anastasios Douvikas, who lifted his finish over Lammens to double the lead.
Paz struck again in the 57th minute. Winning possession from Baleba in a dangerous area, the midfielder advanced towards goal and bent his shot beyond Lammens to put the home side three goals clear.
Como continued to find openings against United’s defence. In the 76th minute, Kaiki delivered a cross from the left, allowing centre-back Jacobo Ramon to arrive unmarked and head home the fourth.
Substitute Joshua Zirkzee pulled a goal back for United in stoppage time, meeting Amad’s delivery, but it offered little consolation after the visitors had been comprehensively outplayed.
The result marked another setback for Carrick, whose side has now conceded six goals across its last two Champions League fixtures while scoring just once. United has also managed only one victory in its last 11 away matches in the competition.

Saudi Arabia reportedly executed two Bangladeshi nationals, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akhtar (also identified as Siti Akhtar), on 14 October 2026, after they were convicted of committing an “indecent” act inside a mosque in Mecca. Official statements did not specify the exact nature of the act. In this context, a video (here & here) showing a public execution is being shared on social media, linking it to this incident. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Viral video depicts the October 2026 execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia.
Fact: While the October 2026 execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia is a real event, the viral video is unrelated to this incident. The video actually dates back to 2015 and shows the execution of a Myanmar woman convicted of murder. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same video (here & here), which has been available since at least 2015, stating that it shows the punishment of a woman for torturing her child to death. This indicates that the viral video predates the event and is unrelated to the October 2026 execution of the Bangladeshi nationals.
Further research led us to media reports (here, here & here) from January 2015 covering this incident, which state that the video showed the beheading of a Myanmar woman named Layla bint Abdul Mutaleb Bassim. The woman was reportedly found guilty of the severe abuse and murder of her stepdaughter.
To sum it up, an old, unrelated video is being shared as visuals of the execution of the Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia.

A 32-year-old woman with a recurrent ovarian tumour delivered a healthy baby after undergoing fertility-preservation treatment and in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) despite having very low ovarian reserve following two previous surgeries.
The woman was diagnosed with a borderline seromucinous ovarian tumour with microinvasion at the age of 30. Fifteen months later, an MRI revealed a large cyst in the left ovary, prompting a second surgery. The tumour recurred in the same ovary within three months.
Consequently, the woman was referred to Milann Fertility and Birthing Hospital in Bengaluru. She wished to have a child using her own eggs, even as specialists assessed the risks associated with the condition and the limited ovarian tissue remaining.
Cyst in left ovary
At Milann hospital, scans showed a complex cyst in the left ovary and only two visible follicles, which contain eggs. Her right ovary could not be visualised, and her anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) level was 0.6 ng/ml, indicating very low ovarian reserve.
The case was managed by a multidisciplinary team that planned treatment to address the recurrent tumour while preserving the possibility of pregnancy. Although removal of both ovaries and fallopian tubes, along with the omentum, was recommended as definitive treatment, the couple wanted to explore the possibility of having a genetically related child.
Two-stage approach
The team adopted a two-stage approach, first removing the affected ovarian tissue while preserving access to the remaining tissue, and then proceeding with fertility treatment. Testing confirmed a borderline tumour with microinvasion but found no evidence of spread into surrounding tissues.
To limit hormonal exposure, the team used a low-oestrogen stimulation protocol for IVF. The first embryo transfer did not result in pregnancy. Further evaluation suggested chronic endometritis, or inflammation of the uterine lining, which was treated with anti-biotics followed by pro-biotics.
Frozen embryo transfer
For the next attempt, the team opted for a natural-cycle frozen embryo transfer to avoid additional hormonal stimulation. A single high-quality embryo was transferred, and a pregnancy test 14 days later was positive. An ultrasound at seven weeks confirmed a singleton pregnancy. The woman continued oncological surveillance alongside pregnancy care and, subsequently, delivered a healthy baby.
“Our priority was to preserve her fertility while minimising hormonal exposure. A personalised IVF approach and natural-cycle embryo transfer helped us achieve pregnancy,” said T. Shilpa Reddy, consultant in Reproductive Medicine and Gynaecology at the hospital.

While I had the Apple TV app running, I tuned into some live MLB soccer. The action: sharp and smooth (and dull, obviously, because soccer), and the same was true when I switched over to an NFL game on DirecTV. That’s as expected with a 120-Hz refresh rate.
Speaking of which, that rate, coupled with low-latency game mode (which kicked on automatically) served my Xbox experiences well. From the 1930s palette of the cartoonish Cuphead to the candy-colored arcade racing of Burnout: Paradise, everything looked crisp and vivid, with fast response times and zero blur.
For my color investigations, I clicked into Planet Earth II on HBO Max, Pixar’s Coco on Disney+, various “8K” nature videos on YouTube, and an Inglorious Basterds 4K Blu-ray played on the Xbox. Across the board, the Roku Pro Series produced vibrant, richly detailed color—but with less of the “pop” I’ve witnessed on high-end LG and Sony OLEDs. That’s partially due to the panel’s limited brightness.
Whether that’s a bad thing is open for debate; some would argue that higher-end OLEDs oversaturate, the shiny colors more of a distraction than an enhancement. Discuss.
A notable Roku innovation is Smart Picture Max, which automatically detects the type of content you’re watching and adjusts various display settings accordingly. Though it’s hard to gauge the impact of this on things like color and brightness, there’s one clearly quantifiable benefit: motion-smoothing. Smart Picture Max disables it for most TV shows and movies, meaning you don’t get the dreaded soap-opera effect. That alone gives the Pro Series a leg up over most OLEDs, which require manual tinkering to disable this heinous feature (and again to re-enable it for sports and gaming, the only situations in which it’s not heinous).
The one catch here is that any Dolby Vision content overrides Smart Picture Max, leaving motion-smoothing switched on. Fortunately, Roku makes it refreshingly easy to modify that and other picture settings; just press the star button on the remote. I found (and toggled off) smoothing with just a few clicks. Another nice perk: Any change you make applies instantly to whatever you’re viewing, so you can immediately gauge whether it’s what you want; you don’t have to exit the menu to see the results.
On the audio front, the presence of Dolby Atmos does nothing to improve the TV’s speakers, which produce plenty of volume but get harsh and shrill the higher you go. Indeed, the opening measures of Nick Perito’s “The Green Leaves of Summer” in Inglorious Basterds were deeply unpleasant, even at a modest volume. This came as something of a surprise, as Roku’s previous Pro Series TV sounded much better overall. The speakers here are tolerable at low volumes in a small room; for everything else, you’re going to want a soundbar.
In the end, Roku’s first OLED won’t win over any die-hard fans of premium panels; it’s a budget model through and through, probably on par with LG’s similarly affordable B6. But it’s still an OLED, with all the vivid color, pitch-black black, and strong contrast that technology affords. And the Roku remote, interface, and automated image adjustments contribute to a splendid user experience. Watch for the next sale (Black Friday, anyone?) and you’ll feel like you’re getting a steal.

Actor Saif Ali Khan has sold a 797 sq ft carpet-area apartment in Mumbai’s Bandra West for Rs 4.11 crores. The transaction also includes two open parking spaces, according to property registration documents accessed by CRE Matrix.
Saif Ali Khan sells Bandra west apartment for Rs 4.11 crores
The sale deed was executed and registered on October 19, 2026. However, the agreement to sell was signed on March 7, 2024, and registered on March 11, 2024. The buyers took possession of the apartment on March 7, 2024. The transaction attracted stamp duty of Rs 24.66 lakhs, as per the registration records. The apartment is located in Hi-Cons Residency, a residential building in Bandra West.
According to property registration records, Khan had purchased a 6,000 sq ft carpet-area unit spread across two higher floors of the same building from developer Hi-Con Constructions on March 30, 2007. The property was acquired for Rs 9.7 crores and included parking facilities.
The original unit was subsequently divided into three separate apartments on June 19, 2014. These comprised a flat measuring approximately 2,997 sq ft on a lower floor, another apartment measuring 2,205 sq ft on the same floor, and the 797 sq ft apartment that has now been sold. According to CRE Matrix, the original purchase price of Rs 9.7 crores covered all three apartments.
Saif Ali Khan’s Other Real Estate Transactions
Apart from the Bandra West sale, Khan has also leased commercial property in Mumbai. According to property registration documents accessed by CRE Matrix, the actor leased two commercial units spanning 5,692 sq ft of RERA carpet area on Andheri Kurla Road to Durva Fintech Private Limited for a monthly rent of Rs 22.76 lakhs.
The leave and licence agreement was registered on September 29, 2026, for a five-year period, from May 10, 2026, to May 9, 2031. The documents identify Vikaas Mohan Sachdeva, a director of Durva Fintech, as the licensee. Khan acted as the licensor through his constituted attorney.
Khan also owns an apartment in Mumbai’s Satguru Sharan building, where he lives with his family. The over 6,500 sq ft residence was purchased from real estate developer Satguru Builders in April 2012 for Rs 23.50 crores, according to property index-2 documents accessed by IndexTap.com.
Before moving to Satguru Sharan, Khan and his wife, Kareena Kapoor Khan, lived in the Fortune Heights apartment complex in Bandra. In April 2016, the actor purchased an apartment measuring more than 950 sq ft in the complex for Rs 7 crores, according to property registration documents accessed by Zapkey.com.

The continuing mumps outbreak in Keralam, which began in late 2023 and has persisted into 2026, has renewed demands for including the mumps-measles-rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP). Outbreaks have forced the closure of schools and hostels for weeks in Alappuzha, Thrissur and Kottayam.
The demand has gained strength following studies from Keralam documenting immunity gaps among children, complications that can cause long-term disability, and genetic differences between the circulating mumps virus and the strain used in the vaccine, indicating how the continued exclusion of the MMR vaccine from the UIP represented an important gap in disease prevention.
From an annual average of over 2,000 cases, mumps infections began surging in November 2023. Keralam reported 74,907 cases in 2024 and 26,462 in 2025. A further 6,606 cases have been reported so far this year.
Low priority
Despite being vaccine-preventable, mumps has remained a relatively low priority in India’s immunisation policy, largely because of its low mortality. Although a time-tested combined MMR vaccine is available, the UIP provides two doses of the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine, which does not protect against mumps.
The Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) has long recommended MMR in place of MR, a vaccine combination available to children through the private sector since the 1980s. It has argued that mumps’ public health significance is underestimated because clinical cases, complications and long-term outcomes are inadequately documented.
With outbreaks also occurring regularly in other States, several have urged the Centre to include MMR in the UIP.
In a response to the Tamil Nadu government obtained through an RTI application, the Centre said decisions on introducing vaccines under the UIP consider disease prevalence and incidence, mortality, vaccine efficacy and cost-effectiveness, among other factors.
According to the response, the National Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (NTAGI) considers mumps-associated disability not a significant public health concern. Adding the mumps component, it said, would more than double the vaccine’s cost compared with MR, without proportionate additional health benefits.
‘Poorly documented’
Paediatricians contest this assessment, arguing that the disease burden and long-term complications of mumps remain poorly documented.
“The increased cost argument is being made in a setting where the mumps burden and associated long-term complications are poorly documented. Systematic surveillance, documentation of complications and disabilities, transparent vaccine-price comparisons and an economic evaluation factoring in health-care costs, school absenteeism and complications should settle this,” they say.
“Mumps may not cause mortality, but its morbidity is significant, particularly during epidemics among unimmunised children. Complications include acute pancreatitis, encephalitis and aseptic meningitis. The virus can affect the reproductive glands in both sexes, with long-term consequences that may not be immediately apparent. It is also a leading cause of acquired sensorineural hearing loss in children, sometimes resulting in permanent, irreversible deafness due to nerve damage,” says K.K. Purushothaman, former Professor of Paediatrics, Government Medical College, Thrissur.
He also questions whether the Centre has applied consistent standards of evidence and affordability when deciding which vaccines merit public funding, given the subsequent inclusion of relatively expensive vaccines such as the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) in the UIP and later the HPV vaccine (as a special initiative). MMR, he argues, is a time-tested and safe option that has not been assessed against current evidence using comparable cost-effectiveness standards.
Molecular characterisation
A study by the Keralam unit of the National Institute of Virology, published in Infection, Genetics and Evolution in September 2026, adds another dimension to the debate. Molecular characterisation of mumps viruses circulating in Keralam during 2024–25 identified genotype C, genetically different from genotype N (L-Zagreb), the strain used in the mumps vaccine.
The researchers emphasised the need for continued molecular surveillance to track viral evolution and evaluate the current vaccination strategy. However, genetic differences alone do not establish that the vaccine is ineffective.
The study noted that available seroepidemiological evidence and outbreak patterns indicate a considerable mumps burden. The continued exclusion of a mumps vaccine from the UIP, it suggested, leaves an important gap in disease prevention.

The video is authentic but does not show recent gatherings, as some people falsely claimed. It features clips of larger "No Kings" rallies that occurred on Oct. 18, 2025 — almost one year ago to the day.
This week, people shared a video displaying a collage of aerial clips allegedly showing "No Kings" gatherings, specifically the Oct. 17 "No Kings: Vote Early" event. Cities featured in the video included Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Washington, D.C., Chicago, New York, San Diego and Boston.
The NoKings.org website describes "No Kings" as a movement against kings, dictators and tyrants, primarily focused on U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration. A footer on the homepage explains, "No Kings events are nonpartisan and are designed to increase participation from all eligible voters."
As an example of posts currently spreading the "No Kings"-labeed video, a Facebook user's repost of it (archived) on Oct. 17 received millions of views. The post's caption read in part, "When citizens stand together and make their voices heard, the country should pay attention." That same user later claimed (archived) the video showed moments from Saturday's event and that "the news is ignoring it, and social media is censoring it."
In sum, our research found the video clips were authentic but also about a year old. Therefore, we've rated the video miscaptioned.
Others reposted the same video on Bluesky, Facebook (archived) and X (archived). Those users either claimed the clip showed last Saturday's gatherings or displayed comments from people who believed that it did. Some commenters falsely suggested the video was an AI-generated fake.
The video was a montage of clips of "No Kings" rallies that took place on Oct. 18, 2025. On that day, the progressive activist group Indivisible — one of nine partner organizations mentioned on the NoKings.org website — posted the video on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram and other platforms. Others prominently posted the video on or around the same day.
Snopes emailed Indivisible to officially confirm that the organization was the first to post the video and whether they compiled it themselves. We'll update this article if we receive further information.
Reverse image searches for each city in the video found matching clips or photos from the 2025 rallies, including for Minneapolis (at 2:42), Philadelphia (at 1:46), Washington, D.C. (at 0:17), Chicago (at 1:15:10), New York, San Diego and Boston.
Fact checkers reported at the time that some users falsely alleged the 2025 Boston footage broadcast by MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) really originated in 2017.
Earlier this year, some people also reposted the October 2025 footage to falsely represent "No Kings" demonstrations as occurring on March 28.
Saturday's 'No Kings: Vote Early' gatherings
The most recent "No Kings" event on Saturday, dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," reportedly featured smaller demonstrations than past "No Kings" occasions — with a singular focus on the upcoming midterm elections — including community gatherings such as block parties and cookouts.
The Indivisible organization posted an authentic video that they said showed glimpses at some attendees participating across the U.S.

Carrick carrying on as normal as Man Utd eye possible replacements
- Published
While head coach Michael Carrick is expected to be in charge for Sunday's match against Bournemouth, Manchester United have already begun the process of identifying possible replacements.
Eddie Howe, Antonio Conte and Julian Naglesmann are understood to have their eyes on the Old Trafford job.
Sources say Carrick is carrying on as normal and has not been made aware of any imminent change following Wednesday's humiliating 4-1 defeat by Italian side Como.
That defeat was followed by captain Bruno Fernandes questioning Carrick's tactics in the Champions League loss.
The players have been given Thursday off, while United are still to confirm arrangements for Friday's planned news conference to preview the Bournemouth match.
Some senior figures at United are of the view that chopping and changing mangers so regularly in recent years has failed to arrest United's decline, and that Carrick has been let down by players who are under-performing.
That does not necessarily mean that Carrick is safe, of course.
There remains major uncertainty over his future. But there is also an appreciation in some quarters of the progress that he and his squad made last season, and a view that he should be given more time to turn things around.
For weeks, managers - in and out of work - have grown aware that the United job may become available.
Howe, for example, is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated that the former Newcastle boss is open to returning to management with Manchester United after leaving St James' Park in the close season.
Former Chelsea boss Conte and ex-Germany manager Naglesmann, who are also out of work, are also interested.
Aston Villa head coach Unai Emery and Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler's stock is high with those in the corridors of power at United - but extracting them away from their respective clubs would be difficult.
- 'Not what a captain should be' - the debate around Fernandes' outburst 
  - Published2 hours ago
Carrick's possible fate echoes predecessors
For the third year in a row, United have publicly and financially backed a manager in the summer, but positive results have not followed.
Ruben Amorim staggered on to January, but the shock League Cup defeat at League Two side Grimsby last August and the awful performance at Brentford less than a month later stripped away his safety net and gave United's hierarchy nowhere to go when he attacked their influence.
United looked extensively at other candidates, including Thomas Tuchel and Roberto de Zerbi, in the summer of 2024 before deciding to stick with Erik ten Hag. The Dutchman was dismissed in the October.
Now, we have Carrick.
There were dissenting voices when he was appointed on a permanent basis in May, but the majority of supporters felt 12 wins from 17 in interim charge and a place in the Champions League after a two-year absence meant the 45-year-old former United midfielder deserved a crack at the job.
But, as ever, results shape everything.
There are numerous reasons behind the club's poor form this season and blame can be apportioned across a variety of departments and to the very top of the club.
However, the brutal truth is two wins from 11 games, and none in seven, their worst run since 2015-16 when eight matches without a win took Louis van Gaal to the brink of dismissal, is simply not good enough. And as head coach, Carrick bears significant responsibility for that.
What happens now?
Accusations of a lack of passion, desire and intensity have dogged United all season, having won just two of their matches in all competitions.
The team has also been hampered by injuries and players failing to reach the level anticipated.
While they have struggled in attack, they have also only kept a single clean sheet all season as form, results and confidence have all dipped.
Mixed into that negativity has come explosive post-match comments from experienced defender Lisandro Martinez, attacking the recruitment, and Fernandes, attacking Carrick and his tactics.
In between was the interview in the Athletic with Ten Hag when he spoke of 'broken promises' and a 'toxic culture'. It all smacks of a club lacking control, discipline and a clear forward-looking strategy.
There is certainly a view from senior figures around the club that while overall recruitment can be questioned – specifically the strategy of strengthening midfield in the most recent transfer window, at the expense of bringing in striking support for Benjamin Sesko or competition at left-back for Luke Shaw, part of a long list of absentees in Como – the players have to take a significant amount of responsibility for the current situation.
Whether that helps Carrick is another matter.
The proximity of United's next Premier League game doesn't make immediate change straightforward even if that was the thinking.
Following Amorim's dismissal in January, former United midfielder Darren Fletcher took over as interim manager for two games. Fletcher subsequently returned to his role as Under-18 coach, but two of the coaches who helped him, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, stayed with the senior set-up as part of Carrick's team.
United have a clear midweek coming up following their EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, who came back from two down to win at Old Trafford last month. That, in theory, would allow time to take stock without the immediate pressure a match can bring.
Bournemouth secured their first Premier League win under new boss Marco Rose last week. They drew 4-4 in a memorable encounter at Old Trafford last season, prior to that, they won 3-0 on both of their previous two visits.
It remains to be seen if Carrick will be in charge, and if so, how long after that.
It seems the only certainty around Manchester United just now, is the sense of uncertainty – again.

A pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.
The analysis from the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.
A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.
Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.
They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.
Another reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.
Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”
There is increasing recognition of the importance of Indigenous stewardship of the Amazon and other biomes that sequester carbon, shelter biodiversity and provide vital ecological services to the planet. But this role is increasingly difficult as Indigenous lands are threatened by miners, loggers, farmers and land grabbers, and as many of the young people of these often economically poor communities are exposed to the internet or lured away to wealthier cities.
How to sustain, encourage and reward Indigenous stewardship is a hot debate in the international aid and environmental community. Many previous payment schemes came with strings attached, such as the Brazilian government’s bolsa família, which has child education obligations, or bolsa verde, which has conservation activity requirements.
The authors of the new study say the project – which was drawn up with local women’s groups – is the first to offer an unconditional basic income to an Indigenous community in the Amazon.
The lead author, Dr Neil Howard, said: “All of this helps ethical conservation. The incentive to exploit or abandon land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”
To boost the impact, the project delivered a voluntary “cash plus” complementary programme of community-led education on finance, conservation and climate change.
Other academics are more cautious about the environmental impacts of cash transfers, pointing out that similar studies elsewhere have found they can lead to an increase in deforestation as people use the extra cash to expand agriculture.
In some parts of the Amazon, cash payments are used to buy motorbikes and cars, which increases demand for more roads. There are also reports of Indigenous communities becoming more exposed to drugs when they visit cities to collect transfers.
The authors of the new report acknowledge that wider research is needed on the ecological impacts of unconditional basic income. Their two-year study was small, covering little over 500 hectares (1,235 acres) of forest. They did not measure changes in vegetation or soil quality, nor account for the influence of any separate projects that might have been affecting community behaviour.
Despite these limitations, they say the early results have excited the cash-for-conservation network of civil society organisations.
“Yes, this is an experimental pilot and and we could do with something much larger,” Howard said. “But this is very pioneering. My hope is that the trade-off between scale and innovation tips in this direction.”

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives.
The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump.
Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s.
Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states.
The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed.
The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population.
At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union.
So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it?
No country for young men?
Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.
Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.
When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.
The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.
Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.
Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.
Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.
The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.
In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington
But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively.
The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39.
There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.
So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her.
Age versus issues
Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too.
The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%.
Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast.
Campaigners argue that these demographic trends matter because they leave some issues underrepresented.
"Yes, that might result in older people being elected, but I think it really skews, too, what issues are important; what issues politicians are incentivised to talk about and to take care of," says Grace Mausser, the co-chair of the New York City wing of the Democratic Socialists of America.
Mausser campaigned for Zohran Mamdani in his winning bid last year to become, at age 34, New York City's youngest mayor since 1892. Mamdani was held up as an example of a rare youthful success story, but his ally Mausser is less concerned with a politician's age than with their outlook.
Mausser says it is not necessarily a problem if someone has been in politics for a long time. Rather, the problem can be what may result from that: "You become so used to the language and the ideas of the political establishment that anything else - any new ideas, whether they come from young people or old people - seem crazy."
She invokes left-wing Democratic senator Bernie Sanders, 85, as an example of an older politician with a long tenure on Capitol Hill who has embraced change and had ideas that have resonated across generations.
Disaffected youth
In the US, older people hold politicians in far higher esteem than younger people - even more so than in many other countries, according to a Pew survey from spring 2025. Some 62% of 18-34-year-olds were likely to say few or none of their elected officials are honest, compared with 45% of people aged over 50. Of the 25 countries surveyed by Pew, only Greece's young adults had a more pessimistic view of the honesty of politicians.
For one expert who studies political engagement on both sides of the Atlantic, disaffection among young people helps to explain their unwillingness to participate in politics. The issue is not helped by the fact Congress has minimum age requirements for members, he says. Candidates must be 30 to serve as a senator, and 25 to be a representative.
"The one leads to another," remarks James Sloam from Royal Holloway, University of London. "If you don't have enough young people engaged in politics generally, then they won't become representatives."
What is more, Sloam says, young people in the US and the UK alike are alert to the fact that power does not just lie in politics. They are aware there are many other areas of work in which they can wield influence - including over elected officials.
For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs.
Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary."
Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave.
JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids."
Two-horse races
America's two-party system is cited as another barrier to young people getting involved with politics.
Sloam, the London academic, says this is because only a relatively narrow range of views are represented. He highlights research that indicates young people are more energised by social movements or issue-based campaigns than by party politics.
And within party politics, he notes the example of Mamdani and others on the political left who appear to be galvanising youth support outside the Democratic Party mainstream. But he cautions that "it's a little bit sporadic at the moment".
The Republican Party has been through its own splintering over the last decade with the advent of Trump's MAGA movement, which appealed to a swathe of young men in the 2024 presidential election.
Some European democracies show a more pluralistic political environment can increase youth engagement, Sloam says. Scandinavian countries, for example, which are more likely to be multi-party, provide a clear counter example because the parties of government in those countries "work with those social movements to try and bring them into the political systems". Citing countries such as Norway, Sloam suggests there is a cycle whereby stronger youth turnout and youth trust in the political system leads to more involvement in politics.
Looking ahead
It is true that some lawmakers should know when to call it a day, some experts argue, but equally, voters should not lose sight of the qualities of age. Nor should they confuse age with competency.
"Age alone is a very poor predictor of anything," says Tracey Gendron, a professor of gerontology at Virginia Commonwealth University whose research challenges the presumption that ageing is always linked to decline.
"You can have a 45-year-old who is experiencing depression or substance abuse who may not have the cognition necessary for the job," she says. And equally: "You can have an 85-year-old with incredible integrity and political judgement and wisdom who is fully capable of doing the job."
Gendron accepts the point that US politicians are not representative of the nation's age profile, but says this just shows that there are many ways in which Congress could afford to diversify.
"It's funny when we call it a gerontocracy and we focus just on age alone," she says. "When you look at most other aspects of representation - gender, sexuality, religion, race - we're not representative there either."
Owen, the Republican, fancies his chances in Utah, despite his opponent's much larger war chest.
Discussing what energises him as a Gen Z candidate, he identifies issues including the role of tech in public life, immigration and cost-of-living concerns. "I'm on the front end of starting my own family and looking at the costs and [asking] how am I going to make it work?" he says.
Asked if he sees any similarities between his campaign and the campaigns of young political candidates on the opposite side of the political spectrum, he says: "I'd break down the 'us versus them' framework, and maybe discard that a little bit… [there is] a bipartisan message that a lot of Americans on both sides of the aisle are feeling: that Washington isn't working for them."
He takes a similar view to Mausser, the democratic socialist in New York, that voters should not necessarily pick a candidate because they are young: what matters is their ideas.
"For me, it's much more about what you support, what you're who you're fighting for, than what year you were born," she says.
