Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
At least 11 Canadians arrested as Trump administration intensifies efforts to root out alleged voter fraud
Robert Harold Corbett was sure he was an American citizen until federal agents showed up at his door with an arrest warrant earlier this month.
Corbett was born in Canada, but raised in the United States, he told reporters outside a federal courthouse in Raleigh, N.C.
"I did not find out I was adopted until I was 51 years old," said Corbett, who has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) says he voted in six elections since 1998.
Corbett is among at least 11 Canadians who have been caught up in a crackdown on non-citizen voting by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa drew a direct connection between those prosecutions and what it described as Canadian interference in American politics.
In a statement, the embassy accused Canadian politicians of openly attempting to influence the U.S. election through trade policy, political campaigning and public remarks. It also singled out Canadians for illegally voting, claiming Canada has the second-highest number of its citizens facing fraudulent or illegal voting charges of any country.
"All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections," said the statement, which comes amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Canada over tariffs and trade.
Since late last year, federal prosecutors have charged dozens of non-citizens, many of them longtime U.S. permanent residents, with illegally voting in federal elections. But several of those accused say they didn't know they were breaking the law, with some saying they didn't even know they were registered to vote.
Investigations have consistently found that illegal voting by non-citizens is highly uncommon, says David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research.
"This is likely an attempt to sow doubt about the elections in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.
A Reuters investigation published in September found that software glitches and clerical errors across a dozen states could have added more than 30,000 self-declared non-citizens to voter rolls since 2000.
Becker says the DOJ has an "election crimes manual" that cautions prosecutors against taking enforcement actions close to elections because of the potential to influence voters.
"There's no reason these arrests couldn't have been made on Nov. 4 or some time after," he said.
Aaron Cohen, a Florida criminal defence lawyer who represents several non-citizens facing voting-related charges, says some of the confusion among his clients stems from election officials failing to properly verify eligibility when registering voters.
"I feel strongly that it's a policy decision for whatever policy outcomes are that the current administration is seeking," Cohen said of the U.S. efforts to prosecute non-citizens for voter fraud.
Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned last month.
Handcuffs, prison time
The DOJ's news release including information about Corbett's arrest features images of people handcuffed with their arms being held by police officers and faces blurred.
A video posted by the department on X Tuesday features a COPS-style montage of masked officers and a man in pajamas being led down a brightly lit hallway, advertising the arrests of 28 people in Californian for non-citizen voting. Two Canadians were among them.
Corbett told WRAL, a North Carolina NBC affiliate broadcaster, that he spent the night in a crowded and dirty jail cell with "people peeing on the floors." He said he was certain he was a dual citizen of Canada and the U.S.
Paige Adamson, a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years, was accused by U.S. border agents of illegally voting and questioned for several hours in September, CBC previously reported.
Adamson, who was heading back to the States after a birthday dinner in British Columbia, was told the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) believes she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen in order to vote in Washington state.
The department also alleged Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election and cited those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S. Adamson says she has no memories of ever voting in the U.S.
A North Carolina Election Integrity Team sign in Spanish, seen Oct. 25, 2024, in Durham, N.C., warns non-citizens not to vote and that doing so could lead to deportation — a notice that advocacy groups say could intimidate legitimate voters who speak Spanish. (Jonathan Drake/Reuters)
The consequences for the accusations can be serious. The Trump administration has sought to deport non-citizens convicted of voting illegally and in June, another North Carolina-based Canadian, Denis Bouchard, was sentenced to two months in federal prison.
Others have successfully challenged their charges. In August, a federal judge in Florida acquitted Gaynell Jeffries, a Canadian citizen accused of illegally voting, after she argued that an election official had mistakenly told her permanent residents were eligible to cast ballots.
Broader implications for democracy
Frédérick Gagnon, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and the head of the university's Observatory on the U.S., says the prosecutions in the U.S. are unfolding under a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants and other non-citizens living there.
"People are worried about profiling. They're worried of getting arrested and we can see that ICE wants to operate so quickly that sometimes they're proceeding with arrests that aren't justified," Gagnon said.
He said Trump's repeated allegations of widespread voter fraud also serve a political purpose by mobilizing his supporters.
Both Becker and Gagnon see no indication Canadians in particular are being singled out.
"They're looking at anybody they can possibly find because they are desperate to make the lie of widespread non-citizen voting look a little better," Becker said.

Cabinet Secretariat declines to act on complaints against senior EC officer: RTI
Two Election Commissioners separately asked the Cabinet Secretary to act over a senior officer's conduct. The Secretariat held back, citing the Commission's constitutional independence and absence of a collective communication.
The Cabinet Secretariat declined to act on complaints filed by two Election Commissioners against a senior Election Commission officer, saying that the letters had been submitted in their individual capacities and did not constitute an official communication from the Commission as a whole.
The details emerged from documents released under the Right to Information (RTI) Act, according to news agency Press Trust of India (PTI).
The Secretariat said that taking action without a formal communication from the Election Commission could be inappropriate and might be viewed as interference in the functioning of a constitutional body.Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi sent separate letters to Cabinet Secretary TV Somanathan on July 29, raising concerns about the functioning of Senior Deputy Election Commissioner Maneesh Garg.
According to the documents cited in the PTI report, the complaints alleged that Garg had revised work allocations among senior deputy election commissioners, deputy election commissioners, directors general and officers of equivalent rank without consulting the Commission or the officials concerned.
In a note released in response to an RTI application filed by activist Commodore Lokesh K Batra (retd), the Cabinet Secretariat said the communications had to be taken seriously but could not be treated as formal representations from the Election Commission as a whole.
“The above communications are from the ECs in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the Commission as a whole,” the note said.
The Secretariat recommended acknowledging both letters, with a copy to the principal private secretary to the Chief Election Commissioner for information. It also placed the matter on record for consideration in future decisions concerning the officer.
The Cabinet Secretariat’s decision has renewed questions over why Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi approached the Cabinet Secretary instead of addressing the matter through the Election Commission’s internal mechanisms. In an interview with India Today, former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa questioned the circumstances behind the move and said the Commission needed to clarify the full facts, including whether the objections were considered and discussed.
During an India Today TV debate, political analyst Yogendra Yadav questioned the move, asking why Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had not sought a meeting of the full Election Commission and, if that mechanism failed, approached the President.
ELECTION COMMISSIONERS RAISED CONCERNS OVER WORK ALLOCATION
In their letters, Sandhu and Joshi alleged that Garg, after taking charge as link officer of the Deputy Election Commissioner (Administration), issued an order revising the distribution of work among senior officers without prior discussion with the Commission or the officials concerned.
The Election Commissioners said the changes were made despite repeated oral and written instructions that such decisions should not be taken without prior discussion with or approval from the Commission.
Joshi also alleged that the Administration Division did not provide him with the relevant file when he sought access to it.
Both commissioners contended that the changes went against established practices and violated provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
Garg, an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer, was posted to the Election Commission by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet on September 2, 2024, according to the documents cited by PTI.
The Cabinet Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the two letters on August 5 and forwarded copies to the Department of Personnel and Training, the Establishment Officer and the office of the Chief Election Commissioner.
CABINET SECRETARIAT CITES POLL BODY'S INDEPENDENCE
In its note, the Cabinet Secretariat emphasised that the Election Commission is a constitutional body designed to function independently and remain insulated from executive interference.
“The Commission is a Constitutional Body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner,” the note said, adding that its functioning is governed by its own rules and guidelines.
The Secretariat also referred to Section 18 of the 2023 Act, which provides that the Commission's business should, as far as possible, be conducted unanimously, with differences of opinion resolved by a majority.
The note stated that although Garg had been appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet, his work and conduct were now subject to the Election Commission's rules and guidelines.
The Secretariat said that, in the absence of an official communication from the Commission as a whole, taking action on the individual letters could be inappropriate.
“ECs have sent these communications for appropriate action; however, in the absence of any official communication from the Commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate,” the note said.
It added that any intervention could be construed as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body.
A copy of Somanathan's letter was also marked to the Secretary of the Department of Personnel and Training and the Establishment Officer so that the matter could be taken into account in future decisions concerning Garg.
EC SAYS WORK REDISTRIBUTION ORDERS WERE NOT IMPLEMENTED
The controversy followed an internal work-allocation order that raised concerns among Sandhu and Joshi about the distribution of responsibilities relating to electoral rolls.
The Indian Express reported in September that the commissioners believed the changes could centralise powers relating to the addition or deletion of names and updates to electoral rolls, instead of leaving these functions with state-level officials.
In a statement issued on September 26, the Election Commission said the work redistribution orders issued by Garg had not been implemented following directions from the two commissioners.
The Commission also clarified that the letters sent to the Cabinet Secretary concerned an officer on deputation and were not related to policy matters or the functioning of its information technology division.

- Capcom has reported a major data breach affecting 11.7 million email records linked to CAPCOM ID users worldwide.
- Moreover, the breach exposed 43 records of birth dates, gender, and country details, alongside 196 unauthorized password changes.
- Capcom says it has already taken steps to contain the breach and urges players to avoid suspicious links impersonating the studio.
Capcom has suffered a major data breach via unauthorized third-party access on October 22, 2026, affecting more than 11.7 million accounts worldwide linked to its CAPCOM ID online service.
CAPCOM ID provides access to various online services and account features across Capcom’s gaming ecosystem, including titles such as Resident Evil Requiem and Onimusha: Way of the Sword.
In Capcom’s latest press release, the studio has apologized for the incident and has disclosed the number of CAPCOM ID accounts affected. Among them, the data breach has affected 11,774,247 e-mail records of users worldwide, particularly linked to date and time of account creation, last login, number of logins, client IP address used during last login.
Capcom’s breach also exposed 43 records containing birth dates, gender, country or region, and nicknames. The company also confirmed 196 unauthorized password changes and says it has reset the affected passwords since.
In the same press release, Capcom confirmed that the data breach didn’t expose user-created custom passwords and credit card information. The studio has already notified affected users of the incident and reported the incident to Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.
Capcom detected signs of a possible breach on October 19, 2026 and formed an internal team to contain the incident. After confirming data leaks and unauthorized password changes on October 20, the company reported the breach to police on October 21.
Despite the major data breach, Capcom has confirmed that players can their email registered with the CAPCOM ID service to play titles like Street Fighter 6 and Pragmata without any hindrances. However, the studio has warned players to refrain from clicking any suspicious links or fraudulent emails impersonating Capcom.
“Based on the findings of the investigation, it will implement measures to prevent recurrence and further strengthen its information security framework,” concluded Capcom along with an apology to all affected users.
The studio also confirmed that it has “identified and addressed the attack method involved in this incident.” That said, was your CAPCOM ID account affected? Tell us in the comments section below.

- The claim that North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un is dead is unfounded.
- The rumor stems from U.S-based Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie, who has a history of spreading false or unverified claims on social media.
- Snopes found no verifiable evidence confirming Kim had died. North Korean state media posted photograhs claiming to show Kim touring a garment exhibition on Oct. 19, but we could not verify when they were taken. If Kim were dead, there would likely be more speculation and reporting from South Korea and reputable news agencies worldwide.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the North Korean permanent mission to the United Nations and await a response.
In October, rumors spread online that North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un had died from a serious health condition.
Some posts claimed he died after a brain hemorrhage led to a coma, while others said he died from myocarditis, a heart condition.
Snopes readers also asked us to verify Kim's condition and whereabouts.
(X user @xie_wanjun)
Snopes found no verifiable evidence confirming Kim had died. North Korea's supreme leader has been the frequent subject of death hoaxes in the past.
North Korean state media posted images that they claim show him visiting a garment and footwear exhibition on Oct. 19, but we were unable to definitively confirm when they were taken. Furthermore, we could not independently verify claims about Kim's health or medical history. Until we know more, we've left this claim unrated.
Snopes reached out to the North Korean permanent mission to the United Nations to learn more and will update this story accordingly.
The earliest example of this rumor originated from U.S-based Chinese dissident Wanjun Xie, who also claimed on X that Chinese President Xi Jinping was dead. Xie alleged that due to poor medical facilities in North Korea, Kim went to Beijing, China, to receive treatment.
As seen above, Xie shared a video claiming to show a North Korean news announcement of Kim's death. This video is from 2011, not 2026, and shows a North Korean newscaster announcing the death of Kim Jong Il, Kim's father and predecessor.
On Oct. 20, North Korea's state news, Korean Central News Agency, released images of Kim on an official tour. The news release read:
Respected Comrade Kim Jong Un, General Secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and President of the State Affairs of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, went round the venue of a garment and footwear exhibition in light industry on October 19.
He was accompanied by leading officials of the Party and the government.
Comrade Kim Jong Un was greeted on the spot by senior officials of the Light Industry Department of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea.
A series of photographs published by Rodong Sinmun, the official newspaper for the ruling Workers' Party of North Korea, showed Kim and his daughter Kim Ju Ae inspecting garments and shoes on display.
(Rodong Sinmun)
(Rodong Sinmun)
(Rodong Sinmun)
There were no obvious signs of AI generation or manipulation in the images, but Snopes could not definitively confirm when they were taken. Signage in the background indicates the photos may have been captured sometime in 2026 without pointing to a specific date. While this does not prove that Kim is alive, there is no evidence of his death either.
Xie has circulated unverified claims before, including ones stating Xi had stepped down or been ousted from power in China. There is no evidence to support such claims amid news that Xi is preparing for a possible meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
If there were authentic sources discussing Kim's death, this news would have been widely covered by reputable news outlets like The Associated Press or Reuters. That was not the case.
According to BBC News, if Kim had died, China would likely be tightening security along its borders in anticipation of refugees. North Korean defectors to South Korea also would have received information through their whisper networks. 
News reports over the years have said Kim is a heavy smoker, overweight and has cardiovascular issues, but there's no evidence he suffered a brain hemorrhage or has myocarditis, as posts suggested.
As we've previously reported, North Korea is a black hole for independent media coverage so verifying any information coming in or out is difficult.
For further reading, Snopes has dug into numerous rumors about the dictator over the years.

Austin track bumps out of control - Verstappen
- Published
Max Verstappen says the bumps on the track that hosts this weekend's United States Grand Prix are "unacceptable" and "out of control".
The Dutchman said drivers had complained about the condition of the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas, and attempts by the organisers to resolve it had not worked.
Red Bull's Verstappen said: "I love this track, I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the best venues, best city to be at.
"But for me the bumps are unacceptable. Over time they've been grinding a little bit here and there but it's just putting a plaster on the big problem.
"But that of course means you need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that's the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control."

The track is built on former marshland and that has made it difficult for organisers to keep it in good condition, but the four-time champion rejected that as a reason not to try to solve the issue.
"You can use the excuse that the soil is the problem but then you should have known that and you need to make sure that you reinforce it more," Verstappen said.
"Last year, for example, you pull around 5-6G in a corner, but I had some impacts, vertical load, which was over 9G on my spine, which I can tell you is really not fun, and especially the older you get, you think about that more and more."
Verstappen said the problem was likely to be exacerbated this year because although the cars from 2022-25 had lower ride-heights overall, the way the cars are run under the latest regulations means they are running lower in corners than last season.
That's because of the switch between having the front and rear wings open in drag-reduction mode on the straights and closing in corners means the cars drop down towards the ground when they brake.
"You bottom out way harder, because when the wings close and the ride-height comes down, under braking is actually a very stressful moment, and I know around here in some places, it's very bumpy under braking," he said.
"Especially when it's like these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting older, but the surface underneath the soil just moving up and down, sometimes (it's) very hard to expect, or if you're like a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there, because no-one really drives here sometimes.
"I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great.
"I know that's part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it's also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years.
"And now if we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more."
World champion Lando Norris, of McLaren, backed Verstappen's opinion, saying: "The regulation of building a new track, the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small. It certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what those regulations are now.
"It's an old track, not a new track so it's pretty bad. There's a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it's so bumpy and you're hitting your head pretty hard against the headrest and things because of the bumps so it's certainly not a nice thing. There's not much we can do. I mean, we complain about it so it's stuff we've brought up many, many times but there's only so much we can complain about things. But he's right."
But Mercedes driver George Russell said: "It's bumpy, but I think it's just part of racing. I'd say my general view is F1 tracks probably need to be repaved every couple of years just to make it a bit more consistent. Because we're going to tracks now where Tarmac's coming up, it's falling apart, it's causing more issues than not.
"Not ideal, but not much we can do."

Gilead Sciences agreed to pay $45 million to settle allegations of paying kickbacks that improperly influenced prescriptions paid for by the Texas Medicaid program, the latest pharmaceutical company to reach a deal with the state over marketing practices.
The state pursued its claims alongside a whistleblower who also filed a lawsuit claiming Gilead paid another company to hire registered nurses to recommend its drugs. The lawsuit also accused Gilead of offering free support services to doctors to prescribe its drugs, which resulted in false claims being filed with government programs.
Nearly a decade ago, Health Choice Advocates and some related firms filed whistleblower lawsuits against several drugmakers, accusing them of hiring third-party contractors to deploy nurses — sometimes by phone, sometimes at patient homes — to ensure that prescriptions were refilled.

Relatives of gravely ill detainees at two Florida immigration jails say authorities are about to deport their loved ones to unknown countries in Africa despite worsening medical conditions.
Flights are scheduled as early as Wednesday, according to the families and the immigration advocacy group the Workers Circle, which has been monitoring conditions and speaking with detainees inside two Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facilities in south Florida.
The group said multiple sick detainees with varying conditions have been targeted for imminent deportation, and learned about the operation only in the last few days.
“I received a call from several detainees letting me know that men were being pulled in to interviews with deportation agents, where they were being informed that because of their medical conditions, Mexico would not be accepting their entry, and they will be sent to Africa,” Arianne Betancourt, the group’s immigrant rights organizer, said at a Tuesday night press conference.
“We know that once they are deported and sent to these third countries, they are not receiving medical care in detention. They have difficulties getting medicine.”
The affected detainees are at the Krome North processing center in Miami, which was found to be experiencing severe overcrowding by a government inspector’s report last month, and the Broward transitional center in Pompano Beach. Both facilities are privately run on behalf of ICE.
Anisley Cortés, the wife of Noslén Sendra, a 41-year-old Cuban national, said her husband has been incarcerated since last November, first at the now closed “Alligator Alcatraz” immigration jail, and at Krome since April. She said he has uncontrolled diabetes and acute pancreatitis that resulted in a weeks-long hospital stay earlier this year.
“He lost over 50 pounds. They wouldn’t give him his medication, and they would not give him enough food. It was a nightmare of a time for all of us,” she said. “He is very sick and needs the right healthcare.
“Cuba will not accept him as a deportee, and we now have proof that Mexico will not accept him as a deportee because he is so sick. And so they told him that because he could not be accepted at either of those two countries, ‘Oh well, we’re going to have to send you to Africa’.
“They told him that Mexico would not accept him because he has too many medications that he requires, and so they said, ‘Well, we have to deport you anyway’. We’re left with the uncertainty of not knowing how he is, or if we’ll see him again.”
Shalyn Fluharty, an immigration rights attorney, said information from the detainees indicated deportation flights were imminent.
“We understand that just this week, within a couple of days, likely Thursday and Friday, there will be two flights going to Africa, in particular to the Central African Republic, and we also believe Burundi,” she said.
Fluharty said previously deported immigrants were shackled at their hands, ankles and waists during lengthy flights, and some who complained were placed in full body wraps with no ability to move.
“This is what we anticipate will be happening this week for these individuals, based upon what we’ve seen in the past,” she said.
“Travel can last sometimes up to 24 hours. What if you’re somebody who has a heart condition? Who has a high risk of stroke? Who is experiencing diabetes and requires regular access to food or insulin? These conditions take your already vulnerable medical state and make them, unfortunately, often life-threatening.”
Responding to a request for comment, a spokesperson for the homeland security department demanded to know the affected detainees’ personal information. The department did not respond further when provided with Sendra’s details.
Betancourt said families risked retaliation for their relatives by coming forward. “This is not a single one-off story,” she said.
“The inspector general’s report confirmed that there is a lack of medical care inside of the Krome detention facility. Families have been demanding oversight, and every day they are experiencing real fear to speak up and advocate for their loved ones.”
During two unannounced visits to Krome in May, government inspectors found multiple violations of noncompliance with detention standards, including severe overcrowding. Holding 1,102 detainees in a facility with a maximum capacity of 882, the report said, “jeopardizes the safe and orderly operations within the facility”.
Other listed violations included an inadequate number of operational toilets, sinks, and showers, and previous complaints included female detainees made to use toilets in full view of men, and arriving detainees held for more than 24 hours in a bus in the parking lot because of a lack of space.
Advocates say Donald Trump’s massive second term immigration crackdown has caused overcrowding in detention centers nationwide that DHS has attempted to alleviate by ramping up deportation flights to so-called third countries.
The controversial practice, approved by the US supreme court last month, has seen hundreds of detainees deported to at least a dozen African countries where they have no ties.
A Human Rights Watch report earlier this month found countless examples of abusive treatment during and after the flights, and detainees subjected to persecution, arbitrary incarceration and torture following their arrival.

The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.
It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”
The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.
The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.
The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.
It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.
The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.
Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.
“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.
The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).
“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”
Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.
“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.
“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.
The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.
It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.
Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.
“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”
Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.
“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

Tonbo Imaging’s promoters and investors have realised substantial gains from the company’s IPO, which closed earlier this week post witnessing an overwhelming demand from investors. The company’s three cofounders — CEO Arvind Lakshmikumar, CBO Ankit Kumar and chief commercial officer (CCO) Cecilia D’Souza — collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr from the defence tech company’s ₹852 Cr IPO. CEO Lakshmikumar raked in ₹80.5 Cr by offloading 11.5 Lakh shares at the upper end of the ₹665-700 price band. He continues to hold around 38.18 Lakh shares, making him one of the largest shareholders of Tonbo Imaging. Cofounder Kumar, who serves as the CBO and CRO of Tonbo, offloaded 5.8 Lakh shares worth ₹40.6 Cr and continues to hold 24.6 Lakh shares. Meanwhile CCO D’Souza, offloaded around 2.3 Lakh shares for ₹16.1 Cr. The largest selling shareholders in Tonbo Imaging’s IPO were its related entities, Bengaluru-based CEAQ Technologies Pvt Ltd and Singapore-based CEAQ Technologies Pte Ltd. The cofounders are the directors of these aforementioned entities as well. While CEAQ Technologies Pvt Ltd offloaded its entire shareholding of around 50 Lakh shares for ₹350 Cr, the Singapore-based entity sold 41.6 Cr shares to rake in ₹291 Cr. The Singapore-based entity continues to retain 1.05 Cr post the IPO. Early Investors Cash In Among other shareholders, Artiman, an early-stage sector agnostic venture fund, has made ₹13.8 Cr by selling 2 Lakh shares, clocking a return multiple of 4.8X on its investment. It will retain another 2 Lakh shares, valued at ₹13.8 Cr at the upper price band. Amit Dilip Shah, who is a partner at Artiman, individually sold 84,000 shares for ₹5.9 Cr at ₹700 apiece, translating to a 4.1X return, while his remaining 1.4 Lakh shares are worth ₹9.8 Cr. Ramesh Radhakrishnan, also a partner at Artiman, offloaded 80,000 shares for ₹5.6 Cr, realising a 4.8X return on his initial investment. He will retain 1.2 Lakh shares valued at ₹8.7 Cr. Promoter group entity Vinimaya Advisory LLP sold 3.4 Lakh shares for ₹23.8 Cr, implying a 3.6X return multiple. It will retain 3.2 Lakh shares worth ₹22.4 Cr. Tonbo’s Road To The Bourses The trio cofounded the defence tech company in 2003 as a defense electronics and embedded vision business. The company grew into a major global OEM for thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, and missile guidance systems serving government agencies, military organisations, and defense contractors across 24 countries. The company's operating revenue declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit fell to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year. In Q1 FY27, the company reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr. The Indian government is a primary customer, making up 71% of Tonbo's revenue in FY26. Tonbo Imaging’s ₹852 Cr IPO consisted entirely of an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares, with no fresh issue component. The IPO valued the company at ₹4,009.8 Cr (about $480 Mn) at the upper end of the price band. The IPO closed for subscription on October 19 with a 136X oversubscription. Investors bidding for 115.87 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer. The allotment of shares materialised today. Ahead of the IPO, Tonbo Imaging allotted 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 anchor investors raising ₹255.4 Cr. 12 domestic mutual funds, SBI Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund, Mirae Asset, anchored the IPO.

A disability rights group has written to the Central government seeking the classification of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices and prostheses as essential assistive products under the draft Rights of Persons with Disabilities (Amendment) Rules, 2026.
Doctors with Disabilities: Agents of Change (DwDAoC), an organisation of health professionals with disabilities, said in its communication that the Centre should classify communication aids and prostheses as essential products.
In a representation to the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the group noted that these products, put in the specialised assistive products category, could create uncertainty over access to insurance coverage, public financing, replacement and maintenance.
The draft rules, issued under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, propose a framework for standards and accessibility of assistive products and technology. The notification follows a Supreme Court directive calling for clear, non-negotiable accessibility requirements under Section 40 of the Act. The draft invites objections and suggestions before finalisation.
AAC devices include picture-based communication boards, speech-generating devices and applications that convert text or symbols into speech. In its representation, DwDAoC argued that the need for specialist assessment, customisation, fitting or rehabilitation should not determine whether a product is essential. It called for the classification to reflect the role assistive products play in enabling autonomy, participation and the exercise of rights.
The group said the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, recognise augmentative and alternative modes of communication. It also cited the World Health Organisation’s Priority Assistive Products List, which it said includes communication aids and artificial limbs, and ICMR’s National List of Essential Assistive Products (NLEAP), 2023, which has prostheses among its prioritised products.
DwDAoC urged the government to align the draft rules with these frameworks and consult AAC users, prosthesis users and other persons with disabilities before finalising the rules. It has urged the government to ensure equitable access to assistive products, regardless of the complexity of the services required to provide them.

WHO and Switzerland have announced the renewal of their cooperation strategy for the period 2024-2028. In 2013, Switzerland became the first high-income country in the WHO European Region to pilot a cooperation strategy with WHO (hereafter referred to as the WHO-Switzerland Cooperation Strategy). In 2022, WHO and Switzerland jointly decided to update and renew this cooperation strategy, which was done on 4 March 2025 at the Regional Office of the WHO in Copenhagen, Denmark.

Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.
Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.
What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.
What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.
Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.
So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

IPS officer Sumit Jha became a recurring figure on social media during students' protests over the NEET examination in June-July, and later in October when the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) called for large-scale demonstrations in Delhi against Chief Minister Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Many on social media circulated a "fake" video showing Jha announcing his resignation from his post as Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP), Delhi Police, amid the protests. However, the Delhi Police had dispelled the rumours in July. It fact-checked the video clip and clarified on July 28, "The viral video claiming Delhi Police DCP Sumit Jha resigned over student protests is completely fake and AI generated." In the original video posted on July 23, Sumit Jha appealed “to students and youth to be wary of such foreign accounts spreading rumours to mislead the situation.” He stated in the video message that “480 Pakistan-based social media handles involved in coordinated misinformation campaigns were identified and blocked.” This video of Jha, posted by the Delhi Police's X handle on July 23, was altered using AI to show Jha announcing that he has stepped down from the Delhi Police service amid the protest. The fabricated video showed him saying, "I was being pressured to lie about the student protests. I won't lie anymore, so I'm resigning." On July 28, the Delhi Police fact-checked the video and dismissed it as fake. The viral post reportedly resurfaced during the CJP's October protest. The misleading content was uploaded on Facebook, Instagram and X, prompting the police to take up the matter with the platforms, officials told news agency PTI. Kara Swisher on Elon Musk: 'He's unelected, unaccountable, enormously wealthy'
Elon Musk says Tesla and SpaceX are exploring a possible merger, a move that could bring two of his biggest companies under one roof. But what is the business case for combining an electric vehicle manufacturer with a space and artificial intelligence company?
Longtime tech journalist Kara Swisher, who hosts the podcasts On and Pivot, spoke with Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep about Musk's expanding business empire and political influence.
"He's got to do something with Tesla as it descends downward," Swisher said, pointing to growing competition from Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers.
She argued that Musk missed an opportunity to develop an affordable electric car while competitors such as China's BYD expanded globally.
Swisher said data, AI and connectivity are increasingly central to Musk's businesses, though she questioned whether demand for computing power would hold up if the AI boom falters.
Swisher also discussed what Musk could face if Democrats regain control of Congress, as the billionaire spends hundreds of millions of dollars supporting Republican candidates.
"They could look into what happened at DOGE. I'd start there," Swisher said, referring to the Department of Government Efficiency. She also pointed to previous investigations involving Tesla crashes.
The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk ordered a slowdown of military-grade Starlink service used by Ukrainian forces, disrupting drone operations and air defenses. The decision reportedly caught Ukrainian officials and some in the Trump administration by surprise.
According to the same report by the WSJ, Musk said restrictions on the satellite network are determined by the U.S. military and ultimately the president. But Trump said he did not know who was responsible, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration had neither requested the slowdown nor known about it in advance.
"One single person who happens to be the world's richest man should not be making wartime decisions or decisions about our defense or anything else like that," Swisher said.
"He's unelected, unaccountable, enormously wealthy," she added. "One single person who has no guardrails on him to be able to make these decisions that results in the deaths of people across the globe."
NPR has repeatedly sought comment from Musk, who has a standing invitation to speak with the network. NPR also reached out to SpaceX for comment on this story.

The sale of books has emerged as the latest political flashpoint in West Bengal, with under-construction book stalls run by Left parties allegedly vandalised in Kolkata’s Dhakuria and elsewhere, amid chief minister Suvendu Adhikari’s call to deny the CPI(M) space at Durga Puja venues.
The alleged attack in Dhakuria on Wednesday left senior activists of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation and local Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M), workers injured. The structure of a book stall being set up by the Communist Party of India (CPI) was also vandalised.
The incidents come weeks after Adhikari, on September 10, urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for book stalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated the position two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Left-wing parties have been setting up book stalls during Durga Puja and other festivals in Bengal for decades. The practice dates back to 1954, when the undivided CPI set up the first festive book stall in Park Circus under the leadership of communist leader Muzaffar Ahmed.
Despite repeated electoral setbacks since 2011, the CPI(M) continues to have a network of festive book stalls across the state. The CPI, CPI(ML) Liberation and the Socialist Unity Centre of India (Communist), or SUCI(C), also set up stalls according to their organisational strength. Such stalls are set up during Kali Puja, Christmas and Eid as well.
In recent years, the Trinamool Congress, the BJP, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and its affiliated organisations have also begun setting up book stalls. However, the public call by a sitting chief minister to deny Left parties space at festive venues marks an unprecedented escalation in the dispute.
Attack on Book Stall in Dhakuria
According to eyewitness accounts, the CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI have been setting up book stalls near the Dhakuria bus stand during Durga Puja for decades. On Wednesday, around 5.30 pm, a group of 10 to 12 men arrived while CPI(ML) Liberation workers were supervising the construction of their stall. The men allegedly ordered them to stop work, identified themselves as BJP-RSS workers and demanded that the site be vacated, claiming they intended to set up their own stall at the same location.
Manas Chatterjee, also known as Babun, a member of the CPI(ML) Liberation’s Kolkata district committee, said the party had been operating its book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since at least 1985.
“From the very beginning, the body language of the group was extremely hostile. They said that beef is consumed at our book stall and that they would not allow us to set up our stall this time,” Chatterjee said.
According to him, the group claimed to have permission from the police to set up a stall at the same location and demanded that the Left workers produce their own permission. “When I confronted them, asking who they were to demand such permission, they said that their ‘Raj’ had started and that now everything had to be done according to their whims,” he said.
Chatterjee alleged that the group repeatedly claimed to have permission from the joint commissioner of Kolkata Police and said this entitled them to set up a stall wherever they wanted.
When Chatterjee tried to prevent the group from tearing down a hammer-and-sickle flag, he was allegedly assaulted. Between 10 and 15 youths pinned him to the road and kicked and punched him on his waist and chest, he said. The under-construction stall was subsequently ransacked and uprooted.
Chatterjee alleged that police personnel were present near the site, but left when the assault began.
Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old CPI(ML) Liberation activist, was also allegedly assaulted when he tried to protect Chatterjee.
As the confrontation escalated, local CPI(M) leader Achyut Chakraborty intervened. He alleged that members of the group splashed hot tea on him and assaulted him.
Chakraborty said the CPI(M) had been setting up a book stall at the Dhakuria bus stand since 1977, with the CPI and CPI(ML) Liberation subsequently joining the practice.
“What happened this year is unprecedented,” he said. According to Chakraborty, the group aggressively demanded to see police permission for the stalls and began assaulting Left workers when questioned about its authority to do so.
He alleged that the BJP workers initially outnumbered the Left activists after mobilising around 40 to 50 people over the phone. Party workers and local residents then gathered at the spot, but the Left workers tried to prevent the confrontation from escalating further.
“Book stalls during the puja have always been a defining feature of the festive season in West Bengal. The BJP’s fascist brigade is vandalising such stalls. At a book stall near Dhakuria bridge in Kolkata, our local committee secretary and State Committee member Comrade Babun Chatterjee has been seriously injured by the fascist goons. Veteran octogenarian Comrade AB Chowdhury has also been beaten up. Condemn this fascist assault on comrades and on the progressive cultural tradition of West Bengal,” CPI(ML) general secretary Dipankar Bhattacharya said in a Facebook post.
Police Permission Becomes a Point of Contention
Following the incident, CPI(M), CPI(ML) Liberation and CPI workers approached Lake police station to lodge a complaint. According to the Left parties, police said the stalls did not have the required permission and that, since the parties had only informed the police about their plans to set them up, and not sought formal permission, the police could not intervene.
Chakraborty said the police repeatedly asked whether the parties had obtained permission from the joint commissioner of police. “It intrigued us that the tone of the BJP workers and the police sounded similar on this issue,” he said.
The Left parties maintain that the land belongs to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC), to which they have paid the required fees to set up their stalls. They said the established practice has been to inform the local police station rather than obtain police permission, and that this arrangement has been followed for close to 50 years.
Chakraborty said police were unable to produce a notification establishing that the rules had changed and that prior police permission was now mandatory.
According to CPI(M) and CPI(ML) Liberation leaders, the issue of police permission has not arisen in other parts of Kolkata, where stalls have been set up after informing the police.
On Thursday, Left party workers marched from the Dhakuria bus stand to Lake Police Station. The rally was attended by CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh, former CPI councillor from KMC Ward 92 Madhuchanda Deb and CPI leader Prabir Deb, among others.
Police, however, maintained that the stalls lacked the required permission and that they could not assist the parties because the joint commissioner had not approved them.
“It won’t be an overstatement to say that the Lake Police Station tried using the BJP workers, who are mostly outsiders, to heckle us so that the stalls would not come up,” he said.
Alt News contacted Lake police station, but officials declined to comment. The Left parties said their stalls would be inaugurated on Friday despite the dispute.
Voice of Opposition Should not be Suppressed: HC
The Dhakuria incident is not the only controversy involving Left party book stalls. The CPI(M) has also reportedly faced opposition to setting up stalls in other places in the state. According to a report in Anandabazar Patrika, similar incidents have been reported from Behala and Kasba in Kolkata, Shibpur in Howrah, Naihati in North 24 parganas and elsewhere.
The CPI(M) approached the Calcutta high court on Wednesday in this regard. In their petition, the party mentioned an incident of October 6 in Bongaon. As the party started work for building a book stall there, people allegedly from Hindu Jagran Mancha stopped them. Left workers were allegedly assaulted and threatened against putting up the stall.
Justice Sougata Bhattacharya, hearing the petition, sought the police’s response and observed that the state could not “pick and choose” while granting permission. The opposition could not be denied permission in a manner that effectively stifled its activities, the court said.
“It is not right to allow one party and deny permission to others. The voice of an Opposition political party should not be suppressed in this manner. They are not setting up a lottery shop; they want to sell books. What is the problem?” Justice Bhattacharyya observed.
The state subsequently approached a division bench, arguing that the proposed stall was to be set up on Public Works Department land without permission and that a report should be sought from the department rather than the police. On Thursday, the division bench sent the matter back to Justice Bhattacharya.
Later that day, Justice Bhattacharya directed that the CPI(M) be allowed to set up its book stall within 100 metres of the intended location. The court held that the police would be responsible for dealing with any untoward incident and assigned responsibility for maintaining law and order around the stall to the superintendent of police of Bongaon Police District and the inspector-in-charge of Bongaon.
In its order, the court observed that if other people were allowed to set up stalls selling different items during the festive season, the CPI(M) should not be prevented from selling books.
It added that the dissemination of different political thoughts and ideologies was welcome in a democracy because it made democracy “fruitful, deep-rooted and matured”. The court also said it expected the ruling dispensation to create an atmosphere in which people aligned with different political ideologies would not hesitate to express their views.

WASHINGTON – U.S. President Donald Trump’s moves in recent weeks to ease economic pressure on Russia while stepping up criticism of Ukraine have triggered bipartisan opposition in Congress, potentially complicating his agenda after next month’s midterm elections.
Seeking to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and waived newly enacted sanctions against Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state enterprises.
At the same time, he has increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for him to be replaced as the country’s leader. A satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations was throttled following an order from inside the White House, Reuters reported last week.

Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
- Published
The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said.
The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation.
The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds".
Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.
- How US mansion of Gambia's ex-president was seized 
  - Published27 May 2022
- Profile: Former Gambian President Yahya Jammeh 
  - Published22 January 2017
On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.
It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".
Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.
He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.
Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.
In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.
A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.
There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.
Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.
A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

Food regulator FSSAI has asked food business operators (FBOs) to transport perishable items under controlled-temperature conditions across the supply chain to safeguard public health.
In a social media post on Sunday (October 18, 2026), FSSAI said it has issued an advisory on “handling, storage, and transportation of perishable foods like khoa, paneer, meat, and fish under controlled temperature conditions throughout the supply chain”.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also asked State food safety officers to maintain strict vigilance and take action if rules are not followed.
FBOs must ensure strict adherence to hygiene and temperature standards, it added.
FSSAI mentioned that it has specified hygienic and sanitary requirements for FBOs under Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.
"It has been brought to the notice of FSSAI that perishable food commodities such as khoa, paneer, meat, fish, etc., are at times not handled, stored or transported under appropriate temperature conditions," the advisory noted.
Because of their perishable nature, these food items are highly susceptible to microbial growth and spoilage if not maintained under appropriate temperature conditions.
As per the conditions laid out under licenses, FBOs are required to maintain the prescribed temperature throughout the supply chain, from procurement/sourcing to delivery to the end consumer.
"Subjecting these food products to temperature abuse may adversely affect public health and constitute non-compliance with the hygiene and sanitary requirements," the advisory said.
The regulator has asked FBOs to transport only in clean, covered, and hygienic vehicles or conveyances suitable for food transportation.
FBOs have also been told to use only food-grade packaging and suitable secondary packaging materials.
"Protect the product from dust, moisture, pests, physical damage and cross- contamination during storage, loading, unloading and transportation," FSSAI told FBOs.
Further, FBOs have been told to maintain appropriate records and traceability of consignments.
The regulator has also advised the commissioners of food safety at the state level, Indian Railways and Regional Directors of FSSAI to direct the concerned licensing authorities and food safety officers to maintain strict vigilance during inspections and transportation checks to ensure compliance with the law.
In case of non-compliance, they can initiate appropriate action, including seizure and destruction of the food items.

While security cameras are ostensibly for, well, security, they can also be super handy for making sure your kids came home at the right time, checking up on your pets when you’re away, and investigating that weird sound in the middle of the night without having to get out of your toasty bed.
I’ve tested so very, very many security cameras, and there are a few reasons I think you should snap up this particular Eufy Security Wall Light Cam S4 deal at $80 off. I’m also going to highlight a couple of other Eufy options currently on sale.
The Eufy Wall Light Cam S4 looks and acts as a modern, motion-activated wall light, perfect for illuminating a driveway, porch, or back gate, which is where I have mine (no more stubbed toes when I take out the trash at night). Eufy has also packed in a 4K camera that you can swivel to get the right angle, offering a wide, crisp view of your chosen spot. It records locally, with 32 GB of storage built-in, and it's subscription free, including the on-device AI detection, which can accurately distinguish between people, vehicles, and pets. Installation is quick and easy, and it connects directly to your Wi-Fi. You’ll just need a decent signal at your chosen spot.
To sweeten the deal, there’s a solar panel to keep the battery topped off. It sits neatly on top, but you can detach it for better placement to catch the sun’s rays. Despite being in a busy spot, mine has stayed charged for the last couple of months, though I suspect that may change as we head into winter.
What I like best about this security camera is the wall light functionality. You can set the brightness and color temperature (I like a warm light). I also love that it doesn’t scream outdoor security camera; you only notice it if you look closely.
Some downsides: the frame rate is just 15 fps, so fast-moving subjects can appear blurry, particularly in the dark (though the light helps with that). Some folks will also need to top off the battery off on occasion, so you’ll want to keep it somewhere within reach. I also feel it’s overpriced at the original $250, but at $170 ($80 off), that's less of an issue.
If you need an indoor camera, the Eufy S350 is also on sale right now at $100 ($40 off), and it’s a wonderfully versatile, feature-packed, dual-lens camera. It even has automatic tracking, making it ideal for checking in on your cat or dog throughout the day. It regularly dips down to this price, so you might want to wait for Black Friday, when I predict it will drop another $20.
The EufyCam C35 2-Cam Kit at $130 ($70 off) is also worth considering right now. These cameras work inside or out with an easy magnetic mount and come with a handy HomeBase Mini for local recording and onboard AI that includes facial recognition. This is a common discount, but it's still a great deal for a two-camera kit with hub.
