A day after the Old Rao Tula Ram (RTR) flyover ramp was closed for structural safety repairs, long queues of vehicles and traffic congestion on National Highway-48 (NH-48) left commuters stranded for hours on Thursday, affecting traffic between Gurugram and Delhi.
New Delhi Traffic Deputy Commissioner of Police Vikas Kumar said the congestion on NH-48 was a spillover effect of the flyover closure, as commuters who previously used the flyover switched to alternative routes.
“People who were earlier using the Old RTR flyover are now using other routes, including NH-48. With this, the load has increased significantly, causing congestion. The flyover was helping commuters bypass several junctions, and its closure has led to traffic pile-ups at multiple junctions also, with Mahipalpur being the worst affected area,” he said.
The congestion added at least 35 minutes to journey times, with vehicle queues stretching up to 1.5 km and backing up towards Gurugram, Mr. Kumar said.
The Old RTR flyover ramp, which handles an average of two lakh vehicles a day, was closed for urgent repairs to a damaged road surface. The situation worsened during the evening peak hours as employees returned from Gurugram to Delhi.
Commuters took to social media platform X to share photographs and videos of long queues, with some reporting that ambulances were stuck amid the congestion. Several said journeys that would ordinarily take a little over an hour had stretched to more than two hours.
“It is taking over one and a half hours to cover a 20-km stretch from Cyber Hub in Gurugram to Teen Murti in Central Delhi,” a commuter posted on X.
Another commuter said it had taken two hours to reach Connaught Place from Gurugram, blaming the congestion on NH-48 and the disruption around Dhaula Kuan.
A third commuter warned travellers to leave early to avoid missing flights, reporting that NH-48 had remained choked for hours. “It’s been 3 hours since it has been choked and the cops have hundreds of trucks on the highway,” the commuter said.
Another commuter said ambulances were stuck in traffic and unable to move. “There were trucks and goods carriers everywhere; I could see at least 25 from my car alone. Restricting their movement during the day could have made a significant difference,” the commuter said.
Mr. Kumar said the Delhi Traffic Police had informed the Gurugram Police to prevent heavy vehicles from entering the affected stretch. Additional traffic personnel had been deployed at several junctions, including Mahipalpur and along NH-48, to regulate traffic and ease congestion.
The Public Works Department (PWD) had initially said that the repair work would be completed by Thursday morning. However, Mr. Kumar said on Thursday night that the work was still under way and was expected to be completed by Friday. The ramp will remain closed for 48 hours after the repairs are completed to allow the concrete to cure and develop adequate strength.

Two more original Glee cast members are eyeing a return for the Disney+/Hulu reboot. Heather Morris, who portrayed ditzy, high-spirited cheerleader Brittany, and Chord Overstreet, who played Sam Evans in the original series are in talks to return for the reboot, sources have confirmed to Deadline.
Overstreet’s Sam Evans was a transfer student to William McKinley High School, who joined the football team and the school’s glee club, New Directions.
They join Lea Michele, who we reported Wednesday is in talks to reprise her Rachel Berry character from the OG.
Disney+ and Hulu announced a series order for the reboot earlier this week.
Watch on Deadline
Co-creator Ryan Murphy said last month that he had been in touch with “around 10 of the original cast members” of the show, though no casting was announced as part of the series order.
The original Glee cast included Chris Colfer, Jane Lynch, Kevin McHale and Matthew Morrison as well as Dianna Agron, Cory Monteith, Amber Riley, Mark Salling, the late Naya Rivera and Darren Criss.
Set at William McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio, Glee followed the members of the New Directions, a glee club competing in the show choir circuit, while dealing with social issues. Each episode featured a musical performance.
The reboot hails from original show producer 20th Television.
The original Glee, created by Murphy, Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan, aired for six seasons from 2009-2015, on Fox. It won six Emmys, including for Murphy and Lynch as well as guest stars such as Neil Patrick Harris and Gwyneth Paltrow, and currently streams on Hulu.

After losing 60 pounds on weight-loss drugs over the past year, Atlanta resident Lorraine Scott faced a common wardrobe dilemma.
"Most of the things in my closet didn't fit anymore," said the 42-year-old, who is known to her YouTube followers as Lorraine Kamesha. Rather than buying an entirely new wardrobe while her weight fluctuates, Scott has spent at least $300 tailoring her favorite jeans and pants, turning to fast fashion for the remainder of her clothing.
Across the United States, consumers taking weight-loss medications such as Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro are turning to tailors and cobblers to save money as they lose weight.
The shift is driven in part by broader cost-of-living pressures and rising out-of-pocket expenses for the medications, as more US employers reduce insurance coverage for GLP-1 treatments.
Over the past year, leather repair specialists have seen a sharp increase in demand for their services as people lose weight quickly. Requests extend beyond belt alterations to include adjustments for shoe and handbag straps tailored to fit customers' trimmer bodies.
This uptick in demand illustrates how weight-loss drugs are reshaping the retail market, benefiting specific service industries while traditional clothing retailers adapt.
According to Gallup, roughly 11% of US adults are taking GLP-1 medications to lose weight, leading millions of consumers to seek budget-friendly options to update their wardrobes.
Cobblers Direct, an online footwear and handbag repair business with 25 storefronts in Texas and a nationwide mail-in operation, has recorded double-digit year-over-year growth in belt shortening, according to CEO Stephen Kelly.
The company, whose team of around 100 craftspeople will soon move into a new 30,000-square-foot facility in Austin, is currently shortening up to 500 belts each week, Kelly said.
He noted that customers regularly enter stores carrying five or six belts across their shoulders. After having additional holes punched, some clients ask to keep the trimmed leather remnant as a "badge of honor."
"They'll pull their belt out and show how long their belt originally was. And then they tuck it back into their waistline," Kelly said.
According to a survey of more than 700 US adults on weight-loss drugs conducted by telehealth platform Trimi, about 80% of GLP-1 users continue wearing clothes that no longer fit, waiting an average of six months before buying replacement items. Jeans are the most affected clothing item, with 90% of respondents reporting a poor fit.
Reluctance to purchase a new closet is further reinforced by University of Cambridge research released this year, which found that patients regain an average of 60% of their lost weight within a year of stopping the medications.
At family-owned Jim's Cobbler Concierge in Manhattan, clients began bringing in belts by the dozen last year, according to client relations director CJ Burgos — a trend the shop named "belt-zempic." Burgos noted that GLP-1 users are also experiencing reductions in foot size, leading to more footwear adjustments.
"It's helped the business, but we've also helped clients save," said Burgos, who has altered his own belts after losing about 60 pounds using Ozempic.
The rising popularity of GLP-1 drugs in the US is also driving business for thrift stores, discount chains, and secondhand clothing platforms, as consumers refrain from spending on new garments while their sizing remains unpredictable.
What sets GLP-1s apart from other commercial tailwinds is "the scale and speed," said Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at online thrift platform ThredUp.
Shoppers are actively transitioning to smaller sizes, particularly when purchasing denim: 43% of buyers who started above a waist size 28 are now purchasing smaller jeans than when they registered with ThredUp, Rotem noted.
Online personal styling company Stitch Fix is introducing expanded adjustable sizing and stretch fabrics so that clients undergoing rapid weight loss have the "right apparel to help them bridge multiple sizes," said CEO Matt Baer.
He estimated that at least 20% of the platform's new customers are taking a GLP-1 medication and seeking assistance with finding updated sizes.
"We've always known that resale and thrift are very popular choices for people in life transition," said Rotem of ThredUp. "As we see that there are many more people in life transition with the advent of GLP-1s, we're leaning into that."

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.
“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.
The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

Eight private keys underpinning part of listed digital trust company eMudhra’s certificate infrastructure were so weak that researchers could recover them from publicly available certificates. The discovery prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft to block the affected certificates, triggering a wider effort to protect browsers, applications, and enterprise systems. The incident also rattled investors. eMudhra shares hit their 20% lower circuit at ₹431.55 on the BSE today. The immediate concern is whether software still trusting the compromised keys could accept fraudulent certificates. A related challenge is replacing legitimate certificates affected by browser makers’ decision to withdraw trust in a parent certificate. Here is what happened, how the flaw arose, and what it means for businesses. What Happened In The eMudhra Security Incident? Digital trust company eMudhra disclosed that eight of its digital certificate authorities had a serious security flaw after a researcher discovered that their private keys could be reconstructed from publicly available certificates. The keys were not stolen from eMudhra's systems but instead generated using extremely small numbers that were easy to guess. The eight values were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The discovery prompted major technology companies, including Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft, to block or distrust the affected certificates. The incident has also raised concerns about the security of systems that rely on digital certificates to establish trust online. What Is eMudhra And Its Significance In The Digital Ecosystem? BSE-listed eMudhra provides digital identity, authentication and security solutions to businesses, financial institutions and governments. Its services include digital signature certificates (DSCs), electronic signatures and tools that help organisations secure digital transactions and manage identities. In India, its DSCs are used for activities such as filing documents with government portals, including GST, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and income tax systems. Its eSign services also support paperless digital workflows. The company operates internationally as well, providing digital certificates that help websites establish secure connections with users by acquiring digital certificates. eMudhra said the incident affected its global website-security business, not its Indian DSC and eSign operations. Its Indian services run on separate infrastructure and continue to operate normally, according to the company. How Were Keys Weakened? The problem began during a key-generation ceremony on April 30, 2025. According to eMudhra, a flaw in the process created a second set of weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. Staff mistakenly used the weak keys when preparing the certificates, and the company is still investigating the exact error. On October 17, 2026, a researcher identified as Wayne discovered that he could reconstruct the private keys from publicly available certificates. He demonstrated control over each key by signing a message with it and reported the findings to browser security teams. Mozilla independently recovered the same keys on the day of the report, confirming the vulnerability. The eight affected keys included six used for website security and two intended for code signing. What Has eMudhra Said About The Incident & Its Impact? eMudhra said its core infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached, and its physical and digital security controls remained intact. The company said the incident was confined to eight intermediate certificate authorities and did not affect its root CA private keys or other intermediate authorities. It also said none of the eight affected authorities had issued certificates to end users or websites, an assessment it said was supported by public records of issued certificates. The affected global TLS business contributes around 1% of eMudhra's revenue. However, the company acknowledged that the reputational impact could not yet be quantified. eMudhra said it was working with customers who might be affected to provide replacement certificates and prevent disruptions to critical services. Its investigation into the root cause and security controls is ongoing. How Could Compromised Keys Affect The Internet's Security Infrastructure? Digital certificates help browsers establish whether a website is what it claims to be. They are a key part of the security system that allows users to connect to websites over HTTPS. If someone obtains a certificate authority’s private key, they may be able to create fraudulent certificates that make an unauthorised website appear legitimate. In certain circumstances, this could enable an attacker to impersonate a website and intercept or modify communications. There is no public evidence establishing that the compromised keys were used in a successful malicious attack Google said no certificates issued through the six affected website-security authorities appeared in public Certificate Transparency logs before the company blocked them. Chrome requires such records for publicly trusted certificates, helping prevent fraudulent certificates from being accepted by the browser. Other software, including applications and devices that do not enforce the same checks or use updated certificate lists, could face different risks. India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned that the compromised code-signing keys could be used to make malicious software appear to have been signed by a trusted publisher, extending the potential risk to software whose authenticity is verified through digital signatures. It asked organisations to consider applications, servers and devices that rely on certificate trust stores. How Have Technology Companies Responded? Technology companies have moved to block the affected certificates and update their systems. Mozilla: Blocked the certificates in Firefox within hours of receiving the report. It also released browser updates and is updating its wider certificate store to protect other applications. Google: Blocked the affected keys in Chrome and took additional steps to remove the eMudhra’s root certificate authority from its Chrome Root Store. The removal is scheduled to reach supported Chrome devices on October 27, 2026. Apple And Microsoft: Took steps to distrust the affected certificates through their respective security and certificate-trust programmes. Cloudflare: Updated critical services, shared certificate stores and products including Cloudflare One and Cloudflare Tunnel. The company said its investigation had not identified active exploitation of the vulnerability on its own services. These measures are intended to prevent systems from trusting certificates linked to the compromised keys. However, organisations using separate or outdated certificate stores may still need to update their software and infrastructure. What Should Businesses & Developers Do To Mitigate The Risk? Businesses should check whether their websites and applications rely on the affected certificates and follow the relevant software vendors' advisories. Google has asked website operators using certificates linked to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, which is eMudhra’s root certificate authority, to obtain and install replacement Transport Layer Security certificates from another trusted certificate authority before Chrome removes the root from its trust store on October 27. Developers and IT teams should also update affected certificate stores, software dependencies and applications. Cloudflare has warned that applications using their own certificate stores may require separate remediation, including rebuilding or redeploying affected systems. Developers should not disable certificate verification to work around resulting errors, as this would remove the security protection the updates are intended to restore. What Happens Next? The incident has prompted scrutiny of eMudhra’s wider certificate infrastructure. Google said it is reviewing whether the company’s remaining certificate authorities should continue to be trusted by Chrome. eMudhra is still investigating how its key-generation process produced weak keys and why they were used in the certificates. Another unresolved question is whether the keys were accessed or misused by anyone else before the affected certificates were revoked. The issue has also snowballed into a wider debate about the viability of digital trust infrastructures. The Internet Freedom Foundation today said it is preparing representations for the IT ministry, the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) and CERT-In regarding the vulnerability.

The Best Phones You Can’t Buy in the US
Featured in this article
There’s a world of excellent phones—flagship smartphones that push photography to new levels, and budget buys that defy expectations—that you won’t find in the US for various reasons. Some Chinese phone manufacturers are banned domestically, while other brands prefer to focus their efforts in countries where Apple doesn’t have a massive market share. Whatever the explanation, I have a strong grasp of the best phones you can’t officially buy in the US, having tested global handsets for years.
Many of these phone manufacturers release multiple devices under sub-brands. With that in mind, here’s some basic information: Xiaomi is the brand behind Poco and Redmi; Nubia came from ZTE; Honor was a subsidiary of Huawei but separated after Huawei was banned in the US; and Realme spun out of Oppo. Folks in the UK and elsewhere in Europe can buy many of the phones in our guides to the Best Android Phones, Best iPhones, and Best Cheap Phones that are for sale in the US.
Updated October 2026: I added the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, Nothing Phone (4b), mentions of the TCL P80 Ultra, Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra and Pro, and Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro Max, and removed some older devices.
Other Good International Phones
Haven’t seen anything you like? The following phones are also worth considering:
TCL P80 Ultra for £480: I love that the 6.8-inch AMOLED screen transforms into an e-ink screen at the flick of a switch; it’s also wonderfully matte, even in AMOLED mode, which makes it more comfortable to read for hours than most phone screens. TCL has also packed in a versatile camera, including a decent telephoto lens, and solid battery life. But the plain design and occasional sluggishness make it a tough sell at this price. If reading is your main priority, the compromises may be worth it.
Xiaomi Poco F9 Ultra for £999 and F9 Pro for £799: This year's unfortunate price jump, combined with Xiaomi's weird pricing (low early-bird prices and frequent discounts, but very high MSRPs), makes these phones tough to recommend. Both are actually very good, with lovely displays, good battery life and performance, great stereo speakers, and versatile triple-lens cameras. Naturally, the Ultra is slightly bigger and better. Sadly, they signal a major departure from Poco’s budget roots, but if you see them discounted (I’ve seen the Ultra for £669 and the Pro for £579), they are worth considering.
Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 Pro Max for £499: With a huge battery that easily lasts two days, a big screen, great build quality, and impressive durability, the Redmi Note 17 Pro Max makes a strong first impression. Performance is mediocre, the camera is limited, and it’s packed with bloatware. Unless battery life is your top priority, I’d pick something else.
Honor Magic 8 Pro for £894: This phone boasts excellent camera performance and AI assistance across the board, with a raft of refinements over Honor’s Magic 7 Pro. Its slimmed-down design with subtle curves makes it a pleasure to handle, and Honor has managed to pack in a much larger silicon-carbon battery. The versatile camera also zooms farther (3.7X optical zoom) and handles low light and shaky hands with aplomb (night photography is especially strong). That said, the image processing can be heavy-handed at times. The 6.71-inch screen is gorgeous, razor-sharp, and gets very bright. Honor’s Magic OS 10 is seriously slick on top of Android 16, and Honor AI genuinely adds value, from photo editing to contextual task handling; you can bring it to life with the dedicated AI button. There’s also support for Google Gemini, if you prefer. This is definitely not a phone for AI skeptics. Throw in secure face unlock, incredibly fast wired (100 watts) and wireless charging (80 watts) with the right gear, plus seven years of Android and security patch updates, and you get a supremely sophisticated smartphone with very few discernible weaknesses. But with its successor due to land shortly, you should only snag this right now if you can get a decent discount.
Xiaomi Poco X8 Pro for $390 (£479) and Poco X8 Pro Max for $510 (£599): If anything, a slight step down from the now-discontinued F7, the X8 sports a smaller 6.59-inch AMOLED screen, a MediaTek Dimensity 8500 Ultra chipset, and 8 GB of RAM in the basic model. Performance is solid (though it’s worth noting I used a 12-GB RAM review unit). And the slightly smaller body is a touch easier to handle. You get a big 6,500-mAh battery with plenty of stamina, plus 100-watt charging that gets you back to full in under an hour. The main camera is a solid 50-MP shooter, though the 8-MP ultrawide and 20-MP front-facing cameras aren’t great. I like the mint green model, but it also comes in black or white. There’s still too much bloatware to deal with, and Xiaomi’s software is not my favorite, but you get decent support, including four Android versions and six years of security updates. There’s no wireless charging, but that’s par for the course in this bracket. Overall, the Poco X8 Pro is the best phone for its price. If battery life is a priority, consider the X8 Pro Max, which jumps up to 8,500 mAh. It also has a bigger screen, a better processor, and Wi-Fi 7 support.
Xiaomi 17T for £649 and 17T Pro for $780: Without Honor’s aggressively low pricing, one of these phones (probably the 17T) would have claimed the best mid-range spot above. Compared with the Honor 600, the 17T offers slightly better performance with more RAM and a more reliable camera that has superior zoom capability. Unfortunately, it also comes with a lot of bloatware, and the software needs some tinkering to get the best it offers. The 17T Pro adds wireless charging, a bigger battery, much better performance with a faster chipset, and a larger screen—but it’s even more expensive, pushing the top end of what I’d consider midrange.
Oppo Find N6 for $1,899: Touting an 8.12-inch display, the Find N6 is a beautifully engineered folding phone that’s impossibly slim and light. Despite its creaseless promise, the fold is still discernible. You’ll hardly notice it with the screen on, but you’ll feel it if you use the optional stylus. Performance is impressively slick, with enough stamina to see you through a busy day, and the camera system is excellent. It’s a big step up from last year’s N5, with a 200-MP main shooter, 50-MP telephoto, and 50-MP ultrawide, though it can’t quite compete with the Xiaomi 17 Ultra above. The global model supports familiar Google apps, but you’ll have to import them, since the phone won’t officially launch in the West, which is why it can't edge out Honor’s foldable above.
Xiaomi 17 Pro Max for $1,129: The Xiaomi 17 Pro Max differs from the 17 Pro mainly with a refreshing design that adds a second, smaller screen on the back to house the camera lenses. Xiaomi offers several creative ways to use this auxiliary display, including a selfie preview for better main-camera selfies, music controls, customizable themes, and virtual pets. There’s even a retro gaming case that lets you play Angry Birds, though it feels a bit silly when there’s a 6.7-inch screen on the other side. Aside from the second screen, the 17 Pro Max is a typical Xiaomi specs beast, and the 17 Pro isn’t far behind, but neither has been officially released outside China yet.
Oppo Find X9 Pro for £1,099: Photography fans simply must check out the Oppo Find X9 Pro. The 200-megapixel telephoto lens supports 3X optical zoom and can take excellent shots at 6X zoom by cropping images down to 50 megapixels. To maximize camera capabilities, though, you’ll need the detachable Hasselblad Teleconverter Kit ($400). This enormous lens slots into place on the case and adds another 3.28X zoom, though it’s tricky to use without a tripod. An additional trio of 50-MP lenses, with all supporting 4K video recording at 60 fps with HDR, makes this a great pick for creatives. Impressive specs include a 6.78-inch flat display, IP66/68/69 ratings, and a 7,500-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’ll last for two days.
Xiaomi Poco F8 Ultra for £649 and F8 Pro for £406: Xiaomi’s cheaper, youthful brand Poco provides room for experimentation, but the company’s own 15T Pro is a better buy in this price bracket. What the F8 Ultra offers that you won’t find elsewhere is a fun (or awful, depending on your tastes) denim finish on the back. There are also Bose-tuned speakers, an excellent 6.9-inch display, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. It also has a flagship-level Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and generous RAM and storage. There’s even a trio of 50-MP lenses in the camera. The F8 Pro is slightly smaller but has similar specs, making it the better bargain.
Honor Magic 7 Pro for $985: Honor’s Magic 7 Pro features a solid triple-lens camera, a gorgeous 6.8-inch screen, speedy performance, good battery life, and dual IP68 and IP69 dust- and water-resistance ratings. Honor’s Magic OS boasts polished AI features, and Honor announced an increased commitment to seven years of Android version and security patch updates with this phone. The Magic 7 Pro’s downsides include its large camera cutout on the front, camera processing that’s sometimes heavy-handed, and an ultrawide camera that struggles to match the other two lenses.
Doro Aurora A20 for £250: Doro is a Swedish company focused on providing devices that are accessible for older folks. It primarily offers phones but also sells a decent video doorbell. The Aurora A20 is an odd spin on the flip phone that may help some people transition to a touchscreen device. It’s like an old candy bar HTC Android phone with a flip-out keypad attached to the bottom. There are lots of thoughtful features, including an alarm button, a spacious keypad, and simplified software. It’s also fairly cheap, but I found the performance sluggish, the camera poor, and the design a bit chunky and heavy.
Realme 14 Pro+ for €369: The color-changing finish may be gimmicky, but it's fun, and this phone looks and feels far more expensive than it is. There are more highs than lows on the spec sheet: You get a triple-lens camera, an IP68/69 water-resistance rating, a 6,000-mAh battery, and a 6.83-inch OLED display with a 120-Hz refresh rate. But the Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 chipset is limited, there's no wireless charging support, and you don’t get a charger in the box. Even so, it’s still quite a bargain.
Xiaomi 15 for $690: Folks seeking a compact phone could do a lot worse than the Xiaomi 15. It feels lovely and has a 6.36-inch screen, a decent triple-lens camera, and top-notch internals. But it’s a conservative design, and it has software and bloatware issues.
Honor Magic 7 RSR for £1,550: Designed with Porsche, this souped-up version of the 7 Pro above has a fancier design with a hexagonal camera module, a slightly improved telephoto lens, 24 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and a bigger battery (5,850 mAh). It’s lovely, but it doesn’t justify the extra cost.
Avoid These Phones
These aren’t necessarily bad phones, but I think you’d be better served by an option above.
Nothing Phone (3a) Lite: Nothing’s translucent hardware and pixelated software give it a retro-cool vibe, and it is currently the cheapest phone it offers in the UK (it wasn’t released in the US). The screen, battery life, and software are decent, but the camera and bloatware were disappointing. I don’t think the Nothing Phone (3a) Lite is the worst, but you can do better.
Nubia Z80 Ultra: Like my gaming pick above, the Nubia Redmagic 11S Pro, the Nubia Z80 Ultra trades a better camera for slightly lower performance and screen quality. It’s also a real brick, with an enormous camera module on the back that makes it awkward to handle, though I do like the dedicated camera button. Despite a very impressive spec sheet for the money, it manages to feel like less than the sum of its parts. Nubia’s software is subpar, and for this phone, it commits to only three years of security updates and a single Android version upgrade.
Oppo Reno 13 Pro 5G: This slim, lightweight midrange phone boasts a 6.8-inch screen (brightness is limited), a triple-lens camera (solid 50-MP main and telephoto lenses with a disappointing 8-MP ultrawide), and an impressive IP69 water-resistance rating. Battery life is good, and wired charging is fast, but there’s no wireless charging. It’s packed with bloatware, but it also adds AI features and tools for transcription, summarization, image editing, and more that may add value for some folks. After some time with the 13 Pro, I feel you can do better for the money.
Xiaomi Mix Fold 4: Officially released only in China, the Xiaomi Mix Fold 4 is a stylish folding phone with a 6.56-inch outer screen that folds open to reveal a 7.98-inch inner screen. It also offers solid performance and battery life, but despite having a large quad-lens camera module, the camera is underwhelming. The crease is also pronounced, and using a Chinese model is a bit of a pain, as various items are not translated and getting the apps you want takes work.
Realme GT7 Pro: This potential flagship killer has a 6.78-inch OLED screen, a Snapdragon 8 Elite chip, and an enormous 6,500-mAh battery. You also get a triple-lens camera, but the 50-megapixel main and telephoto lenses are let down by the 8-megapixel ultrawide. It also lacks wireless charging, and it only seems to be for sale in Germany.
Xiaomi Redmi Note 14 Pro+: Here, you get an attractive, durable design (IP68), a 200-megapixel Samsung camera sensor, and decent battery life with superfast charging (120 watts). But those wins come at the price of middling performance, poor ultrawide (8 MP) and macro (2 MP) lenses, and a ton of bloatware. Ultimately, there’s little improvement over last year’s Redmi Note 13 Pro+. Not only are there better phones for the same money, but there are also better Xiaomi phones.
Should You Import One of These Phones?
While some phones are not officially sold in the US (or certain other countries), you can still get your hands on them if you’d like. They're often easy to buy online, and you may even find some on Amazon, often via third-party sellers. But before you buy, you’ll want to consider a few factors.
Phone Model and Supported Bands
The technologies and specific bands upon which cellular networks rely differ from country to country. While models described as “global” and even specifically UK or European models are likely to work in the US, they may not support all the bands your carrier uses. Missing LTE or 5G bands can mean patchy service or even relegate you to 3G. Chinese and other country-specific models will almost certainly lack some common US bands and may not work on some carrier networks.
You will often find this information in the listing or aggregated on websites like Kimovil, but I recommend checking directly with the manufacturer and your carrier.
Customs Charges
Depending on where you buy, importing a phone can lead to customs charges and add a significant expense to the overall cost. Do your research and factor in any extra fees before you buy.
Android and Google Services
It is common for phones released only in China to ship without any Google services, including the Google Play Store. Many Chinese manufacturers have their own app stores or preinstall third-party app stores for the Chinese market. Sometimes it's a simple case of checking a box to unlock and download Google services, but it’s not always so easy.
Even where Google services are supported, some Chinese phones won’t work properly with certain apps, such as Android Auto. Lack of support can leave you stuck with specific Chinese default apps and services, and many banking apps won’t work as they would on a US or global model.
With regard to Huawei phones in particular, the company developed an independent ecosystem of apps and services following its US ban. The latest models run HarmonyOS. Although it was originally forked from the Android Open Source Project, it is now completely separate, and Huawei phones can no longer run Android apps.
How I Test Smartphones
I try to use every smartphone I test as my main phone for at least a week, sometimes longer. I stress-test performance by playing the most demanding mobile games and recording videos at the highest resolution. I make calls to test the smartphone's microphone and speaker quality.
I often test the camera side by side with a competing phone and analyze the photos on a larger, more color-accurate screen. I've been reviewing all kinds of smartphones, from budget devices to flagships, for more than a decade.

The United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed military strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, according to a report by The New York Times.
Meanwhile, Tehran has threatened to unveil a weapon it calls the “Father of All Bombs” amid escalating tensions in West Asia.
The proposed US-Israeli operation could involve a short but intensive campaign targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenal.
Citing US officials and others briefed on the deliberations, The New York Times reported that the two militaries had stepped up exercises, including flights over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres.
US war secretary Pete Hegseth also met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss the possibility of renewed strikes, according to the report.
Some US officials believe another round of attacks could push Iran's economy to the brink and pressure Tehran into making diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.
However, it remains uncertain whether US President Donald Trump will approve a fresh operation.
A White House official said the administration did not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist”, adding that Trump was keeping all options on the table to ensure Iran could not acquire nuclear weapons.
Iran threatens to unveil ‘Father of All Bombs’
Amid reports of possible renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any fresh military action.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said Iran was preparing to unveil a weapon described as the “Father of All Bombs”, according to statements carried by Iranian media outlets.
“The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them,” Mohebbi said, according to Iran's Student News Network (SNN).
In separate remarks carried by Iran's Young Journalists Club news agency, Mohebbi said, “We are in the stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs.’ This is something new for the enemy.”
He did not provide details about the weapon or explain its capabilities.
Mohebbi also said Iran's missile stockpile had increased 1.5 times following the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, without providing specific figures. He claimed that missile quality, range, destructive power and accuracy had improved significantly.
The IRGC spokesperson said Iran was moving towards a defence doctrine based on permanent deterrence and asymmetric warfare.
“Now, we say that if a country attacks us, we will not only respond but also launch an offensive,” he said.
“Our doctrine will no longer be merely offensive; it will be asymmetric. We will attack the enemy in a way that makes them feel the intensity of our response,” Mohebbi added.
Questions over possible use of ‘Mother of All Bombs’
The Iranian threat follows reports that Trump has considered using the US GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), commonly known as the “Mother of All Bombs”, against Iran's deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.
The conventional bomb weighs approximately 9,800 kg (21,600 pounds) and is among the largest non-nuclear weapons in the US arsenal. Trump authorised its first use during his initial presidential term, when it was deployed against an Islamic State tunnel complex in Afghanistan in April 2017.
However, weapons specialists have questioned whether the bomb could destroy Iran's underground nuclear facility, which is believed to be protected by layers of granite.
The MOAB explodes above ground rather than functioning as a deep-penetration weapon. Military officials have also raised concerns about its delivery, as the bomb would have to be carried by a relatively slow-flying MC-130 transport aircraft that could be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire.
A separate report by CNN last week said US military planners had developed strike options that included the potential use of the MOAB against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The report also highlighted doubts over whether the weapon could penetrate deeply enough to destroy heavily fortified underground facilities.
The bomb could cause extensive destruction at the surface but might not achieve the intended military objectives against deeply buried targets.
US builds up military presence as diplomatic efforts continue
According to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November. The planned deployment includes three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces.
The report said political considerations, including Trump's earlier pledge not to launch strikes against Iran before the midterm elections, could affect the timing of any operation.
The US and Israel reportedly came close to launching another attack earlier this month, but Trump postponed the operation shortly before it was due to begin, despite extensive preparations and heightened alert levels among their air forces.
Washington is also seeking to use the threat of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran's nuclear programme and control of the Strait of Hormuz, the report said.
Iranian negotiators, however, have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that it be addressed later in the talks.
Some US planners believe a three-day campaign could inflict enough economic damage to change Tehran's position.
However, previous US-Israeli strikes between February and April drove up energy prices and inflation worldwide, affected security across West Asia and severely strained the Pentagon's supply of missile interceptors, according to the report.
Iranian officials have warned that any renewed conflict could extend beyond commercial shipping and energy infrastructure to data centres and underwater internet cables.
Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran's negotiator General Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, rejected the prospect of a swift end to renewed hostilities.
Describing the idea that the US could conclude another round of strikes within 72 hours as a “fantasy”, Mohammadi said Iran would determine when the war would end.
“Our attacks will be more fierce, creative and different,” he said. “We are determined and confident and strong planning has been put in place.”
Pezeshkian says Iran faces a ‘super-challenge’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has described the situation as a major challenge for Tehran.
Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, “The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world.”
He added, “We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm.”
Iran's representative to the United Nations also alleged, according to SNN, that Starlink had been used to identify and target locations in military attacks against Iran, adding that the country's space and scientific infrastructure had come under attack.
The timing of any renewed operation could also be affected by Israel's October 27 election.
Analysts believe Netanyahu could face difficulties initiating a war if he loses and becomes a caretaker prime minister.
Others believe the prospect of joint US-Israeli strikes could be used to pressure political rivals into joining a unity government.
With military preparations continuing and negotiations yet to produce a breakthrough, uncertainty remains over Trump's decision and the scale of Iran's potential response.

Can't postpone your Paris trip? Here's what you should know
From sudden museum closures to transport strikes and curfews, the unrest in France is creating uncertainty for visitors. Here's what you should know before you go.
Anti-government demonstrations across France escalated into widespread violence over the weekend, as thousands of protesters clashed with police, set municipal buildings and cars on fire, and ransacked storefronts.
The unrest, which began last month as largely peaceful, student-led protests over the quality of the public education system, spiralled into the country’s worst rioting in decades, with more than 2,000 arrests and nearly 1,000 police officers injured, according to the French Interior Ministry. To reassert control, authorities issued curfews in parts of several cities on Monday, including Paris, Nice and Lille.
More demonstrations have been planned over the next two weeks. Here’s what you need to know if you plan to travel to France soon.
WHAT PARTS OF FRANCE HAVE BEEN AFFECTED?
Paris became the epicentre of demonstrations over the weekend, with major clashes and rioting at Place de la Republique and surrounding avenues. Many of the shops across Les Halles were looted and vandalised, while the Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde became flash points for standoffs between the police and protesters.
Marseille, France’s second-largest city and a popular tourist destination, also saw significant unrest, with protesters breaking into City Hall and ransacking the building, leaving graffiti and knocking over the bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic. In response, authorities banned public gatherings in the city between noon and 8pm.
In Lyon, tens of thousands of protesters marched through the city on Saturday, and some set fire to the city’s tourism office. Other major cities like Bordeaux, Lille, Calais and Limoges also experienced violence and damage to public buildings.
IS IT SAFE TO VISIT PARIS?
While Paris is generally considered safe, travellers are advised to check travel advisories issued by their respective governments or embassies, avoid protest areas and exercise increased caution because of civil unrest. They should also follow local media outlets for updates on planned demonstrations.
The next major protests are scheduled for Oct 24, Oct 31 and Nov 5, with the Yellow Vests, a populist protest movement, calling for gatherings at Place de la Bastille and Place de la Republique, although times and routes have not been finalised and are awaiting police approval.
By Tuesday, major streets in central Paris had been cleaned up and Parisians had returned to work, although many storefront windows remained broken, and burned cars and bikes littered the streets. Parks, including Luxembourg Gardens, Tuileries Garden and Parc Monceau, were calm. At cafes, people sat on patios with coffee and wine, and tourists and tour guides went about their days as planned.
Sophie Gacheny, an independent tour guide based in the city, urged visitors to stay on the Left Bank, or the southern bank of the River Seine, which is typically quieter during protests. Like other guides, Gacheny is planning her tours around the protests and won’t run any on the days when demonstrations are scheduled.
Kiana Tiese, who offers private tours of Paris, said she took a group of visitors out for a tour on Sunday, a day after the protests, and said everything went well.
HOW ARE TOURIST ATTRACTIONS AFFECTED?
While most major Paris landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe remain open, local authorities can close them on short notice if large-scale protests pass through them. On Monday, the Louvre was forced to shut down after protesters blocked the entrance, causing anger among tourists who had paid for their tickets. (The museum has not announced when it will reopen.)
The tourism board, Paris Je T’Aime, advises travellers to monitor live updates through its website and dedicated city pass app, which provide real-time updates on operating hours for major landmarks and venues.
Municipal buildings, shops and outdoor monuments have been damaged across other major cities, too, creating road closures and areas with restricted access. Be sure to check the status of a landmark and surrounding areas before traveling there.
HOW IS LOCAL TRANSPORTATION AFFECTED?
French unions have called for a nationwide general strike on Nov 5, which could affect the national rail, public transit networks and roads. Under French law, transportation workers must file notice of a strike at least 48 hours before the planned action.
On demonstration days, police shut down metro stations and roads along protest routes, and bus and tram schedules are reduced.
ARE THERE CURFEWS?
French authorities imposed curfews on Monday across parts of several major cities, including Paris, Lille, Lyon and Nice.
In Paris, the authorities enacted strict curfews in areas where demonstrations turned violent, such as Place de la Republique and the Les Halles commercial district. Authorities banned public gatherings in those areas between 8pm and 6am, and prohibited people from being in public outdoor spaces across dozens of districts between 11pm Monday and 6am Tuesday. Police set up checkpoints around the perimeter of the curfew zones to verify the identities of residents and exempt emergency workers. It was unclear how long the curfews would last.
At the five-star Hotel Lancaster Paris, steps from the Champs-Elysees, hotel guests sipped drinks and ate French tapas on Monday night in the lobby’s plush Copperbay cocktail bar. The rest of the neighbourhood was equally tranquil, with no police or sirens in sight. Along the tree-shaded grand boulevard, international crowds strolled under the wrought-iron streetlamps, window-shopping at big global stores like Sephora and Zara.
Lauren Bell, 38, who was visiting the city with her sister from Madrid over the weekend, said that while the city felt calm on Tuesday, people also seemed to be preparing for the next wave. “We were shocked to see how quickly and badly the situation got violent and out of control,” she said. “It feels like it’s not over.”
WILL MY TRAVEL INSURANCE PAY IF I DECIDE TO CANCEL?
Whether your travel insurance will cover trip cancellation depends on your policy. Travellers are advised to check with their insurers to understand what is covered and whether they are eligible for reimbursement.

How I Used Claude Code to Make My Slow Android TV Faster Again
You can use any AI model, but I prefer Claude because some models might hallucinate and break things, potentially bricking your Android TV. Other requirements include having your Google TV or Android TV connected to the same Wi-Fi as your computer or Mac/Windows device. And download the Claude Code app on your Mac or Windows. Once you have the requirements, turn on Developer Options on your TV first. To do that
Step 1. Turn on Developer options on the TV
On the TV, open Settings, go to System, and tap About.
Scroll down and tap Android TV OS Build seven times until you see a message saying you are a developer.
Step 2. Enable wireless debugging
Next, you need to enable wireless debugging.
Go back to Settings, tap System, open Developer options, and enable them.
Scroll down to the Debugging section and open Wireless debugging.
Now enable it.
The TV will ask you to allow wireless debugging on your Wi-Fi network; tap Allow and tick Always allow on this network. Scroll down and find the TV’s IP address and port. In most cases, Claude finds the TV on its own, but if it doesn’t, this address will come in handy.
Step 3. Ask Claude Code to find the TV and connect
Open Claude on your Mac or Windows, go to Claude Code, and start a new chat. From here, enter the following prompt. Again, make sure your TV and your Mac or Windows PC are connected to the same Wi-Fi, so Claude can find your TV on its own.
Prompt: Hey Claude, my TV is on this network, and wireless debugging is enabled. Could you please check and debloat my Android TV? It is super laggy
Now wait until Claude successfully finds your Android TV. Once it’s done, authorize Claude to connect to your Android TV. Press Allow on your TV.
Step 4. Remove unwanted apps and bloatware
Once you authorize the connection, you don’t need to do anything. Claude will analyze and diagnose why your TV is slow. It will check your RAM, the installed apps, and what’s taking up more memory and all.
Once it finds the issues and unwanted bloatware, it checks what’s running on your TV and automatically uninstalls it. It also removes unnecessary packages.
In my case, Claude successfully removed Sony’s Digital Demo and Sony’s Select Echo Dashboard, along with other Google apps such as Google Play Games, Play Movies, Calendar Sync, Camera Gallery, and apps I haven’t used in over 50 days.
Step 5. Replace Google TV launcher with Projectivy Launcher
Next, Claude will start removing the Google TV launcher because it slows the TV down.
A Projectivy Launcher on the Google Play Store is significantly faster, and Claude recommended it to me. Once again, you don’t need to do much. You can ask Claude to download the launcher, install it, and remove the Google TV launcher on your TV.
Since Claude also uninstalls the Google TV launcher, it also removes unnecessary packages such as Android Easter Egg, Services on Device Personalization, Federated Compute, Google Feedback, Text-to-Speech, and much more.
Once the launcher is downloaded, it installs on your device, and Claude automatically sets it up. If it finds any issues during setup, it fixes them automatically. However, keep note that some Android manufacturers ship with a boot receiver that re-enables the Google TV launcher and several Sony apps on every boot. However, Claude also removes those options.
Step 6. Remove ads using Private DNS
While Claude removes the Google TV launcher, many streaming apps still show ads that can slow your TV. Fortunately, you can use AdGuard private DNS to stop ads on your Android TV.
Most Android manufacturers hide this option, including Sony, which hid my private DNS option from my network menu on my specific TV model. However, you can ask Claude to set it directly using ADB. It will run multiple commands, and you can use this prompt to ask Claude to set private DNS to AdGuard.
Claude Code Did What Years of Android TV Tweaks Couldn’t
That’s it. Once finished, ads will be blocked on your device. You can check by opening any streaming app and seeing whether it serves you ads. The Projectivy Launcher might not be as user-intuitive as the Google TV launcher, but it strips out sponsored content, ads, and everything else, making your TV feel faster, like new. And I am happy to make this trade-off for a faster, ad-free TV experience.

ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోలోని ఘటన నిజం కాదు. ఇది కేవలం సామాజిక అవగాహన కోసం బంగ్లాదేశ్కు చెందిన మొహమ్మద్ రుహుల్ రూపొందించిన ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో మాత్రమే. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దీనికి సంబంధించిన అసలు వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) “Ruhul vlog” అనే బంగ్లాదేశీ ఫేస్బుక్ పేజీలో 24 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ పేజీలో మొహమ్మద్ రుహుల్ అనే వ్యక్తి సామాజిక అవగాహన, వినోదం కోసం ఇలాంటి వివిధ స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలను రూపొందిస్తుంటారని తెలిసింది.
ఇక వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా, ఒక వీధి వ్యాపారి చెరుకు రసంలో స్యాకరిన్ (Saccharin) అనే కృత్రిమ స్వీట్నర్ (Artifical Sweetener) కలిపి ప్రజలను అనారోగ్యానికి గురి చేస్తున్నాడంటూ మొహమ్మద్ రుహుల్ అతనితో వాగ్వాదానికి దిగి దాడికి పాల్పడతాడు. అయితే, వీడియో చివర్లో రుహుల్ మాట్లాడుతూ, ఇది కేవలం అవగాహన కోసం తీసిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని, తాము సామాజిక అంశాలపై ఇలాంటి వీడియోలు చిత్రీకరిస్తామని స్పష్టం చేశాడు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ అవుతున్న వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, కేవలం అవగాహన కోసం తీసిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో అని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
అయితే, ఆహార పదార్థాలు, పానీయాల్లో స్యాకరిన్ వాడకంపై భిన్నాభిప్రాయాలు ఉన్నాయి. ఆరోగ్యంపై దీని ప్రభావం గురించి మరిన్ని అధ్యయనాలు జరగాల్సిన అవసరం ఉందని నిపుణులు చెబుతున్నారు. FSSAI దీనిని పరిమిత మోతాదులో మాత్రమే వాడటానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది. అయినప్పటికీ, భారత్, బంగ్లాదేశ్ వంటి దేశాల్లో ఎలాంటి నాణ్యతా పరీక్షలు లేకుండా, పరిమితికి మించి దీనిని పానీయాలు, ఆహార పదార్థాల్లో వాడుతున్నట్లు పలు మీడియా కథనాలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పేర్కొన్నాయి.
చివరిగా, ఫుడ్ జిహాద్ పేరుతో వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదు, ఇది బంగ్లాదేశ్లో రూపొందించిన ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో.

Americans are furious about the state of our healthcare system.
The 2026 election could reshape healthcare
Why everyone who cares about healthcare reform should vote in the midterms.
A recent KFF poll found 60 percent of US adults worry about the cost of medical care — more than gasoline, food and groceries, or their rent or mortgage. One in three Americans say they worry every day or almost every day about their ability to afford healthcare, per a new survey from the Pew Research Center. There seems to be a growing appetite for reform, too: More than 65 percent of Americans say they support the government spending more tax dollars to lower healthcare costs.
Democrats are trying to weaponize those frustrations against the Republicans who currently hold Congress and the White House. By a 2-to-1 margin, voters say they trust Democrats over Republicans on healthcare. That could mean single-payer Medicare-for-all or a new public insurance option or maybe something else. What all this energy leads to will depend on what happens in November. The candidates themselves are framing the stakes in those existential terms.
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here.
“Medicare for all is where we need to go,” Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Michigan Senate race whose support for the policy has been widely covered, said during an August interview with CNN. “And my hope is, both coming out of the 2026 midterms and then out of 2028, that we’re going to be on our way to a Senate majority to be able to get this done.”
Real change will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election and a new occupant in the White House. But this year’s midterms are still a make-or-break moment: The candidates who get elected this year, and how they shape the upcoming presidential primary debate and actions in Congress, will determine whether healthcare reform happens at all.
If you’re fed up with the state of American healthcare, and you want to see a change, you should show up for the midterms on Tuesday, November 3.
Big midterm wins can beget big healthcare wins
The classic pattern in American elections is that more voters go to the polls during presidential campaigns than during the midterm elections when only House and Senate seats are on the ballot. Turnout has started to tick up for the midterms in recent years, but it still trails behind presidential years. Midterms suffer from the perception that there’s not as much at stake if the White House is not on the line.
But that’s never been strictly true.
Midterm elections are extraordinarily important in shaping the future of policymaking, even if the payoff is delayed. They help determine both the character of the Congress that could eventually pass a major bill after the next presidential election, and the kind of ideas and policies that are going to be prioritized.
“Voters should see 2026 and 2028 as the elections that will guide the next big change in our healthcare system,” said Natalie Davis, CEO and co-founder of the advocacy group United States of Care, in a statement to Vox. “These elections will be how voters’ demands are heard — and will tell us whether the next real window for change will come with serious reforms or missed opportunity.”
A walk through the recent history of healthcare reform should help make the stakes of the 2026 elections clear.
In 2006, the national mood looked similar to what we’re seeing today. A very unpopular Republican president was in office, and the country had soured on his agenda. George W. Bush’s foreign wars and his misguided attempt to overhaul Social Security gave Democrats an opportunity to win big in the 2006 midterms — and they did. Dems won more than 30 seats and secured a comfortable majority in the House. In the Senate, they won six seats and narrowly took control of that chamber too.
It was a resounding rejection of the Bush administration, and it set up the next decade of Democratic policymaking. At the highest level, the midterms gave energy to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, united as they were around their opposition to the Iraq War, and that energy carried over to the presidential primary. Barack Obama defeated Hillary Clinton and won the presidency, springboarding off of the excitement that started with the 2006 elections.
Dems’ success in the midterms also helped put lowering healthcare costs at the forefront of the Democratic agenda. That encouraged both Obama and Clinton to develop detailed healthcare policy proposals during their primary campaigns and ultimately set the stage for the Democrats to pursue the Affordable Care Act once they had full control of the government in 2009.
And then there is the literal size of the congressional majorities that parties need to pass their agenda. Voters may not spend much time thinking about whip counts, but one or two elections in a midterm year can ultimately decide the fate of the next president’s agenda.
Part of the reason Democrats were able to pass the ACA was that they built on their huge wins in 2006 with more wins in 2008 and held massive congressional majorities once Obama was sworn in. And once the debate over healthcare reform really got started, they needed every single vote. It was especially important in the Senate: Democrats had exactly 60 votes in 2009. That meant if all of them united together, they could pass filibuster-proof legislation — so long as nobody defected. That was only possible because in 2006 Mark Pryor won a Senate seat in Arkansas, Sherrod Brown triumphed in a Senate race in Ohio, and Jon Tester beat an incumbent Republican in Montana.
Without those wins in 2006, the Democratic legislative agenda in 2009 would probably have looked different. They might’ve had to pursue a more limited healthcare reform plan; maybe the ACA wouldn’t have passed at all.
What kind of Democrats will be on the rise in 2028?
The 2006 midterms both created the opportunity for the ACA — and set the limits on what the legislation could actually achieve. Democrats had that 60-seat Senate majority, but within it were many more moderate members. Policies like the public option (which would have authorized the government to create its own health insurance plan to sell alongside private insurance) couldn’t get sufficient support. That is the dilemma of policymaking: You need those swing-seat members to win, which often means tacking to the center, but you also can’t pass anything they won’t get on board with.
Nevertheless, that is a good kind of political problem to have, one which Democrats would be thrilled to face in January 2029. All of which brings us to 2026. What are we going to do now?
It all starts with the vote count. Most projections expect the Democrats to win between 10 and 20 House seats. But the difference between 10 and 20 could be substantial. The cushier the majority, the further you can push the policy agenda. More than 30 House Democrats actually voted against the ACA, but they could still narrowly pass the bill because of the huge majority that they had started building in 2006.
If you live in one of the districts — like Arizona’s Sixth or Colorado’s Eighth or Florida’s 22nd, to name just a couple of the 21 toss-up races identified by the Cook Political Report this year — that forecasters say is competitive this year, you could have an outsized say in what the future of policymaking looks like. But even in safe districts, you should vote: Elections are the most reliable way we have to gauge public opinion, and strong victories for the candidates who prioritize healthcare send a message.
The same goes for the Senate. If Democrats sweep all of the competitive races, they could have up to 55 seats in the Senate in 2027 — with a chance to build on it in 2028. If you are a voter in Kansas, Michigan, Ohio, Texas, Alaska, Maine, New Hampshire, or Iowa, your ballot carries extra weight for the next steps in US healthcare reform. If the Democrats can reach 60 votes again in 2029, they would have much more flexibility about what to pass. Even if they fall short of that magic number, the more of a cushion they have above 50, the more likely that their Senate leaders can find support for altering Senate rules for the filibuster and get an ambitious bill approved.
How you can get involved this election
If there is ever going to be a path to a true healthcare overhaul, it starts with this year’s elections. If you want to see a change, you can vote — and you can do more than that.
- Talk to your neighbors.
- Phone bank for candidates you believe in.
- You can even sign up to drive people to the polls on Election Day.
The results of this year’s midterms will also set the terms of the debate among Democrats. We are likely to see “show” bills advanced by Dems next year that may have no chance of being signed by President Donald Trump, but that will give us a sense of what kind of policies the party wants to pursue and how much support there is for them. Believe it or not, the first Medicare prescription drug negotiations bill passed the House in 2007 after Democrats’ big wins in 2006 — even though the policy didn’t become law for another 15 years. The broader public may not pay much attention to this kind of doomed-to-fail legislation, but it is often a window into the future.
“One challenge for Democrats is finding the next big health care idea beyond the Affordable Care Act that will resonate with voters and respond to their affordability concerns,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “One big difference between now and 2006 is that back then there was already a lot of coalescing around ideas that ultimately led to the ACA. All the major Democratic candidates for president in 2008 supported something like that. I’m not sure that’s true now, at least not yet.”
Democrats are already aligning on a wide range of healthcare ideas, from reviving the public option to free primary care to the full-blown Medicare-for-all supported by progressive candidates, some of whom are in competitive elections. If El-Sayed wins the Senate race in Michigan, for example, that could supercharge a debate around Medicare-for-all. It could also provide momentum to any progressives who run for president — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to name one obvious example — and decide to make Medicare-for-all a pillar of their platform.
But if El-Sayed and other progressives were to fall short, that could make Democrats more timid about being ambitious in the 2028 campaign and afterward. Still, he’s far from the only candidate in a crucial race to put their support behind Medicare-for-all. There is Randy Villegas in an important California House race. Troy Jackson has bet on it as part of his bid to topple Sen. Susan Collins in Maine. All of these races will send a signal to the party about what the public wants and is willing to turn out for.
In some ways, winning elections is the easy part. Legislating is hard, and any eventual healthcare law will surely involve compromises and unexpected surprises. Who knows what will be happening in the world in 2029?
“The bottom line is: 2026 is a healthcare election,” the leaders of the advocacy group Protect Our Care wrote in a campaign memo this month. “After November, it’s up to Democrats to keep up the fight to deliver relief to families and make healthcare affordable and accessible for every American.”

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

The Delhi Police crackdown on the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led protest on October 10 has drawn international scrutiny, with human rights bodies and press-freedom organisations flagging police excesses, and international media outlets reporting on the severity of force used against young protesters.
Police detained over 2,000 protesters and used force to suppress the mobilisation in the national capital. In arguably the most brutal assault on press freedom in India since the Emergency, journalists from both independent and mainstream media outlets were stopped from doing their work and detained in a display of police excess that bordered on madness. Some were dragged by their clothes, pushed and manhandled, some had their phones snatched, and pressured to delete footage of police action.
‘Restrictions Violate India’s Obligations under Int’l Law’
The global human rights non-profit Amnesty International on Friday put out a statement urging Delhi police to ensure that the fundamental right to peacefully protest is guaranteed to Indian citizens. In the statement, titled, ‘Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital’, Amnesty highlighted that “approximately 22,000 armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi police officers expected to be deployed.”
Aakar Patel, chair of board, stated: “From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law.”
After reports of rapid mass detentions began to surface on Saturday, the United Nations Human Rights Commission published a press release: ‘Concerns over mass detentions before and during protests’. Spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called for the unconditional and immediate release of all those arbitrarily detained. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled. Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality. The Indian authorities should also ensure law enforcement forces exercise utmost restraint in response to peaceful protesters, consistent with the country’s democratic traditions and human rights obligations,” read the statement.
Similarly, the global media watchdog Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Delhi police to “immediately release all detained journalists and media workers, return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests…and the police response without interference.”
