A video showing Maharashtra FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe filming himself with a crowd is being shared (here, here) with the claim that he is expressing support for protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid the ongoing anti-CEC agitation. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A video showing Maharashtra FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe filming himself with a crowd expressing support for protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: This video was recorded during Maharashtra FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe’s visit to Sydenham Institute of Management Studies, Research and Entrepreneurship Education in Mumbai for Management Conclave 2026 in October 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using Google Lens led us to an Instagram post shared by thebmssociety_sydenham, with the description “When the system meets the student. Tukaram Mundhe at Sydenham’s Management Conclave ‘26.”
Further searches led us to a video posted on Maharashtra FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe’s official Instagram account, @tukaram_ias, showing him recording himself with a group of young people. A comparison of the visuals confirmed that the viral video matches the video shared on his Instagram account.
To sum up, the video of Maharashtra FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe with students is unrelated to the anti-CEC protests.

McDermott calls for Super League to accept NRL investment
- Published
England head coach Brian McDermott has called for Super League to accept investment from Australia's NRL in order to improve the English game.
Talks are currently ongoing after Super League clubs rejected a £35m package from the Australian Rugby League Commission and a second deadline of 15 October was allowed to pass without an agreement being reached.
Formalising a partnership between the sport's two leading competitions is seen as as a key step in helping to grow the European competition's revenue.
"I think the NRL's investment in Super League could be very, very positive," said McDermott, who is also the assistant coach of the Gold Coast Titans.
"The product's brilliant. It has always being brilliant. The product's never been the problem. The players have never been the problem. The coaches have never been the problem.
"It's just how it's marketed and how it's presented to people. I think there's some dominoes could start falling our way if the NRL invests and we accept their investment."
Super League is yet to agree a new title sponsorship deal, finalise broadcast negotiations or even its fixtures for the 2027 campaign with London Broncos' position yet to be fully determined.
The Broncos came in16th on the yearly grading list, below fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders, despite a season in which they won the second tier's Grand Final, the 1895 Cup and were runaway champions in the regular-season standings.
The Broncos were overlooked 12 months ago when Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique joined the expanded 14-team competition.
But with the backing of Australian businessman Grant Wechsel and former Brisbane Broncos star Darren Lockyer, and with a squad full of internationals, they do still harbour hopes of playing in Super League in 2027.
It is understood any completed deal would involve the Australian governing body insisting on Broncos featuring in the top flight in the near future.
The financial gulf between the northern and southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record $5.3bn (£3.97bn) television deal over seven years in July.
Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.
"I know there's some positive notes around Super League at the moment, especially with crowds," McDermott added.
"It's been a really interesting competition this year and Wakefield winning the Grand Final puts a brilliant marker down that all the teams can win it.
"It would be a real positive validation of Super League if the NRL were to invest."

- 'NRL investment in Super League benefits both parties' 
  - Published2 September
McDermott also stressed that an injection of finance into the English game would help widen the pool of talent for future England coaches to call upon. NRL clubs have oversight of players in several age groups leading up first-grade level.
"The TV deal that the NRL's just signed is enormous and [with that you get] preparation, the facilities and the teams coming through that support each NRL club.
"I don't think Super League clubs could populate three teams underneath them with a genuine six, seven, nine and one [the spine of the team].
"So you end up playing a version of rugby league in the UK at junior level, which is good, it's well coached, it's dedicated and it's full of commitment. But you don't have the genuine six, seven, nine and one influence over a game. This is not a new opinion. This has been going on for a long time.
"If you're asking me, is there a big divide between the competitions? Yeah, there is. It's nothing to do with commitment, nothing to do with good-quality coaching or commitment from players. It's just the size of the competitions and the standing in their country."

2027 BMW iX5 first drive: You'll love the range, but maybe not the look
BMW's latest EV will do over 450 miles on a charge and even close its own doors.
Too many manufacturers are getting too clever in trying to reinvent the humble door handle lately, sometimes with fatal consequences. BMW is certainly joining that crowd with the upcoming electric SUV, the iX5. It's the effective replacement for the iX, the next step up the model line from the recently released iX3, and a battery-powered alternative to the two-row X5.
The iX5 has little winglets at the top of the front and rear doors containing strain meters that can detect a subtle pull without actually flexing. It's a vastly complex system that enables something surprisingly nice: power doors that actually work.
Reinventing the door handle
Pull the little winglet and the door swings itself open as far as it can, relying on embedded sensors to avoid slamming into you or the car you parked next to. Get inside, step on the brake pedal and the door quickly closes itself. This isn't novel technology by any means. A fair few cars (mostly expensive ones) have offered this in the past, but I tend to find them extremely annoying.
Most are so slow that I never want to wait for them, so sluggish that they're hard to close manually or so unreliable that I couldn't trust them to not create a power-assisted ding into the next car over. In the iX5, they actually work, adding a little more luxury to the electric version of BMW's second-best-selling machine in the US.
It's far from the only luxurious touch. The SUV I drove was the 570-horsepower, 593-pound-foot iX5 60 xDrive model, outfitted with plush, massaging seats. The matte silver paint on the outside gave it a premium look, even if the styling is polarizing, to say the least.
A shared safety experience
The driver assistance system also has some decidedly premium touches. BMW evocatively calls it "Symbiotic Drive," and though that sounds vaguely alien and ominous, it just means that the system works with you. On the highway it'll steer itself, and you can take your hands off the wheel. But if you want to change lanes, you can either tap the turn stalk, or just grab the wheel and execute the change, then let it go again.
You can speed up and even slow down manually without the system disengaging, something that definitely takes some getting used to. This isn't like an old-school cruise control system that turns off the second you touch the brake pedal or launches itself up to full speed as soon as it's engaged. You can apply the brake to bring yourself to a complete stop for a light, then lift off again and the car will smoothly resume.
It works excellently, as does the infotainment system, which runs on a curiously inclined, 17.9-inch touchscreen in the center of the dashboard. Everything is quick and responsive, and though the integrated AI assistant was a little over-eager to chime in whenever anyone in the car said "BMW," it was at least able to find restaurants and answers to all of the inane queries we expect from our agentic future overlords.
Panoramic Vision
Above that touchscreen, situated far back on the dashboard, is BMW's Panoramic Vision display. It runs from pillar to pillar, with six segments that you can customize to show everything from the current weather to arbitrary pictures of vintage BMWs. It looks a bit much at first, but it's actually quite nice to have, and is a lot easier to see than your average gauge cluster hidden behind the steering wheel.
It's certainly more useful than the final display in the iX5, the optional 14.6-inch passenger display. This is situated to the right and slightly behind the central display, to obscure it from the driver's view. That's because BMW opted not to use the same kind of perspective-limiting display technology that many other premium SUVs have used.
Instead, the system relies on the driver-monitoring camera to detect when the driver's gaze wanders to the passenger display. When it does, the screen goes blank and whatever video the passenger is watching pauses. The screen turns back on again when the driver looks away, but the passenger has to manually resume the video. As far as user experiences go, it's not ideal.
Range-topper
The iX5's most luxurious feature might be the range. The iX5 carries a prodigious 144-kilowatt-hour battery slung down below the passenger compartment. It charges at a remarkable 460kW via NACS port, enough to get from 10 to 80 percent in 22 minutes if you can find a charger with enough juice.
BMW hasn't completed its EPA testing, but says to expect more than 450 miles on a charge. To prove that's attainable, one of BMW's engineers drove over 500 miles from San Francisco to LA without stopping and still had 50 miles remaining.
My road trip was a fair bit shorter, but I did spend about six hours behind the wheel of a pair of BMW's new SUVs. The first half I was in the X5 40 xDrive, the internal combustion version. The second half was in the electric, and it was my clear preference.
Though the gasoline-burning X5 had good power at higher speeds and made a nice sound when I floored it, the throttle response on the iX5 was infinitely sharper. It is certainly heavier, but the lower center of gravity made it feel that much more engaging in the corners, and it can do the same stopping trick as the iX3, relying on the electric motors to come to a standstill so smoothly that if you close your eyes you literally can't tell when the wheels stop rolling.
Wrap-up
But there's honestly not much between the gas-powered X5 and battery-powered iX5. That's a big change of positioning compared to the even more polarizing iX and the prior-generation X5. Though similar in many regards, those two looked and drove nothing alike.
For this generation, BMW is bringing the family together, making the internal combustion and battery-electric versions look nigh identical. They're even pricing them similarly, with the plug-in X5 50e starting at $77,500, and the iX5 starting at $79,800.
Maybe this, combined with the generous range, will finally help break down some of the EV stigma that still poisons the American automotive landscape. If not, perhaps the cool, automatic doors will woo people over. Yes, you can get them on the gas-powered X5, too, but they cost extra there.

Tokyo – Japan will switch to a post-departure refund system for consumption tax paid by foreign visitors starting Nov. 1, following a series of cases in which purchased tax-free goods were resold in Japan at prices including tax.
Foreign visitors can currently buy goods at prices excluding the consumption tax at tax-free shops in Japan.
Under the new system, which is intended to prevent illegal acts by ensuring that purchased items are taken out of Japan through customs inspections at ports and airports, foreign visitors would buy goods at tax-inclusive prices and receive refunds equivalent to the tax after departing.
On Thursday, Tokyo Customs demonstrated tax exemption procedures for the press at Tokyo’s Haneda Airport in the run-up to the transition to the new system.
While predeparture customs checks are conducted after security inspection at present, inbound visitors, from November, will need to have their passports scanned by a dedicated machine before security inspection to be eligible for consumption tax refunds.
“To prevent any confusion, we will establish a solid operation system,” including by deploying staff to guide travelers, a Tokyo Customs official said.
Seven busy international airports — including Haneda Airport, Narita International Airport in Chiba Prefecture and Kansai International Airport near the city of Osaka — will allow foreign travelers to conduct the procedures through a dedicated smartphone website to reduce congestion.
In recent years, many foreign visitors were known to have bought large quantities of goods at tax-exclusive prices and resold them in Japan at prices including tax before leaving the country.
According to government statistics, however, only 10% of the 690 departing foreign visitors who bought ¥100 million or more worth of tax-free goods in fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2023 were confirmed to have possessed the items in predeparture customs inspections at ports or airports.

A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining “userland” access that he says “lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO.”
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called “tethered” hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI’s Codex to poke at SmileBasic’s language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After “substantial effort for ~2 weeks,” that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.
From there, Hajhamid writes that he started poking around for access to the Switch 2’s internal sysmodules, looking for ones that could provide more privileged access to the console’s core functions. Eventually, he found a buffer overflow in the console’s FileSystem services module that exposed a cached data pointer, granting arbitrary read and write privileges. From there, Hajhamid writes that he could execute “privileged filesystem actions” and eventually achieve native code execution through a faked filesystem process.
Hajhamid, who goes by Pepsipu online, showed off a host of new modded characters in Mario Kart World as a proof of concept for the exploit. Others are similarly showing off simple demos and in-progress developer tools running on exploited hardware.

Nostalgic bumper stickers show how Americans voiced their views before social media
They were also a rare benefit to being stuck in traffic, either as entertainment or another way to annoy the driver behind you

Before there was social media, Americans used bumper stickers to share their strongest and strangest views with people who didn’t necessarily care.
The medium back then was cars. Slap a belief on the rear end and go. If people agreed, they honked. If they disagreed, they honked. Drivers figured it out, usually without crashing.
The original Twitter with its character limits was nothing. With bumper stickers, a sentiment had to be packed into a dozen words or less or it was just a blur.
“America: Love it or leave it.” That one rode around the country widely in the 1970s, a divisive time with anger over war, soaring gas prices and shady practices documented at the government’s highest levels. Ah, the past.
That bumper sticker, among others, is now in the collection of the Smithsonian, repository of Americana big and small.
Vote. Back Off. Coexist. Save the Whales. For decades, and seemingly peaking with the baby boomer generation, the stickers were a low-cost, low-key hum of diverse voices at a time when just three broadcasters announced the national news.
They were also a rare benefit to being stuck in traffic, either as entertainment or another way to annoy the driver behind you.
On the move, there was a breezy satisfaction in leaving a hint of yourself for others to consider, like perfume. Maybe your bumper sticker told the world where you studied, what music you liked, what sports teams you supported, what turned you on and why.
It was possible to go too far. The content of some bumper stickers over the years was taken to court, where the very American freedom of speech and expression was debated. According to the Washington-based Freedom Forum organization, some of them suggested that the driver behind them eat something that rhymed with spit.
Don’t laugh, it’s paid for. Keep on truckin’. God Bless America. How’s my driving?
The snappy, scrappy lines were so effective that more than once, U.S. lawmakers referred to “bumper sticker politics” while calling for action, not shallow slogans. That’s according to the Congressional Record.
If you’re rich, I’m single. If it’s rocking, don’t come knocking. Keep honking, I’m reloading.
And remember: If you can read this, you’re too close.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

A study on Internet use among school-going children, supported by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR), recommends that digital literacy must be encouraged for children and parents with active support from schools.
Anxiety, sleep disturbances, and mood changes among children are the most reported health consequences, indicating that Internet use impacts children emotionally and physically. Based on the findings, the study has recommended a “collaborative multi-stakeholder framework” to digitally empower children in the era of emerging technologies.
A report based on the study, titled ‘Empowering Children in the Digital Age: Analysing Experiences and Vulnerabilities within the Framework of Vision Viksit Bharat and Sustainable Development Goals’, has found 97.6% children are accessing the Internet from home, with smartphones as the primary device.
“Most of the children are spending 4.5 hours per day using the Internet. Their primary purpose for using the Internet is studying, followed by playing online games, watching videos, and talking to friends,” Moina Khan, faculty with Bennet University, Uttar Pradesh, which conducted the study for ICSSR, said.
For the study conducted in 2025, Ms. Khan interviewed more 2,000 children in the 9-14 years age group studying in schools in Delhi, and about 500 parents. “Children, schools as well as parents reported various benefits of digital platforms, including social media for children, from information, upskilling and community-building to collaborative learning and creative expressions. Children confidently use digital spaces exhibiting high technical or functional skills. However, what they lack are critical skills,” Ms. Khan said.
She pointed out that at home, adults think children are tech savvy and better than them. “However, we are living in a bubble thinking they know it all. What they do not understand is systematic power manipulation and persuasion, algorithmic influence, and exploitation. The majority of children, irrespective of their perceived digital skills, reported feeling lonely when they did not use the Internet for long periods, experiencing anger when they did not find what they wanted online, and struggled to stop using the Internet even when they wanted to, reflecting signs of addiction,” she added.
47% children mentioned talking to unknown people in the past six months while many played games online with strangers, according to the study. “Talking to strangers online, playing games with them, and watching content inappropriate for their age was more common in the age group of 12-13 years. Few reported experiencing cyber bullying and impersonation. Most of the children have mentioned not reporting uncomfortable experiences to parents or teachers. However, many of them considered parents as a preferred choice for reporting such incidents,” the report added.
The report also indicates gender-based differences in Internet use, with boys generally using the Internet more than girls. “Boys’ greater social freedom often leads to less controlled Internet use, increasing their exposure to harmful content and online risks. Girls’ restricted access could create a different threat by limiting their digital literacy and self-protection skills,” it said.

Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”
The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves.
“As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.”
“Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied. “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.”
A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.”
Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out.
“The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.”
Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by listing cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites includes asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers.
In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read "Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task."
Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.”
If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed, or be banned from the platform entirely.
In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike.
“Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.”
Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.”(Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable, but against current Airbnb policy.)
“First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’" another person said, though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans.
Unwanted smoking and other serious scenarios—like letting dirty dishes become “health hazards,” leaving “permanent stains on sheets,” and creating “mountains of rotting garbage" —were invoked by several hosts. But these policy adjustments, seemingly, will not change how any of these things are treated.
Airbnb already has its own ground rules that all guests must agree to. The general credo is to "treat your host’s home like your own," which translates to things like putting trash in the trash can, and not leaving moldy dishes.
If a host finds anything was damaged or went missing during a stay, guests are expected to pay a “reasonable” amount to repair or replace it. Hosts are also protected through the platform’s protection program, AirCover, which will reimburse up to $3 million for certain property damage caused by guests, including furniture, cars, and other belongings.
Additional cleaning costs, such as performing "smoke odor removal" or handling "pet accidents” are also covered by AirCover. Airbnb notes that the cleaning fees hosts are allowed to set are only meant to cover standard guest turnover tasks like laundry and vacuuming. Hosts can’t “charge guest fees for failing to perform specific cleaning or checkout tasks,” though they can still leave guest reviews “based on cleanliness.”
In the Airbnb Hosts subreddit, a few lurking guests were quick to bring up the cleaning fees, which are famously the subject of their ire. One self-described “mostly guest” said they’re not opposed to running the dishwasher or stripping the bed. “Just don’t charge me a cleaning fee over $100 then,” they said.
“Truth nuke,” another person replied. “Why would I have to pre-game the cleaners?”

eMudra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.
V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers.
Don’t let the door hit you on the butt
“However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”
The announcement came two days after researchers revealed eMudhra had issued eight certificates with private keys so defective they were trivial to discover. Anyone who took the time—which was measured in milliseconds—could crack them and then use them to generate TLS certificates that would be trusted by all major browsers, as well as an untold number of email servers, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, and unmaintained CLI tools that ship their own copy of the roots.
Whereas NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private keys—used in the type of certificates eMudhra issued—are supposed to contain roughly 384 bits of entropy, the eight compromised certificates had key sizes ranging from 3 to 8 bits. Stated differently, whereas there are supposed to be 2384—a number with 116 digits—different key possibilities, the strongest of the defective keys had a maximum of just 256. The private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

Influencer charged after capturing great white shark on Cape Cod
Christopher Stefanou, known as LISHARKMAN on YouTube, has been accused of capturing animal known as ‘Aaron’ on a trip with a client

A New York influencer has been accused of targeting and capturing a great white shark on Cape Cod.
Angler Christopher Stefanou allegedly took a European client onto the eastern shores of Cape Cod to capture the shark as part of a days-long trip in October last year. Known as LISHARKMAN on social media, Stefanou has more than two million subscribers on YouTube.
Stefanou posted footage to social media showing the men using a drone and other equipment to capture and drag a great white known as “Aaron the Shark” onto the beach, Cape & Islands District Attorney Robert J. Galibois says.
The group photographed themselves with the animal before releasing it, prosecutors added.
A year later, on October 21, Stefanou was arraigned in the Barnstable Superior Court, where his bail was set at $10,000.
He faces a slew of charges, including animal cruelty to a shark, fishing for shark, mechanical deployment of bait, attempt to capture a shark, and possession of a protected species shark, prosecutors confirmed.
Stefanou has been ordered to surrender his fishing license and remove the video of the shark, as well as being told to stay out of Massachusetts unless for legal reasons.
In a statement given to CBS News Boston, Stefanou’s attorney, Jon A. Ciraulo, said that his client maintains that he is innocent.
“There can be no question that Chris respects the sport, actively participates in conservation practices, assists in marine tagging and research efforts, and volunteers his time to educate enthusiasts on safe and responsible angling,” Ciraulo said.
“The charges against Chris are allegations only. He maintains his innocence and intends to fully challenge the allegations against him.”
Stefanou, from Long Island, is next due to appear in court on December 11.
In one video posted to his channel, he can be seen pinning a sand tiger shark to the ground while removing a hook with just his hands. In another, he can be seen capturing an alligator in Florida.
“He is an extremely passionate angler who specializes in Land Based Shark Fishing on Long Island, New York, but often ventures out to different states along the east coast (sic) of the U.S.,” Stefanou is described on his website.
“He also books private land-based shark fishing charters for anyone interested!”
Massachusetts law states that great white sharks are a protected species and that fishing for them is prohibited. Boaters and anglers are banned from intentionally luring, churning or attempting to catch the sharks.
Cape Cod is the only great white shark aggregation site in the western North Atlantic Ocean, something driven by the large local population of gray seals.
Aaron the Shark, who measures 9 and a half feet in length, has been detected over 5,000 times off the coast of Massachusetts via acoustic detection, according to the White Shark Logbook.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
- Published
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
- Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war 
  - Published3 hours ago
- Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism 
  - Published1 day ago
- US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin 
  - Published12 minutes ago
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
All rather vague.
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
"Of course!"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

Rogers to charge new fee for bills paid by credit card, says practice is ‘increasingly common’
Rival telecom firm Telus rolled out similar fee in 2022, before scrapping it a year later
Rogers Communications says it will roll out a new fee early next year for customers who pay their bill with a credit card.
The Canadian telecom giant says a 1.6 per cent “credit card processing charge” will apply starting Jan. 17. The company says this will impact both auto-pay and one-time credit card payments.
“The charge applies every time you pay your Rogers bill with a credit card,” Rogers says on its website.
“This reflects the fees we are charged by credit card companies.”
According to Rogers, the fee is not applicable to customers in Quebec, as well as those on certain “specialized plans,” or former Shaw Mobile customers who migrated to Rogers when it acquired Shaw Communications in 2023.
Other forms of payment are not subject to the new fee. These include direct debt and online banking payments, cheques, Rogers gift cards, prepaid cards, Debit Mastercard and Visa Debit.
“If you choose to pay your bill by credit card, it's increasingly common across many sectors for a credit card fee to apply,” Rogers said.
Telus scrapped similar fee
In 2022, rival telecom provider Telus asked the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) for permission to add a 1.5 per cent surcharge to the bills of some landline phone customers who pay their bill using a credit card. The CRTC rejected this request.
However, the regulator’s approval was only required for a fee on landline services. Telus rolled out a 1.5 per cent credit card fee for mobile and home internet customers.
Telus scrapped the fee in 2023, following a settlement between credit card companies and merchants allowing merchants to pass on the cost directly to customers.

As Peddi gears up for its World Television Premiere on Sony MAX on October 24 at 8 PM, Ram Charan has opened up about the physical demands and personal challenges he faced while filming the sports-action drama. The actor revealed that he spent nearly 50 days shooting in traditional wrestler’s attire, an experience that pushed him out of his comfort zone.
Ram Charan reveals challenges of wearing wrestler’s attire for 50 days during Peddi shoot; says, “Have hurt my eye, legs and many other parts”
The film’s sports sequences required considerable physical effort, with Ram Charan sustaining injuries during the shoot. The team also worked with real wrestlers and a national-level runner to bring authenticity to the sporting scenes.
Reflecting on the challenges he encountered while filming, Ram Charan shared, “I have hurt my eye, legs and many other parts but we expected all this to happen. When we shot for a sport, we always worked with real players. We shot with real kusti players, and for the running scenes we worked with a national-level runner. I enjoy doing physically tough roles so I was prepared for it.”
Apart from the physical demands, wearing the wrestling attire for an extended period was another challenge for the actor. Ram Charan spoke about his discomfort with being in the outfit in front of a large number of people throughout the shoot. The experience involved performing various activities and sequences while dressed in the traditional attire.
Speaking about stepping outside his comfort zone, the actor candidly shared, “I am quite a shy person. I wouldn’t really call myself an introvert, but wearing the wrestling attire and working in it for 50 days was quite challenging for me. I was not used to it and here I had to do all of this in front of so many people for 50 days. Whether it was riding a bicycle, working in the fields, training in the akhada, or performing scenes with my co-star, I had to do it all in that attire. It was quite uncomfortable for me.”
Headlined by Ram Charan and Janhvi Kapoor, Peddi combines sports, action and drama against the backdrop of a remote village in Andhra Pradesh in 1990. The story follows Peddi, a gifted sportsperson whose passion for the game earns him recognition in his village. However, when his community and its way of life face a threat, the game takes on a deeper meaning, becoming a fight for the people and their dignity.
The film brings together cricket and wrestling while exploring themes of pride, identity and community. As audiences prepare to watch the film on television, Ram Charan’s account offers a glimpse into the physical preparation and personal challenges involved in bringing his character to life.

Longtime audio giant Bose announced on Wednesday that it's acquiring Skullcandy, the lifestyle brand known for its bass-heavy headphones. Skullcandy will remain a separate company within Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business and will still be based in Park City, Utah.
The acquisition isn't out of left field. Bose has lent its audio expertise to Skullcandy over the past year under its Sound by Bose licensing program. Skullcandy designs the headphones and then works with Bose on the audio front. The relationship began with the Skullcandy Method 360 ANC earbuds in 2025 and more recently, with the Crusher 1080 ANC headphones in July.
When WIRED spoke with Skullcandy CEO Brian Garofalow in July about the partnership, Garofalow highlighted the 23-year-old company's ability to build community and culture, specifically around the board sports community (the first Skullcandy product was designed on a ski chairlift). But he admitted the company wasn't “the greatest at the engineering part of innovation with products.”
This is hardly Bose's first audio acquisition (though it may be the most mainstream). Bose acquired McIntosh Group, owners of luxury audio brands McIntosh Laboratory and Sonus Faber, back in 2024. But Bose seems to be after Skullcandy's connection to its community.
“What does the brand stand for? Does it have meaning for consumers? Is it relevant to a group of consumers that, frankly, we otherwise aren’t reaching?" Bose CEO Lila Snyder tells WIRED. "If you think about McIntosh, Sonus Faber, and Skullcandy, they all fit into that realm. Skullcandy gives us access to a customer base that we think we’re largely missing with the Bose brand.”
That's why Bose has no plans to relocate Skullcandy from Park City, Utah, which Snyder says is the epicenter of board sports culture. “We want to make sure we’re right at the heart of it, as they always have been,” she says. Skullcandy products are also affordable, especially compared to other Bose products and Bose-owned brands, which lets Bose compete at both ends of the market.
As WIRED's headphone reviewer, I find Bose and Skullcandy an odd pairing. In consumer audio, Bose pioneered active noise-cancelation (ANC) in headphones, and maintains that legacy with ANC-leading products like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds (2nd Gen). Skullcandy, on the other hand, has often been viewed as the butt of the joke when it comes to audio quality. It has had a reputation for middling sound, bass-over-everything headphones, and a loud, bold aesthetic.
Recent collaborations have started to change those perceptions—WIRED rated the Method 360 ANC earbuds an 8/10, noting good sound quality and ANC for the money. Snyder says those buds and the recent Crusher collab are just the tip of the iceberg. “It’s the beginning of what we think we can do together,” she says.
I’m very curious about what comes next from Skullcandy, headphones or otherwise. Either way, we’ll see if Bose's acoustic muscle can give the lifestyle brand the permanent glow-up it’s been chasing.

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group is rescuing a boat carrying 14 Indian nationals that was attacked off Jabal Zuqar island near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the group’s military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Thursday (October 22), blaming Saudi Arabia for the incident.
The development comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with attacks targeting Saudi energy infrastructure and airports. India has strongly condemned the continued attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including the October 21 strikes on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province.
Saudi authorities did not immediately respond on the alleged boat attack. The circumstances of the incident were not independently established in the information available.
In a statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said the attacks on Saudi Arabia had resulted in civilian deaths and injuries.
“One Indian national unfortunately died and two others were injured in the attack on Dammam airport, while another Indian national was injured in the attack on the Shaybah oil field,” the ministry said.
The MEA conveyed its condolences to the family of the Indian national killed in the Dammam airport attack and wished those injured a speedy recovery. It added that the Indian Embassy in Riyadh was in contact with Saudi authorities and would provide all possible assistance.
India also called for an immediate halt to attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure, describing them as “completely unacceptable”. It said it stood in solidarity with the people and government of Saudi Arabia in safeguarding the kingdom’s sovereignty and expressed hope that peace and normalcy would return to the region.
Separately, Saudi state oil giant Saudi Aramco has instructed employees to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely, Reuters reported, citing six people with knowledge of the matter.
The instruction follows a wave of Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, including Saudi energy facilities and airports. The reason for the evacuation was unclear, and Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis have claimed responsibility for attacks on Aramco facilities in the Red Sea city of Yanbu and the Saudi defence ministry in Riyadh. Saudi authorities have not confirmed the reported strikes.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted drones over Riyadh and Medina on Thursday. Earlier, a Houthi attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday evening killed two people, including an Indian national, and injured eight others, according to the report. Saudi aviation authorities said airport operations had resumed and air traffic had returned to normal.
The renewed fighting has also raised concerns about oil supplies. Saudi Arabia’s benchmark stock index fell 2.5% on Thursday, according to LSEG data, while oil prices rose to their highest levels since May amid fears of further escalation in the Middle East.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh had earlier urged Indian nationals in Saudi Arabia to remain calm and vigilant amid the evolving security situation.
In its October 13 advisory, the embassy asked Indians to stay indoors in the event of an aerial attack and follow instructions issued by local authorities through official channels. It also advised them against circulating or reposting videos or news related to the ongoing events.
The embassy said it had opened a 24-hour control room to assist Indian nationals and urged travellers to remain in regular contact with their airlines and verify flight updates before travelling.
The embassy also said Indian nationals whose visit, tourist, Umrah or business visas had expired because they were unable to leave due to flight unavailability would be permitted to exit Saudi Arabia without paying fines, according to information provided by Saudi authorities.
(With Reuters inputs)

Would a Democratic Congress change course on Israel?
Public opinion on Israel has changed. But it doesn’t rank among most voters’ top midterm priorities.
Israel felt inescapable in the midterm primaries, especially for Democrats, where centrists and progressives clashed — memorably! — over military aid, Gaza, and (of course) AIPAC.
But with the Election Day almost upon us, the subject seems less prominent. When I Googled “Israel US elections” this morning, all the top results concerned next week’s Israeli parliamentary elections.
In less than two weeks, however, Americans will also head to the polls. They’ll decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.
As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms. We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November.
Previously, we dug into how both parties are changing, the bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers, and the politics of high costs. This week, we’re tackling Americans’ growing disillusionment with Israel — and how that will (or won’t) show up at the midterm ballot box.
Go a little deeper
You know the first part of this story already, because we’ve discussed it quite a lot: Americans’ views of Israel have nosedived over the past 18 months.
That shift helped shape the Democratic primaries and will likely figure prominently in the coming presidential contest. But how much Israel matters in a general midterm election, to people outside the political left…well, November will really test that.
Voters rarely rank Israel policy among their top priorities. In a poll that the Associated Press and NORC Center for Public Affairs Research conducted earlier this month, about 80 percent of registered voters said Congress should highly prioritize the cost of living during its next term, and roughly 70 percent said the same about ending the Iran war. By comparison, less than a third of voters said they prioritized cutting off aid to Israel.
There’s another way that Israel factors into US elections, of course — and that’s in fundraising. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has become one of the biggest spenders in US elections and a repeat flash point in this year’s Democratic primaries.
But in the general election, even AIPAC has been overshadowed by the GOP’s big-business donors, many of them in tech, who have given Republicans a historic spending advantage in this year’s contests. On Wednesday, the lobbying group actually announced it would no longer endorse political candidates or make direct campaign contributions.
In either case, whatever happens in the midterms won’t likely transform US policy toward Israel. President Donald Trump is still in charge of foreign policy, after all, and even if Democrats take back the House, they’ll have little ability to reverse his agenda.
But a Democratic majority would gain “new congressional tools to act on Israel-Palestine issues,” Hady Amr, the former US Special Representative for Palestinian Affairs, wrote in a new analysis for Chatham House. Those tools aren’t flashy (think: hearings, funding restrictions, and reporting requirements), but they could certainly set the stage for a broader policy shift under a Democratic president.
Races to watch:
- Florida’s Senate race, where Democrat Angie Nixon has criticized her party’s ties to the pro-Israel lobby;
- Michigan’s Senate race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign grew out of pro-Palestinian activism;
- Michigan’s (deeply purple) Seventh District, where progressive William Lawrence has vocally criticized US support for Israel.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.
“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.
Previous visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.
The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.
Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.
After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.
By Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.
It said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”
The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.
“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.
The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.

Sundar Pichai (allegedly) draws the line at oceans
President Trump claimed that the Google CEO refused to rename the Atlantic Ocean in Maps.
Capitulating to a bully might seem like a good idea in the short term. But do it once, and you've proven that you'll acquiesce to an escalating series of demands. Take Google, for example. The company, which appeased Trump by renaming the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario in Google Maps, has (allegedly) had to field a call about renaming the Atlantic Ocean.
That's the scenario President Trump recounted at a rally on Wednesday in South Carolina. He said he called Google CEO Sundar Pichai to ask whether Google Maps could "handle" a new name for the Atlantic. The president said he'd weighed whether to use "Trump" or "America" on either the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean. Pichai's response was, reportedly, "Please don't ask us to do that."
According to Trump, Google's compliance finally hit a limit. "No, no, no, this time I'm not doing it," Trump quoted the CEO as saying. "Oceans are different, sir." The stated rationale was that oceans "cover a lot of countries." Of course, the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario also touch more than one country: three for the former and two for the latter.
Trump said he'd "probably pass" on the Atlantic. However, he also floated renaming the Pacific Ocean "the American Ocean" instead.
Google didn't stumble into this. In early 2025, it relabeled the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" for US users following Trump's executive order. This August, it did the same to Lake Ontario in the US, which now reads as "Lake America." In both cases, Apple followed suit. It's increasingly clear just how low Big Tech will stoop when tariff exemptions, regulatory favors and government contracts are on the line.
Meanwhile, inflation is rising, gas is at $4.27 a gallon and diesel is at $6.31, according to AAA. The Iran war has dragged on for 236 days despite Trump suggesting in March that it could be over in four to five weeks. With the midterms less than two weeks away, at least we have a president who's laser-focused on the real issues.

Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
- Published
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.
The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.
Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.
Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
'Critically important'
Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.
After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.
It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.
And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday accused the Congress of undermining movements that sought to hold the government accountable and push for reforms.

He accused the Congress of sidelining young opposition leaders and keeping only one person in the limelight. “The Congress does not allow others to get an opportunity. It wants to keep only one person in the limelight and does not listen to the voices of young leaders in the opposition,” he said.
His remarks come amid a series of protests in Delhi over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls, demands for chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and restrictions on the right to demonstrate.
Modi's ‘angoor khatte hai’ jibe at Congress

“I don’t know how long Congress will continue putting the country’s interests at stake to launch its failed product. In a year, there are not as many launches from Sriharikota as the number of failed attempts Congress makes to launch its leader,” he said.

Student groups, including AISA, and youth organisations have protested in Delhi over the SIR exercise, alleging that 13 crore eligible voters’ names could be deleted and demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
