Two European women held captive for more than a year in Niger freed in Libya
- Published
Two women - a Swiss and an Austrian – have been freed after more than a year in captivity in Niger and handed over to authorities in the Libyan city of Benghazi.
Swiss national Eva Gretzmacher, 76, and Austrian Claudia Abbt, 69, were kidnapped separately in the northern Nigerien city of Agadez in January and April last year.
No details have been given about who was holding them or their demands, although some reports have previously linked the kidnapping to Islamic State militants. The circumstances of their release were not disclosed.
Libyan officials were reported as saying the women would be handed over to authorities in their respective countries after necessary procedures were completed.
Libya's al-Masar TV showed the two women entering what looks like an ambulance and later being attended to by a health worker.
Speaking in French, the women thanked Khalifa Haftar, military commander of eastern Libya, and his son, Saddam Haftar, for their release.
Gretzmacher was an aid worker who had lived for many years in Niger, while Abbt had spent several years living and working as a community worker in Agadez.
A plane was expected to leave Benghazi on Thursday, first stopping in Vienna to transfer Gretzmacher to Austrian authorities before continuing to Switzerland with Abbt, privately owned Air Info Agadez news outlet reported.
Libya has struggled to recover from the chaos that followed the 2011 Nato-backed uprising that toppled long-time ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
It is split between two administrations - one in the east backed by Haftar, and the other in the west in the capital Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah.
Niger and the broader Sahel region have faced years of jihadist violence, including kidnappings and deadly attacks, carried out by different groups linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State.
The country has been under military control since 2023 when Gen Abdourahmane Tchiani deposed the country's elected President, Mohamed Bazoum.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) called for a Tricolour March on 16 October 2026. Police were deployed across Delhi, while CJP member Abhijit Dipke was picked up from his residence in Jhandewalan and Neha Bora was detained at Mandi House, both in Central Delhi (here, here, here).
Against this backdrop, a video showing a crowd marching with Tricolour flags is being shared on social media (here, here), claiming that it shows the Tiranga March organised by the Abhijeet Dipke-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) in Delhi on 16 October 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows the Tiranga march called by the Abhijeet Dipke-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) in Delhi on 16 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video shows a protest march led by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav near Gandhi Maidan in Patna, Bihar, on 19 August 2026. It is unrelated to the CJP’s Tiranga March in Delhi on 16 October 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to social media posts (here, here) from August 2026 mentioning that the visuals show a march organised by RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav in Patna, Bihar. This confirms that the video predates the CJP’s Tiranga March scheduled for 16 October 2026.
Based on this clue, a keyword search led us to reports stating that RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav led a protest march in Patna on 19 August 2026 towards Raj Bhavan. The protest was held over issues including question paper leaks, unemployment, and the alleged firing on student protesters in Siwan, Bihar.
We also geolocated the viral video and confirmed that the location shown in the clip is near Gandhi Maidan in Patna, Bihar. The comparison between the viral video and geolocation can be seen below.
To sum up, the viral video shows Tejashwi Yadav’s August 2026 protest march in Patna, not CJP’s Tiranga March in Delhi.

Trade, H-1B visas, Pak factor: Marco Rubio on key issues in India-US relations
Marco Rubio defended US immigration curbs, urged India to diversify crude imports, backed deeper nuclear and defence cooperation, ruled out Pakistan ties coming at India's expense and called for a diplomatic end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday said India and the United States are close to reaching a trade agreement, with only a few issues remaining under negotiation, expressing optimism that the deal would provide greater certainty for businesses in both countries.
In an exclusive interview with India Today TV, Rubio said he could not foresee anything preventing an agreement, although he declined to disclose the remaining points of contention or whether Washington would offer India the competitive tariff advantage it was seeking in an interim trade deal.
"We are very close," Rubio said, adding that only a few items remained under discussion. He said the agreement must benefit both countries and provide businesses with clarity on the rules governing bilateral trade and investment.
"The point of having an agreement is to be able to have certainty so that people know they can invest, people know what the rules are that are going to govern trade and commerce between the two countries," he said.
The top Trump official was responding to concerns about continuity in trade policy and the possibility of repeated tariff revisions, including in the context of the Super 301 provision of retaliatory tariffs. He did not spell out how the proposed agreement would address these concerns but said predictability was one of the principal objectives of the negotiations.
US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who joined Rubio for the interview, described the bilateral relationship as stronger than ever across several sectors, including trade, information technology, pharmaceuticals and defence.
Gor said bilateral trade had increased from around USD 20 billion 15 years ago to usd 240 billion, arguing that investments by Indian and American companies were creating jobs in both countries.
He cited investments by Indian companies in the US, including multi-billion-dollar facilities being developed by the Essar group, as examples of the economic benefits flowing in both directions. Gor also said American technology companies operating in India complemented employment in the US rather than simply shifting jobs overseas.
H-1B VISA RESTRICTIONS NOT AIMED AT INDIA, SAYS RUBIO
Addressing concerns over higher visa costs and restrictions affecting Indian professionals and students, Rubio defended the Trump administration's immigration policies, saying they were part of a broader reform and were not specifically directed at India.
He acknowledged that the changes affected Indians seeking to work in the US and American businesses seeking to hire them, but said the policies applied to countries across the world.
"The United States has had a broken immigration system," Rubio said, citing unlawful immigration, alleged fraud and abuse in business-related immigration programmes and concerns among American workers about competition for jobs.
He said the administration wanted an immigration system that worked for the US economy and its citizens.
The Secretary argued that concerns over foreign workers taking up highly skilled jobs needed to be addressed as the administration pursued its goal of rebuilding American industry. He maintained that the policy changes were not India-specific, even if their impact was more pronounced in countries whose professionals make extensive use of US work visa programmes.
Gor echoed Rubio's position, saying the changes were not targeted at any individual country and arguing that Washington needed to reset its immigration policies.
He said the principle of "America First" did not mean the US wanted to act alone, adding that Washington expected other countries to understand its decision to prioritise its own national interests.
US WANTS INDIA TO BUY MORE AMERICAN CRUDE
On energy cooperation, Rubio said Washington wanted New Delhi to diversify its sources of energy by purchasing more crude oil from the US and other countries in the West, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing imports from Russia.
Asked about President Donald Trump's decision to allow additional energy flows into the global market, including a temporary waiver of sanctions affecting Russian oil purchases, Rubio said the administration was considering the wider effects of the Russia-Ukraine war and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
He said the temporary measure was intended to increase supplies in the global market at a time when diesel prices were high across the world.
Rubio stressed US foreign policy had to account for the wider global economic consequences of conflicts rather than be viewed through the lens of a single country or crisis.
Rubio argued that India had already been diversifying its energy sources and that greater reliance on a wider range of suppliers would serve its interests.
"It's not so much about buying less Russian oil than it is about buying more US crude or Venezuelan or others from the Western Hemisphere," he said.
He also highlighted India's refining capacity, saying the country could process more crude oil and attract investments to expand its refining infrastructure.
Rubio's visit to a refinery operated by Reliance Industries in Jamnagar in Gujarat, was an opportunity to understand its operations and its potential role in processing more crude from the Western Hemisphere, he said. He also pointed to the company's investment in a facility in Brownsville, Texas, which he said was expected to come online by 2029.
INDIA COULD BE AMONG FIRST COUNTRIES TO GET US SMALL MODULAR REACTORS
The US State Secretary also indicated that India could become one of the first international markets for American small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs), following India's decision to open parts of its civil nuclear sector to private participation.
He credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government with passing the SHANTI Bill, which he said enabled private technology and new equipment to enter India's nuclear sector.
Rubio acknowledged that regulatory challenges remained and that the process would take time, given the complexity of nuclear technology and the long-term nature of the partnership.
"India is one of the first places that the United States is looking at possibly to have our first SMRs internationally," he said.
He added that discussions had taken place in Washington, New Delhi and Mumbai, where India's nuclear regulatory agency is based and expressed confidence that cooperation would progress.
According to Rubio, the regulatory process was still under way, cautioning that the partnership would take time to develop because of the complexity of the technology and the long-term implications of nuclear cooperation.
'US-PAKISTAN TIES WILL NOT COME AT INDIA'S EXPENSE'
Marco Rubio sought to reassure India that Washington's engagement with Islamabad would not undermine its relationship with New Delhi or its position on counterterrorism.
Asked how the US would ensure that closer ties with Pakistan did not come at the expense of India's fight against terrorism, Rubio said Washington had longstanding relations with both countries and hoped to use its engagement with Pakistan to influence its decisions.
"In no way does the relationship with Pakistan come at the expense of our relationship with India," he said.
Rubio said the US shared India's concerns about terrorism and cited American operations against Islamic State and al-Qaeda, as well as the killing of al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, as examples of Washington's counterterrorism efforts.
He also referred to US counterterrorism operations in parts of Africa, arguing that Washington had demonstrated a sustained commitment to combating extremist groups and ideologies that threaten both countries.
Asked about his diplomatic engagement during Operation Sindoor following the Pahalgam terror attack, Rubio declined to disclose details of his conversations with the Indian and Pakistani leadership.
He said the US was willing to play a constructive role whenever tensions between countries risked escalating into a wider conflict.
The objective, he said, was to prevent war and encourage countries to pursue cooperation in business and commerce.
Rubio added that any diplomatic solution would require both sides to engage and make concessions, while acknowledging that getting the parties to the negotiating table would not, by itself, resolve their differences.
DEFENCE COOPERATION AND QUAD GAIN MOMENTUM
Ambassoder Gor said defence cooperation between India and the US was at an all-time high, pointing to joint military exercises, co-production and the presence of American defence companies in India.
He cited the participation of around 500 US Army personnel in the Yudh Abhyas exercise and the involvement of American F-35 fighter jets in the Tarang Shakti exercise as examples of expanding military engagement.
The envoy added that Tarang Shakti marked the first time F-35 fighter jets had participated in a joint exercise in India and the aircraft were deployed only to countries Washington trusted, presenting their participation as an indication of the depth of the defence partnership.
Gor also named Lockheed Martin and Boeing as American companies involved in India's defence sector, arguing that joint production could create jobs in both countries.
He described India as a valuable partner in the Quad, the grouping comprising India, the US, Japan and Australia.
Rubio said the Quad was increasingly moving beyond diplomatic meetings to practical cooperation, particularly in maritime awareness and supply-chain security.
He added that Washington was working towards a leaders-level meeting, which he expected could take place around December, while seeking further engagement before the end of Trump's term.
He cited efforts to monitor potential threats to undersea cables and said the four countries were working to reduce excessive dependence on any single country for critical goods and technologies.
Rubio said India and the US could develop domestic capabilities in sectors including artificial intelligence, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and critical minerals.
Gor, joining the topic, said Washington had invited India to join the Pax Silica initiative, describing New Delhi as a trusted partner in strategic supply chains.
He also said senior US officials, including the attorney general and representatives of American law enforcement agencies, were expected to visit India for discussions on counter-narcotics cooperation.
RUBIO SAYS RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR MUST END DIPLOMATICALLY
On the Russia-Ukraine war, Rubio said a settlement would require diplomacy rather than a military victory.
He described the dispute over the Donbas region as central to the conflict, saying Russia wanted territory that Ukraine was unwilling to surrender because of concerns about sovereignty and long-term security.
Responding to a question about Russian President Vladimir Putin's reported willingness to consider a trilateral meeting involving Russia, the US and Ukraine, Rubio did not outline a specific negotiating framework. Instead, he focused on the territorial dispute over Donbas, describing it as the central obstacle to ending the war.
The question, he said, was whether both sides could agree to an arrangement involving concessions.
"This war is not going to be solved militarily. This war is only going to end diplomatically," Rubio stressed.
He added that Washington was willing to help bring the parties together but acknowledged that negotiations would not guarantee an immediate settlement.
Rubio said the territory at the heart of the dispute accounted for about 11 per cent of the relevant part of Ukraine and that Russia had been unable to take it militarily while Kyiv remained unwilling to surrender it. He said both sides would have to weigh concessions against their respective interests if a settlement was to be reached.
GOR SAYS TRUMP, MODI REMAIN IN REGULAR CONTACT
Ambassador Gor further said Trump and Modi maintained a close relationship and were in regular contact, including through multiple phone calls during the month of the interview.
He described both leaders as focused on delivering results and said their relationship helped advance bilateral cooperation.
"They're, they're dear friends and it works well because of that, because they see eye to eye on moving the ball forward, on getting things done, on delivering. And so he holds the Prime Minister in the highest regard. They've known each other for many years," Gor said.
Rubio, meanwhile, praised Trump's approach to foreign policy, describing him as a leader willing to pursue decisions that traditional politicians might consider difficult or unconventional.
He described Trump as a business-minded and unconventional leader who was willing to pursue ideas that others considered impossible, saying this approach had shaped the administration's foreign policy. Gor similarly predicted that Trump's presidency would be viewed as historically significant.
Asked whether he would contest the 2028 US presidential election, Rubio declined to discuss the possibility, saying his current responsibilities as secretary of state and national security adviser occupied his time and attention.
The interview covered a wide range of issues, but the trade agreement remained one of the most immediate areas of bilateral engagement. Rubio's optimism about the negotiations came with a qualification: the remaining issues still had to be resolved and the final terms had not yet been announced.

The One Question AI Could Not Answer
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Why Children Need More Than Screens to Master the Future
Hong Kong is moving decisively into the age of artificial intelligence in education. The government has committed significant funding to digital education, supporting schools in purchasing AI tools, digital resources and related training. The message from policymakers is clear: our children must learn to master technology.
They are right. But true mastery requires much more than screen time.
To master AI, children must first master something far older, subtler and more profound themselves.
Artificial intelligence can calculate, translate, summarise, generate images and simulate conversation at astonishing speed. Used well, it can support learning and open new possibilities. But AI cannot replace the experiences through which children become grounded, confident, imaginative and fully human.
This is why, at Garden House Waldorf School, our approach to education begins not with the screen, but with the child.
The Senses Are Not Optional
Children do not become fully human through information alone. They become human through experience.
The evidence on screen time is alarming. Studies tracking children aged two to five have found that as screen time increases, so does emotional fragility, irritability, difficulty calming down, and an inability to complete tasks. These patterns persist across age groups from six to seventeen. Children with high screen exposure struggle to remain calm when faced with challenges. Their curiosity declines. The risks of anxiety and depression escalate.
These behaviours are not signs of dysfunction. They are signals of confusion — of a child who has lost their internal compass. The problem is not merely the screen itself. It is everything that screen time displaces: physical activity, imaginative play, face-to-face interaction, and the rich sensory engagement that builds resilience.
For those of us living in cities, there is another urgent concern. A landmark study involving over 300,000 children found that for every additional hour of daily screen time, the risk of myopia increases. At four hours per day, the risk roughly doubles. In parts of Asia, myopia rates have surged from modest levels in the 1970s to 80 or even 90 percent today. The eye is designed for flexibility — alternating between distant horizons and nearby objects. Locked onto screens for hours, it loses that adaptability.
The Sensory Imbalance of the Digital Age
Consider the online meetings that have become part of our daily lives. They engage at most two senses: vision and hearing. The sense of warmth — that tangible experience of human presence — is entirely absent.
This is the deeper risk of the AI era. A mode of perception dominated by vision and hearing will only intensify, leaving the lower senses — touch, smell, taste, life sense, balance and movement — chronically underdeveloped. AI excels at recognising words. But it operates on a dangerous assumption: that understanding words is equivalent to understanding thought, and that understanding thought is equivalent to understanding another human being. Everything becomes confined to the literal, with no warmth to complete the circuit.
There are people who "know" each other through social media, yet find themselves completely lost when meeting in real life. They possess information about one another, but they lack the sensory experience of one another. Their sensory pathway is incomplete.
Wisdom Cannot Be Downloaded
None of this means that technology is bad, nor that AI should be kept out of education forever. Children must eventually learn to understand it, question it and use it wisely.
But the key word is wisely.
The question for our age is not whether children will use AI. They will. The question is whether they will bring to it a fully developed humanity — bodies that are awake, senses that are alive, hearts that can feel, and minds that can judge.
That is the one question AI could not answer. It can only be answered by how we choose to educate our children.

Etsy is announcing stricter rules about how AI can be used in listings to reduce the volume of AI slop on the platform. In a post, the company says that “many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content” and that sellers are “concerned about your work appearing alongside items that use AI in misleading ways,” spurring the new policies and restrictions.
Etsy is cracking down on AI slop listings
Etsy’s new AI policies, among other changes, require that a listing’s first photo is unedited.
Under the new policies, every listing must include “at least one unedited photo of the actual item against a real background,” and all photos must “accurately represent the item a buyer will receive.” The photos that aren’t the first one can be edited with software or AI-powered tools, as long as “the final result remains an accurate representation of the physical product.” The company shared a few examples to demonstrate the type of misleading images that are prohibited, including the cat stuffed animal at the top of this post.
While uploading images for a listing, if Etsy detects that any may be AI-generated, the platform will show a pop-up where you can note if an image was made with AI or not, as shown in a video. If a buyer reports that what they receive is “materially different” from a listing, a seller may be responsible for a refund.
For sellers who offer “functional guides,” which include patterns, recipes, or instructions,” Etsy says that the information in those products “must be your own work, not generated by AI.” Sellers will have to show an “actual result” made from a guide. The company also says that listings made by bots are no longer allowed.
Selling AI-generated art is still allowed on the platform, but a seller must disclose that it was made with AI, Etsy says.

Bandipora, Oct 22: A late-night operation to evict the District Drug De-addiction Centre and an adjacent old age home in north Kashmir’s Bandipora has drawn sharp criticism.
Medical staff have accused authorities of acting like thieves, while officials cite property disputes and unpaid rent.
Both facilities are operated by a local non-governmental organisation funded by the central Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, functioning locally under the Social Welfare Department. However, the premises belong to the health department and the municipal committee respectively.
The facilities were inaugurated just some years ago. The old age home opened in October 2022, followed by the de-addiction centre in February 2023. Both were inaugurated by then deputy commissioner of Bandipora Dr Owais Ahmad.
The closures occured when officials reportedly arrived under the cover of darkness, breaking locks and removing medical equipment, luggage and staff belongings. This left vulnerable patients arriving for treatment the following morning completely blindsided.
The human toll of the sudden eviction was starkly visible at the old age home.
"I was having dinner when some men came and told me to leave the premises immediately. They didn't even let me finish my meal before forcing me out," said Ghulam Mohammad, an elderly man sitting outside the home, who has been living at the facility for the past three years.
"They went upstairs, broke in, and started throwing furniture and belongings out of the windows. When I asked where I would go, they told me the administration hadn't paid the rent and said they were not responsible for me."
Dr Anjum, a medical officer at the de-addiction centre, expressed shock over the execution of the eviction. She confirmed no staff members or officials from the centre were notified or present during the night-time operation.
"It was a sudden action and no member of the centre was kept in the loop," Dr Anjum said. "It was like a robbery. They came, broke the locks and brought all the luggage down. If the district administration will do these things, what can you expect from thieves?"
She added that while the health department may have a legal claim to the property, the method of reclaiming it was flawed.
"They are saying it is their building and they can take it, but you need to take it legally, not like thieves," she said.
The closure has disrupted a critical healthcare lifeline in the district. The de-addiction centre has around 1,400 registered patients. Dr Anjum noted that patients arriving for scheduled outpatient treatments the next morning were forced to flee in distress upon finding the doors locked and operations suspended.
An official from the Municipal Committee Bandipora, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Greater Kashmir the old age home was evicted because the occupants had failed to pay rent since taking over the municipal property.
"It was given to them as a temporary accommodation, but they ended up occupying it permanently," the official said.
He noted the rent was originally fixed at 17,000 rupees per month, but no official rent assessment was conducted over the years, leading to massive outstanding dues.
Defending the eviction of the de-addiction centre, Additional Deputy Commissioner Zaffar Shawal distanced the core district administration from the specific execution of the move, attributing the action directly to the health department.
He explained the premises originally housed the old district hospital, noting the health department reclaimed the building because they required the space for their own operational needs.
"The building was under the occupation of somebody else and they took it back," he said, refusing to answer if the action was a departmental matter rather than a broader administrative directive.
Block Medical Officer Bandipora Dr Tahir Malik confirmed this, telling Greater Kashmir the health department was taking back its own property.
"Obviously, it was a government hospital, so the health department will occupy it," Malik said.
When asked about the sudden, night-time execution, Malik declined to provide specific operational details, stating only that government procedure was followed and noting the wider dispute is now sub judice.
Repeated calls from Greater Kashmir to Chief Medical Officer (CMO) Bhajan Kour, for further comment on the operation went unanswered.
Health workers and social staff are now scrambling to locate displaced equipment and secure alternative spaces to resume care for their stranded patients. "There is no place to stay put, neither has any information been shared with us," Dr Anjum said.

I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”
Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”
That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.
They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start?
Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.”
Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event …
Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing.
There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.”
Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important.
How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees??
Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load.
Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine.
Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.”
Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.”
You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend?
Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy.
Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with?
Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.
One woman came to an event with a mother who was dealing with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, and she wanted to know whether her mother was qualified for long-term care because she had an insurance plan. Well, the insurance carrier sent her a 300-page packet. Who is going to read through that? This is how insurance companies keep you from using your insurance policy. So of course, she fed it to AI. And the AI came back saying, yes, your mother is absolutely qualified for care, and would you like me to write a letter to the insurance company to argue your case?
When I first started out as a consultant, I, in a typical female way, completely lowballed my consulting fee. I fed my proposal to Claude and said, “What's wrong with this? Make this bulletproof.” And it came back and said, “You're not charging enough for this scope of work.” And I was like, “Well, what should I charge?” And it said, “Start by doubling your rate.” I took a deep breath, and I did it. The client did not blink.
I feel that a lot of people don’t want to get near AI because they see slop and get the ick. But you’re talking about something different—using AI for economically valuable tasks.
Berger: The economic value piece is really important, because women have long suffered from being stuck at home as domestic laborers, because we weren't seen as economically valuable in the marketplace, right? So the idea behind Aged Intelligence Society is that if anyone needs to optimize their time, it's women.
In some ways, AI is the new washing machine or the new laundry or whatever it is. It's giving women many, many hours of the day back by offering them automation.
The reason we narrowed the aperture to people 40-plus is that we feel like the product-market fit for women who are over 40 is so spot on. One, because we have very discerning taste after many decades of honing it. We know how to ask really sharp questions. We have very strong bullshit meters, so we're not going to take just the first answer. We're going to keep probing and pushing.
And so we feel like in some ways this tool was built for people who have a certain level of intelligence and accrued experience. It's not really built for young people. It's not built for people who have not already gone through the failure and the friction of life and learned for themselves what makes for a good question.

Dream night for Bournemouth - win over Milan a sign of Premier League power

At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation.
That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture.
Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final.
Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008, not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts.
"It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports.
"So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special."
To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two).
While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point.
In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A.
The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years.
For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare?
Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance?
Premier League sides make strong start
English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once.
In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them.
In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them.
Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21.
The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams.
But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years.
So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory?
Money talks
Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List.
It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League.
Premier League clubs earn more than £1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined.
Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30.
Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'.
Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final.
In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively.
In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League.
All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates.
The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of £3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues.
Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.
You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings.
Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent.
"With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August.
"A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer."
Europe still rules in Champions League
Despite the success of Premier League sides in the Europa League and Conference League, the Champions League is a harder nut to crack.
While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered.
Over the past two campaigns, eight of nine English teams have been knocked out by one of the Deloitte Money League's big four, according to the last report produced in January 2026.
Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Liverpool were eliminated by an aggregate score of 25-6 last season.
No English club appeared in the top four of Deloitte's Money List, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain leading the way. Three of those have won the Champions League five times between them in the last seven years.
English clubs are certainly very much in the mix for the Champions League, with Arsenal losing last season's final on penalties and Manchester City winning in 2023.
But, with just one English club in the past three finals, the Premier League elite are yet to take their European domination to the very top.
Come May, it could well be Bournemouth, Brighton, Crystal Palace or Sunderland leading the English charge in Europe.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.
* With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

New Delhi,Oct 22: The Road Ministry has proposed mandating Advanced Emergency Braking Systems (AEBS) for all new car models starting October 2030 to curb road accidents.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), in a draft notification dated October 19, 2026, said that for pre-2030 still-in-production models, AEBS would be mandatory from October 2032.
AEBS provides automatic braking in the event of failure of the driver to respond to emergency situations to either avoid a crash or reduce the impact of a collision.
"Provided that, M1 category of vehicles manufactured on and after 1st October 2030 in the case of new models and 1st October 2032 in the case of all models shall be fitted with Advanced Emergency Braking System, conforming to AIS-185, as amended from time to time," the draft notification said.
The government has mandated multiple measures, especially focused on braking systems, to enhance the safety of medium and heavy-duty vehicles.
To enhance brake performance, a revised braking standard has been mandated for trucks effective October 1, 2027.
Braking systems have been advanced with the mandatory implementation of electronic stability control systems (AIS 162) for trucks from October 1, 2027, which provide stability, especially in the event of braking at curves.
The draft rules will be taken into consideration after the expiry of thirty days from the date on which the copies of this notification, as published in the Gazette of India, are made available to the public.

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.
It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.
However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, Trailblazer, released in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.
The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’
The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.
Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’
At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.
As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.
It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.
But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.
Mary is part of a legacy of tall women in Indian health care that helped sculpt systems that are propping the nation up today, including Muthulakshmi Reddy, Kadambini Ganguly, and Anandi Joshi. They are the forebearers who chipped away at the glass ceilings that prevented them from rising, and cleared the ladder for women who came after them, though history has not given them their due space.
But it is now time for reparation, it is time to say their name loud. Say her name: Say Mary Poonen Lukose, so every one can hear, and celebrate.

One death due to measles, 161 confirmed cases and 116 suspected cases have been reported in Kozhikode district so far this year.
Health department officials, at a review meeting on Wednesday (October 14, 2026), said the disease was spreading mainly among unvaccinated people. They said preventive measures would be strengthened and vaccination coverage expanded with the help of other government departments in the coming days.
They pointed out that measles vaccination was available at all government health centres. The two doses of the measles-rubella vaccine, administered between nine and 12 months and between 16 and 24 months, are an effective preventive measure. If children miss vaccination, they can receive the injections up to the age of five.
L.T. Saritha Kumari, District Medical Officer, presented a report at the meeting chaired by Assistant Collector Malavika G. Nair.

- Social media posts claim grocery giant Kroger plans to cut 3,000 U.S. employees and replace them with artificial intelligence and outsourced workers in India. Due to the lack of access to primary evidence, we have left these claims unrated.
- The claim about replacing the workers with AI is based on reliable news reports. Bloomberg and Reuters reportedly viewed a company memo from CEO Greg Foran saying the company plans to cut 3,000 corporate jobs in the U.S., while noting it hopes to increase its use of AI tools. Snopes has not been able to view the memo, so we cannot independently verify its contents.
- Meanwhile, the claim about outsourcing jobs to India appears to come from Brittain Ladd, a self-described "business strategist and consultant." In July, Ladd said anonymous sources at Kroger told him the company planned to move some of its jobs to a "capability center" in Bengaluru, India.
- Ladd's claim also is supported by reliable reporting. Multiple Kroger executives have spoken on quarterly earnings calls about outsourcing as an opportunity to save money. Furthermore, The Charlotte Observer found an August 2026 post announcing that Kroger planned to move its technology and digital operations to India on a LinkedIn page that helps fill outsourced positions.
In October, social media posts claimed grocery giant Kroger is planning to replace 3,000 U.S. workers with a combination of artificial intelligence tools and outsourced workers in India.
Snopes readers contacted us asking whether the claims were true.
We found solid secondary evidence suggesting they are true, but because we could not independently verify them with primary evidence, we leave this claim unrated for now.
Is Kroger laying off 3,000 workers?
Bloomberg and Reuters, both reliable sources for business news, separately reported the claim that Kroger plans to lay off roughly 3,000 workers. In turn, the outlets sourced the news to a company memo they viewed that CEO Greg Foran, who joined Kroger in February, wrote. We reached out to Kroger for additional information but had not received a reply by the time of publication. 
The reports say the layoffs, which would affect approximately 37% of Kroger's 8,200 corporate employees, will be spread out over three years, but the exact details have not yet been determined. They also note the layoffs were part of a larger shift at Kroger toward adopting more artificial intelligence tools into its workflows. Foran's memo reportedly says the company needs to cut duplicative work while adapting to new technologies, which would allow the grocery chain to reduce prices and invest in in-store staff.
Snopes has not been able to view the memo so cannot independently verify its contents. The company has not appeared to refute the above reports, as of this writing.
Is Kroger outsourcing jobs to India?
At least one social media post notes that Foran — a Walmart executive from 2014 to 2019, who Bloomberg said helped "turn around Walmart's US business" — has a history of outsourcing roles to India.
While Foran was at Walmart, the company announced it was outsourcing its "finance and accounting back-office operations" to Genpact, an outsourcing company founded in India as a subsidiary of General Electric. (It is unclear to what extent Foran was involved in this decision.)
The claim about Kroger outsourcing jobs ultimately originates from a July 2026 LinkedIn post from Brittain Ladd, who describes himself as a "business strategist and consultant." His post cites "sources from Kroger." The Cincinnati Business Courier and The Charlotte Observer picked up and recirculated Ladd's analysis in July and August, respectively. Snopes attempted to contact Ladd but he did not reply before publication. (We relied on Ladd's post and the Observer's reporting for our investigation, as the Courier's coverage was paywalled.)
According to Ladd, the idea for Kroger's new global capability center (a euphemism for an outsourced office) was initially floated in 2019, long before Foran's entrance, but it was put on hold while the company pursued a merger with Albertsons, because "pursuing mass layoffs during [a Federal Trade Commission] antitrust review would have been reckless." That proposed merger fell apart in December 2024. Since then, Kroger has actively worked to implement its outsourcing plan.
The Observer reported that multiple Kroger executives, including Foran and Chief Financial Officer David Kennerley, have repeatedly mentioned the center during quarterly earnings calls as an opportunity to save costs. "We need to operate more efficiently," Foran reportedly said during the June 2026 call. "That means fewer organizational layers, smarter ways of working, standing up our Kroger capability center and applying AI across the business."
The Observer also found a July LinkedIn post from GCC ERA, a website helping fill outsourced positions in India, announcing that Kroger Technology & Digital was outsourcing roles to the country. According to that post, at least some jobs at Kroger are being outsourced to India.

Jammu, Oct 22: A fire broke out in the Bhagwah area of Doda district, gutting six shops and two stores and causing heavy losses to local shopkeepers, officials said.
There were no casualties or injuries from the fire.
The incident occurred late Wednesday night in the Dessa-Bhagwah belt. Fire and Emergency Services personnel, along with local police and community members, worked together to bring the fire under control, officials added.
Abdul Rahman, a local shopkeeper, said the fire spread rapidly before the fire brigade arrived, destroying a substantial portion of the shopkeepers' stock.
"We were at home when we heard people shouting that the market was on fire. By the time we rushed here, the fire had spread. Much of the shopkeepers' stock was destroyed before the fire brigade arrived. Around 8 shops, including mobile and electronics shops, were affected," Malik said.
The extent of the losses and the cause of the fire were not immediately known.

‘Rahul Gandhi should become PM’: Revanth Reddy's appeal in Telangana
Reddy said the country was at a critical juncture and urged members of the Nehru family to take responsibility for its future.
Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy on Thursday called for Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, to become prime minister, saying his leadership was necessary to secure justice for backward classes and steer the country towards progress.
Addressing the 174th birth anniversary celebrations of Panduga Sayanna Mudiraj, a figure associated with the struggle for backward-class rights, Reddy said the Nehru family chose other leaders to head the government despite having opportunities to take the top post after Rajiv Gandhi's death, news agency PTI reported.
"Rahul Gandhi should become prime minister if justice is to be done to the backward classes. They could have become (PM) long ago had they wanted it. After Rajiv Gandhi's death, Congress came to power many times," he said.
He also appealed to people to set aside their differences and make a positive choice when the next Lok Sabha elections are held.
Telangana government considers Mudiraj community's BC-A status
Reddy said his government was committed to strengthening the political representation of all backward-class communities. He announced that a cabinet sub-committee would be formed to examine the demand for including the Mudiraj community in the BC-A category.
The community currently falls under the BC-D category in Telangana. According to Reddy, the matter would be taken up at the next cabinet meeting, with officials and legal experts consulted before a decision is made.
He also asked Backward Classes Welfare Minister Ponnam Prabhakar to engage with other backward communities, including Gangaputras, who are already classified under BC-A, to address concerns about the distribution of reservation benefits.
Revanth Reddy highlights caste survey and welfare measures
Referring to the caste survey conducted by his government, Reddy said the findings had enabled different communities to raise their concerns more effectively.
He also highlighted the government's food distribution programme, contrasting it with the subsidised rice scheme introduced by former undivided Andhra Pradesh chief minister N T Rama Rao.
While Rama Rao had launched a scheme providing rice at two rupees per kilogram, Reddy said his government was supplying fine-quality rice free of cost to 3.48 crore people through the Public Distribution System (PDS).
He added that his government was continuing policies pursued by former chief ministers N Chandrababu Naidu and Y S Rajasekhara Reddy in undivided Andhra Pradesh, as well as K Chandrasekhar Rao after Telangana was formed.
Statues of Telangana figures planned at Tank Bund
Reddy also announced plans to install statues of prominent Telangana personalities, including Doddi Komuraiah and Panduga Sayanna, at Tank Bund on the banks of Hussain Sagar lake.
Recalling Sayanna's legacy, he said the social figure had stood up for marginalised people when feudal landlords encroached on their lands during Nizam rule.
Reddy said Sayanna was arrested by the Nizam's police, after which the queen of Wanaparthy Samsthanam, a feudal estate, paid a substantial amount to secure his release.
He said Sayanna was killed unjustly and noted that songs celebrating his contributions continued to be sung during agricultural activities such as sowing, even more than a century after his death.

Pakistan arrests man hunted by US over $126m postage fraud case
- Published
Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.
Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.
He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.
The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.
Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

Reuters has contacted PSG, Lyon, the LFP and the Paris police prefecture for comment.
