My Oura Ring now feels like a keepsake from a former self. I picked it out with the company’s sizing kit, but within a month, it no longer fit the same way. Since January, I have shed over 40kg of fat. The ring, once snug, now slips and spins, holding on with costly accuracy to the shape I used to be. I knew I’d need new clothes as my body changed, but I barely considered the fate of my health tracker.
There’s a quiet satisfaction in letting a beautiful watch claim your wrist. A smart ring grants that luxury, quietly gathering the data we now expect from ourselves. It never lights up a dinner table or interrupts with a sleep report until you ask for it. The appeal is clear: you can care about your health without announcing it to the world.
For Indian buyers, however, the introduction came with an awkward timetable. Oura Ring 4 went on sale here on March 18, 2026, starting at ₹28,900, with membership priced at ₹599 a month. On May 28, Oura announced Ring 5 globally, with shipping from June 4. The new ring in the shop was suddenly the previous ring in the range. After waiting for an official Indian launch, it was difficult to feel especially courted by the sequence.
On the move
Then comes the reality of daily life. If you eat with your hands, the ring joins you at lunch, its polished surface flirting with unruly masala. Cooking means kneading dough; cleaning up means plunging into a sink of dishes. You can take the ring off, but then you need a safe spot for it. For something prized for its low-maintenance charm, it still demands attention at unexpected moments.
Oura’s instructions acknowledge some of this domestic life. You can clean its titanium rings with mild soap and water, then dry them thoroughly. Showering is permitted. The company advises considering removal when handling hard cookware or lifting weights, where friction can scratch the finish. Wearing it directly beside another ring can scratch either piece.
Jewellery brings its own negotiations. Delhi-based certified fitness professional Aarja Bedi, who is engaged, has begun wearing her smart ring on the corresponding finger of her right hand. She likes the idea of a titanium band alongside traditional pieces, but is less sure about the comfort of wearing them together. “You don’t want to be figuring out finger real estate the week before a big occasion,” she says. Oura recommends the index finger, with the middle or ring finger also suitable. The wedding band need not surrender its place to the sleep score.
The data debate
Chennai-based fitness coach Raj Ganpath, author of Simple, Not Easy, stopped wearing an Oura he had bought from the United States. The fit troubled him; changing sizes from India was inconvenient, and the morning readings didn’t consistently match the morning he thought he was having. His Garmin has stayed. He chooses information relevant to his training, including its VO₂ max estimate of aerobic fitness, without feeling obliged to attend to everything it produces. “You need to know what data is important for you and what you need to track,” he says.
Raj describes someone waking quite happily, reading an unfavourable sleep report, and beginning to feel tired. The number has acquired the authority to revise the experience. Mumbai-based Ritesh Shaiwal, athlete and director of Easyhuman, wants clients to pay attention to sleep scores and heart rate variability, the variation in timing between heartbeats, without waiting for permission from a gadget to feel motivated. “It is ok to use it, but don’t get dependent,” he says. There is a difference between being interested in your sleep and having it marked every morning.
Those subtleties could be introduced more warmly at the sales counter. During my visits to over a dozen stores in Delhi and Mumbai, I noticed it was a challenging to find staff who could confidently explain Oura. Instead, conversations often shifted towards Gabit. While this was my experience, not a national audit, but with Gabit available at Croma and Ultrahuman already in Indian retail, Oura might need to ensure that its reputation alone isn’t the only thing guiding demonstrations. When someone is buying for the first time, they really benefit from having someone who can clearly explain what happens after opening the box and why the monthly payments continue.
The software provides part of the answer. GLP-1 Insights was launched for English-speaking users in India starting June 4, including on Ring 4. Users can log medication doses, record side effects, and track weight alongside sleep or recovery data. Between medical visits, days can blur: when did the tiredness start? How did last week go? Having a record could make discussions with healthcare providers more effective. This update matters beyond simply adding a new app feature.
A record still requires interpretation. A readiness score cannot establish that a medication caused a change, and a weight entry cannot tell you how much of the loss is fat. Oura says the feature does not recommend dosage changes or replace a clinician. It can help someone arrive at an appointment with a better account of what happened, without supplying the medical conclusion.
One size doesn’t fit all
On June 23, Oura announced a collaboration with LillyDirect, Eli Lilly’s US healthcare platform, offering eligible customers a complimentary Oura sizing kit. That detail really matters. The company is there to help people find their perfect ring size, especially for treatments that might change it. The kit starts by answering that question early on. But what about the answer later on? Not everyone taking medication to lose weight will need a smaller ring, but the possibility doesn’t require much imagination. Oura is inviting these customers to wear its product through the process. A paid plan with a defined size-change benefit would let them buy with confidence about what follows. Eli has no reason to organise an exchange of my ring. The company selling it as a companion to my changing body has every reason to consider one.
Oura’s published warranty says replacement rings come in the original size. Its sizing guidance directs people with a poor fit to support, leaving room for an individual solution, but I could not find a published Indian benefit guaranteeing a replacement after weight loss. Retail exchanges follow the retailer’s policy, which might cover situations like selecting the wrong size at checkout. In my case, I was confident that I chose the right size from the start.
Ultrahuman has provided clearer details. Its two-year UltrahumanX plan, available to eligible users, allows a Ring AIR wearer to request a smaller replacement after losing weight, according to its terms. Only one ring replacement is permitted for the reasons listed, whether due to weight change or fit adjustment. While the limit matters, it’s equally important to understand the offer thoroughly before you put the ring on your finger.
I would gladly pay Oura for a size-replacement plan in India. I am invested enough in its insights to want to keep wearing it, especially with the new GLP-1 features. There is still lunch to get through, the question of where I left it before doing the dishes, and a steadily loosening fit. Mine may soon need to be a different size. I would like that to be a conversation about continuing to wear it, rather than buying it all over again.
So, should you consider getting one? If you’re looking for a subtle health companion that offers useful insights without another screen demanding your attention, Oura is definitely worth thinking about. Its GLP-1 features provide even those starting treatment with another reason to consider it, though I would suggest keeping an eye on the potential size change. Many users won’t experience the same issues I do. They’ll simply wear the ring, go about their day, and discover helpful information whenever they open the app. Despite my own concerns, I still believe Oura is a great choice. I just hope the company makes it easier to keep the ring fitting perfectly as I get smaller.

Bukele says military operation launched to rescue Salvadorans held by gangs in Haiti
SAN SALVADOR — El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday he had launched a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran aviation technicians kidnapped by gangs in Haiti, warning of a more forceful response if they are not released alive and unharmed.
Gangs in Haiti had opened fire on an armored vehicle three days earlier the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country. The four Salvadoran soldiers have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.
Addressing Haitian gang leaders, Bukele demanded that they return the Salvadorans "alive, unharmed" and warned that, if they do so, "everything will go back to the way it was before the kidnapping." If not, the Salvadoran leader — who drew international attention for his contentious war on his own country's gangs — said it would result in a more powerful operation.
"Today's attack is nothing compared to what is coming if they do not release the four hostages alive. And do not take our words as empty threats," he wrote on the social media platform X.
It was not immediately clear if Bukele intended any further action to be carried out by Salvadoran, Haitian or international security forces in the area.
In his post, the Salvadoran leader shared video of armored vehicles with shattered windows driving through plumes of smoke.
Haiti's government issued a news release Wednesday evening saying the "abduction" of the aviation technicians was an "absolute priority."
It noted that a meeting was held at the prime minister's office "to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force."
"The release of the abducted soldiers is an absolute priority, and all necessary resources are being mobilized to achieve this goal," the government said.
It wasn't immediately clear if Haitian authorities received confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.
A spokesperson for the gang suppression force did not immediately respond to a message seeking details.
Bukele said the four men are aviation technicians and that the Salvadoran mission in Haiti "consists only of pilots and technical personnel" whose main job is to carry out medical evacuations, "not to wage war."
The U.N.-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday's attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops and it comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador is among a number of countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form a part of a gang suppression force with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.
The U.N. in 2025 originally approved up to 5,550 security personnel and more than 50 civilian staff to be sent to Haiti to dismantle armed gangs.
In early October, El Salvador passed a law extending its armed forces' participation in the force for a year. The law also authorized the mission to "deploy civilian and military personnel according to the mission's needs," expanding its role beyond medical evacuations, as stipulated in the previous decree.
The multinational force received at least a six-month extension through March 2027 from the U.N. Security Council.
Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years, with more than 5,700 people killed or injured from January through mid-September and more than 230 people kidnapped, according to the United Nations.
The area where the armored vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitelhomme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou. Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the U.N. and the U.S.

The federal government has sent an offer to the European Space Agency (ESA) to send the Australian of the Year, astronaut Katherine Bennell-Pegg, to the International Space Station.
The mission, slated for 2028, will mark the first time a qualified astronaut has flown to space under the Australian flag.
The ESA offer for Bennell-Pegg to join a future ISS mission garnered support from philanthropists and the Australian space industry, but has previously described by the office of the science minister, Tim Ayres, as “a very expensive undertaking” which no government alone could fund.
Announcing the decision on Friday, Ayres said:“The government has been engaging extensively with the private sector, philanthropists, and other levels of government to raise funding to support a space flight – which is a significant cost.
“We are grateful to the philanthropists who have committed over $6m in cash, plus in-kind support, and some indicative support from some state governments.”
Bennell-Pegg is director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency (ASA) and completed astronaut training with the ESA in 2024.
She is not the first Australian astronaut, but she is the first to qualify under the Australian flag. Dr Andy Thomas and Paul Scully-Power, both Australian-born, went to space as US citizens on Nasa missions. Elaine Hyde, a dual Australian and US citizen, last year took a suborbital flight aboard Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin NS-30.
In May, the ASA announced it had entered into “treaty-level discussions” with the ESA, which “would establish a formal framework for enhanced cooperation between Australia and Europe”.
In August, Ayres and the assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, wrote to state and territory leaders asking them to “partner” with the federal government to fund the mission. The letter, according to The Australian, described it as a “complete Australian mission that includes locally developed experiments and technology”.
South Australia, where the ASA is headquartered, has publicly committed to supporting Bennell-Pegg’s space bid.
“South Australia stands ready to partner with the commonwealth in what should be a national endeavour,” the premier, Peter Malinauskus, said. “Katherine Bennell-Pegg has the potential to inspire a new generation to dream big and address the single biggest challenge to our economy which is productivity.
“Australia has a massive shortage of young people taking up the fields of science, technology, engineering and maths, and we need more of it if we’re going to grow the nation’s productivity … Nothing would motivate young people more to take up these fields of endeavour than seeing Australia’s first ever flagged astronaut in space.”
A campaign to secure Bennell-Pegg’s spaceflight mission was supported by entrepreneurs Dick Smith and Jim Whalley – who had each pledged $1m funding for the mission – and former prime minister Kevin Rudd, who said on social media that the “project makes long-term economic sense for Australia beyond the usual sensibilities of the Treasury bean counters”.
Richard de Grijs, a professor of physics and astronomy at Macquarie University, said of Bennell-Pegg: “She is qualified, she has undergone significant training, so she is set to go up if a suitable mission can be found.
“The government has actually contributed quite a lot of money to that education already,” he said. The ASA paid $466,000 for Bennell-Pegg to complete her astronaut training at the European Astronaut Centre in Cologne, Germany.
“There is an inspirational value in sending a citizen from your country to space who is also the Australian of the Year … but the question is, is that worth $100m?” De Grijs said.
“It’s a lot of money, but on the other hand, it might actually lead to returns that are way more than the estimated number.”
De Grijs pointed out that Australia was also involved in “inspirational spaceflight” by another means: an Australian-built lunar rover, named Roo-ver, will be sent to moon on a Nasa mission in 2030.
Darin Lovett, chair of the Space Industry Association of Australia, said the industry had “a strong track record of return on investment”.
“For around $100m, less than the price of a single coffee for every Australian adult, this is not a ticket to space. It is a down payment on Australia’s future in one of the defining industries of this century.”
In a speech Bennell-Pegg delivered earlier this month, she described space as “a gateway – a lure – into the full breadth of STEM fields. Especially for those that dream of going up there.”

For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.
Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI. “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.
Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.
Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.
AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.
It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely.
Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster. These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals.
Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it.
Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress.
Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says.
Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely.
I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers.
I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here.
It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights.
Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab.
Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.”

India’s manufacturing story is moving beyond assembling finished products. Startups are developing specialised components, materials and engineering systems that power industries ranging from electric mobility and aerospace to energy storage and computing infrastructure. The semiconductor industry offers one indication of this shift. At SEMICON India 2026 in September, the government outlined the next phase of the India Semiconductor Mission, spanning chip design, materials, manufacturing equipment, fabrication, advanced packaging and research. The push reflects India's ambition to build domestic capabilities across the semiconductor value chain. Policy support is also extending to other manufacturing-intensive sectors. On October 13, the Ministry of Heavy Industries extended the bid submission deadline for a programme to establish 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity for grid-scale energy storage. The initiative is part of the government’s effort to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing. These developments are creating opportunities for startups building real technologies behind industrial growth. However, developing a promising technology is only the starting point. Startups must validate their products, establish reliable production processes and translate engineering capabilities into commercially viable businesses. Against this backdrop, Inc42 is back with the October edition of its ‘Five Manufacturing Startups To Watch’. This edition features Nautical Wings Aerospace, Magron Novus, NuSynth, Refroid and Xbattery Energy, five startups working across aerospace propulsion, electric motorcycles, chemical process innovation, data centre cooling and battery management systems. With that said, here are the five manufacturing startups that caught our eye in October. Editor's Note: This list is not a ranking. It is a curated selection of manufacturing startups that have stood out to the Inc42 editorial team this month. Nautical Wings Aerospace | Developing Electric Propulsion Mechanism For Aircraft Aircraft propulsion systems must balance power, efficiency and reliability against strict constraints on weight and operating conditions. As electric aviation and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) evolve, developing propulsion systems suited to these requirements could open up opportunities for specialised aerospace manufacturers. Bengaluru-based Nautical Wings Aerospace is developing electric propulsion systems, motors and composite components for aircraft and UAVs. Founded in 2020, the startup also offers custom engineering capabilities for aviation applications. Its product portfolio includes fixed-wing UAV propulsion configurations with rotor sizes of up to 120 inches and power outputs of up to 150 kW. The company's work spans electric motors, propulsion integration and lightweight composite components, bringing several critical elements of aircraft propulsion engineering under one roof. Its focus is on developing indigenous hardware for aviation and unmanned platforms. Nautical Wings operates in India's emerging electric aviation market, which is projected to grow at a CAGR of 7.8% through 2029. Its progress will depend on validating its systems for specific aircraft applications and establishing repeatable manufacturing processes. Magron Novus | Fully Forged Carbon Fibre EVs Building an electric motorcycle involves more than replacing a petrol engine with an electric motor. Manufacturers must engineer the powertrain, battery architecture and vehicle controls to deliver the performance riders expect. Bengaluru-based Magron Novus is attempting to bring these elements together through its own technology stack. The startup is developing electric motorcycles and related technologies, including wireless power transfer and connected riding features. Founded in 2022, the startup showcases two platforms: the C-20, designed for everyday riding, and the H-35, aimed at the performance segment. According to the company's published specifications, the C-20 features a 22.5 kW motor, while the H-35 has a 35 kW motor. Its proprietary technology stack includes the Apex Drive system, battery architecture and vehicle intelligence features. The startup is also developing wireless power transfer technology and a virtual assistant to enhance the charging and riding experience. E2Ws command a significant share of India's booming electric vehicle market, which is poised to reach $132.2 Bn by 2030, according to Inc42's India's Electric Vehicle Startup Landscape Report. A healthy uptick in sales supports this market's rally. In September, total E2W sales stood at 2.07 Lakh units, a 12.2% month-on-month increase from 1.84 Lakh units registered in August. Magron's ability to turn its technology into reliable, manufacturable products and bring its motorcycles to market will determine how it develops in India's increasingly competitive electric mobility sector. NuSynth | Re-Engineering Chemical Manufacturing Processes Chemical manufacturers often face challenges when developing processes for complex molecules. Existing synthesis routes can involve high material costs, difficult reaction conditions, safety risks or production steps that become harder to control at commercial scale. Improving these processes can therefore be as important as developing new chemical products. Bengaluru-based NuSynth Technologies is a chemical manufacturing startup focused on process innovation for complex chemistry. Founded in 2026, the company aims to redesign chemical synthesis rather than rely solely on incremental improvements to existing methods. Its initial focus areas include pharmaceutical intermediates and electronic chemicals, with the ambition to develop proprietary process technologies for global markets. The startup combines chemical research with an AI-enabled platform that uses experimental data to guide subsequent research and development. By recording experimental outcomes as structured data, the platform aims to prioritise future experiments and accelerate the development and commercial scale-up of chemical processes. NuSynth's operations include an R&D facility and pilot plant in Mysuru, alongside a Bengaluru facility under development. The company also reports working with more than 20 manufacturing partners across India, providing a potential route from process development to commercial production. Its services include custom synthesis, process development, scale-up and commercial supply. NuSynth operates in India's speciality chemicals market, valued at approximately $37 Bn in FY25, according to NITI Aayog's report on India's chemical industry. The segment accounts for around 18% of the domestic chemicals industry and includes high-value products used in pharmaceuticals, electronics and other industrial applications. Refroid | Developing Cooling Systems For AI Infrastructure Data centres require cooling systems. As facilities accommodate increasingly intensive workloads, conventional air-cooling approaches can face efficiency and capacity constraints. Liquid cooling offers another route, transferring heat more directly from computing equipment to a cooling system. Hyderabad-based Refroid Technologies is an industrial machinery manufacturer developing cooling solutions for data centres and other mission-critical computing applications. Founded in 2021, the company focuses on liquid cooling technologies for hyperscale facilities, edge computing and high-performance computing environments. Its technology portfolio includes immersion cooling, direct-contact liquid cooling, coolant distribution units and hybrid load banks used in testing environments. These systems are designed to support the thermal management requirements of high-performance computing. Refroid has also highlighted its work on indigenous cooling technologies. The company announced a collaboration with Bharat Petroleum Corporation to develop an indigenous liquid coolant and has introduced domestically developed coolant distribution units for liquid-cooled data centres. The startup operates in India’s data centre industry, where installed capacity increased from approximately 375 MW in 2020 to around 1,500 MW by 2025, according to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Xbattery Energy | Building Indigenous Battery Management Systems Batteries are central to electric vehicles and renewable energy storage, but their performance and safety depend on the electronics that monitor and control them. Much of this technology remains import-dependent, creating an opportunity for Indian manufacturers to develop indigenous battery management systems. Hyderabad-based Xbattery Energy is a deeptech startup manufacturing battery management system (BMS) electronics for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Founded in 2024 by Satish Reddy, Sonu Mishra and Varshith Veeramaneni, the company aims to replace imported electronics with locally developed hardware and software. Its flagship platform, BharatBMS, supports applications ranging from 5 kWh home backup systems to megawatt-scale energy storage and high-voltage electric vehicles. The company also offers battery monitoring through a cloud platform, allowing customers to track battery parameters and diagnostics. Its customers include automotive and battery manufacturers, although names remain confidential under non-disclosure agreements. Xbattery operates in India’s BMS market, valued at approximately $281.6 Mn in 2024 and projected to reach $699.6 Mn by 2029, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 20%, according to MarketsandMarkets' India BMS market report. The market covers electronics used to monitor and manage rechargeable batteries across electric mobility and energy storage applications. In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.
I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.
In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.
Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.
The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.
Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.
It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.
In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.
Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.
What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.
But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.
And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

- Published
Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid.
"With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MSN NOW, external.
In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation.
The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.
More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out."
Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed.
"We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".
The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".
Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one.
She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.
The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.
Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating.
Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".
Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.
He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".
At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it".
"You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

Viral "looksmaxxing" streamer Braden Peters — the self-proclaimed online beauty guru who built a massive following as "Clavicular" — pleaded not guilty in a Massachusetts court on bombshell criminal charges alleging he intoxicated and raped a 17-year-old girl at his family's Cape Cod home.

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

Meta wants more than rank-and-file employees at the office. It wants CEO Mark Zuckerberg there, too — even if that comes at a hefty price.
The tech giant's board said in a securities filing Wednesday that it would create a new class of non-voting stock in part to keep Zuckerberg in control and give him a financial incentive to continue living near its headquarters. It described his presence at the office as "critically important" to its future success. Meta has required employees to come in at least three days a week since 2023.
Zuckerberg previously told the board he was considering moving in response to a proposed California billionaire tax. The stock deal would give the CEO $20 billion in "immediate liquidity" to cover the tax by selling stock without losing control of Meta, the filing said.
That arrangement carries particular weight at Meta, where Zuckerberg is leading the company's AI push. It also speaks to a common belief that has driven return-to-office mandates: The best work happens when people — including senior leaders — are physically together.
Staying local
Cole Rubin, cofounder of sports technology company FanFeed, said CEOs and other execs are sending a message to employees by physically working alongside them.
"You're not going to question why you're working long hours if you actually can see the leader doing the same," Rubin told Business Insider.
Having bosses in the office can also help a company move faster when unexpected opportunities arise, he said. Employees can walk into a leader's office, get an immediate answer, and act before the moment passes.
"It's not the scheduled calls where the magic happens," Rubin said. "When you have the decision-maker there, it gives people a lot of freedom to be able to feel heard."
A leader's presence is especially important during crises, said Bill George, former chairman and CEO of Medtronic, a medical-technology company. Being together lets executives quickly assess what has happened, gauge employees' reactions, and decide on a course of action.
"We've got to really feel what's going on emotionally, and we actually physically have to discuss it," he said.
George also noted that RTO demands placed on workers can ring hollow if the CEO doesn't follow them. "You've got to be there if your employees are there," he said.
Long-distance tradeoffs
Meta wouldn't have been the first company with a long-distance CEO if Zuckerberg had opted to leave the Golden State.
Brian Niccol was living in California when he was named CEO of Seattle-based Starbucks in 2024. The coffee chain had agreed as part of his hiring package not to require him to relocate. Later, it built a 4,624-square-foot satellite office five minutes from his home so he could work alongside colleagues, Business Insider first reported. Niccol has since purchased a property in Seattle.
Companies with long-distance CEOs don't perform as well on average as those with leaders on-site, according to a 2025 study by Boston College and Arizona State. They also have lower valuations and worse insider reviews, the findings show.
Meta's decision to woo Zuckerberg to stay in California was made by a special committee on its board, which said it was informed by challenges the company faced when he couldn't be physically present with management during the pandemic.
The committee said it didn't want Meta "to face similar challenges going forward."

Menopause may not be a gradual process taking years as is commonly thought -- instead, the female body could be traversing a "physiological cliff" around the time of the last menstrual period, a new study has found.
Analysing more than 300 million laboratory test results from over one million women in the US and Israel, researchers at Weizmann Institute of Science identified abrupt changes in dozens of measures of bodily health and function, far beyond the familiar shifts in sex hormone levels and the loss of fertility.
Findings published in the Nature Medicine journal showed that the changes appeared in 52 of the 90 types of laboratory tests examined, covering nearly all body systems, including tests of bone health, liver and kidney function, and cholesterol levels.
The changes were found to be less pronounced among women receiving menopausal hormone therapy.
Further, the sudden shifts were preceded by accelerating changes in sex hormone levels that began more than a decade before menopause -- several years earlier than previously thought.
None of the abrupt changes were observed in men of similar ages, the study found.
It "revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP (final menstrual period) including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems," the authors wrote.
Because most of the abrupt changes identified in the study are associated with increased disease risk, the findings could help women take preventive steps, such as exercising and improving their diet, years before menopause, the researchers said.
"Our study extends the window for potential preventive care to almost a decade before menopause. More broadly, the method we developed may help study other major changes in life, such as puberty, pregnancy or the onset of disease," author Uri Alon, from Weizmann Institute of Science, said.
Two sets of data were analysed -- results from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, conducted over more than two decades, and medical records collected over around 20 years by Israel's health insurer Clalit.
The researchers said that such large datasets are rarely used in menopause research because they generally lack information about the age at which women had their last period.
To overcome the limitation, the team developed a computational method which they said is inspired by astronomy.
Just as astronomers can sharpen an image by mathematically correcting distortions caused by a telescope, the new method removed the 'blur' in medical data caused by differences in the age at which women reach menopause, the researchers said.

Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a clinic.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said three of the missiles carried cluster warheads. One struck the Pecherskyi district, damaging several historic structures, including a monastery.
“This is another extraordinarily revealing strike – revealing, because it was no accident,” Zelenskyy said. “The choice of weapon was deliberate; the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible.”
He said the strikes showed Russia was not serious about peace, adding: “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.”
During negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Putin, who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.
In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply: “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles.”
Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors that could bring down enemy missiles, and more sanctions against Moscow.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, added that “appeasement, servility and flattery” would not stop Russian aggression.
Downing Street said it did not recognise Witkoff’s description of Putin, pointing out that the Russian president had killed “thousands” of Ukrainians and his own frontline soldiers.
On Wednesday, the Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the coming weeks, leaving millions in the dark and cold, officials in Kyiv believe.
According to Zelenskyy, the US has resumed intelligence warnings of Russian missile attacks. The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump called Elon Musk to ask him to reverse the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, which had left Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes. Some Ukrainian officials reportedly told the Journal that the system had been working better since the call, though still not at its previous capability.
The New York Times reported that when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.
Vladimir, the commander of an air-defence unit protecting Kyiv, said the US restrictions had hampered his unit’s ability to intercept Russian drones. “Of course it’s hindering us. Our drones can no longer reach the speeds needed to intercept enemy targets,” he said, adding that he felt betrayed by Washington.
The decision to cripple Ukraine’s successful drone programme came amid the most serious row between Washington and Kyiv since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. It began after Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, to lower US fuel prices, a move that Zelenskyy criticised as “weak”.
The Trump administration denies it is deliberately helping the Russians. But European diplomats concede that the US appears to have switched sides. Ukrainian civilians are dying as a result, they say.
Russia, meanwhile, said it had shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones launched in overnight attacks. One man was killed and another was wounded as a result of a Ukrainian aerial strike in Russia’s Belgorod region, local authorities said.
Details also emerged of a Ukrainian counterattack through a tunnel in the north-eastern city of Kupiansk, which Russia partly occupies. As part of Operation Veles, the Khartia corps carried out the world’s first underground counteroffensive, advancing 15km into enemy rear lines.
“We observed how the enemy operates underground and studied their methods. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to infiltrate the rear of our forces. So, we went underground ourselves,” Khartia’s commander, Brig Gen Ihor Obolienskyi, told Ukrainian media.
The Ukrainian soldiers crawled 15km through tunnels – without communication, GPS or light – having developed their own navigation and life-support technologies in advance. About 100 Russians were killed in the operation, and 30 taken prisoner, the Khartia corps said.
- Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber

Hong Kong watchdog warns of hacking risks from flaws in web programming language
Cybersecurity watchdog urges website operators to install updates immediately to fix two critical PHP flaws that could let hackers take over servers
A Hong Kong information security watchdog issued an “extremely high risk” warning on Thursday morning over two critical flaws in a widely used web programming language that could allow hackers to execute code remotely and take control of servers.
The warning followed similar alerts from governments and cybersecurity agencies overseas, which urged website operators to install updates to fix the vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language.
The Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) said a remote attacker could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code on a targeted system.

Ex-West Brom & Stoke striker Berahino retires at 33
- Published
Former Premier League striker Saido Berahino has retired from football at the age of 33 to concentrate on his role as a coach with Burundi's national team.
The Midlands-bred Burundi international made his name with boyhood club West Bromwich Albion, where he had one especially prolific season of 20 Premier League and cup goals in 2014-15 before joining Stoke City for £12m in January 2017.
But, having already faltered at Albion in his latter days under Tony Pulis, Berahino flopped badly for Stoke, who went on to suffer relegation from the Premier League in April 2018.
After being given a second chance by then Stoke boss Gary Rowett, he scored five times in 2018-19. But he soon fell out of favour again until he was released by mutual consent with still three years remaining on his contract.
Having left Stoke in August 2019 for Belgium, Berahino played at Waregem and Charleroi before being signed by former Baggies boss Darren Moore at Sheffield Wednesday in August 2021.
He has since played in Cyprus, India and Slovenia, as well as for his native country, having previously been capped by England at all age levels up to and including under-21.
Berahino was twice called up for England's full squad by then manager Roy Hodgson - but was not picked to play.
Berahino's 'Letter To The Game'
Berahino reserved special thanks for his first club, for whom he scored 36 goals in 121 appearances in all competition, including a hat-trick on his first start, as a 20-year-old, against Newport County in the EFL Cup in August 2013.
In a statement, entitled 'A Letter To The Game', posted on Instagram, Berahino wrote: "I want to thank West Bromwich Albion for believing in me when I was a boy.
"Those years at the club, the goals, the fans, the moments, they will always be special. There were highs and lows, mistakes and lessons. I learned that the game can lift you up and test you at the same time.
"The time has come to hang up the boots. My body and my heart are ready for the next chapter. I am proud and grateful to now serve the Burundi national team as a coach. Giving back to the country that made me, and helping the next generation, feels right.
"To my family - you have been my strength. To the fans who stayed with me through every chapter - I will never forget your support. This is not goodbye to football. It is simply the end of one story and the beginning of another.
"Football has given me everything. From the streets of Bujumbura to The Hawthorns, from the Premier League to places I never imagined I'd play - this game carried a young refugee kid through life."

A blood donor from Chikkamagaluru travelled over 300 km to Dharwad to donate a unit of blood to a three-year-old boy with the rare Bombay blood group, who was undergoing treatment for an inherited bleeding disorder at a private hospital.
The child, Abhinandan, was in a critical condition after severe bleeding caused his haemoglobin level to fall sharply. He urgently required a compatible unit of blood. Finding a suitable donor was challenging because the Bombay blood group (hh phenotype), an extremely rare blood type, is distinct from the usual ‘ABO’ blood groups, including ‘O’ positive and ‘O’ negative.
People with this phenotype lack the ‘H’ antigen on their red blood cells and generally cannot receive ordinary ‘O’-group blood; they require compatible blood, usually from another Bombay phenotype donor.
Following an appeal by the child’s father, Mahantesh, the Swami Vivekananda Blood Donors Foundation launched a search for a compatible donor. Its founder, Shivakumar Rattihalli, contacted Mahesh Kumar, a rare blood donor from Chikkamagaluru and explained the child’s condition.
Mr. Mahesh agreed to donate blood and travelled for over five hours to reach SDM Hospital in Dharwad, where, after completing the necessary procedures, he donated a unit of Bombay-group blood to the child.
The incident highlighted the importance of coordination among rare blood donors, as patients with the Bombay phenotype require specially matched blood and cannot generally receive blood from ordinary ‘O’-group donors.

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.
The Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names of millions of living Indian citizens.
Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.
In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries who detained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.
On Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government – drew tens of thousands of supporters as they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action, have vowed to “fight on” in their protests against SIR.
Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.
The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.
Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.
In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”
A Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.
“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.
Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.
“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”
Critics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.
“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.
By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.
Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.
“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”
Three former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.
Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”
None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”
The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.
Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.
Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exercise left millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.
A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued notices to Nestle India and Zydus Wellness over “misleading claims” in certain products and has asked the companies to provide scientific proof to support their advertisements.
In a social media post, the FSSAI said notices were sent to Nestle India for misleading claims and non-compliant promotions involving two food products ‘Lactogen Pro 1 Powder’ and ‘Nan Excella Pro Stage 1’.
The regulator also issued notice to Zydus Wellness Product Ltd citing misleading claims and advertisement on its food product Complan.
In the notice issued for Lactogen Pro 1 powder, the FSSAI said the company has claimed, in its labelling and advertisement material, that the product “contains whey protein, which is a part of milk protein that is easy to digest”.
The food safety regulator has asked Nestle to furnish scientific substantiation for the claim regarding whey protein being easy to digest.
In the product Nan Excella Pro Stage 1, the FSSAI said that the claim “5 HMOs [human milk oligosaccharides] helps support normal immune system” was considered to imply that the product was suitable for supporting the immune system.
“The claim was considered non-compliant with provisions prohibiting claims relating to the prevention, alleviation, treatment or cure of any disease, disorder or particular physiological condition, unless specifically permitted under applicable regulations,” the regulator said.
In the case of Complan, the FSSAI said the product label displays images of two children and claims include “2X Faster Growth”, “Supports Concentration and Memory” and “Pro Immunity+ 34 Vital Nutrients”.
The claims were found to be in violation of the FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.
The regulator has asked Zydus to provide scientific justification for such claims.
The advertisement claim “Growth Comes in 4 Flavours” was found to violate regulations of the FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018.
The companies have been directed to show cause within the stipulated period as to why action should not be taken against them, the regulator said.
