Anthropic has unveiled Claude Duet, a proactive AI agent designed to monitor connected apps, prioritise tasks, and carry out work in the background, including when users switch off their devices. The offering targets professionals and small business owners. Powered by Claude Opus 5.5, it is available as a research preview through a waitlist for Claude Pro and Max subscribers in the US. Users can access Claude Duet through standalone iOS and Android apps or on Claude’s website. It is included in existing Pro and Max subscriptions but shares usage limits with other Claude products. Background checks count towards these limits, while complex assignments consume more usage, Anthropic said. Unlike conventional AI chatbots, Claude Duet is designed to identify work that needs attention without waiting for a prompt. It sends users a daily briefing covering important items across connected apps, including emails and calendars, and provides updates when tasks are completed or require a decision. Users can assign tasks through text or voice messages, ranging from scheduling meetings and drafting email replies to building dashboards, financial forecasts and web applications. The agent can also search past conversations and use existing Claude memories, skills and connected apps. Claude Duet connects with more than 6,000 tools and plugins available through the Claude Marketplace, including Gmail, Slack, QuickBooks, Stripe, Gusto, LinkedIn, DocuSign, HubSpot and Shopify. For instance, it can identify unpaid invoices through QuickBooks or Stripe and draft payment reminders. It can also prepare payroll information, draft job postings, create follow-up emails using customer and deal histories, and help businesses set up and manage online stores. The agent runs on its own cloud-based virtual machine with a browser, allowing it to continue working even when users close the app or switch off their devices. Anthropic said it checks connected accounts every few hours rather than continuously, partly to limit subscription usage. Claude Duet can also help users make business purchases through Link, Stripe's digital wallet, and Shop Pay. Payments require user approval, while Link uses a virtual card to avoid sharing the user's actual card number. Integration with 1Password for accessing saved website logins is also planned. Anthropic said the agent requires approval before sending messages, making payments, signing documents or deleting information. Trading securities and transferring money between accounts remain prohibited, even with user approval. Users can disconnect apps, and only they can mark tasks as finished. Safeguards And Early Limitations Anthropic said Claude Duet includes safeguards designed to prevent unauthorised actions, prompt injection, and sensitive data leaks. Prompt injection involves malicious instructions hidden in content an agent encounters, such as emails or websites. The protections include an automated system that assesses proposed actions and controls designed to keep passwords and sign-in tokens out of the agent’s direct view. A separate message-checking system is designed to block requests to share highly sensitive information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health and personal finance details, can be shared only on explicit user instructions, Anthropic said. The company said Claude Duet has undergone adversarial testing and external penetration testing, and is covered by its public bug bounty programme. However, Anthropic acknowledged that the early version may misinterpret conversations, misjudge urgency, or miss information arriving between checks. It is currently better suited to work assignments than personal errands, such as booking tickets, and users cannot yet view its browser. The launch adds to the growing competition in always-on AI agents that work across apps with limited human intervention. OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse target similar use cases, while Bengaluru-based Emergent’s Wingman handles tasks across email, calendars, and workplace software through WhatsApp and Telegram. As agents gain access to more business systems, their permissions and accountability are also coming under scrutiny. Recently, CERT-In warned about unauthorised AI agent access to Indian organisations’ systems, highlighting the risks associated with deploying increasingly autonomous tools. Anthropic said feedback from early users will inform further development. The research preview does not currently include Team and Enterprise subscribers.

Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) on Wednesday (October 23, 2026) ordered legal action against officials responsible for discrepancies in the electoral rolls of the Pilibhit Assembly Constituency, where searching certain voters’ EPIC numbers online displayed details of other electors.
“Legal action will be taken against both the current and former election officials responsible for the discrepancies found in the voter list for constituency 127 – Pilibhit. In addition to the legal action being taken against the two voter registration officials, instructions have also been given to initiate departmental action. The computer support staff will be terminated. The District Election Officer, Pilibhit, has received a detailed report regarding a complaint concerning the display of the EPIC number of one voter in the voter list of Assembly constituency 127 (Pilibhit), indicating the details of another voter,” reads an official statement by the State election commission.
According to the investigation report, the computer operator of the voter registration centre for Assembly Constituency 127 – Pilibhit, entered a total of 13,779 Form-8s between May 31, 2026, and August 29, 2026, to update voter details. Of these, a total of 4,717 forms were entered between July 16, 2026, and the remaining 9,062 forms were entered between July 17, 2026, and August 29, 2026. No Form-8s corresponding to any of these entries were found in the office records. A total of 10,470 Form-8s were approved, while 3,309 were rejected. This revealed discrepancies in 10,470 of the entries,” says the official statement.
The Election Commission of India has directed that the computer operator at the voter registration centre in 127-Pilibhit and the election registration officers (EROs) assigned to the Pilibhit constituency for the period between July 16, 2026, and July 17, 2026, be held responsible for the irregularities in the voter registration process.
“The commission has instructed that legal action be taken against them under Section 32 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and relevant sections of the Indian Penal Code. Furthermore, the commission has directed a thorough investigation into the role of the relevant assistant election registration officers in this case, with a report to be submitted. The District Election Officer, Pilibhit, has been instructed to direct the computer assistants at voter registration centres to conduct a thorough review of all Form 6s and Form 7s submitted for voter registration and deletion, respectively, between April 10, 2026, and October 21, 2026, and to provide a detailed report within one day. In addition, all discrepancies found in Form 8 entries are being addressed according to established procedures and standards,” added the official statement.
The Congress on Wednesday (October 21) alleged large-scale manipulation of electoral rolls in the Pilibhit Sadar Assembly constituency, claiming that the names of 13,150 voters were changed while their EPIC and serial numbers remained the same. The party accused the Election Commission for the manipulation.

Can a dream help you solve a problem? Here's how to try tonight
We spend about two hours every night making home movies in our minds. Over a lifetime, that adds up to about seven years of dreaming.
For most of human history, those movies were considered sacred. Many early civilizations believed dreams were messages from the gods. In ancient Greece, people slept in temples hoping a dream would bring guidance or healing.
By the 1970s, scientists took a far less romantic view. A few psychiatrists likened dreams to the brain's attempt to make sense of random signals, and their theory threw cold water on the idea that dreams were meaningful.
Psychologist Rosalind Cartwright, known to colleagues as the "Queen of Dreams," pushed back. She believed dreamwork could be a form of therapy and made her case in books including Crisis Dreaming, co-written with Lynne Lamberg and The Twenty-Four Hour Mind. She published many studies from her lab experiments.
Today there's a resurgence of interest and new research. And one ancient practice is getting a fresh look: dream incubation, planting a question in your mind before sleep in hopes your dreams will offer insights.
It may sound mystical, but there's research behind it. In a small study from the 1990s an instructor at Harvard Medical School asked college students to focus on a problem at bedtime. About half reported a dream related to it, and many felt the dream contained a solution.
Jungian analyst Lisa Marchiano uses the practice with people navigating challenges and midlife transitions. The first step, she says, is asking a good question, and that takes time. "You want to ask a question that could be answered," Marchiano says. Skip yes-or-no questions. Instead, make it targeted but open-ended. If you're weighing a job offer, ask, "What would it look like if I took this job?" or "What would it look like if I went on another date with this person?"
Next, write down what you already know about the problem. "You're looking for the stuff you don't know," she says. "You want to invite your unconscious to fill in the gaps."
In other words, consult your inner "dream maker." As Marchiano puts it, "Instead of going to ChatGPT, try going to your dream maker."
Finally, turn it into a ritual so it doesn't feel like one more chore. You could take a bath as a way to wind down as you set an intention or "ask" for a dream. Marchiano says she writes her question in her journal, then copies it onto a slip of paper, folds it and tucks it into a small velvet bag to put under her pillow.
How to try dream incubation tonight:
- Think of a challenge, decision or problem you face. Write it down as an open-ended question.
- Review it before lights out. If you can, place a related picture or object by your bed.
- As you drift off, tell yourself you'd like to dream about it.
- Keep a pen and notebook on your nightstand.
- When you wake up, lie still before reaching for your phone. Jot down anything you remember, even a fragment or an emotion.
That last step matters. Many people say they don't remember their dreams, and the window is short. "You only have about three to five minutes to remember," says Dr. Harrison Shong-Wen Chow, a Stanford anesthesiologist. Writing a dream down or telling someone helps move it into long-term memory, he says.
Chow's own research explores something even more surprising: how dreams under anesthesia may help people process fear and trauma. There's also research into how an electronic device may help deliver dream prompts for targeted dream incubation.
Be patient. Dream incubation may not yield anything the first night, and dream recall is subjective. But over time, the practice may lead to a fresh insight, or at least a new way of listening to yourself.
To hear more about how to unlock the power of your dreams, listen to the new episode of Your Turn w/ Allison Aubrey wherever you get your podcasts and follow our Your Turn newsletter to help navigate the twists and turns of midlife.

Commentary: Do parents project PSLE stress to their kids?
Parents unwittingly place pressure on their children when they take leave or sabbaticals for PSLE preparation, says father-of-three Malminderjit Singh.
SINGAPORE: When children hit the age of 12, some Singaporean parents are ready to take on the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) even decades after they left their primary schools.
We can tell when the parents among us have children sitting for PSLE. Their annual leave is all saved and reserved for September. Some even take sabbaticals from work or say no to new projects and roles.
On the surface, these sacrifices appear commendable. But at what cost?
Parents unwittingly lay more stress on their children when they make such monumental sacrifices for their PSLE journey. “I have taken a year off from work for you, you better do well for your PSLE!” “We didn’t go for any family holiday this year, you better appreciate it by doing well!”
Suddenly a 12-year-old is now not merely sitting for an examination. He is apparently responsible for Mummy’s career progression or Daddy’s leisure and wellness.
We frequently talk about the stress children experience from PSLE. According to a recently published study by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS), around two-thirds of parents surveyed agreed that the education system caused unnecessary stress to their children. But whose stress is this, anyway?
HEIRS TO STRESS
In the IPS study, the proportion of parents who felt stressed about their children’s education increased from 73.1 per cent in 2016 to 87.9 per cent in 2026. And those who argued with their spouse over their children's education jumped from 42.8 per cent to 59.7 per cent over the same period.
Guess who has to bear the brunt of this pressure, on top of sitting for a milestone examination?
In a CNA exercise involving 20 Primary 5 and 6 pupils, parents emerged as their biggest source of stress. Some children described worrying about disappointing parents because of the money spent on tuition, being compared with friends, or internalising parental messages connecting good schools with future success.
One 11-year-old explained that a good secondary school would help him further in life. Asked where that idea came from, he answered simply: “My parents.”
Children learn not merely from what we tell them but what we react to. We may tell our kids, “Your marks don't define you.” Then ask after they walk through the door, “How well are you going to do on that paper?”
We insist, “Don't compare yourself with other people.” Then WhatsApp another parent: “How much did Sarah get?”
Children are extraordinarily good at detecting the difference between our values and actions.
TOO LONG A VIEW?
So, is the problem really with the PSLE examination? The IPS study found that most parents support PSLE, with 85.9 per cent of respondents indicating that it is a useful checkpoint for children. A similar percentage of parents felt that the PSLE is necessary to assess students fairly.
On the one hand, parents recognise the usefulness and relevance of PSLE, but on the other hand, they are getting more stressed by it. What exactly are parents anxious about?
The IPS study found that parents are less stressed about homework and preparing children for examinations. Instead, they increasingly worry that their child is not achieving the grades he or she is capable of, is falling behind or might lose out in the education system in the longer run.
That last phrase is revealing. A 12-year-old experiences PSLE as something happening this year. A parent sees it as a consequential event in a 15-year chain.
PSLE results determine which secondary school their kids go to, which influences which junior college or polytechnic they are admitted to and whether it can lead to a good degree and a respectable career.
Our children see an exam paper while we, as parents, see their entire lives flashing before our eyes. And then we wonder why everybody is anxious.
A HOLISTIC ARMS RACE
The IPS study tells us that there is light at the end of the PSLE tunnel. Parents increasingly value their children’s holistic development. They see character, self-discipline and other developmental outcomes as important goals of primary education.
But will the stress from an educational arms race just dissipate or will it diversify? The data offers a warning.
Average monthly tuition expenditure has risen from an inflation-adjusted S$386 in 2016 to S$677 in 2026. Average enrichment expenditure has more than doubled from an inflation-adjusted S$152 to S$355.
Nearly nine in 10 parents believe children spend too much time on tuition and enrichment. Yet 70.2 per cent say they would spend even more on tuition and enrichment if they had the resources.
That contradiction is striking. Collectively we think children are doing too much. Individually we worry that ours might not be doing enough.
The risk is that we simply expand the parental scorecard. Not too long ago, success meant, “What did you get for Maths?” Going forward, it could be “What did you get for Maths, what instrument do you play, are you in student leadership, do you volunteer and have you started coding?”
A PSLE PRISONERS’ DILEMMA
We should be careful not to turn every childhood interest into a credential. Sometimes a child should be allowed to play badminton because he likes badminton and not because his parent has identified a strategic Direct School Admission (DSA) pathway.
It is a tricky dilemma, though. If everyone else is running and I tell my child to walk, am I being enlightened or irresponsible?
Parents might prefer a less competitive environment, but nobody wants their own child to be the first to test it. This is why simply telling parents to “relax” will not work.
Singapore has created more pathways for children of all abilities to succeed. But parents still worry that missing a school, programme or opportunity puts their child at a lasting disadvantage. Perhaps the challenge is not just about creating credible pathways, but convincing parents to let their children take them.
Malminderjit Singh is Founder and Managing Director of Terra Corporate Affairs and a parent of three children.

Bypoll to Madhya Pradesh Rajya Sabha seat vacated by L Murugan on November 12: Election Commission
Murugan's term was due to end on April 2, 2030.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Thursday announced that the bypoll to a Rajya Sabha seat from Madhya Pradesh vacated by former Union minister L Murugan will be held on November 12.
The seat fell vacant on October 14, a day after Murugan, the Union minister of state for information and broadcasting and parliamentary affairs, quit the Council of Ministers and sought to give up his Rajya Sabha membership. His term was due to end on April 2, 2030.
Murugan was a Rajya Sabha member since September 2021 and was re-elected from Madhya Pradesh in April 2024. He is a former Tamil Nadu BJP chief and joined the Union Cabinet in July 2021.
In his resignation letter, Murugan said he wanted to return to the grassroots and work full-time to strengthen the BJP in Tamil Nadu ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.
He also spoke about what Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership meant for him. “It has been the greatest honour of my life to serve India and Tamil Nadu under your leadership. I do not come from a political family. I come from a very poor family,” he wrote. His parents, who worked as daily wage labourers and cattle grazers, “continue to lead a simple life in Konur village”, he said.
Murugan credited Modi and the BJP’s culture of recognising grassroots karyakartas and giving him opportunities far beyond his expectations. He described every responsibility he received as “an expression of your trust” – from the National Commission for Scheduled Castes to the Rajya Sabha and the Council of Ministers.

The notification for the bypoll will be issued on October 26, and the last date for filing nominations is November 2. Scrutiny will take place on November 3, and candidates can withdraw by November 5.
Voting will be held from 9am to 4pm on November 12, with counting at 5pm the same day. The whole process must be completed before November 16.

Twenty-one-year-old Saouhum Sharma, a 4th-year History honours student at Hans Raj College, joined the October 12 rally led by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi to the Supreme Court. By the end of the day, a knife had been slashed across his throat.
The Assault
Sharma and three friends met at Barakhamba Road at 2 pm. They subsequently met more friends and made their way to Mandi House.
“It wasn’t too chaotic at first,” he told Alt News. “We got the call from some Indian Youth Congress (IYC) people who were leading the protest around the area that Rahul Gandhi and everyone was reaching the Supreme Court; we should also reach the Supreme Court. The route from Mandi House to the Supreme Court is a straight road. So we decided to just start walking there. It was two groups of IYC workers and us.”
By 5.40 pm, the group had made some headway towards the Supreme Court when they encountered police barricades. “Some of the IYC people tried to topple the barricades but could not. So we went through a cut onto Sikandra Road.”
As they walked along Sikandra Road, they came across around 15 men standing beside a jeep. Sharma said some appeared to be Hindutva workers, based on what they were wearing.
“They were donning some markers of Hindutva workers. A couple of ‘gamchas’, one in a saffron-coloured T-shirt. Nothing overt, but definitely visible,” he said.
Initially, the men were provocative rather than violent, Sharma recalled. “They were whistling at the female IYC workers — whistling and calling after them. They called a few of them ‘chikni’. They were calling them while standing 20 metres ahead on the side of the road; arms around each other’s shoulders. From afar, they did not look like they would interfere because we outnumbered them. So we didn’t really think of turning back.”
However, as the group approached, the men began taking saffron flags with long poles out of the jeep. “They still weren’t exactly being violent, just provocative.”
Asked whether the men identified themselves as members of any organisation, Sharma said they did not. The flags, too, did not name any organisation, he said. They were generic saffron flags bearing images of an angry Hanuman or the Ram Mandir.
“The men decided to swing the poles, and the IYC workers got a bit agitated, and a bit of a brawl ensued between them; the IYC workers got into an argument with the goons,” Sharma said.
Amid the confrontation, a young man, whom Sharma estimated to be 18 or 19, entered their group. He was not wearing any of the visible markers that Sharma had associated with the men beside the jeep.
“Then this one guy, he was probably 18-19 years old, made his way inside our group. He wasn’t wearing any of those identifiable markers. So we couldn’t tell that he was from the other group. He stood beside me for about five seconds and then… it happened quite quickly.”
“He pulled out a barber’s knife. My friend saw it and dragged me towards herself at which point he swung the blade. He missed my face, and it grazed my neck. He walked away after that.”
Sharma said it took him some time to realise what had happened. “I felt a sting in my neck and realised I was bleeding. At that point, we walked away from the group and decided to head home.”
Encounter with Police
After walking around 500 metres from the spot of the assault, Sharma and his friends encountered a police official on Sikandra Marg, who spotted the blood on Sharma and called out to them.
“He was drinking chai by a police vehicle, wearing a light green vest. There wasn’t a lot of police presence at that point, as we were a little far from the protest site. He offered to give us a ride after he saw the blood,” Sharma said.
As the group considered the offer, the officer turned to the driver seated in the vehicle and asked him to detain them, Sharma alleged. “We got scared, turned him down and left. He insisted at first but didn’t follow us when we left. We immediately left the vicinity of the protest site, went to the Jama Masjid metro station and left.”
According to Sharma, the police official was not wearing a name tag.
“Thankfully, the cut wasn’t that deep as he missed my face and the knife only grazed my neck. After returning, I cleaned the wound a bit and then got a tetanus shot,” he said.

Celebrity shark returns to South Korea canal after failed rescue
- Published
A famed dusky shark in South Korea has returned to the canal where she had been stuck for a month, just one day after authorities said they had successfully guided her out, local media report.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after she was spotted lingering in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
South Korea's oceans ministry said on Wednesday evening they had led Bukangi out of the canal into an open harbour - but reports later said the shark had swum back to the mouth of the canal, having apparently broken through a barrier installed by authorities.
Another operation to relocate Bukangi has been scheduled for Thursday.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In recent weeks, more than 1.6 million visitors have descended upon a park in Busan to catch a glimpse of Bukangi, named after the canal in which she was spotted.
Her popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating. There were concerns that she would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans cheered and waved goodbye to their shark, unaware that she would still be lingering in the canal by the next day.
Before Wednesday's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
- Published
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.

Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. "We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".
He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.
Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.
"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."

According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.
It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.
Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.
David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".
France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.
BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.
The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.
The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.
Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.
The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.
It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.
While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.
Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

A U.S. judge on Thursday (October 22, 2026) issued President Donald Trump a December 11 deadline to testify under oath in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC.
Judge Enjolique Lett in Miami gave the order in response to complaints by the British broadcaster that Mr. Trump has refused to sit for a deposition, including canceling a previously agreed date of October 16.
If Mr. Trump fails to attend the deposition by then, he risks sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, the court said.
Mr. Trump has accused the BBC of deceptively editing its documentary "Trump: A Second Chance" to make it seem as if he was inciting violence when he told supporters to march on the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, after losing the presidential election.
The crowd proceeded to storm Congress in an attempt to stop the formal certification of Democrat Joe Biden's victory.
While the BBC has apologised for the incident, which prompted the resignation of multiple senior executives, the broadcaster has denied it caused Mr. Trump any real injury and moved for the case to be dismissed.
Mr. Trump filed his suit against the BBC in December 2025 and is seeking at least $5 billion on each of two counts.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said in court that Mr. Trump had no real excuse not to testify and that on October 16, he had only been campaigning, "participating in party politics."
"No plaintiff is above the law," Mr. Tobin said.
In a court filing Wednesday (October 21), Mr. Trump's legal team argued that he was not seeking to avoid a deposition but had been constrained by "matters of national importance."
The lawyers said Mr. Trump would be able to give a deposition between January 11 and 22.
Mr. Trump has made attacks on the media a signature of his two presidential terms, insulting reporters who ask questions he doesn't like and seeking to ban outlets airing critical reports from the White House.
Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.
With his approval ratings in the low 30% range and polls showing his Republican Party likely to lose control of the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterm elections, Mr. Trump faces increasing headwinds as he approaches his final years in power.

A Bharatiya Janata Party worker was killed in Malda district’s English Bazaar area on Wednesday night (October 21, 2026). Clashes also broke out in Arambagh and Nalhati during Durga Puja immersion celebrations. Police used force to control the mob as tensions escalated in both places.
The 38-year-old worker Samir Ghosh was allegedly attacked outside his home and shot dead. Police said that they detained one suspect and are looking for other suspects as Mr. Ghosh was allegedly attacked by a group of miscreants.
The reason for the murder and the details of the incident are being investigated. Malda police visited the spot on Wednesday night (October 21).
Mr. Ghosh was a BJP worker, his brother Vivek Ghosh alleged that the deceased was murdered by Trinamool Congress workers. However, local Trinamool leadership has denied these allegations.
“He was alone in the house when this happened, 10-12 people attacked and killed him,” Vivek Ghosh said. Others were reportedly busy in Durga Puja celebrations when this incident happened.
English Bazaar MLA Amlan Bhaduri also blamed Trinamool for the attack and said that he has asked for immediate action against those involved in the crime. Meanwhile, local Trinamool leader Biswajit Ghosh said that the clashes were due to personal family feud and had no political relations.

Two neighbourhoods got into a scuffle at Arambagh in Hooghly district as tensions escalated over Bijaya Dashami celebrations. The groups attacked each other with sticks which also led to vandalising houses. Police baton-charged the crowd to disperse the violent mob.
Clashes reportedly erupted after some miscreants from a neighbouring locality were accused of forcefully entering a celebration, which led to locals resorting to attacking the miscreants.
A similar clash erupted in Birbhum district’s Nalhati area where the locals objected to people bursting crackers during Bijaya Dashami celebrations and procession. Police resorted to baton-charging at Nalhati as well to control the violent crowd.

2026 సెప్టెంబర్లో విద్యా వ్యవస్థలో సంస్కరణలు చేపట్టాలని, పాఠశాలలకు నిధులు పెంచాలని డిమాండ్ చేస్తూ ఫ్రాన్స్లో హైస్కూల్, యూనివర్సిటీ విద్యార్థులు, ఉపాధ్యాయులు పెద్దఎత్తున నిరసనలు చేపట్టారు. వీరికి తోడుగా పెరుగుతున్న జీవన వ్యయం, ఆర్థిక సంక్షోభం కారణంగా సామాన్యులు, రైతులు, కార్మికులు జతకలవడంతో అక్టోబర్ మూడవ వారం నాటికి ఇది దేశవ్యాప్త హింసాత్మక ఉద్యమంగా మారింది. ఈ నిరసనల్లో విపరీతమైన ఆస్తి నష్టం, భవనాల దహనం, వేలాది మంది అరెస్టులు చోటుచేసుకున్నాయి. ఉద్యమం హింసాత్మకంగా మారడంతో ఫ్రాన్స్ ప్రభుత్వం పలు నగరాల్లో పాక్షిక కర్ఫ్యూ విధించింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పారిస్లోని ఈఫిల్ టవర్ మీద పాలస్తీనా జెండాను నిరసనకారులు ఎగురవేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026 ఫ్రాన్స్ నిరసనల్లో ఈఫిల్ టవర్ మీద పాలస్తీనా జెండాను నిరసనకారులు ఎరుగవేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది ఆర్టిఫిషియల్ ఇంటెలిజెన్స్ (AI) ఉపయోగించి సృష్టించిన వీడియో.అయితే, ఈ నిరసనల్లో భాగంగా ఫ్రాన్స్లోని పలు ప్రాంతాల్లో ఆందోళనకారులు పాలస్తీనా జెండాలను ప్రదర్శించినట్లు మీడియా కథనాలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోను (ఆర్కైవ్) “jaranor.films” అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీ 18 అక్టోబర్ 2026న పోస్ట్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. అయితే, ఇది నిజంగా జరిగిన ఘటన కాదని, ఇదొక AI వీడియో అని ఆ పోస్ట్ వివరణలో పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ పేజీలో పోస్టు చేసిన ఇదే తరహా వీడియోలని ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.

Govt proposes mandatory automatic emergency braking in new car models from October 2030
The road ministry's draft rules propose AEBS for new car models from October 2030 and all existing models still in production from October 2032.
The Road Ministry has proposed mandating Advanced Emergency Braking Systems (AEBS) for all new car models starting October 2030 to curb road accidents.
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), in a draft notification dated October 19, 2026, said that for pre-2030 still-in-production models, AEBS would be mandatory from October 2032.
Also Read: MoRTH pushes for an intelligent and clean construction
AEBS provides automatic braking in the event of failure of the driver to respond to emergency situations to either avoid a crash or reduce the impact of a collision.
"Provided that, M1 category of vehicles manufactured on and after 1st October 2030 in the case of new models and 1st October 2032 in the case of all models shall be fitted with Advanced Emergency Braking System, conforming to AIS-185, as amended from time to time," the draft notification said.
Also Read: MoRTH mandates automatic load covers for tippers, dumpers from April 2027
The government has mandated multiple measures, especially focused on braking systems, to enhance the safety of medium and heavy-duty vehicles.
To enhance brake performance, a revised braking standard has been mandated for trucks effective October 1, 2027.
Also Read: ‘Results visible next winter’: MoRTH secy on Delhi-NCR fleet renewal scheme
Braking systems have been advanced with the mandatory implementation of electronic stability control systems (AIS 162) for trucks from October 1, 2027, which provide stability, especially in the event of braking at curves.
The draft rules will be taken into consideration after the expiry of thirty days from the date on which the copies of this notification, as published in the Gazette of India, are made available to the public.

Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
- Published
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.
"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.
Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.
The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.
Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".
This was just the start of the problems.
Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.
In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.
GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.
Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.
Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.
"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.
Hopes for the future
Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.
But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.
Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.
Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

A private key meant to vouch for the security of websites around the world turned out to be the number 4. That was one of the weaknesses researchers found in eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates issued by Bengaluru-based eMudhra. The discovery prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft to block the affected certificates, triggering a wider effort to protect browsers, applications, and enterprise systems. The incident also rattled investors and eMudhra shares hit their 20% lower circuit at ₹431.55 on the BSE today. The immediate concern is whether software still trusting the compromised keys could accept fraudulent certificates. A related challenge is replacing legitimate certificates affected by browser makers’ decision to withdraw trust in a parent certificate. A digital certificate acts as a digital identity that allows a browser to verify a website’s authenticity. Certificate authorities issue these certificates and vouch for their authenticity. eMudhra is among the certifying authorities licensed by India’s Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA). The incident goes beyond one company. It shows how much of the internet’s security rests on a chain of trust that one weak link can undermine, raising questions about how India oversees companies that participate in this global infrastructure. What Happened On October 17, a researcher named Wayne notified the Chrome Root Program, which forwarded the report to Mozilla, and also contacted eMudhra and the Apple and Microsoft root programmes, reporting that he had obtained the private keys corresponding to eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. He demonstrated control of each key by signing a message with it “We have a problem here – Wayne”. The full details of how the flaw was discovered and fixed have now been published by Dennis Jackson, a cryptographic engineer at Mozilla. Intermediate CAs can issue certificates that websites use to establish their identity. Anyone holding the corresponding private keys could potentially issue fraudulent certificates for websites they did not control, allowing affected clients that still trusted those CAs to accept the certificates. The keys were not stolen, but the researcher found that they had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them easy to reconstruct from the public certificates. Six of the eight intermediates were intended for website security through TLS, while two were intended for software signing. Chrome, Apple, Microsoft, and Firefox blocked the affected TLS intermediates. What eMudhra Says In a statement on its website, eMudhra said it was investigating the incident and reviewing its security controls and operating procedures. The company said the eight intermediate CAs were created during a key generation ceremony on April 30, 2025, and the hierarchy entered browser trust lists in mid-2025. It said its roots and issuing CAs had undergone independent audits in each of the previous two years, but did not identify the auditors or disclose the scope of those audits. eMudhra said only one of the eight affected intermediates had been deployed in production and that none had issued end-entity certificates. It said it revoked all eight intermediates and was working with affected customers and root programmes to address the incident. The company also said the incident did not affect its Indian Digital Signature Certificate (DSC) and eSign businesses, which operate on infrastructure separate from its global TLS business. On October 21, eMudhra said the affected global TLS business accounted for around 1% of its revenue. India faced a similar trust-related incident in 2014, following the misissuance of certificates for Google domains by the National Informatics Centre. At the time, Google restricted the India CCA root certificate in Chrome to a limited set of domains, including gov.in and nic.in. eMudhra has been a licensed certifying authority under India’s IT Act since 2008. The company has also worked with public- and private-sector organisations, including banks and government agencies. The company provides digital identity, authentication and security solutions to businesses, financial institutions and governments. Its services include digital signature certificates (DSCs), electronic signatures and tools that help organisations secure digital transactions and manage identities. In India, its DSCs are used for activities such as filing documents with government portals, including GST, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and income tax systems. Its eSign services also support paperless digital workflows. Many critical government websites, including the Aadhaar issuer UIDAI as well as websites of the Indian postal services and the income tax filing portal, use eMudhra certificates or other technology developed by the company. Why It Matters Beyond eMudhra Browsers and operating systems rely on lists of trusted certificate authorities. A compromised intermediate CA can therefore threaten trust beyond the authority’s direct customers. With the compromised keys, an attacker could potentially issue fraudulent website certificates to impersonate legitimate sites and intercept traffic, provided the affected systems still trusted those certificates and the attacker’s other technical requirements were met. The two code-signing intermediates also raised concerns about malicious software being presented as coming from a trusted publisher on systems that accepted their signatures. “When news like this comes out about a company that supports our PKI infrastructure, it raises concerns about both the company’s reputation and the country’s reputation. Even a relatively small mistake or a gap in the validation process can affect confidence in the wider industry. People may start to question whether PKI infrastructure provided by Indian companies can be trusted,” said Abhijeet Zilpelwar, cofounder and chief technology officer at pi-labs. The Long Tail: Software And Devices Updated browsers received protections quickly. The harder problem is software and devices that do not receive the same updates or reliably check certificate revocation. Applications, programming languages, package managers and build pipelines can use their own certificate bundles or the operating system’s trust store. Some do not reliably check revocation status, meaning they may continue to accept certificates unless their trust configuration or software is updated. Embedded devices can be harder to update. Routers, cameras, payment terminals and industrial controllers running old firmware may continue to trust affected certificate chains if their software does not receive the relevant protections. For Indian enterprises, exposure does not depend solely on whether they bought certificates directly from eMudhra. The company says none of the eight affected intermediates issued certificates to end users, and Google found no certificates chaining to the six website-security intermediates in public Certificate Transparency logs before blocking them. However, systems that continue to trust the affected intermediates may remain exposed if they lack effective revocation checks or have not received relevant security updates. Potentially affected systems include backend applications, servers and devices running outdated software, including those operated by organisations that use another certificate provider. Banking, fintech, e-governance and other businesses relying on certificate-based authentication should assess their exposure, though the incident does not establish that these sectors have been disproportionately affected. “Mid-sized organisations, SaaS providers and those with lots of vendor-managed systems are most exposed as they often do not keep track of their certificates,” said Rajesh Chhabra, general manager for India and South Asia at global cybersecurity giant Acronis. The Ministry of Electronics and IT has issued a statement saying that the impact of this incident on Indian websites and applications have been very limited and for a very short interval. Additionally, the department has also formed a special team to investigate the matter and is engaging with relevant stakeholders. According to CERT-In’s advisory issued on October 21, organisations should update browsers, operating systems and applications, ensure servers and devices receive current trust lists and revocation information, identify affected certificates and services, and replace them where necessary. CERT-In also advised organisations to verify certificate details and not bypass certificate warnings or disable certificate checks. Venkata Satish Guttula, former director of security at Rediff.com India, said the eMudhra incident raised wider concerns about security audits. “Titles keep getting bigger while the people holding them get more junior. Audits look clean on paper, but the skill behind them is thin,” he posted on X, describing what he called an “illusion of competence” in security audits.

Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström confirmed on this week’s earnings call that the company is trying to catch Spotify Family plan users who don’t actually live together with a new QR code verification method that requires scanning the plan manager’s phone. TechCrunch reports that in response to a question about the “crackdown,” he called it a “routine improvement” instead:
Spotify says yes, it is busting people for using Family Plan sharing too widely
Spotify’s co-CEO said it will keep tweaking verification as people ‘find holes around’ methods like its new QR codes over time.
This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base.
As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.
This isn’t the first time Spotify has tried to limit sharing Family plans, which it says are only for people living in the same household. The new QR code verification method has forced some users to get creative to stay on their shared Premium subscriptions — the code refreshes every few seconds and anyone who misses the seven-day window to scan it gets banned from joining a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months.

Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993
- Published
Rwanda has signed a 10-year deal with Formula 1 to host races in the African country, starting "in the early 2030s".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali and next to the city's new international airport. It will be the first F1 race in Africa since 1993.
A statement from F1 said the project came as a result of "years of collaboration to ensure the right foundations, with the best partner, are in place to deliver a successful, sustainable and world-class grand prix for generations to come".
The circuit, designed by the former F1 driver Alex Wurz, has been "designed to work in harmony with the natural landscape, using the area's elevation changes to create a unique and challenging racing experience while delivering exceptional viewing opportunities for fans," the statement added.
F1 hopes the race will provide an opportunity for the sport to expand its profile in Africa, a relatively unexplored market compared to Europe, Asia and the Americas.
It has not yet been established where the race may best fit into the schedule during the year.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published7 hours ago
The sport is likely to want to avoid holding the race in the main rain season of March to May. There is a shorter, less disruptive rain season from October to November.
F1 is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: "For more than three decades, the world's premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.
"Rwanda is proud to host the Formula 1 African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa, many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.
"The circuit in Bugesera, alongside the new international airport, will bring jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come, because our aim was never a single race weekend, but a lasting benefit for our people."
F1 president Stefano Domenicali said the new contract was "a landmark moment for F1", which would mean the sport was racing "on every inhabited continent".
Domenicali added: "Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."
Sportswashing controversy
The race is likely to lead to opposition from human rights groups accusing Rwanda of sportswashing, as has been the case with its sponsorship of Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa.
Rwanda's east-central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
A spokesperson for F1 said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."
The track's build process will be overseen by three companies, with long-time F1 track architect Tilke and DAR working alongside WurzDesign as the creator of the circuit.
It is designed to be fast and flowing, with significant elevation change, using the natural contours of Rwanda's hilly landscape.
The first grand prix in Africa was the final round of the World Championship in Morocco in 1958.
South Africa hosted a race during the apartheid era - from 1960-66 in East London, now known as KuGompo City, before the race moved to Kyalami near Johannesburg from 1976-85.
Kyalami returned for two races in 1992 and 1993 as apartheid was coming to an end.
The country has held talks with F1 in recent years about a return at various venues, including Kyalami and Cape Town, but a deal has not proved possible.

Pakistan has appointed nine retired senior military officers to diplomatic missions abroad as part of a group of 17 non-career ambassadors and high commissioners, according to a disclosure by Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar in the Senate, CNN-News18 reported.
The appointments have also drawn attention to Army Chief Asim Munir’s influence within Pakistan's power structure. Munir travels with Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif on major deplomatic missions and sometimes lead them.
The appointments, which span postings across the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia, have renewed questions about Islamabad's selection of diplomatic representatives and the balance between non-career appointments and its professional foreign service.
According to a report by CNN-News18, the details were provided in a written response by Dar to Senator Muhammad Talha Mahmood, who had sought information on non-career diplomats serving overseas, including their professional backgrounds, places of domicile and the procedures governing their appointments.
The Senate response identified nine former senior military officers appointed or designated to diplomatic positions in different countries.
They include Major General (Retd) Kamran Tabrez Savera, High Commissioner-designate to Abuja, Nigeria; Major General (Retd) Khurram Sarfraz Khan, posted to Amman, Jordan; and Major General (Retd) Nayyar Naseer, posted to Colombo, Sri Lanka.
The other six are Air Marshal (Retd) Muhammad Mughes Afzal, posted to Damascus, Syria; Lieutenant General (Retd) Muhammad Aamer, posted to Doha, Qatar; Major General (Retd) Kanwar Adnan Ahmad Khan, posted to Kyiv, Ukraine; Vice Admiral (Retd) Faisal Rasul Lodhi, posted to Male, Maldives; Major General (Retd) Muhammad Irfan, Ambassador-designate to Sarajevo, Bosnia; and Major General (Retd) Mumtaz Hussain, Ambassador-designate to Tripoli, Libya.
The postings place former officers from the army, air force and navy in diplomatic roles across several regions.
The Senate disclosure also listed eight other people from outside Pakistan's regular foreign service who have been appointed or designated to overseas diplomatic positions.
They are Dr Yousaf Junaid, posted to Ankara, Turkey; Dr Faryal Leghari, posted to Ashgabat, Turkmenistan; Kohdayar Marri, posted to Hanoi, Vietnam; and Muhammad Irfan Tarar, Ambassador-designate to Niamey, Niger.
The remaining names are Zaheeruddin Babar Thaheem, posted to Phnom Penh, Cambodia; Aqil Gillani, posted to Rabat, Morocco; Dr Najeeb Samie, Ambassador-designate to Tunis, Tunisia; and Muhammad Sami-ur-Rehman, posted to Warsaw, Poland.
Together, the 17 appointments show Pakistan's use of personnel outside its career diplomatic service for overseas representation.
The inclusion of nine retired senior military officers has brought renewed attention to the criteria used to select non-career diplomats and the role of professional foreign service experience in senior overseas postings.
Career diplomats typically build expertise in international negotiations, bilateral relations, international law and consular affairs through years of service. Appointments from outside the regular diplomatic cadre can therefore raise questions about how candidates' qualifications are assessed and how non-career appointments affect career officers' prospects.

New Delhi, Oct 22: India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen ties in defence, space, and nuclear energy domains, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk pledging to boost bilateral strategic partnership amid growing global instability.
Following the talks, Modi said both sides believe in democratic values and the rule of law and that India will continue to support every meaningful effort in bringing peace to Ukraine and West Asia.
Tusk is on a three-day visit to India amid renewed global push to end the conflict in Ukraine.
"Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space, and nuclear energy. We invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India in all these strategic areas," Modi said.
"In critical minerals and coal gasification too, we will develop new partnerships with Polish expertise," he added.
Modi said the friendship between India and Poland is based not only on diplomatic relations but also on a shared heritage of humanity and compassion.
"During World War II, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur sheltered thousands of Polish children and families in India."
"Poland also extended this spirit of humanity by supporting the safe return of our students from Ukraine in 2022," he added.
In his media statement, Modi also made a mention of the growing economic engagement between the two countries.
"The world is going through a period of uncertainty and change. Even at this time, both India and Poland are emerging as important centres of growth, technology, and innovation," he said.
The prime minister said the growing economic strength of the two countries has created new opportunities for India-Poland partnership.
"And the India-European Union free trade agreement has further expanded these opportunities. Upon entry into force, this agreement will open up new opportunities for exports of machinery, chemicals, plastics, and engineering goods from India to Poland," he said.

Like someone in mourning, Sam Altman said mathematicians went through phases after OpenAI began its blitz into the field.
First, there was disbelief. Then, there was pain.
"The day one reaction was like, 'We're cooked, and our field is over,'" OpenAI's CEO said. "'We're telling our grad students to switch majors.'"
After that, there was anger.
"The day three reaction was maybe like: 'It's horrible that OpenAI did this,'" Altman said at a recent talk at Stanford, before hundreds of students jittery about the viability of their future careers.
Come day five, though, in Altman's telling, mathematicians began to come around to what he described as AI's now-inalienable role in the study of numbers and proofs.
"We've now seen a lot of people say, actually, I'm going to have a different but hopefully better kind of career as a mathematician," Altman said.
Altman's buoyant assessment contrasts sharply with what some in the math community have described as an existential transformation.
After OpenAI abruptly broke into the field's prerogatives in September, announcing its models had solved the Navier-Stokes equations — a famously challenging math puzzle that stumped the industry's brightest since the 19th Century — preeminent mathematicians erupted in fury.
A pair of academics, one at New York University and another at Anthropic, accused OpenAI of using data from their chat logs to help crack the problem. Mathematicians also complained that while an AI model might have solved the problem, it didn't show its work, leaving them with the less celebratory task of verifying it.
And in the wake of all that controversy, there was more controversy.
A group of undergrads at Caltech, wary of how rapidly AI was disrupting their field and wanting to stay relevant, advertised a "mathathon" where participants were encouraged to use AI to solve long-standing problems.
OpenAI dropped out of sponsoring the event after more than 700 academics signed an open letter denouncing the competition for promoting AI "slop." (Organizers have since made adjustments to the rules, and the competition is set for November.)
More recently, Terence Tao, a math prodigy at UCLA who earned his doctorate at 20, said math's "romantic era" is over, as top academics like him adjust to a workflow that involves verifying AI's work rather than solving problems individually.
"Some things are being lost," Tao said after OpenAI this month said it solved over 700 more problems.
Meanwhile, Altman, sitting on the opposite side of the debate, has adopted the optimism of the disrupter.
"I don't think there's going to be like a job apocalypse," Altman said of AI causing companies to restructure their workforces. In the field of math, however, Altman said the disruptions came more quickly than in other disciplines and industries.
"That was the fastest that I think we've all gotten to watch a field go through this cycle," he said.

Consolidation is underway at David Ellison's Skydance just a few weeks after the company closed its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Skydance's chief product officer, Dane Glasgow, laid out the product and tech leadership structure of the combined entity in a memo viewed by Business Insider.
Four top WBD executives are leaving, according to the memo.
They include:
- Avi Saxena, Warner Bros. Discovery's chief technology officer
- Tyler Whitworth, chief product officer for WBD's streaming business
- Dave Duvall, WBD's chief information officer
- Trish Collins Weedon, WBD's chief information security officer (CISO)
Duvall, Saxena, and Whitworth will stay on in an "advisory capacity as we undergo this transition," Glasgow wrote.
The company is mostly keeping Paramount executives in charge of its combined tech and product organization.
These leaders include:
- Lakshman Nathan, Paramount's chief information officer
- Carlo Joseph, its chief information security officer
- Jim Harrison, its executive vice president of infrastructure, broadcast, and distribution
- Nick Lee, Paramount's executive vice president of media systems
A few WBD executives are staying on in Skydance's post-merger leadership, per Glasgow's memo.
They include Brinton Miller, formerly WBD's media technology and operations lead, who will serve as Skydance's executive vice president of production and studio technology, and James Crossland, formerly head of global content operations at WBD, who will serve as its EVP of global content operations.
Skydance has spent the past year revamping its tech and product team, often recruiting talent from tech companies.
Glasgow joined Paramount from Meta, while Lee joined from Microsoft's AI division. Other team leaders in its post-merger structure include head of design Suzanne Pellican, formerly a Google exec; Hugh Williams, a former Google, eBay, and Microsoft exec; and Barak Turovsky, who came to Paramount after serving as chief AI officer at General Motors and VP of AI at Cisco.
Bringing technical expertise to Paramount has been a priority for Ellison, who wants to turn the century-old media brand into a modern, tech-forward business like Netflix. The company revamped its data and insights strategy in January, and merged some engineering teams in March to bolster its streaming tech.
"We are building a product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley," Ellison told CNBC earlier this month.
In his memo, Glasgow expressed gratitude for the work of both Paramount and WBD staffers, writing that he was "encouraged by the early collaboration, the bold new ideas you're bringing forward, and your openness to exploring new ways of working with your colleagues."
He also acknowledged the structural changes could be disruptive.
"I know a change of this scale brings questions, especially as we get to know new teams and colleagues," Glasgow wrote. "Your leaders will share more about their organizations in the coming weeks and we'll bring our teams together soon to keep building with and learning from each other."

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
