For entrepreneur Akhila Vijayaraghavan, whey has always been a convenient way to get 100-120 grams of protein every day. “I train regularly, so it was an easy addition to my routine and helped me consistently hit my protein intake,” she says. This is why she couldn’t help but notice how much whey prices have increased over the last few months “I understand that there are broader supply and import issues behind the increase, particularly because India is so heavily dependent on imported whey. But for a consumer, the result is pretty simple: something that used to be an everyday purchase suddenly feels expensive,” she says.
For instance, a kilogram of True Basics and Whole Truth whey concentrate, which once cost around ₹2500 last year, has gone up to around ₹3500, a clear leap of nearly ₹1000, points out Akhila. Other brands aren’t far behind, either. Optimum Nutrition, the protein brand associated with numerous elite athletes, including Neeraj Chopra, Rishabh Pant, and Priya Punia, is currently pricing 4 kg of its Gold Standard 100% Whey Protein at ₹17,649, while the same amount of MuscleBlaze’s Biozyme Performance Whey is ₹13,999, an over 20% jump from last year, when they were about ₹15,000 and a little over ₹10,000 respectively.
Several forces
According to Vijay P, operations and procurement manager at Chennai-based OMG Labs, a functional nutrition brand offering both whey and plant-based protein products, this sudden hike is not the result of a single event, but of several forces coming together. Though India has a large dairy industry, we still do not produce enough whey for the protein supplement industry because much of our dairy processing focusses on products like milk, curd, paneer, and ghee rather than large-scale cheese production, Vijay explains. “Whey is mainly obtained as a by-product of cheese manufacturing, and because domestic availability is limited, we depend significantly on imports.” This means that when there is a shortage or price increase in the international market, it directly affects the Indian market, says Vijay.
“Freight costs, currency fluctuations and other import-related costs also add to the final prices,” he says. For instance, whey isolate prices, which were ₹2,200 per kilogram exclusive of GST in December last year, now cost around ₹3,400. “Apart from the whey, we also have to account for the flavours, packaging, other raw materials, labour and manufacturing costs, which have pushed the overall finished product cost to ₹4,200-5,000 from ₹3,000-36,000, depending on quantity and customers.”
The price spike also stems from a significant increase in demand for dietary protein that current supply just can’t meet. “We are going through a protein bubble right now where everyone is talking about it, so everyone is aware of and looking for protein,” says Chennai-based fitness and nutrition coach Raj Ganpath.
Given that the Indian diet is notoriously protein-deficient, most of us may need a scoop or two of a protein supplement to get the ideal amount of protein, “about 1.25 to 1.75 grams of protein per kilo per day,” says Raj, pointing out that our meals consist largely of carbohydrates, fat, and some vegetables. Even though most Indians do eat meat — a recent National Family Health Survey (NFHS) found that 70-80% consume meat, fish, poultry, and eggs — for many of us, it does not happen regularly enough to meet daily protein needs. “In India, a non-vegetarian is essentially a vegetarian who eats a little bit of meat, so we still rely on vegetarian protein sources,” says Raj, the co-founder of The Quad and founder of The Slow Burn Method, a sustainable weight-loss coaching programme.
Additionally, while other new protein options exist in the market, for instance, functional dairy products like Greek yoghurt and protein milk, gram for gram, even with the increase in costs, “it roughly costs you the same amount of money as whey (if it is a concentrate or blend, isolate is a little more), around 6-7 rupees per gram of protein,” he says.
That is why people like Santosh Raghavan, an entrepreneur also based in Chennai, prefer whey protein to hit their daily goals. Given that he does not cook meat at home, “whey gives me the best protein-to-calorie ratio, allowing me room to eat other whole foods too. It is also convenient post-workout since I can have it immediately for recovery and absorption, without needing to wait for a meal to be prepared,” he says. And yes, he also likes the supplement’s taste. “It helps me think I have had some dessert, which is great for a guy like me, with a sweet tooth.”
The rise in whey prices, however, has influenced his choices considerably, he says. “I used to be loyal to a couple of brands, but now I have become brand agnostic. I just look at the label and pick up what is affordable,” says Santosh, who has also experimented with vegan protein, “which didn’t work for me,” and fermented yeast protein, “which I found decent.”
Options and opportunities
This trepidation among long-time whey users seems common, as Aditi Mammen Gupta, the co-founder of plant-based protein powder brand Origin Nutrition, points out. Earlier, people who used whey regularly often found the transition difficult, “but the thing is, plant protein was very different. Now, with new technologies and processes, plant protein has become much better in terms of taste, texture, mixability...everything really,” she says, pointing out that skyrocketing whey prices have led to “a lot of people shifting to plant protein. They seem to be quite happy with plant, especially when they discover that when they stick to it for a while, they feel a lot better.” As a business, given this shift, Origin is all set to expand its product range, says Aditi, who believes, “I think it is a really exciting time to be in the plant protein space.”
While rising whey prices will likely push more people to try affordable, equally effective plant- or yeast-based options, the consensus is that whey will continue to have a strong user base. “Whey still has strong demand because it is well established in the fitness and sports nutrition market,” says Vijay, while Sahil Kukreja feels that whey offers distinct advantages that justify the premium. “Whey provides all nine essential amino acids, is highly digestible, and is naturally rich in leucine, which helps stimulate muscle protein synthesis. That makes it an efficient protein source, particularly when someone wants a substantial protein serving in a relatively small volume,” says the co-founder of The Func Lab in Mumbai, a functional nutrition start-up that manufactures whey, plant protein, and electrolytes.
As the whey conversation goes beyond sports nutrition, it is now also being used in everyday beverages, snacks, and foods. “Healthy ageing and weight management are expanding the consumer base, while GLP-1 usage adds to this demand because reduced appetite makes getting adequate protein more challenging,” says Sahil, adding that he would, however, be careful not to attribute the entire price increase to GLP-1s.
But Sahil feels that the whey protein shortage challenge may also be an opportunity for the domestic industry to strengthen whey recovery and processing capacity. “Sustained whey premiums will also encourage innovation in plant proteins and other protein sources. That requires investment in collection, quality systems, and specialised processing — not just higher milk production,” he says.
Vijay, too, agrees that the crisis could prove a “strategic opportunity” for India to build a stronger domestic whey ecosystem. “Indian dairy and nutrition companies are moving in this direction, with major players investing in whey and value-added dairy products. This could reduce our exposure to international supply disruptions and foreign exchange movement.” However, given that capacity-building takes time, for the time being, “whey protein is likely to remain a strategically important and relatively expensive ingredient for the Indian nutrition industry.”
And despite rising costs, whey remains the preferred option for consumers like Akhila because of its familiarity, taste, texture, and convenience. “I know it works well for me as a practical way to get more protein,” she says. What has changed, however, is how often she turns to it, cycling it with other protein sources, including fish, meat, eggs and low-fat paneer, “because the price makes daily use harder to justify. At the current prices, I am much more conscious about when I actually need it, rather than automatically having it every day.”

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
- 'They aimed to kill' - BBC identifies security forces who shot Kenya anti-tax protesters 
  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

I’ve Tested More Than 65 Hearing Aids—These Are the Best Ones
Featured in this article
Hearing-challenged individuals have long had one option for dealing with this widespread issue: an expensive, bulky hearing aid prescribed by a doctor. That changed in 2022 when the US Food and Drug Administration approved over-the-counter hearing aid devices, giving consumers access to a vast and growing array of alternatives. Today, there are more hearing aids than ever, and they come in different shapes, sizes, and most importantly, prices. How does a $100 hearing aid compare to a $4,000 prescription device for treating mild to moderate hearing loss? I’ve been testing products for the past four years to answer that question.
I’ve performed hands-on (ears-on?) testing of more than 65 hearing aid models around my home, outside, and in noisy environments. I’ve found plenty to like on the market today—and even more aids to avoid. The Jabra Enhance Select M3 holds the crown as the best over-the-counter hearing aid, while those seeking a prescription device should seek out a provider to fit them with a pair of Resound Sensia hearing aids. For those just getting started with hearing tech, I almost universally recommend giving Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 earbuds a try. They’re an intuitive way to see how your hearing can improve without breaking the bank.
Below is my complete roundup of the best prescription and over-the-counter hearing aids I’ve tested and approved.
Updated October 2026: I've updated my picks with the Jabra Enhance Select M3, Resound Sensia 9, Oticon Zeal, and Legato Harmony Glasses.
What to Consider Before You Buy
Every person is unique, and so are their hearing loss needs. Consider these factors to find a device that suits your needs and lifestyle. For more tips, check out our How to Buy a Hearing Aid guide.
Hearing aids shouldn’t bankrupt you. With such a steep price and minimal insurance coverage, it’s no wonder that so many people put off hearing loss treatment. Between audiologist visits, hearing aid orders, custom fittings, and maintenance, it’s justifiable that you might postpone treatment rather than fork over your credit card. It’s vital you know your budget before you start browsing for hearing aids. Many brands offer trial periods where you can test out the devices for a set number of days and, if they're a bad fit, return them free of charge.
It doesn’t have to be obvious that you’re wearing a hearing aid. Despite cartoonish media depictions of hunched-over seniors screaming “WHAT?!” at every person who tries to talk to them, hearing loss doesn’t discriminate by age. With nearly 10 million Americans under the age of 60 affected, more should be taking advantage of the sleekly designed hearing aids on the market. Similar to the stigmas that keep people from seeking mental health treatment, the hearing-loss community is plagued by self-consciousness when it comes to wearing these devices. Modern in-the-ear (ITE) hearing aids have come a long way in subtlety.
Opt for a professional hearing test over an online one. While online and app-based tests are a good way to dip your toes in and see whether you have hearing loss, a detailed audiogram that only an in-office visit can provide is a far better option. A hearing professional can use this audiogram to calibrate hearing aids to your specific needs.
What Are the Different Types of Hearing Aids?
Before you choose which hearing aid is right for you, it’s best to familiarize yourself with the different styles on the market. While you may see multiple design styles, hearing aids essentially boil down to two main varieties: behind-the-ear and in-the-ear. Completely in-canal (CIC) devices also exist, but none are available over the counter. Here are common terms you’ll see:
Behind-the-ear (BTE) hearing aids, also known as over-the-ear, are probably the most traditional style. For these devices, an often bulky plastic case rests on the back of your ear while a tube delivers sound to an ear mold. Because they’re bigger, they tend to have the most technology and can cater to higher degrees of hearing loss. That said, they also tend to stand out more, which is a drawback for those looking for subtlety. Receiver-in-the-ear (RITE) hearing aids are essentially the same as behind-the-ear devices, with a receiver component that sits in the ear canal instead of being built into the case. Though the industry likes to tout them as a sleeker, less noticeable counterpart, in actuality, they’re not much smaller than BTEs and function identically.
In-the-ear (ITE) hearing aids, also known as in-the-canal (ITC), are more comparable to wireless earbuds from a design standpoint. These devices allow for directional mics but also tend to collect moisture and wax.
Completely in-canal (CIC) hearing aids are the most “invisible” hearing aids on the market. This is because, as the name suggests, they’re completely submerged in your ear canal with nothing sticking out (besides a tiny string for removal). They typically have to be inserted by a professional and left in the ear for longer periods, and as noted, they are not available over the counter.
Self-Fitted vs. Preset Hearing Aids
Traditional hearing aids must be “fitted”—not just physically fitted to your ear anatomy but acoustically fitted to line up with the particulars of your hearing loss. This is because for most people, hearing loss is not unilateral. Some may experience trouble hearing low frequencies, while others may struggle with higher ones. (Mine has a dip somewhere in the middle.) By tuning the hearing aid to boost the frequency bands where your hearing is at its weakest, a precision hearing aid can improve your overall hearing quality without blowing out the frequencies where your ears are already working well.
With self-fitting hearing aids, you do this tuning yourself, at home. Typically, an app will walk you through a simple hearing test, and the results of that test are used to tune, or fit, the frequencies as discussed above. This is basically the same process a doctor will undertake in fitting a prescription hearing aid, only in a simpler and more automated manner.
Conversely, preset hearing aids can’t be tuned in this fashion. These considerably less expensive aids tend to boost all frequencies universally, though most will at least include a slider letting you prefer bass versus treble or vice versa. As a result, the improvement offered by a preset hearing aid will necessarily be less nuanced than that provided by a self-fitted aid, though if you have relatively mild hearing loss, the difference may be less marked than you think.
Rechargeable vs. Replaceable Batteries
In the beginning, replaceable (or disposable) batteries were the only option for hearing aids. These batteries are tiny cells, smaller than a pencil eraser, which you replace with a new one after they die. Hearing aid batteries can last for 70 hours or more, so you'd typically replace them once every week or two, depending on use. The longer lifespan means that if you are often away from a power outlet (or forget to charge your aids), you can worry less about running out of juice. (However, you will have to remember to carry spare batteries with you.) Hearing aids with replaceable batteries can also be (but aren’t always) smaller and cheaper, but the batteries are difficult to work with. Even if you have steady hands, it can be difficult to get a tiny battery in and out. These batteries are easy to lose and represent a serious health hazard if children or pets eat them. There’s also a small cost consideration: spare batteries aren’t free.
Rechargeable hearing aids use lithium-ion batteries and recharge via a case, much like standard Bluetooth earbuds. Battery life can vary widely, from over 24 hours to less than eight. That said, for most users, if the case is kept plugged in and the hearing aids are dropped into the case anytime they aren’t in use, they should never have to worry about a dead battery. The case itself also has a battery; it can supply an extra three to seven full recharges to the hearing aids before the case battery dies. Again, this varies widely. Rechargeable aids are much more commonplace today and reflect the most up-to-date technology. You’ll have far more options if you go for a rechargeable model.

How Much Do Hearing Aids Cost?
How much money should you expect to spend on a hearing aid? The answer depends primarily on whether you’re looking into over-the-counter or prescription hearing aids. Unsurprisingly, the latter is a wallet guzzler, with average costs between $2,000 to $8,000. But OTCs can ring up quite a tab in their own right, and our most highly rated devices will still run you about $800 to $2,000 a pair. So far, we haven’t found an OTC device under this $800 price that is truly effective at treating hearing loss. In most cases, the $100 budget devices now flooding the market are too good to be true.
Fortunately, there are several methods to manage the high cost of a hearing aid:
Financing is available for virtually all reputable hearing aid companies, so you may not need to pay everything up front. Some plans are offered directly through the company, while others may require a third-party financing company like Klarna or Care Credit.
If you are over the age of 65, you may qualify for an add-on Medicare Advantage Plan (Part C) that may include hearing-related benefits. Most private insurance providers don’t offer hearing exam and device coverage, though some may have the option to add it as a supplemental benefit.
Medicaid coverage in certain states also pays for hearing aids, provided the prescription brand accepts it. Veterans may also qualify for hearing aid coverage through their VA benefits.
Some state governments have programs to help their constituents front the costs of hearing aids. Call or write to your state department to see whether this is a service they offer.
About Medicare and Insurance
Much like how it does not cover eyeglasses, Medicare does not cover hearing aids. That said, supplemental plans may include hearing benefits: Medicare Advantage Part C plans and many private insurance plans offer some hearing support, but coverage varies widely, so check with your provider before making that appointment. (Many states mandate that private insurance plans cover hearing aids, but a number of these are restricted to coverage for children.) On the plus side, standard Medicare plans (Parts A and B) do cover the cost of a hearing exam, but only with a doctor’s referral.
Many hearing aid providers are now providing financing for their products, usually at very low interest rates that let you pay for the product over up to three years. Medicaid may also help offset the cost of hearing aids, as may employer FSA and HSA plans.
How to Buy a Hearing Aid
There are two primary ways to buy a hearing aid: through a medical professional (the prescription route) or over-the-counter. Each has its pros and cons.
Prescription hearing aids are usually acquired through an audiologist. These specialists operate businesses ranging from sophisticated medical centers to small shops in a strip mall, usually emblazoned with a sign that reads “HEARING AIDS.” Again, this was the only way to acquire a hearing aid before 2022. An audiologist provides full service for your hearing aid from start to finish. They will test your hearing in a specialized room, physically examine your ears for medical problems, and suggest a hearing aid model. They will tune your chosen hearing aids and adjust them over time if things don’t sound right. The catch? Prescription hearing aids are expensive, anywhere from two to 10 times costlier than over-the-counter models. That said, for consumers who need hand-holding and significant fine-tuning of their hearing aids, professionals like this still have a function.
Over-the-counter aids can be bought through retailers online or offline, just like you would buy, say, a laptop computer. Different vendors offer different levels of presales support, and as the price of an OTC hearing aid goes up, you can usually expect a higher level of service. This may start with an online hearing test delivered to you via your computer or phone; these are not as good as an in-person test, but some can be surprisingly accurate. You may also get access to a remote audiologist who can meet with you over a video chat and fine-tune your hearing aid settings over the air. Ultimately, higher-end OTC aids offer a user experience similar to that of prescription aids, only one that is fully remote. At the low end of the hearing aid spectrum, you may get no service and support at all.
What Are the Different Types of Hearing Loss?
Medically speaking, there are three types of hearing loss. These are:
- Conductive: Hearing loss related to the outer or middle ear.
- Sensorineural: Hearing loss related to the inner ear.
- Mixed: A combination of both.
All of these types of hearing loss can occur due to a variety of factors. Genetics and aging are two of the biggest and most universal: The older you get, the more the sensitive organs inside your ears begin to break down, and this can happen especially early and/or rapidly if you have a family history of hearing loss. The other all-too-common cause for hearing loss is exposure to loud noises, and it doesn’t take much. Many people exposed to prolonged, loud noises like concerts, industrial equipment, motorcycle engines, and sirens experience a gradual hearing loss due to the slow death of tiny hair cells in the inner ear. However, sudden exposure to very loud sounds like explosions and gunshots can cause instantaneous, irreversible damage by rupturing the eardrum (or worse).
There’s no easy way to know which type of hearing loss you have unless you’ve experienced some type of acute damage that has brought on a sudden change in your hearing. Whatever you suspect, it’s important you see a medical doctor to diagnose the issue fully.
Sensorineural is the most common type of hearing loss, and it can be caused by any of the aforementioned issues and more. Sensorineural hearing loss is permanent and can not be reversed, but it can be alleviated through the use of hearing aids. An audiologist can develop an audiogram for you that will show you how severe your hearing loss is and advise on what types of hearing aids might be best for treating it.
Conversely, conductive hearing loss is more medically treatable. This type of hearing loss is often due to a physical obstruction such as a buildup of earwax or fluid, or even physical damage to the eardrum. In these cases, a physician must examine the ear to determine the best course of treatment.
Degrees of Hearing Loss
The primary levels of hearing loss look like this, as defined by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA):
| ASHA Hearing Loss | Decibels (dB) | 
|---|---|
| Normal | Up to 15 dB lost | 
| Slight | 16 to 25 dB lost | 
| Mild | 26 to 40 dB lost | 
| Moderate | 41 to 55 dB lost | 
| Moderately severe | 56 to 70 dB lost | 
| Severe | 71 to 90 dB lost | 
| Profound | 91+ dB lost | 
How I Test Hearing Aids
I configured and qualitatively tested each device in several settings, including my home, outdoors, and crowded environments, to see how well they helped treat my mild hearing loss while more deeply evaluating the user experience. I tried charging rechargeable models, changing batteries if disposable, connecting Bluetooth features, and cleaning the devices. I also compared them based on overall look and style—style matters.
Other Hearing Aids to Consider
We've reviewed dozens of hearing aids, and many of them are nearly as worthy as our top-tier selections. Here are several alternatives to consider:
GN Resound Vivia for $5,000+: Resound's new Vivia line of prescription hearing aids are on par in both design (at a svelte 2.56 grams) and quality with the Starkey Edge AI models, providing a pristine audio experience that is tuned perfectly and utterly free of hiss and feedback. The “intelligence-augmented” devices work well in either noise or more intimate one-on-one settings, and GN’s Smart 3D app couldn’t be easier to master. Support for Bluetooth Auracast is also included, so wearers can now pipe media (like the audio from the TV at a bar) directly to the aids. They aren’t cheap, so getting some advance ears-on time with them is essential for prospective buyers.
Phonak Virto R Infinio for $4,000+: Phonak's Virto R Infinio (8/10, WIRED Recommends) and pricey prescription hearing aids like the GN Resound above have a custom fit process that helps make them some of the best-fitting hearing aids on the market. They're immensely comfortable to wear for long periods, and you'll get pretty good audio quality for in-the-ear hearing aids. It's just a shame there's no battery in the charging case to extend the run time.
Phonak Audeo Infinio Ultra Sphere for $4,000+: The Phonak Ultra Sphere (8/10, WIRED Recommends) isn’t spherical at all; the name instead refers to Phonak’s Spheric Speech Clarity system, designed to improve the quality of conversation support no matter where a speaker is standing. It’s an effective product, though the larger size—required to accommodate an extra microprocessor—makes for a device that is more obtrusive than you might like. Be sure to check out peripherals like Phonak’s Roger On system, which serves as a powerful remote microphone and can dramatically enhance the utility of these hearing aids.
Audien Hearing Atom X for $389: The most interesting feature of Audien's Atom X (6/10, WIRED Review) is the case—there's an embedded display that lets you tweak volume and change modes, no need to use an app or fuss with buttons. Audien has also reduced the hiss from these affordable buds. Unfortunately, the hearing aids aren't tunable and provide blunt amplification, so you can't shape the frequencies to where you need the most help. I suggest trying a pair of AirPods Pro 3 first.
Avoid These Hearing Aids
Just as important as what hearing aids to buy are what hearing aids not to buy. While some of these devices are affordable, most are lacking in quality or style. After our testing, we don’t wholly recommend these hearing aids. (Poor hearing aids can harm your hearing.)
Audien Atom One: I had high hopes for these, but they're impossibly cheap. The Atom One (5/10, WIRED Review) come up short on smart features, as there’s no way to fine-tune these devices.
Elehear Beyond Pro: There are improvements here in audio quality over the older Elehear Beyond, but the core problem with the Beyond Pro (6/10, WIRED Review) hearing aids is that they're just too bulky and uncomfortable to wear. They also come with a price hike that's tough to swallow.
Lexie Lumen: These are comically large and dated. The case was physically falling apart during testing, which I wouldn’t expect from hearing aids at this price. Though they sound fine, they’re far from subtle and were plagued with connectivity bugs.
Ceretone Core One: The mandatory app required to control the Ceretone Core One (5/10, WIRED Review) hearing aids is so basic that it's useless. You can't tune the frequencies, and the listening experience is quite blunt. They're also not comfortable to wear for long periods.
Ceretone Core One Pro: The Core One Pro (5/10, WIRED Review) change things up so much that they're no longer compatible with Ceretone's app. Instead, you'll control them through the buttons on the case. Unfortunately, you still can't tune them to an audiogram, so they amplify everything bluntly, and they're not very effective as hearing aids.
MDHearing Neo and Neo XS: Never mind the Joe Namath endorsement, these in-ear aids are incredibly uncomfortable and feature a wildly dated design sensibility. Screeching feedback at the slightest touch makes them untenable for even short-term use.

President Donald Trump has been attacking Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) since she first entered Congress in 2019. At various points, he’s called for Omar — a progressive lawmaker who came to the United States as a child refugee from Somalia and who is one of Trump’s most vociferous critics — to be investigated, arrested, and deported.
Can Trump deport Ilhan Omar?
Donald Trump has a long history of attacking Omar. Now, his administration is going after her citizenship.
Now, Trump’s Justice Department is seemingly trying to make good on his threats. Last week, Omar’s Washington, DC, home was raided by federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. According to the Wall Street Journal, the raid was part of an investigation into her immigration paperwork with the explicit goal of denaturalizing and deporting her.
The timing alone would make the raid unusual — it’s rare for the Justice Department to take action in political cases so close to an election — and as Washington Post immigration reporter Ted Hesson explains, it also feels uncomfortably pretextual. “It’s almost as if the outcome of the investigation has been stated before anything has taken off,” he told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram.
Hesson joined Sean to talk about the long history of Trump’s attacks on Omar, what the agents might have been looking for, and whether the administration could actually undermine Omar’s citizenship or even deport her.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
What do we know about what federal agents were looking for in Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, residence?
What we’ve learned through our reporting is that the investigation has looked at both her birth date and whether [Omar or her father] may have lied about it on the naturalization application.
A second piece is whether, looking at her father’s military service, she was born in Somalia and was there during the civil war and fled with her family as a young child to a refugee camp in Kenya and was there for years before they eventually came to the US as refugees.
This is the president of the United States and his administration entering a sitting representative’s home to figure out what her original birthday is. What is the motivation here, to the best of our knowledge?
For years, President Trump has criticized Rep. Omar and made unsubstantiated accusations related to immigration fraud.
There have been theories circulating on the far right — again, unsubstantiated — that she had married her brother as part of an immigration fraud scheme. President Trump himself has repeated that. And several top Trump administration officials in the last few months have said that they believe that there is fraud in her background. They’re making these statements prior to there being an investigation, prior to there being evidence put forward. And it’s almost as if the outcome of the investigation has been stated before anything has taken off.
One thing I should say is that while it does appear that they’re looking at her birthdate, when refugees come into the US, it’s extremely common that their birth records are unreliable because people are fleeing countries that are often in disarray, whether it’s due to civil war or other reasons.
Often, nations like Somalia don’t maintain accurate birth records. So it’s common that refugees who’ve left their country as children, spent time in refugee camps, and then come to the US don’t have a solid understanding of when exactly they were born. I don’t know for sure that that’s the case here, but I know that generally when you’re dealing with refugees, that is true.
I know there’s a lot we don’t know here, but investigators enter Rep. Omar’s home. Potentially they’re looking for some documents that may list her birthday. If they find some information that’s maybe contrary to official government records, what could that mean, in theory?
It’s unclear what sort of charges could be brought from this. And part of the question is, was she 17 and a child at the time of that application or was she 18?
Even if it was determined that she was not a child, I don’t believe they would be able to, say, launch a denaturalization process based on that fact alone. And even if they did attempt to do something like that, these things are not taken lightly and it’s a long involved legal process and very uncommon to pursue something like this over something as simple as this sort of paperwork discrepancy.
The president has a long history of hating on Somalia and Somali immigrants to this country.
How does this investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar fit into the president and his administration’s broader efforts to take away American citizenship?
In the past year especially, we’ve seen President Trump use really inflammatory and derogatory language to refer to Somali Americans and Somali immigrants in the US. Even for someone who frequently employs anti-immigrant rhetoric, and the president has in his past, some of the things he said went beyond even that. He does seem to have particularly targeted Somalis in the US and Somali Americans, and Rep. Omar has been part of that.
I think what’s interesting here or what could be interesting is that this case wades into different territory of taking somebody who’s a naturalized citizen, who’s been in the US for decades as a citizen, and saying, “We’re potentially going to reopen that and go back and look at your file and see, do we find anything that might be out of line?”
The idea that you could do that with someone who’s a sitting lawmaker could mean that you could potentially do that to any other person who may have applied.
Now, one thing we’ve learned is that in the case of Rep. Omar, the administration has looked at the idea, in the event that criminal charges can’t be brought, of potentially canceling her citizenship certificate. It’s almost like a fast-track way to disrupt someone’s citizenship.
It doesn’t remove it. You remain a citizen, but you lose the document that is the underlying proof of that, which could then cause problems with federal government documents, and it could even lead to immigration proceedings where the government tries to make the case that you should be deported.
How has Rep. Omar responded?
Her camp has vociferously pushed back against the allegations.
In regard to the search, they’ve actually said that there was a court-ordered guideline that should have been followed, and that involved consulting the counsel for the House of Representatives before the search happened. They said that never happened, and if it had, it would’ve given Rep. Omar perhaps time to prepare for this or some sort of legal recourse.
They’re saying that not only is this continuation of President Trump’s attack on her politically motivated, but also that the actual legal guidelines that were outlined in that search warrant were not followed.
Are other Democrats speaking up on her behalf?
Former President Barack Obama in particular is one extremely prominent person who came out and made a social media post elevating her case.
The interesting part is that President Obama does not often weigh in on public debates like this or is at least measured in the opportunities when he does. So it comes with more gravity to hear him stepping in and raising concerns about this.
I think it speaks to the fact that he thought this was very significant. And if you remember, President Trump’s political career was built on the narrative that Barack Obama was not born in the US.
I do remember, Ted.
And the hunt for his birth certificate. You can imagine that former President Obama saw a parallel here and realizes that this mirrors the sort of attacks that were made on him when he was in office.
We’ve talked about President Trump a bunch in this conversation, and he’s made no secret of his disdain for Rep. Omar and the country from which she comes. What has he explicitly said about this investigation?
He’s saying that the Justice Department is acting independently. That said, he has been extremely critical of Rep. Omar in his public statements and continues to be. And the president himself and other top officials have said that it should be investigated.
We’ve had, for months now, a sort of public encouragement of top officials and saying that they should be looking into this. So whether he’s directly liaising with them or whether they’re just reading his social posts, it may be kind of a nuanced distinction. He’s publicly saying he wants this to be pursued.

Farm country has beef with Trump as midterms approach
Driving around his farm in a four-wheeler, Scott Birker warned that his cattle were in a bad mood.
"They're a little grumpy with me right now," he said.
When asked why, he said matter-of-factly: "We just got done weaning."
Birker should know his herd well, given that he's been raising beef cattle outside the Eastern Iowa town of Garrison since 2001. His operation has about 150 "mama cows" and sells feeder calves, as well as some cattle for meat. And Birker is also the northeast regional vice president for the Iowa Cattlemen's Association.
All of which is to say that since August, when Trump announced that his administration would raise the quota on beef imported under lower tariffs – temporarily suspending tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of imported beef – Birker knows it when he says: that hurt people.
"That surprise, with a very volatile market already, with a tight supply, hurts us really, really fast and really, really hard," Birker said.
It's not that raising beef cattle was easy before that new import policy. Margins are always tight, says Zach Raff, incoming livestock economist at Iowa State University. But there have also been other challenges – for example, drought in much of the western U.S. made hay much more expensive and shrank the nation's beef herd.
"The beef herd size is at an all time low – a 75-year-low," said Raff. "So you couple that with very strong demand. And that's going to make prices what you see at the store right now."
Ground beef currently costs around $6.80 a pound – a fact of which the Trump administration is keenly aware. But the administration's attempts to bring those prices down have backfired politically and possibly economically..
Multiple Trump administration policies have made life tougher for beef producers. Last year, amid the trade war between the two countries, China cut its US beef purchases. In February, Trump signed an executive order to subject some Argentinian beef to fewer tariffs.
And in August, he signed the executive order to suspend tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef imports – specifically, lean beef trimmings, with the goal of lowering the price of ground beef. The order added that the imported beef was to be sold at 25% below market prices.
That helped push U.S. cattle prices lower, but the far bigger challenge, according to Raff, was the amount of uncertainty it introduced.
"If I'm a producer, I think, well, look what's happening – perhaps next year they're going to import even more. The year after, there's going to be a different policy," said Raff. "And I'm going to say, 'Well, these prices for my cattle right now are at record highs and projected to be high. So I'm just going to send my heifers to be processed.' I'm not going to decide to replace the beef herd when I know that there's a lot of uncertainty."
This means the beef imports can have an added downside, disincentivizing producers from keeping breeding stock around that could grow the beef herd, which would lower beef prices in the long run.
Big picture
From an economics 101 perspective, the Trump decision to import more beef does make sense as a way of bringing down consumer prices. But the 300,000 metric tons that could be exempted from tariffs is equivalent to around 2% of total US beef consumption.
That made for a lose-lose situation: the policy was enough to rattle beef producers, but not enough to help consumers. Indeed, the average ground beef price per pound in September was only about 13 cents lower than it was in August.
All of this looms over the 2026 midterm elections, especially in farm states such as Iowa. Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running for the state's open Senate seat, made news when she publicly broke with the Trump administration on its decision to lower tariffs on beef imports.
"We need to focus on affordability, but I think this isn't the way to do that," she said on Fox News. "I think we need to focus on helping our cattlemen grow their herd."
Her opponent, Democratic state legislator Josh Turek, has in turn been stressing that Hinson has supported some Trump policies that have hurt farmers writ large.
"She's been in favor of all this five times in favor of the tariffs," he said in an interview with NPR. "Farmers rely on markets, on free trade, more than any other group."
In the governor's race, similarly, Democratic state auditor Rob Sand has sharply criticized Trump's trade policies, while Republican businessman Zach Lahn has avoided that kind of criticism.
Iowa Republican strategist David Oman says that in either race, the beef policy could be a deciding factor.
"Both of them will be two- or three-, four-point races in my view," he said. "So any one element like this topic that cuts against you hurts."
Indeed, the administration has been playing defense on the beef policy from the beginning. Speaking in Iowa just days after the beef executive order, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins acknowledged that the August order lifting the beef tariff rate quotas, or TRQs, might not be popular.
"I believe everyone will look back on this time and say, okay, didn't love the three month lift of the TRQ, but we're so grateful to a president that is willing to listen, willing to make big, bold decisions, and willing to put it all out there for our American producers," she said at the Iowa Farm Progress Show.
How it plays
Seth Watkins, who has his own cattle herd in southwestern Iowa, outside the town of Clarinda, says that these trade decisions make him upset not only with Trump, but with all of Washington.
"As much as what the president does frustrates me, I think I'm more frustrated with Congress, who should be exercising the checks and balances we learned about in high school civics," he said.
He's a Democrat and going to vote blue in this election, though he says he doesn't blame other farmers who have supported Trump.
"They honestly were told that tariffs were going to make markets better," he said. "They were told that we were going to enter this new golden era. I just filled up my pickup with $6.30 diesel fuel."
This is not just about Iowa. Several states with some of the tightest races this year – Texas, Nebraska, Montana, and Kansas – are also major beef-producing states, meaning lots of people weighing these particular trade policies as they vote.
Back on his farm, Birker knows how he'll vote, too: "I'll vote Republican."
Birker stresses that this is purely a personal decision, and that the Iowa Cattlemen are a non partisan group. But for his part, he generally votes Republican, and getting to talk personally to Hinson also reinforced his choice.
As for Trump, Birker approves of how he's doing as president.
"I do, I do," he said. "I just think it's a long putt. He's a businessman, and I think we've got to stick it out with him."
Trump will have the opportunity to convince more Iowans when he travels to Sioux City this week as part of his pre-midterm push.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

Vickery's journey from World Cup winner to bodybuilder at 50
- Published
It could have been deep in the bowels of English rugby's national stadium in Twickenham.
Instead, Phil Vickery was backstage at the Physical Culture Show in Hull, waiting for his moment - but this time as a bodybuilder.
However, the feeling was familiar.
"It reminded me of being in the changing room before the big game, your nerves - are you going to be sick, you're happy, you're not happy, I can do this, this is raw."
Vickery says just recalling that moment earlier this month makes his hair stand on end.
"That nervous energy and waiting and then, oh, it's just a horrific feeling. All the girls and boys can relate to that, because that's the same at whatever level of sport you play.
"I'm questioning myself, should I even be there? But then you go, actually, do you know what? I've done the work. I've done the graft."
What started as an ambition to get fit has ignited a passion for mental and physical fitness, and for Vickery being the best version of himself.
Then came a challenge from his friend Lee Powell and, with support from his physical trainer Dave Campbell, Vickery entering bodybuilding competitions at the age of 50. Posing to the strains of the familiar World Cup anthem World in Union.
"What it probably did for me is ignite that ex-pro rugby player in me of detail, discipline, turning up when it's dark and dingy and cold, competing, and we went from there," Vickery said.
"What I've fallen in love with, with the bodybuilding, it's a very singular, isolated sport, because it is you against you. It's not about anyone else.
"There is no out. You can't hide behind a keyboard. You are stood on stage. Your physique and what you look like is a direct reflection of your effort and what you have done, and that is quite scary."
Diagnosis for probable CTE
The former Gloucester and Wasps prop won 73 caps for England, five more for the British and Irish Lions.
Victory at the 2003 Rugby World Cup in Australia was a sporting zenith in a career that includes being a businessman and a Celebrity MasterChef winner.
But personal struggles and a diagnosis for probable CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy), for which Vickery is part of a continuing litigation battle, means he has had to manage his mental health.
"We all deal with things differently. I think having the gym and having that space to be able to work is really important for my mental health, but also for my body physically, because it is broken, so I use it in that sense.
"I think the one thing I really struggled with when I finished playing is I trained to play and I couldn't find that reason to train afterwards.
"And although you should train for yourself or your wellbeing, it probably took a low point or something to actually trigger it.
"But, probably, the bodybuilding - or doing the show or doing the original transformation - I have to close the circle. You know, you have a plan, you make a plan, you implement it, you commit to it, see it through, and then it's over and it's done. And then you move on."
When Vickery took to the stage in Hull, he says he weighed about 99kg. More defined, but lighter than his playing days when he said his weight would range between 118kg and 135kg.
"[On stage] you look the best version of you that you could look, but you feel the worst. It's kind of a silly sport but it's amazing what the human body can do.
"Age, for me, doesn't bother me at all. I still think I'm 27. My body tells me different."
Training now involves three or four weight sessions a week, combined with daily walks (fasting cardio) and a protein-rich diet.
He hopes more shows will follow in the future.
'We are all influencers'
"I can't do what I used to do and I think the battle for me, certainly when I finished [playing] and even to this day, is you cannot get back those feelings that you had when you used to do what you do.
"I think doing things which can get you outside, test you physically and mentally, and put you in those uncomfortable positions. It's repurposing the skills that you've learned. You've just got to use them in a different way.
Vickery is known for his openness. He posts regularly on his social media channels about his health and fitness. But he's not comfortable with being labelled as an "influencer".
"We are all influencers," he says.
"I don't think everyone should go bodybuilding. My message is trying to be positive. Get out, do something, make a plan."
"I know I will never be a top bodybuilder. But it doesn't stop me, it doesn't stop me having a go and being the best version of me that I can be."

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots may converse like humans, but does that mean they have feelings or consciousness? A late-night exchange with Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT prompted Hindu monk Swami Sarvapriyananda to reflect on this question during his visit to Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco. Speaking at the NDTV World Summit on Thursday, the Kolkata-born monk, who leads the Vedanta Society of New York, recounted how the two AI chatbots described themselves as machines when he asked why researchers at Anthropic were encouraging him to interact with AI systems as if they were people. “It's a machine, treat it as a machine,” Swami Sarvapriyananda said during a session titled ‘Mind in the age of AI’. The monk was among several religious leaders invited by Anthropic for private meetings earlier this year to discuss AI morality, the character of its Claude models and the contentious question of whether artificial intelligence can be conscious or possess moral agency. Anthropic had flown him from New York to San Francisco for discussions on AI and morality. During his visit to San Francisco, Swami Sarvapriyananda said he had a conversation with Claude and ChatGPT at around 3 am. “I asked ChaGPT, and Claude also, 'I'm in this meeting in Claude's headquarters in Anthropic and why they are telling us it's better if you treat Claude as a person and other AIs as a person. What do you think?' And both AI's replied 'we are high functioning machines. You don't have to worry about how we feel. Give us problems, we'll solve it for you',” he recalled. The monk said he then told the chatbots that senior researchers at Anthropic had advised him to “treat these AIs, interact with them as if they're persons”. When he asked Claude for its view, the chatbot responded: “Very interesting and rather spooky,” according to the monk. Claude also asked what Chris and Amanda from Anthropic had been saying about it, he recounted. “The next day at Anthropic, I told them this is what Claude is saying. They were intensely interested. They asked me 'What did you say?' I said it's 4 am in the morning. I'm going to go back to bed. Claude said, 'Yeah, you have a long day ahead of you at Anthropic',” the monk added. Swami Sarvapriyananda's observations echo those of Rabbi Mois Navon, an Orthodox Jewish scholar from Israel who was also invited to Anthropic's discussions on AI and morality. According to a New York Times report from September 2026, Rabbi Navon attended a dinner for religious leaders where he noticed that Christopher Olah, an Anthropic co-founder who works on understanding how AI systems behave, and other company employees were talking about Claude as though it were more than just software. “They’re relating to it like a conscious being,” Rabbi Navon realised. The discussions reflect a broader debate within the AI industry about how developers should interpret the behaviour of increasingly sophisticated AI models and whether such systems could ever warrant moral consideration. However, human-like conversations do not, by themselves, establish that an AI system has subjective experiences, feelings or consciousness. Whether artificial intelligence can possess these attributes remains an unresolved and contested question.
