There is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.
Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.
He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.
The accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known as yarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.
It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).
Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.
The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.
Saijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.
In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed in fundoshi loincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.

O'Neill bemoans marginal moments but are Celtic just not good enough?
- Published
Three Europa League games. Three defeats for Celtic. They are 35th of 36 teams in the competition after another European collapse, this time against Celta Vigo.
Only Ararat-Armenia and their inferior goal difference keeps the Scottish champions from propping up the table.
Off the back of Sunday's 7-1 drubbing of Hearts, there was hope Martin O'Neill's team had turned a corner. Instead, the disparity between their domestic dominance and European shortcomings was laid bare once more.
After Mika Baur swept Celtic in front on 47 minutes, they went into their shells and succumbed to a timid 2-1 defeat as Javi Rodriguez struck twice in three minutes.
O'Neill bemoaned refereeing decisions and marginal moments that went against his team, but are Celtic simply "not good enough" to compete in Europe?
That was the verdict of former Scotland attacker James McFadden after a Celtic collapse that is becoming all too familiar.
"The performances at this level haven't been good enough," he said on Sportsound. "Celtic are way short."
Celtic looked nailed on for the Champions League this season when they went into a 4-0 aggregate lead against Austrian champions LASK in the play-off round, before shipping five goals in 77 minutes to drop into the Europa League.
O'Neill's side have now lost their last four European matches, conceding 14 goals in the process. Only once before had they done so in the same season - in the 2017-18 Champions League.
"It seems as though Celtic struggle when there's a bit of adversity," McFadden added. "If something goes against them, the confidence drops, their heads drop, they stop playing forward.
"The ball goes back and across, inviting pressure, and there's no way they take the pressure off. That has been a theme."
'Deserved' loss or night of nearly moments?
After another disappointing night, O'Neill focused on moments that went against his team - a free-kick not given before Celta's equaliser and a Liam Scales header that flicked the top of the bar at 1-0.
"We conceded a free-kick and I thought a second before that we should have had a foul for us," O'Neill said. "They score from the free-kick and it knocks us a little bit. It gave them a bit of momentum.
"I think if [Liam] Scales' header goes in to make it 2-0, we get the three points. We've lost three matches now, remarkably we're still in with a chance [of progressing]. We've got to win here and got to win away from home.
"We take the lead in the game, if we get the second goal we win the match and it changes the whole dynamic. It didn't happen, that's it - we need to try to find a way to win European games."
Centre-back Liam Scales had by far the most touches of any Celtic player with 121, well ahead of left-back Kieran Tierney (79) and goalkeeper Sam Johnstone (69).
Goalscorer Baur admitted they did not do enough to win and was at a loss when asked what needs to change. "How we played second half, last 30 minutes, we deserved it in the end," Baur said.
When asked if he knew why his team collapsed in such a manner, he responded: "I cannot tell you, sorry.
"It can happen that you get a goal, they can score too, good team - you should then get control back, hold the ball a bit longer to take the momentum away from them. You should break that."
Celtic did not get control back, did not break Celta's momentum and ultimately paid the price.

China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built
China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority.
The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC).
The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a technical director with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases.
“The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
Efforts to understand how classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD summon powerful changes in consciousness tend to focus on what's happening inside our head.
That's because these compounds bind tightly to serotonin receptors that densely populate certain structures of the brain, and a growing number of studies demonstrate they can exert long-lasting changes in mental health and well-being for people with a range of psychiatric conditions. 
Increasingly researchers have started to probe how these drugs elicit other physiological changes, given that many cells and tissues beyond the brain possess those same receptors, known as 5-HT2A.
Now, new research offers some of the first evidence in humans that psychedelics may also hold potential for treating diseases characterized by inflammation and immune dysregulation throughout the body.
The data, published Wednesday in the medical journal JAMA Psychiatry, draws from a small pool of patients with Parkinson's disease, but it reflects what's been observed in lab studies with animal and cell models for years. For certain diseases, psychedelics appear to combat inflammation and even help restore stressed mitochondria, the energy-producing factories of the cells.
The team at the University of California, San Francisco, who conducted the study, used blood tests to measure five different signaling molecules involved in inflammation in participants, both before and after two sessions with psilocybin.
The participants had significantly lower levels of inflammation following the treatments, compared to baseline, and those changes persisted a month after their final dose of psilocybin. The researchers also tracked a blood marker of mitochondrial stress. Here, too, there were substantial improvements immediately after participants were given psilocybin, though not during the longer-term follow up.
"This gives us an initial biological signal to investigate," says Dr. Ellen Bradley, an associate professor of psychiatry at UCSF who helped lead the analysis.
The findings were based on 12 participants in a pilot study to evaluate the feasibility and safety of giving psilocybin to people with Parkinson's disease. Patients with neurodegenerative conditions are typically excluded from trials on psychedelics and mental health for safety concerns.
The original study, which was published last year, assuaged researchers' concerns about the risks. Bradley says they found a "really promising safety profile" and that "symptoms even seemed to get a bit better."
The researchers emphasize that the study has limitations: they did not have a control group, and the participants knew they were receiving the drug. So the data on what was happening in their blood needs to be confirmed in follow-up studies before making definitive claims, says Aoife O'Donovan, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at UCSF and co-author of the paper.
Still, O'Donovan says the findings reflect "objective markers" that changed over time and that gives them confidence to pursue this line of research.
Parkinson's disease is characterized by dysregulated inflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction. This data, Bradley notes, could help explain why the participants appeared to benefit from the drugs during the trial.
Beyond that, the results raise the proposition that psychedelics may help address others diseases that are characterized by troubles with inflammation, says D. Parker Kelley, a research scientist in the Mitochondrial PsychoBiology group at Columbia University who was a first author on the paper with Bradley.
"It's a potential jumping off point for a lot more research in this area," he says, "that may apply not only to Parkinson's, but also neuropsychiatric disorders like depression and anxiety, and even cardio-metabolic and inflammatory disorders."
While previous studies have looked at biomarkers of inflammation after psilocybin, those have generally included healthy volunteers – not people with real disease, says Charles Nichols, a professor of pharmacology, biochemistry and experimental therapeutics at LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans.
"I think it's really exciting," says Nichols, who didn't work on the study, but whose lab discovered that certain psychedelics could have powerful anti-inflammatory effects about fifteen years ago.
That insight came from studying lab-grown cell culture that simulated inflammation of blood vessels and hardening of arteries, also known as atherosclerosis.
In that experiment, they found a psychedelic acting on the 5-H2TA receptors functioned as a "potent anti-inflammatory," even at doses well below what would cause a psychoactive trip, he says.
Since then, Nichols' group has run numerous experiments in animal models of disease including asthma, arthritis, and cardiovascular disease, but the field has needed to test whether these protective effects hold up in humans.
He says this new study in Parkinson's patients is a proof of principle.
"We can only draw so much from those conclusions," he says. "But I do think it validates a lot of the pharmacology that we've been doing over the last 15 years on the anti-inflammatory, the mitochondrial protective effects."

New video shows just how massive Trump’s White House ballroom is
Work on the project continues following a federal ruling over congressional approval and ongoing lawsuits surrounding its six-story underground facility

Newly released aerial footage shows the scale of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, captured from a helicopter as construction continues.
The clip, shared on X by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino Jr., shows the massive frame of the structure adjacent to the White House complex. Scavino said the video was recorded from Marine One while Trump traveled to Joint Base Andrews for a flight to South Carolina.
The project has faced legal and political opposition since work began. A federal judge ruled in August that Trump lacked the authority to demolish portions of the White House without congressional approval, raising questions about the future of the project.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation previously filed a suit that temporarily paused above-ground construction, though work was permitted to continue on a six-story underground bunker replacing the Presidential Emergency Operations Center. The underground portion is set to include a military hospital and research facilities.
The original East Wing of the White House was demolished in October 2025 to make way for the 90,000-square-foot facility, proceeding without congressional authorization.
Initial estimates in February 2025 placed the cost of the project at $100 million. The figure later rose to $250 million and has since grown to $600 million.
Trump has consistently defended the initiative, arguing it will offer a secure location for state visits, official ceremonies and inaugurations. The design also features a drone port intended as a defense mechanism.
Details about how the project is being funded were revealed in leaked internal campaign records obtained by The Washington Post, which show $333 million in private gifts across 67 major pledges. Major corporate backers include Nvidia and Apple, which pledged $25 million each, as well as $5 million commitments from companies such as Amazon, Microsoft and T-Mobile.
Political allies and administration members also contributed, though Trump himself is absent from the donor list despite past claims that he was financing the build directly.
The funds are collected through a D.C.-based non-profit, the Trust for the National Mall, before being transferred into a White House account. This structure allows the project to avoid standard campaign disclosure rules, with at least $77 million coming from anonymous donors — a setup that has drawn criticism from ethics experts and Democratic lawmakers.
The documents also show that several major pledges coincided with favorable agency decisions or federal contract awards, including a $25 million pledge from Dish Network chairman Charles Ergen before the FCC dropped an inquiry into his firm, and a $3 million pledge from Salesforce around the time it secured a multi-billion-dollar Army deal.
“This is a shield that protects everything that’s inside, everything that’s on top,” Trump told reporters near the site in May, adding that it would be the “safest building ever built, in my opinion.”
Earlier this month, Trump visited the site with White House communications adviser Margo Martin.
“President @realDonaldTrump checks on the progress of the White House Ballroom construction,” Martin wrote on X with video of the inspection.
Following the helicopter flight shown in the new video, Trump attended a campaign rally at Clemson University in South Carolina on Wednesday that was repeatedly interrupted by demonstrators. The event turned violent after a protester was struck by an attendee.
Trump reacted to the incident from the stage, as reported by The Guardian: “That was great, man. Wow. Man, I loved that. I watched that. That was incredible. Wow. That was unbelievable. Is everybody OK?
“Who’s the guy that threw that punch?” he continued. “You know, you reminded me of Evander, the real deal, Holyfield.”
Former heavyweight boxing champion Evander Holyfield was in attendance at the rally.
“You gotta give them credit,” Trump said. “It takes courage to do that at a Trump rally. He got whacked.”

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.
During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.
Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, the Wall Street Journal reported at the time.
His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.
Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments into AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.
All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”
Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. Many California companies left for Texas, Nevada, and California in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.
But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.
In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.
On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality, and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.
Bowing to the inevitable
Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we’ve gone over it no matter which records you choose.
The UN relies on temperatures averaged over a few decades to determine where we’re at, which means we have technically not gone above the limit yet. But, as temperatures seem stubbornly disinterested in dropping much even after extremely hot years, we’re likely at the start of the period where the 1.5° goal is passed. So, while it’s not technically too late to get on a pathway that keeps us below this, practically it’s already too late.

An analysis of 33,159 cancer journal articles revealed tell-tale patterns of fake citation numbers across 4,000 articles by 'research paper mills', or fraudulent research organisations.
The suspect papers received 50-100 per cent more citations than other articles within one to three years of publication, yet had fewer readers and were accessed less often online, findings published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Researchers said suspect papers tended to cluster in a subset of journals including 'Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research' and 'Molecular Cancer' whereas other journals were only marginally affected.
They said 'research paper mills', the fraudulent organisations that make money by offering to list people's names on fake research papers, may also be manipulating citation counts -- a key measure of academic performance.
Artificially inflated citation counts distort the evidence base to misinform future research and clinical translation, the team said.
"Just as likes and shares indicate social media influencers' audience engagement, citations from other researchers are an important academic measure for evaluating scientists' research impact," author and statistician Adrian Barnett, from Queensland University of Technology's Australian Centre for Health Services Innovation, explained.
"Because citation counts are now a key measure of academic performance, they can incentivise journals and researchers to maximise citations counts," Barnett said.
The author said the researchers documented a pattern that suggested widespread, coordinated manipulation of citation counts by paper mills.
"Artificially high citation rates can inflate journal impact factors, amplify unreliable findings, and slow scientific progress," Barnett said.
The team evaluated the impact of paper mills on citation patterns in 33,159 articles published in 20 journals between 2012 and 2023.
"Applying our previously developed detection model, we flagged a total of 4,085 articles as potentially associated with paper mills, based on their textual similarity to the titles and abstracts of retracted paper mill articles," co-researcher Baptiste Scancar said.
Papers flagged by the model had many more citations, compared to non-flagged papers, but had fewer readers, the researchers said.
"Having more citations but fewer readers makes no sense, as citations come from readers," Scancar said.
"Flagged papers mostly cite and are cited by other flagged papers, measurably inflating the citation metrics of some cancer research journals," the co-researcher said.
"Flagged papers tended to cluster in a subset of journals including Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research and Molecular Cancer whereas other journals were only marginally affected," Scancar said.
Our results support the screening of articles and journals for the patterns of citation manipulation we have described, the researchers said.
"Across leading cancer journals, clusters of interconnected papers bearing the hallmarks of paper mill products accumulate far more citations than other papers despite having fewer readers," the authors wrote.
"This study provides evidence that citation manipulation leaves measurable traces in citation patterns, offering a practical basis for future screening and intervention," they said.

As Laika debuts its latest stop-motion animation, Travis Knight is standing firmly against generative AI.
The Wildwood director and Laika CEO explained that GenAI “is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” also emphasizing that he hopes people “see the danger” in the technology’s potential as much as the “value.”
“But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist,” he told The Verge. “When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition. And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that.
Knight continued, “When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. That’s theft.”
Watch on Deadline
While he conceded that “AI is extraordinary technology” that could reap great benefits in medicine and science and “benefit humanity tremendously,” he also sees “a world where they can be devastating.”
“I fear for the latter, I hope for the former, but it requires people to be good stewards of this technology,” he explained. “As a group of humans we have not shown generally that we’re good at that. But I’m ever an optimist, and I hope that collectively we can see the value in the technology and use it responsibly, and see the danger in the technology and push back against it.”
Knight’s comments come amid ongoing concerns around AI’s plagiarism of copyrighted materials and the threat it poses to jobs in Hollywood and beyond, as well as recent warnings from those working in AI that continued progress could “cause a billion deaths.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order last month to fast-track stringent oversight and control of AI. Convening “a group of world-leading experts” within the next 60 days, the order lays out a discussion of “safety plans” and “an emergency shutoff, or ‘kill switch,’ for frontier models.”
On a federal level, Trump has brushed off concerns about AI as “a hoax,” insisting the U.S. government “already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies.

Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests. The research, published Thursday in the journal Science, uses samples of ancient vegetation and rock records to analyze the growth—and sudden retreat—of an ice cap that is the last vestige of an ice sheet that once covered much of North America.
The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.
“A question that’s in the popular consciousness is, have we caused enough global warming to stop the next ice age from happening?” says Andrew Wickert, an associate professor of environmental science at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, who was not involved in the research. The new research shows that “even as we were just starting to ramp up emissions, we’ve already done enough damage to cause the major North American ice sheet to already start retreating. That’s significant.”
The planet regularly goes through phases where ice extends down from the high latitudes—what we colloquially call "ice ages"—due to natural shifts in the Earth's rotation and orbit, known as Milankovitch Cycles. Those are followed by interglacial periods where ice retreats toward the poles.
The last ice age ended 12,000 years ago. At its peak, what's known as the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered all of Canada and extended as far south as New York and the Midwest. It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.
Unlike glaciers, which can move, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the bedrock, preserving the vegetal record of what grew around it under the ice. That quirk allowed the scientists leading the new study to glean information about how much it has grown—and shrank.
To determine when it first reached its modern size, they used an exposure dating technique to calculate roughly how long rocks several meters from the glacier’s edge had been exposed to the sky. Using measurements of Beryllium-10, an element that forms on the surface of exposed rock, the authors calculated that the ice sheet first reached the size it is today around 3,600 years ago.
Next, they wanted to see how much the ice cap had regrown from that point. To do this, they turned to the humble denizens of the tundra in front of the glacier: mosses and lichen.
“After the ice cap retreated, mosses eventually colonized this newly exposed land,” says Nicolás Young, a paleoclimatologist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University and lead author of the new paper. “These mosses are living there, and things are normal—then, eventually, the ice cap starts to re-expand. The ice covers the moss, and kills it.” The traces of the dead moss are preserved in newly reexposed land, allowing Young and his team to piece together a timeline of how the ice has moved across the landscape.
Thanks to these records, Young and his coauthors estimate that the glacier started growing again around 2,000 years ago. This may have signaled the start of another glaciation period.
But starting in the 1960s, the ice cap has done something that wouldn’t correspond with another ice age: It started getting smaller again. The team used historic aerial photos that showed that the ice has reversed course, retreating significantly back from its new margins. The Barnes Ice Cap’s edges have retreated an average of 4 meters per year since the 1980s. That coincides with a period of rapidly increasing carbon emissions, which has caused ice to go into retreat worldwide. The ice cap offers a particularly stark example, though, given the growth prior to the 1960s.
“Modern retreat of this glacier has reversed 2,000 years of net expansion—that’s a pretty decent chunk of time,” Young says.
Meredith Kelly, a professor of earth sciences at Dartmouth, says the data gathered in the study is “awesome” and that the study shows a “clear pattern of what the ice cap was doing.” However, Kelly says that she would like to see a comparison of some of the data to other sites around the world to more fully grasp how, exactly, the Earth was moving into its glaciation period before the effects of human-caused warming kicked in. While we have a broad understanding of what kicks off periods where ice can grow, the exact mechanisms are still something that require more research.
The evidence presented in this paper, Young says, could also validate a decades-old hypothesis that has long been held up by climate deniers as “evidence” climate change is a hoax. In the early 1970s, scientists gathered for a meeting at Brown University to discuss hypotheses of when the next ice age might happen. (Young says that two of his coauthors on this paper were at that meeting.) The scientists concluded that a glaciation period was so imminent that they sent a warning letter to President Richard Nixon.
“I think this study actually helps show that scientists were right about a pending glaciation,” Young says. “
Media coverage of the meeting, as well as a colder period of weather in the 1970s, have long been pitched by climate deniers as “proof” that global warming isn’t actually happening. It very much is, though, and the new research actually adds to the evidence.

On Monday night, Georgie Purcell shared a statement on social media in support of Helen Haines, who earlier that day had been allegedly attacked by a constituent in her regional Victorian electorate.
Purcell, a Victorian upper house MP whose region partly overlaps with Haines’s federal electorate, wrote that the alleged attack had sent chills down her spine. Being a woman in politics, she said, had changed the way she moved through the world – where she parked her car, which route she took home, even whether she held public events at all.
It didn’t take long to receive validation of why her precautions were necessary: a constituent commented on her Haines statement, saying he wished it had happened to Purcell. Another, a little while later, said: “You should be scared.”
Purcell reported them both. Beyond that, she says, there is “nothing else she can do” as the threats lack the specificity police require to take further action.
It leaves her on “high alert” with just five weeks until the Victorian election.
“One thing that is on my mind is there is 10 days of prepoll approaching where anyone who does want to undertake a targeted attack on a candidate or a member of parliament, it won’t be hard to work out where they are,” she says.
Purcell is not alone. Nationals MP Annabelle Cleeland, whose electorate of Euroa covers 11,452 square kilometres, says, due to threats, she shares her live location with her husband and staff when on the road.
“I don’t feel like I signed up for this job to put my children in harm’s way and, right now, I’m frightened about that,” she told ABC Radio Melbourne on Thursday.
“It’s sexualised, it’s violent and they target your weaknesses and your vulnerabilities – your children, your home.”
MPs across Victoria’s political spectrum – predominantly women – have said that threats to their safety intensified during Victoria’s prolonged Covid lockdowns and have remained a constant since.
Few Victorians can forget that during the pandemic, an effigy of the then premier, Daniel Andrews, was subjected to a mock execution on the front steps of parliament amid debate over pandemic legislation.
The next day, Andrews said: “There are some people who are threatening me. They’re threatening my family. They are essentially attacking the safety of my family.”
It is understood the premier was receiving around-the-clock close personal protection at the time. During the 2022 election campaign, Andrews’ press conferences were largely kept out of public view. One exception, an event at a Caulfield dog park, drew a man intent on heckling him. In 2023, another man faced court on charges of stalking and harassing Andrews.
When he resigned in 2024, Andrews lost his security but remained as much a public figure. Just recently, images of where he has been living appeared on the front page of a national newspaper.
His successor, Jacinta Allan, also faced much hostility, particularly in regional Victoria, where communities opposed the government’s emergency services levy and laws that allow state body VicGrid and its contractors access to private land for transmission projects – without a landholder’s consent.
There was the 2025 Bush Summit – a day after the latter laws passed parliament – where, during her speech, Allan was relentlessly heckled, including by an audience member who stood on her chair with a noose around her neck. Allan’s staff left in tears.
On other occasions, cars believed to be carrying the premier have been blocked or followed, only for those inside found to be staff members or other ministers – including at a press conference during the January bushfires.
For six weeks a mobile billboard carrying the message “ditch the witch” and AI-generated images of Allan travelled around Melbourne’s CBD before being reported on.
Each incident generated footage that was widely shared by the media and on socials.
A former staff member of Allan’s said the former premier “legitimately feared for her safety”.
“She would say ‘Someone is going to be killed.’”
‘A turning point’
For the entire four years she has been in parliament, Purcell has received abuse, rape and death threats on social media over her positions on issues including duck hunting and racing.
But since beginning a relationship with federal Labor MP Josh Burns, Purcell has had access to more security measures – not because she is a Victorian MP, but because her partner is a federal one.
In Canberra, the Australian federal police manage threats against federal MPs, building up intelligence about repeated behaviour and patterns over time. In Victoria, Purcell says, individual complaints are dealt with separately by police.
With a state election looming, this may be about to change.
On Wednesday, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, met with the Victorian electoral commissioner and the chief commissioner of police, Mike Bush, as well as his cabinet, to discuss stronger safety measures for MPs.
“This work will happen progressively and as soon as possible. What has happened must be a turning point for political debate in Victoria and around Australia. We must go forward with more respect and understanding of one another,” Carroll told reporters.
Earlier that morning, Bush said police were working to establish a centralised process for monitoring threats against MPs.
“We want a single-stop shop to report these things and have the ability to be very proactive,” he said.
As of Thursday afternoon, changes were yet to be communicated to Victorian MPs, who have been asked to attend a briefing with police on Friday. For now, their only guidance remains a Tuesday morning email from the Department of Parliamentary Services that advises them to monitor and control access to their electorate offices, check external areas on CCTV before leaving, and to remember that a duress button is available in an emergency.
It leaves MPs weighing the risk of being out in public with their constituents against the possibility that one may try to harm them.
- Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

Delhi HC refuses to stay release of Sourav Ganguly-inspired film Doosra
The Delhi high court declines to stay the release of Doosra: India’s Other Freedom Struggle after Sourav Ganguly and Luv Films challenge its release.
The Delhi high court on Thursday declined to stay the release of “Doosra: India’s Other Freedom Struggle”, a Hindi sports drama inspired by former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly, which is scheduled to hit theatres on Friday.
“I have said no stay, so the film can go on,” Justice Dinesh Bhatt said.
The court was hearing a petition filed by former India cricket captain Sourav Ganguly and Luv Films LLP to restrain the release of the film, citing the unauthorised use of events from the former cricketer’s life, particularly his captaincy in the NatWest cricket series final and his shirtless celebration at Lord’s.
The suit, argued by senior advocate Balbir Singh, alleged that Doosra amounted to the unauthorised commercial exploitation of Sourav Ganguly’s personality rights and infringed Luv Films’ exclusive contractual rights over his proposed biopic.
It contended that the film used the former cricketer’s name, image, likeness and iconic cricketing moments without his consent or a licence.
According to the suit, Ganguly entered into an agreement with Luv Films on August 5, 2021, granting the production house exclusive rights to develop, produce and commercially exploit audiovisual content, including a biographical film based on his life and cricketing career.
Luv Films claimed to have made substantial investments in the authorised biopic, titled Dada – The Sourav Ganguly Story, which is scheduled for release on May 14, 2027.
The suit further stated that the trailer and promotional campaign for Doosra, launched on October 12, prominently referenced Ganguly’s leadership of the Indian cricket team and its historic victory in the 2002 NatWest Series final at Lord’s.
It also cited an October 13 interview in which Deo discussed how the 2002 final and milestones in Ganguly’s career had influenced the film’s fictional character, Tara.
However, Deo’s lawyer Saurabh Kirpal argued that the movie was not a biopic of former India captain Sourav Ganguly, but the story of a girl from Rajasthan who draws inspiration from him. Kirpal further submitted that the filmmakers had obtained a licence from the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) to use footage from the NatWest Series, contending that Ganguly had no rights over the footage itself.
The matter will be heard again on Friday.

You can build a portfolio website for free without coding using AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Google AI Studio, or Perplexity. Simply provide your details or resume, ask AI to create a personalized website, download the HTML file, and publish it for free using Netlify Drop or GitHub Pages.
A resume is a standard way to showcase your skills and experience while applying for jobs. Most companies still evaluate candidates through resume screening. However, resumes follow a standard template and don’t truly visualize users’ skills.
On the other hand, portfolio sites have become popular for showcasing candidates’ creative skills. However, most portfolio sites were previously limited to developers with web development and website-publishing skills. But thanks to AI, that restriction no longer applies to regular users.
Anyone can now create a personalized portfolio website to showcase their skills and experience creatively without writing code. Web hosting services like Netlify and GitHub also make it easy to publish a simple portfolio site for free.
If you are a beginner, have never written code, and want to publish a portfolio website to showcase your skills and stand out, this guide will show you how to create one for free.
I will show you how to create a free portfolio website using Claude, ChatGPT, Google AI Studio, or even Perplexity, then guide you through a detailed, step-by-step process to publish it for free without writing code.
Table of Contents
How to Create and Publish a Portfolio Website for Free Using AI
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Claude
You can create a portfolio site using any free AI model. First, let’s create one using Claude. If you’re not aware, Claude also offers a limited free version, enough for most users to create a great portfolio site.
Step 1: Go to Claude.ai and sign in or create a free account.
Step 2: Once you’re done, paste this prompt into the prompt box and press Enter. You can modify the prompt to add or remove details, or to guide how your portfolio website looks. Remember that the possibilities are endless. Even if you generate a site, you can edit and customize it later, but the free version is very limited. So, ensure that you specify every detail before submitting your prompt.
Step 3: Now wait for Claude to create your portfolio site. You will see a message such as “Creating site.html” with a timer. Leave the tab open until it finishes creating.
Step 4: Once it’s done, Claude shows a preview of your website in the side panel canvas. You can preview what Claude built. You can also see how it looks on different devices, including mobile, and whether it’s responsive.
Step 5: Next, you need to download the file. To do that, in full screen, click the small arrow icon next to the copy icon at the top right of the screen, then choose Download as HTML and save the file locally on your device.
Once the site is created, you can publish using the steps below. You can also create portfolio websites with other free AI tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini AI Studio, and more. Those offer better free rate limits than Claude.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using ChatGPT
Unlike Claude, ChatGPT offers a completely free version with much more generous rate limits, letting you create a fully personalized portfolio website.
Step 1: If you don’t have a ChatGPT account, go to chatgpt.com and sign in with your free account.
Step 2: Now, enter the prompt in the prompt box and press Enter.
Step 3: Wait for ChatGPT to plan, build, and write the code.
Step 4: In my case, building a portfolio site took six minutes. You can tap the HTML file to preview it. Like Claude, ChatGPT also opens it in a preview.
Step 5: However, it also offers a direct download option, and when it’s done, click on the download portfolio.html, and it opens a preview, and click on the download icon at the top panel, and select HTML option, and save it locally on your device.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Google AI Studio
Next, let’s build a free portfolio site using Google AI Studio.
You can also use Gemini to create a website, but here I am using Google AI Studio. It gives access to the latest models, is free to use, and offers plenty of customization options. However, if you are a beginner, it can sound complex, so we created this simple guide to help you understand Google Gemini AI Studio.
Step 1: To create a portfolio website using Google Gemini AI Studio, go to aistudio.google.com and sign in with your Google account. Next, in the sidebar, under the Build section, tap on New app.
Step 2: Now Google AI Studio directly shows the preview on the right side. Since Google offers free rate limits, you can re-enter the prompt and make the changes you want. To proceed, click the code icon at the top of the preview.
Step 3: Now find the index.html option. Google AI Studio creates several project files, but index.html holds your entire website. In the file list, hover over index.html, click the three-dot menu next to it, then click Download.
Step 4: Once downloaded, open the file from your downloads folder and check that everything works properly without breaking anything. However, I highly recommend skipping the Export and Publish options here. Export lets you download the whole project, while Publish hosts the app within Google; both steps are unnecessary if you want to publish a simple portfolio site.
How to Create a Free Portfolio Website Using Perplexity
Next, you can also build a website using Perplexity. The free version allows you to create a simple portfolio site.
Step 1: To do that, go to Perplexity.ai, sign in with your free account, and click on the Ask Anything box.
Step 2: Paste the prompt and tap Send.
Step 3: Wait for Phubloxity to create a portfolio website. Once done, it will show you the portfolio.html file. Click on it to preview.
Step 4: After you check the preview, click the download option, download it as an HTML file, and save it locally on your device.
How to Publish Your Portfolio Website for Free
To publish your portfolio site, there are plenty of options, but in this guide, I will show you two free, reliable options: Netlify Drop and GitHub Pages.
Method 1: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using Netlify Drop
Step 1: Create a free Netlify account. First, go to netlify.com and sign up with your email. You can also sign up using Google or GitHub.
Step 2: Go to app.netlify.com/drop and drop the index.html you created using Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Google AI Studio from your downloads folder, or click the file and select it.
Step 3: Next, it automatically creates a free address. After a few minutes, your project shows as published with a random address such as sunny-tulip-tf52.netlify.app in my case. You can also click on that link to see the live site.
Step 4: However, if you think it can have a better name, open the project settings and change the project name to something short, such as meera-ai. Your address becomes meera-iyer.netlify.app. Make sure your site name is unique, since there will be hundreds of free Netlify sites out there.
Step 5: Once you have hosted the site successfully, you can share your link. Your portfolio is now live for anyone on any device to access it.
Method 2: Publish Your Portfolio Website Using GitHub Pages
Now let’s look at how to publish it for free using GitHub Pages.
GitHub also lets you host a simple website for free, and you can do everything on the GitHub website without installing anything. However, it takes a few more clicks than the Netlify Drop process.
Step 1: First, create a GitHub account. To do that, sign in to your free account at github.com, then go to github.com/new and create a new repository. For example, you can create ramesh.portfolio and set it to public. Remember that free accounts need a public repository for Pages to work. Turn on “Add a README” and finally tap on Create repository options.
Step 2: Once done, you can upload a file to the repository. Click Choose your files or drag and drop the index.html file, and at the bottom type a short message such as “Add portfolio website” and click on the Commit changes button.
Step 3: Once done, open the repository and go to Settings. Then click Pages in the left sidebar. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, pick main and / (root), and click Save.
Step 4: Now wait until GitHub says the changes can take up to 10 minutes. Wait for your site to go public, refresh the page, and wait for it to update. Once it’s done, click Visit site.
That’s it. GitHub will create your page under your name using a GitHub subdomain.
Final Thoughts
This is how you can use free AI tools to create free portfolio websites. Whether you are a beginner and have never written code before, you can follow this simple step-by-step process to create your first portfolio website.
If you have never built one and don’t even have an idea of creating profile sites, you can simply upload your resume into the AI tool and ask it to convert it into a portfolio website and generate an index.html page. If you have any issues while deploying the site, let me know in the comments, and I am happy to guide you.

Anti-CEC protest: Mapping key players, organisations shaping overseas campaigns
The CJP protests have drawn support from opposition-linked political networks, international advocacy organisations and diaspora groups, with connections spanning the Global Progressive Alliance, George Soros-funded institutions and overseas campaigns.
The Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) protests over the NEET paper leak, that rocked New Delhi in June, have since broadened into a campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. With the Congress, Left parties and other opposition groups joining the protests, questions have emerged over whether the mobilisation is entirely organic or is being amplified by a wider network of domestic political actors, overseas advocacy organisations and international campaign groups.
Are international NGOs, global activists and India's political Opposition working in tandem to put pressure on the Indian government? An examination of the connections cited by the groups involved offers a broader picture of how a domestic political protest has gained international visibility.
From prominent political figures and foreign institutions to overseas events featuring YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, this report examines the organisations, individuals and networks associated with mobilisation.
This investigation does not establish direct financial funding linked explicitly to specific domestic protests in India, but it maps out the transnational networks and personnel driving their international mobilisation.
RAHUL GANDHI AND THE GLOBAL PROGRESSIVE ALLIANCE CONNECTION
One of the key institutional links cited in this network is the Global Progressive Alliance (GPA), an international grouping of left-wing, socialist and social-democratic political parties.
Top leadership post for Rahul Gandhi: Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, serves as a member of the GPA's Presidium for Asia, while his close adviser Sam Pitroda is an active board member.
December 2025 German Tour: When Gandhi undertook a five-day visit to Germany in December 2025, Pitroda publicly confirmed that the trip was connected to Gandhi's role in the GPA.
International reaction to domestic protests: In July 2026, when Delhi Police detained Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra during student demonstrations over the NEET paper leak, the GPA issued a statement on X criticising the police action and saying it was monitoring the situation closely.
The statement drew attention to the involvement of an international political grouping in a domestic Indian controversy involving one of its leadership members. However, the GPA's public support for the protesters does not, by itself, establish that it directed or coordinated the demonstrations.
BJP'S ALLEGATIONS: THE GEORGE SOROS FUNDING ANGLE
The involvement of international progressive networks in Indian political protests has drawn criticism from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Allegations of foreign funding: At a press briefing in December, 2025, BJP national spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi alleged that the GPA network was linked to institutions backed by billionaire philanthropist George Soros and his Open Society Foundations (OSF).
Alleged indirect channels: The BJP also pointed to links involving European civil-society organisations, including Germany-based Campact, which has received OSF funding. The party alleged that such connections helped link Western political circles with Indian Opposition strategies.
These remain political allegations. Evidence of funding received by an organisation does not, on its own, establish that the donor directed its activities or coordinated a particular protest.
DHRUV RATHEE'S LONDON EVENT AND OVERSEAS ACTIVIST NETWORK
The international dimension of the mobilisation came into focus during overseas events, including a London gathering featuring YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and demonstrations in support of the CJP in New York.
Hindus for Human Rights (HfHR) has been associated with campaigns critical of the Modi government and has promoted protests under the slogan "Jantar Mantar Is Everywhere!" across cities in the United States and the United Kingdom. The organisation also participated in the London event featuring Rathee.
Similar demonstrations were organised or announced in several international cities, including:
- Austin, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and Chicago in the United States
- Melbourne in Australia
- London, Dublin, Berlin and Manchester in Europe
- Toronto and Vancouver in Canada
HfHR ORGANISES NEW YORK RALLY IN SOLIDARITY WITH CJP
HfHR promoted a rally at Union Square in New York on October 18, featuring speakers including Abby Govindan, Aatish Taseer, Shaifali Puri, Mandeep Minhas, Shruti Ganguly, Shivani Parikh, Yashica Dutt and Anurima Bhargava.
Several of these individuals have publicly criticised the BJP-led government's policies on issues including the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), citizenship, Kashmir, farmers' protests, minority rights and caste. Their criticism has often focused on allegations of majoritarianism and authoritarianism.
Among the speakers was Aatish Taseer, a British-born writer and journalist who wrote Time magazine's 2019 cover story, "India's Divider in Chief", which was critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The Indian government revoked his Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) status, citing issues relating to his father's Pakistani origin. Taseer has challenged the decision.
HfHR also shared posts supporting Neha Bora after her detention during a protest in Delhi. Its co-founder, Sunita Viswanath, publicly expressed solidarity with Bora and amplified calls for her release.
On October 19, Viswanath posted images and videos from Union Square with the caption, "Jantar Mantar is everywhere!"
HfHR also helped mobilise international expressions of solidarity with the CJP's July 20 protest at Jantar Mantar, with demonstrations reported or announced across North America and Europe.
The locations included New York's Union Square, San Jos City Hall, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Fremont, Austin, London, Dublin, Berlin, Manchester, Toronto and Vancouver.
According to organisers, more than 500 students and community members gathered near the Mahatma Gandhi statue at New York's Union Square on July 24.
KEY PLAYERS IN THE MOBILISATION NETWORK
Several individuals and organisations have featured prominently in the activities surrounding these protests. Their documented associations, however, need to be distinguished from claims that they jointly coordinated the mobilisation.
1. Sunita Viswanath and Hindus for Human Rights
Founding and organisational links: Sunita Viswanath is the co-founder and executive director of HfHR, a US-based advocacy organisation. She has also participated in events alongside groups such as the Indian American Muslim Council (IAMC).
The Alliance for Justice and Accountability: HfHR was established in 2019, alongside IAMC and the Organisation for Minorities of India (OFMI), as part of the broader network associated with the Alliance for Justice and Accountability (AJA). The coalition spearheaded protests against Prime Minister Modi's “Howdy Modi” event in Houston in September 2019.
Some accounts have alleged that these networks overlap with Western and Pakistani intelligence interests, including Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). Such allegations require specific, independently verifiable evidence and should not be treated as established facts merely because the organisations share campaign platforms or political positions.
Soros-linked funding: US financial records, including Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 990 filings, reportedly show that Open Society Policy Centre Inc. awarded USD 60,000 to HfHR in 2020. Viswanath also leads Women for Afghan Women, an organisation that has received funding from the Open Society Foundations.
These funding links establish financial associations, but do not, without further evidence, demonstrate that Soros or his organisations directed HfHR's activities or the CJP protests.
Sunita Viswanath at Rahul Gandhi's 2023 US event: During Gandhi's US visit in May and June 2023, which included San Francisco, Washington, DC, and New York, he participated in a discussion on US-India relations with policy experts at the Hudson Institute in Washington.
A photograph from the event shows Gandhi seated at a table with Viswanath nearby. Viswanath has said she was among approximately 50 attendees at the gathering, which she described as a public "DC town hall". The Hudson Institute also publicly acknowledged hosting Gandhi for the discussion.
The photograph and accounts of the event establish that Viswanath attended the gathering. They do not, by themselves, establish a formal political partnership or operational coordination between her and Gandhi.
2. Who is on HfHR's advisory board?
HfHR's official website lists the following individuals on its advisory board:
- - Harsh Mander
- - Aakar Patel
- - Rev Abhi Janamanchi
- - Anand Teltumbde

- - Martin Macwan
- - Medha

- - Syeda Hameed

- - TM Krishna
Important qualification: HfHR's website states that advisory board members do not necessarily endorse every statement or position taken by the organisation, just as the organisation does not necessarily endorse all their views. Membership of the board should not, therefore, be interpreted as blanket endorsement of the organisation's campaigns.
3. Salil Shetty's association with Rahul Gandhi
On October 11, 2022, Salil Shetty, then a vice-president of George Soros's Open Society Foundations and a former secretary-general of Amnesty International, was seen walking alongside Rahul Gandhi during the Bharat Jodo Yatra.
The public appearance established an association between the two at the event. It does not, on its own, establish coordination between the Open Society Foundations and the Congress party.
THE LONDON EVENT: SOUTH ASIA SOLIDARITY GROUP, CPI-ML AND UK PARLIAMENTARY LINKS
The London gathering featuring Dhruv Rathee brought together activists and organisations with links to South Asian political campaigns.
The South Asia Solidarity Group (SASG) was identified as the principal organiser of the London event. Its founders are Amrita Wilson and Kalpana Wilson.
Who is Amrita Wilson?
Amrita Wilson is an author and activist born in Kolkata in 1941. Her book *Finding a Voice* received the Martin Luther King Award. Her OCI status was revoked over alleged anti-India activities, a decision she is challenging.
Who is Kalpana Wilson?
Kalpana Wilson is a senior lecturer. She was accused of heckling and interrupting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant during a lecture at Birkbeck, University of London, in June.
The CPI-ML connection: Kalpana Wilson is married to Deepankar Bhattacharya, general secretary of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, or CPI-ML. Neha Bora, president of the party's student wing, the All India Students' Association (AISA), has also been associated with the protests.
These relationships and organisational links provide context for the political affiliations of some participants. They do not, on their own, establish that the organisations acted under a common command structure.
SASG backs the 'Jantar Mantar 2.0' march
The South Asia Solidarity Group expressed support for the planned “Jantar Mantar 2.0” march on October 10, 2026.
The group's campaign echoed several demands raised by the CJP concerning the Chief Election Commissioner and the SIR controversy. These included action against Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate halt to the SIR process, restoration of voting rights for people whose names were allegedly deleted from electoral rolls, cancellation of elections conducted under the SIR process and greater transparency and accountability in the Election Commission of India's functioning.
SASG also urged members of the Indian diaspora to amplify the movement's demands and expressed solidarity with the protesters.
UK parliamentary amplification
British MP Zarah Sultana, associated with Your Party, founded by former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, was among the political figures cited in connection with efforts to mobilise diaspora networks in the United Kingdom.
Sultana, whose family has roots in Mirpur, has used her political platform to raise issues concerning South Asia. HfHR publicly praised her on X for her role in mobilising support for the protests.
Her public support illustrates how the campaign's demands reached political platforms outside India. Establishing whether parliamentary activity formed part of a coordinated international strategy would require further evidence.
WHAT THE CONNECTIONS ESTABLISH, AND WHAT REMAINS UNPROVEN
The organisations and individuals examined here are linked through a combination of formal political affiliations, advocacy campaigns, funding relationships, public appearances and overseas demonstrations.
Three broad strands emerge:
1. Formal political networks: The Global Progressive Alliance provides an institutional link between Rahul Gandhi and an international grouping of progressive political parties.
2. Philanthropic and civil-society links: Funding records and organisational relationships connect some advocacy groups to philanthropic institutions, including entities associated with George Soros. Such links do not, in themselves, establish direction or control of political protests.
3. Diaspora mobilisation: Organisations such as HfHR and SASG have promoted campaigns and solidarity demonstrations in cities across North America, Europe and Australia, helping bring the CJP's demands to an international audience.
Taken together, these connections point to an international ecosystem of political organisations, advocacy groups and diaspora activists engaging with Indian domestic issues. However, the existence of overlapping affiliations, shared political positions or parallel protests is not sufficient to prove that the participants were operating in concert or under a centrally coordinated plan. Establishing that stronger claim would require evidence of direct coordination, instructions, funding tied to specific activities or other demonstrable links between the actors involved.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing “fake polls,” amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media.
Carr’s post on X said, “Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis… Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations.”
Carr urged broadcasters to “provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered.” In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very “context” that Carr said is needed.
Carr’s post did not mention any specific fake polls or any specific broadcasters that aired them. The vagueness of Carr’s post may be useful for his and Trump’s ongoing battle against the news media. In August, Trump demanded that the FCC punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in election endorsements, and wrote that the FCC must do something about “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA.”
Ex-FCC chairs: Carr wants “self-censorship”
Carr’s latest warning to broadcasters came as no surprise, given that he has spent much of the past two years threatening broadcast licenses and opening investigations into Trump’s least favorite news companies. Former Republican and Democratic FCC chairs and commissioners recently said Carr is seeking to censor and chill the speech of broadcasters through a proceeding that threatens the licenses of ABC-owned stations.
“FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s threat against broadcasters over their reporting on political polls is yet another truly outrageous attempt to censor and control the information available to Americans as they prepare to vote… Carr is now seizing on reports about fabricated political polling as an excuse to once again try to scare broadcasters into self-censorship,” said a statement today from a group of former FCC chairs and officials.
Today’s statement was attributed to former Chairman Tom Wheeler, a Democrat; former Chairman Mark Fowler, a Republican; and seven former high-ranking FCC officials. “Good-faith reporting on public polls—even ones that turn out to be made up—is not a violation of the FCC’s news distortion or hoax rules. And the FCC has zero authority to dictate editorial decisions,” they said.
Wheeler, Fowler, and others previously signed a letter objecting to the ABC investigation. The letter called it “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and the Trump administration of threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes.”
Anna Gomez, the only Democratic commissioner on the current FCC, wrote today that “Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”
Pollster admits hoax
An entity called Wedgewood Polls said yesterday that it published fabricated polling data “to test whether media outlets, aggregators, and commentators would report on data without verifying the source, methodology, or underlying firm legitimacy.” It claimed to be running an experiment on the modern political polling industry.
“Despite having no history, formal credentials, or real data behind the vast majority of our releases, Wedgewood Polling was added to major polling aggregators, including The New York Times, FiftyPlusOne, and VoteHub, and repeatedly treated as a legitimate news source,” the statement said.
Notably, the three polling aggregators mentioned in the statement are not broadcast stations or news networks whose programming is carried on local broadcast stations. That’s relevant because Carr has repeatedly said he merely uses the FCC’s regulatory authority over broadcasters with licenses to use public spectrum, and not media outlets that do not have FCC licenses. Carr’s post yesterday warned broadcasters to “comply with their public interest obligations” under “the terms of their federal licenses.”
While Wedgewood Polls claimed that its data faced no scrutiny from news organizations, FiftyPlusOne said it was preparing to publish an article exposing the fraud and had sent a request for comment to Wedgewood. “They did not respond to our request, but instead posted a public statement on social media admitting that they had been fabricating data,” FiftyPlusOne wrote.
FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and VoteHub all say they did some vetting of Wedgewood before deciding to use its polls. FiftyPlusOne wrote:
Their statement alleges that FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and other poll aggregators did not conduct appropriate vetting of their firm prior to aggregating their polls; this is false. We reached out to them to ask who they were and confirm the methodology statement on their website. We were given two names, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. We were able to independently confirm that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry and reviewed their methodology statement in detail. It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different. Wedgewood operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm, including collecting money from donors to conduct crowd-funded polls, and sharing raw survey data (which we now have confirmed was fraudulent) with FiftyPlusOne on Oct. 15, 2026.
NYT and VoteHub explain poll inclusion
VoteHub Head of Data Science Zachary Donnini said that after talking to Wedgewood’s “head pollster,” Votehub “assigned them a D grade and included their polling data on our site.” Meanwhile, the New York Times updated its polling page with a statement about Wedgewood.
The New York Times said it sends all new pollsters “a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding.” Wedgewood answered the questions, and the NYT used 15 of its polls for state and congressional-district races.
The Wedgewood “polls were never included in the tracker or average of President Trump’s approval rating or of the national polls tracking overall preference for control of Congress,” the NYT said.
In the previous incident this year, a group called Median Strategies admitted it faked poll results as part of a “social experiment.” The NYT said it never included that group’s results in its trackers “because the group did not respond to our questions about its methodology.”
Nate Silver removed Wedgewood from his polling site today. Wedgewood polls tended to be about 1 percentage point more favorable for Democrats than other polls, according to Silver.
