The rising French star whose dad won Rugby World Cup with England
- Published
Accents quickly reveal a lot about a person.
So speaking to Leeds-born Felix Balshaw - the 20-year-old son of England Rugby World Cup winner Iain - it soon becomes clear why he is representing France on his climb up the professional tennis ladder.
There is no mistaking a strong Gallic twang as Balshaw, who celebrated the first ATP Tour victory of his career this week, discusses his journey.
Balshaw was born in West Yorkshire while his father played for Premiership club Leeds Tykes, before the family moved to Biarritz when Iain - an electrifying full-back/wing who scored three tries in England's iconic 2003 campaign - joined the cross-channel exodus to the French Top 14.
The Balshaws have remained in the luxurious Basque coastal city, known for its Belle Epoque architecture, Atlantic seafront casinos and world-class surfing.
"We came down in Biarritz in 2009 and we just loved the place," said Felix, who broke into the world's top 200 last month for the first time.
"I grew up in France and, as each day went by, I felt more and more French.
"Since I've been little, from when I started playing in Tennis Europe juniors, I have always had the French flag by my name."

  - Published12 hours ago
Balshaw pledging allegiance to his adopted country is understandable given the limited contact with his birthland.
Trips back across the English Channel have been "very rare" for the Balshaw children, largely restricted to Christmas family gatherings.
Their maternal grandmother lives in Bath, although Felix has never visited his father's hometown of Blackburn.
But the world number 178 is fully aware his dad will forever be ingrained in the fabric of English sporting history.
The then Bath player scored three tries in the pool stage of England's historic 2003 World Cup campaign, helping secure a 20-17 victory over Australia in the final when he came on as a second-half substitute.
On the eve of the biggest match of his career - facing fellow Frenchman Corentin Moutet in the Lyon Open second round - Felix tried to draw inspiration from watching highlights of his father playing in 2003.
"I just had a massive smile [watching] because I can say 'this is my dad'," he said.
"When he was at Biarritz I was always stood in a little corner in the stands with the rugby gang. It was very, very inspirational to watch him.
"As a father he's tough, but it's always important that he has a lot of experience in rugby, so he's got a lot of stuff to teach me.
"He's always been a great, great part of my life. He's always had my back."
Balshaw started playing tennis at the age of four, but unsurprisingly also had a talent for rugby.
At 13, he needed to make a choice about which sport he wanted to pursue more seriously with the prospect of a professional career looming.
"When I was little, and your father is a rugby champion, of course you always want to follow in his steps and do the same journey as him," Balshaw said.
"But I just felt that rugby was not going to be my sport.
"Tennis, I guess, is more difficult for me than rugby because it's an individual sport, but there was a little more fire in me [playing tennis].
"That meant it was the right choice to choose tennis."
Balshaw is essentially an inverted Arthur Fery - the French-born British number one who became a household name with a stunning run to the Wimbledon semi-finals in July.
The pair actually met for the first time at this week's ATP 250 event in Lyon, where Balshaw beat Portuguese world number 56 Jaime Faria for his maiden win at tour level.
Possessing a Roger Federer-style one-handed backhand, and a Thor-inspired hammer celebration, Balshaw announced his arrival in some style.
Next week Balshaw will rise into the world's top 180, having starting the 2026 season ranked 718th.
His success will no doubt catch the attention of Lawn Tennis Association (LTA) chiefs, who are desperate to increase the pool of British players at the elite level.
Was Balshaw ever approached by the LTA to represent the country of his birth?
And was there ever a conversation with his parents about who he should represent?
"Maybe my parents are hiding stuff and I don't know, but I have never been personally contacted by the LTA," Felix said.
"I think for [my parents] the most important thing is if I'm happy, they'll be happy as well."

The Allahabad High Court directed the Special Task Force (STF) to verify the appointment letters and educational records of all teachers posted in government-run basic schools in Uttar Pradesh that teach students in Classes I to VIII.
According to Live Law, a bench of Justice Vinod Diwakar directed teachers of Classes 1 to 8 to furnish legible copies of their appointment letters and educational documents to the Basic Shiksha Adhikari (BSA) concerned within a week of receipt of the notification issued from the office of the BSA.
These documents include those relating to High School, Intermediate, Graduation, B.Ed./B.T.C. (D.El.Ed., B.El.Ed., etc.), TET/CTET.
The Allahabad High Court passed an order on October 16.
Why did Allahabad HC take this action?
The direction was issued after the court was apprised that a large number of teachers in Uttar Pradesh had obtained employment based on forged documents or by using another person's documents.
The matter came to light when a writ petition was filed before the court by one Kusumlata, seeking a direction to the District Basic Education Officer, Sant Kabir Nagar, to approve her appointment as an Assistant Teacher and release her salary.
As per Live Law, the woman claimed that she was appointed in Siddharth Nagar district on January 2, 2006 and was promoted on July 12, 2010.
However, she was placed under suspension on February 11, 2021, over the allegations that she used forged documents to secure her appointment.
According to the State's counsel, an inquiry initiated against her had found that she had used forged educational documents belonging to another teacher, Kusumlata Srivastava, who is posted at a school in Gorakhpur district, the report added.
On October 8, the court had directed the petitioner to appear before the Additional Superintendent of Police, Special Task Force (STF), Lucknow, on October 12 and 13, along with all her documents and claims.
The court had also directed the STF to inquire into the validity and genuineness of the documents within one week and submit a report to the court.
However, the petitioner did not appear before the STF on either date and also avoided submitting her educational qualifications for verification.
Her counsel claimed on the previous date that she had recently undergone surgery and was on bed rest. However, no one appeared on her behalf when the matter was taken up.
According to the report, the bench was also informed that the Special Task Force (STF) investigation even revealed that a large number of teachers in the State obtained employment by forging documents.
The bench was further apprised that in several instances, 10 or more persons have obtained employment against a single set of educational documents.
The bench referred to an earlier order passed by a coordinate Bench, where directions were issued for action against teachers who had secured appointments by playing fraud upon the authorities, including cancellation of appointments and recovery of salary wherever permissible.
In that case, the court had also directed disciplinary and penal action against officials found to have colluded with, abetted, or deliberately ignored such fraudulent appointments.
Taking into account the state of affairs, the court directed a statewide verification exercise.
While teachers have to submit legible copies of appointment letters and educational documents, they have also been directed to file notarised affidavits disclosing the particulars of specified immediate relatives, whether serving or retired, who have held office in the Uttar Pradesh Education Department at the level of BSA and above.
The specified relatives include spouses, parents, children, in-laws, siblings-in-law and first-degree cousins. Teachers without such relatives must file an undertaking to that effect.
The high court directed BSAs to issue instructions to school headmasters to ensure compliance. Their offices must compile an Excel sheet recording each teacher's name, appointment date, qualifications, the minimum qualification required at the relevant time, and the merit score under the applicable Gazette notification.
The documents and compiled information must be forwarded to the concerned STF Range Office.
The Director of Education will supervise the exercise, while the Additional Director General of Police, STF, will supervise verification and investigation, as per Live Law.
The court also cautioned that any "laxity or dereliction of duty" by the officers concerned would be viewed seriously and that they may be held personally accountable.
The court also linked fraudulent appointments to the deteriorating quality of primary education, observing that the closure of many primary schools due to declining student numbers was not due to a lack of resources alone.
"A teacher should always bear in mind that subject knowledge at the level taught is not the only quality of a good teacher," the court observed.
It highlighted the importance of pedagogic ability, regular attendance, patience and fairness towards children.
It noted that a large number of primary schools have been closed down, principally on account of a shortfall in the number of students.
"That shortfall is not attributable to a want of resources, but to the deteriorating quality of the education imparted and to the inadequate performance of the teachers," it remarked.
The matter has been listed for November 4.

Brazil's Congress's shift to the right could change Latin America's powerhouse. Here’s what to know
Brazil’s elections have shifted Congress further right, regardless of who wins the presidential runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
SAO PAULO -- Brazil’s elections have shifted its Congress to the right regardless of who wins Sunday's presidential runoff between Flávio Bolsonaro and incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Many lawmakers taking office in February 2027 are keen to reshape the nation’s Supreme Court, economy, human rights protections and environmental policies.
If right-wing and centrist lawmakers unite, they will command a simple majority in the 513-seat lower house and could even assemble a supermajority in a broad alliance to change Brazil’s constitution. A similar dynamic is expected in the Senate. Analysts and politicians agree there could be long-lasting impacts in Brazil and in Latin America.
Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won an additional 23 seats in the lower house and nearly doubled its Senate seats, mostly at the expense of centrist parties. Lula's Workers' Party held onto roughly the same number of seats.
Those figures could still change as some lawmakers change parties after their election.
Here is a look at how this right-leaning Congress could reshape Brazil’s agenda.
Bolsonaro’s congressional allies want, above all, to impeach Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who chaired the investigation that put former President Jair Bolsonaro in prison for his attempted coup.
They need 54 votes in the Senate, and many of the future members ran precisely on an impeach de Moraes platform. Brazil’s next president will be able to appoint at least three new justices.
Right-leaning lawmakers have also expressed their wish to curtail individual rulings from Supreme Court justices, who have often suspended laws, issued sweeping injunctions and made high-impact orders without the authorization of the full bench. Some lawmakers also want to discuss term limits for justices.
Even leftist lawmakers support to some of those ideas in the wake of a corruption scandal that ensnared the court.
Many elected lawmakers support Bolsonaro’s hard-line proposals for public security. They want to reduce the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 years of age. Several also support chemical castration as a penalty for convicted rapists and pedophiles.
Some of those lawmakers also want structural shifts in the country’s penal system, drawing inspiration from the mass-incarceration model of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, if Bolsonaro wins and wants to spend funds toward that end.
“Far-right proposals for public security are focused more on addressing people’s fear than on solving the problem. These proposals center on punishment,” said Melina Risso, a research director at think-tank Instituto Igarape.
“Such measures are typical of those who neither understand the problem nor wish to resolve it. What is the point of increasing penalties when only 36% of homicides in the country are solved?”
Many right-wing lawmakers want Brazil to halt public spending, but don't say what will be cut — which is why leftist lawmakers tried to warn voters that welfare initiatives will be their main target, as they were during the Jair Bolsonaro presidency.
Some aligned with Bolsonaro propose lowering corporate taxes and reversing tax code changes set to take effect in January. Lula's administration sees a new value-added tax (VAT) at the moment of every financial transaction as key to prevent fraud. Bolsonaro’s allies say it will suffocate companies — and they’re looking to repeal hundreds of administrative rules, decrees and bureaucratic constraints to lower costs for businesses.
Bolsonaro's bloc also includes strong advocates of privatizing state-owned enterprises who will insist on helping Brazil's powerful agribusinesses by providing more access to rural credit, protecting private land ownership rights and allowing more flexible employment contracts.
A few lawmakers also want more distance from China, Brazil's main trading partner, to side instead with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Many elected lawmakers of Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party have campaigned on loosening environmental licensing requirements, weakening regulatory agencies and giving out amnesties for illegal land grabbing. They say they need to foster economic activity in the Amazon and beyond, so local populations don’t starve. Some of those initiatives depend on the president’s pen, and others can be authorized by Congress.
“Coupled with a denialist government under Flávio Bolsonaro, this could bring environmental chaos,” said Suely Araújo, a public policy coordinator at the nonprofit Climate Observatory.
About 70% of the members of Brazil’s lower house and 80% of the Senate are considered to be hostile to environmental and climate agendas, according to the observatory.
“This scenario points to four years of immense effort for those working on climate and environmental issues, as well as deep concern regarding both serious setbacks and the dire consequences all of this holds for the climate crisis,” Araújo said.
Many right-wing lawmakers are poised to move beyond aggressive social media rhetoric and take concrete legislative action to counter progressive politics, as they promised.
Their efforts focus on dismantling measures supporting transgender populations, particularly by restricting gender-neutral bathroom access and slashing dedicated welfare programs and specialized healthcare services. These lawmakers also intend to secure leadership of congressional commissions to oppose gender-neutral language initiatives and promote a biological definition of womanhood.
New demarcations of Indigenous lands are expected to be frozen, under the argument that reserving territory hinders mining, agricultural expansion, and growth.
State-mandated quotas and identity-based affirmative action frameworks for university admissions and public service jobs will be challenged. Lawmakers plan to advance faith-based legislative agendas to restrict abortion access and reshape civil liberties protections.

Swimmer, 65, killed in shark attack off South Africa's east coast
- Published
A South African woman has been killed in a shark attack off the country's east coast, in what is the first recorded such fatality this year.
Janine Lochrenberg was swimming off a beach in KuGompo City (formerly East London) on Tuesday morning when she was attacked.
Witnesses said the 65-year-old was bitten in two places and died before she was brought to shore.
Shark attacks are rare in South Africa, with about 10 fatal ones since 2012, according to the Florida Museum's International Shark Attack File.
Lochrenberg was out on a daily morning swim with her local open water swimming club when she was attacked at around 08:00 (06:00 GMT). Fellow swimmers brought her to shore, but it's believed she died before they could get her out of the water.
She was bitten on her thigh and her upper arm, one of her fellow swimmers told the BBC. They also said she had been wearing a magnetic shark repellent band on her ankle at the time.
Lochrenberg's sister Margot said she was holding her sister's head as they brought her to shore but believed she bled out in the water.
She told the BBC that her sister had "loved the water so much" despite knowing there was an "elevated shark presence in East London".
"She'd made peace with that. She had a deep affinity with the water and was a remarkable person," she said.
Barbara Briceland, Lochrenberg's partner, told the BBC the retired medical physicist was a good swimmer, who often swam far out into the breakers, and described her as very brave.
"She was highly intelligent, lots of fun, kind, in a quietish way, thoughtful, well-loved with a love of life."
Briceland added they were looking forward to retirement and were about to leave for a three-week road trip together.
Orient Beach, where the attack took place, has been closed alongside another nearby beach, authorities confirmed.

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.
The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.
The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.
The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.
Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.
“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.
The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.
Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.
Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.
The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.
Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.
Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.
The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.
“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”
The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.
“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Sit-ins, mass cease-work mark 3rd day of protest amid Manipur ethnic violence spike
A committee formed in connection with the killing of three Meiteis urged people to observe a day’s mass cease-work
Hundreds of protestors on Thursday staged sit-ins amid a day-long mass cease-work call following two days of street protests in Imphal valley districts against the killing of three Meitei farmers three days earlier amid a spike in ethnic violence in Manipur.
A 45-year-old Kuki man collecting bamboo shoots was killed, and at least six Kuki houses were set ablaze after the three Meiteis were killed in an ambush on Monday. The ambush was the first incident of violence between Meiteis and Kukis after July 13, when armed Kuki groups attacked Meiteis in Bishnupur’s Torbung Bangla. In the last few months, at least 50 people have died in the state, mostly in Naga-Kuki clashes.
A committee formed in connection with the killing of three Meiteis urged people to observe a day’s mass cease-work and stage sit-ins in their respective localities, offices, educational institutions, and marketplaces. Marketplaces, including Khwairamband Ima, opened around 9.30am before businesses were made to shutter.
Shutdowns paralysed much of Manipur on Tuesday and Wednesday when at least six protestors were injured as police dispersed a mob when protestors tried to storm a stadium to meet chief minister Yumnam Khemchand.
Protestors blocked the Imphal-Dimapur national highway at Khurai Lamlong junction. An altercation between security forces and protestors in Khurai Lamlong forced police to fire tear gas, mock bombs, and stun grenades to disperse the crowd and clear the highway. The protesters retaliated with slingshots and threw stones instead of clearing the highway.
The protesters have refused to take the bodies of the three slain Meiteis until all involved in the killing are held. Meitei protesters on Monday left two bodies in front of the main gate of the Chief Minister’s residence to protest the failure to protect civilians after suspected armed Kuki militants carried out the ambush.
Security forces fired tear gas shells to disperse the mob that breached security outside the residence and parked a truck carrying two bodies.
The families of the victims claimed that the attackers belonged to the Kuki community.
The ethnic clashes in Manipur first broke out between the dominant Meitei and tribal Kuki communities in May 2023 and have left at least 360 people dead since 2023. A breakdown of law and order led to the creation of ethnic enclaves, displaced around 55,000 people, and left 49,000 missing.
On May 13, four people, including three church leaders, were killed in a twin ambush in Kangpokpi. On the same day, 48 civilians from the Kuki and Naga communities were taken hostage from both groups.
Two days later, 14 people from each community were released. But 14 Kukis and six Nagas remained in captivity. After 27 days of protest and appeals for unconditional release of the hostages, 14 Kukis were released on June 9. But on June 10, mutilated bodies of six Naga hostages were recovered, fuelling tensions.

India hits back at UN report on migrant rights, calls findings imprecise, unsupported
India challenged a UN migrant rights report over its Assam reference, sourcing and legal claims. It sought accurate country references, clear legal distinctions and child protection grounded in due process.
India has strongly rejected what it called “imprecise and unsupported” references to the country in a report by the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Human Rights of Migrants, questioning its geographical terminology, sourcing and treatment of legal findings.
Delivering India's statement at the Interactive Dialogue with the Special Rapporteur, Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of External Affairs Barkha Tamrakar flagged inaccuracies in the report by Gehad Madi, arguing that unverified allegations and broad policy recommendations should not be presented as established findings of the United Nations.
“India must place on record a serious concern about the report's treatment of law, evidence, and state responsibility,” Tamrakar said. She added that a thematic report must not convert broad policy preferences, unverified allegations or advocacy submissions into settled UN findings.
INDIA QUESTIONS REFERENCE TO 'ASSAN AND NORTHERN INDIA'
Highlighting what she described as a glaring inaccuracy, Tamrakar pointed to paragraph 27, footnote 32, of the report, which states: “For instance, in Assan and Northern India.”
She said this was the complete reference, without identifying any specific case, proceeding, authority, date, law or source.
“Assan is not the name of an Indian state or a recognised jurisdiction. If the intended reference is Assam, the report should say so accurately. Northern India is not a legal or administrative jurisdiction,” she said.
Tamrakar argued that a country-specific allegation could not be made through a typographical error and an unidentified geographical expression. India therefore rejected the reference as “imprecise and unsupported” in its present form.
She added that if the Special Rapporteur intended to refer to citizenship-related processes in Assam, the report should have identified the precise process and distinguished between an allegation, an expert concern, an administrative decision and a judicial finding.
“These are not interchangeable categories,” she said.
India also expects country-specific assertions to be properly sourced and to respect the concerned state's opportunity to respond, Tamrakar said.
INDIA CHALLENGES REPORT'S INTERPRETATION OF CHILD RIGHTS
Tamrakar also addressed the report's treatment of children's rights, noting that India is a state party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child and supports Articles 3, 9 and 10 in their proper context.
Article 3 requires the best interests of the child to be a primary consideration. However, Tamrakar argued that this does not make that consideration the only factor in every case or automatically override lawful decisions relating to public order, border management, criminal conduct, nationality or immigration status.
“India cannot accept the report's categorical propositions as though they were universally binding legal treaty rules,” she said.
India supports humane and lawful migration governance but does not agree that irregular migration should be treated solely as a matter of vulnerability, without recognising that it can also constitute a breach of immigration law.
INDIA CALLS FOR THREE CORRECTIONS
Outlining India's position, Tamrakar called for three key corrections in the treatment of migration and child protection in the report.
First, country references must be accurate, specific and verifiable.
Second, recommendations must be clearly distinguished from binding treaty obligations and the policy preferences of an independent mandate holder.
Third, the protection of children must be advanced through due process, family-sensitive procedures, cooperation between states and child protection authorities, and safe and regular migration pathways. Such protection, she said, should not come at the cost of denying legitimate state functions or relying on generalised allegations.
Tamrakar said India would continue to engage constructively with the United Nations and other states on these objectives.
She stressed that cooperation is strengthened by accuracy and that human rights advocacy is strengthened, rather than weakened, when it is grounded in verifiable facts, applicable law and respect for the sovereign equality of states.

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said if the opposition brings any fresh impeachment motion against the country's top poll officer, it will be examined according to rules and procedures.
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum after The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.
If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.

Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.
But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.
It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.
GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.
GM also says it will use AI to speed up new-vehicle development, eventually cutting its four- to five-year development time in half—the speed at which Chinese carmakers create new vehicles today.
The automaker plans to expand its “eyes-off” highway driving technology to its most popular cars, inching closer to its years-old promise of making a personal self-driving car. It previously said the system was coming to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. Today, the company’s Super Cruise feature lets drivers take their hands off their steering wheels on hundreds of thousands of miles of pre-mapped highways. Reaching true autonomy will take time, but GM isn’t ready to talk about that publicly. “This industry is rife with promises that were not fulfilled. I am not keen on making them,” Anderson says.
But GM is taking a different approach from, say, Tesla. The electric carmaker sells a driver-assistance feature called “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” that can navigate many highways and local roads but requires drivers to stay alert and ready to take over at any moment. That kind of system “presents the illusion of autonomy without its benefits,” Anderson says, who for a time led Tesla’s Autopilot program. If drivers can’t do other things while their car is doing most of the driving, it’s less useful and “comes with the direct expense of the safety of your vehicle and the people around you,” he says. “That would not be a responsible way to operate.”
GM’s method, by contrast, is to slowly expand “eyes-off” capabilities to more sorts of roads, letting drivers text or eat or watch YouTube first on some highways, and then on more highways, and then on local roads, and then maybe everywhere.
That’s when the automaker's vision gets bigger and blurrier. The cabin, the company says in a blog post, can become a space to “relax, work, and unwind. … In time, this will pave the way for a future where your car can take on everyday errands,” the company says. The personal self-driving car will pick up groceries, drop off children, and then maybe even find a parking spot at the end.
Urban planners and infrastructure experts have worried about this vision. If you lower the price of a car trip, in money and time spent driving, won’t everyone send their cars out for every task? Won’t the roads be crowded with pods full of people sleeping, emailing, and YouTubing while their vehicles slowly pilot them onward—or worse, cars with no one in them? Won’t cities become sprawlier?
Anderson says yes. If you have cheap, personal driving robots, “you will very likely incur more of those robots on the roads. And so there's a lot of societal and infrastructural considerations to make here,” he says. But he argues we have time, and that cities take time to sprawl. “I wouldn't call this an imminent thing, but it certainly is something we should be thinking about.”

It's a little hard to review the iPhone Duo. I've been toting Apple's first folding smartphone for the past week, and several apps I've tried to open on the sprawling 7.6-inch screen look awful. Thick, black bars on the sides, with a phone-sized app in the middle of this tablet-like display. But you likely won't encounter this problem once the Duo is in your hands.
In the past day, a handful of apps I use regularly updated to add full support for the iPhone Duo's screen sizes and vertical user interface elements. Instagram, Threads, Slack, and even the Google app now have navigational icons on the right rail instead of the bottom center, and the app content is better laid out to make use of the larger screen.
Developers need to target the iOS 27.1 software development kit (SDK) for full Duo compatibility. That will take some time. But it is a little maddening that some app developers, who for years have never seemed to care about optimizing their app for Android folding phones, are so quick to embrace Apple’s fold. Slack, for example, never offered the two-pane view of its desktop app in the Android version, but it's on the Duo. C’est la vie. Hopefully, Apple’s entry into foldables will result in a “rising tide lifts all boats” situation and Android fold lovers will get to enjoy those optimizations.
In Duo Time
The iPhone Duo's Standby mode turns on when the phone is propped up via a kickstand.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
The iPhone Duo arrives seven years after Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold. In Apple tradition, its first entry into an existing category feels fully mature; the Duo has significantly less jank than the first few generations of its Android counterparts. The infamous crease—where the phone folds—is hardly visible thanks to Apple’s display stack and clever use of a matte-finish nanotexture screen. The phone is IP68 dust- and water-resistant (though avoid taking the Duo to the beach, as sand is notoriously detrimental to phone hinges). The software experience, barring the unoptimized apps, feels carefully considered.
Apple has also landed on the right shape, months after Samsung realized it following seven years of narrow, somewhat awkward book-like folds. The wider, shorter “passport” design feels better than what’s come before in this category. The 5.4-inch outer screen is still big enough to be useful, and the hinge glides open gracefully and stays put at various angles. The hardware feels polished.
That’s not to say Apple has completely trounced the competition. I still appreciate that Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold8 is super lightweight at 201 grams, as the iPhone Duo’s hefty 254 grams (heavier than an iPhone 18 Pro Max) can get tiring after extended doomscrolling. I don’t love the fact that, when closed, one side of the Duo has angled corners and the other is curved—the Fold8 looks better in that regard. Touch ID also takes a little getting used to after years of relying on Face ID, mostly when you’re holding the Duo with your left hand and you suddenly have to authenticate an app or purchase with your right hand. (It can mercifully auto-unlock if you're wearing an Apple Watch.)
Apple also tightly controls the multitasking experience. If you have two apps split-screen on the Duo, Apple won't let you resize one app to be slightly bigger than the other like you can on Android. Here, a 50-50 split is always enforced. You can't add a floating third app when in split-screen either, even though Apple has offered a similar capability on iPads for years. (The exception is video apps—you can have them float in picture-in-picture mode.) In portrait orientation, you can split-screen only with a video app; Apple won’t let you stack two apps, something Android has enabled for years.
That rigid software philosophy extends to basic input handling, too. I am typing this review on the iPhone Duo using a compact folding keyboard with a tiny attached trackpad. The trackpad works OK, but I could only get it to work after turning on AssistiveTouch in iOS’ accessibility settings. If the Duo is the iPhone that lets you do more, Apple should natively enable cursor support just like it does on iPads.
Then there are the physical quirks. The Duo supports MagSafe, so you can magnetically stick the phone to MagSafe tripods, mounts, and the like. (When it’s open, the Duo's weight makes the phone sag to one side.) But what about MagSafe wallets? They’ll work, but Apple’s official wallet sticks out past the phone’s lower edge—not what you’d expect from a company that pores over every detail. Apple doesn’t have an official solution, so you’ll have to rely on a third-party accessory (and I suspect there will be many Duo accessories).
The iPhone maker follows the industry standard with a dual rear-camera system, lacking the third zoom camera from its Pro iPhones, which I sorely miss. At least the selfie cameras—the one on the outer screen and the “hidden” under-display inner camera seem to produce good results. On a Zoom call, my editor remarked that the video quality looked “really good” with both selfie shooters. (Zoom, by the way, wasn't optimized.)
Dynamic Duo
When an app is properly optimized, the experience is chef’s kiss. Multi-pane views let you see a lot more in an app than candy-bar phones, a boost to productivity. Split-screening two optimized apps looks excellent, with plenty of room for each app to breathe and let you multitask. I haven’t found myself putting the Duo in angled positions much, mostly because I’ve really enjoyed using it with Apple’s Folio With Kickstand case, so much so that I wish the kickstand were integrated into the phone itself; I strongly recommend investing in an accessory to prop the Duo up.
Battery life has been pretty great. With average use, I’ve ended most days with around 40 percent left by bedtime. Right now, with over six hours of screen-on time because I’ve been working off the Duo for most of the workday, it’s almost 6 pm, and I’m at 45 percent. Impressive.
Duo Preview lets the photo subject see themselves in the frame.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
The dual rear cameras are reliable, too. You don’t get the fun variable-aperture wizardry of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera, but after comparing photos I’ve captured on both devices, the results aren’t drastically different. That brings us to the features I think will help bring folding phones into mainstream appeal—Smart Take and Duo Preview.
The latter is a staple of folding phones, letting you show the camera’s viewfinder to the photo subject—good news for anyone who has ever complained about their Instagram husband. Now you can make sure they’re angling the camera just right before hitting the shutter button. You can also take better-quality selfies with the rear camera yourself— open the camera app on the larger screen and flip the phone; you’ll get an option to view the camera controls on the outer screen, letting you see a live preview while snapping with the superior 48-megapixel cameras.
Smart Take is similar to Google’s Magic Capture. Set the phone down in a partially folded shape (so it looks like a tiny laptop) and tap the shutter button. The camera will then wait for you to get into position and snap a series of photos when it thinks you’re posing. You can forget about asking someone to take a picture for you. It’s not as smart as the Pixel feature—I ended up deleting a bunch of awkward Smart Take photos—but it’s convenient.
I’m sure Kids Cue will be popular too. I don’t have a kid, so I couldn't vet how well it works, but it loops cute Snoopy animations on the outer display to capture a child's attention and make them smile. Google and Samsung have similar versions on their folding phones, but neither has Snoopy—a big win for Apple.
The nanotexture finish on the inner screen is the star of the show. The matte surface reduces the crease's visibility, while also minimizing glare and reflections. It also feels like e-paper, which I imagine will be very welcome when Apple Pencil support is added later this year (via a software update). Writing on a screen always feels better when the screen isn’t entirely smooth.
You don’t get the crisp video quality, deep blacks, and sharp contrast of the iPhone 18 Pro when watching movies and shows on apps like Netflix on the nanotexture panel. However, colors are still just as vibrant, and the experience is very similar. I didn’t have any issues with screen brightness—the Duo gets up to 3,000 nits at peak outdoor brightness—even with the textured finish, though off-axis viewing isn’t great in direct sunlight.
Much of my time this past week has been thinking about wasted space. Sometimes I questioned Apple’s decision to move all the navigation elements of iOS to the right rail—there’s so much wasted space in some apps! Then I use an app that uses all that space, and I’m content. That’s probably my takeaway. If you want to try Apple’s first folding phone, wait a few months for developers to optimize their apps. (It might actually help that the phone is backordered until January.) Waiting might help in other ways too—Apple plans to add Reachability later this year for the Duo, letting folks with small hands more easily access the left or right edges of the screen with a tap.
You'll likely spend most of your time on the outer screen of the Duo.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
This is often the case with first-generation products, but it may be prudent to wait for the Duo 2—not because there are glaring issues here, but I suspect Apple may tackle the weight problem with the next version, just as Samsung did on its latest iteration.
Folding phones will never be for everyone. Some people do not care for the bigger screen. Others have durability concerns, and a device with more moving parts will never be as repairable or robust as its single-slab counterpart. Price is a barrier for others—but on that note, the Duo is surprisingly on par with its competitors (though still expensive).
But the folding category is here to stay. I know people who swear by the fold and won’t buy anything else. I’m starting to convert, especially with the newer passport-style shape. Now if only someone could figure out how to put a real zoom camera on there.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.

Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
- Published
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.
They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.
When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.
What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.
"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."
As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."
By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.
Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.
Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.
The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.
Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.
The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.
Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.
The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.
The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.
Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.
We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.
"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."
Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.
"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."
Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.
Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."
As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.
There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.
That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.
"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.
"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."
A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.
Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.
The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.
"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."
They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.
"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."
She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.
Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.
As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.
So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping.
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.
On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.
In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”
In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.
“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”
