Daler Mehndi row: CM Dhami speaks to Mika Singh, says misunderstanding can be resolved
Pushkar Singh Dhami spoke to Mika Singh after Subodh Uniyal publicly reprimanded Daler Mehndi during a performance. The chief minister urged an amicable resolution as calls mounted for the minister to apologise.
Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Thursday spoke to singer Mika Singh over the controversy surrounding state minister Subodh Uniyal's public reprimand of Daler Mehndi during a performance, saying any misunderstanding could be resolved through dialogue.
Dhami said he had spoken to Mika, Daler Mehndi's brother, and stressed that the matter should be settled amicably. Mika had earlier demanded an apology from Uniyal and urged the chief minister to intervene.
In a post on X, Dhami said, “Today, I had a telephonic conversation with the renowned singer Mika Singh. While discussing matters concerning Daler Mehndi, I emphasised that any misunderstandings should be resolved through mutual dialogue and cordiality.”
He added that Uttarakhand, known as Devbhoomi, upheld the tradition of Atithi Devo Bhava, or treating guests as divine, and that artists were always welcomed and respected in the state.
Earlier, speaking at a press conference in Dehradun, Dhami said he would also speak to Daler Mehndi and described both singers as his friends. He suggested that Uniyal might have been under pressure from the audience during the incident.
“I believe the minister must have been under pressure from the public at that time. The minister himself has stated that he was unaware that Daler Mehndi was unwell,” Dhami said.
WHAT HAPPENED AT KUNJAPURI FAIR?
The controversy erupted on Sunday night when Uniyal went on stage during Daler Mehndi's performance at the Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair in Narendra Nagar, in the New Tehri area.
A video of the incident, which went viral on social media, showed the minister questioning the singer's condition and asking whether he was drunk because he appeared unable to speak properly. Mehndi, 59, was heard apologising.
The incident drew criticism from several members of the entertainment industry, who backed the singer and called for artists to be treated with dignity and respect.
Mika Singh, in a post on Thursday, said Uniyal should apologise to his brother. He also said Mehndi had agreed to perform at the event after another singer, Sunanda Sharma, fell ill.
Mika said it was painful to see his brother being accused of being drunk while performing on stage. He appealed to Dhami to intervene, adding that artists deserved dignity and respect.
MINISTER SAYS HE THOUGHT SINGER WAS UNDER INFLUENCE
Uniyal, who faced criticism over his conduct, said on Wednesday that Mehndi should have informed the organisers in advance that he was unwell and should not have come to perform.
Speaking to PTI, the minister said he had expected the singer to perform at the fair but felt that Mehndi was lip-syncing rather than singing live. As a local representative associated with the organising committee, he said he felt pressure from people who wanted the matter questioned.
Uniyal also claimed that Mehndi appeared unable to speak or walk properly, leading him to suspect that the singer was under the influence of a substance. He acknowledged, however, that no medical examination had been conducted.
The minister said he later learnt that Mehndi had been unable to speak because he was unwell.
Dhami's intervention comes amid calls for Uniyal to apologise, with the chief minister urging both sides to resolve the dispute through dialogue.

After moving to West Virginia last year, Steve Kuo signed up for a new insurance plan that would cost him $500 a month. But there was one upside: He knew he was entitled to a free preventive visit. He wanted to take advantage of it, so he made an appointment at a clinic near his new home.
You’re supposed to get one free doctor’s visit every year. So why are so many Americans being charged?
Why Americans are fed up with “preventive” doctor visits.
But then when he got there, they asked about his medical history and he mentioned prior kidney problems. When he received a bill a few weeks later, he had been charged twice for the same appointment: Once as that free preventive visit, once as an “office sick visit” because of the kidney conversation. He was flummoxed — and very annoyed, as he shared on social media. “No copayment means no copayment, exactly as stated in the insurance guidelines,” Kuo told me over email. “What is written and agreed upon should be honored.”
He is far from alone. On Reddit, I easily found more than a dozen examples in just the past year of people getting a surprise bill for what they thought was going to be a free visit.
One woman posted a nearly $1,000 bill she’d received for what she thought was going to be a preventive gynecology visit. Another woman said that she ended up facing roughly $3,000 bills because she was given an ultrasound (which she said she didn’t request) at a preventive visit, and then her blood draw was sent to an out-of-network lab. Another person lamented that they had been billed $170 for an office visit because they had briefly mentioned back stiffness.
It’s not supposed to be like this. Americans don’t get much when it comes to our healthcare, but most of us are supposed to be entitled to at least one thing: Once every year, no matter your health insurance, you can go to the doctor with the goal of preventing future health problems by discussing important vaccinations, cancer screenings, and cardiovascular health screenings. The Affordable Care Act made that the law in 2010.
But more than 15 years later, people all over the country are walking into their doctor’s office, thinking they’re entitled to that one free visit every year, and walking out being billed for a sick visit, blood labs, and more. Researchers estimate that Americans spend tens of millions, maybe hundreds of millions of dollars every year on services that are supposed to be free under the ACA.
Dr. Yalda Jabbarpour, a family physician in the Washington, DC, area and medical director of the Robert Graham Center for Policy Studies, told me she still deals all the time with people’s confusion about what a preventive visit really means.
“Every single time I’m in the clinic, this issue comes up with a patient. And it’s sad that it comes up,” Jabbarpour told me. “In my mind, the blame is not to be put on the patient. The blame is not to be put on the physician. Really, this points to a bigger system issue that we need to solve.”
How could a seemingly simple promise of one free annual doctor’s visit result in a situation so convoluted that patients and doctors are still struggling with it nearly two decades later? And how might we fix it?
Patients are getting surprise bills from their doctors — and they’re pissed off
The goal of the ACA was to expand coverage and make sure health insurance would be comprehensive to actually help people stay healthy. As part of that project, the authors of the law added a mandate for insurers to cover those services, including an annual wellness exam. The problem is, they did not define what the parameters of that preventive visit actually were, said Alex Hoagland, a healthcare economist at the University of Toronto.
“It didn’t establish a clear definition of…all the diagnosis codes and procedure codes and how frequently you get that combination within a year,” he said. “They don’t define what actually is preventive care and what’s not.”
Do’s and don’t’s for a preventive visit:
- Topics that should be free to talk about: routine vaccinations, many cancer screenings, screenings for diabetes and cardiovascular health, contraception.
- Topics that could lead to you getting charged: chronic pain, prior medical problems, other physical and mental health symptoms (including depression).
- If you are a first-time visitor at a doctor’s office, you may also be charged a “new patient” fee.
That has left each insurer to define a preventive visit on their own — and that’s where the perverse incentives that leave patients in a lurch begin. Preventive visits are supposed to be reserved strictly for screenings and talking about other preventive measures you can take to protect your long-term health, but you may get billed for an “office visit” or a “sick visit” if you talk about any specific symptom you’re experiencing, the same as if you had come in because you had the flu.
Health insurers have an incentive to keep the definition of preventive care as narrow as possible, so they have to pay fewer claims without any contribution from the patient. At the same time, doctors want to be paid for the actual services that they are providing. If somebody does bring up a bigger health problem during a preventive visit, then the doctor reasonably wants to be paid accordingly.
“I know, particularly in the healthcare space, it’s really popular to blame one party or another, and here I don’t think it’s a matter of corporate greed or physician incompetence or whatever,” Hoagland said. “It’s just a natural mismatch of incentives.”
So the reality is that “one free doctor’s visit” sounds straightforward, but, in practice, it’s much more complicated. You as the patient might think of it as one visit, but in our fee-for-service healthcare system, where providers bill based on each specific thing they do, it’s not. The conversation about your vaccination may be free — but asking about your back pain is not. If you get blood tests ordered, that’s another line item. The list goes on. “It’s not like you walk into a doctor’s office and it’s just one thing that happens, right?” said Sabrina Corlette, co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University. “It’s multiple different things that are happening when you go into a doctor’s office.”
Part of the problem may be that it’s one free visit. We Americans are consumers at heart: Tell us we’re going to get something for free and we want to take advantage of it. But having just one free visit may also lead to people bringing a laundry list of questions to that preventive visit, because they think of it as their only chance to ask everything of their doctor.
That makes it easy for the discussion to tip over into a sick visit — and not only does that lead to a surprise bill, it can also crowd out the conversation about prevention that the visit is supposed to be focused on.
“What ends up happening a lot…is that a patient comes in for their annual visit, and in their mind, that is their time to bring up every single thing that’s been happening during the year, because they see it as the free visit to bring up everything that’s happened during the year. For some patients, that takes up the entire visit,” Jabbarpour told me. “They leave, and it’s like, ‘Oh my god, we forgot to do all the screening things: the vaccinations, the cancer screenings, and the cardiovascular risk screening.’ And then something happens down the line because you never address those screenings.”
A 2021 study by Hoagland and Paul Shafer, both of Boston University at the time, estimated that Americans with employer-sponsored insurance had in 2018 alone paid between $75 million and $219 million in medical bills that should have been free. They were more likely to be charged for things like contraception or cholesterol and diabetes screenings, with individuals sometimes paying hundreds of dollars for those services.
Hoagland told me he had been billed for preventive visits because he has type 1 diabetes and the system automatically categorized his appointment as a diabetic visit. Earlier this year, he co-authored a study that found people with chronic conditions were more likely to be charged for preventive care. Corlette said that she too had recently been charged for what was supposed to be a preventive visit after she mentioned an issue as an aside. And these are folks who study health care for a living.
“It was literally maybe a 10-second conversation where I would ask the doctor a question about something,” she said. “And that triggered it.”
Colonoscopies are another dramatic example of how this issue plays out in real life; Corlette told me the procedure was one of the first services where this fuzzy line between prevention and treatment under the ACA became obvious. People go under for what is supposed to be a preventive colonoscopy. But then their doctor finds a polyp and decides to remove it — good clinical practice, but as a result, their patient could end up being charged thousands of dollars because the colonoscopy was no longer preventive once that polyp was snipped.
“All of a sudden, that would trigger what the patient thought was a preventive service into a cost-sharing obligation,” Corlette said. “Colonoscopies can be thousands of dollars. That was when we were first like, ‘Oh, yeah, this is a more complicated area than I think the lawmakers that drafted this provision originally envisioned.’”
How the US could fix our preventive visit headaches
The ACA’s preventive visit promise was clearly well-intentioned and it’s worth remembering that, if you look in the aggregate, more Americans are getting more free preventive care than they did before the law was passed. The problem, as much as anything, is expectations: People think they’re entitled to a free visit and are understandably frustrated when they get billed for it.
“The difference is before the Affordable Care Act, maybe they anticipated some kind of cost-sharing,” Hoagland said. “But after, they expect it to be free.”
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here.
It doesn’t have to be this way. Corlette’s team at Georgetown University recently released a proposal that Americans be entitled to three primary care and two urgent care visits every year with no cost-sharing. This approach has two virtues, she told me: It will help people feel like they are actually getting value from their insurance — the very complaint that Steve Kuo raised — and, because we know primary care helps prevent problems down the road, it should also improve people’s health in the long term. Take the pressure off that one free visit and let people see the doctor a few times a year without worrying about being charged.
“In employer-based insurance, a lot of people feel like, ‘What the hell am I getting for my premium each month?’” Corlette said. “We wanted people to feel like they’re getting good value, and we wanted to get to better population health.”
Hoagland also endorsed the idea of at least one free physician’s visit every year, no matter what’s discussed. In the long term, Jabbarpour said she’d like to see copays eliminated entirely for primary care.
But any payment reforms are not going to happen immediately. What can we do right now?
For one, doctor offices could make an effort to be as transparent as possible. Jabbarpour’s MedStar system has started calling people a couple of days before their appointment with a brief script that tells the patient that they could be charged if the conversation with their doctor touches on additional medical problems. If your doctor’s office doesn’t proactively bring it up, ask when you schedule your appointment or when they call you to confirm it. Worst-case scenario, ask your provider what they consider preventive care when your visit begins. You might also want to educate yourself on what services are generally considered preventive and should be available for free: Your insurer may make that information available on their website, or KFF has a database you can peruse.
It’s not a perfect solution. “What ends up happening is patients come in, and they say, ‘I know I’m not supposed to talk to you about anything else, so I’m not going to tell you about anything else.’ And you don’t want that to happen,” Jabbarpour said. You should ask your doctor directly: What do you consider to be preventive care? Establish boundaries at the start. That way, you can at least be aware if you are going to get charged because the conversation crossed the line to discussing an active health problem.
And if you want to see the underlying laws change, start organizing. Contact your state and federal reps and ask them what they are doing to ensure this stops happening. Things could be different: Jabbarpour said she hopes to one day work in a health system where the cost of a single primary care visit isn’t so high-stakes, where doctors and their patients can manage their health according to their particular needs, rather than worry about how to bill for one specific conversation that covers the whole range of somebody’s health — like primary care is supposed to do.
“I think some patients can be managed by seeing us once every year, once every two years, and some patients need to see us monthly,” Jabbarpour told me. “To put all patients in the same box and say you can only see your primary care physician once a year if you want it paid for, it makes zero sense.”

In November 2009, I joined 10 other economists in a letter urging Congress to pass a bill that became the Affordable Care Act. I could hardly imagine what would come next.
The ACA promised to expand coverage, and it did. But I signed the letter primarily because the ACA promised to “bend the cost curve” of American health care, which was getting out of control. A 2010 Institute of Medicine report found $750–$765 billion in wasteful health spending in 2009, roughly 30 cents of every health care dollar.
Today, similar analyses find up to $1.6 trillion in wasteful spending annually. That is still roughly 30 cents of every health care dollar.
The curve did not bend, and I now wish I hadn’t signed my name to that letter.
I, and many of my economist colleagues, didn’t foresee how many of the ACA’s cost-control and financing provisions would be stripped out by Congress, on a bipartisan basis, or watered down over the following decade.
The Independent Payment Advisory Board, which was supposed to force automatic Medicare cuts if spending exceeded target growth rates, was repealed in 2018 without ever becoming operational.
The “Cadillac tax” — an important way to discourage excessively generous insurance and a reform I vigorously supported — was repeatedly delayed and ultimately repealed in 2019.
As lawmakers chipped away at the ACA, the political push to find new ways to spend health care dollars more wisely seemingly began to flag. Efforts to move health care away from fee-for-service models and to encourage greater efficiencies had mixed results at best.
But the big mistake, ironically, was the ACA’s lack of focus on affordability. The ACA did nothing to slow — and indeed likely accelerated — the trend toward consolidation in health care, which drove prices higher. The ACA’s design and compliance costs favored large insurance carriers, and the ACA exchanges’ narrow-network model gave insurers reason to bulk up for negotiating leverage against providers. The ACA goal of improving care coordination helped hospitals justify stepped-up mergers and acquisitions of physician practices, thereby strengthening market power.
As costs kept climbing, many health economists were reluctant to probe the wasteful spending that accompanied the consolidation frenzy. This work was chilled by the ascendent political viewpoint that attempts to rationalize expensive end-of-life care would result in “death panels” — a term effectively coined and leveraged by former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin (R).
It embodied a distrust of government involvement in medicine and a suspicion that experts would value some lives more highly than others. But that is already what we do. Some medical treatments are more valuable than others. I wrote a New York Times opinion piece in 2009 titled “I am a Death Panelist. I Am Not the Problem.” That essay has aged better than my letter to Congress. In it, I argued that cost containment efforts must prioritize high-value, life-improving treatments over endless, ineffective interventions.
Seventeen years and trillions of dollars later, that idea has never been more important.
Health care reform proposals like “Medicare for All” are doomed to fail if we can’t contain costs. The current administration’s focus on rooting out fraud is a good start. But more needs to be done. Armed with new tools to better measure what patients want and identify valuable innovation, we can discourage the 30% of care that does no good without heavy-handed government interventions such as rationing or price controls.
The USC Schaeffer Center for Health Policy & Economics and the Aspen Institute jointly recommended in 2021 that Congress establish an independent Institute of Health Technology Assessment. The institute would bring together leading scientists, economists, physicians, and, importantly, patients to evaluate new and existing evidence on the effectiveness and value of devices, medicines, procedures, and other innovations that end up on a medical bill. The idea would be to equip all parties, from payers to providers to patients, with insights into effectiveness, cost, and value. The independent, publicly funded institute should be set up without regulatory authority — for instance, it cannot set prices — but in a way that can nevertheless influence private and public decisions about clinical care.
The ACA also came up short here. It set up the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute (PCORI), which has awarded more than $5 billion to support over 2,600 research studies and projects across the United States. One study showed that antibiotics could prevent half of all appendectomies, resulting in an estimated 27,410 fewer surgeries over five years.
Unfortunately, in the wake of the death panel debate, Congress was so fearful that PCORI could be used to ration care that it prohibited the institute from conducting formal cost-effectiveness analyses. It cannot try to quantify health benefits or rank treatments on a “cost-per-dollar” basis.
That restriction starkly illustrates the challenges that continue to bedevil the movement to put value at the center of health care policy. We are unlikely to get control of costs unless we can see what procedures and technologies are worth to patients and society in dollars over time.
I stopped endorsing legislation after the ACA passed. But if anyone introduces a bill to establish an Institute of Heath Technology Assessment, or to unleash PCORI to do cost-benefit analysis, I’m ready to sign.
Dana Goldman is the founding director of the USC Schaeffer Institute for Public Policy and Government Service.

Nigeria confirms an Ebola case in Abuja as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive
LAGOS, Nigeria — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.
Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. "We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had," he said.
Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the latest outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections.
Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that "we are facing an extremely serious threat," with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
"This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa," he said.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country's preparedness for a potential outbreak.
"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers," the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola task force in June following the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.
"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,000 people and killed more than 4,300 people.
The latest outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said. Nigeria was one of the countries affected, recording 20 cases before it was declared over in the country after three months.

I was reporting on the ground near Connaught Place, close to Rajiv Chowk metro station, when Delhi Police detained me and several other journalists at around 11:20 am on October 10, 2026.
Delhi Police and central security forces had cordoned off the area around Jantar Mantar, preventing protesters and journalists from approaching the designated protest site. I was filming the police action and speaking to people present at the scene when officers began pushing and shoving individuals standing at the intersection of Connaught Place and Kharak Singh Marg. Several people were holding placards to express their dissent when police arrived and began detaining them.
While I filmed the detentions, one officer thrust his hand towards me and attempted to grab me. I showed him my press card. He backed off but continued gesturing aggressively. On camera, I asked him what legal guideline or constitutional provision allowed him to detain or attempt to assault a journalist on duty. He became enraged, and a heated exchange followed. The police then detained several journalists, including me.
We were shoved into a bus and driven across the national capital. When we repeatedly asked the officers which legal procedure they were following to detain us, they did not respond. They also refused to tell us where we were being taken.
The journey lasted around two hours. We travelled along Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, crossed the Yamuna, passed Shahdara flyover and Burari, and eventually reached the Delhi-Karnal highway. We became increasingly concerned about our destination. At 8 am, when I had begun reporting on the ground, I had noticed several police vehicles bearing HR and UP number plates. Our apprehensions grew as the bus continued along the Karnal expressway for another 20 minutes or so.
During the two-hour journey from Connaught Place towards neighbouring Haryana, we were not provided with sufficient drinking water or other basic necessities in the scorching heat. We managed to get some water only when a truck driver passed his bottle through the bus window. However, packed food, including bananas, biscuits and kachori, were already available on the bus.
Around 2 pm, we arrived at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium in Bawana, Delhi, approximately 65 km from Connaught Place. The stadium had been converted into a detention centre, where around 100 people detained from different parts of Delhi were being held.
I began documenting the situation inside the detention centre, speaking to detainees and trying to understand the circumstances in an area that had been without internet connectivity since the previous night.
A Cockroach Janta Party coordinator, reportedly picked up from his residence in Burari around 3 am on October 10, described his experience to me. “No food, no proper water, and a contingent of police officials who were not cooperating with anything since I was detained,” he said.
The stadium, usually filled with the sounds of athletes and cheering fans, now echoed with protesters’ slogans. “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chor” (The vote thief needs to resign) rang out across the premises.
A few minutes later, another bus brought in a group of protesters. They alleged that the police had shoved them into the bus and assaulted them. Despite this, they continued raising slogans against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the BJP-led Union government. Those detained included supporters and activists of the Muslim Students’ Federation (MSF), the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), and leaders of the Communist Party of India (Marxist).
CPI(M) leaders Sujan Chakraborty and Manik Sarkar, the former chief minister of Tripura, were also at the detention centre, along with several other leaders from across the country. Sudip Dutta, general secretary of the Centre for Indian Trade Unions (CITU), a prominent national trade union affiliated with the CPI(M), had also been detained and brought to the stadium.
I spoke to a student from Delhi about how they intended to pursue their demands. Aman, an AISF member, said voter deletions and irregularities in Form 6 could affect future generations of voters.
“See, this issue of voter deletions is going to impact the upcoming generations who are going to vote tomorrow. As college students, it is our responsibility to make our peers aware about these issues. After today, we would hit the classrooms, reach out to our friends and make them aware of how this issue of ‘vote Chori’ that has come to light is going to impact them and the generations to come,” he said.
Another student, Ali, spoke about police brutality and the use of central security personnel to curb the right to protest.
“We were picked up from Minto Road. The police had barricaded the entire area. Around ten police officers were charging at a single protester, and dragging them to the police van. CRPF, BSP, ITBP, CISF, and even Uttar Pradesh Police are on duty. Why is the government acting like this to curb the voices of the students,” he said.
I spent another hour documenting events at Rajiv Gandhi Stadium, where protesters continued raising slogans despite being detained. Around 3:30 pm, after repeated negotiations with police officers, I was released along with another journalist.
As we left the premises, we were asked to provide our personal details. When we identified ourselves as journalists, several officers appeared astonished and initially thought we were lying. They believed us only after we showed our press cards.
The exchange lasted around ten minutes. It became clear that the officers at the detention centre had received no instructions or communication informing them that journalists were also being detained.
During the four to five hours I spent under detention, the same ort of resentment came up in every conversation: Allegations, an investigation and protests against Gyanesh Kumar had prompted the Union government to take preventive measures in the name of maintaining law and order. These measures were so extensive that people seeking reforms to Indian democracy were being detained. The scale of the restrictions was equally alarming.
Metro services, railway stations, roads and shops in parts of Delhi were directed to be shut down, affecting daily commuters, roadside hawkers and shopkeepers. Internet services were also suspended within a four-kilometre radius of the Janpath-Kartavya Path area and in and around makeshift detention centres across Delhi. Internet connectivity was suspended in the area surrounding Rajiv Gandhi Stadium as well.
A shopkeeper in Bawana, near the stadium, told me that the internet shutdown had caused significant losses because customers could not make online payments. The preventive measures affected not only protesters but also ordinary people, disrupting the lives of commuters, daily-wage labourers, shopkeepers, railway platform-based workers, auto drivers and others going about their daily routines.
Why was Delhi being subjected to what resembled a state of emergency?
Article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution guarantees individuals the right to express their opinions and protest, subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions and the rights of others. The government can also take measures to maintain law and order. But how far can such measures legally and constitutionally extend?
I continued to think about these questions as I travelled to Samaypur Badli metro station, approximately 17 km from the detention centre. The 30-minute journey offered no concrete answers.

- There is no evidence that a legitimate trans rights advocacy group sent mailers to Texas homes, purportedly sharing resources for transgender and LGBTQ+ minors with unsupportive families.
- Credible reports indicate that pamphlets with resources for trans minors were sent en masse to Texas families. However, public business records indicate the return sender listed on the envelopes these flyers came in — the "Texas Transgender Student Union" — is based at an address in Wyoming, not Texas. That address is known for its ties to scam operations and shell companies.
- The main organization promoted within the pamphlets, the Transgender Education Network of Texas, is a legitimate advocacy group that has denied all involvement with the mailers and said the messaging within them does "not represent the official position or communications of the organization."
- Wyoming allows business creators to be anonymous, so the name of the person who is actually behind these flyers is not known, as of this writing. Snopes has reached out to the registered agent tied to the so-called Texas Transgender Student Union for more information. We await a response.
In October, photos spread purportedly showing mailers sent to Texas homes, apparently sharing resources for transgender and LGBTQ+ minors with unsupportive families.
Pictures of the pamphlets, titled, "Texas Trans & LGBTQ+ Student Resource Guide," were shared on X, Facebook and Reddit.
They include directions to advocacy organizations that could supposedly help minors navigate emancipation, or the legal process that allows minors to become legal adults before they turn 18.
The flyers also share resources to allegedly receive gender-affirming care outside of Texas, where prescribing hormone medication for gender dysphoria is prohibited for youth under the age of 18. However, the "guide" does not appear to actually contain any detailed step-by-step instructions for anything.
This was sent to my home. Addressed to the "students" of our family from the "Texas Transgender Student Union." It coaches minors on what to do if their parents are not supportive of their "trans" identity and walks them through getting emancipated. THIS IS EVIL!!!!! https://t.co/lTTy7cz18N
— Sara Gonzales (@SaraGonzalesTX) October 19, 2026
Photographs of the envelopes the flyers came in show the sender was the "Texas Transgender Student Union."
Snopes readers who found the mailers suspicious contacted us to ask about whether they originated from a legitimate organization.
Skepticism is, in fact, warranted. As of this writing, there is no organization based in Texas named, "Texas Transgender Student Union." Public business records indicate that a Wyoming-based LLC registered under that name on Sept. 2. The LLC uses an address that multiple reporters have previously linked to scams and shell operations. 
We have not rated this claim as information continues to emerge about this incident. Here's what we know.
No evidence of 'Texas Transgender Student Union' in Texas
A search (screenshotted) of Texas' business records found no evidence of any organization named "Texas Transgender Student Union." The return address attached to the envelopes is also not a valid mailing address, according to a USPS search (screenshotted). A nearly identical address, 11611 W. Airport Blvd., leads to a nearby mailbox at a UPS store. Therefore, it is possible the address on the envelopes includes a typo.
There is no online presence for any group called Texas Transgender Student Union aside from a Wyoming business license (more on that below), per searches on Google and social media platforms, including X, Facebook, Bluesky and Instagram.
It is unclear how widespread the mailing list is for whichever organization sent the pamphlets. On Oct. 20, Houston Chronicle reported that the so-called resource guide "appears to have been sent in recent days to many past GOP voters, including a handful of prominent right-wing influencers who posted images of them on Monday."
Wyoming address tied to campaign
Reporters on X were quick to connect the Texas Transgender Student Union to a Wyoming-based LLC called Northwest Registered Agent, which is listed in Wyoming business records as the agent for the so-called Texas Transgender Student Union.
Northwest Registered Agent is one of the largest registered agent companies in the United States and offers LLC formation for as little as $39 (excluding state fees). Snopes contacted the Northwest Registered Agent organizer listed on the business license — Taylor Newman — to see if they had any additional information about the so-called Texas Transgender Student Union. We await a response.
Records also list "30 N Gould St" in Sheridan, Wyoming, as the Texas Transgender Student Union's principal office and mailing address. There are thousands of companies represented by registered agents at that address, according to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and The Sheridan Press, the community's daily newspaper. Wyoming's business laws are permissive, allowing anonymous individuals to set up shop without actually living in the state. (In fact, Northwest Registered Agent advertises its services as involving "privacy by default.") 
The businesses connected to that address "include a mix of reputable companies and those that have a history of scamming customers out of money and hiding behind a Sheridan address to do it," a Sheridan Press reporter wrote in 2024.
According to Sheridan Press, the Sheridan County Chamber of Commerce "receives about five calls a week from customers desperate to get ahold of a 30 N. Gould company to get their money back," and the paper itself "receives dozens of correspondence regarding the issue weekly."
No evidence legitimate groups are involved
The main organization listed as a resource in the mailer — the Transgender Education Network of Texas, or TENT — has denied any involvement with the document.
TENT, which has a legitimate business registration in Texas, released the below statement on its website, updated as of Oct. 17:
We are aware of text messages and now physical mailers that have been circulated concerning TENT that appear to have been issued by or on behalf of the organization.
These text messages and mailers were not authored, authorized, approved, or distributed by TENT and are not affiliated with our organization. The texts do not represent the official position or communications of the organization.
We will continue to monitor the situation and remain committed to our organizational values of unequivocal support for trans Texans, their families, and their loved ones. Trans Texans belong here. This is our home and we're not going anywhere.
Underneath the statement, TENT included a GIF of singer Mariah Carey with the caption, "Why you so obsessed with me?"
Reporters have also pointed out that TENT likely lacks the resources to launch a widespread mailing campaign. The organization lost its nonprofit tax-exempt status in 2021 after failing to file tax forms for three consecutive years, but its most recent filing in 2017 states it made only $13,300 in revenue that year. USPS' bulk mail cost calculator suggests sending even 10,001 to 50,000 mailers would cost more than $44,000, depending on how big the pamphlets are. 
The documents spread as Texas news outlets reported that TENT sent cease-and-desist notices to two digital messaging companies over a series of texts that linked to TENT resource guides.
Are conservatives behind the pamphlet?
Following the texts, state Rep. Jeff Leach, a Republican from Texas, asked state Attorney General Ken Paxton to investigate organizations like TENT for supposedly "violating" state Senate Bill 12, an act that prohibits diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and programs and instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in K–12 public schools.
As of this writing, there is no evidence Paxton had anything to do with the flyers. We reached out to the Texas attorney general to ask whether he had any involvement and await a response.
The cryptic campaign has caused some online infighting among Republicans, some of whom also seem to believe that conservatives sent the pamphlets as a political tactic ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

No law or regulation mandates that U.S. presidents salute armed forces personnel, though the act is considered standard practice in the modern era. Ronald Reagan is usually credited with initiating the etiquette, which Trump more often than not continues to follow.
This week, people shared a video they claimed showed U.S. President Donald Trump neglecting to salute two Marines upon disembarking Marine One (the call sign officials use when a president flies on a special fleet of helicopters).
For example, on Oct. 20, a Bluesky user posted (archived) the video, writing that Trump forgot to salute when exiting the helicopter.
Trump forgets to salute while exiting Marine One then lumbers across the tarmac to his Qatari bribe jet. Natalie Harp is the first one up the stairs to join him on the plane.
[image or embed]
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar.com) October 20, 2026 at 2:47 PM
Other users shared the same video and claim on Facebook (archived), X (archived) and YouTube (archived).
This video truly showed Trump neglecting to salute two Marines standing next to Marine One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, as part of his travel plans to speak at a North Carolina rally. The clip showed no signs of AI generation or alteration of its contents.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask whether Trump simply forgot to salute, as some people alleged. We will update this article if we receive further details.
Looking at the full video
A longer video, as well as photos of the same deboarding, showed no evidence that Trump saluted the Marines.
Following deboarding, Trump appeared to have a cordial discussion with another armed forces member while walking to Air Force One and saluted that person. He then saluted Air Force airmen and others potentially not visible in the frame before boarding Air Force One.
Other photos showed Trump saluting a Marine earlier on the same day when departing the White House, as well as saluting a different Marine upon arriving back at the White House later that evening.
Famous saluting incidents involving Obama, Trump
This matter resembled claims about former presidents failing to recognize members of the military or to perform other patriotic acts. For example, former President Barack Obama once saluted a Marine after boarding Marine One, then deboarded to briefly speak with him and shake his hand, then boarded again without saluting.
At other times, Obama saluted Marines next to Marine One while holding a cellphone on one occasion and a coffee cup on another. We also reported about moments when Obama allegedly failed to salute the nation's flag and place his hand over his heart during the national anthem.
In a famous video from Trump's first term, he attempted to retrieve and return a Marine's hat, officially known as a cover, after the wind appeared to knock it off of his head. He then walked up the steps to Marine One without saluting.
No regulation mandates that U.S. presidents salute armed forces personnel, though the act is considered standard practice in the modern era.

First responders
Many a time, it is the peers who are in the best place to spot early signs of mental distress. That is a reason why the Department of Social Work (Mental Health) at Madras School of Social Work in Egmore trains its second year students to offer peer support in mental health.
Although the programme is offered to all, not all students sign up to become a first responder, the diffidence stemming from the fact that being a first responder requires niche skills.
J. Damen Queen, associate professor, Department of Social Work - Mental Health, says this is a sustainable support service within the system that addresses three As - accessibility, affordability and availability. For students, this is an opportunity to offer care and support while they are still studying, boosting their confidence, knowledge and practical skills to recognise and respond to early signs of mental distress.
The faculty says that they are next working on a pilot programme where they want to reach out to 20 colleges in Chennai to train them as trainers and thus create mental health ambassadors in these institutions.
The gratitude wall
Research says that practising gratitude can reduce stress, improve mood, and strengthen relationships. So once in every two or three months, Gratitude Walls are sure to be spotted on the campus of CTTE College for Women in Perambur. They come in all shapes, sometimes taking the form of a tree with branches, many a time on a specially designed notice board and placed at strategic locations so that a good number of students can take part in this mindfulness activity.
Some are guided on the objective behind the wall — a space to celebrate life’s little and big things one is thankful for.
Alima Zahra, head, Department of Psychology, says the gratitude wall actually does bring in a measurable difference in a short time. “It is easy to execute and is a space to reflect. We have some faculty who have started doing this activity with their students,” says the HOD. She adds that one therapeutic event involving music, sand, movement are among activities they conduct to address mental health issues. The college also has a mental health and wellness club.
Teenagers break the stigma
This year-long volunteer peer support initiative at Chettinad Vidyashram empowers students across classes to speak up, reach out for help, tackle stigma and inspire change. Led by psychology students of Class XII, the “Young Helper Project” was started in 2024.
In Class XI, they are given a primer on mental health and the next year, they start taking mass sessions for students across classes I to XI, spread across the academic year, at least one a month and on a range of topics such as bullying, peer pressure and self-esteem.
What makes these sessions engaging are they are sometimes play-based or involves seniors sharing their respective journeys.
Sometimes a class XII student is sent to engage with a child through a drawing activity and in the process make him/her open up about certain topics disturbing him.
G. Parvathi, head of department, Psychology, says when teachers don an additional role as counsellor there is some hesitation from children to open up or reach out for help. “Young Helper Project was started to bridge that gap. Besides giving students an opportunity to be a trainer, the sessions nudge children to reach out to the counselling department in case of pressing issues bothering them and never hesitate to ask for help,” says Parvathi.
Nature as therapist
Two nature-based outdoor activities at Women’s Christian College on College Road in Chennai are linked to positive mental health outcomes such as improved focus, lower stress and better mood. Community gardening has been in the curriculum at this sprawling green campus for some years and what makes it special is the flexibility quotient that it offers students. The Centre for Environment Studies at the College invites students across disciplines to sign up, allowing them to choose a plot and work on growing vegetables and greens. Seeds and tools for gardening and the necessary guidance are offered.
There are no timelines given or number of hours they have to clock; students choose to work as and when they wish, but they are encouraged to come as a group. A student with a bad day might choose to spend more time at her green patch.
C . Anupama, Dean, Centre for Environmental Studies, WCC, says they have 25 students across departments who have enrolled for this in this academic year and updates on progress of veggies are shared on a WhatsApp group to motivate them.
The Centre also initiated Forest Bathing, a walk on the campus where they encourage participants to slow down, breath deeply and engage their senses while spending time with trees.
Both activities are therapeutic, and in Forest Bathing the strategy changes depending on the group. If there are literature students then they write poetry or if it is an mixed group they hug trees, says Anupama.

One was central to facilitating the bogus Cyber Ninjas audit of the 2020 vote in Maricopa County that found no evidence of voter fraud but cost taxpayers $4 million. Another is friends with a Covid-denying former boxer turned MAGA influencer who was filmed on the steps of the Capitol on January 6, 2021 shouting “1776.” Another was set to headline a rally with MyPillow founder and election denial funder Mike Lindell.
This is not a list of edgy MAGA influencers sharing hot takes on X, or podcast hosts on Rumble boosting wild conspiracy theories. No, this is a list of some of the Republican candidates running for attorney general in states across the US.
A WIRED review has identified a slate of GOP attorney general candidates in more than half a dozen states, including key swing states, who have repeatedly expressed their belief that the 2020 election was stolen. If elected, several have said, they are willing to relitigate 2020 once again—and all will potentially play a key role in the 2028 presidential election.
“Any attorney general should be dedicated to upholding the rule of law,” Christina Beeler, senior counsel for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, tells WIRED. “The office of attorney general is a powerful office, and it is deeply important that anyone in that role is dedicated to upholding the rule of law and the results of elections.”
The role of attorney general in the administration and protection of elections differs from state to state, but in general, as their state’s chief legal officer they are required to be a check on both the governor and the federal government. The functions of the role have been highlighted in recent months, as attorneys general across the country have repeatedly stood up to President Donald Trump and his administration's efforts to take control of elections, seize ballots, and obtain voter rolls containing sensitive information on US citizens.
Here, WIRED has looked at GOP candidates for attorney general in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, and Kansas, where some have openly espoused baseless allegations about the 2020 election.
Arizona
Warren Petersen, an Arizona state senator, was one of the most vocal supporters of Trump’s baseless claim that the 2020 election was stolen. In 2020, he signed a document that asked Congress to accept 11 alternate electoral votes for Trump, and later signed another demanding the US Senate reject Arizona’s slate of electors.
Petersen was also central to getting the bogus audit in Maricopa County approved, a process run by a firm called Cyber Ninjas. The audit ultimately showed that Joe Biden had won by more votes than originally thought. The whole process cost Arizona taxpayers millions.
Earlier this year, Petersen complied with a grand jury subpoena, handing over files on the Cyber Ninjas audit to the FBI as part of its investigation into the 2020 election in Maricopa.
And the lawmaker has also signaled a possible desire to relitigate the 2020 election if he’s elected, calling for an expansion of the attorney general’s Election Integrity Unit. “People will know we’re serious about it,” Petersen said during his primary campaign in July. “Just like they know the Trump DOJ is serious about it right now.”
Polls show Petersen tied with his Democratic opponent, Kris Mayes.
Georgia
In Georgia, the focus of much of Trumpworld’s conspiracy theories about elections, the GOP’s nominee for attorney general is Brian Strickland. In 2020, as a state senator, Strickland shared a press release that called for officials to consider launching an investigation into “fraudulent activities” in the 2020 election, a forensic audit of the election in Georgia, and new voting laws in the state.
Strickland has also signaled his willingness to fall in line with the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to investigate the 2020 election. When FBI officials raided Fulton County’s election offices earlier this year and seized ballots from the 2020 election, Strickland called it a “transparency” measure. “Fulton County can't run elections,” Strickland wrote on X in February. “That's the simple truth. Every Georgian, regardless of party, should have faith in our election process.”
An Atlanta Journal Constitution poll published this week shows Strickland in a tie with his Democrat opponent Tanya Miller.
Kansas
Unlike the other election deniers on this list, Kris Kobach is already in the position he’s running for in November, having won the attorney general’s race in 2022.
A long-time promoter of baseless conspiracy theories about fraudulent elections, Kobach previously served as Kansas’ secretary of state from 2011 to 2019. During his time in office, Kobach claimed that an estimated 18,000 noncitizens were on the state’s voter rolls based on non-peer reviewed research that initially found six people who may have attemped to register or registered to vote. In 2017, Trump appointed Kobach to the short-lived “election integrity” commission that found no evidence of widespread voter fraud.
In the wake of the 2020 election, Kobach was an adviser to Texas’ effort to overturn the results and assisted a member of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers who tried to rescind her vote to certify Michigan’s 2020 presidential election results. In 2022, Kobach was announced as a headliner at a Kansas rally with prominent election denier Lindell.
Recent polling suggests Kobach is in a tight race with his Democratic opponent, Chris Mann.
Michigan
In Michigan, Eaton County prosecutor Doug Lloyd won the GOP nomination for attorney general earlier this year, in a race that had once included Matt DePerno, a lawyer facing felony charges for undue possession of a voting machine and conspiracy in the wake of the 2020 election. (DePerno pled not guilty to the charges, and the case is still pending in the district court.)
Unlike DePerno, Lloyd is not typically labeled as an election denier, and he has claimed to be more moderate than his Democratic opponent, Eli Savit. But in a recent podcast interview reviewed by WIRED, when asked about “credible concerns raised by voters about the 2020 election,” he signaled his willingness to relitigate the six-year-old issue.
“I believe the attorney general has the ability to actually use their investigative officers within their office or the Michigan State Police to actually go back and look at those items,” Lloyd told the MI True Red podcast. “And so as I look at it, you know, I want to take those things in.”
Recent polling shows Lloyd tied in his race against Lavit.
Nevada
In Nevada, Trump has endorsed lawyer Adriana Guzmán Fralick for the position of attorney general. That may be because she has said she would push for Nevada’s version of the SAVE Act, which Trump has failed to force Congress to approve on a federal level. The act would impose severe restrictions on eligible voters by requiring those registered to produce a passport or birth certificate, documents that tens of millions of Americans readily do not have.
"President Trump is fighting for secure elections—but DC keeps dragging its feet,” Guzmán Fralick wrote on Facebook earlier this year. “Nevada shouldn't have to wait. As your Attorney General, I will push for the SAVE Nevada Act to remove non-citizens from our voter rolls, count all ballots on Election Day, and end universal mail-in voting. What Washington won't finish, Nevada will.”
Experts have repeatedly said the SAVE Act would disenfranchise millions of voters.
Guzmán Fralick has also touted the endorsement of Joey Gilbert, a far-right boxer turned MAGA influencer who gained fame for spreading conspiracy theories about the Covid-19 pandemic. Gilbert, who calls Fralick a “friend,” was also present at the rally at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. While he didn’t enter the building, he was captured on video near serial conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, chanting “1776.”
Recent polling shows Guzmán Fralick trailing her Democratic opponent Nicole Cannizzaro by 8 points.

Microsoft’s Surface Line has a product to fit a variety of needs and budgets, including flexible 2-in-1 tablet-laptops. The company also recently announced new versions of its Surface Laptop and Surface Pro as follow-ups to its 2024 models, making it even trickier to pick the best model that matches your priorities.
When those 2024 Surface models launched, they were among my favorite devices of the year. Over the past couple of years, those models have held up, making them great buys—especially when on sale. But now, with the new Surface Laptop 8th Edition and Surface Pro 12th Edition (not to be confused with the Surface Pro 12), we finally have some next-gen silicon to pair with them. Just bear in mind that the new Snapdragon X2 chips come at much higher prices, bringing the devices’ value into question.
I weighed these details, among others, in outlining which Microsoft Surface device is best for every need.
Be sure to read our other buying guides for more, including the Best Laptops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best 2-in-1 Laptops, Best MacBooks, and our tips for choosing a laptop.
Updated October 2026: I've rewritten this guide with notes from my testing of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra and updated pricing for other models.
Best for Most People
Recommending a laptop from 2024 as my top choice feels embarrassing. Not for me—but for Microsoft. I adore this laptop, and I actually still find myself returning to it over newer, flashier options. The 3:2 aspect ratio screen is my favorite feature, and it can't be found almost anywhere else right now. The taller shape of the display is preferred if you spend most of your time on a laptop looking at documents, spreadsheets, or websites. Beyond that, it gets great battery life, performs well (in just about anything other than games), and has a gorgeous, high-resolution display.
But I hear you say, why not the 2026 model (also known as the 8th Edition)? Microsoft launched a refresh this year with new chips inside (the Snapdragon X2 lineup, if you care to know). I've tested these chips in other laptops, such as the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x, and they speed things up in meaningful ways—especially on the graphics front. Unfortunately, Microsoft made the poor decision not to send these out to reviewers for independent testing, so I've never had one to try myself.
The real problem, though, is the pricing. Like many laptop manufacturers this year, Microsoft has dramatically increased the price of its products. You can thank the ongoing memory shortage for that. Right now, you can still buy the 2024 Surface Laptop with 512 GB of storage for $999 on Amazon. It's only for the Dune color right now, whereas the Black and Silver models are $50 more. These are not quite as cheap as they were in 2025, but it's a great deal. It's especially affordable compared with the 2026 version. It's over $400 more for an otherwise identical configuration, and sometimes it jumps to the retail price of $1,600. That's just too much for what you're getting. I just don't think the performance difference is worth that much. It'd be a different story if the 2024 model were unavailable, but I have a hard time suggesting someone buy the newer one at the moment.
The Surface Laptop comes in two main variants: 13.8-inch and 15-inch screen sizes. Both are great, but I think the 13.8-inch model offers plenty of screen real estate for the average person, especially with this aspect ratio.
| Specs | 
|---|
| Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite or Plus | 
| Memory: 16 GB, 32 GB, or 64 GB | 
| Storage: 512 GB or 1 TB | 
| Display: 13.8-inch at 2304 x 1536 at 120Hz (IPS) or 15-inch at 2496 x 1664 at 120 Hz (IPS) | 
The Most Powerful Surface
The Surface Laptop Ultra might bear some resemblance to the standard Surface Laptop, but it's a completely different animal under the hood. It's no thicker than the 15-inch Surface Laptop, despite offering far more performance. That's thanks to the Nvidia RTX Spark N1X chip inside, which delivers GPU performance typically found only in discrete graphics cards, like those in gaming laptops. In many ways, this is Microsoft's answer to the MacBook Pro—a laptop designed for content creators, media pros, and a burgeoning new demographic: AI enthusiasts. It can be configured with up to 128 GB of unified RAM, allowing you to feed that GPU tons of memory to access larger AI models—all running entirely on-device. I tested the 32-GB version of the Surface Laptop Ultra, which limits you from running larger AI models (such as 70-billion parameters and above). In reality, you need something with a more powerful GPU to handle foundation-tier models that really compete with the cloud-based services people are used to. I don't know if the case for running local AI models is fully made yet, but the Surface Laptop Ultra lets you dip your toe in.
It can play games, too, but don't be fooled by the “Nvidia” brand into thinking it will perform anywhere near a proper discrete graphics card in a gaming laptop. Some very popular multiplayer games still aren't compatible at all (such as PUBG and League of Legends), though Nvidia says it's working on it. The Surface Laptop Ultra is for someone who wants to dabble in content creation, gaming, and AI on their work laptop. And yes, if that sounds like the M5 Pro MacBook Pro, that's the point.

|---|
| Processor: Nvidia RTX Spark (18-core with 5,120 GPU cores or 20-core with 6,144 GPU cores) | 
| Memory: 24 GB up to 128 GB | 
| Storage: 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB | 
| Display: 15-inch at 3270 x 2180 at 120 Hz (Mini-LED) | 
The Best Surface Pro 2-in-1
I’ve always liked the idea of a smaller Surface Pro, and in theory, the Surface Pro 12 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) checks the right boxes. It keeps the premium look and feel of the Surface Pro line, retaining the Snapdragon X Plus chip (with two fewer cores) while making slight changes to lower the price and make the tablet even thinner. I can live with the incremental downgrades in the webcam and display. My problem at launch, when I first reviewed the Surface Pro 12, was the pricing. Microsoft tried to slot this cheaper, smaller Surface below the Surface Pro 13.8, then immediately stopped selling the lower-tier configurations of that larger device to make room. But these days, the Surface Pro 13.8 has gotten so expensive that I no longer think it's worth buying. If you really want a 2-in-1 Windows tablet, the Surface Pro 12 is your best option.
Microsoft has even started selling a version of the Surface Pro 12 with only 8 GB of memory. That could work if your needs are fairly light. You wouldn't want to use that configuration as your primary work device, though. The Surface Pro 12 also doesn't include a bundled power supply, so you’ll need to pay an additional $70 to add one. Like every Surface tablet, you also have to pay extra for the corresponding keyboard or Surface Pen.
| Specs | 
|---|
| Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus | 
| Memory: 8 GB or 16 GB | 
| Storage: 256 GB or 512 GB | 
| Display: 12-inch, 2196 x 1464 (IPS) | 
Surface Devices That Are Hard to Justify
I’ve already mentioned that both the new Surface Laptop and Surface Pro are priced high for a standard, generational chip refresh. That already makes me doubt whether these devices are worth buying, but I only make official recommendations on products I’ve tested myself.
Another wrinkle: Microsoft isn’t running a typical media review program for these new devices. Unlike nearly every high-end laptop a major company releases, Microsoft isn’t sending review units to independent media for testing, according to a Microsoft spokesperson. That doesn’t necessarily make these devices inherently bad, but it’s a very uncommon choice and, frankly, not a good sign.
Microsoft Surface Laptop 13 (2026): Be careful with this one. It's named dangerously similar to the 13.8-inch model, but it's actually a midrange-type laptop. It has a more basic display, and frustratingly, it's not even in a 3:2 aspect ratio. And $950 for a laptop with only 8 GB of RAM is absurd. If you really want something cheap with only 8 GB of RAM, the Dell XPS 13 only costs $700 and is a far better laptop.
Microsoft Surface Pro 13 (2026): $1,500 for a tablet is really hard to justify. This is for the model with an IPS display, putting the upgraded OLED model at over $2,000. And don't forget: It doesn't come with a keyboard either. When the iPad Pro is cheaper, you know this is overpriced. This does tend to drop down in price on Prime Day or Black Friday, though you'll really need to do some price checks to make sure this is worth the money—even on sale.
Microsoft Surface Laptop 13 (2025): I haven’t tested this model yet, but it’s hard to recommend given the price alone. The 256-GB base configuration is sold out on Amazon, while Microsoft sells it for a whopping $950. That's way too expensive to even consider.
Microsoft Surface Go 3: These days, there isn’t a good reason to pick up any Surface device older than the 2024 models. Shockingly, though, you can still buy the Surface Go 3 new. It costs $700, and it comes with only 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. Even in 2026, that’s insanely overpriced for the specs.
Microsoft Surface Laptop for Business: I haven’t tested this model yet, either, but it’s currently the only way to get an Intel-powered Surface Laptop. It’s also the only way to get a Surface Laptop with 5G connectivity. This is primarily for commercial use, though anyone can currently buy one directly from Microsoft.
Should You Wait to Buy?
It’s been two years since the Snapdragon X platform launched alongside the Surface Laptop 7th Edition and Surface Pro 11th Edition. While I still wholeheartedly recommend these devices, I don’t know how much longer they will be available. Even so, now’s a great time to buy these, especially while they’re still on discount.
Qualcomm announced its Snapdragon X2 chips last fall, and you can buy the Surface Laptop 8th Edition and Surface Pro 12th Edition with those new chips inside. But they’re very expensive and weren't sent out for review. In most cases, they're still too expensive for me to recommend buying over the 2024 model.
The Surface Laptop Ultra just started selling, and it's among the first devices to use Nvidia's new RTX Spark platform.
Things That May Annoy You
There are a few things about Surface devices that may annoy you. With the Surface Pro, the keyboard is not included—and you’ll definitely want to buy one. While the tablet works fine detached for occasional use, Windows just isn’t as cut out for touch-only functionality as Apple’s iPadOS is on iPads. So, when you buy a Surface Pro, don’t expect Windows to help you navigate much without a mouse or touchpad.
Ports are a bit of a mixed bag for Surface devices. You’ll find USB-C ports throughout the Surface line, and the high-end models support Thunderbolt 4. Some models, like the Surface Pro 11th Edition and Surface Laptop 7th Edition, also use the magnetic Surface Connect charger, despite having USB-C ports available. The new 13-inch Surface Laptop and 12-inch Surface Pro ditch the Surface Connect port. The real kicker on the Surface Pro lineup, however, is that it doesn't have a headphone jack. It also lacks USB-A and other legacy ports, while the Surface Laptop includes USB-A, which I find handy to keep around.
Lastly, all modern Surface devices (outside of the commercial models) use ARM-powered Qualcomm processors rather than x86. While Microsoft and Qualcomm have done a lot of work to get nearly all major applications to run natively, you’ll still run into niche software that won’t run, or will run slowly, through emulation. This has become much less of a problem recently, but if you rely on a specific application, make sure it has a native ARM version before moving forward with a Surface device.
Laptop vs. Tablet
Microsoft Surface devices currently come in two forms: clamshell laptop and detachable 2-in-1 tablet. The laptop is simple enough and targets the MacBook Air audience. The major difference is that all Surface Laptop models have always included a touchscreen. This is what most people interested in a Surface device should choose, primarily because it’s the most versatile and comfortable form factor.
The detachable 2-in-1, meanwhile, is a tablet you can attach to a keyboard cover. It has a sturdy kickstand built into the back, which allows you to prop it up to use with the keyboard. It’s a lot like the iPad Pro when paired with a Magic Keyboard. But the idea is that it can function as a tablet alone, handy for one-handed use, or as a laptop when attached to a keyboard. The problem is that Windows doesn’t have an interface as touch-friendly as iPadOS. It also doesn’t have an expansive touch-friendly mobile app ecosystem. That means you’ll primarily be using the Surface Pro as a highly portable laptop replacement.
Do You Need Microsoft Complete?
If you’re rough on your gadgets, the Microsoft Complete extended warranty might be a good idea. Starting at $99, it gives you additional warranty coverage, plus two accidental damage claims with a $49 deductible. Microsoft will provide up to four years of coverage for Surface devices specifically and will cover things like cracked screens, drops, and spills.
You can get Microsoft Complete in a few different ways. You can buy it with your Surface device. But if you’re not sure whether you need it, you can either book an appointment with a Microsoft product expert, add it directly through the Surface App, or contact Microsoft Store Support after you’ve already purchased your device. You have up to 45 days after buying your Surface product to add a protection plan.
Great Surface Accessories
You’ll have to purchase these accessories separately (unless they’re available as a bundle), on top of shelling out money for the device itself. I’ve got a few first- and third-party recommendations.
Surface Pro Flex Keyboard for $330: Microsoft redesigned its signature keyboard cover for the new Surface Pro 13 (11th Edition). It’s detachable, so you can position it anywhere you’d like while using the tablet. The touchpad is also larger this time around. There’s also a bold key option to assist people with low vision and reduce eyestrain. I like that it allows you to space out the tablet and keyboard on your desk for a more comfortable experience.
Surface Pro Type Cover for $158: This Type Cover is one of my favorite accessories. The cover is easy to attach, the clicky keys feel satisfying, and it’s the least expensive option in the Surface Pro lineup. It’s compatible with the Surface Pro 8 and earlier.
Surface Slim Pen 2 for $136: With the second-generation Slim Pen, Microsoft added haptic feedback and lower latency (sketching and writing should feel more responsive). I liked using it with the Surface Pro 11th Edition, but it’s also compatible with some older Surface devices, like the Surface Pro 8, and it pops into the storage slot right above the keyboard. It’s an ideal accessory if you rely on your tablet for taking notes or drawing.
Microsoft Arc Mouse ($90): This hyper-portable wireless mouse is great if you need something compact to travel with, especially when paired with the Surface Pro. For storage in your bag, the ergonomic shape can snap to being flat, while providing a comfortable angle when you need it. Battery life is also fantastic, which is important when you’re on the road. I wouldn’t choose this as my daily mouse due to the limited buttons, but it’s a great mobile mouse and matches the graceful Surface aesthetic perfectly.
Microsoft Adaptive Accessories ($15 to $99): Microsoft offers a range of PC hardware for people who have limited mobility, including a programmable button, an adaptive mouse, and a hub to connect them to a PC wirelessly.

Crowd of 50 beats foreigner to death in South Africa
- Published
A foreign national has been beaten to death by a crowd of about 50 people in Durban, South Africa, police say.
According to police, the unidentified man, believed to be in his late 30s or early 40s, was first approached by two men by the roadside before being assaulted by a larger group. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police have launched an investigation into the murder, with the motive yet to be established.
The killing follows a wave of protests against immigrants in South Africa this year, some of which have turned violent. Earlier this month, shops and cars were set on fire in Durban, as well as Soweto, near Johannesburg.
Provincial police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda told the BBC they cannot speculate on the motive for the killing in Durban and that more information would be shared once verified.
- 'We have to prioritise South Africans': Anti-migrant movement blocks foreigners from healthcare 
  - Published18 October 2025
- The uniformed group targeting foreigners in South Africa 
  - Published18 September 2023
The government has urged the demonstrators to act peacefully, while also accepting the need for immigration reforms. It says tens of thousands of foreign nationals have been deported or repatriated since it launched a crackdown earlier this year.
One of the groups behind the protests, March and March, had initially set a deadline of 30 June for all undocumented migrants to leave South Africa.
Several protests were held ahead of that deadline, with reports of attacks on people from other African countries.
These prompted several countries, including Zimbabwe, Nigeria and Ghana, to take steps to repatriate their citizens amid fears of further violence.
Nigeria accused South African authorities of responsibility for the deaths of two of its citizens that month.
Ghana also confirmed the death of a citizen, Bashiru Isak, a father of three who was fatally shot in Cape Town during demonstrations targeting foreign nationals.
His death led to a diplomatic row with South Africa, which said the scale of the violence had been exaggerated.
One of the leaders of the March and March movement, Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, denied that she was xenophobic.
"We can't be living with these people for so many years and now when we say it is too much, it is enough, we are told that we are xenophobic," she told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals.
The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce.
Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence.
Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent's main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.

The Delhi Traffic Police has shut the Old Rao Tula Ram (RTR) flyover's carriageway connecting the IGI Airport side to Vasant Vihar until October 25 after identifying cracks at two points on the stretch, officials said on Wednesday. With the route blocked, motorists travelling towards Vasant Vihar are being directed to use the adjoining service road. The diversion has led to slow-moving traffic and long queues near the flyover. The traffic police informed the Public Works Department (PWD) about the damage and requested repairs to avert any potential accidents. Repair work is underway at both locations, with officials expecting the carriageway to be ready by the morning of October 26. A traffic police official said the extent of the damage made it necessary to close the entire carriageway, as allowing vehicles to use even a portion of it was not considered safe. To help commuters navigate the diversion, the traffic police has updated Google Maps to show the service road as the alternative route and the flyover as closed. Traffic personnel have also been deployed in the area to manage vehicle movement. The department has shared details of the closure and diversion through its social media channels. The PWD is carrying out repairs on the two damaged sections in coordination with the Delhi Traffic Police. “Deterioration of concrete, visible cracking, and exposure of reinforcement were observed in the gap slab section of the old RTR Flyover. Given the structural distress, traffic was temporarily suspended, and PWD initiated the necessary repair and rehabilitation works,” PTI quoted a PWD official as saying. The repair works are expected to be completed by tomorrow morning. Traffic will be restored after allowing a curing period of 48 hours to ensure adequate strength development of the repaired concrete," the official added. The Gurugram Traffic Police has diverted vehicles travelling from Jaipur towards Delhi on the RTR Flyover towards Dhaula Kuan, directing commuters heading to Vasant Vihar to take alternative routes. According to the advisory, motorists can reach Delhi via NH-48 and the KMP Expressway; the Narsinghpur Cloverleaf, Dwarka Expressway and UER-II; or the Narsinghpur Cloverleaf, Southern Peripheral Road (SPR), Ghatta T-Point, Gwal Pahari and Mandi Border. Other suggested routes include IFFCO Chowk–MG Road–Aya Nagar Border/Bandhwari Toll, Rajiv Chowk–Sohna–Ballabhgarh, and UER-II from beyond the Rajokri Flyover. Commuters from Udyog Vihar have also been advised to use UER-II to reach Delhi. The traffic police has clarified that only passenger vehicles travelling to the airport should take the NH-48 route towards Mahipalpur. Other motorists heading to Mahipalpur have been asked to use the suggested alternative routes. "Commuters are requested to follow the designated alternative routes and comply with the instructions issued by traffic police personnel.
