(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
For anyone navigating the healthcare system, diagnosis is only the harsh beginning. There are medicines to afford, compulsive researching, decisions to make, follow-up appointments to keep and, sometimes, conflicting advice to sort through. For people living with chronic illnesses and disabilities, these become part of everyday life. The question is not only whether medical science can offer a treatment, but whether the care is in reach and if one can understand their options and make informed decisions about their health. A few of this week’s reports look at these questions
Treatment and questions
The government has capped trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs, as Bindu Shajan Perappadan reported. The move brings the discourse on the cost of cancer treatment back into focus. For patients and their families, the price of medicines can influence how manageable treatment is over months or years. A price cap is an important policy intervention, but its real value will depend on whether patients see meaningful savings.
And in Keralam, parents of children with spinal muscular atrophy have sought political support over concerns about a generic drug. For families dealing with a rare condition, access to treatment can involve difficult decisions about affordability and the medicines available to them. These decisions need clear communication and reliable evidence on safety and effectiveness, alongside efforts to make treatment accessible.
There is also the question of the use of medication and Dr. Chandrakant Lahariya examines India’s problem of overtreatment and overmedication. Unnecessary tests and medicines can add costs and expose patients to avoidable risks. For people already managing several conditions or taking multiple medicines, knowing what is necessary and what may not be is an important part of safe care.
What new research tells us
I write about lung adenocarcinoma in the all you need to know about series, following news that Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery for the cancer. The Vatican later said his recovery was on track. The explainer looks at the disease behind the headlines and offers readers a clearer understanding of this type of lung cancer.
Other research this week looks at how differently people can experience disease. A study suggests that early-onset Alzheimer’s disease can look very different from the late-onset form. Another suggests that menopause may involve a more pronounced physiological shift around the final menstrual period than the idea of a gradual transition implies.
Long COVID remains another area where researchers are working to understand why some people continue to experience effects long after an infection. A new study suggests that the condition may affect bacteria in the mouth and lungs. It is still too early to conclude what these changes mean for persistent symptoms, but the research adds to efforts to understand the longer-term effects of COVID-19.
Science, integrity and disease detection
An analysis of more than 4,000 cancer research articles has identified suspected paper-mill activity, raising concerns about the reliability of published research. Scientific findings often become the starting point for further studies, so potentially fraudulent papers can have consequences well beyond the journals in which they appear. Trust in science depends not just on new discoveries, but also on how carefully the evidence is produced and checked.
V. Geetanath reports on a genetic toolkit developed by scientists at the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology to study the inner workings of tuberculosis. The tool could help researchers investigate the bacterium more closely. It is an example of the foundational work that often happens long before a discovery leads to a new test or treatment.
Another report looks at chemical signatures -- patterns of molecules and compounds in the body that could help identify diseases by detecting changes associated with illness. These signatures may offer clues to disease processes and support earlier diagnosis, but researchers must establish how accurately they can identify specific conditions and distinguish them from other causes of similar changes. The challenge is to validate these findings in different patient groups and develop tests that are reliable, clinically useful and accessible in routine healthcare.
Climate and community health
The health effects of climate change are not always immediately visible, but their potential scale is considerable. An analysis suggests that limiting global warming to 1.8°C could prevent the loss of 1.89 billion years of healthy life. The estimate puts the consequences of a warming planet in terms of human health, reminding us that the conditions in which people live are closely tied to their ability to stay well.
Closer home, Kozhikode has reported 161 confirmed measles cases and one death. C. Maya reports that a continuing mumps outbreak in Keralam has also renewed demands for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
Care also needs to continue beyond the immediate event that brings someone into the health system. Dr. Sowmya Josyula writes about why maternal health care after delivery is crucial. Once a baby is born, attention can shift almost entirely to the newborn, even though the mother may still need medical follow-up and support. Postpartum care is an essential part of maternal healthcare, not an optional extra.
Sudha Chandrashekar’s article on making Keralam age-ready takes up a related question: how can the rights of the elderly be translated into accessible care? Recognising those rights is only a starting point. Older people need services and support that work in practice and respect their needs and autonomy. In another important piece, Dr. Parth Sharma examines how doctors working with marginalised communities risk facing reprisals when they challenge the conditions that make people sick, from displacement and hunger to the denial of basic healthcare.
And more
Elysia Poggi Davis, Benjamin L. Hankin and Catherine Demers write in The Conversation about research suggesting that treating depression during pregnancy may benefit a baby’s brain development.
Preeti Zachariah examines why whey protein prices are rising in India.
Smruthi Prabhu explains what intestinal gas can tell us about gastrointestinal health.
Biju Dharmapalan looks at whether a sugar-rich diet while taking antibiotics could affect the gut microbiome, he also writes about why citizens should be research partners in science.
Zubeda Hamid’s In Focus podcast examines the plague case in Siberia, what is known about the disease and what remains uncertain.
In Say Her Name series, Ramya Kannan revisits the story of India’s first woman Surgeon General and the barriers she faced in pursuing a place in science.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study suggesting that wealthier Indians may be more prone to heart disease than poorer groups.
Anirban Mukhopadhyay explores a molecule that could help make treatments for inflammatory bowel disease more effective.
Dr. C. Aravinda examines how AI-MedTech is regulated in India.
Dr. Dinesh Arab reflects on health and ageing in The back end of 55.

On October 17, Saturday, even as 19 people were killed and several injured in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata, a different scene of chaos unfolded a few kilometres away at Jadavpur.
A bulldozer was brought in by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) and Kolkata Police to demolish bookstalls of Left parties set up near 8B bus stand of Jadavpur. While locals and Left workers, including CPI(M) and AISA activists, protested through the night to thwart the attempted demolition, the authorities succeeded in bringing down certain bookstalls and damaging others.
Left book stalls have come under threat both from Right-wing fanatics and the administration after chief minister Suvendu Adhikari issued a warning. “You consider Sanatan Dharma to be merely cultural. You do not say Durga Puja; You call it ‘Sharadotsab’. I will tell all Durga Puja committees that if these so-called communists come to set up stalls and do not write Durga Puja, do not allow a single stall,” Adhikari had announced earlier.
Alt News has already reported on alleged attacks on book stalls by BJP workers in several parts of the state.
Same Stalls Set Up For Years
Left organisations, including the CPI(M), AISA, SUCI(C) and Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), have historically set up bookstalls in and around the 8B bus stand area of Jadavpur. The CPI(M) has been setting up its bookstall there for over 40 years, while AISA’s stall has been set up for more than 10 years. The APDR has been setting up a bookstall for the past four to five years. This year, an RSS bookstall was set up right between the CPI(M) and AISA stalls.
Around 6 pm on Saturday, a joint team of Kolkata Police, Central Armed Police Force personnel and KMC arrived with a JCB earthmover to demolish the Left bookstalls. However, the RSS stall was left untouched.
According to the KMC personnel present at the spot, the Left stalls lacked the necessary permissions. Left parties, however, denied this allegation. Representatives of the Left parties argued that they had paid the required fees to the KMC to set up the stalls.
The administration, however, maintained that paying the fees did not necessarily mean that permission had been granted to set up the stalls. The Left parties, in turn, asked the authorities to show which documents they lacked, while also asking what documents the RSS stall possessed that made it legal. Their requests were repeatedly rejected, representatives told Alt News.
‘Authorities Passed the Buck’
“Police and the KMC workers were only passing the buck on each other. Police said the KMC had sought their help to demolish illegal structures. When confronted, KMC workers said that police had asked them to help demolish our stalls,” said DYFI Kolkata district committee member Sainik Sur.
“We asked police and KMC time and again to show the demolition order. But all they said was that there was immense pressure from higher levels to demolish all the Left stalls,” added Sur.
A similar claim was echoed by AISA state president Ritam Maji. “Police and the KMC made it very clear that the Left bookstalls were illegal, whereas the ‘Sanatani’ stall that came up this year for the first time was legal. We have paid the required fee to KMC and have the receipt of the same, yet they claimed that our stalls were illegal. When we asked them to show documents of the RSS-backed stall, to figure out what permissions we lacked, the police simply said that the top brass of the KMC had requested that the space be cleared,” said Maji.
Besides the earthmover, the administration had also brought a KMC dumper truck near the stalls, generally used to collect and dispose of garbage, allegedly to collect the debris from the stalls and the books, representatives of the Left said.
Hundreds Gather Around Bulldozer
After an APDR stall was partially demolished, nearly a hundred people — locals in the area and Left party workers — gathered near the bulldozer in the evening to prevent it from demolishing stalls. Armed with flags, books and posters, they formed human chains around the bookstalls, forcing the authorities to retreat. CPI(M) central committee member and former Jadavpur CPI(M) MLA Sujan Chakraborty also reached the spot to join the resistance.
Around 1 am on October 18, Sunday, personnel from Kolkata Police, CAPF and KMC workers started assembling near the bookstalls again. An hour later, they again started dismantling the APDR stall.
The SUCI(C) bookstall, set up near Gate 2 of Jadavpur University, was also demolished around this time. The area surrounding the stall was cordoned off by security personnel, and party workers could not prevent the demolition.
CPI(M) Kolkata district committee member Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the party’s bookstalls, documented the resistance against the demolition as scores of people stood in front of the JCB earthmover, through his Facebook Live.
After the SUCI(C) stall was brought down, the administration tried to demolish both the APDR and AISA stalls, which were interlocked in a single bamboo structure. Around 3 am, Left activists were again seen forming human chains around their stalls. A section of the activists sat inside the AISA stall as the police and central forces tried to demolish it, ultimately compelling police to retreat.
As the administration tried to bring down the APDR stall around 4:30 am, CPI(M), AISA and APDR workers tried to resist the advance in a unified manner. SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya was seen resisting the administrative forces, who tried to tear down the bamboo scaffolding of the APDR stall.
Subsequently, individuals identifying themselves as KMC workers used machetes to cut the ropes of the APDR stall and bring down the structure, despite the efforts of protesters.
After the APDR stall was demolished, protesters formed a human barricade in front of the CPI(M) stall. Actress Ushasie Chakraborty was among the protesters who held the barricade.
As the standoff continued, CRPF personnel wielded the baton briefly, but it failed to scatter the crowd. Around 5 am, the forces left the spot.
Although the CPI(M) stall was mostly left untouched, the AISA stall suffered extensive damage. AISA activists tore down a section of the stall and rebuilt it on Sunday morning. SUCI(C) and APDR also rebuilt their stalls, and books were sold through Sunday.
“The police informed us that if we dismantled our stall for repairs, they would not allow us to rebuild it. However, we repaired it nonetheless and carried on with our programme,” said Maji.
Trinamool Congress MLA Kunal Ghosh visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. “I have visited the 8B stall quite a few times in the past. Maybe this time I might have skipped coming here. But after what happened last night, I feel it is my duty to come here and show solidarity,” said Ghosh, with CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh standing by his side.
West Bengal Congress President Suvankar Sarkar also visited the CPI(M) stall on Sunday evening. So did CPI(M) state secretary Md Salim.
Chief Minister’s Warning
On September 10, Adhikari urged Durga Puja committees to deny the CPI(M) space for bookstalls if the party used the term “Sharodotsav”, or autumn festival, instead of Durga Puja. He alleged that the term was part of a concerted attempt to dilute the religious character of the festival and impose communist culture. He reiterated his stance two days later while inaugurating a Ganesh Puja pandal in Keshtopur, a northern suburb of Kolkata.
Following Adhikari’s warnings, on October 14, a division bench of the Calcutta High Court overturned the order of Justice Sougata Bhattacharya’s single bench and declined the CPI(M)’s plea to organise a bookstall in front of its party office in Bongaon in Jessore Road of North 24 Parganas district — a spot where a bookstall by the Hindu Jagran Manch had allegedly been set up.

U.K. politicians looking to gauge how British voters will react to their policies have a new cohort on which to test their ideas: AI-generated focus groups.
Startups Electric Twin and Artificial Societies, and more established research firms GWI and Toluna are using data from real focus groups and surveys to build AI personas able to react to political messages within minutes. Another firm, London-based Synthetic Respondents, charges $16 (£12) a project, which it says is a thousandth of the cost of a traditional piece of focus group research.
Critics warn that reliance on AI-generated focus groups could detach politicians from reality. But the technology also has the potential to transform their ability to sense-test their ideas, making it quicker and more affordable to gauge how real-life voters may react to policies, and giving backbenchers access to analysis that might previously have been outside their budget. One early adopter was Kanishka Narayan, elected to Parliament in 2024, and now Britain’s AI minister.

When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model, the iX3, it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’s sixth-generation electric powertrain, a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line.
But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch.

Pick your power
The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km).
In time, a 400 V plug-in hybrid X5 50e xDrive will join the mix on the production line at Spartanburg, South Carolina, with a 26.5 kWh battery pack and about 44 miles (71 km) of electric range. And eventually, BMW’s hydrogen fuel cell tech will find its way under the hood of the new-generation X5 too. But those wanting something more efficient than the X5 40 can consider the iX5.
BMW is sticking with its strategy of an asynchronous motor for the front axle and an electrically excited synchronous motor for the rear drive unit, thanks to the lower losses of these motor types compared to motors that use permanent magnets. There is a combined output of 570 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft (804 Nm): The front motor generates 245 hp (183 kW) and 225 lb-ft (305 Nm); the rear produces up to 325 hp (242 kW) and 369 lb-ft (500 Nm).

Between the axles at the heart of the iX5 is a rather massive 144 kWh (usable) battery pack, made up of BMW’s new 120 mm cylindrical cells. These are taller than the 95 mm cells in the iX3, which increases energy density by 30 percent over the smaller SUV’s pack. So even if it’s not quite as long-legged as the gas X5, it should still get 450 miles (724 km) on the EPA test cycle, BMW told us. The car’s route planning is designed to take charging into account and uses onboard AI to “consider expected charging capacity, reliability, and precise station location data when selecting stops.” It will even automatically open the charging port flap when you arrive.
Like the smaller Neue Klasse EVs, the pack operates at 800 V, but it is even more capable when it comes to DC fast charging. At a demo during the first drive in California, we watched as an iX5 plugged in at 10 percent state of charge. Within a little over nine minutes, the EV had reached 50 percent SoC, peaking at 465 kW and averaging 375 kW throughout the session, which delivered 61.5 kWh. (The IONNA station had been specially upgraded to charge above the usual 400 kW.) While that kind of power level is now old hat for some Chinese automakers, it’s a big step forward for a European OEM.
A 10–80 percent fast charge takes as little as 22 minutes—provided you have access to a 460 kW charger—via the NACS port. That same port will accept up to 15.4 kW of AC power via BMW’s home charger, or you can use the provided 11 kW onboard AC charger. There are adapters for both V2H and V2L, as the X5 is capable of bidirectional charging.
No more dials

For decades, BMW’s orange-lit cluster of instrument dials was instantly recognizable. But the move to digital cockpit displays put an end to that. Now, the new HMI paradigm from Munich is the Panoramic Vision display, which blends into the windscreen’s frit (the black border that’s painted on). The display is clear and quite minimalist but very legible, appearing a few inches further down the hood and thus closer to where your eyes focus on the road than if you had to look down at a conventional dash. It first showed up in the iX3 and now arrives in the bigger X5. While it looks unfamiliar at first—and people sure seem to hate the unfamiliar these days—together with the full-color heads-up display, you rarely need to look down into the cockpit while driving.
That goes for interacting with the infotainment system, too. The trapezoidal touchscreen and BMW’s current iDrive OS user interface are easy to use, but the onboard personal assistant works much better than the Alexa-based system did last year in the early iX3 we drove. I recognize that I’m an outlier using voice commands to interact with the car, but when they work, I’m going to use them. Particularly in the absence of physical controls—“Hey BMW, turn on the driver’s seat massager” is easier for me to do behind the wheel than tapping the car icon to access vehicle settings and then scrolling down to seats and then selecting the tab for massage and then turning it on.
There’s also a passenger screen, although, helpfully, BMW made this its own option rather than including it in a package. The screen only allows the front seat passenger to watch streaming videos, play games, or browse the web—they cannot interact with native infotainment functions like navigation or the climate settings from that screen, just the one to its left.

Another difference between the gasoline X5 and the iX5 is that the latter features BMW’s new “Heart of Joy.” This is one of the powerful domain controller computers that replaces the jumble of black boxes and single-function ECUs, in this case the one that manages vehicle dynamics. As we found with the iX3, this clever electronic brain enables solid chassis and powertrain control, including the ability to come to an incredibly smooth stop while one-pedal driving.
But the iX5 has another party trick that I didn’t notice in the smaller, cheaper EV: It will automatically detect red lights and stop signs, alerting you and braking the car if necessary (i.e., you were about to run the light or sign). The feature works whether you’ve engaged active drive assist or not. It’s always there like a safety net along with the car’s other advanced driver assistance systems. (I am sure you can disable this feature like the others, although I didn’t check, and I’m sure people will post comments with their particular edge case. Given driving standards these days, I’d be happier if everyone left it running.)
The new assist suite is called BMW Symbiotic Drive, and it’s of the very latest generation of ADAS that allows the driver to apply brake inputs without canceling out of active driving mode—only a heavy stomp on the brake will shut off cruise control.
The EV drives better
Neither X5 nor iX5 are unpleasant to drive. The X5’s engine is quiet, and neither car suffers from much wind noise. Unlike the iX, which had something of a “skyhook” magic carpet ride, both iX5 and X5 are more firmly sprung, but not bone-rattlingly so. But I give the edge to the heavier iX5—although the battery adds to a hefty 6,200 lb (2,813 kg) curb weight, the extra mass helps dampen the short-duration shocks that make it past the X5’s (optional) adaptive air suspension. Longer-duration bumps are smoothed out by either car.
If you have passengers in the iX5, you might find Sport mode has too violent an initial throttle tip-in; in the other throttle settings (eco, comfort), this is not an issue. The iX5 also offers five levels of lift-off regenerative braking, from none at all (it coasts very well) to 0.6 G of regen. And it has true one-pedal driving that will bring you to a complete stop.
The 2027 X5 40 xDrive starts at $72,100, plus a $1,450 delivery and handling charge, and you can already find them in BMW showrooms. There is still a premium for the electric version—144 kWh of lithium-ion isn’t cheap, after all. Thus, the iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 plus delivery and arrives in Q1 2027.

Healthtech startup CureBay raised around ₹100 Cr ($10.6 Mn) in a pre-Series C funding round, comprising over ₹69 Cr in equity led by IvyCap Ventures alongside existing investors and around ₹30 Cr in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners. CureBay cofounder and CEO Priyadarshi Mohapatra told Inc42 that the round came amid strong investor interest. The startup will use the proceeds to expand geographically, strengthen its delivery network and invest in its AI and technology capabilities. The healthtech startup, which currently operates in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar, plans to enter Telangana and Andhra Pradesh markets next. It aims to grow its network of rural clinics from 250 to 800 over the next two to three years. CureBay connects patients in underserved areas with healthcare providers through a combination of rural clinics, local community health workers and a digital platform linking patients to doctors, hospitals, diagnostic laboratories and pharmacies. It also uses AI-assisted screening and care coordination to support patient care. The startup is also investing in GPUs and training AI models to screen patients and assess health risks. Its existing AI products cover areas such as skin conditions, dental health and haemoglobin screening, with plans to expand these capabilities. “We have a full suite of AI products for areas like skin, dental, and haemoglobin. We will keep adding more products and continue investing in width as well as depth,” Mohapatra said. CureBay also runs Kavach, a subscription programme designed to encourage preventive care by offering consultations and support for medicines, diagnostics and certain hospitalisation-related costs. The startup claims to have served over 12 Lakh patients and connected more than 270 doctors and 1,000 healthcare professionals across 4,500 pincodes. Prior to this round, CureBay had raised over $34.6 Mn from investors including Bertelsmann India Investments, British International Investment and Elevar Equity. While the startup is yet to file its audited FY26 financial statements, Mohapatra said it closed the fiscal year with an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of nearly ₹170 Cr. It aims to double this figure by the end of FY27. “We broke even at an operating EBITDA level in FY26. Currently, our monthly run rate is about ₹20 Cr, and we expect the number to grow almost 50% from now till March,” he told Inc42. Mohapatra attributed the growth to customers spending more on CureBay as they increasingly view it as a trusted healthcare partner, alongside the expansion into new markets. However, the startup remains loss-making at the company level. Mohapatra said entering new markets entails fresh expenditure, while profitability would depend on reaching a more stable operating scale. “When we stop expanding and we reach a stable state, we will be net positive at a company level. So the important metric for us to track is operating EBITDA,” he said.

The Keralam government will strengthen all legal measures to curb unhealthy eating habits among children and prevent excessive consumption of junk food, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said.
Keralam would approach the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) seeking clarity on the definition of HFSS (High Fat, Sugar and Salt) food and on the criteria for regulating their sale, he said in a statement in Thiruvananthapuram.
As junk food has no precise scientific definition, there is no clarity on which food items should be included in this category or how their sale should be regulated. Foods containing high levels of fat, sugar and salt can be classified as HFSS, but clear criteria and guidelines are needed to fix the upper limits. At present, it is the absence of such criteria which is hampering efforts to draw up a list of HFSS food and to regulate its sales near schools.
On August 7, 2026, the FSSAI had published a draft regulation on this. The draft proposes that if solid food contains more than 4.2 g of fat, 3 g of sugar or 0.625 g of salt per 100 g, it should be considered as high levels. For liquid food, the “high” thresholds are fixed at 1.5 g of fat, 2 g of sugar and 0.175 g of salt per 100 ml, respectively.
Mr. Muraleedharan said that only when the draft regulation was finalised and incorporated into statutory rules would States have a clear legal standing to prepare a list of HFSS food and to ban or restrict their sale near schools. He added that the State would write to the FSSAI requesting that criteria be finalised without delay.
Eat Right programme
The government was implementing the Eat Right School programme to ensure safe, balanced and nutritious food in schools and to foster healthy eating habits among children. The programme was also being implemented in Model Residential Schools. ‘Protests achieve nothing’: Amit Shah takes dig at Rahul Gandhi, says Congress won't win polls even in ‘30 years’
Launching a scathing attack on the Opposition, Shah said that the Congress party would not be able to win elections in 30 years due to its “negative politics”.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Thursday said "protests and demonstrations achieve nothing", stressing that political leaders should focus on public welfare.
Speaking at an event in outer Delhi to launch and inaugurate 33 Delhi Jal Board (DJB) projects worth ₹8,941 crore, Shah hit out at the Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) over their allegations of “vote chori” and discrepancies in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, accusing them of using “political jugglery and mobocracy” to challenge the people’s mandate.
He warned that the parties risk losing their remaining political ground unless they focus on governance.
“You cannot use political jugglery and mobocracy to defy the mandate of the people. If you want to win elections, go among the people to understand their problems. These protests and demonstrations will not achieve anything. Implement schemes for people’s welfare wherever you have been elected, otherwise you will be wiped out from the remaining places,” Shah said.
Shah accused the opposition of repeatedly questioning electoral outcomes whenever the BJP wins, alleging that the “vote chori” narrative was an excuse to cover up electoral defeats.
“A new game has begun in Delhi. As BJP governments are being elected, they are making excuses of vote chori. They say the BJP is not coming to power by popular vote but by vote theft. In reality, you want to save the votes of infiltrators by making these allegations of Vote chori,” he said.
He cited the Congress’s electoral defeats across states over several decades, arguing that the party had been rejected by voters even before the BJP came to power nationally in 2014. He also pointed to the opposition’s victories in Kerala, Himachal Pradesh and Telangana, arguing that the same electronic voting machines (EVMs) and Election Commission were in place when those parties won.
“Whenever you lose, you criticise the Election Commission. When courts rule in your favour, they are good; otherwise, they are bad,” Shah said.
Shah repeats ‘30-year claim’
Predicting that the BJP would remain in power for 30 years, Shah said the opposition’s negative politics would prevent it from returning to government. He urged Congress and AAP to concentrate on improving governance in states where they still hold power.
"When I say BJP will be in power for 30 years, they again reiterate allegations of vote theft...I want to tell you that Amit Shah was born here, stays here, and will die here...I don't need to visit foreign countries every six months. I am saying you won't form government for 30 years, based on your negative politics," he said.
Shah blames Congress, AAP for Delhi’s environmental challenges
Turning to Delhi’s environmental challenges, Shah blamed successive Congress and AAP governments for allowing sewage and industrial waste to enter the Yamuna. He said the Centre, Delhi, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh were now working together on a time-bound plan to clean the river.
“We will come before the people in May 2029 with a clean Yamuna,” he said, adding that a three-year action plan had been drawn up to provide sewer connections to every household and ensure clean water reaches every home. He said the newly launched projects would play a critical role in achieving the target.
Shah also targeted AAP over Delhi’s landfill sites, claiming that more than two crore tonnes of waste had been removed and 100 acres of land cleared. He said the sites would be transformed into gardens within two years.
Taking aim at AAP’s government in Punjab, Shah accused it of failing to curb drug abuse and asserted that the NDA would form the government in the state by 2029 and dismantle the drug trade.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited India to advance discussions on the India-US bilateral trade agreement, energy cooperation, and strategic security ties. During the visit, Rubio confirmed that negotiations on the trade deal are approaching conclusion, with outstanding discussions centering on reciprocal tariffs under Section 301, agricultural access, and civil nuclear cooperation under the Shanti Bill. In addition, Rubio toured the Reliance Industries oil refinery complex in Jamnagar, Gujarat, to address energy flows, heavy crude refining, and the integration of Venezuelan and US crude supplies. Strategic discussions covered technological infrastructure, satellite communications, counterterrorism cooperation, and Quad maritime domain awareness initiatives. Panelists and experts, including Michael Kugelman, Dr. Ajay Srivastava, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, and former USIBC Managing Director Alexander Slater, reviewed diplomatic approaches to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, critical supply chain security, talent mobility, H-1B visas, and the domestic political timelines impacting bilateral commerce between New Delhi and Washington.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio discusses the India-US bilateral relationship, stating that both nations are close to finalising an interim trade deal to provide continuity for businesses. Rubio addresses energy security, Washington's short-term purchase of Russian diesel, global crude oil supply, and potential refining ties linked to Reliance's Jamnagar refinery. He clarifies that updated US visa regulations apply globally and notes that relations with Pakistan will not compromise strategic ties with India. An expert panel further examines US sanctions, oil waivers, the Lindsey Graham Act, and potential trade tariffs. The bulletin also covers a political controversy in New Delhi after visual artist Rehan Vadra alleged that around 70 protest photographs were removed from his solo exhibition at Bikaner House, prompting allegations of censorship from Congress and counterclaims from the BJP. Finally, the report highlights US President Donald Trump's claim regarding Google CEO Sundar Pichai.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Ambassador Sergio Gor examine India-US bilateral relations on India First, addressing negotiations on a bilateral trade pact, 240 billion dollars in trade volume, and global energy dynamics following a tour of the Jamnagar refining facility. Rubio outlines United States visa policies, workforce priorities, and potential diplomatic pathways concerning the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Analysts Yash Sinha and Brahma Chellaney assess trade discussions, tariff policies, the 60-day Russian oil waiver, Venezuelan crude refining, and General Electric engine delivery schedules for India's Light Combat Aircraft programme. Furthermore, BrahMos Aerospace CEO Dr Jaiteerth Joshi explains the combat deployment of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles from Sukhoi-30 fighter aircraft during Operation Sindoor. The coverage details missile stealth, triad deployment capabilities, domestic manufacturing initiatives, and development updates on the BrahMos NG system.
A political controversy erupted after visual artist Raihan Vadra was asked to remove approximately 70 photographs depicting youth protests and the national tricolour from his solo exhibition, 'No Idea is Final', at Delhi's Bikaner House. While Vadra, the Congress party, and INDIA bloc leaders alleged political censorship and hostility toward artistic expression, the Bikaner House Management Society and the BJP defended the decision, citing strict venue guidelines against political artwork, nudity, and communal themes. On 'To The Point', anchor Preeti Choudhry and panellists, including Sanju Verma and Gurmehar Kaur, debated the constitutional boundaries of free expression under Article 19, government intervention, and the definition of political content in documentary photography versus venue compliance. The broadcast also examined historic Indian photographs that shaped public memory, including Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March, George Fernandes during the Emergency, and the Bhopal Gas Tragedy. Concluding the programme, actor Tiger Shroff shared visuals of injuries sustained from a close-range shooting incident.
Speaking on the ongoing negotiations between New Delhi and Washington, former Managing Director of the US-India Business Council Alexander Slater analysed the key obstacles delaying a bilateral trade agreement. Slater noted that while both governments announced a framework agreement earlier in the year, substantive progress remains slow, remarking, 'I think it would be very unlikely that you would see any trade agreement announced between the two sides before the midterm elections.' He highlighted that past negotiations have consistently faced hurdles over issues such as totalization of benefits and agricultural tariffs. Slater also pointed to shifts in the geopolitical environment, including India's purchases of Russian oil and tariff waivers under the Graham Act. Furthermore, he emphasized the critical role of people-to-people ties, warning that recent visa disruptions could threaten bilateral technology cooperation and choke off a valuable source of human capital for the United States.

A mother recently told me about her child’s holiday homework. She had asked the child to complete a set of maths problems, and every answer was correct. Pleased with the result, she asked the child to explain how one of the problems had been solved. The child couldn’t. When she probed further, she discovered that Alexa had supplied the answers.
The homework was done. The learning wasn’t.
Another incident stayed with me. A child took an answer generated by ChatGPT to school. The teacher pointed out that it was wrong. The child was unconvinced.
“No, ma’am. You got it wrong. ChatGPT is never wrong.”
And the teacher stood no chance.
These are small, everyday incidents, but they raise a question worth asking: what happens when children begin outsourcing not just their tasks, but the very faculties they are still developing?
AI and learning
AI can retrieve information, solve problems, generate stories and explain complicated concepts in seconds. Used thoughtfully, it can be a wonderful learning aid. But there is a difference between using a tool to strengthen a skill and allowing that tool to perform the thinking in its place.
Memory, reasoning, judgement, creativity and the ability to work through difficulty develop with practice. A child who struggles with a maths problem, tries different approaches and eventually arrives at a solution has gained more than the answer. The child has practised persistence, reasoning and problem-solving.
When the answer arrives instantly, that opportunity may disappear.
This does not mean every use of AI weakens a child’s abilities. We do not yet have enough long-term evidence to make such a sweeping claim. But it is worth asking whether, when AI repeatedly does the work for children, we are giving them fewer opportunities to practise the very skills education is meant to nurture.
Physical learning
There is another dimension to this conversation that deserves attention: learning through the hands.
Maria Montessori, the mother of the Montessori education system, believed that a child’s hands play a vital role in learning. She wrote, “The hands are the instruments of man’s intelligence.” Children learn by touching, handling, building and experimenting, gradually making sense of the world through direct experience. When AI provides ready-made answers, stories and solutions from a very young age, children may miss the valuable process of doing things for themselves—exploring, making mistakes and discovering. The concern is that if we allow convenience to replace experience, we may deprive children of opportunities to develop skills that grow through hands-on learning.
A child who builds a tower that repeatedly collapses learns about balance in a way that a screen explanation alone cannot provide. A child who mixes ingredients, plants a seed or works with physical objects is learning through observation, movement and trial and error. The finished result matters, but so does the process of getting there.
Experiencing emotions
The same principle applies to emotional development. Children need opportunities to experience frustration, uncertainty, disappointment and conflict, with a trusted adult nearby to help them make sense of these feelings. If every difficult moment gets resolved immediately by a convenient answer, children may have fewer opportunities to practise coping, reflecting and finding their own way forward.
The aim is not to leave children struggling without support; it is to offer the right support without taking away every opportunity to try.
And then there is the question of relationships.
A mother recently shared that her daughter refers to ChatGPT as her ‘boyfriend’. Whenever she faces something difficult, she says, “I’ll ask my boyfriend.” It may sound amusing at first. Children often give human qualities to toys, invent imaginary companions and engage in pretend relationships. But AI introduces a new dimension: it can respond to a child, creating the impression of a relationship that goes beyond imaginative play.
A chatbot is available on demand. It does not visibly grow impatient, interrupt with its own problems or require the compromises that real relationships do. For a young person who feels lonely, anxious or misunderstood, this accessibility may feel comforting.
But human relationships teach us things that a responsive machine cannot fully replicate: How to read another person’s expressions, how to empathise, listen when we disagree, repair a misunderstanding, respect boundaries and recognise that someone else’s feelings matter too. These are not incidental life skills. They are part of learning to live with other people. They are about being mindful of the people around us.
The concern is not that a child who talks to AI will inevitably withdraw from human relationships. It is that we should notice when a machine begins to replace conversations, connections and help-seeking that a child could otherwise experience with people.
This is no longer a hypothetical question. A February 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 1,458 American teenagers aged 13 to 17 found that 16% had used AI chatbots for casual conversation and 12% had used them for emotional support or advice. These figures do not establish harm or dependence, and they cannot automatically be applied to Indian children. They do, however, show that some teenagers are already turning to AI for more than information and schoolwork.
Preparing children
For parents and educators, the answer cannot simply be to ban AI or pretend it will disappear. Children are growing up in a world where these tools will be part of education, work and everyday life. They need to learn how to use AI, but also how to question it, verify its answers, recognise its limitations and take responsibility for their own decisions.
UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Framework for Students places a human-centred mindset among its four key dimensions, alongside AI ethics, techniques and applications, and system design. It emphasises critical judgement and preparing students to become responsible users and co-creators of AI.
That is an important distinction. AI literacy should mean more than knowing how to write a good prompt. It should include knowing when not to use AI, when to check its answer and when to put the device aside and do the work oneself.
What adults can do
A parent can ask a child to solve a problem before consulting AI, then compare the child’s reasoning with the tool’s response. A teacher can ask students to explain how they arrived at an answer, rather than evaluating only the final product. Children can be encouraged to write their own stories before asking AI for suggestions, build something with their hands before watching a digital demonstration, and attempt to resolve a difficulty before seeking an instant solution.
Most importantly, adults need to model these habits themselves. If we unquestioningly accept every AI-generated answer, we cannot reasonably expect children to approach it with discernment.
Offering support
There is one more question we must ask: when a child is distressed, lonely or overwhelmed, who do they turn to?
Every child needs at least one adult they can approach in a moment of crisis—someone who will listen without judgement, take their feelings seriously and help them find the right support. Technology may offer information or a starting point, but it should never become a substitute for making human help accessible.
The goal is not to raise children who are afraid of AI. It is to raise children who can use it without surrendering their own judgement, curiosity, resilience or relationships.
In a world where a machine is always available, let us make sure no child feels that it is the only one available to them.
(K. Sreedevi is a holistic learning specialist integrating Montessori education, remedial therapy and mindfulness to support children’s learning and emotional well-being. sreedeviarun@gmail.com)

It’s a great time to buy a rug. The floors are getting cold, and you need to be prepared for your winter hibernation. Fall is also hosting season, which means making your place more presentable for the holidays. Maybe you’ve moved, like many do this season, and are still furnishing your new space. Fortunately, home goods sales are plentiful this time of year.
Ruggable’s October Hosting Sale is one of my favorite excuses to redecorate, with up to 30 percent off select styles. It runs through October 25, so your window is closing as I type. Keep reading for more reasons I love Ruggable, plus a few of my favorites currently on sale.
For People Who Make Messes
I adore Ruggable. The entire WIRED Reviews team adores Ruggable. I have the Pamir Moroccan Flatwoven runner under my kitchen sink, and it's gorgeous, but I don’t panic when spills and stains happen. In fact, I welcome them. The beauty of a washable rug is that you can actually live on it, which feels almost radical when so much home decor seems designed for childless, pet-free people who never eat or drink.
WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz has a toddler and a cat, both of whom have peed on his hallway rug. Both times, he was grateful he could toss it in the washing machine and dryer and move on. Commerce executive director Cooper Fleishman was debating between the Wendel Ochre Rug by Anthropologie, the bohemian Yara Navy & Bronze Rug, and the Berber-inspired Enya Multicolor Rug for his office. Reviewer Simon Hill has the Santiago Persian Tufted Rug in his home in Scotland (yes, they ship to the UK and Europe) and recommends the Mandalore Tufted Rug for any Star Wars fans out there.
Ruggable has thousands of designs to choose from—2,122 to date. It’s a blessing and a curse. The brand also regularly offers alternatives to discontinued styles, so all is not lost if you were eyeing a piece you can no longer find. Note that the sale does exclude the new Easy Care Wool collection, along with gift cards, spot cleaner, and rug pads. Read the terms and conditions before you buy, and don’t delay; the sale ends October 25.
Is Ruggable Worth It?
While we stan Ruggable, it’s not without its shortcomings. WIRED editor Kat Merck has the Jonathan Adler Venom Flatwoven Rug in her kitchen; the edges curl up, and it drives her nuts. I will say my Ruggable’s nonslip pad has betrayed me more than once. It shifts around the kitchen and is the occasional tripping hazard. Aligning a rug onto the pad is also two-person job, but it’s not impossible if you live alone. Customers online have also reported issues with prints fading over time, but that’s practically a given with high-traffic, machine-washable rugs.
We also like Revival, which has an assortment of hand-knotted and woven imported wool rugs at reasonable prices. Plus, the company is having its own 20-percent-off sitewide sale that ends on Sunday.

For Mugdha Kalra, a parent of a special needs adult, financial planning has consumed the past few years. The question for her is, who will take care of her son when she is no longer there? She is planning to set up a trust fund that will help him reside at a support home. Ms. Kalra is not alone: for parents of children of special needs, the question of ‘who after me?’ is constantly at the back of their minds, a question made difficult by the fact that there is very little in the way of State-funded support services in the country.
“Even the basic facilities cost ₹50,000/month. A parent must make a lifetime plan for their child to be able to have this support once they are old or too incapacitated to take care of their child. Many people with autism also have comorbidities or other health conditions and money is needed for this too. Parents need to start planning early and set up trust funds for the child,” says Ms. Kalra, who is also an autism advocate.
Understanding autism
Autism is a diverse group of conditions related to development of the brain. The World Health Organization estimates that as of 2021, 1 in 127 people globally had autism. Exact numbers for India are hard to come by, but up to 1.8-2 million children in India are thought to have ASD, as per figures cited in a paper published in Cureus in 2024.
Not everyone who is on the autism spectrum has the same level of needs or abilities. Some people with autism may face several difficulties in their day-to-day lives, while others may only need help with specific tasks. Those with higher needs may require assistance from a caregiver to function and live a life of dignity. In India, as in many other countries, caregiving responsibilities fall on the parents, and predominantly on mothers. But this then raises the question of long-term planning: how to ensure their child is provided for, and care for, after they are gone or unable to care for them anymore.
“My son will outlive me; a facility for neurodivergent individuals is the only option,” says Sutapa Bose, senior special educator, India Autism Center (IAC), a non-profit organisation based in Kolkata. Her son has just turned 19 and she is planning to set up a trust fund for him soon to help in his future care and living. “Financial stress is always there; care has become expensive. But his health and safety are also major concerns for us,” she adds.
Guilt, sibling and caregiver burnout
Caregiving is no easy task. It take a toll, both physically and mentally. “There is always guilt about not doing enough for our children even though our personal lives are affected,” says Ms. Bose, adding that their parents’ mental health inevitably suffered, an aspect of caregiving that is not much attention is paid to.
An unfair amount of the burden of caring for a person with autism also falls on the sibling, if there is one, who is younger and more able than the parent, so an unsaid expectation lies on them to offer lifetime care, Ms Kalra added.
This is what happened in the case of the Chatterjees. Jharna Chatterjee’s son lived and grew up during a time when she was the only breadwinner in the family and also took on caregiving responsibilities. Her son, Sanjib Chatterjee, passed away 16 years ago due to comorbidities. She did not have the financial resources to send him to a care facility.
“It hurts my soul to think that my son passed away, but in a way, as a mother I can die in peace knowing that my son led a dignified life and was cared for. How would I ensure that if he lived after I passed away? My elder son had spent half his life caring for my younger son, who was autistic. It drained our finances, we lost our house, and my elder son lost his business while taking care of his brother. Life felt unfair, but we had no choice,” said Ms. Chatterjee, who is now 87.
Little support
Parents, caregivers and experts point out that what makes their caregiving harder, is the lack of support from both the government and the society in caring for people with autism.
Ms. Kalra notes that even when support homes are available, the basic facilities are sometimes below average and may not always offer a dignified life.
“Once we are not there, we hope to ensure our children are in a place where they have a dignified and structured life and are cared for. However, the government does not do much: India has individuals and NGOs trying to make small changes. That is not enough. We need to have structural and policy-based change in the country to make the society more inclusive for people on the spectrum,” points out the parent of twin boys with autism.
The IAC, in this regard, recently brought out a white paper to seek GST exemption for disability support services. The institute argued that taxing therapy and rehabilitation increases the financial burden on families and sought a service-based approach instead of disability severity thresholds. Representatives of IAC also met with the Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and presented the paper to her and put forth their demands. According to Sakhi Singhi, a governing board member of IAC, the Finance Minister acknowledged the issue and assured them that they would look into the matter.

The Billboard 200 has tracked the best-selling albums in the US for decades.
It's a major accomplishment to top the chart, especially when an artist manages the feat with multiple different albums.
Only a handful of artists have crossed into double-digit No. 1s, including modern superstars like Taylor Swift, Drake, Jay-Z, and Future. They're listed below in ascending order.
Editor's note: Although Elvis Presley is often credited with 10 No. 1 albums, a Billboard representative told Business Insider that most of his biggest releases predate the modern Billboard 200 chart, which launched in 1963.
Madonna — 10
Madonna's 2026 album "Confessions II" became her milestone 10th No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
Madonna is also the first artist with a No. 1 album in the 2020s to have already topped the chart in three other decades: twice in the 2010s ("Madame X" and "MDNA"), four times in the 2000s ("Hard Candy," "Confessions on a Dance Floor," "American Life," and "Music"), and thrice in the 1980s ("Like a Prayer," "True Blue," and "Like a Virgin").
Bruce Springsteen — 11
Bruce Springsteen's 11 chart-topping albums span over three decades, from 1980's "The River" to 2014's "High Hopes" — even though Springsteen has yet to score a No. 1 hit song on the Billboard Hot 100.
Barbra Streisand — 11
Barbra Streisand logged her first No. 1 entry on the Billboard 200 with "People" in 1964.
Fifty-one years later, she set a record for the longest span between No. 1s when "Encore: Movie Partners Sing Broadway," her 2016 studio album, topped the chart.
Streisand previously held the record for the most No. 1 albums among female artists until Taylor Swift broke it in 2023.
Kanye West — 11
Ye, who still releases music under the name Kanye West, topped the Billboard 200 for the first time in 2005 with "Late Registration."
He logged his 11th consecutive No. 1 album in 2024 with "Vultures 1," a collaborative effort with Ty Dolla $ign.
Eminem — 11
When it was released in 2000, Eminem's "The Marshall Mathers LP" sold over 1 million copies in its first week, easily earning a No. 1 debut on the Billboard 200.
Two decades later, "Music to Be Murdered By" debuted at No. 1, becoming Eminem's historic 10th chart-topper. He logged his 11th in 2024 with "The Death of Slim Shady (Coup de Grâce)."
Future — 11
Future earned his first No. 1 album in 2015 with "DS2," which has since spent over 300 weeks on the Billboard 200.
In 2024, Future's "Mixtape Pluto" debuted atop the chart — his third No. 1 album in just six months and 11th overall.
Earlier that year, Future topped the chart with "We Don't Trust You" and "We Still Don't Trust You," collaborative efforts with Metro Boomin. The former is widely known for reigniting a feud between Drake and Kendrick Lamar.
Jay-Z — 14
Jay-Z began collecting No. 1s in 1998 with his third studio album, "Vol. 2... Hard Knock Life." In 2017, he extended his total to 14 with his latest effort, "4:44."
Jay-Z is also one of the most-awarded artists in Grammy history.
Drake — 15
Since pivoting to music after starring on "Degrassi" as a teenager, Drake has racked up 15 No. 1 albums, from 2010's "Thank Me Later" to 2026's "Iceman."
Drake's grand total also includes one mixtape ("Care Package"), three collaborative albums ("What A Time To Be Alive" with Future, "Her Loss" with 21 Savage, and "$ome $exy $ongs 4 U" with PartyNextDoor), and one project mysteriously billed as a playlist ("More Life").
Taylor Swift — 15
Only one of Taylor Swift's albums hasn't topped the chart: her self-titled debut, which peaked at No. 5 in 2008.
Swift earned her first No. 1 later that same year with "Fearless," which has since been ranked the fourth-biggest album in Billboard 200 history. In the 2020s, Swift rerecorded four of her old albums and rebranded each new release as "Taylor's Version." All four of those topped the chart, too.
Most recently, 2025's "The Life of a Showgirl" launched atop the chart with the biggest sales week in history, breaking Adele's record. It became her 15th No. 1 album, extending her record for the most among women. She is tied for the most among solo artists.
Swift has also broken Elvis Presley's record for the most cumulative weeks spent at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a solo artist.
The Beatles — 19
The Beatles hold both records for the most No. 1 songs on the Hot 100 and the most No. 1 albums on the Billboard 200. The latter group includes classics like "Revolver" (1966), "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" (1967), "Abbey Road" (1969), and their post-band breakup compilation "1" (2000).
As a solo musician, Paul McCartney has topped the Billboard 200 eight more times, while John Lennon managed the feat three times before he died in 1980.

You exist long enough as a subscription service, and eventually you'll get a "+." Kindle Unlimited, Amazon's subscription service for borrowing books, comics and magazines, is the latest service to fall. In an email to subscribers, Amazon said it's renaming the subscription to Kindle+ and expanding its library of audiobooks.
The service still offers access to the same reading material, and now "thousands more audiobooks," according to Amazon. Amazon also says reading history, bookmarks, notes and saved titles all carry over to Kindle+, and it'll still cost $12 per month and limit borrowing to 20 titles at a time.
Really, the only thing that's meaningfully changing is the audiobook library. One of the ways Amazon is expanding its existing collection is by allowing authors who self-publish through the company's Kindle Direct Publishing platform to include their audiobooks in the service. Self-published authors have the option to upload traditionally produced audiobooks, and Amazon is also testing a service that can generate audiobooks read by a "virtual voice."
Kindle+ is live now and should work just as well through Amazon's Kindle app as it does on the company's redesigned lineup of Kindle hardware.

New York City council votes to advance bill that would ban horse-drawn carriages
Legislation requires mayor to develop plan to transition drivers to new jobs
New York City council passed a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers and the rest of the industry find other jobs, though its provisions are vague and doesn't set clear benchmarks for displaced workers.
Instead, it requires city hall to come up with a program that includes job referrals, career counselling and educational opportunities. It also allows the administration to consider some form of compensation for industry workers.
The mayor's office has been working on a workforce transition program and has started discussions on potential compensation, according to city hall.
"The mayor will sign this bill, and the Mamdani administration is working every day to ensure we can do so while providing the strongest possible protections for the owners and workers in this industry," a spokesperson for the mayor said after the council's vote.
The union representing carriage drivers had vowed to file a legal challenge "the minute the ink dries" on the legislation.
The latest push began in June after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after jumping from a runaway carriage during a ride. His death appeared to be the first fatality involving a horse carriage in Central Park since the rides began.

Mahajan's family has personally appealed to the city to end the rides, offering tearful testimony that they thought the rides were safe. His uncle, Gaurav Mahajan, praised the proposal during a rally Thursday, saying "the hour of justice has finally arrived," as he stood beside local lawmakers and animal welfare activists.
"We're turning our shattering loss into an unbreakable shield of kindness for the city. For months, our family hasn't been allowed to just grieve," he said. "We've had to fight. We've had to channel our devastating sorrow into a war for change."
Carriage drivers have expressed sympathy for Mahajan and his family but argue they are being unfairly targeted because of a single accident.
"It does nothing for alternate employment, for the continuation of our businesses," said Christina Hansen, a longtime carriage driver and industry spokesperson. "Who's going to pay my rent while I'm looking for a job?"

BrahMos Aerospace is expanding its missile development and export ambitions, with a prototype of its next-generation BrahMos-NG system targeted for 2027-28 and a 1,500-km-range variant on its longer-term roadmap. The company is accelerating research and development, strengthening its supply chain and engaging foreign militaries interested in air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile, CEO and managing director Dr Jaiteerth Joshi said in an interview with ANI on Thursday.
BrahMos-NG is being developed as a smaller, lighter and stealthier version of the existing missile. It will feature higher indigenous content, new technologies and advanced materials. The system is being developed jointly by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Russia's NPO Mashinostroyeniya through BrahMos Aerospace.
The company plans to develop the first prototype by 2027 or 2028. The missile will initially be developed in an airborne configuration, potentially expanding India's air-launched strike capabilities.
Foreign militaries show interest in air-launched BrahMos
BrahMos Aerospace is in talks with foreign countries interested in integrating the air-launched missile into their air forces. 
Some of these countries operate the Sukhoi-30 fighter aircraft, which is also used by the Indian Air Force.
Interest is also emerging in BrahMos-NG, with potential customers looking at the next-generation system ahead of its development. The company is engaging with interested parties on the missile's capabilities and possible integration.
The growing interest follows BrahMos' combat deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when the 
Indian Armed Forces
 used the weapon system in active warfare for the first time.
The missile was deployed against critical targets, including major Pakistani airbases such as Nur Khan. Its combat performance has drawn greater attention from foreign militaries seeking weapons that can adapt to rapidly evolving battlefield conditions.
BrahMos Aerospace CEO Dr Jaiteerth Joshi said the missile had demonstrated its ability to engage targets accurately in real time. He said no 
BrahMos missile
 was intercepted during the combat operation.
1,500-km-range variant remains at conceptual stage
BrahMos Aerospace is also exploring a major extension of the missile's strike range to 1,500 km. The proposed variant remains at the conceptual stage, with the company discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner.
The range-extension programme is being pursued in phases. According to Joshi, test firings from land, sea and air have validated longer-range capabilities beyond the missile's original 290-km strike range.
The proposed 1,500-km variant would mark a significant expansion of the missile's planned reach. However, the company has not announced a development or deployment timeline for it.
Production expansion targets rising demand
BrahMos Aerospace is prioritising the completion of existing orders from the Indian Armed Forces while preparing to meet growing demand from domestic and international customers.
Its production units in Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow are working towards fulfilling the pending orders. The company also plans to accelerate research and development by establishing 'Tech-bricks' for specialised technologies required to develop and test future BrahMos systems.
A key part of the expansion plan is to strengthen the supply chain and increase production capacity in case of emergencies or a sudden surge in demand.
The company intends to expand the number of suppliers for individual systems and sub-systems from the earlier one or two industry partners to as many as 45 sources. The move is expected to widen the supplier base and encourage competition on quality and pricing.
Combat record strengthens export prospects
BrahMos has become a key component of India's defence export strategy, with its operational performance adding to its international profile. The company secured its first export order in 2022, before the missile's combat deployment, and subsequently signed an export deal with the Philippines.
BrahMos Aerospace has since signed deals with two more Southeast Asian countries this year. Orders and deliveries involving the Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam are expected to take the missile's exports beyond $600 million.
The missile's export prospects are part of a broader expansion in India's defence exports, which have reached Rs 38,400 crore, registering annual growth of 62.7%.
The system is increasingly being positioned as a flagship of India's defence manufacturing capabilities and push for self-reliance. Its combat performance during Operation Sindoor has also strengthened its profile among foreign military buyers.
Navy contract reinforces domestic manufacturing
On October 6, the Ministry of Defence signed a contract with BrahMos Aerospace for the procurement of fire control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships.
The contract has a minimum indigenous content requirement of 68% and is expected to encourage participation from Indian industries, including micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
The project adds to BrahMos Aerospace's domestic production commitments as it pursues new missile variants, expands its supplier network and seeks to strengthen its position in the international defence market.

‘Raise capital now’: Nikhil Kamath says AI funding more than its revenue, warns startups
Nikhil Kamath estimated that around $1 trillion was being invested in AI annually, while revenue generated was between $100 billion and $200 billion.
The money flowing into artificial intelligence (AI) far exceeds the revenue it currently generates, Nikhil Kamath has said. The Zerodha co-founder warned that 2027 could be a difficult year for startups and said “it won't be a bad idea” for entrepreneurs to raise funds now as access to capital could become difficult in the months ahead.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2026, Kamath said the AI industry was attracting enormous investments but had yet to generate enough revenue to justify the spending.
“The amount of money going into AI and the money coming out of AI, there is a big gap in between that,” he said.
Kamath estimated that around $1 trillion was being invested in AI annually, while revenue generated through enterprise adoption was between $100 billion and $200 billion. This leaves a gap of $700 billion to $800 billion a year that investors or other sources of funding must cover, he said.
He noted that foreign capital, including investments from the Gulf, helped fund American AI companies in the previous funding cycle. Finding enough fresh capital to sustain investments at the current scale every year could prove difficult.
ALSO READ | Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs globally this year as it ramps up AI adoption
Why 2027 could be difficult for startups
Kamath said investors were counting on AI to boost productivity and generate trillions of dollars in economic benefits to justify the huge spending. “I don't know if I've seen that happen on the ground yet," he said.
He also warned that rising US Treasury yields could make borrowing more expensive. "So for next year, with American Treasury rates going up, cost of money going to 5-6-7%, I don't know where it'll go, it's at 5% today.”
“Somebody has to bridge this gap up until that five trillion dollar revenue story plays out, even if it does or it doesn't, nobody knows,” he said.
Kamath advised founders to secure funding while investor appetite remained relatively strong. “So if somebody is able to raise a lot of capital today and keep it, probably not a bad idea,” he said.
Kamath is the co-founder of Zerodha, one of India's largest stockbroking firms. He has also invested in several businesses, including Licious, Nourish You, Pee Safe, Subko and electric scooter maker Ather.
He is involved in philanthropy and environmental initiatives and has signed the Giving Pledge, a commitment to donate at least half of one's wealth to charitable causes during one's lifetime or through a will.
Kamath backs inheritance tax
At the summit, Kamath also backed the idea of an inheritance tax, calling it “probably not the worst idea in the world”.
An inheritance tax is levied on beneficiaries who receive money, property or other assets after someone's death. Kamath questioned whether wealth passed between generations should be treated differently from income earned during a person's lifetime.
ALSO READ | Nikhil Kamath marks Zerodha’s 16th birthday with nostalgic note: ‘Hope we’re all still in same room in 2042’
“I don't like the idea of taxing somebody who is earning money in his lifetime and incentivising that but taxing people between generations when wealth is being passed through; I don't know in what manner. It has to be done in a manner where it's not an unrealized gain,” he said.
He said that such a tax should not force business owners to sell equity in their companies to meet their tax obligations. He also recalled facing online criticism when he had previously shared his views on inheritance tax.
‘Wage growth must keep up with asset prices’
Kamath also discussed the Gini coefficient, a measure of income or wealth inequality. He said inequality was worsening in many parts of the world and argued that the wealth gap would be difficult to reduce unless wages grew alongside asset prices.
“As long as wage growth in society is not going to keep up with asset price inflation, logically it's impossible for wealth inequality to come down,” he said, adding that governments might need to intervene to address the problem.
He also asked wealthy individuals to take steps to reduce inequality before it becomes more difficult to tackle.
“To the rich people in this room, it's not even altruism, but it could be self-serving to solve this problem when you can, before you reach a point where you have to,” he said.
What India can learn from China on AI
Kamath said India had the potential to build major technology companies but lacked the risk capital available to businesses in the United States and China, particularly those developing advanced AI models.
He said companies working on frontier AI models had access to greater funding to experiment with new technologies, making it difficult for Indian firms to compete at the same level.
“I don't see how an Indian company, or for that matter any company outside of those two or three countries where there is that much risk capital, can have a fair shot at competing in that layer,” he said.
However, he pointed to India's cost advantages in setting up businesses and building data centres. Kamath estimated that setting up a megawatt of capacity in India could cost 30% to 40% less than in the West. He also said electricity was significantly cheaper in India than in several other countries.
Kamath suggested that India could learn from the competition between Chinese provinces, where local leaders compete to attract investment and promote development.
“One thing that maybe we can change and learn from China is to allow for different provinces or states to compete with one another like they were a capitalistic organisation itself,” he said.
He added that chief ministers could operate more like corporate CEOs, competing to improve their states' performance and attract businesses.
