A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.
But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.
Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.
"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."
Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.
Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.
Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for "Medicare for All" and called out Valadao for a vote "that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families," since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.
Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said "there are no actual cuts" to Medicaid.
An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.
Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.
Fertile Ground, High Unemployment
Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River's bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields.
Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.
Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao's district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections.
Valadao has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last remaining Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.
"This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters," Cummins said.
But California's congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao's Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.
"Valadao knows that he's on notice," Cummins said.
Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump.
On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.
"The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes," Villegas said during the debate.
At campaign event, no mention of healthcare
On Sept. 30, Valadao held a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser. It was hosted by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber.
Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.
Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience.
After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News' questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents' Medicaid coverage, saying, "I think you are distorting the truth."
Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao's district.
They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao's votes closely. She called him "a hero for the Central Valley," citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the "breadbasket of the world."
Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong's district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.
A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults on Medicaid to prove they're working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.
"It's not an actual cut," Valadao said. "We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask."
$32 million in campaign ads for one swing district
In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats have each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.
"When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that's pretty high," Cummins said.
Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.
Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays.
"David Valadago is going on vacation again, Mom," he'll tell her, mispronouncing the congressman's name. Her son doesn't realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.
Maese is undecided. Even though she's a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn't sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.
For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.
"He just hasn't come through with anything he said," she said, "especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid."
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

New Delhi, Oct 22: An virtual meeting of the INDIA bloc will be held on Thursday evening to deliberate on the roadmap for protests over the "vote chori" issue and on ways to press for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, sources said.
Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge will chair the meeting, which will also review the preparations for the INDIA bloc's rally in Delhi on November 1, they said.
The INDIA bloc leaders would brainstorm on charting out the roadmap of protests, review the preparations for the November 1 rally and ways to corner the government over the 'vote chori' issue.
The meeting also assumes significance as it comes at a time when there is speculation over the government convening Parliament for passing a Constitution amendment bill, involving delimitation, for the early implementation of the Women's Reservation Act.
Last week, the protests over the "vote theft" charge reached the Supreme Court's doorstep.
On October 12, opposition stalwarts, joined by activists and civil society members, took part in a "March for Democracy" along a heavily barricaded route and filed a joint petition against Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, alleging poll irregularities, in a major show of strength in the national capital.
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi also hosted INDIA bloc leaders for tea at his home on October 13. After the meeting, the opposition bloc vowed to continue resisting and take the "vote chori" fight to its logical conclusion.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

In GTA 6, the phone is no longer an in-game menu to receive calls and messages. Rockstar Games is turning the phone into a physical device that Jason and Lucia pull out of their pockets and use in person. With a fully functional GTA 6 phone, you might wonder what apps are available on it.
Well, GTA 6 previews shared with content creators detailed apps for social media, vehicle theft, fast travel, fitness tracking, entertainment, and vehicle delivery. Yes, your in-game phone in GTA 6 does more things now. In this guide, learn about all the apps on the GTA 6 phone and what each does.
Full GTA 6 Phone Apps List
Plenty of apps have already been revealed through the GTA 6 extended look, trailers, and creator previews. Some exclusive interviews also confirm certain mechanics, confirming the legitimacy of the apps.
| App | Use | Status | 
|---|---|---|
| WAINK | Scans parked cars and reveals their locks, alarm, tracker, value, registration cost, and theft-related information | Confirmed (Rob Nelson to IGN, August 27, 2026) | 
| Snapmatic | Browse social posts and follow accounts, but Jason and Lucia cannot publicly upload photos | Confirmed (IGN, August 27, 2026) | 
| Ryde Me / RideMe (rydeme.app) | Book rides for fast travel and interact with the driver during the journey | Confirmed (IGN and Kotaku, August 27, 2026) | 
| Fitness App | Tracks Jason and Lucia’s sleep and helps monitor how tired they are | Confirmed (TGG, September 3, 2026) | 
| On Demand | Provides podcasts and shows, with creator-safe music also supported | Confirmed | 
| Scooter Bros | Delivers a personal vehicle to the player | Confirmed | 
| BuckMe (buckme.app) | Digital banking app used to manage the player’s banked money | Confirmed | 
| WhatUp (what-up.app) | Messaging and communication between characters | Unconfirmed | 
| LifeInvader | Social networking platform returning from GTA 5 | Unconfirmed | 
| Bleeter | Twitter-style social media platform | Unconfirmed | 
| Fruit Pay | Mobile payment service similar to Apple Pay | Unconfirmed | 
| Unknown Social Media App | Short-form video and social content similar to TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts | Confirmed existence, exact identity unknown | 
| LeonidaGov (leonidagov.org) | Potential Leonida government website or service | Unconfirmed | 
| BrianAndBradley (brianandbradley.com) | TBA | Unconfirmed | 
| HookersGalore (hookers-galore.com) | TBA | Unconfirmed | 
| WipeoutCornSkin (wipeoutcornskin.com) | TBA | Unconfirmed | 
| MyBoyHasACreepyCorndog (myboyhasacreepycorndog.com) | TBA | Unconfirmed | 
| Bunko Jack’s App | A store app advertised through an in-game sign, potentially tied to Jack’s Liquor Store | Unconfirmed | 
All Confirmed GTA 6 Phone Apps
Now that you know about all the apps in brief, here is a full breakdown of each of them so you know what to look for in your GTA 6 phone:
WAINK Vehicle Scanner
WAINK is one of the most useful phone apps for players who enjoy stealing cars in GTA 6. When you approach a parked vehicle, WAINK can scan it and provide information before you decide whether to steal it. The app can identify whether the vehicle is locked, whether it has an alarm or tracker, and provide information about its value.
It can also show the vehicle’s registration cost and potential resale information. The app therefore gives players more information before committing to a car theft, especially when avoiding tracked or expensive vehicles.
Snapmatic
Snapmatic app from GTA 5 returns, but its role is different in GTA 6. Jason and Lucia can browse the feed and follow accounts, allowing them to keep up with activity happening around Leonida. The game also uses social media posts as part of the wider story.
However, Jason and Lucia cannot publicly upload their own photos. Rockstar explained that the pair are hiding from authorities and do not want to leave a digital trail. They can still send photos to each other privately. It is important, given that you must work for that relationship in GTA 6.
Ryde Me / RideMe
Fast travel in GTA 6 is possible thanks to the ride-hailing (taxi) service app on the phone. Players can book a ride and talk to the driver during the journey. Rides can also be shared, allowing other passengers to join the trip and interact with the player, including strangers.
Fitness App
The extended look at GTA 6 already showed how weight mechanics, gym, and food choices work. Looking at all the GTA 6 screenshots, we can understand that both Jason and Lucia will have to maintain their body fat for different types of attributes. That is where a fitness app comes into play.
Confirmed through the creator previews, there will be a proper fitness app on the GTA 6 phone. It will also track how well the protagonists sleep. The information is also tied to the game’s tiredness system.
Rockstar explains that fatigue can affect how certain attributes regenerate. This gives the phone a practical role in tracking the characters’ physical condition.
On Demand
On Demand is an entertainment feature on the phone used for podcasts and shows. As per reports, Rockstar had a dedicated team working on the in-game entertainment content. These shows might be available through the On Demand app.
It gives the characters access to entertainment while moving around the GTA 6 map. The same phone system also includes creator-safe music.
Scooter Bros
Just like a taxi app in GTA 6, the phone also includes a private car app called Scooter Bros. The service can deliver a personal vehicle to the player, giving Jason or Lucia another way to access their rides without manually searching for them.
BuckMe
BuckMe is the game’s digital banking app. It is a part of the GTA 6 money system. It allows players to manage money that they deposit rather than carrying all of their cash physically.
In GTA 6, money exists in separate forms, with physical cash being more vulnerable to loss. That is where banked funds are safer, as you can access them anytime using BuckMe.
Unconfirmed GTA 6 Phone Apps
Beyond the confirmed apps, some rumored and unconfirmed ones might appear in GTA 6. Here is the list:
- WhatUp: A rumored messaging app and parody of WhatsApp. It is expected to handle messages between GTA 6 characters.
- LifeInvader: The GTA parody of Facebook could return, but its presence as a GTA 6 phone app remains unconfirmed.
- Bleeter: The GTA equivalent of X/Twitter may return, although Rockstar has not confirmed it as a GTA 6 phone app.
- Fruit Pay: A rumored payment app that could handle digital transactions, but there is no confirmed gameplay or previews showing how it works.
- LeonidaGov: A rumored government website for Leonida based on the discovered leonidagov.org domain. Its purpose and availability in game remain unconfirmed.
- BrianAndBradley: A rumored website that could parody a personal injury law firm. Its connection to an actual GTA 6 feature is unknown.
- HookersGalore: A rumored website with an unclear purpose. Despite fan theories about its function, there is no confirmed information about what it does in GTA 6.
- WipeoutCornSkin: A mysterious domain discovered alongside the other suspected GTA 6 websites. Its purpose is currently unknown.
- MyBoyHasACreepyCornDog: Another unexplained domain that could be connected to an in-game website.
- Unknown short video app: The GTA 6 extended look has shown social media and livestreaming activity. But we don’t know much about the exact app responsible for a TikTok or YouTube Shorts-style feed.
Those are all apps available on the in-game GTA 6 phone. Which apps are you clicking the moment you enter GTA 6? Let us know in the comments.
Can you post photos on Snapmatic in GTA 6?
Rockstar confirms that, due to their digital footprint, Jason and Lucia do not post photos on Snapmatic.
What is the use of WAINK in GTA 6?
WAINK is a vehicle scanning app that lets you inspect parked cars before stealing them. It can reveal details such as locks, alarms, trackers, value, and registration costs.

The national telemedicine consultation helpline e-Sanjeevani has integrated an AI-enabled clinical decision support system for healthcare providers. This is just the latest example of AI’s increasing integration into medicine and medical care worldwide, and in India. As AI begins to influence clinical decisions, such as reassurance, referrals, or investigations, its regulation has now become an urgent patient-safety question. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation’s (CDSCO) July 2026 guidance on software in medical devices becomes important in this context. The document brings software (including AI-enabled) used for a medical purpose into a clearer approval pathway. However, it explicitly says that it reflects existing practice and is not a new regulatory control.
What is MedTech?
Medtech refers to instruments, apparatus, implants, software, or related devices used for diagnosis, prevention, monitoring, or treatment, whose primary action is not achieved through pharmacological, immunological, or metabolic means. A thermometer, glucometer, blood pressure apparatus, pacemaker, dialysis machine, and CT scanner are considered MedTech. Software is the set of instructions that makes a digital device work. A digital blood-pressure monitor, for example, uses embedded software to control cuff inflation, read pressure sensors and calculate the final BP value. Within software are algorithms, which are step-by-step rules that convert inputs into outputs.
AI (built on advanced algorithms such as machine learning and deep learning models) learns patterns from large amounts of data and uses them to make inferences. All AI depends on algorithms, but not every algorithm is AI. Netflix and YouTube recommendations are familiar examples of algorithms. But a medical algorithm is not a film recommendation. AI may reduce workload, improve consistency and extend specialist support to places where it is scarce. But a false positive can send a healthy person through anxiety and unnecessary tests, while a false negative can do the opposite. A model trained on one population, or one hospital network, may behave differently elsewhere. So, a model that works in Boston is not automatically ready for Bihar.
Risk before labels
India currently regulates medical devices by stretching the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which was intended mainly to penalise spurious drugs. In 1982, an amendment allowed the government to classify devices as ‘drugs’. The Medical Devices Rules, 2017, established the first dedicated rulebook. The rules introduced four classes - Class A for low risk, B for low-to-moderate risk, C for moderate-to-high risk, and D for high risk. The manufacture of devices under classes A and B is generally handled by State licensing authorities, while the central authority regulates manufacture of devices under classes C and D as well as the import of all classes. In 2020, all devices meant for medical use, including software, came under the law. While AI does not create a fifth class, the risk it poses depends on its intended use and the consequences of incorrect output.
The July guidance translates this risk-based approach classification specifically to software as Software in a Medical Device (SiMD - embedded in or controlling hardware), or Software as a Medical Device (SaMD -where the software itself performs the medical function). Software that only stores or transfers patient information is treated differently from one that influences diagnosis or treatment. Standalone medical software is assessed according to both the severity of the clinical situation and the extent to which its output guides medical decisions. Software intended solely for general wellness or routine tracking of body parameters may remain outside the medical-device framework.
Proof followed by surveillance
Validation for AI-enabled devices is sought uniquely. The CDSCO seeks evidence of a sound clinical association between the output and the condition; whether the software technically produces the intended result, and whether it performs clinically in the population and setting (deployment) where it will be used.
Developers are expected to describe training, validation and test datasets, including demographic, geographic and clinical diversity when using AI. Models developed outside India may require justification and validation in representative Indian populations. Bias, generalisability and subgroup performance matter because even ‘95% accurate’ means little without asking — accurate at what, in whom, and against which reference standard? Approval is also a continuous process as algorithms can be retrained, software can be upgraded, while performance can drift. The CDSCO discusses change in management, retraining, rollback, version control and post-market surveillance of the system.
Guidelines, not law
India’s AI regulation is outlined in policy papers of NITI Aayog, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. In 2018, NITI Aayog released the National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, which named health care a priority. ICMR then, in 2023, issued ethical guidelines for AI in health care, stressing the need for accountability, fairness and patient autonomy. In November 2025, the Electronics & IT Ministry’s AI Governance Guidelines chose not to propose a separate AI law, leaving each sector’s regulator to act.
In February 2026, the Health Ministry launched the Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India (SAHI), which addresses governance, data, validation, deployment and monitoring of AI across healthcare. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has developed AI-specific lifecycle approaches, including predetermined change-control plans for defined future modifications. Europe combines medical-device regulation with the EU AI Act, which adds requirements for high-risk AI such as risk management, data quality and human oversight.
Way forward
The new guidance raises a larger question: can a technology that decides who is sick and who is sent home be governed by guidelines alone? India’s guideline-led approach has enabled regulators to move quickly without waiting for Parliamentary legislation. While its insistence on Indian data is ahead of many similar guidelines elsewhere, a dedicated statute for AI-enabled medical devices could make Indian validation mandatory for high-risk tools, clarify liability, and create a public registry of approved AI devices.
The question is whether technologies that can influence life-and-death decisions should continue to rely on guidance built on an 80-year-old law or be governed by a clear statutory framework that patients and clinicians can trust.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Greetings from the Brazil-Argentina border, where waterfalls are flowing at near-record rates
IGUAZÚ NATIONAL PARK, Argentina — Few times in my life have I felt the enormity and power of nature. Standing at the edge of Iguazú Falls, on the Brazil-Argentina border, was one of them.
Iguazú isn't just one imposing fall, but a complex of cascades spanning more than a mile across both countries. A rain-soaked October in Brazil has sent near-record volumes of water surging over its towering cliffs. Scientists link the relentless rains to this year's Super El Niño, causing extreme weather events across the globe.
But what a spectacular force of nature for the lower-than-average number of tourists who braved the deluge this month. The roar of the rushing Iguazú river under your feet penetrates your body; your eyes strain to keep up as the rusty swells disappear over the steep precipice. 
One day during my recent visit, officials registered nearly 12 million liters (more than 3 million gallons) of water per second tumbling over the falls. That's 10 times the normal flow. As the Iguazú river's red, muddy waters raced furiously toward the falls' edge, they lapped the bottom of the narrow metal catwalks that usually hover a few feet above the falls during normal-rainfall years.  
Officials closed the spectacular walkways as the river level kept rising. When asked why access was shut off, the national park's director simply said, "It just keeps raining." 
That's an understatement. I'm still drying out.

Max Verstappen: Red Bull driver hits out at 'unacceptable' bumpy United States GP surface at COTA amid safety concerns
Max Verstappen has criticised the bumpy surface at Circuit of The Americas ahead of this weekend's race in Austin, Texas; watch every United States GP session live on Sky Sports F1, starting with first practice at 6pm on Friday evening
Friday 23 October 2026 00:28, UK
Max Verstappen revealed concerns over the state of his spine as he unleashed a scathing criticism of the "out of control" bumpy track surface at Circuit of The Americas.
The four-time world champion arrives in Austin for Sunday's United States Grand Prix after claiming his first two victories of the season in back-to-back races.
Speaking to the media on Thursday, Verstappen was unexpectedly passionate over the state of the circuit, which is generally considered as one of the most popular among the drivers on the F1 calendar.
"You see also the track state from what I saw in WEC (World Endurance Championship), it was extremely badly bumpy," Verstappen said.
"I'm not really looking forward to that to be honest, for your spine. I was joking about that in the last race but it's not really a joke to be honest because we mentioned this already for years that it's actually getting a bit out of control.
"I'm sure it's going to be quite tough to find the right compromises around this track in places where it's just extremely bumpy. I don't know how our car is going to respond to that."
The Red Bull driver appeared to be urging the event organisers to place greater emphasis on improving the surface for the event in future.
"Of course, you can use the excuse that the soil is the problem, but then you should have known that you need to make sure that you reinforce it more," Verstappen continued.
"I love this track. I love this place. It's one of the best layouts ever and it's one of the venues, best cities to be at. But for me, the bumps that we have are unacceptable.
"Over time, they've been grinding a little bit here and there, but it's just putting a plaster on the big problem - that's just what's coming underneath.
"That's what you need to actually tackle in the first place. Of course, it means you need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time, but honestly, that's the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control."
Verstappen then explained that medical checks had shown that "the bottom end" of his spine "doesn't look that great".
The 29-year-old said: "That I think sometimes people don't really understand that because I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great, the spine.
"I know that's part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it's of course also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years.
"Now, if we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then, you are going to suffer with that much more."
Norris: I need to take headache tablets
Reigning world champion Lando Norris revealed that he takes headache tablets before driving at certain tracks due to their bumpiness.
Norris also explained that if COTA was a brand-new circuit, it wouldn't meet the requirements to be added to the calendar.
"If you build a new track now, the rules, the regulation of building a new track, the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small," Norris said.
"It certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what those regulations are now, but it's an old track, not a new track.
"It's pretty bad. There's a lot of places… I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it's so bumpy and you're hitting your head pretty hard against the headrests and things because of the bumps. It's certainly not a nice thing.
"There's not much we can do. We complain about it. It's something we've brought up many, many times, but there's only so much we can complain about things."
Mercedes driver George Russell said the bumpy nature of the circuit is "just part of racing," but expressed concern over the general standard of surfaces throughout the year.
"It's bumpy, but I think it's just part of racing," Russell said.
"I'd say my general view is F1 tracks probably need to be repaved every couple of years just to make it a bit more consistent because we're going to tracks now where tarmac's coming up, it's falling apart, it's causing more issues than not.
"We're not an IndyCar or an F2 car that run their ride heights, reasonably high. Our ride heights are 10mm at the end of the straight, a centimetre from the ground, so any time you bump you really feel it.
"The side profile of the tyres now since we've been at the 18-inch is substantially smaller.
"The circumference of the tyre is the same. The circumference of the rim is far greater, so you've lost all of that effective suspension in the tyre, which was a damper, which we kind of don't have anymore. Not ideal, but not much we can do."

OpenAI’s venture capital arm as well as Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund are investing in Coherence Neuro, a startup developing a brain implant to detect and treat cancer.
The investments are part of a $45 million seed funding round for Coherence and reflect Big Tech’s burgeoning interest in brain data. Coherence’s CEO and cofounder Ben Woodington says there is “growing synergy” between the big AI labs and companies building devices to decode the brain, known as brain-computer interfaces.
“The idea of capturing data to train better models and use it to optimize treatments is going to be super important,” he says. “The AI companies seem to be aligned with this thesis as well—that this novel data source is going to be valuable.”
Woodington says AI is a “perfect use case” for brain-computer interfaces because developers of these devices generate massive datasets that are too large for humans to analyze themselves. AI models can help read raw neural data and link it to actions, such as moving a computer cursor or producing synthesized speech.
In January, OpenAI announced that it was directly investing in a new brain-computer interface company, Merge Labs, cofounded by its billionaire CEO Sam Altman. Merge Labs came out of stealth with $252 million in initial funding to pursue ultrasound technology that can decode information from the brain. At the time, OpenAI said it was funding Merge Labs because of a belief that brain-computer interfaces “will create a natural, human-centered way for anyone to seamlessly interact with AI.” (The name Merge Labs comes from the idea popular in Silicon Valley that humans will eventually merge with machine intelligence.)
Thiel’s VC firm has also backed Elon Musk’s Neuralink as well as CTRL-labs, the creator of a wristband that translates neural signals from arm and hand movements that was acquired by Facebook in 2019.
Rather than focusing on restoring function for paralyzed individuals, San Francisco–based Coherence is developing AI models to decode subtle electrical signals associated with brain tumors. The company says it already knows how to detect these signals in animals to determine whether cancer is growing, shrinking, or recurring. The team is working to translate these findings for human research and, eventually, clinical trials.
This summer, Coherence briefly tested the recording ability of its implant in the brains of three people who were already undergoing brain tumor removal surgery at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia. The implant was in place for roughly 30 minutes before being removed, providing an initial safety check. Next, Coherence is testing both the recording and stimulation capabilities of the device in an additional seven patients.
The implant is also designed to emit mild electrical stimulation to halt the growth of tumors. The idea is that over time, the device would learn to detect signals associated with cancer and provide real-time treatment. Coherence plans to use the new funding to launch a clinical trial to implant the device long-term in patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain cancer. The company also aims to develop implants to treat cancers in other parts of the body.
“Coherence's approach to developing a cancer therapy capable of improving from data is incredibly innovative,” Ian Hathaway, partner at the OpenAI Startup Fund, says in a statement. “We are proud to be backing them on this exciting mission.”
Woodington says that OpenAI will not have access to its data. “There's nothing in the contracts or arrangements that would mean that we would share, or they would have access to, any brain data or other health data that we're generating,” he says.
That is seemingly different from OpenAI’s relationship with Merge Labs. In its January announcement, OpenAI said it would “collaborate with Merge Labs on scientific foundation models and other frontier tools to accelerate progress.”

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

Swiggy’s consolidated net loss narrowed 16% YoY to ₹922 Cr in Q2 FY27 but widened 17% from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. Instamart’s segment loss increased to ₹764 Cr from ₹651 Cr in Q1 FY27, offsetting an improvement in food delivery profitability. Operating revenue grew 36% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹7,571 Cr, while total expenses rose 30% YoY to ₹8,703 Cr. Foodtech major Swiggy reported a consolidated net loss of ₹922 Cr in the September quarter of FY27, narrowing 16% from ₹1,092 Cr in the year-ago quarter. However, its loss widened 17% from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue increased 36% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹7,571 Cr, according to its stock exchange filings. Including other income of ₹212 Cr, total income stood at ₹7,783 Cr. Swiggy’s consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹760 Cr from ₹695 Cr a year earlier and ₹651 Cr in Q1 FY27, with higher losses at Instamart and its newer businesses weighing on profitability. Across its consumer-facing businesses, gross order value (GOV) increased 25% YoY to ₹20,793 Cr. Average monthly transacting users rose 21% to 27.8 Mn. Total expenses increased 30% YoY to ₹8,703 Cr. The purchase of stock-in trade rose about 55% YoY to ₹3,607 Cr, while employee expenses lowered by about 2% to ₹676 Cr. Food delivery continued to be the bread winner for Swiggy, with operating revenue increasing by 22% YoY to ₹2,338 Cr along with a 39% jump in operating profit to ₹349 Cr. “Our food delivery business delivered its highest ever profits and margins while we continue to unlock new category growth through Toing, our standalone offering for affordable meals,” Swiggy cofounder, MD, and group CEO Sriharsha Majety said. Instamart EBITDA Loss Peaks Ahead Of Inventory Model Pivot Meanwhile, Instamart’s revenue contribution continued to pick pace during the quarter. The quick commerce arm’s revenue grew by 33% YoY to ₹1,306 Cr while operating loss increased by 3% to ₹749 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier and ₹778 Cr in Q1 FY27. Adjusted EBITDA margin improved marginally to -9.7% of GOV from -9.8% in the preceding quarter. Swiggy said it believes Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA losses peaked in Q2 FY27. Amid mounting losses, the company announced today that it would begin pivoting Instamart to an inventory-led model by the middle of the ongoing December quarter (Q3 FY27). The company completed its pivot to an Indian-Owned and Controlled Company (IOCC) within the previous quarter, enabling it to move Instamart to this model. The company is eyeing shifting Instamart to the inventory model within the upcoming three quarters. "This has the potential to add 80 bps to Instamart’s contribution margin when fully rolled-out while giving us greater flexibility and control over assortment, pricing, availability and day-to-day operations. As we transition to the inventory model, we expect to improve our overall working capital cycle by 8-10 days which should offset the additional investment in holding of the inventory on our balance sheet," the company said. During the quarter under review, Instamart’s contribution margin stood at -1% of GOV, deteriorating 82 basis points sequentially while GOV increased 31% YoY and 17% QoQ to ₹9,230 Cr in Q2 FY27. Swiggy attributed the sequential decline in margins to targeted pricing investments to reactivate dormant users and encourage repeat purchases, changes in customer and category mix, and the initial costs of new dark stores. The renewed spending follows Instamart’s achievement of contribution breakeven in Q1 FY27, after which Swiggy stepped up investments to accelerate growth. Instamart added 1.3 Mn average monthly transacting users sequentially, taking the total to 14.8 Mn. Orders increased 29% YoY to 130.3 Mn, while net average order value rose 4% to ₹506. Over two months after attaining the IOCC (Indian-Owned and Controlled Company) tag, Swiggy announced that it will shortly commence transitioning its quick commerce business, Instamart, to an inventory-led model. Swiggy expects the transition to improve Instamart’s working capital cycle by 8-10 days. “As we have mentioned in our previous communications, this has the potential to add 80 bps to Instamart’s contribution margin when fully rolled-out while giving us greater flexibility and control over assortment, pricing, availability and day-to-day operations,” the company said. The inventory model will give Instamart greater control over product assortment, pricing, availability and day-to-day operations in comparison to its current model where Instamart operates as a marketplace hosting seller entities. Eternal’s quick commerce arm Blinkit was the first to complete the inventory-led model pivot. The company has seen a significant improvement in its bottom line performance since then. Blinkit has emerged as the largest revenue contributor for Eternal, contributing ₹19,152 Cr to the company's total ₹24,138 Cr operating revenue for Q2 FY27. Swiggy has been bidding to undertake a similar transition for some time now. Its initial May 2026 special resolution to become an IOCC failed after receiving 72.36% of shareholder votes in favor, narrowly missing the required 75% threshold It managed to get shareholder approval to enable the transition earlier in August. Today, the company said its domestic ownership has increased to over 58%. Instamart Margins Under Pressure Swiggy’s quick commerce margins further weakened in the September quarter (Q2 FY27). The quick commerce business reported a contribution margin of -1% of gross order value (GOV), compared with -0.2% in Q1 FY27 on the back of higher spending on pricing and customer retention. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹778 Cr in the preceding quarter. Its net order value rose 34.8% year-on-year to ₹6,594 Cr, while Swiggy added 69 net dark stores during the quarter, taking the network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities. “Contribution margin was -1.0% of GOV within the range guided earlier, as we added 69 net stores, taking the network to 1,240 stores across 133 cities, and invested in differentiated assortment, availability and service quality,” the management added. While Instamart NOV grew 13.4% sequentially to reach ₹6,594 Cr and orders were up 29.3% YoY to 130 Mn, the adjusted EBITDA loss rose to ₹895 Cr in the quarter. At the consolidated level, Swiggy’s revenue from operations increased 36.1% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr in Q2 FY27. Its net loss narrowed 15.6% year-on-year to ₹922 Cr, but widened from ₹791 Cr in Q1 FY27. Alberta's referendum count still not complete, results to be delayed
Results delayed, not expected to be released on Thursday as required
The final ballots for Alberta's remaining referendum questions have still not been counted, and Elections Alberta has no estimate for completion.
In a statement issued shortly after 1:30 a.m. MT on Thursday, officials with the Elections Alberta media team said its teams had not yet completed counting all of the ballots.
"Our teams continue to work around the clock and we are not estimating a time for completion for Oct. 22, 2026," agency officials wrote. "We knew hand counting the referendum was going to be a monumental task."
'Just hasn’t been possible'
In an interview on Wednesday evening, as the deadline for the final count approached, officials with Elections Alberta confirmed that the agency had called in additional staff to help get the work completed overnight but that it wasn't enough.
"Despite the efforts of more than 47,000 election workers, it just hasn't been possible," officials said. "We'll continue to count ballots until the job is done."
Elections Alberta had previously said it had a 48-hour deadline from the closing of the polls on Monday to complete the count and publish the results in order to meet the parameters set under Alberta's referendum regulations.
- Alberta premier says UCP must be pro-Canada, separatists can 'join a different party'
- More than 4 in 5 Edmonton voters want to stay in Canada, early Alberta referendum count suggests
However, in their statement on Thursday, election officials said that the legislation was "silent" on a deadline for a vote containing more than seven questions.
"Note the legislation is silent after 7+ questions ... it's 12 hrs for 1 to 2; 24 hours for 3 to 4; 36 hours for 5 to 6," the statement reads.
Alberta's referendum regulations dictate that a count must be completed "48 hours after the close of voting on referendum voting day for a referendum in which 7 or more questions are put to the electors."
Elections Alberta had a strategy set to tackle the historic referendum, first counting the ballots for Question 10 — which explored the possibility of Alberta separation — before moving on to the nine remaining questions that ask Albertans to weigh in on a series of questions about constitutional issues and immigration policies.
As of Thursday morning, 97 per cent of polling stations were reporting across Alberta.
Complete voter turnout won't be known until all votes have been counted, but Elections Alberta was expecting record turnout.

Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's access after Starlink row
- Published
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's internet access, Donald Trump has said.
The US president was speaking hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk has previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russia.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report he had put pressure on Musk to restore access to the service, but when asked about it said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration has previously insisted it did not instruct Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move which has been criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Ukraine relies on Starlink - owned by Musk's SpaceX company - for a range of battle communications and early warning systems during Russian missile attacks.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
Speaking at a press conference , he said the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal, external reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX to ask for an explanation.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.
Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

Canadian diplomats based in U.S. advised to avoid appearing with midterm candidates
Global Affairs Canada says issuing advice to diplomats around elections is routine
The government of Canada has issued advice to all embassy and consulate staff to avoid appearing with U.S. midterm candidates, according to a source with knowledge of the notices.
Two separate notices were sent out in the last month, the source said.
Those instructions, which Global Affairs Canada describes as routine, come as Trump administration officials level accusations of "potential interference in U.S. elections" at Canadian officials.
In addition, the source said the government told diplomatic staff to be careful with their social media, not pick sides and not pose for photos with candidates. Bloomberg first reported news of the government notices.
The source characterized the advice as basic reminders.
"As part of regular business, Global Affairs Canada provides instructions to its Canadian missions abroad. Government officials are always instructed to limit public events and stakeholder engagement during election periods in their host country," a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada separately told CBC News.
The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" on Wednesday that lists a number of instances it alleges could amount to "potential" interference, including a reference to Bernadette Jordan, Canada's consul general in Boston, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates last week.
The source told CBC News that the most recent bulletin was sent out last week before the U.S. Embassy issued its statement.
The embassy statement came after two Trump administration officials — trade adviser Peter Navarro and U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra — warned Canadians not to get involved in the U.S. midterms.
Hoekstra specifically mentioned Industry Minister Mélanie Joly in his comments on potential meddling. Four of the nine instances listed in the embassy release also reference Joly's comments about Canada's counter-tariff strategy, going back to March 2025 when she was in charge of foreign affairs.
Joly has pushed back on assertions that she's trying to influence the midterms and did so again on Thursday, saying she has met with both Republicans and Democrats during recent trips to the U.S.
"That is diplomacy, that's what we do," she told reporters during a news conference in Toronto.
The embassy's recent release also mentions the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Regan ad that ran in the U.S. last year and comments made by Premier Doug Ford.
Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.
"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."
Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."
"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.
The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates in border states like Michigan and Maine.
The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.
"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.
