Sherrock one of 24 'amateurs' taking on Littler
- Published
Women's world number three Fallon Sherrock has been named among 24 contestants bidding to beat Luke Littler and walk away with £501,000.
The 'amateurs' will each take on Littler in a single leg of 501 and anyone who can beat the two-time reigning world champion will be in line for the cash prize.
It is part of Netflix's new special 'Beat Luke Littler', which will be broadcast live from the Manchester Central Convention Complex on 30 October.
Sherrock has been a pioneering figure in darts since she became the first woman to win a match at the PDC World Championship when she beat Ted Evetts in 2019.
Fellow teenagers Mitchell Lawrie and Jayden Walker will also be among those hoping to defeat 19-year-old Littler, who shot to fame in 2024 when, aged 16, he reached the final of the PDC World Darts Championship.
Scotland's Lawrie, 15, became the first teenager to reach a WDF World Championship final last year, while he is a two-time world youth champion.
Walker, meanwhile, won the England International Open earlier this month to become the youngest winner of a senior WDF title - a record previously held by Littler.
Littler became the youngest world champion in history by winning the 2025 world title at the age of 17 - a title he defended 12 months later.
The audition process took place across London and Manchester in September and started with participants trying to complete a leg of 501 in 24 darts or fewer.
Successful players then progressed to an interview with the show's producers before a final stage assessment with a judging panel, which included 16-time world darts champion Phil Taylor, Matchroom founder Barry Hearn and professional darts player and TV pundit Laura Turner.

A man accused of making threats while armed with “improvised nunchucks” at a Western Australian MP’s electorate office could have been holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, a court has been told.
John Lawrence Smart appeared on Thursday in the WA magistrates court where his lawyer expressed concern for his mental health. He was not required to enter a plea.
Smart was accused of making verbal threats at the office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley in the inner-Perth suburb of Victoria Park on Wednesday afternoon.
He was charged on Thursday with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making an unlawful threat and possessing cannabis. Police alleged Smart “made verbal threats while in possession of an improvised martial arts weapon (nunchucks)”.
During the court hearing, the highly agitated 56-year-old held his head in his hands and said he had been a musician for 20 years and he was holding claves.
“People, they don’t understand what I’m going through,” he said from the dock. Smart claimed people had “destroyed” his head.
Prosecutors said Smart entered Beazley’s office physically agitated and screaming, and holding two pieces of wood tied together.
He had a second similar implement attached to his belt, the police prosecutor said.
Smart allegedly demanded to see the politician while raising one of the implements above his head in a threatening manner before leaving the premises.
Smart’s lawyer said he was known to carry percussion sticks in the community and play drums.
The magistrate Heidi Watson suggested to the prosecutor that Smart might have been holding “drumsticks”.
The court heard Smart had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia and displayed delusional persecutory beliefs. He believed he had the “devil inside him”.
Watson ordered that Smart remained in custody for further medical assessment.
Beazley earlier said two of her staff were present in the electorate office when Smart allegedly entered.
“It was confronting,” she said in a social media post. “My staff did an amazing job and did everything right.”
No one was injured in the alleged incident, which comes after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was struck by a 4WD vehicle outside her electorate office in northern Victoria on Monday.
That incident sparked a nationwide debate about whether public officials were sufficiently protected from threats against their safety.
The WA premier, Roger Cook, said state parliament had been shocked by both incidents.
“We have got to start to turn the temperature down,” he said.
Cook said discussions were under way about potential upgrades to security measures to protect parliamentarians and their staff.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe at work, at home and in their communities,” he said.
“It’s not OK for people to take out their aggressions, their disagreements on staff in a politician’s office.”
Cook said security measures could be improved at state parliament, but they must be balanced with the need to maintain public access.
The Labor leader said he would support making an allowance available to MPs for security upgrades at their homes.
Beazley is the Labor state minister for local government and the daughter of former federal Labor leader Kim Beazley.
Smart was scheduled to return to the same court next Thursday.

Last year, we reported on Red Viper, a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo’s famously failed red-on-black “portable” 3D headset from the ’90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color, has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame.
Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy’s four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color’s readme files explain how the emulator’s game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8×8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash, for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game.
The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force, where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements.

Christina Applegate, the actor who has been one of the most visible faces of multiple sclerosis since her 2021 diagnosis, made a stunning revelation this week: She does not have MS after all. And her doctors still don’t know what is causing her debilitating symptoms.
What Christina Applegate’s misdiagnosis reveals about MS
About 15 percent of MS diagnoses may be wrong. How is that possible?
“I’m back at square one,” Applegate told fellow actor Jamie Lynn Sigler, who does have MS, on Sigler’s podcast MeSsy. “I was not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”
It is a harrowing predicament for Applegate, and hopefully her medical team is able to get her the diagnosis and treatment she needs. But the fact is, her experience is not unique. Even as more and more Americans get diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, misdiagnosis remains all too common. According to one meta-analysis, roughly 15 percent of MS diagnoses may actually be false positives.
How could such a common medical condition — roughly 1 million Americans are living with the disease, about one in every 350 people — remain such a mystery? After Applegate’s announcement, I called some leading experts on MS to ask why diagnosing the disease is such a challenge, and what they want people to know. Here’s what I learned.
Why MS can be challenging to diagnose
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune condition: The body mistakenly attacks cells meant to protect your brain and spinal cord, and the resulting damage interrupts nerve signals and causes the disease’s telltale symptoms of motor impairment, tingling sensations, and vision problems. Some people experience a rollercoaster of relapses and remissions; others see the disease steadily progress, eventually leading to serious disability.
The reality is, scientists still don’t really know what causes MS to develop, said Dr. Andrew Solomon, a neurologist at the University of Vermont who specializes in MS. Smoking is a known risk factor. Obesity and metabolic problems play a role, but we need more research. Even the precise role of genetics remains something of a mystery. “We don’t really know what causes or triggers the autoimmune response in any given individual,” Solomon said.
And that’s where the challenge in diagnosing it begins.
First, the testing can be imprecise; there is not a single test that reliably diagnoses MS. If a doctor suspects their patient may have MS, they usually undergo an MRI, which their physicians then scour for lesions that are typically associated with the disease. But those scans are still subject to interpretation: Other rare conditions sometimes resemble MS in imaging, as can diseases of blood vessels in the brain. You can also receive a spinal fluid analysis to check for abnormalities in your immune system, which the vast majority of MS patients have.
The nature of MS symptoms adds to the difficulty. They can often be vague early on: brain fog or fatigue or a general malaise. The tingling or vision problems can be similar to symptoms for other conditions that are not MS, and they are easily dismissed if they go into temporary remission, as often happens during the initial phases of the disease.
“Neurological symptoms sometimes can be vague — numbness, pins and needles — and it’s usually short-lived,” Dr. Saud Sadiq, chief research scientist and director of the Tisch Multiple Sclerosis Research Center of New York, told me. “Unless they’re taken seriously initially, they may be ignored because by the time the patient goes through the healthcare system and is actually referred to a neurologist, the symptoms have abated.”
If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence?
One 2025 study by Solomon and his colleagues found that 40 percent of people who had later been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis were initially misdiagnosed with a different disease.
“Because it’s so heterogeneous, it doesn’t present in the same way in everybody and can have varying severity, it can be hard to diagnose sometimes,” Solomon said.
Lastly, when people are experiencing debilitating symptoms, there is pressure to deliver some diagnosis — and that may push some doctors to leap to MS even if they are not sure, Solomon said. The recent advent of effective treatments that help manage the disease’s symptoms, especially when it is caught early, may add to that pressure, even if the better course would be to continue monitoring the person before they start a medication.
“There may be a lot of clinicians who, if they can’t find a better explanation than MS, may be inclined to diagnose MS, even if they don’t really meet our diagnostic criteria, because they’re worried about missing a window of opportunity to treat somebody,” Solomon said.
There is reason to hope the MS misdiagnosis problem could get better. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society released new diagnostic criteria in 2024 that Solomon said more physicians should become familiar with to better distinguish MS from problems like migraines or vascular disease. And because imaging is involved in diagnosis, there is optimism that AI could be a powerful new tool in delivering more accurate results.
What everyone should know about MS symptoms and diagnosis
The good news is that MS, when diagnosed properly, is a treatable condition these days. “The prognosis with new drugs is extremely good for long-term care,” Sadiq told me. “If patients stick to treatment at a good MS center, you can look forward to a life without disability in 2026.”
So it is worth being vigilant and talking to your doctor if you experience any concerning symptoms. You should seek care if you have numbness or pins and needles that persists for more than 24 to 48 hours, Sadiq said, or have motor problems, like one hand won’t work as you try to play piano. Dr. Annette Langer-Gould, who develops and evaluates programs for MS care at Kaiser Permanente, said numbness in your abdomen, chest or back, as opposed to your extremities, is a particular cause for concern. If one eye has normal vision and the other is blurred, that’s another good reason to get checked out.
If you do get tested, make sure the actual images of your MRIs end up being reviewed by an expert in MS. “The most common reasons the disease is still misdiagnosed are related to the providers’ lack of expertise usually in reading MRI scans,” Langer-Gould said. The spinal tap may sound scary, and doctors sometimes don’t recommend them because their insurance reimbursement is low — but they add to the confidence of a diagnosis. They are worth it, she said.
“American patients are very afraid of the spinal tap,” Langer-Gould said. “My message to patients is: Listen, just get the spinal. This way we’ll be sure.”
And do not be afraid to seek a second opinion for such a serious diagnosis, Sadiq added. Every state has a recognized MS center. If your doctor is diagnosing you with MS, ask directly: What’s the evidence? If your doctor is recommending that you start treatment, it could also be worth checking whether they have a relationship with a pharmaceutical company that affects how you perceive their judgment, Langer-Gould said.
People who have already been diagnosed may also be shaken by the Applegate news and question whether their own diagnosis might be wrong. Solomon said that folks should have a frank conversation with their physician about how exactly their case met the diagnostic criteria. With proper imaging and the spinal fluid tests, you can get to a confident diagnosis for the vast majority of people. But be your own advocate to make sure you’re satisfied.
“For many people, the diagnosis actually can be very straightforward,” Solomon said. “We really have no question about what it is.”

The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.
Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.
It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.
Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.
“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.
Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.
“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.
She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.
“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.
“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”
Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.
“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.
After the attack, Nathaniel wrote: “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”
He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.
Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.
“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”
The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.
Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.
On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”

Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives in November. A staggering 13 years and two console generations after the release of its predecessor, the long-awaited sequel has effectively become one of gaming’s holy grails—a title that some thought they’d never actually see, its development cycle so legendarily long that there’s a dedicated “we got [x] before GTA 6” meme.
The latest criminal opus lets players control Jason and Lucia, a modern-day Bonnie and Clyde, and bears all the hallmarks of Rockstar's incredible attention to detail. Leonida, the open-world setting based on Florida, looks almost impossibly vast yet meticulously detailed, with its own weather systems and hundreds of animal species roaming around.
It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing.
The Human Cost of AAA
At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is. On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade. Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition).
Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online. With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game.
Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.
The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis. It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios. Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches.
Take 2025’s Battlefield 6 as an example. Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation. A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though).
It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch.
With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback. Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”)
Same Old, Same Old
Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games. It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns.
However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience. Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost. Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay.
The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways. Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer. But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments.
Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2? Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it?
Less Is More
The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller.
That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles. In short, rediscover the “AA”-scale game.
The textbook example of how successful this can be is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded. The RPG earned rapturous reviews and endless fan acclaim, celebrated for its challenging dodge-and-parry twist on turn-based combat, its stunning world—a breathtaking blend of belle epoque and dark fantasy imagery, wrapped in a gorgeous painterly flourish—and its mature and emotionally complex story of explorers battling the inevitability of death.
In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either. Clair Obscur has motion-capture performances, a voice cast featuring Hollywood heavyweights like Charlie Cox and Andy Serkis, a full orchestral score, and dazzling visuals. It even packs a solid 60-odd hours of playtime, making it feel significant and not daunting. It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026.
While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff. The game was hugely successful for its budget, letting the studio continue without resorting to painful layoffs. Sandfall’s success isn’t a one-off. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences.
The Not-Quite Bleeding Edge
Another major benefit of aiming smaller is that it lets companies mitigate rising development costs for themselves and consumers. The memory crisis is forcibly extending the hardware life cycle, delaying new console generations and blocking supplies of powerful PC graphics cards, leaving many players without the means to reap the benefits of the most demanding games.
As Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi—no stranger to hugely ambitious games with incredibly long development cycles—says, “There isn't a single console that you can say, ‘As long as I have this, I'll be able to play everything, to do everything.’ Personally, I think that over the course of the next 10 years, if someone said, ‘Here's the next generation of consoles,’ the market and the audience are not necessarily going to just jump over.”
Hamaguchi says the industry will still straddle the lower-spec options, like a Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch 2, providing broader experiences to a wider base. It won't be so much about cutting-edge technology, but how developers can compete in game design. "I think we're going to be entering an age where that's really the focus of competition,” he says.
Sadly, this approach has one big problem: Developers are already trying it but failing to draw investment. There’s no easy answer—investors follow the money, and the money points to GTA-scale games, even though AAA development increasingly leaves carnage in its wake.
Even Rockstar appears to realize the current approach is unsustainable, with studio veteran Phil Hooker telling Bloomberg that “the engine, the tools, and the team we've built during the [GTA VI] project will allow us to do things more quickly” in the future. Hopefully, good news for fans who fear another decade-long wait for GTA VII.
Grand Theft Auto VI will be a success, and its longevity is already certain. But when every other publisher sees the inevitable slate of sales records the game will shatter, they’d do well to think twice before chasing it—the games industry might not survive if they do.

Canada Post starting weekend parcel delivery in Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa this fall
Financially troubled Crown corporation gives update on restructuring
Canada's national mail carrier says it has begun delivering parcels on the weekend to homes in Ottawa and Montreal, with plans to expand to Toronto in late November.
The financially troubled Crown Corporation also says it plans to provide weekend delivery to other urban centres like Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary next year.
It aims to offer weekend delivery to seven million households by the end of 2027.
Private carriers have successfully outpaced Canada Post by offering weekend and evening delivery for years. Until recently, the Crown corporation had said it was unable to do the same because of the previous collective agreement it had with its mail carriers.
Senior leadership provided an update on Canada Post's restructuring efforts and finances during its annual public meeting on Thursday.
Canada Post continues to lose money, including $482 million in the first half of 2026 before tax. Leadership said they expect the company will still need to rely on federal loans to stay afloat.
Canada Post employees and supporters rally at Canada Post headquarters in Ottawa during the November 2024 national strike that completely shut down mail service in the country. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)
"The continued reliance on government funding is not a long-term solution and we are committed to reduce the reliance on government support as quickly as we can," said Rindala El-Hage, Canada Post's chief financial officer.
Despite the continued losses, Canada Post is showing signs of early recovery, El-Hage said, as customers return after a long period of labour disruption.
Parcel revenue grew by 20.7 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. Operating costs also declined by $119 million.
The Canadian Union of Postal Workers (CUPW) and the corporation signed a new collective agreement in June which stays in effect until 2030.

After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.

More than 80 nutrition researchers and experts are calling on the White House to release the federal government’s proposed definition of ultra-processed foods, after its unveiling in August was canceled at the last minute under pressure from major food companies.
The Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, led by cardiologist Dariush Mozaffarian, is scheduled to meet with the Office of Management and Budget on Friday to present the petition. The Department of Health and Human Services wants the definition to be released before the upcoming midterms, said Mozaffarian, who spoke at the HHS event where the definition was originally slated to be announced.
“This is part of what the Make America Healthy Again movement that many independent voters and swing voters voted for,” Mozafarrian said. “I think HHS sees this as a win for the administration before the election to show they’re taking real action.” 
On the other hand, Mozaffarian said, the Consumer Brands Association, a food industry trade group, has argued that a proposed definition will raise food prices — a position he called “absurd and false,” but one that could make the White House nervous with midterms around the corner.

Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.
The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.
Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music and news criticising Pyongyang.
If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.
At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.
The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.
Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.
Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.
The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.
The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.
Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.
North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.
Speaking after a meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.
Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but may have to use alternative routes.
The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”
Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the Republic”.
“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was later overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for that day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.
Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of the Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.
Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.
However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.
France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big city mayors later in the day.
The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Elysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.
The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections that will choose Macron’s successor.

It’s getting harder to dodge “You Can See Everything” spoilers, but you know what I’ll never dodge? STAT’s award-winning journalism.
Speaking of, today’s newsletter features two stories from the illustrious Tara Bannow, who explains why CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz called a New York disability services program “a plague to the state.”
Telehealth companies eye GLP-1’s next act: addiction
Telehealth companies aren’t waiting for approval from the Food and Drug Administration to test the popular obesity medications GLP-1s for other indications. Their next target? Addictions like alcohol use disorder.
Experts are hopeful that these drugs can fill a significant unmet medical need, as the FDA has not approved a new medication for alcohol use disorder in two decades. The hype is certainly real. Telehealth brands are buying ads on Facebook. Biotech companies like Eli Lilly and Altimmune are testing drugs for their effect at curbing alcohol cravings.
But will these drugs actually work? Read more from STAT’s Katie Palmer.
‘A plague to the state’
Federal officials have announced their latest target for fraud in health care: New York’s Social Adult Day Care program.
The Medicaid-funded program provides socialization, personal care, and meals for adults with physical and cognitive disabilities, but federal officials say it’s rife with fraud. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz even called it “a plague to the state.”
Oz joined law enforcement officials in Queens at dawn on Tuesday as they searched offices and delivered warning letters to almost 100 providers informing them that their Medicaid billing far exceeded their peers and that they would be expected to provide documentation to support it. Two providers were arrested on Wednesday for allegedly defrauding Medicaid for more than $500,000.
New York is the latest state to come under the fire from the Trump administration’s war on fraud, which some say is disproportionately aimed at punishing blue states such as Minnesota and California. Read more from STAT’s Tara Bannow.
Personalized ‘prehab’ while awaiting liver transplant tied to better survival, study says
People who need a liver transplant face daunting odds against living long enough to receive one. An individualized exercise and diet program can improve their chances of survival while on the waiting list, a study published Wednesday in Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology found, with the frailest patients often benefiting the most.
A team from Northwestern Medicine and the University of Pittsburgh tested a home-based exercise program in 355 patients who had met with a physical therapist and a dietitian to design a plan aiming for 150 minutes of weekly activity.
Overall, two-thirds of patients did better on a frailty score that measures grip strength, chair stands, and balancing. And patients who attended at least three follow-up visits improved by at least 0.4 on that 4.5 frailty scale, associated with an approximately 50% lower risk of dying while on the waitlist. The authors hope to confirm these results in a larger trial. – Elizabeth Cooney
Health insurance premiums jumped 9% in 2026
Workplace health insurance coverage costs just keep rising.
The amount that workers pay in premiums for a family health insurance plan jumped 9% in 2026, to $7,471 on average, according to KFF’s 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey. Workers at small businesses faced even larger increases.
Premiums are jumping largely because the overall cost of health care is climbing. So far, employers have shouldered most of that increase, but it’s come at a cost: Small businesses are increasingly retreating from offering coverage to their workers and experts say that employers are reaching a “breaking point.” Premium increases could increase even further next year.
Tara has the full readout from the gold-standard survey, which puts some hard numbers to the nationwide feeling that health insurance is too expensive.
More Americans don’t have health insurance
Working-age U.S. adults without health insurance rose in 2026. And half of all uninsured people did not seek needed care because of cost concerns, according to a new survey.
The Commonwealth Fund Biennial Health Insurance Survey found that the uninsured rate rose from 8.9 percent in 2024 to 11.2 percent in 2026, a bump that they attribute to the expiration of Affordable Care Act marketplace premium tax credits and the rollback of pandemic-era protections that kept people enrolled in Medicaid.
The bad news is likely to get worse. In 2027, major Medicaid cuts and Affordable Care Act marketplace restrictions will make it even harder for Americans to access health insurance. Read more of the survey’s findings.

Michael Gray, the star of the 1970s “Shazam!” television series, died on Friday in Palm Desert from natural causes. He was 75.
Gray first got his break in television in 1972 when he was cast in NBC’s “The Little People” alongside Brian Keith and Shelly Fabares. Early in his career, he held several supporting roles across series including playing Marcia’s boyfriend Jeff on “The Brady Bunch” as well as appearing on “Dynasty,” “Marcus Welby, M.D.,” “Room 222” and “The Flying Nun,” as well in films such as “Run, Simon, Run,” “Beyond the Valley of the Dolls” and “Myra Breckinridge.”
In 1974, he joined the cast of “Shazam!” as Billy Batson, starring alongside John Davey and Les Tremayne in the series, which ran for three seasons until 1976. Gray became a teen idol, frequently appearing on the covers of Tiger Beat and other teen magazines.
Popular on Variety
“From my very first day on ‘Shazam!,’ Mike and Les [Tremayne] welcomed me like a king,” Davey said about Gray. “Mike was just a loving, sweet guy with a great sense of humor. He loved acting, loved doing the show and, in recent years, loved appearing at comic cons. He really enjoyed meeting and chatting with the fans. Mike was a wonderful man. I don’t think he ever stopped smiling.”
“Shazam!” was remastered in 2012 for distribution on DVD, which sparked a career resurgence for Gray. In recent years, he appeared in several episodes of the FX series “Archer” as one of the titular character’s boyhood idols, as well as appearing in “Surge of Power” on AMC’s “Comic Book Men.” When “Shazam! Fury of the Gods” released in 2023, Gray made a brief cameo where he interacted with Zachary Levi’s Captain Marvel as a nod to the original series.
Gray was born in Chicago on Sept. 2, 1951, and was raised in Miami Beach, Florida, before moving to Los Angeles to study acting at the Pasadena Playhouse and pursue his career in entertainment. After landing his role in “Shazam!,” Gray began to feel typecast and took a hiatus from acting. During this time, he worked in children’s theater education and men’s fashion, as well as owning and operating a floral business with his wife, Stacy.
Following the 2012 resurgence of “Shazam!,” Gray frequently attended fan conventions and reconnected with his fanbase while also pursuing roles in projects such as the “Surge of Power” franchise.
“I meet people [everyday] who say, ‘You have no idea what you did for me as a child.’ ‘You helped me get through life.’ ‘You made me the better man, or woman, that I am today,’” Gray told Fanboy Planet in 2012. “And that’s a nice feeling. I didn’t know the show had that much strength and power back then.”
Gray is survived by his wife, Stacy Benon Gray, whom he married in 1994; step-children Ryan Cooper and Laurel Cooper; and son-in-law Lee Barker.

‘Unacceptable’: India slams Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia, moves to help stranded pilgrims
An attack on King Fahd International Airport on Wednesday evening killed two people, including an Indian, while two Indians were among eight people injured.
India on Thursday expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia while condemning continued attacks by Houthi rebels on civil infrastructure, including a strike on Dammam airport that killed an Indian national, and backing the early restoration of peace and normalcy in West Asia.
The Indian side also said it is working with airlines and tour operators to facilitate the early return of Indian pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia because of the suspension of flights by Indian carriers following the recent escalation of hostilities.
An attack on King Fahd International Airport on Wednesday evening killed two people, including an Indian, while two Indians were among eight people injured. Another Indian was injured by debris from a drone intercepted over Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday.
“We strongly condemn the continued attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including the attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield in the Eastern Province on October 21,” the external affairs ministry said in a statement.
Such attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure are “completely unacceptable and must cease immediately”, the Indian side reiterated. “We stand in solidarity with the people and the Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its sovereignty, and hope that peace and normalcy would return to the region at the earliest,” it said.
While conveying condolences to the family of the Indian killed in Dammam and wishing the speedy recovery of the injured, the statement said the Indian embassy in Riyadh is in touch with Saudi authorities and providing assistance to the affected Indian nationals.
The latest attacks on Saudi infrastructure reflect the escalation of the conflict between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen. One Indian was killed, and 10 more were injured in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10.
External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on social media that the Indian embassy in Riyadh and the consulate in Jeddah are “engaging with concerned airlines and tour operators to facilitate the early return of affected [Indian] pilgrims”.
Jaiswal’s social media post followed a claim by AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi that 4,000 Indian pilgrims were stranded in Makkah and Madina after Indian carriers such as Air India, Indigo and Akasa Air cancelled flights.
Jaiswal said about 3,000 stranded Indian pilgrims have returned from Saudi Arabia on available flights over the past week. This was in addition to more than 10,000 pilgrims who were not stranded and returned to India during the same period. “Arrangements are being discussed to facilitate the return of other Umrah pilgrims at the earliest,” he said.
The Indian missions in Riyadh and Jeddah, with the support of community volunteers, are extending all possible welfare assistance to the pilgrims, Jaiswal said.
Nineteen Indians, including 11 seafarers, have been killed so far in the West Asia conflict, which was triggered by attacks by Israel and the US on Iran in February. Dozens more have been injured across West Asia. The Indian side has been concerned by these casualties and has repeatedly called for a return to dialogue and diplomacy while urging all stakeholders to stop attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure.

'Agent Layla': A sex assault victim went undercover to bring her abuser to justice. Now he's out on parole
Parole Board decision comes as victim receives praise for telling her story
A woman who went undercover to get a confession from the man who sexually assaulted her says she's "fed up" and "retraumatized" by a parole board decision to release him.
The parole board decision comes as Vienna Luke has received support from people across Canada and abroad who have heard her extraordinary story of going undercover as an RCMP agent in the CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla.
"I feel deflated," said Luke of the decision to release Justin Sewell early. "My story being out there is like, 'Wow, look.' But there's still so much work to be done."
18 years of fighting for justice. 6 months in prison. 7 months in a halfway house.
The parole board made its decision to release Sewell on Oct. 6, citing his low assessed risk to reoffend and his compliance and participation in therapeutic programs during his time in a halfway house.
Justin Sewell (left) was a trusted brother-in-law to Vienna Luke (second from right) and Shawnessy Luke (right). Vienna met him when she was 10 years old. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
As described in the Personally: Agent Layla podcast and in court documents, Sewell drugged, assaulted and photographed Luke in 2007 when she was 20 years old.
After wrestling for years with what really happened the night she was drugged into unconsciousness and assaulted, Luke decided in 2019 to report the assault to police after she and her sister, Shawnessy Luke, recorded a phone conversation with Sewell's ex-lover who said he disclosed putting ketamine in Vienna's drink. In court, Sewell has denied it was ketamine, but a provincial court judge found it was either ketamine or Valium.
RCMP proposed a plan to put Vienna Luke undercover, giving her the code name Agent Layla. They used emails to entice Sewell to meet her face to face at a hotel lounge at the Vancouver International Airport under the premise that him telling the truth might be a path back to family reconciliation.
In the recording from the sting, obtained by CBC and included in Episode 3 of the Agent Layla podcast, Vienna Luke pushes Sewell to describe the specific details of his offence. He admits to drugging and assaulting her, and to watching her through her bedroom window on two separate occasions.
Eventually, Sewell pleaded guilty to sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism.
Sewell was a successful veterinarian in the northern B.C. community of Fort St. John at the time of the assault. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
After what was described in court as an unusually lengthy sentencing hearing in which Sewell took the stand arguing that a self-diagnosed addiction to pornography was the root cause of his offences, a provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to two years less a day of house arrest in April 2025.
Seven months later, a panel of B.C. Court of Appeal judges overturned that decision and imposed a sentence of 33 months less a day to be served in prison.
After serving about six months in a federal institution, Sewell was granted day parole and transferred to a halfway house in April 2026.
Since then, according to notifications provided to his victims and viewed by CBC News, Sewell has been granted permission to leave the halfway house and travel to his home in Fort St. John or to "recreate" in Grande Prairie, Alta., for 70 days over a period of less than seven months.
Discrepancies in 2 Parole Board of Canada decisions made 6 months apart
The Parole Board first considered Sewell's applications to be granted full parole in an April 2026 face-to-face hearing. His case was up for review again six months later in early October. This time he was subject to a paper review, a parole decision-making process that assesses documents written about the offender's behaviour and programs they have completed, but does not interview the offender.
The two boards came to a few markedly different conclusions.
The parole board members in April 2026 found in their decision that Sewell "engaged in considerable rationalizing and minimizing" of his offences. Instead of addressing the "key issues leading to your violence," the board found he focused on "[his] use of pornography and the problems in [his] marriage, as though solving those particular problems was a solution also for the behavioural issues that led to the sexual assault."
"The Board believes that a day or full parole release to your home community is not adequate to the task of protecting the community from your risk."
With support of her sister Shawnessy Luke (left), Vienna Luke went undercover in her own case and obtained a confession. The sisters continue to work together seeking justice in the case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Six months later, despite letters from Vienna and Shawnessy Luke imploring the board to weigh heavily the findings of the April board members who interviewed Sewell and decided against full parole, the October parole board members found Sewell's "compliance, community adjustment, ongoing therapeutic involvement, and low assessed risk" support a reduction in supervision and that release on full parole "will not present an undue risk to society."
That board granted full parole on Oct. 6. Correctional Service Canada confirmed the end of Sewell's sentence is Jan. 1, 2028. For the 14 months that remain, Sewell is required to report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with females, and he is prohibited from accessing pornography.
'How is [he] allowed the freedoms to go on a recreational hunting trip?'
For Vienna Luke, it has been an intense time. On the one hand, she's received messages from podcast listeners commending her for sharing her story of confronting her abuser, which led to a conviction and prison time. On the other hand, she's found herself still advocating behind the scenes for justice in her case.
"I'm a person that chose to report," she said. "You can understand why people are just like, 'I'm going to move on with my life.'"
In the most recent parole board decision, board members cited a letter from the Luke sisters questioning the 70 days Sewell was allowed to leave the halfway house, including his release "for the purposes of a hunting trip."
Justin Sewell in a photo where he is hunting. This image is from before he faced the courts for his assault on Vienna Luke. Sewell is now under a 10-year prohibition on possessing firearms. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
The sisters say that in September they began to suspect that some of Sewell's trips might be to participate in hunting, an activity he described as an important hobby in court.
Concerned he might be violating a 10-year ban on using firearms, the Luke sisters say they called the Fort St. John RCMP non-emergency line to alert the police. They say the officer on the line told them Sewell had been granted permission to go hunting with an "approved associate."
Vienna Luke said she met with Correctional Service Canada and parole board officials to express her concerns.
"As they talked and continued to justify how they were handling him ... and their allowances to him, I started shaking. I was so upset," she said.
The sisters weren't worried for their personal safety. They live in Vancouver, about 800 kilometres from Fort St. John as the crow flies. Their concern was that the decision to grant him time to participate in a hobby was at odds with the seriousness of the crime.
"We had a hunch he was going hunting, but we didn't think he was approved to go hunting," said Vienna Luke.
"We were livid," said Shawnessy Luke.
CBC News reached out to Correctional Service Canada to confirm the details of Sewell's permission to go hunting. In an email, it says the organization cannot provide details of travel permits because of the Privacy Act.
The statement adds that "[w]hile we cannot talk about specifics of this case due to privacy, please note that if, at any time, an offender's risk increases or there is a change in their behaviour ... we take immediate action."
The Luke sisters' concerns were summarized by the parole board, who wrote in the October decision: "It is also concerning that your index offence involved violence and yet you are requesting to engage in an extended activity which involves weapons."
Vienna Luke wants systemic change
Vienna Luke knows the outcome of her case – a conviction in a historic sexual assault – is rare. But throughout the lengthy process since she first reported the assault seven years ago, she has found herself questioning whether the justice system is working for sexual assault survivors.
"You would think that maybe the fact he went to jail, he went to a halfway house, the justice system is telling me that I should feel grateful. Look at what you got," she said.
"I feel ungrateful. What did we do all this work for?"
Vienna Luke told her story in honour of other women who have told their stories of surviving sexual assault. (Vienna Luke/Submitted)
In interviews for the podcast and elsewhere, Vienna has emphasized she is telling her story to honour sexual assault victims who went before her. She told their stories, including their struggles with the justice system, which gave her strength in the hardest times.
Now she's receiving emails from other women telling her she has become a symbol of strength for them.
"I've come so far," she said. "To be in a place where I can speak about what happened to me, what was done to me publicly, and everything I did in this process is unbelievable and really I just feel so proud."

The row over the distribution of “experimental drug” meant for “clinical trials” to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) patients assumed political dimensions in the State, with the Opposition quick to latch on to the issue, demanding that the government assuage the concerns of the parents.
All hell broke loose on Tuesday, with parents of SMA children claiming that the SMA drug given free of cost at the SMA clinic in SAT Hospital was an “experimental drug” as the marking on the carton said “physicians’ samples/ for clinical trials only.”
Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan expressed concern whether “the sick children were being treated like mere guinea pigs” as well as shock at the Health Minister’s “criminal negligence.” On Wednesday, senior CPI(M) leader K.K. Shailaja too said the government cannot “change the drug just like that merely because it is cheaper.”
However, the fact remains that the decision to shift to the generic version of SMA drug had been taken during the previous government so that uninterrupted supply of the drug can be ensured. The purchase processes were initiated in February 2026 itself.
SAT Hospital authorities had clarified on Tuesday itself that no “experimental drug” was being given to children and that only the generic version of the original molecule, approved by the Central Drugs Standards Control Organisation (CDSCO) was given to the patients.
“We had a shortfall in the supply of the drug. On Monday, rather than send SMA patients away, we procured some samples of the generic version from Natco and distributed it. There is no change in the drug and the scaremongering about “experimental drugs” is unnecessary,” sources at SAT Hospital said.
“No experimental drug was given to SMA children. What was given was the generic version of Risdiplam, the patented original formula by Roche, now manufactured by the Indian firm Natco Pharma and which has been approved by drug regulatory bodies in the country. The drug is priced at 97% less cost than its patented version and makes it possible for the government to give the drug free of cost to more patients,” a hospital statement said.
On Wednesday, SAT Hospital authorities said they too back the physician samples. “We received the government supply on Tuesday evening and, hence, we opted to replace the drug,” Superintendent of SAT I. Riaz said.
SAT Hospital has been running an SMA clinic since 2022. At the time, Roche Pharma was the only firm licensed to produce and market the drug Risdiplam for SMA. The cost of one 60 ml bottle was ₹6.3 lakh.
Keralam is the only State to utilise public funds for providing free SMA treatment to children. With more children being identified with the disease and getting registered for free treatment, sustaining the free drug supply was becoming a problem.
It was in 2025, after the patent period of Risdiplam expired, Natco obtained the licence of the Drugs Control General of India to manufacture the generic version of Risdiplam. The generic drug is priced at ₹15,900 a bottle.
According to the National Policy for Rare Diseases (2021), manufacturing and licensing of drugs for rare diseases by Indian pharma firms is an important objective so that the precious medication can be accessible to more patients at a lower cost.
“The generic version has all regulatory approvals and is being used by all premier medical institutions in the country to treat SMA patients. Keralam cannot continue to procure the original molecule at high prices when an approved generic formulation is available at a fraction of the price. The government’s decision to embrace generics is a patient-centric move and it is highly commendable because it prioritises equitable access to life-saving drugs over vested commercial interests,” public health expert B. Ekbal said.
IMA representative N. Sulphi, too, pointed out that the controversy was nothing but a fallout of the rivalries between two pharma firms.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said the generic version of Risdiplam had been approved by an expert committee and that any concerns about the quality or efficacy of the drug were misplaced. The government’s only intention was to make the drug accessible to more patients, he said.

Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.
“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”
The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.
Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.
The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.
Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.
Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.
On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.
He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.
In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”
