As written, the updated terms and conditions will require companies to let Meta use automated software to "access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, webpages, or URLs" associated with the company in question. This includes the ability to create "test credentials," which are sometimes used to bypass paywalled content.
The updated policy applies only to Meta's business-related products and accounts. It won't affect normal users, whose public posts already fall under Meta's standard privacy policy, which allows the company to scrape those posts to train AI models.
When first posted, the updated terms explicitly said Meta could use the scraped data to "train" its products, strongly implying the data would be fed into AI models. The word "train" was removed from the terms sometime between Oct. 15 and 20, so it's unclear whether, or how, that slight language change affects what Meta may do with the data.
In October 2026, reporting from Harvard University's Nieman Journalism Lab revealed that Meta, the technology giant that owns and operates Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, among others, planned to change its commercial terms of service in a way that would allow it to freely collect data from the internet using bots and crawlers (a practice often called "scraping") to train artificial intelligence models. The terms of service document noted the updated terms would take effect Oct. 30.
Snopes found that Nieman Lab's reporting was generally accurate. The proposed new terms do appear to include a clause that would allow Meta to scrape data and information from the internet without paying to license it, including from news sites. Therefore we've rated this claim mostly true.
After the publication of Nieman Lab's story, however, Meta changed the language in the proposed update. That change, Snopes found, might affect Meta's ability to use that data to train AI models.
In email and phone statements to Snopes, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said the updated terms and conditions did not actually change how the company collected or used any data, and that the new paragraph was simply attempt at consolidating existing terms and conditions policies into one place.
Roberts also disputed the idea that the new terms and conditions language would be used to scrape data from news sites. "As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences," he said, referring to a file that tells web crawlers how they can access sites. "This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don't give us new rights that supersede those preferences."
Here's what to know about the proposed changes:
Meta's business model
The best way to understand the proposed changes is to review how Meta makes money. Mostly, that's through advertising. Put simply, companies pay Meta a lot of money in order to run advertisements on its social media platforms.
Because the vast majority of Meta's income comes from advertising, the company is incentivized to make it easy and effective for businesses to purchase that advertising. There are two main ways Meta does this.
First, advertisers want the ability to reach as many eyeballs as possible, so the more users there are on a given platform, the better. However, users are a limited resource — you can't add more more of them if everyone already has a Facebook account. Third-party data suggests Meta's social media platforms see approximately 3 billion active users each month, meaning that by now, Meta has mostly optimized the size of its advertising network.
Second, advertisers want as much data as possible, which allows them to target advertisements to specific users and see which advertisements are actually effective. Meta collects and stores practically everything it can, according to the company's large and sometimes convoluted privacy policies. (The YouTube creator Reject Convenience, who makes videos about data privacy, runs a second channel on which companies' privacy policies are read aloud. His video on Meta's policies is 2 hours, 22 minutes long.)
These two practices allow Meta to act as a one-stop shop for advertising. Instead of selling customer data to advertisers, Meta stores user data itself, using its own in-house software and algorithms to decide what advertisements to show to whom. On the business side, Meta also maintains tools that allow companies to adjust and experiment with their advertising techniques, relying on Meta's algorithms to do much of the heavy lifting.
Because Meta's platform is so big, it's effectively a must-have for smaller and medium-size digital businesses (including Snopes — we use it to advertise our newsletters and membership by buying ad space on Facebook and Instagram, according to CEO Chris Richmond). As with any software, using Meta's business products means accepting a set of terms and conditions and a privacy policy.
The previous terms and conditions (archived) for Meta business products appeared to mostly protect Meta from lawsuits. Under those terms, companies agreed to give Meta a license to intellectual property for the purpose of advertising, agree to abide by applicable U.S. laws when using Meta products (including legal restrictions on data sharing), and release Meta from some liabilities, such as actions carried out by a third party.
The changes, as featured in Nieman Lab
The updated terms (archived), which will go into effect Oct. 30, include several new sections that might expand Meta's authority, if accepted.
Most importantly is this paragraph from Section 1, presented as it appeared Oct. 15, when Nieman Lab reported its story:
You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users' use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products.
To put it bluntly, this language initially appears to give Meta permission to scrape all data on the websites of companies using Meta's business tools, including information that would normally be hidden behind a paywall.
Nieman Lab spoke to several media law experts for its report, all of whom agreed about the paragraph's purpose.
"This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market," said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney.
"For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves," said James Grimmelmann, a digital and information law professor at Cornell University.
As previously noted, Meta claims the updated terms of service are a simple consolidation of information, and do not change its ability to access and scrape data. Roberts, the company spokesperson, repeated that customers have the ability to opt out of data scraping by changing the settings in a website's robots.txt file, which theoretically controls how bots can access websites. (Some crawlers ignore the robots.txt file, according to Richmond, so Snopes uses additional protective measures to stop bots as well.)
According to Ars Technica, however, Meta's older terms and conditions documents mentioned scraping in limited circumstances, while the language in the updated terms and conditions is significantly broader. It could allow for data scraped for one particular use to be reused in an entirely different manner.
It's worth noting that publishers have filed several lawsuits against large AI companies, including Meta, arguing that the companies illegally scraped data protected by copyright in order to train artificial intelligence models, without compensating the publishers.
The second change
The claim that Meta reserves for itself the right to scrape companies' data for the purpose of training AI models relies on the inclusion of the word "train" in the terms of service contract. Here's the critical snippet from those terms again, as they appeared in Nieman Lab's Oct. 15 article: "… in order to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain advertising and business products."
When Snopes archived the terms of service for readers on Oct. 20, however, the word "train" was conspicuously missing. The Verge reported the same change on Oct. 17.
In its questions to Meta, Snopes asked why it removed the word "train" from the terms of service between Oct. 15 and 20, and whether that would affect how it planned to use the data.
The company provided the following statement in response:
"We removed 'train' because there was some confusion," it said. "As we previously said, the consolidation of terms were for business and advertising products, not scraping news websites."
When speaking to Roberts via phone, Snopes asked several times how the removal of the word "train" would affect how Meta used the data. Roberts never answered the question, but repeated that the change was made due to "confusion."
As such, it's unclear how the removal of the word "train" would affect how Meta uses any data it scrapes from websites who accept the new terms and allow data scraping in their robots.txt file.

Meta board placates Zuckerberg after threat to leave California if voters approve wealth tax measure
Polls suggest a tight result on Prop 40, as some tech barons threaten to move out of state if it passes
Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg, Reuters has reported, in a move spurred by a California ballot measure, part of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, that has sparked heated debate and hundreds of millions in campaign spending.
Under the deal, Zuckerberg will get non-voting shares he can sell to potentially foot a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event the proposal is approved, in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday.
Zuckerberg, the world's sixth richest person according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because Proposition 40, the ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth tax," could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.
Proposition 40 asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5 per cent tax on the state's billionaires, and needs over 50 per cent support to pass. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth upwards of $2 trillion US.
State health care programs would be the biggest beneficiaries of proceeds raised through the fund, with money also going to state food assistance programs and public education.
- Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
- How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
The parent company of Facebook and Instagram said Zuckerberg needs to continue to manage the company from its Menlo Park headquarters at a time of "unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry." Meta says it needs to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years to finance its AI-related growth plan.
Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027. Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20 per cent of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10 per cent of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill from Prop 40 without losing voting control.
Brin equates tax to Soviet-style oppression
Backers say California's measure would generate $100 billion US for health care, food assistance and education. But skeptics peg the revenue estimate at closer to $40 billion US and say it could also drive some billionaires out of the state, depriving California of future tax revenue and investment.
Sergey Brin, Google co-founder, has spent more than $100 million US to defeat the ballot measure.
"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don't want California to end up in the same place," Brin recently told the New York Times.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin is shown on Oct. 8 during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C. Brin has spent millions trying to defeat California's Proposition 40 ballot measure. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)
Darien Shanske, a law professor at the University of California-Davis, who helped draft the proposal, told CNBC that relocating wouldn't limit the tax exposure of the ultra wealthy. Any billionaire residing in the state on Jan. 1, would still be taxed, given the state's tax laws, he said.
Prop 40 is supported by, among others, California Democrat Ro Khanna in the House of Representatives and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
"Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?" Sanders said at a rally in California earlier this month.
Passage of the measure far from certain
The measure hasn't elicited a tidy split of progressives and Democrats in favour versus billionaires against, however.
Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, for example, has shrugged off the proposal.
"The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang told CBS News earlier this week. "I feel it's a privilege. It's a responsibility. And nothing would give me more joy than to be able to pay even more taxes."
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, seen at a Los Angeles campaign stop on Oct. 15, doesn't believe Proposition 40 is an adequate way to fund state services. (Mike Blake/Reuters)
Meanwhile, outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes Prop 40 and backs the Brin-introduced Proposition 42, which would seek to amend the state constitution to ban such tax proposals after Jan. 1, 2026.
Newsom's position earned a rebuke from outspoken actor Mark Ruffalo, who called it "beyond sad" on social media. Messaging directly to Newsom's account, Ruffalo said Democrats need someone who is "tough when it comes to the real imbalances people are struggling with every day: billionaires vs. people and the planet."
But current Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and the California Teachers Association (CTA) are also among the individuals and groups opposed to the measure, arguing that while well-intentioned, it is a complex and unsustainable funding measure. The CTA is focused on Proposition 3, which would raise funds through a state income tax hike on high earners.
Becerra's Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, is staunchly opposed to Prop 40.
California voters have only approved one in three citizen initiatives historically. As well, California ballot measures typically need robust early support, political analysts say, as history has shown the undecided are more apt to choose No when it comes to time to vote.
"California ballot measures tend to lose support over time, and if it's polling below 50 per cent in August, that's not a good sign for its prospects," John Pitney, a professor of politics at Claremont McKenna College, told Reuters in a report published Sept. 30.
A Citrin-Politico poll released this week indicated that, of those who took a position, 46 per cent of survey respondents favoured Prop 40 while 43 per cent were opposed.

Abby Choi got share of ex-husband’s luxury watch profits, murder trial told
Watch dealer tells court Alex Kwong transferred HK$6 million from a luxury watch sale to Hong Kong socialite
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung received a share of the profits her ex-husband made from investing in luxury watches, the model’s murder trial has heard.
Chan Leong-hang, an employee of Aristo Watch & Jewellery in Tsim Sha Tsui, said on Thursday that Alex Kwong Kong-chi sold upmarket timepieces to the shop and asked that the shop transfer part of the proceeds to Choi via bank transfer.
Chan said the company transferred HK$6 million (US$764,580) to Choi’s bank account after her ex-husband sold a watch to the shop in October 2021. He also recalled Kwong selling a Richard Mille watch worth HK$10.5 million and asking for part of the profit to go to his former partner.

Bihar is set to host an international sporting event to mark 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand.
As part of the “100 Years of Unity Through Sport” initiative, the India-New Zealand Under-20 Rugby Series will be held at the Rajgir Sports Complex from October 23 to 28. in Nalanda.
The main matches of the series will take place on October 27. The event will bring together young players from both countries to promote cultural exchange and mutual cooperation alongside sporting competition.
The Under-20 men’s and women’s teams from India and New Zealand have arrived in Bihar to participate in the series. The New Zealand teams received a traditional welcome at Patna airport on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
During their stay, players from both countries will participate in joint training sessions and share their sporting techniques, experiences and cultures.
New Zealand’s Under-20 Rugby teams have travelled to India for the first time for an event of this kind. New Zealand’s men’s team, Tama Toa, and women’s team, Hine Toa, comprise a total of 24 young Maori players selected from different regions.
The event will provide young athletes with an opportunity to showcase their talent on an international platform apart from strengthening the historic sporting ties between the two countries.
The selection of seven players from Bihar for the Indian Under-20 men’s and women’s teams is a matter of pride for the state. Bajrangi Kumar and Rohit Kumar have been included in the men’s team, while Alpana Kumari, Aarti Kumari, Beauty Kumari and Saloni Kumari have secured places in the women’s team. Sagar Prakash is also part of the Indian contingent.
Sagar Prakash, Alpana Kumari and Aarti Kumari previously represented India at the Asia Rugby Emirates Under-20 Sevens Championship held in Bihar in 2025.
According to official of Bihar Sports Deparmtent, four rugby sevens matches will be played at the Rajgir Sports Complex on October 27. These will include matches between the men’s teams and the women’s teams of India and New Zealand, along with two mixed matches.
The official asserted that players from both countries will come together to form joint teams for the mixed matches. The initiative aims to promote not only competition but also sportsmanship, cooperation and international friendship, the official said.
Rajgir is strengthening its reputation as a major destination for Rugby tournaments. The city hosted the Asia Rugby Emirates Under-20 Championship in August 2025 and the Senior National Rugby Championship in April 2026.
Hosting India-New Zealand series will further highlight Bihar’s sporting infrastructure and its capacity to organise international competitions.
Bihar State Sports Authority Director General-cum-CEO Raveendran Sankaran said hosting the series was a proud occasion for Bihar and Rajgir. He noted that the event would strengthen international sporting relations, encourage cultural exchange and inspire young people in the state to take up Rugby.
He added that the state government was committed to providing athletes with better training facilities and more opportunities to compete.
Indian Rugby Football Union President Rahul Bose said the completion of 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand was a historic milestone. Playing against New Zealand on home soil would give Indian players an opportunity to learn international techniques and improve their understanding of the game.
Meanwhile, Manu Albert, head of the New Zealand Rugby delegation, expressed enthusiasm about sharing sporting experiences, developing the sevens format and supporting the training of Indian players and coaches.
Training workshops were organised at Kalinga stadium in Bhubaneswar for 35 Indian coaches, with support from New Zealand Rugby coaches in May 2026. The upcoming series in Rajgir represents an important step towards taking this collaboration forward.

Brook underlines status as world's best all-format batter in remarkable defeat
- Published
Just under a year ago, Harry Brook was left wondering if he would be sacked as England white-ball captain and what damage he had done to his international career.
What a turnaround in 12 months. From whacked in Wellington to the run-fest in Rawalpindi, Brook is undeniably England's most important cricketer and probably the best multi-format batter in the world.
Brook's 202 in England's defeat against Sri Lanka was an astonishing display of stroke-making. There can be no higher praise than to compare Brook's dismantling of the Sri Lankan attack to the sort of innings once played by South African genius AB de Villiers.
It was the first double hundred scored by an Englishman in an ODI, passing England's previous best individual score of 182 by Ben Stokes against New Zealand in 2023. In reaching 200 in 114 balls, Brook registered the fastest double ton by anyone in an ODI, bettering the 117 deliveries of India's Shubman Gill against West Indies only last month.
Brook has joined one of international cricket's most exclusive clubs. In completing the set of a hundred in a T20, double hundred in an ODI and triple century in a Test, Brook has matched the previously unique treble of West Indies' legend Chris Gayle.
In the moment, the collection of another landmark might not mean a great deal to Brook. Despite his efforts, his team were beaten as the spirited Sri Lankans pulled off the second-highest run-chase in history in one of the most astonishing ODIs ever played.
For a man who has previously spoken about prioritising match-winning contributions over individual achievements, Brook the captain was left dejected that his innings ultimately counted for nothing. He is the first man to make a double ton in an ODI and end up on the losing side.
Still, it further underlined his status as the premier run-getter across all kinds of international cricket. Perhaps only Australia's Travis Head can challenge Brook for the crown.
Ranked by the International Cricket Council as the best Test batter in the world, Brook averages 53.08 in the longer format of the game. No England player with a minimum of 20 innings since 1968 has a better average than Brook – he stands above Joe Root, Alastair Cook, Geoffrey Boycott, Graham Gooch and everyone else to have batted for England in the past seven decades.
In T20 internationals, Brook averages 36.21 at a strike-rate of 164.92. No batter to have played at least 20 innings for a major nation averages more at a better strike-rate.
Brook is learning to play List A cricket in one-day internationals. Sri Lanka was his 61st List A match, 45 of which have been ODIs. After a slow start to his international 50-over career, Brook averages just under 50 in his past 29 matches and almost 57 in 2026.
The responsibility of captaincy suits him. In ODIs, Brook averages 31 runs more as captain compared to when not. In T20s, his average jumps 19 runs when wearing the metaphorical armband.
Brook's workload is an issue, the Yorkshireman having played in every England fixture since being rested for a T20 series in Ireland last September and, fitness permitting, he will be the only man to play in every game this winter – that's five tours to four countries across three continents. He left home last week and will not again see his own bed until mid-January.
He says his time to rest is during the Indian Premier League, the riches of which he has turned down in order to focus his energy on England. Brook probably does not get enough credit for making such a decision.
There is the question of how good Brook could become. Ben Stokes revealed that, at the end of the Ashes, he took Brook to one side to say he should be averaging 60 or more in Test cricket.
Speaking to the BBC in August, Brook admitted to not being the "finished article".
"I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games," he said.
In terms of improvement, Brook has already shown a willingness to do the hard yards to become a better cricketer.
As a youngster, he struggled with his fitness, but has worked hard to become one of the best athletes in the England team. He has spoken at length about being better able to run twos – he is one of the best runners between the wickets in the world. Brook has also turned himself into one of England's most reliable catchers.
As for the batting, well-qualified judges don't hold back in their praise. Last month, Stokes said Brook may have more talent than Kevin Pietersen. In 2024, James Anderson said Brook could surpass Root as England's highest Test run-scorer. Just last week, Chris Woakes labelled Brook as "next level".
The missing achievement is a starring role in winning a major series or tournament.
Brook's magnificent century should have been enough for England to win the fifth Test against India at The Oval last year, only for him to throw away his wicket with victory in sight. He has not made a century in 10 Ashes Tests against Australia and was only a bit-part player as part of the England team that won the T20 World Cup in 2022.
Maybe his moment is approaching. Next summer is a home Ashes, followed by the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. Brook will be 28 and at the peak of his powers. There is the chance to play a major part in regaining the urn and to become one of the few British athletes to lift a World Cup in any sport.
To do that, he will have to iron out the flaws that have arisen in England's one-day cricket across the first two matches of the tri-series in Pakistan.
In the opening match, against Pakistan, dropped catches and poor strokes left them well beaten in a contest they could have won.
Against Sri Lanka, England somehow lost from what seemed an impregnable position, their bowling and fielding falling apart amid a growing realisation they were in danger of failing to defend a target of 430.
There was some mitigation. Dew made the ball incredibly slippery, while their attack was weakened by the absence of the rested Jofra Archer and benched Adil Rashid.
Nevertheless, the bowling was awful, particularly Sam Curran, who conceded 103 from nine overs to return the worst figures by an England bowler in an ODI. It was an error by Brook to continue to show faith in the left-armer, while not using the full allocation of 10 overs from either Josh Tongue or Gus Atkinson.
It is one of the first major missteps of Brook's captaincy career and the sort of performance that shows England still have some way to go to be seen as serious World Cup contenders.
Now, England will have to win their next two matches to reach the tri-series final, to be played on 31 October, exactly 12 months on from Brook's horror show in Wellington.
England need the sort of turnaround their captain has managed over the past year

Titans release Elliott for pulling gun in car park
- Published
Defensive tackle Jordan Elliott has been released by the Tennessee Titans after he pulled a gun in the car park of the team facility.
Titans coach Robert Saleh confirmed on Tuesday reports that Elliott retrieved a gun from his car after an altercation with JC Latham during practice on 15 October.
The 28-year-old did not play in Sunday's victory against the Indianapolis Colts and was released by the Titans on Tuesday over what the club called an "incident".
"Just pause with regards to the news that Jordan had a gun," Saleh said.
"This is a man who is a father, a great husband. This is a man who has never committed a crime in his entire life.
"And he pulled a gun in the parking lot. Why did he go off the rails and grab a gun? To me, those are small signs of a cry for help. Obviously there is something greater happening."
Offensive tackle Latham called the altercation with Elliott an "unfortunate situation" that happened "just in the heat of the moment".
"Never been no bad blood between us two. We never actually had an argument leading up to it," Latham said.
"I do think mental health is extremely important and that's just one of those situations where you pray for a guy like that and, if you can, reach out to him, hope for the best for him. It's nothing personal on my end."
Elliott, who previously played for San Francisco and Cleveland, has appeared in five games this season.
Saleh said he would still recommend Elliott to another franchise.
"My message to 31 other teams would be if you need a hell of a run-stopping D-tackle that can help you on a play-off run, give me a call, I'll tell you everything you need to know about him," he said.
"I will stand on the table for Jordan's character. Unfortunately rules are rules with regards to guns on property, and sometimes it's far greater than the knee-jerk reaction of kicking somebody when they're down."

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

A senior South African cricket official has pledged to order a review into the low crowd which attended the first Test against Australia in Durban.
Despite South Africa being the reigning world Test champions and Australia the number one-ranked side in the world, fewer than 20,000 fans attended across the five days.
Australia, who are touring South Africa for the first time since the 2018 sandpaper scandal, won by 214 runs and can wrap up the three-match series when the second Test gets under way in Gqeberha on Sunday.
"It is impossible to overlook our disappointment that just under 20,000 fans attended across the five days," said KwaZulu-Natal Cricket Union chief executive Heinrich Strydom.
"A Test match of this quality deserved greater support in the stands. This is something we will reflect on through a thorough internal review.
"We need to listen to our supporters, reconnect with our communities and continue to find ways to make Test cricket more accessible, engaging and appealing.
"Test cricket is part of our sporting heritage and its future depends on all of us."
Attendances for Test cricket have been declining in many places around the world, most notably in South Africa and the West Indies.
However, live sport does remain a big draw in South Africa.
While the Test against Australia was ongoing, a football cup final between Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns was being held across town in Durban which attracted more than 50,000 fans.
"While we recognise supporters face competing demands on their time and finances, we must also understand better what influences their decisions to attend and what more we can do to make live cricket an attractive and worthwhile experience," added Strydom.

Tamil literature is replete with references to Siddha practitioners, traditional healers, and the faith, or lack of it, that people have in them. A segment of Tamil literature that has focused on class and caste hierarchies has also looked sharply and sensitively at the socio-economic determinants for access to health care. Among the pioneers of drawing technology and science into his writings in Tamil was the legendary, prescient novelist and screenwriter Sujatha. But in modern Tamil fiction, the employment of medicine and medical issues as the central theme and plot has been rather minimal.
While there might be only a few texts in popular, modern Tamil fiction that weave the story around a medical condition, these form a significant contribution to the genre. Muthumeenal’s Mul focuses on leprosy, and Sivakami’s Pazhayana Kazhithalum offers a health perspective couched in caste discrimination.
Among the Tamil writers who have formed a strong bond between their stories and health issues, Imayam stands tall, not merely through sheer numbers, but through depth of content. Many of his short stories and novels couch the essential human experience he portrays in medical conditions, each wrapped in the other, not distinct, but influencing and impacting each other.
Health in Tamil fiction
But before we dip into Imayam’s work, a full-length novel of note on a core health issue is Mul (thorn) by Muthumeenal, a deep and personalised account of living with leprosy. The narrator is a young girl whose life has been upended when she finds suspicious patches on her body. She moves into an institution where medical care is provided, around which the story is built, and the multiple angles, including stigma, politics, loneliness, and internal struggle, are woven into this autobiography. The public-health message is stigma-busting: that leprosy is treatable, and early therapy can cure it.
In retired IAS officer Sivakami’s work, a Dalit feminist treatise, Pazhayana Kazhithalum (The Grip of Change), the text deals strongly with the social determinants of health — caste violence, gender-based violence, bodily autonomy, and the mental and physical toll of bigotry.
In Imayam’s Ippothu Uyirodirukkiren (I’m Alive… For Now), the author artfully folds in the themes of both the above novels — crafting a social commentary within the nephrology ward of a government hospital where a teenager with end-stage kidney disease has been admitted. It follows his rapid decline, his transition onto dialysis, and organ donation. Reviewers have praised its ‘authentic’ portrayal of nephrology, the disease, and the treatment.
But this is an achievement across various novels that Imayam, a school teacher and politician, has penned. While known for his sharp critique of caste and gender hegemonies, Imayam has also built a strong subgenre of medical literature. Unlike authors who use disease as a generic plot device or a melodramatic tool to lead up to a crisis, he treats medical conditions with gripping sociological depth and clinical accuracy.
A Sahitya Akademi winner, Imayam attempts to explain the human condition through pain, suffering and debility, and as his longtime collaborator-translator Justice Prabha Sridevan says, “an astonishingly astute understanding of the feminine condition.” His recent novel, Noiputtru (disease), also talks of life derailed by leprous patches.
Set in a Tamil Nadu leprosarium in the 1960s, the novel documents the lived experiences of patients ostracised from their families and confined to State-run institutions, including detailed descriptions of the diagnostic and treatment processes. The descriptions of the impact of leprosy are merciless — thickening ears, flattened noses, and physical disfigurement — there’s no way to conceal this in the deliberate, yet sparse prose of the author.
Imayam’s world of illness
Very few novels in Tamil come with the searing commentary that he delivers in Sellatha Panam (A Woman Burnt). Unlike in the case of the protagonist of the above-mentioned novels, here, Revathi, an upper-caste woman who is forced to take the extreme move after her inter-caste marriage, is trapped in a liminal world and confined to bed. Around her, in the waiting corridors of the burns ward, social realities are exposed, the niceties ripped off, though his most effective literary tool is conversations between people. It is said Imayam spent time observing the JIPMER burns ward while researching the book.
Just launched, the English translation of Uppu Vandikaran (The Salt Vendor) harks back to the dark, panic-driven emergency of the pandemic lockdown. It’s not just about falling ill with COVID-19; instead, it exposes the lacunae and inadequacies in the medical system, as Chellamuthu goes from one hospital to the other, being rejected by each one of them since he cannot produce a certificate confirming his infection- a situation the world was familiar with during the first couple of years of the 2020s. Similarly, his short story Government Pinam (The Government Corpse) is situated in the pandemic, focusing on a boy quarantined with his sick father in a house sealed shut by government officials.
In Imayam’s debut novel Koveru Kazhudaigal (Mules), over three decades ago, a significant segment is about how the women of the Vannar community deliver through traditional midwifery practices, outside of medical institutions. He also broaches the subject of patient attendants, a subject gaining currency in a nation growing increasingly grey, and the care of the elderly comes into the spotlight. In Pinathuku Sondhakkari (Owner of the Corpse): Meenakshi, a live-in attendant, is left alone to handle her elderly employer Ramanan’s sudden death, his children away and slow to return.
Manamurivu (Divorce) deals with the gendered nature of infertility, dragging the reader through IVF clinics, menstrual cycles, hormone injections, and the inordinate stress to bear children on the woman in the relationship.
Since the COVID-19 pandemic drew science and medicine into drawing rooms and headlines, willy-nilly, it remains to be seen whether Tamil literature will now make room for more health-related content.

New Delhi, Oct 22: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday received a telephone call from his Israeli counterpart Benjamin Netanyahu, during which the two leaders exchanged views on recent developments in West Asia and underscored the urgent need to restore peace and stability in the region.
Modi and Netanyahu also welcomed the sustained momentum in India-Israel relations and reaffirmed their shared commitment to further strengthening the Special Strategic Partnership between the two countries.
"The leaders also exchanged views on recent developments in West Asia and underscored the urgent need to restore peace and stability in the region. Prime Minister Modi reiterated India's call for dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward," the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) said in a statement.
In a post on X, Modi said he received a phone call from the Israeli prime minister.
"We reviewed the sustained momentum in our bilateral ties and reaffirmed our commitment to further strengthening our partnership. We also exchanged views on recent developments in West Asia and underscored the urgent need to restore peace and stability in the region," he said.
Prime Minister Modi had made a state visit to Israel from February 25 to 26. The two leaders had then agreed and decided to elevate the Strategic Partnership to a new level -- 'A Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity'.
Modi had then said that India's security interest was linked to peace and stability in the Middle East, adding that New Delhi fully supported the Gaza Peace Initiative.
They also had telephonic talks during the US-Iran and Iran conflict.
Earlier this month, Netanyahu had called Indian pilot Smit Machchhar a "hero of the entire world" for foiling an alleged attempt by his co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound flight, as he spoke with him over the phone.
Captain Machchhar was attacked and seriously injured by his co-pilot in the cockpit of flydubai flight FZ1073 while the aircraft was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month.

Bangladesh off-spinner Aliss Al Islam has been reported for a suspect bowling action following his team’s seven-wicket defeat to Afghanistan in the ODI tri-series at Sharjah on Wednesday.
The 29-year-old, who made his ODI debut in the match, went wicketless while conceding 47 runs in 8.3 overs as Afghanistan chased down Bangladesh’s total of 160.
The International Cricket Council (ICC) confirmed on Thursday that the match officials had questioned the legality of Aliss’ bowling action in their report.
The spinner will now undergo an independent assessment at an ICC-accredited testing centre in accordance with the governing body’s Illegal Bowling Action Regulations.
Under ICC regulations, a bowler’s elbow extension must not exceed 15 degrees between the bowling arm reaching the horizontal position and the release of the ball.
Aliss is permitted to continue bowling in international matches pending the outcome of the assessment.
This is not the first time the spinner’s action has come under scrutiny. He was reported during the Bangladesh Premier League in 2019 and again in 2025, although he subsequently received clearance to resume bowling.
Aliss made his T20I debut earlier this month against Sri Lanka at the Asian Games before earning his maiden ODI appearance against Afghanistan.
Bangladesh’s defeat on Wednesday ended its campaign in the three-team ODI series, having previously lost to Zimbabwe.
Afghanistan and Zimbabwe will contest the final on October 23.

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

A hearing in downtown L.A. is on the books for Friday to address the requests. The parties are aiming to have the trial moved to March 22 next year.
Out of what has been an extremely contentious battle even by Hollywood standards between producers Amanda Ghost, Gregor Cameron and Vince Holden and Deb director Wilson over allegations of misconduct on the film, this latest twist has a much more personal origin.

The Delhi High Court has imposed a token cost of ₹1 on Niva Bupa Health Insurance Company Limited for invoking its Intellectual Property Division to pursue a ₹5 crore suit against social media influencer Vishal Rattewal over allegedly disparaging posts, holding that the dispute did not involve trademark infringement.
Justice Anup J. Bhambhani, in an order passed on September 21, observed that merely using an insurance company’s name or trademark to identify it in social media posts did not, in the circumstances of the case, amount to trademark infringement.
Niva Bupa had approached the court seeking the removal of allegedly disparaging posts published in late August this year by Mr. Rattewal on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and X.
It submitted that Mr. Rattewal, a social media influencer and content creator with a substantial following, had deliberately used its distinctive name, trademarks, logo and other brand identifiers, including ‘NIVA BUPA’, prominently in the titles, thumbnails, captions, visual presentation and content of his publications. The company alleged that he had simultaneously associated the brand with allegations of “fraud, dishonesty, deception, and unfair trade practices”.
It sought an apology, ₹5 crore in damages and litigation costs, alleging that the content had harmed its reputation and infringed its registered trademark.
The dispute stemmed from a consumer complaint filed by Mr. Neeraj Kumar against the insurer before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Charkhi Dadri, Haryana. In an order passed on October 9, 2024, the commission ruled in Mr. Kumar’s favour and made certain observations concerning medical insurance companies.
Niva Bupa alleged that Mr. Rattewal subsequently published offensive and disparaging content about the company in connection with the consumer proceedings.
In this backdrop, Niva Bupa contended that, by publishing allegedly offensive content on his social media accounts, Mr. Rattewal has infringed its registered trade mark by harming its reputation in India.
The court, however, held that Mr. Rattewal was neither engaged in the insurance business nor connected with it. Using Niva Bupa’s name or trademark to identify the company in the alleged posts did not amount to use “in the course of trade” or constitute infringement under the Trade Marks Act, it said.
“In the opinion of this court, this suit is not maintainable before the Intellectual Property Division of this court, since it is not a matter relating to infringement of any intellectual property right of either of the plaintiffs,” the court held.
After the court dictated its order returning the plaint, Niva Bupa sought permission to withdraw the suit and pursue its claims through an ordinary civil action. The court allowed the request, granting them liberty to file a fresh suit on the same cause of action, subject to payment of ₹1 as costs to Mr. Rattewal.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday called for stronger global institutions, a greater voice for the Global South and effective international cooperation during crises, while accusing the Congress leadership of repeatedly failing to launch its leader politically.Addressing the NDTV World Summit 2026 in New Delhi, PM Modi said institutions such as the United Nations were struggling to keep pace with the changing world order and emerging challenges, according to news agency ANI.PM Modi warned that trade, technology and sea routes were increasingly being “weaponised”, stressing the need for a global system that prevents the strong from exploiting the vulnerable. Citing ancient Indian statesman Chanakya, he referred to the Sanskrit aphorism ‘apranitah tu matsyanyayam udbhavayati’, which he explained as a situation where the absence of law and order allows the strong to prey on the weak.“The world does not need such a situation. It needs a system that stops this 'matsya nyaya' from happening,” PM Modi said.Highlighting India's role in global cooperation, Modi cited the country's humanitarian assistance during the Covid-19 pandemic. “During the Covid-19 pandemic, the world experienced India taking on such a role. India sent vaccines to every country in need; sent medicines to over 100 countries,” he said.
“The changing world order calls for stronger global institutions, a greater voice for the Global South, and international cooperation that stands firm in times of crisis,” he added.PM Modi said India's vision of becoming a developed nation, or Viksit Bharat, by 2047 went beyond domestic ambitions. “It is also a guarantee for a better world,” he said, adding that international cooperation must remain effective during crises and not just in favourable circumstances. “India is strengthening its own capabilities to help strengthen the world,” he said.

Parents of children suffering from Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a serious genetic disorder, in Keralam are trying to get political support for their opposition to the State government’s decision to replace the life-saving medication being administered to their kids with a generic drug.
A section of them recently met Opposition leader Pinarayi Vijayan and Industries Minister P.K. Kunhalikutty. Mr. Vijayan also wrote to Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, urging him to address the concerns related to the efficacy of the new medicine. Mr. Vijayan, in the letter, sought to reconsider the decision to cut the ₹30 crore sanctioned during the previous government’s tenure for the free drug distribution scheme for those aged up to 12 till they turn 25.
Risdiplam, a life-saving drug
Children with SMA are being given Risdiplam, a life-saving drug patented by the company Roche Pharma, since 2021. It costs ₹5.4 lakh a bottle. The then Left Democratic Front government procured it at a negotiated price of about ₹1-₹1.25 lakh, to be distributed for free among the children. However, the United Democratic Front-led State government recently issued an order to procure its generic version manufactured by Natco Pharma, whose price is 97% lesser than its patented version. Government officials claim that the attempt is to widen the drug access to more SMA patients.
However, Cure SMA Foundation of India, an advocacy organisation representing those affected by the condition, along with the parents of the affected children, claim that the efficacy and safety of this generic version have not yet been established.
They point out that the medication currently being administered has been proven to have a high level of safety and efficacy through long-term scientific studies. The 118 children at present receiving the free drug are showing significant health improvements, they say. They are requesting the authorities to continue the same medication until scientific study results demonstrating the efficacy and safety of the generic drug are made available.
“SMA is a neurodegenerative disease, and timely and effective treatment is crucial. If the new medication lacks the same level of efficacy or safety as the current one, there is a risk that the condition of children who have already regained their health could deteriorate once again,” one of the parents says. The parents also express the concern that a sudden, unannounced switch to a generic medication—for which bio-equivalence or therapeutic equivalence studies have not been completed—could seriously impact their children’s health. The parents and patients claim that though multiple petitions were submitted highlighting their concerns, all of them were disregarded.

EA is home to some of gaming’s biggest RPG franchises, including Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Now there’s nobody working on a game, or games, within the organization, and chances are there never will be, which might make them more likely to sell off those IPs.
However, Darrah thinks EA may forget these legendary IPs exist, and instead of selling Mass Effect or Dragon Age, the company would “bury them in the vault.”
“I think we still are gonna have to wait a little bit before we see if EA has any interest in selling off some of its dormant IPs. Right now, they seem in cost control mode. They might start in a revenue-generation mode where selling IPs might be more desirable,” concluded Darrah.
EA is indeed in cost-control mode as it focuses on multiple launches, including Motive Studio’s Marvel’s Iron Man and Star Wars Jedi 3, reportedly targeting a 2027 release with Respawn leading development. Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
- Published
When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.
But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.
"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?
"Those thoughts haunt me every night."
Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.
Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.
But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.
"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.
"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."
Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.
Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.
Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.
"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."
Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.
In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic.
"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."
Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.
"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."
Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.
Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.
Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.
"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."
The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.
Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.
"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."
But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.
For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.
"It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air".
"The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."
Thousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.
Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.
Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.
Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers.
"Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months.
"We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."
What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before.
"So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.
In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.
Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out".
"However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."

An Austrian and a Swiss woman freed in Niger after a year and half in captivity
Two women from Austria and Switzerland have been freed in Niger after spending more than a year and half in captivity, officials and local media reported Thursday
NIAMEY, Niger -- Two women from Austria and Switzerland have been freed in Niger after spending more than a year and a half in captivity, officials and local media reported Thursday.
The Austrian woman, an aid worker identified as Eva G, was received by the Austrian crisis team on Thursday, Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said in a statement.
She was kidnapped in Niger’s Agadez city in January last year, months before the Swiss citizen was abducted in the same city in April 2025.
Meinl-Reisinger said Austria worked with Switzerland to find “a safe solution” for the women.
“We are all very relieved that Eva G. is free again after more than 21 months. This time was an unimaginable burden for her and her family,” Meinl-Reisinger said.
Swiss media quoted the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs as confirming the release of the Swiss woman.
Swiss newspaper 20 Minuten reported she was on her way home, quoting Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis.
Officials did not say who was responsible for the abductions or how both women were freed.
The Austrian woman had been working as an aid worker in Agadez, hundreds of kilometers (miles) away from the capital city of Niamey, where she lived for more than 20 years, Nigerien media reported.
The Swiss citizen had also lived in Niger for several years.
Niger has for many years battled a jihadi insurgency linked to al-Qaida and the Islamic State group. Analysts say the country's security crisis has worsened since the military toppled the country’s government in July 2023.
Despite their promise to restore peace in hot spots, the junta’s capacity to improve Niger’s security has increasingly been questioned amid more frequent attacks.

The trailer for Mass Effect 5 has leaked and unfortunately it looks good
'Mass Effect: Universe' looks like it would have focused on a new protagonist and series favorite Liara T'Soni.
A trailer for BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel has leaked on Reddit, just as the possibility of it ever being released has all but vanished following EA's closure of the studio. The trailer was posted from a burner account by a user who claims to be an EA employee, and Bloomberg's Jason Schreier has separately confirmed the footage is the real deal in a Bluesky post.
After opening with text that notes it's made from in-game footage using pre-production assets, the trailer cuts to a man wearing an N7 trench coat (presumably the new protagonist) entering a bar, where an asari approaches him to strike up a conversation. He recounts his experience in the military before sharing that he's picked up a "new line of work," over footage of the galaxy-saving punching, shooting and kissing that should be familiar to fans of the series. After the asari threatens him, Liara T'Soni — an asari ally of the original trilogy's Commander Shepard — reveals herself and the bar breaks out into a fight. The trailer ends on the game's title: Mass Effect: Universe.
The last new Mass Effect game BioWare released was Mass Effect: Andromeda, a 2017 follow-up to Mass Effect 3 that was widely panned by fans and was reportedly the product of a troubled development process. BioWare first teased it was working on more Mass Effect in 2020, while it was still developing its next Dragon Age title. Development on the game has continued since then, through the 2021 release of Mass Effect Legendary Edition, a remastered version of the original trilogy of games, and studio layoffs before and after the release of Dragon Age: The Veilguard. Considering EA said it wouldn't continue development following BioWare's closure, this trailer is likely all we'll get to see of the game.

Carney announces trade and defence partnership with Turkey
PM visits Ankara seeking stronger ties with key NATO ally
Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence co-operation.
It is the latest step in the warming of relations between the two nations and an important moment in the prime minister's plan to co-operate more closely with other middle-power countries.
Carney praised Turkey as an "exceptional" partner.
"No country builds strength alone," he said in a joint statement at the sprawling presidential palace compound.
"The most resilient countries bring together complementary strengths with trusted partners. Our goal isn’t self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience. That’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for Canadians."
There are four pillars to the new partnership — trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and people-to-people ties.
Next month, negotiators will sit down in Ankara for the first round of free trade talks. Also, the partnership includes a new agreement on defence industry co-operation that will better connect Canadian and Turkish companies.
Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, seen here in Ottawa on July 16, is joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
The partnership will also pave the way for investments in the energy and critical minerals sectors. The two countries will also finalize an air transport agreement, increasing passenger flights between the two countries.
The bilateral visit, a first for Canadian prime minister, comes as human rights groups raise the alarm over Turkey's sweeping crackdown last month on dissent and civil society groups, including the dismantling of 2SLGBTQ+ and HIV-advocacy organizations.
"The prime minister has been very clear. We need to engage with the world as it is, not the way we wish it to be," Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said ahead of the trip. He will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials.
People run from the police during a march in support of transgender people and their rights during the 2SLGBTQ+ Pride week, in Istanbul, Turkey, on June 21. (Dilara Acikgoz/The Associated Press)
"Where we have differences of opinion, we discuss those in private."
Carney is looking to diversify Canada's trade to make the country less dependent on the United States. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific.
Turkey, a member of NATO with a growing defence industrial sector, is seen as a key ally on the trade and military production fronts, says Thomas Juneau of the University of Ottawa, an expert in the Middle East.
"What the Carney government appears to be making as a choice is not to restrict diversification efforts only to democracies, only to countries that have positive human rights records," said Juneau.
Turkey has become increasingly authoritarian under Erdogan, who has been president since 2014.
"This is morally a difficult dilemma on the Canadian side, but the calculus appears on the part of the government that if Canada were to choose to diversify only with democracies the ceiling for success would be low."
Immediately after landing in Ankara on Thursday, visited Anitkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who was the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey.
The structure and its 750,000 square-metre grounds are beautifully maintained, divided into the Peace Park with tens of thousands of plants and trees including Canadian maples, and the Monument Block. Carney laid a wreath at the monument.
Carney pays his respects after laying a wreath during a ceremony at the Anıtkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, in Ankara. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Turkey aims to expand its energy capacity significantly in the coming decades, planning to add roughly 20 gigawatts of nuclear power by 2050.
To that end, Ottawa and Ankara are reportedly planning to set up a working group to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's Candu nuclear team in order to build Turkey's planned second or third nuclear power plant.
Asked ahead of the trip to Ankara, Hodgson said he wasn't in a position to scoop the prime minister and told reporters to stay tuned.
- Carney's Turkish balancing act must include business, defence and human rights
- Turkey's president gifted Carney a revolver at NATO summit. Carney gave him maple syrup
Sevag Belian, the executive director of the Armenian National Committee of Canada, says any nuclear deal with Turkey deserves close scrutiny.
He pointed to the previous falling out between the two countries which resulted in Canada imposing a de facto arms embargo, which was mostly lifted in 2024. The lifting of those measures was the price Erdogen demanded of the Trudeau government for getting behind Sweden's membership in NATO.
The fallout started in 2020 when Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to importation of Wescam target acquisition gear used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.
"We know from the disclosed documents that they had said that they will be using the few cameras that they got through the exemption for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria," said Belian.
"But then we know that those cameras were actually diverted illegally to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno.
"We have established through parliamentary investigation that the Turkish side clearly lied."

The IIT-Madras on Thursday announced that it would take up a feasibility study for small data centres to be used for inference across a wide spectrum of subjects, including agriculture, space, manufacturing, health or law.
While large data centres were necessary for large-scale training of Large language models (LLMs), a federated, distributed, and workable model of “pico centres”, developed using frugal engineering methods and aimed at various groups of end-users, could be studied.
Announcing this on the sidelines of an industry conclave titled AI Measurement and Governance at IIT-Madras on Thursday, IIT-M Director V. Kamakoti said Bodhan AI, a Centre of Excellence for AI in Education, funded by the Union Ministry of Education and incubated as a Section 8 Company in IIT-M, was studying the feasibility of setting up frugal AI data centres that would consume lesser electricity and resources, and provide, for example, personalised AI tutors to the 25 crore students studying in India’s schools.
“We should not be using a pistol to kill a mosquito,” Dr. Kamakoti said. He also announced that the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), in partnership with The Better India, would produce 500 videos portraying case studies across the country on how to use AI responsibly and effectively.
He said IIT-M would start work on trusted AI Commons to enhance the accountability and responsibility of AI.
Dr. Kamakoti also launched a software platform for the evaluation of AI tools using over 50 metrics and 100 sub-metrics in multiple languages, and released a white paper on the job scenario projection with the advent of AI.
B. Ravindran, Head, Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI and CeRAI, IIT-M, said the series of working papers released at the event portrayed CeRAI’s commitment to work on what would be an appropriate, right-sized AI approach for India, and the use of frugal engineering in the development of AI.
Gokul S. Krishnan, Research Director, CeRAI, also spoke.
