The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

Citing 'challenges,' AIPAC halts endorsements and direct contributions to candidates
The pro-Israel political organization AIPAC, or the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, announced on Wednesday that it will no longer issue endorsements, make direct PAC contributions or earmark funds for candidates.
A longtime influential lobbying group, AIPAC started its direct political involvement five years ago. Since then, particularly this midterm election cycle, AIPAC has been met with mounting resistance. The group has faced criticism over its stances on various issues, including the wars in Gaza and Iran.
Candidates endorsed by AIPAC have also faced tough opposition from both the political right and the political left for accepting the organization's support and financial contributions as public opinion on the U.S. relationship with Israel has shifted. In order to tame the criticism, some AIPAC-endorsed candidates said they won't accept any money from the organization.
AIPAC first announced the changes in a letter to members, stating "the challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead." In the letter, AIPAC said it wouldn't stop funneling money to candidates that align with the group's mission by mobilizing individual donors.
"We will prioritize increasing direct, organized contributions from individual Americans to candidates—expanding upon our current efforts—and maximizing the emerging political fundraising tools," the letter said.
The letter added that the 2028 cycle will "demand an even stronger commitment by our activists to pro-Israel politics." As a result, the group plans to increase support "for the Republicans and Democrats who are advancing policies that strengthen America's alliance with Israel and standing up against anti-Israel legislation."
A spokesperson for AIPAC did not immediately return NPR's request for comment.
AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through Sept. 30, according to FEC filings. Its affiliated super PAC United Democracy Project contributed $13 million to candidates and political committees and spent an additional $53.5 million in independent expenditures. It's unclear what the role of United Democracy Project will be moving forward.
In recent days, though, several of its individual independent expenditures are being used to campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan. AIPAC also spent heavily to campaign against El-Sayed in the primary, backing his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The Michigan Senate contest is just one of the high-profile races where AIPAC has spent in favor of a pro-Israel politician or in opposition to someone the organization sees as less favorable to Israel.

“Bacchon, police ki maar ka bura nahi maante. Yeh aapko samjhane ke liye kari gayi hai” (Translation: Children, don’t take offence at being beaten by the police. This was done to teach you a lesson.)
This is what a Delhi Police official had to say after protesters were allegedly subjected to a vicious assault inside a prison van fitted with ‘cages’, while being taken to a detention centre at Pandwalan Khurd, a village in the Kapashera tehsil of Najafgarh in South West Delhi, on October 11.
One detainee was called in. Then came the screams. Another followed, and the screams came again. Inside the pitch-dark van, protesters were allegedly punched, kicked and beaten by police personnel before being shoved into cramped, grille-enclosed compartments. They could hear the violence unfold but could barely see who was inflicting it.
Two detainees who were in the same van spoke to Alt News, recounting what they described as a nightmare that would haunt them for the rest of their lives. Each detainee, they said, was made to board the vehicle one at a time, assaulted and then forced into one of the cages inside.
Their offence: Joining a protest on the streets of Delhi against alleged electoral malpractices and supporting the call for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
An Evening of Unspeakable Horror
Twenty-three-year-old Tarang Balani, who works at an e-commerce startup, saw a video posted by Neha Bora urging people to reach R K Ashram at 2:30 pm. “I saw that post at 2. So I reached Connaught Place (CP) directly because I thought if they’re marching from R K Ashram towards Jantar Mantar, and if I’m reaching late, I should definitely find the march somewhere around CP. I reached around 3:30 pm,” he said.
With several routes blocked in the area, Balani had to take multiple detours. He eventually came across a group marching towards Jantar Mantar and joined them. “We were told to form a human chain in case the police came to detain us,” he said.
The group was marching past Chilli’s restaurant and about to turn left when the police moved in to detain them. “As soon as police came, half the crowd had dispersed around, trying not to get detained, and 10-15 people sat down and locked hands with each other to form a human chain. I saw male police officers pulling the women protesters. Then women police officers arrived and did the same thing.”
After a tussle with the police, the protesters were forcibly made to board a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) bus.
In the video below posted by BBC, as Hemansh speaks, a policeman inside the bus can be seen slapping or punching a young man in the face.
View this post on Instagram
“Soon after, they stopped outside the Pind Balluchi restaurant in CP and some police officers started asking us to deboard,” Balani said. The protesters refused to get off the bus since the area was teeming with security personnel and there were no media persons around. “We felt that the media should be able to document what was happening.”
“But if three people are trying to get hold of one person, there’s not much you can do,” he said. According to Balani, police officers began pulling a female protester by her wrists, breaking her bangles and leaving her wrists bleeding. She then clung to the window grille as the officers pulled at her trousers and shoes, leaving her almost suspended in the air. Two women police officers approached her from outside the window and pulled her hair, forcing her to let go. “I saw it happen in front of me,” he recounted.
Outside Pind Balluchi, the protesters were separated by gender. The women were made to sit in a van and taken away, while the men were made to sit on the street for at least half an hour before the next ordeal began.
“If anyone took out their phones, it was immediately snatched, even if they were not recording. They were asking them to open their gallery and delete all media files from the day, even from the recently deleted files. We were told that if we just co-operated, nothing was going to happen to us. So most of us were just sitting quietly,” Balani said.
A Journey that Turned into a Nightmare
Half an hour later, another police van arrived, and the men were asked to board it. Twenty-seven-year-old IIT graduate Hemansh Kashyap recounted how the police allegedly assaulted detainees one by one as they entered the vehicle.
“Some of the policemen started playing good cop, saying that nothing would happen to us if we boarded it. People were taken in one at a time. An official was collecting our phones at the entrance. The first person went in, and then came blood-curdling screams. Then the second person went in, and the same thing happened. We realised that they were being assaulted.”
“We said we wouldn’t board, but the cops said: ‘Aur nahi marenge’ (We won’t hit anymore). But it obviously wasn’t true, and there wasn’t a lot we could do. When I went in, I was immediately slapped very hard, repeatedly, so hard that my glasses flew off. I was shoved into my compartment, and the cops gave me my glasses back,” he said.
Balani said the van had four compartments separated by grille partitions, with a narrow aisle that could accommodate only one person at a time. The vehicle was completely dark, making it impossible for him to see clearly.
“I was beaten up right there in the narrow passage by three policemen. Initially, two of them started beating me up; they punched me and kicked me. And then somebody said, ‘Iska chashma utaar’ (Take off his glasses), and so they took out my specs and started beating me again. I couldn’t even see their faces in the dark; I just saw policemen without name tags,” he recounted.
“I really thought they had confused me with someone else because I was quiet from the start. I was protesting peacefully. As I tried to save myself from the blows, they kept beating me, and beating me, and I just kept pleading with them (to stop). Once they realised that the regular punches and kicks were not working, they started using their elbows. One of them kicked my knee, and I fell in the aisle, and then they hit me more.
“Once I started screaming, that is when they opened the compartment where they pushed me in and just threw my specs. They closed the door behind me and locked it. As soon as I sat down, another person came; he was not wearing glasses, so they literally just took his face and smashed it into a pole in that aisle. I saw it because I was sitting right next to the division between the aisle and my compartment. There was one guy who refused to surrender his phone, and he was beaten by the police as if they had a personal grudge against him,” Balani recounted.
Both Balani and Hemansh Kashyap told Alt News that each of the blocks or cages inside the police van could accommodate six people at most. Each had two benches facing each other, with space for three people on either side. However, 10–12 detainees were crammed into each block, forcing some to sit on the floor and others to sit on fellow detainees’ laps.
The van was completely dark, making it difficult for detainees to even check the time on their watches.
What emerged from both testimonies was the methodical nature of the violence — perhaps its cruellest aspect. One detainee was taken in, beaten and shoved into a cage; then the next was called. The screams were followed by more screams. There was no frenzy, no confusion, but a grim, repeated sequence, with each person left to await their turn, knowing what awaited them in the darkness of the van.
Families Lose Contact as Detainees’ Phones Go Dead
Both detainees had shared their live locations with family members. Kashyap had shared his with his partner, Barshana, who is currently in the United States.
“At 3:45 am Pacific Daylight Time (4.15pm IST) on October 11, Hemansh called me and said he had been detained. He had been detained the day before as well and was held at a farmhouse in Chhattarpur for about six hours before being released. There wasn’t much explicit violence then, so I wasn’t too worried.
“We texted for a while as he told me he was on a bus, and he even sent me a few videos from it. But soon there was complete silence from his side. After two hours of no contact, my calm gave way to worry. I kept checking his location, but it stayed parked at CP for a long time.
“Soon, I received a message request on Instagram from an unknown account. It was Hemansh sending a message from someone else’s phone informing me that he was in a police van and had been assaulted. He told me that his phone was possibly with the cops, and also asked me to track his location. I noticed that the van was moving very fast, heading towards the Haryana border. At around 7 am PDT, the location stopped updating. I had checked, and his battery was at 40%, so it couldn’t have died. I guess the phone was switched off. His friend, who was with him in the van, was also not getting his WhatsApp messages delivered, so both phones seemed to have met the same fate.”
“I kept texting the Instagram account, which, I later found out, belonged to a detainee who had managed to sneak in a phone, but I couldn’t bombard it with messages, as the same phone was being used by thirty others. At around 7:27 am PDT, he called me for a minute, told me they had been brought to a detention centre in the middle of nowhere, and shared the location with me. That is when I mobilised my lawyer and activist friends, who reached the spot to get him out.
“The entire ordeal, from the time he was detained to the time he returned home, lasted about eight hours. It was extremely worrying for me,” Barshana recounted.
Tarang Balani, too, said his brother, with whom he had shared his live location, lost track of him when the police van reached Raota in Delhi. “I’m guessing it was because someone switched it off. An app installed in my phone still shows 70% battery in brother’s phone. The location update was stopped between 6:36 pm and 6:40 pm,” he said.
Kashyap also recounted the assault of a young man, around 19–20 years old, inside the police van. The man allegedly screamed that the police had assaulted him on his private parts and manhandled him. “(He) fell on the ground while being assaulted, and the police started hitting him in between his legs. He told his cellmates after the van started moving. He was probably the first or second detainee to be taken into the van, and he was beaten up brutally. We told him, ‘Don’t get too agitated; they’ll beat you up even more.’ It was very scary,” Kashyap said.
Neither Kashyap nor Balani has got back his phone yet.
Both of them told Alt News that four minors were inside the police van and that all four were assaulted.
Locals Come to Detainee’s Aid at Pandwalan Khurd
The van dropped them at the detention centre around 7:30 pm. The detainees expected their phones back but were told by CRPF personnel that Delhi police had not handed over the phones.
One detainee with a fractured arm received medical attention only at 9:15 pm. “There was just one canister of water, and it ran out pretty quickly. There was no food or medical help. An AIIMS doctor finally came after someone contacted them through their connections,” Hemansh said.
Initially, lawyers were not allowed to enter the detention centre. Meanwhile, a crowd began gathering outside, with some villagers, including children, reportedly protesting the detention.
“They were recording us from outside the gate. We told them to go away or they would get beaten up, but they seemed quite aware of their rights and started asking questions like, ‘How can they beat us up?’ They went away for a bit and came back with their parents, I think. These were ordinary people from the neighbourhood. They came back with water and fruits. Later, when we were released, a man was going around giving everybody 100-rupee notes if they needed to get home,” Kashyap said.
At around 9:30 pm, another van arrived, and some detainees, including 51-year-old journalist Raj Shekhar, were offered the chance to leave. The detainees unanimously refused to go without their phones. The police allegedly told them they could collect their phones from Connaught Place, offering no accountability for their confiscation. Lawyers who had reached the detention centre advised the detainees to call the emergency helpline 112 and submit written applications and complaints.
Between 10:30 pm and 11 pm, buses were arranged to take the protesters to Dwarka More metro station. Unsure whether the buses would actually drop them at Dwarka More, Balani chose not to board one. Instead, he left in a car provided by volunteers, who had been sent sent by journalist Meghnad S to help detainees return home. Kashyap, too, left with lawyers who were present at the scene.
Balani also noted that most Delhi Police personnel involved wore no name tags; only officers with two or three stars had them. He identified one officer as Ashutosh Bishnoi, who, while the detainees waited outside Pind Balluchi, had repeatedly assured them that nothing would happen to them.

President Trump, who floated the idea of renaming ‘Atlantic Ocean’ to ‘Trump Ocean’ earlier this month, has once again raised the possibility of renaming the ocean. Speaking at an event recently, Trump revealed that he called Google Maps and asked to rename the Atlantic Ocean. He said that Google CEO 
Sundar Pichai
 replied to his proposal saying: “No, no, no. This time I'm not doing it.” According to Trump, Pichai said, “Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don't ask us to do that.” This comes months after Google renamed 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the US following an executive order signed by Trump.
Trump wants to rename ‘Atlantic Ocean’ to ‘Trump Ocean’
As mentioned above, Trump first discussed renaming the Atlantic Ocean this month. “We’ve got the gulf. We’ve got a beautiful lake,” Trump said during a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee. “Now, somebody said, you need a river. We need a river. We need an ocean.”
He jokingly said that the new name could be in honor of him. “We call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that,” Trump said further adding “Before I get out, I think we should have an ocean. And we need a great river.”
US previously renamed Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario
Earlier this month, the US administration renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, sparking diplomatic tensions between the US and Mexico. 
In August, Trump also renamed Lake Ontario, between New York and Canada, as “Lake America”.
After an executive order, Google posted a brief update on its Google Maps blog, noting that it follows the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) for its maps. This primarily means that the company has to rename Lake Ontario in Google Maps. Google's update on the name change also made it clear that the change will be only for Google Map users in the US. According to Google, those in the US will only see the new name, which is 'Lake of America'. Meanwhile, Canadians will continue to see the 'Lake Ontario' label. In the rest of the world, Lake Ontario will take precedence, but Lake America will also be there in parentheses. Apple followed the suit renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America on Maps for US users.

Emmy-winning actor Tom Skerritt, with roles in Alien and Top Gun, dies at 93
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement
Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure — whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien — has died. He was 93.
Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.
"While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices," the statement said.
Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for Picket Fences, winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights included playing Shirley MacLaine's patient husband in The Turning Point, Sally Field's husband in Steel Magnolias and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in Contact.
From left, Tom Skerritt, David E. Kelley, creator of Picket Fences, and actor Kathy Baker after the show won best drama series during the 45th annual Emmy Awards in Pasadena, Calif., on Sept. 19, 1993. (Douglas C. Pizac/AP Photo)
"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.
Onstage, he was the narrator in Our Town at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's A Time to Kill, in which The Associated Press wrote that he "nicely pulls off a charming, disgraced and drunken lawyer."
Skerritt's early life
Skerritt grew up in a middle-class family in Detroit. His father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child.
He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by Citizen Kane.
His performance in a Los Angeles theatre production of The Rainmaker led to his first film role — a supporting part as a sergeant in the scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film War Hunt in 1962. The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.
Redford and Skerritt had been vying for the same lead role, with Redford winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, cast Skerritt in A River Runs Through It, as the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times praised his "halting, thoughtful manner."
Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."
Alien and Top Gun
The cast of Alien poses on set. From left, actors John Hurt, Veronica Cartwright, Tom Skerritt, Yaphet Kotto, Sigourney Weaver, Harry Dean Stanton and Ian Holm are pictured in 1979. (Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation/Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)
After War Hunt, Skerritt struggled for screen time, landing a small role in M*A*S*H and Thieves Like Us for Robert Altman, and a bit part as a motorcycle cop in Harold and Maude for Hal Ashby.
Things changed with The Turning Point, which earned him a National Board of Review award. Then came Alien, with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct while hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea."
Then came another memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark Top Gun: "Gentlemen, you are the top one per cent of all Naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."
- REVIEW Top Gun: Maverick is the most Tom Cruise film ever
- The first flight of Top Gun (and two other reasons to visit the cinema) in 1986
Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in Picket Fences, a drama created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — including one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.
Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, who played his doctor wife, in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place of bizarre happenings, including a robber who left a trail of frogs and the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.
"It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'"
Tom Skerritt with his wife Julie Tokashiki in Geneva, Switzerland in 2012. (Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for IWC)
On the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's Brothers & Sisters, Jimmy Ford on TNT's Leverage and the recurring character Evan Drake on Cheers. He starred in the Hallmark movie What the Deaf Man Heard, alongside Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modelled for Guess jeans.
Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie Divided by Hate.  
"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."
He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

TOI correspondent from Washington: The Atlantic Ocean may owe its continued existence, at least under its present name, to 
Sundar Pichai
. By MAGA boss Donald Trump’s own account, the Google CEO rejected his effort to rename the ocean after himself because it touched numerous countries, not just the United States.
At a rally in South Carolina on Wednesday, Trump revealed that he had sounded Pichai about his desire to rechristen the Atlantic Ocean and asked him if he can handle it. The Google honcho, according to Trump, told him, “No no no…this time I am not doing it…please don’t ask us to do that” -- because oceans are different from other water bodies in that they skirt many countries.
“So I’ll probably pass on that..I think we should keep it as the Atlantic Ocean, right?” Trump said, indicating he had backed off from the idea.
Google has not publicly confirmed Trump’s account, which increasingly sound hyperbolic or highly embellished, earning him the sobriquet “Dementia Don" from critics. The episode is the latest installment in the U.S President’s increasingly ambitious campaign to make the world’s geography reflect his understanding of American greatness, which appears to require that the U.S not merely lead the world but also get naming rights over its water bodies.
First came the Gulf of Mexico, transformed by executive order into the Gulf of America. Then Mount Denali in Alaska was restored to its former federal name, Mount McKinley. In August, Lake Ontario, shared by the United States and Canada, became Lake America in the federal nomenclature.
The U.S President has since mused about renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait” and New Mexico “New America.” A river is apparently also required to complete the collection. The Hudson River has been spared, partly because Trump praised its namesake for his historical exploits, while the Mississippi was left alone because he likes the electoral results in Mississippi.
Google Maps has adopted the Gulf of America and Mount McKinley labels for users in the U.S in line with federal naming changes. At a rally in Kentucky last week, Trump boasted that Google had once ignored him but now followed his wishes, declaring that the company was “kissing my ass.” The remark was vintage Trump: crude, triumphant and revealing. The MAGA supremo presented a change in mapping labels as evidence not merely of administrative compliance but of corporate submission, scenes of which he has been rolling out with relish at the White House.
In an extraordinary tableau at a White House dinner last month, tech executives whose companies have spent years presenting themselves as independent, disruptive forces in global affairs took turns to pay tribute to the man who controls the regulatory machinery surrounding their businesses. There were obvious reasons for the pilgrimage: Tech companies face antitrust scrutiny, questions about AI regulation, trade and tariff exposure, immigration restrictions affecting their talent pipelines, and enormous infrastructure requirements. A President who can influence the rules of the game is a president no CEO can afford to ignore.
Trump’s handling – or taming – of Elon Musk offered another instructive lesson to tech oligarchs. Musk, who boosted and bankrolled Trump to victory in 2024, parted ways with the MAGA boss in 2025 after a public falling-out and briefly challenged him. Trump quickly brought him to heel. For Silicon Valley, the message was hard to miss: cultivate the White House, praise the president’s priorities, announce American investments and avoid becoming the next target of his displeasure.
Pichai’s reported refusal to rename the Atlantic may well be a rare instance of a CEO pushing back – politely. It is a small victory for geography and cartography -- and a reminder that even in Washington, where flattery, sycophancy, and adulation is now a flourishing industry, there are limits to what a CEO can put on a map.

The Supreme Court has expressed displeasure over States and Union Territories not responding to the Centre on how its judgment declaring menstrual hygiene as a part of the fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution is being implemented.
“If what we have said in the judgment is only going to remain on paper, how are the Union and states/UTs going to give effect to this fundamental right?” said Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan.
It said the apex court had declared menstrual hygiene/menstrual health as one of the facets of Article 21 of the Constitution, which deals with the protection of life and personal liberty.
The Bench said that on September 1, it had directed the States and UTs to take into consideration the deficiencies highlighted by it and report in that regard by the next date of hearing.
In a significant judgment delivered on January 30, the apex court said that the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution includes the right to menstrual health.
During the hearing in the matter on October 13, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre, told the Bench that the Union of India has taken up this issue very seriously with all the states and UTs to respond to what manner the judgment is being implemented.
“Unfortunately, the states/UTs have not responded to the Union so far. We fail to understand that once the Union calls for the necessary information, why do the states/UTs not respond?” the Bench said.
Also read: Menstrual health is a public health issue
“We are sure that the Union, the states/UTs have realised the importance of the judgment that we delivered, declaring menstrual hygiene as a part of the fundamental right,” it said.
The Bench said the apex court’s verdict was in the interest of young girls who were giving up education, more particularly in remote parts of the country because of the problem of menstrual hygiene, etc.
“We direct the Union to take up this issue very seriously with each state/UT and call for the necessary information in writing as to what steps they have taken so far for giving effect to the judgment delivered by this court,” it said.
The Bench said the Centre should study the verdict once again and accordingly call for information on each and every aspect of the matter.
“On the next date of hearing, if we hear from the Union that some of the states/UTs have not responded, we shall proceed to issue a contempt notice to the concerned chief secretary,” the Bench said.
While granting one last opportunity to do the needful, it posted the matter for the next hearing on December 14.
In its September 1 order, the bench had said the focus should be on the number of schools that lack gender-segregated, functional toilets with usable water connectivity, ensuring accessibility and privacy.
The Centre had then informed the top court that 30,458 gender-segregated toilets with washing facilities had been constructed in schools across the country, while 4,236 were under construction.
In its judgment delivered in January, the apex court had directed the states and UTs to ensure that every school, whether government-run or privately managed, in both urban and rural areas, was provided with functional, gender-segregated toilets with usable water connectivity.
The top court had also directed the states and UTs to ensure that every school provides sanitary napkins to girl students free of cost.
The judgment was delivered on a plea seeking pan-India implementation of the Centre’s ‘menstrual hygiene policy for schoolgoing girls’ in government and government-aided schools from classes 6 to 12.

A total of 2,390 Gram Panchayats in Tamil Nadu have been declared tuberculosis (TB)-free for 2025.
Asha Frederick, State TB Officer, said the ‘TB Free Panchayat’ initiative aimed to make TB elimination a community-owned movement at the grassroots level, with panchayats supporting prevention, early identification, diagnosis, treatment, and patient support. After verification under the national framework, 2,390 gram panchayats in the State were declared TB-free for the year 2025. These panchayats were felicitated in their respective districts recently, and the collective efforts of panchayat representatives, health teams, and communities were acknowledged.
The criteria for declaring a panchayat as TB-free included — achieving a target of examining 30 or more presumptive TB persons through NAAT and/or microscopy per 1,000 population in the year, a TB notification rate of one or fewer per 1,000 population for the year, and a treatment success rate of 90% or more among notified drug-sensitive TB patients.
Recently, the JOSH Team (Joint Squad for Health) was launched nationally by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, in collaboration with the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports and Ministry of Defence. In Tamil Nadu, Thoothukudi, Tiruchi, Cuddalore, Dharmapuri, and Theni were the five districts selected for the phase-I implementation of the JOSH teams’ field activities.
TB-free panchayats
The teams are being introduced at the block level to strengthen community participation. Each team is led by a designated Class-I Nodal Officer and supported by five “MY Bharat” volunteers and five NCC cadets. These teams will support TB awareness, regular community outreach, identification, and referral of persons with TB symptoms, mobilisation for screening, and other field-level TB elimination activities in coordination with the National TB Elimination Programme.
Dr. Asha Frederick said that at the block level, the JOSH Team would mobilise communities to spread awareness about TB, early symptoms, and available free diagnostic and treatment services, conduct village/ward-level awareness drives, and youth-led campaigns. They will be involved in patient support and handholding by acting as local “support buddies” for TB patients adopted under the Ni-kshay Mitra initiative and will also encourage treatment adherence, provide psychosocial support, and reduce stigma. The teams will build a cadre of young TB Champions to strengthen “TB Mukt Bharat” movement.
She added that the JOSH Teams would also facilitate the distribution of nutritional kits provided by Ni-kshay Mitras (donors) to patients and link patients to additional welfare schemes (ration, social security, health benefits).

The first-ever edition of the FIFA Women’s Club World Cup will take place in the United States of America between January 5 and 30, 2028.
The International Federation of Association Football (FIFA) announced the decision through a social media post on Wednesday.
“The inaugural edition of the FIFA Women’s Club World Cup will be hosted in the United States in January 2028,” FIFA said. “The host nation was confirmed by the FIFA Council in view of the maturity of its infrastructure and services, and the level of stakeholder interest in women’s football.”
The tournament will have 19 teams competing for the title. The following seven teams have already confirmed their spots in the World Cup: Arsenal (England), Barcelona (Spain), Club America (Mexico), Gotham (USA), Naegohyang (DPR Korea), Corinthians (Brazil) and Wuhan Jiangda (China).
“Women’s football has reached new heights at national-team level, and now it’s time for global competitions that showcase the best clubs from around the world.
“These FIFA competitions will stimulate growth, inspire athletes, create new rivalries, engage more fans and crown heroes from all over the world,” FIFA President Gianni Infantino was quoted in a media release.
“The FIFA Women’s Club World Cup will be a defining moment in the growth of women’s club football, giving the world’s top clubs the platform they deserve to compete against the best and put the women’s club game in the global spotlight.

Federal judge restricts DHS field operations looking for noncitizen voters
A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states.
In recent weeks, armed Homeland Security Investigations officers have carried out field operations and visited homes to interview people suspected of illegally voting as noncitizens. The targets can include people who became citizens but voted before they naturalized.
In a 19-page order late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that the federal government was using "flawed" data in the initiative and that its efforts likely violated the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.
Martínez-Olguín referenced a disclosure last month from a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower that alleged rushed efforts to match data to create a target list of potential noncitizens on voter rolls, and that the list includes U.S. citizens. She also pointed to HSI's social media posts, including one that showed agents handcuffing a California man accused of unlawfully registering to vote.
The judge wrote that the government's use of unreliable and incomplete data along with highly publicized arrests "lead to an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote."
HSI field operations were planned in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, according to documents produced in the case and CNN reporting.
Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in those states from conducting field operations targeting people they "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens," or that are based "wholly" on USCIS matching data without further investigation.
In a declaration, USCIS official Nicolas Bartell had told the judge his team manually reviews records before referring them to HSI, but acknowledged the "low possibility" citizens could be "erroneously identified as potential aliens" in federal records. He wrote the risks were mitigated by safeguards his office takes "and any remaining risks were outweighed by the need to support the agency's law-enforcement and election-integrity mission."
It's unclear how much of an effect the judge's order will have on the federal government's highly publicized campaign to find noncitizen voters.
States reviews and audits have consistently found voting by noncitizens to be extremely rare.
"DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders," the agency wrote in a statement. "We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."
The order is set to take effect on Friday and would be in effect through election night, though the federal government could appeal.
The judge's ruling came in a lawsuit filed last month by a coalition that includes San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, the city of San Francisco, nursing unions and Voto Latino Foundation. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center are litigating the case against the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.
"Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them," Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer with Protect Democracy, said in a statement.
"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," he added.
A court filing by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United described naturalized citizen members who no longer wanted to attend political rallies, sign up to be election poll workers, or vote in person because of the federal operations.
The order comes as the Department of Justice is suing California and demanding the state segregate 20,000 ballots from people federal officials say they believe are "likely" noncitizens.
A preliminary review of a sample of that list by Los Angeles County election officials found many of the registrations were canceled, inactive or had no voting history, and some pertained to people who indicated they were born in the U.S.
The DOJ announced charges against 28 green card holders across the state on Monday who are accused of illegally voting or registering to vote.

Leh, Oct 22: Ladakh Lieutenant Governor V K Saxena on Thursday laid the foundation stone for an open exhibition ground at Melong-Thang in Leh, calling it a landmark initiative to strengthen Ladakh's cultural, social and economic fabric.
The modern facility will serve as a platform to showcase Ladakh's rich traditions, art, crafts and innovations, besides hosting national and international exhibitions, trade fairs and community events, the lieutenant governor said.
He noted that the exhibition ground would boost tourism and local enterprise while creating opportunities for youth, artisans and entrepreneurs to connect with wider audiences.
The development reflects the UT administration's commitment to building world-class infrastructure that nurtures creativity, fosters dialogue and positions Ladakh as a hub of cultural exchange and sustainable development, Saxena added.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday said he spoke with his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and invited him to light a torch alongside brave Indian pilot Smit Machchhar on Israel's Independence Day.
In a post on X, the Israeli Prime Minister also said that PM Modi appreciated the "strong, long-standing ties" between the two countries.
"I spoke with my friend, the Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, and invited him to light a torch alongside a brave Indian pilot on Israel's Independence Day," said Netanyahu, who is in the midst of a close race for re-election.
"Modi thanked me for the invitation and said that, on the ground and in the air, India and Israel are fighting together against terrorism," he wrote in both Hindi and Hebrew.
Modi travelled to Israel in February on his second visit to the country in nine years. The India-Israel relationship was elevated to the level of strategic partnership during his first visit to Tel Aviv in July 2017.
Earlier this month, Israeli President Isaac Herzog invited Indian pilot Machchhar, who fought off an attack from his co-pilot inside the cockpit of a Tel Aviv-bound flight, to Israel to honour him with the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism.
Machchhar was injured while trying to stop his co-pilot from allegedly attempting to hijack flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv on September 30. The flight was carrying 174 passengers.
Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and avert a possible catastrophe. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers reached Israel safely later that day.
Machchhar, who has been hailed as a "hero" by Modi and Netanyahu for his courage, is undergoing treatment at a hospital in the United Arab Emirates.

- AdHoc has unveiled Dispatch's mobile version, coming to iOS and Android on December 9, 2026.

Indian Railways has brought Rowghat in Chhattisgarh onto the national railway network for the first time since Independence, improving connectivity to remote parts of the state. The Tadoki–Rowghat and Abhanpur–Kurud broad-gauge railway sections were inaugurated on Tuesday, with two new passenger train services also launched.
Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai attended the inauguration, while Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw participated through video conferencing. The programme also included the foundation stone laying for an electric locomotive maintenance facility in Raipur.
The new rail links are expected to strengthen transport infrastructure in southern Chhattisgarh, offering residents better access to essential services and economic opportunities.
The inauguration of the Tadoki–Rowghat section marks the completion of the 95-km Dalli-Rajhara–Rowghat railway line, constructed at a cost of ₹1,628 crore. The project was completed with the opening of its final 17.5-km stretch between Tadoki and Rowghat.
The arrival of trains in Rowghat is a significant development for the region's residents, who have had limited transport options. The new connection is expected to make travel more convenient and improve access to education, healthcare, employment and markets.
Addressing the gathering, Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai said development initiatives across Chhattisgarh, including railway infrastructure projects, were progressing steadily. He highlighted that the state had received an allocation of more than ₹7,000 crore under the current Railway Budget.
Sai said the new railway infrastructure would improve connectivity in remote areas and contribute to industrial growth, trade and broader socio-economic development.
Two passenger train services, Rowghat–Raipur and Raipur–Kurud, were flagged off during the inauguration programme. The services are expected to improve access to Raipur, the state capital, while offering more convenient travel options to people living along the routes.
The new connections could also facilitate daily commuting and regional trade by making travel between smaller towns and major commercial centres easier.
Apart from passenger connectivity, the railway line is expected to facilitate the transportation of iron ore from the Rowghat region. The area has significant iron ore resources that can contribute to India's steel industry, including operations at the Bhilai Steel Plant.
Rail connectivity can make the movement of raw materials more efficient, helping industries meet their requirements and strengthening supply chains. Better transport links could also encourage economic activity and generate employment opportunities in surrounding areas.
Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw congratulated the people of Chhattisgarh on the completion of the railway projects and the introduction of the new passenger services. He said railway infrastructure across the state was being expanded through new lines, gauge conversion and additional tracks.
The projects highlighted included the Dalli-Rajhara–Rowghat railway line, gauge conversion on the Kendri–Abhanpur–Rajim–Dhamtari section and other track development works.
Construction is currently under way on the Kharsia–Parmalkasa double-line project. The Union Cabinet has also recently approved a third railway line connecting Pendra Road, Bilaspur and Uslapur.
These initiatives aim to increase railway network capacity, improve passenger connectivity and support industrial and economic development across Chhattisgarh.
The Abhanpur–Kurud broad-gauge railway section was also inaugurated as part of the programme. The 22-km stretch forms part of the Abhanpur–Dhamtari railway project, which aims to expand broad-gauge connectivity in the region.
Passenger services are already operational between Abhanpur and Rajim following gauge conversion work. Construction on the remaining Kurud–Dhamtari section is continuing and is expected to be completed shortly.
The opening of the Abhanpur–Kurud stretch is expected to provide additional travel options for passengers heading towards Raipur while supporting local businesses, regional commerce and daily commuting.

Mumbai, October 22: Expressing severe displeasure over slum dwellers dumping garbage on public streets, the Bombay High Court asked the Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA) to consider deterrent measures, including forfeiting rights to permanent alternate accommodation for repeat offenders.
A bench of Justices Girish Kulkarni and Neela Gokhale made the observations while hearing a batch of petitions, including one filed by the Kannamwar Nagar CHS Association Ltd, regarding foul odour, toxic gas emissions and health hazards faced by residents near the Kanjurmarg dumping ground.
HC Flags Rights Of Other Citizens
"It cannot be that an encroachment on government land or private property, with an entitlement to receive permanent alternate accommodation, gives them a licence to litter and deface public streets," the bench observed.
"In the event prosecution is lodged or fines are paid on more than two occasions, it would be appropriate for the SRA to take measures to forfeit the right of such slum dwellers to receive permanent alternate accommodation."
Addressing Senior Advocate Birendra Saraf, appearing for the SRA, the court emphasised that unruly action infringes upon other citizens' constitutional rights: "Any misuse of the right to remain in slums cannot be taken to be a right to breach the fundamental rights of other citizens to clean and hygienic surroundings under Article 21."
BMC Cites Challenges In Slum Areas
Senior Advocate Anil Sakhare, representing the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), submitted affidavits detailing steps taken in the K-West ward, Andheri, to clear garbage accumulation. He highlighted that over 42% of Mumbai's population resides in slum clusters where clean-up teams face local resistance and safety threats.
The court criticised the lack of progress on basic enforcement, noting that earlier assurances regarding CCTV surveillance were conspicuously absent from the affidavits filed.
"There is no rule of law for slum dwellers — dump anywhere, construct any number of floors (on their unauthorised structure)," the bench remarked. "Monetary penalties have failed to bring about any result. A deterrent can come only when strict consequences are prescribed."
Court Seeks Greater Civic Involvement
The court directed the BMC to rope in corporators to build awareness, as they are in contact with local citizens. It ordered additional municipal commissioners to submit affidavits on elected representatives' involvement in waste management.
On a court query, advocate Saket Mone, appearing for the plant contractor, cited a recent Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) midnight inspection that reported no foul odour outside Kannamwar Nagar.

Otherwise, we will ask you to deposit Rs 5 lakh per day. When we are concerned with lakhs of citizens, Rs 5 lakh a day is nothing."
The court has kept the matter for further hearing on November 3.

Jagan refuses to allow niece’s wedding at family compound amid dispute with sister Sharmila
The relationship between the siblings is said to have deteriorated after Jagan Mohan Reddy became chief minister
Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party (YSRCP) chief YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has refused to allow his niece’s wedding at the family compound, Yelahanka Palace, in Bengaluru in November amid a property dispute with his sister YS Sharmila, people aware of the matter said.
Sharmila’s daughter, YS Anjili Reddy, got engaged to Somala Raghurami Reddy, who lives in the United States, on September 24. People aware of the matter said Sharmila, the Andhra Pradesh Congress chief, wanted to have their wedding on November 25 at Yelahanka Palace.
An aide to Sharmila said Jagan Mohan Reddy conveyed to her through their mother, YS Vijayamma, that he would not allow the wedding at Yelahanka Palace.
“This has come as a big shock to Sharmila, as she had distributed wedding invitations to relatives, political leaders and prominent personalities. Now, she is compelled to look for an alternative venue for the wedding,” said the aide.
The aide quoted Jagan Mohan Reddy telling Vijayamma that the property was registered in the name of his wife, Bharati Reddy. “Vijayamma tried to persuade him to reconsider his position, but he was firm on his stand,” Sharmila’s aide said.
He added that Sharmila is now left with no alternative but to scramble for another suitable venue. “She has already sent invitations to top Congress leaders in the high command, besides chief ministers including D K Shivakumar of Karnataka and A Revanth Reddy of Telangana, and former Tamil Nadu chief minister M K Stalin. She has to look for another suitable venue to ensure security and logistical requirements associated with their attendance,” he said.
Jagan Mohan Reddy and Sharmila have been involved in a dispute over family properties, including shares in Saraswati Power and Industries Ltd, for the last five years. The issue is pending adjudication in the National Company Law Tribunal.
People close to Sharmila said the late former Andhra Pradesh chief minister Y S Rajasekhar Reddy wanted his son and daughter to receive equal shares in the family’s properties. He arranged for separate residences for them in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Idupulapaya.
In Hyderabad’s Lotus Pond locality, their residences are next to each other. Sharmila continues to live in her house there. Similarly, separate residences were reportedly constructed for the siblings at Idupulapaya, the family’s native place.
Jagan Mohan Reddy is said to have stopped visiting his residence there. Sharmila reportedly stays at hers when she visits Idupulapaya.
In Yelahanka, the family reportedly has two houses constructed next to each other for the siblings across approximately 20 acres. “But the house given to Sharmila was not registered in her name. Rajasekhara Reddy used to stay there whenever he visited Bengaluru. Jagan also has been staying in his palace at Yelahanka during his weekly visits,” Sharmila’s aide said.
Rajasekhara Reddy’s death in a helicopter crash on September 2, 2009, left the division of the family’s assets unresolved, leading to disputes between the siblings. The aide said Jagan Mohan Reddy is denying Sharmila a share in the Bengaluru property.
Sharmila played a key role in the YSRCR and undertook a foot march when Jagan Mohan Reddy was in jail between 2012 and 2013. She campaigned for the party before the 2019 elections.
The relationship is said to have deteriorated after Jagan Mohan Reddy became chief minister in 2019. Sharmila was distanced from the party as disagreements over the division of family assets strained relations.
Sharmila floated a party in Telangana before joining the Congress in 2024 and becoming its chief in Andhra Pradesh. She has been attacking her brother politically since.

Dubai, Oct 22: Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers were either struck by attacks or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight Thursday, possibly the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the Iran war started on February 28.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East. Read our full coverage here.
7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state television reports
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers caught fire and were damaged overnight Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
If verified, it would be the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the start of the Iran war on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran.
Quoting a statement by the Revolutionary Guard's navy, the Iranian report said that four of the tankers were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire. Another three were damaged and immobilised when they hit naval mines.
The report didn't provide details about possible casualties or the flags of the tankers.
The report also warned that the Revolutionary Guard may target US bases in the region if the US tried to allow oil tankers to transit through other parts of the strait.
The Revolutionary Guard had routinely targeted US bases in Gulf countries during the war.

Yemen's Defence Ministry said Thursday that Houthi rallies and mobilisation programmes will be considered legitimate military targets and warned residents in Houthi-held areas against taking part.
The announcement was shared in a social media post and is considered a major escalation against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as civilians living in areas under their control.
Deliberate attacks on civilians could amount to a war crime.
Rallies and what Houthis call “cultural courses” are one of the Iranian-backed group's main tools for mobilisation of supporters and fighters.

The dead are a Saudi citizen and an Indian national who was living in the kingdom, according to a statement. Another eight people suffered injuries in the attack that occurred late Wednesday.
Saudi authorities didn't say who was responsible for the attack or provide any details about the attack reported earlier Thursday. The Houthi rebels issued no statement.
King Fahd Airport on the country's east near Bahrain and Qatar has been attacked previously amid a wider wave of Houthi missile and projectile strikes targeting major airports in Saudi Arabia.

Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun, director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas, at least in his lifetime.
Speaking at an In Conversation event at the Singapore International Film Festival, Chan was asked by an audience member whether he had ever doubted his decision to go into the film industry. His advice to aspiring filmmakers: “This is probably the toughest time for film, but do I believe this medium is going to be lost and gone to short-form entertainment? No.”
He said he would probably use AI as a technique, the way the industry already uses CGI and special effects, noting that CGI has relied on AI for years without calling it that. “Anything that helps me make movies, I welcome. But they won’t know art. Movies are still made by people,” Chan said.
Popular on Variety
Young audiences’ shrinking attention spans have them turning to short and vertical dramas, Chan said, while at the other end, people are listening to podcasts that run for hours, and Christopher Nolan did podcasts around the world to explain his purist approach of making “Oppenheimer” the way movies were made in the ’50s. “So there are two completely opposite ends of the spectrum that are surviving and thriving simultaneously. So I believe that movie will be around for a long, long time,” he told a rapt audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands.
Chan’s latest film, “The Road Not Taken,” premiered in Toronto. “My new movie is about Alzheimer’s, but it’s really not just about Alzheimer’s. It’s about a broken family that has all sorts of problems a family could have,” he said.
The story centers on a couple in the middle of divorce proceedings when the wife, who has early-onset Alzheimer’s, no longer remembers the divorce and drifts back in her mind to the time they fell in love in their 20s. A harsh grandfather and the couple’s relationship with their Gen Z daughter complete the picture. The daughter in the film is 20, the same age as Chan’s own daughter, who is training to become an actor. Chan’s partner is actor Sandra Ng.
The English title comes from the Robert Frost poem, which Chan called his life motto, while the Chinese title, “Ming Tian Hui Geng Hao,” translates as “Tomorrow Will Be Better.” “There’s really no right path,” he said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, it’s all about how you walk it. You make it right.”
While researching the film, Chan visited an Alzheimer’s care institution in Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan province, where he picked up an eight-word Mandarin phrase that he used to sum up his career: go with the flow, and know when to stop. In the ’90s, when he was making romantic comedies at United Filmmakers Organization (UFO), the company he co-founded, gangster pictures and wuxia ruled Hong Kong screens. “We were not exactly going with the flow, but we did make the flow, somehow,” he said.
That same flow later carried him to “The Warlords,” which he described as his biggest film. “Never had I thought that I would ever make a historical epic battle movie with Jet Li. That was never, ever in my agenda for my entire life,” Chan said.
This year marks the 30th anniversary of “Comrades,” which Chan made at 34 as his seventh feature and which captures Hong Kong between 1985 and 1995. He left Hong Kong on Christmas Eve 1996, and only after returning from America around two and a half years later did he grasp how deeply the film had affected filmmakers in mainland China, South Korea and Southeast Asia, even though, he said, it probably only barely recouped its investment.
“That movie gave me a lease of movie life for the next 30 years, until now,” Chan said.
He said 90% of people remember him for that single film, “as if I have not done better afterwards,” calling it a blessing but also a spell he wanted to break.
Chan, who also said the ’90s marked the start of Hong Kong cinema’s decline rather than its golden age, described his DreamWorks film “The Love Letter” as a difficult experience. He was not thrown by working across cultures, he said, having grown up Thai-Chinese and feeling like an outsider even in Hong Kong. What he struggled with was a corporate system where it was unclear who called the shots, and a reliance on test screenings that he likened to today’s algorithms. He said he was probably the first, if not the only, Hong Kong filmmaker to make a non-action film inside the U.S. studio system.
“Had I gone to America or Hollywood with the knowledge that I have of film and marketing and dealing with corporate, I probably would have fared better,” Chan said. “I was too young then, too naive.”
Asked later by an audience member how he navigates censorship in mainland China, Chan said: “Dealing with a corporate is very, very difficult. And if I can survive that, I can survive anything.” He added that limitations of budget, stars, studios or censorship tend to push filmmakers to be more creative.
After Hollywood, Chan set up Applause Pictures, a pan-Asian venture that made 10 films in two and a half years, most of them horror. Its output included “The Eye” franchise and the “Three” horror omnibus films, which brought together directors including Park Chan-wook, Miike Takashi, Kim Jee-woon and Fruit Chan. He also executive produced “One Fine Spring Day” for Korean director Hur Jin-ho – director of SGIFF opener “The Assassin(s)” – whose debut “Christmas in August” he loved. But a planned three-part love story with Hur and Japan’s Iwai Shunji found no investors.
“If we continue this pan-Asian effort, I’m going to be stuck with making horror films my whole life,” Chan said of the decision to move on to mainland China, where his first film was the 2005 musical “Perhaps Love.”
An aspiring screenwriter in the audience asked how he handles a scene that isn’t landing. “I don’t usually fix it for them. I make them fix it over and over and over and over again,” Chan said, adding that after saying “great” to everything at home, he doesn’t do the same with his writers.
He credited nine writers on “The Warlords,” and said screenwriters joke that his films’ writers would not fit in a minibus. “I milk the writer to death, and then I milk another writer,” he said. “So the writers’ community really don’t like me very much. But making movies is not about being well-liked.”
Though he is often seen as a genre-hopper, Chan said the same concerns run through his work, citing the love triangles in his debut “Alan & Eric: Between Hello and Goodbye,” “Comrades,” “Perhaps Love” and even “The Warlords,” which he called a love triangle between three brothers.
“Making every movie is answering some sort of life questions that I have at that stage, in point of my life,” he said. “So in a way, I’ve been making the same movie in my mind in the last 36 years.”

Non-communicable diseases account for three-quarters of deaths worldwide but affect different population groups in different ways, a World Health Organization study showed on Tuesday.
In its biggest-ever look at inequality in health and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), the WHO studied the top four killers -- cancer, cardiovascular diseases, chronic respiratory diseases and diabetes.
It also looked at the five main risk factors driving them -- tobacco use, alcohol consumption, obesity, unhealthy diets, physical inactivity and air pollution.
The report then scanned this across differences in NCD burden, prevention and care -- by age, gender, economic status, education, place of residence, disability status, employment and migration status.
"This is the first effort to systematically measure inequalities in NCDs and their risk factors on a global scale," said Ahmad Reza Hosseinpoor, who leads the WHO's health inequality monitoring team.
"The findings show which populations are being left behind."
NCDs cover eight of the top 10 causes of death, with cardiovascular diseases the biggest killer by far, claiming almost 20 million deaths a year.
The 10 years of national data, collected between 2013 and 2022, confirmed that socio-economic status influences health at every stage -- from initial exposure to risk factors, through to diagnosis, treatment and disease management.
For example, the report found that in low- and middle-income countries, less educated populations suffered higher rates of hypertension and diabetes.
Cervical cancer screening rates are very low among the poorest and least-educated women; while tobacco use remains higher among less-educated men than among more educated men.
Looking at geographical factors, the study found that people in rural areas has significantly more limited access to hypertension diagnosis and cancer screening.
Gender and age also play a role. Men with hypertension are diagnosed and treated less frequently than women, even though they consume more tobacco and alcohol.
Conversely, obesity is more common among women, particularly in developing countries.
The study confirmed that social marginalisation, disability and migrant status were significant factors contributing to increased risk.
The United Nations' health agency urged governments to raise health-related taxes on tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks -- measures that are particularly effective among low-income populations.
Countries were also encouraged to tailor insurance schemes or subsidies for under-served communities and to incorporate inequality indicators into their national health systems.

More than 80% of Bank of Japan watchers anticipate the central bank’s next interest rate increase will come in December, according to a recent survey. None expect a hike when the bank concludes its next meeting on Oct. 30.
Some 83% of economists forecast the bank will raise borrowing costs from the current level of 1.25% at its meeting ending on Dec. 18. Just last month, only 35% forecast a hike in December. In that survey, January was the most popular pick for the next rate hike.
The latest survey results also show that 67% of respondents expect the BOJ to raise rates every three months, up from 46% in the last survey. That points to expectations that the BOJ will maintain the same tempo of rate hikes after it raised rates in September for the second time in three months, the fastest pace since 1990.

Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
- Published
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.
Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.
A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.

Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
What is PHP?
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.
PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.
The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.
Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
'Serious vulnerability'
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.
According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.
"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."
