The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has proposed prohibiting the addition of sucrose and fructose in food products intended for infants up to six months of age.
The draft Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette of India on Friday (October 16, 2026) proposes to amend the existing regulations governing the nutritional composition, quality and safety of infant nutrition products.
The proposed amendment states that “sucrose and fructose shall not be added in the products intended for infants up to the age of 6 months”.
Under the existing Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, lactose and glucose polymers are the preferred sources of carbohydrates in infant nutrition products. Sucrose and/or fructose may be added when required as a carbohydrate source, subject to prescribed limits.
The draft amendment seeks to introduce a specific restriction on their addition in products intended for infants in the first six months of life.
Critical period
“The first six months are a critical period for infant growth and development, making appropriate nutrition particularly important. The proposed restriction aims to ensure that products intended for this age group meet their nutritional requirements without the addition of sucrose and fructose,” the government maintained in a release issued on Saturday (October 16).
It added that early exposure to added sugars is a public health concern because of its potential implications for the development of dietary preferences and long-term dietary habits. Unhealthy dietary patterns are among the risk factors associated with childhood obesity and related health problems.
“The proposal also complements public health recommendations advocating exclusive breastfeeding during the first six months of life. The World Health Organization recommends exclusive breastfeeding during this period, followed by the introduction of nutritionally adequate complementary foods alongside continued breastfeeding,” said the release.
For public consultation
The notification has been issued for public consultation. Stakeholders have been invited to submit objections and suggestions within 60 days from the date on which copies of the official gazette containing the notification are made available to the public.
FSSAI will consider the representations received within the stipulated period before finalising the amendment. The proposed restriction will become part of the regulatory framework only after the amendment is finalised and notified.

Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo. Analysts have speculated that Samsung’s Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that.
In a new blog post, Samsung UK crows that the company’s 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year’s models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn’t talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention.
The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn’t release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn’t mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent.
Samsung noted last month that US preorders for the Galaxy Z8 series were trending 30 percent higher than last year, but it hasn’t confirmed any updated numbers for the US market. This meshes with third-party reports, which claimed Samsung was ramping up foldable manufacturing, particularly of the wider, iPhone-like Z Fold 8. The company isn’t talking about the proportion of Z Fold 8 versus Z Fold 8 Ultra sales, but it seems likely that Samsung’s wider foldable is doing better in the wake of Apple’s foldable announcement.

Chennai YouTuber arrested for allegedly abetting suicide of influencer
The accused allegedly posted defamatory videos targeting the influencer and threatened him in an attempt to extort money, a police official said.
A Chennai-based YouTuber has been arrested for allegedly extorting and threatening a 27-year-old social media influencer who was later found dead at his residence, police said on Thursday.
The influencer, who hailed from Puducherry and had more than 1.4 million followers, was found dead at his rented home in Chennai on October 20. Police are investigating the death as a suspected suicide.
The accused, Jason Samuel Vijayakumar, 30, allegedly posted defamatory videos targeting the influencer and threatened him in an attempt to extort money, a police official said.
The accused also allegedly got the influencer's social media accounts blocked by Meta, the official said.
According to the police, the influencer was facing pressure over his financial advice content, which he was allegedly accused of sharing without a licence from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
“He was under severe mental stress due to this and allegedly died by suicide by hanging himself at his residence on October 20,” the official said.
A case was registered at Kanathur police station under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which deals with abetment of suicide, following a complaint by the victim's father.
Police said witness statements and documents collected during the investigation pointed to Vijayakumar's alleged role in the circumstances leading to the death.
Vijayakumar was arrested on Thursday and remanded in judicial custody by a judicial magistrate after being produced before the court.

A powerful new genetic toolkit that could make it easier to study the bacteria responsible for Tuberculosis (TB), one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases, has been developed by Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, Director of the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB).
Investigate how different proteins work together
Designed for use in mycobacteria, the new system could accelerate efforts to understand how the TB bacterium survives, grows and causes disease. It gives scientists tools to switch genes on, track proteins inside bacterial cells, and investigate how different proteins work together.
Despite decades of research, many genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium that causes TB, remain poorly understood. Scientists typically rely on specially designed DNA molecules known as ‘shuttle vectors’ to introduce genes into bacterial cells and study their functions. However, the complex protein interactions within a cell are difficult to monitor.
New shuttle vectors with fluorescent markers
To address this challenge, Mr. Nandicoori’s research student Asis Kumar used existing knowledge to create a collection of 40 new shuttle vectors. These molecular delivery vehicles carry selected genes into bacterial cells, enabling researchers to study them in different ways.
The new genetic toolkit offers greater flexibility because the shuttle vectors can be equipped with fluorescent markers such as Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) and ‘mCherry’, which make proteins glow under a microscope. This allows researchers to observe where specific proteins are located inside bacterial cells and how they move during growth and division, explained Mr. Nandicoori, in an exclusive interaction.
The team tested the new tools in Mycobacterium smegmatis, a harmless relative of the TB bacterium that is commonly used in laboratories. The fluorescent tags successfully highlighted the locations of key proteins involved in cell growth and division, confirming that the system worked as intended.
The toolkit also enables scientists to study several proteins simultaneously. The research team examined how four different regulatory proteins from the TB bacterium functioned within a single bacterial cell, providing insight into how proteins interact and coordinate critical cellular processes.
Another significant feature is a new purification method that reduces background contamination and improves the identification of proteins that naturally interact inside the cell. This is important because many biological processes are carried out not by individual proteins, but by groups of proteins working together, said the Director.
Mr. Nandicoori said the genetic toolkit could be expanded in the future with new genetic switches, protein tags and regulatory elements, making it adaptable to a wide range of experiments. The study was published in ‘Journal of Bacteriology’.

On Oct. 14, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Facebook (archived) that SpaceX, the spaceflight and telecommunications company Elon Musk founded, had imposed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, its commercial and governmental satellite internet services, in Ukraine.
Beskrestnov wrote that the restrictions came without warning and had disrupted a number of the Ukrainian military's missions.
In the days following the disruption, as speculation abounded about who had ordered the slowdown of SpaceX's internet services in Ukraine, some social media users claimed it was U.S. President Donald Trump or another White House official.
For example, following a Reuters report, one Threads user, whose post was quoted (archived) by activist organization The Other 98% on Facebook, wrote (archived):
So it's official: Reuters has confirmed that the White House gave the order to disrupt Starlink so Russia could attack Kyiv with no advanced warning. The US aided and abetted Putin's killing of numerous civilians in Ukraine. Trump's a traitor, a Russian asset who is using US military technology to help our enemy.
Similar iterations of the rumor spread on X and Instagram as Snopes readers contacted us for more information.
It is unclear, as of this writing, who ordered SpaceX to slow down Starlink and/or Starshield services in Ukraine on or around Oct. 14. The slowdown has been widely reported by Ukrainian officials and reputable news organizations citing affected military personnel in Ukraine, plus U.S. officials have commented on the matter. Therefore, there is no reason to doubt that the slowdown did occur.
On Oct. 15, Reuters reported that Pentagon officials received an order to limit Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade satellite internet service — "from inside the White House." The following day, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that it was Musk who first "approached" Trump with the idea to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. The paper reported that one anonymous source said Trump "agreed" with Musk's idea. On Oct. 20, The Wall Street Journal reported that one anonymous source said Trump and Musk spoke about slowing down Starshield speeds before Musk reportedly "ordered" restrictions.
Trump told reporters on Oct. 16 that neither he nor Musk were responsible for the decision to slow down SpaceX services in Ukraine. Writing on X, Musk said (archived) the "US military and ultimately POTUS" were responsible for the secure Starshield system and that the commercial Starlink product could not be used for "offensive military action."
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 14, 2026
Snopes could not independently verify Reuters', The Telegraph's or The Wall Street Journal's stories because they relied on anonymous sources.
When asked about the reports, the White House referred us to Trump's Oct. 16 comments. A Pentagon spokesperson said via email, "There has been no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
Considering the fact that Trump and members of his cabinet publicly and repeatedly denied having given the order to slow down Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine, in direct opposition to Reuters', The Telegraph's and The Wall Street Journal's reports, we cannot give this claim a rating.
SpaceX did not return a request for comment on who ordered the slowdown of Starlink and/or Starshield services in Ukraine on or around Oct. 14 or on why this occurred. Snopes also contacted Beskrestnov to ask if SpaceX's services are back to full capacity in Ukraine. We await a reply to our query.
Starlink is a satellite internet service. Using SpaceX's rockets, the company has sent more than 11,000 of its own satellites into low-earth orbit. The satellites communicate with each other and Starlink terminals on Earth to connect customers to the internet. Starshield is similar, but is designed for government use.
Ukraine has used Starlink terminals since February 2022. The New York Times reported in July 2023 that artillery teams, drone commanders and pilots could watch drone footage simultaneously using a Starlink connection, which allowed them to find and hit targets faster.
What happened to SpaceX services in Ukraine?
On Oct. 16, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented a speed limit for Starlink terminals while in motion" of 100 mph when those terminals were using the military-grade Starshield network that the company supplies to governments. The restrictions meant that if a terminal moved faster than 100 mph, its internet connection would cut out.
The Associated Press, which interviewed Beskrestnov after the speed limitation came into force, said such a restriction posed a problem for Ukrainian drones, which frequently travel at speeds faster than 100 mph.
For example, the Assocated Press reported that Russian Shahed-class drones could fly at more than 250 mph. Being restricted to 100 mph meant Ukrainian drones could not chase down or intercept Shahed-class drones and were in turn more vulnerable to Russian offenses. (Shahed is the name of an Iranian-designed drone that Russia frequently uses for attacks inside Ukraine.)
On Oct. 16, Zelenskyy told reporters (archived) in Brussels that the Ukrainian military uses Starlink to "intercept jet-powered 'shaheds'" as well as for "mid-range strikes against enemy military targets in our temporarily occupied territories." He added that troops also "receive food and water delivered by drones using Starlink."
That same day, Zelenskyy said speed restrictions had not been fully lifted. It is not clear exactly how long the restrictions have been in place.
On Oct. 17, Zelenskyy reportedly told journalists that Ukraine had driven Starlink terminals at speeds higher than 100 mph outside Ukraine and those terminals had continued to receive a connection, suggesting the speed restrictions affecting the country's troops were deliberate and only applied in Ukraine.
Trump, US officials said they had 'nothing to do' with SpaceX service slowdown
Speaking during NBC's "Meet the Press" on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy blamed the Starlink and Starshield speed restriction on the U.S. government and SpaceX. He said (time code 21:25), "It was the message from American government to limit this bit, and, technically, SpaceX did it."
Zelenskyy made this claim despite Trump saying of the decision two days earlier (time code 11:21), "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," referring to Musk.
Trump did not elaborate on how SpaceX might have suddenly placed limits on Starlink or Starshield speeds in Ukraine without the knowledge of himself, Musk or another decision maker.
Also on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any United States involvement in slowing down Starlink in Ukraine. He said (time code 00:42), "We had nothing to do with it. I don't, I don't — The United States, nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down."
Rubio also repeated Trump's Oct. 16 suggestion that the slowdown somehow occurred without a major decision maker, saying, "It sort of happened."
The Secretary of State also claimed Ukraine does not have access to Starshield, SpaceX's secure network for government entities. This is at odds with Beskrestnov's Oct. 14 statement that said restrictions applied to Starlink terminals on the Starshield network. On Oct. 19, Rubio told journalists in Uzbekistan that Ukraine had "benefited" from Starshield, though did not elaborate on how.
Snopes asked Beskrestnov to clarify whether Ukraine had access to Starshield. We await replies to our queries. The State Department referred us to Rubio's Oct. 19 remarks.
In response to a request from Ukraine's Minister of Defence Mykhailo Fedorov to have speed restrictions on Starshield lifted, Musk wrote on X:
Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.
If Beskrestnov is correct that the October speed restrictions applied to the Starshield network, Musk's statement would likely place the responsibility for any changes with Trump or the U.S. government as the owner of the system. Trump and the Pentagon both denied having made changes to capabilities they provided to Ukraine.
Starlink troubles come at unsettled time for US-Ukraine relations
The sudden restrictions on SpaceX services came amid tensions between Ukraine and the United States. During an Oct. 15 Newsmax interview, Trump said he found Zelenskyy "more difficult to deal with than Putin" and appeared to repeat an earlier call for elections in Ukraine to replace its president.
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy told British broadcast journalist Piers Morgan on Oct. 14 that he felt "betrayed" by Trump after the Starlink speed restrictions. He said he believed this was deliberate act by SpaceX and the U.S. that, he added, resulted in Ukrainian lives being lost.
Additionally, on Oct. 18, Zelenskyy told NBC's "Meet the Press" that intelligence sharing from the United States to Ukraine had been "blocked for some period of time" but that U.S. officials had "de-blocked" it.
The next day, Zelensky posted on X that he had "no early warning from our partners" before Russian strikes on Kyiv and other regions overnight. He added in a separate post that units using Starlink or Starshield services still did not work at speeds above 100 mph "in various sectors of the front."
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that the U.S. has never stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, a claim repeated in the Pentagon spokesperson's statement to Snopes.

Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
- Published
A magnitude seven earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens of others, according to Chinese state media reports.
The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region as on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau.
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa.
Authorities have declared an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 32 others have also been injured.
Power has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, local reports said.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.
Strong tremors were also felt in the cities of Qamdo and Nyingchi in Tibet.
Videos on social media show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

According to the National Retail Federation, a trade association for retail professionals, consumer spending on Halloween in the United States is expected to reach $13.5 billion in 2026. That's more than a billion higher than in 2023, when the total spent reached about $12.2 billion.
American companies — particularly candy and costume makers — pounced on the rising popularity of the trick-or-treat tradition in the 1950s to commodify Halloween and grow their businesses.
That commodification became so commonplace in a short span of years that the co-host of NPR's "Throughline" podcast, Rund Abdelfatah, would eventually cite Halloween as "an American capitalist success story."
What began as a Celtic tradition called Samhain now operates as a billion-dollar holiday across the globe, encompassing everything from religious folklore to secular spooky fun with a particular growth in mass appeal during the 20th century.
One of the most beloved traditions of "spooky season" that predates trick-or-treating and scary movies is carving jack-o'-lanterns; a tradition whose popularity is reflected in the fact that it's projected Americans will spend about $771 million in 2026 on Halloween pumpkins alone.
But where did this strange tradition come from? While the custom itself has a spooky story to go along with it, carving pumpkins was not always traditionally linked to Halloween, nor were the objects carved always pumpkins. While the exact origins are unknown, there is a piece of Irish folklore that purports an explanation: The legend of "Stingy Jack," which first appeared in print in the 19th century.
Snopes has covered the legend of "Stingy Jack" at length previously, including its even older connections to stories about "will o' the wisps," ethereal lights seen floating in the darkness of the woods.
(Getty Images)
In short, it is the tale of a man named Jack who played tricks on the Devil, only to find himself banished from both Heaven and Hell when he died. The legend says the Devil then sent Jack wandering the earthly plane forever, his only light a burning coal placed inside a hollowed-out turnip.
Across Ireland and Scotland, people began carving their own turnips and placing a candle inside to ward off Jack and other spirits who may come around. One early mention of this practice was as early as 1640 in a letter penned by author James Howell, which mentioned "a Turnip cut like a Death's-head with a Candle in't."
The practice was not dissimilar to the Samhain tradition of wearing disguises to protect oneself from wandering spirits. And like that tradition, over time, the legends about Stingy Jack — and thus, jack-o'-lanterns — were integrated into Halloween lore.
When immigrants from Ireland and Great Britain started making their way to the United States, the Halloween traditions followed, and soon the carving object of choice became pumpkins due to their wide availability in America.
An 1885 issue of Harper's Young People magazine reflects the increasing popularity of the tradition at the time:
American boys delight in the funny grinning jack-o'-lanterns made of huge yellow pumpkins with a candle inside. Any lad skillful with a penknife can carve the eyes, nose, and wide mouth with huge teeth that seem like those of a veritable goblin when they appear suddenly at a window or adorning a gate post.
As Halloween's popularity grew, so too did the jack-o'-lantern. Now, companies can be found specializing in pumpkin-carving kits, reality TV shows and pumpkin festivals.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

I set up a digital wall calendar at a friend’s house a couple of months ago. Her first question was one I’ve constantly asked myself as I test these devices in my own home: “Does it have a voice assistant?”
It feels like the one thing missing from these devices. Digital wall calendars have been on the rise in popularity this year, driven by the popularity of the Skylight Calendar. After testing multiple models in my own home, I can see why. These devices take any and all of the digital calendars you already have (Google Calendar, iCalendar, Outlook Calendar—you name it) and put them onto a single device in your home.
It’s great if you’re like my husband and me, who live by our Google Calendars but don’t want to be tied to our phones when discussing plans. These devices can also double as household management tools with meal planning, chore trackers, to-do lists, photo screen savers that double as a digital photo frame, and even financial management for your kids if you go with the Greenlight Family Hub.
The Greenlight Family Hub has been an interesting device in the world of digital calendars because of how many features it offers. It not only adds financial management, as the company was originally a banking tool for parents and their teens, but family location tracking, which uses the Greenlight app on a family member’s phone to show their location, or a GPS tracker that you can separately purchase for younger children.
But there’s one feature behind the paywall (a $10-a-month membership) that finally satisfies the thing I’ve always wanted: a voice assistant.
Greenlight’s proprietary voice assistant has been both easy to use and has given smart, thoughtful answers. So why isn’t there a voice assistant in every digital wall calendar? And conversely, why haven’t smart displays that do have smart voice assistants gained features like full-page calendars and chore charts?
Not Just a Calendar
Part of what makes Greenlight’s hub different from other digital calendars is that the company is using the calendar as a starting point for the offerings it already has. That’s also why it’s called the Family Hub instead of just a calendar like most other devices I’ve tested. Greenlight grew from a banking tool to a way to manage chores and money for kids and teens, and has now become a full family management platform where you can track your family’s calendars, chores, kids’ spending, and even family locations.
Greenlight says it noticed the lack of voice support among competitors’ offerings and baked that into its hub intentionally. “Voice assistants have been around for over a decade, yet when building the specs for Family Hub, we noticed that voice support was absent in the digital calendar market," says Sushil Sharma, chief product officer at Greenlight. "Our goal with Hub was to create an all-in-one command center for busy families to engage with technology in a way that feels natural and seamless. By combining a voice assistant feature with a centralized home display, we are able to limit the number of devices families need in their home.”
It’s also smart for families with younger children—Sharma pointed out that not all kids can read and type fluently, and voice support makes it more accessible for them and the rest of the family. But it’s also a way people are expecting to interact with their home devices after years of smart speakers and smartphones offering voice support.
Voice Report
Greenlight’s assistant reminds me of the modern, AI-powered iterations of Alexa and Google because it’s also powered by AI. Greenlight says its family AI assistant uses frontier large language models with Greenlight’s own proprietary safety tools that it designed with family safety in mind. That means the assistant shouldn’t get into sensitive or inappropriate topics (or accidentally tell your child Santa isn’t real) but will both schedule a timer and answer day-to-day questions. You’ll also see a conversation appear on the right-hand side, reminding me a lot of the Alexa+ experience on an Echo Show device.
Greenlight’s Hub is supposed to only wake at its wake phrase, “Hey Greenlight,” but in the days I’ve been testing it, I’ve found it to be a little sensitive and likely to wake at random. It also tends to keep listening, waiting to see if you’ll continue the conversation or give a new command, so if my family is having a general conversation after asking a question, Greenlight will try to pick up a question from that and answer it. I find myself often ordering Greenlight to stop.
That isn’t an issue just for Greenlight. My Google Gemini-powered smart speaker does the same thing, and both my son and I are quick to yell, “Google, stop!” to get it to stop trying to answer a question we didn’t ask. It’s a problem with these AI-powered voice assistants overall, but I’m finding I’d rather say the wake word multiple times than get interrupted.
Big Brother Energy
When I described to my editor the laundry list of features that the Greenlight Family Hub has, she said it sounded like a “Big Brother machine.” I see why, of course—tracking your location and financial information in a device that sounds like a simple calendar might come as a surprise to most people. It was certainly a surprise to me when I went to set up the hub through the app and ended up stuck on the financial pathway (Greenlight says it’s fixing this issue in the app but I had to have support clear my information so I could set up the hub without setting up a bank card for my child).
Still, I like how much it has to offer, even if it might feel a tad Big Brother-y for some. And while it does have a microphone, it doesn’t have a camera like most smart displays have, so in that sense it feels less creepy to me than other devices I’ve had in my home.
I also really like that most of the features are accessible without needing a premium subscription—notably the photo screen saver feature, which Skylight will charge you for. (Skylight’s business model in general has become charging for storage, for both its calendars and digital photo frames.) Greenlight charges instead for its AI assistant and voice interaction, along with family location sharing. If you’re less voice-inclined than I am, you’d be plenty happy with this hub without the premium subscription.
I am hoping we see more digital wall calendars add at least some kind of voice assistance, as well as offering some control of your smart home devices. Maybe I’m biased coming from a background in smart home technology, but it feels like a huge missed opportunity. Smart displays have existed for years (and Apple just announced its first one) but have lacked the key feature that digital wall calendars have to really make them a touch point in the home beyond your voice. I reached out to both Amazon and Skylight to ask why neither has introduced any such model yet, but both companies declined to comment.
Maybe, for a company like Skylight, it’s the cost of creating an assistant that would work with its platform and needing to change its hardware to include a microphone, but Amazon is well positioned to bring something like this to the market (especially since the newest version of Alexa, Alexa+, is already paywalled). I’m hopeful we’ll see the next generation of smart displays at least make some kind of calendar mode an option; I’d certainly rather see my calendar than another ad or piece of screen clutter on my Echo Show.

San Francisco-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith has raised $66 Mn in a Series C funding round led by Sequoia Capital, bringing its total funding raised till date to $125 Mn. Premji Invest and existing investors Peak XV Partners, Google Ventures, and Y Combinator also participated in the round. The startup raised the fresh capital at an unicorn valuation of $1 Bn, doubling in just over two months. It was valued at $550 Mn when Peak XV led its $45 Mn Series B funding round in August. In a statement, the startup shared plans to bolster its compute infrastructure and expand its technical engineering team. It says that it currently manages nearly 10 MW of compute footprint across data centers in the United States and Europe. It shared plans to expand its total capacity by 5X in 2027 to meet growing enterprise demand. “Even at the start of this year, we underestimated how much code people would be shipping. We expect that volume to only keep increasing as models get better and more engineers embrace AI codegen tools. We’re building Blacksmith to help developers merge code faster and feel confident about what they’re shipping,” Aditya Jayaprakash, Blacksmith’s cofounder and CEO, wrote in a post on LinkedIn. Founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, Aayush Shah and Aditya Maru, Blacksmith operates a specialised cloud platform designed for automatically building and testing software code. It claims to serve more than 10,000 corporate customers worldwide, including high-growth tech firms such as Mercury, Granola, Supabase, and LangChain. As AI agents accelerate the speed at which code is written, the bottleneck for shipping software is moving from writing the code, to validating and testing code before deploying it – a step known as continuous integration (CI). Blacksmith claims its platform is tailor-made to absorb the spiky nature of CI demand with zero operational overhead, compared to general-purpose cloud infrastructure. According to the company’s blog post announcing the latest funding round, weekly CI jobs processed on Blacksmith jumped to over 90 Mn from 5 Mn back in January, driving a 17X jump in ARR over the same period.

Why does one person develop memory problems while another experiences seizures or changes in behaviour? And how do doctors find out whether these symptoms are caused by Alzheimer’s disease, an immune disorder or something else?
Sometimes, the answers may lie in tiny changes in the body’s chemistry. Diseases can cause certain proteins and other molecules to appear in different amounts or behave differently. By measuring these changes, doctors can find clues as to what is happening inside the body, even when the cause is not immediately obvious.
These clues, called chemical signatures or biomarkers, are being studied to improve the diagnosis of several diseases, particularly those affecting the brain and nervous system. The challenge is to establish what these changes mean, how reliably they point to a particular disease and whether patients can access the tests.
According to the World Health Organization, 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia in 2021, with Alzheimer’s disease accounting for an estimated 60% to 70% of cases. The WHO also estimates that nearly 10 million new cases of dementia occur each year.
What are chemical signatures?
A chemical signature is a unique pattern of molecules, elements, isotopes, or by-products identified in a sample by analytical instruments such as spectrometers or chromatographs. “Chemical signatures are like the body’s fingerprints,” says Sreenivas U.M., consultant neurologist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai. When a disease develops, the balance of certain chemicals or proteins may change, providing clues to the problem, he adds.
In Alzheimer’s disease, for instance, doctors and researchers look for changes in proteins called amyloid-beta and tau. Certain forms of these proteins can be measured in blood and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord. Tests measuring phosphorylated tau, particularly p-tau217, can help identify changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease.
Sruthi Degapudi, consultant neurologist, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says these tests help doctors look beyond a patient’s symptoms and investigate the underlying cause. However, finding a disease-associated change does not necessarily mean that a person will develop dementia.
Researchers are also studying alpha-synuclein, a protein associated with Parkinson’s disease. In another condition, autoimmune encephalitis, tests that detect antibodies directed against particular brain proteins can help identify an immune response affecting the brain. This condition can cause seizures, memory problems and changes in behaviour.
The type of sample needed depends on the disease. Blood is relatively easy to collect, while cerebrospinal fluid can provide information about processes affecting the brain and spinal cord. Skin samples are also being studied for certain neurological conditions.
Detecting symptoms
Some diseases begin changing the body long before a person notices anything unusual. Detecting these changes may help doctors identify the underlying disease earlier, although it does not always mean that symptoms can be prevented. Finding these changes also does not always mean an individual has, or is going to have a particular disease.
The distinction is important: a test may identify changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease, but doctors still need to consider the person’s symptoms and overall health before deciding what those results mean.
Chemical signatures can also help distinguish conditions that appear similar. Autoimmune encephalitis, for example, may initially be mistaken for a psychiatric illness because it can cause behavioural changes and problems with memory. Identifying specific antibodies can help doctors recognise the condition and begin appropriate treatment.
“In neurosurgery, examining the molecular characteristics of a brain tumour can help doctors classify it and decide on treatment,” says Aqib M., senior consultant neurosurgeon, Dr. Mehta’s Hospitals, Chennai. Selected molecular tests are already used in specialist practice. Researchers are also studying markers such as neurofilament light, a protein that can indicate damage to nerve cells, he adds.
However, not every promising test is ready for routine use. Some markers indicate damage that can occur in several diseases rather than identifying one specific condition.
Testing and diagnosis
A chemical signature cannot always give the full picture. Age, kidney function, medication and other illnesses can affect the levels of certain molecules. The stage of a disease and the way a sample is collected and tested can also influence the results.
This is why doctors do not rely on a blood test alone. They consider the patient’s symptoms, medical history and examination findings, along with brain scans and other investigations when necessary. In some cases, several biomarkers may be needed to distinguish between diseases that produce similar symptoms.
Cost and availability pose further challenges in India. Specialised tests may not be offered at every hospital, and patients may have to travel to larger centres to access them. Differences in laboratory methods can also affect how consistently results are interpreted.
So, for patients, chemical signatures could mean clearer answers and shorter waits for a diagnosis. But their importance lies not just in detecting changes in the body, but in understanding what those changes mean.

In October 2026, social media users spread an image that claimed to show a woman being punched in the face at one of U.S. President Donald Trump's rallies.
The person in the picture was wearing a shirt that said "RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES." (The Justice Department has released millions of files related to its investigation of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but critics allege the agency made redactions to obscure information.)
The image circulated on platforms such as X and Facebook. Many users sharing the image appeared to believe it was authentic.
"If there's one photo to sum up the Trump era, this is it," one X post said.
While a protester wearing a similar shirt was, in fact, attacked at an Oct. 12 Trump rally in Youngstown, Ohio, the image above was created using generative artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detection software. As such, we have rated this image as fake.
OpenAI's verification tool detected an invisible watermark on the image called SynthID, which the company's AI tools, like ChatGPT, embed in generated images. (As such, the service can only detect images generated with OpenAI's software and does not detect AI generation via other large-language models, such as Google's Gemini.)
(OpenAI)
SynthID detectors are largely accurate but can still be fallible. However, a review of credible footage taken from the Trump rally indicated that the actual protester was wearing slightly different clothing, including an open flannel layered on top of the T-shirt. The T-shirt the real person wore also had variations in the lettering style and coloring, unlike the more uniform version in the AI-generated image.
A reverse-image search could not determine the original creator behind the AI-generated picture.
Numerous reputable news organizations, including NBC News and an ABC affiliate, have published legitimate footage of the event.
NBC News' video shows rally attendees chanting, "USA, USA, USA" as a man in a gray shirt and a baseball cap appears to push down the protester. Another man in a dark blue or black shirt appears to tackle the protester, hit her and put her in a headlock. Security officials then escort the protester away. 
Another clip posted by WKBN, a Youngstown television news station, shows that the same man pulled on the protester's hair:
Images of the incident are also available via credible photo repositories, including Getty Images and Reuters.
NBC News reported that there were no arrests "because deputies didn't see the beating and the woman elected not to file a report, Sheriff Jerry Greene said."
Trump, meanwhile, mocked the protester's weight while watching the attack unfold. "You know they're paid protesters," Trump said, without evidence. "That's a very low-class protester."
The protester has not publicly shared their identity with the media as of this writing.

A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.
Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.
Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.
The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)
Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press releaseAsked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.
“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.
“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”
Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.
Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.
Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has undertaken trade margin rationalisation (TMR) of 137 identified non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs.
“The move is aimed at making cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines,” said a senior Union government official.
The move is expected to bring down the maximum retail price (MRP) of the identified non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs by up to 70%, depending on their existing price structures.
The revised prices will be effective from November 9.
“This intervention builds upon the success of NPPA’s 2019 pilot TMR exercise, under which trade margins for 42 anti-cancer drugs were capped at 30%. Following that exercise, MRP of 526 brands of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was reduced by up to 90%. The present exercise extends this approach to a larger set of anti-cancer drugs, based on the list recommended by the Expert Committee under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS),” notes a release issued by the Centre.
It added that an expert committee comprising leading oncologists, medical specialists, experts from hospitals across the country, and government officers recommended 137 drugs for inclusion under TMR. “This list would be updated periodically,” said the release.
Considering the drugs recommended by the committee, NPPA has capped the trade margin at 30% of the MRP in accordance with paragraph 19 of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013.
“Price of these medicines even after margin cap will remain out of reach of many people. The move alone will not bring down the cost of treatment because hospitals may find ways to charge high prices on other items, consumables, diagnostics, consultation charges, etc,” said K.M. Gopakumar, co-convenor of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments.

PC shipments are in the toilet, plunging over 20 percent from last year
This could reach 27 percent throughout the end of 2026.
Global PC shipments are down 21 percent year-over-year for Q3, according to data accumulated by the market research firm Counterpoint. The industry shipped over 70 million units during this time period last year, but that number has shriveled to 57 million.
As a matter of fact, there's been a quarter-over-quarter reduction of 13.8 percent, suggesting that this downturn is moving quite rapidly. Counterpoint's data has also indicated that this trend will continue, with forecasts for Q4 indicating around a 27 percent reduction year-over-year.
It's not hard to understand why this is happening. PC components keep shooting up in price, thanks to both the ongoing AI-induced RAMageddon and global tariffs, and many people just can't keep up.
"The global PC market is facing mounting pressure as rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases," said Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang. "With affordability becoming an increasingly critical purchasing factor, even market leaders are struggling to maintain shipment momentum."
There's only one tiny sliver of potential sunshine here. These numbers are absolutely dire, yes, but 2025 was actually a great year for PC shipments. The same goes for early 2026, as consumers raced to pick up new computers before prices shot up. Everyone knew this was coming and acted accordingly. Hopefully consumers will come back when prices for memory and other components fall back down to Earth.
However, that probably won't be anytime soon. Counterpoint's research has suggested 2027 will be more of the same.
Some companies are surviving this better than others. Lenovo is still the market leader, though it has experienced a higher-than-average 23 percent year-over-year decline. HP experienced a massive 31 percent decline during that same time period, with Dell at 25 percent.
Apple, however, experienced a smaller decline of 11 percent, which actually increased the company's overall market share. This is likely thanks to the budget-friendly MacBook Neo. ASUS has also managed to weather the storm, more or less. The company recorded the smallest decline when compared to other top vendors, at just seven percent year-over-year.
A 20.1% decline in worldwide PC shipments tells part of the story. The inventory pull-in underneath it tells the rest.
Q3 normally beats Q2. In 2026, it came in 9.1% below.

Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
- Published
A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.
Trump is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer representing the BBC, said in court that "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff" with two months left in the discovery period.
Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance" while he was campaigning in Georgia.
In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings.
The judge in the case, US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett, said that Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December, unless the discovery period is extended.
Last week, attorneys asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.
On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his property in Mar-a-Lago in Florida.
In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year, and claimed that the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action."
Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump made a direct call for violent action".
The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.
In July, Trump's lawyers conceded that they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC select or through US broadcasters.
Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, its commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary.
Typically, depositions take place in a lawyer's office - rather than a courtroom - without a judge physically present.
Depositions, however, carry legal weight and take place under oath. They are recorded verbatim by a court reporter, and the transcripts can later be used as evidence during trials.

Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs
As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure whether the family could pay for the care needed.
"This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?"
— Grace Griffin, Calumet, Michigan
Grace and Daniel Griffin, both 26, knew money would be tight once they had their first child. So, even before the Calumet, Mich., couple tried to conceive, they began crunching the numbers to figure out the cost of pregnancy.
"We wanted to save up enough to pay for those medical bills right away, if possible," Grace said.
But the cost estimator that she found linked to her UnitedHealthcare student plan asked for medical billing codes for each procedure that Grace was likely to receive. That's information she didn't have.
So, she kept digging until she found the Summary of Benefits and Coverage information on the health plan's website, which estimated out-of-pocket costs for a routine pregnancy and delivery at about $2,700.
"We thought, 'OK, that's doable,'" she said. "We should be able to save up that much and pay for that out of pocket."
But as the expenses piled up, it was clear the estimate wasn't even close.
Early in the pregnancy, Grace met her $500 deductible, the out-of-pocket cost she had to pay before insurance pitched in. Her plan also required her to pay 20% coinsurance for in-network care. This meant that for every $100 billed for things like routine blood work and other needed care, she was on the hook for $20.
"When I started getting lab work is when we started realizing expenses would add up quickly," Grace said. Routine blood tests to check iron levels or for gestational diabetes were a couple of hundred dollars every visit, she said.
In June, after what Grace described as a routine pregnancy and delivery, the couple welcomed their daughter. Then the Griffins received an "explanation of benefits" notice that showed the hospital charged about $18,000 for the delivery, with the family on the hook for a sizable portion.
"I thought, 'Oh no, it's going to be a lot,'" she said. "Much more than we budgeted for."
She was right.
In early October, Grace said, her family's out-of-pocket expenses had totaled more than $9,000, over three times the general estimate published by her insurer for pregnancy-related costs.
Meanwhile, Grace and Daniel are scrambling to cover their bills.
For years, federal lawmakers have tried to remedy this issue, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor and co-director of Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms. To make healthcare costs more transparent and accessible to patients, Congress required insurers to provide consumers with an individualized "advanced explanation of benefits" estimating what scheduled care would cost them. The rule, part of the 2020 No Surprises Act, was due to take effect on Jan. 1, 2022, but federal regulators have yet to make that happen, despite ongoing pressure from members of Congress.
"So, it's basically 4 1/2 years since this was supposed to be available, and I think it's a source of a lot of frustration for a lot of folks," Corlette said. "People have a right under the law to know these things."
Meanwhile, she said, another change is pending. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, long-standing maternity billing codes that bundle much of pregnancy care will be replaced with more detailed coding for prenatal care, labor, delivery and postpartum care.
The change could make it easier to see what individual services cost, but Corlette said it's not yet clear whether the change will make it easier for people trying to stick to a budget.
"I could see where it might be advantageous to the provider," she said. "But I'm not sure I'm seeing benefits to the patient."
Until out-of-pocket maternity expenses get easier to estimate, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy.
1. Enroll your baby before the clock runs out
Ensuring your newborn has health coverage is one of the first paperwork responsibilities that parents face in the whirlwind of bringing a baby home.
Birth creates what's known as a special enrollment opportunity, meaning you don't have to wait until the annual open-enrollment period to sign up a newborn.
Many employer health plans require parents to request enrollment within 30 days of birth. Marketplace plans — for those who buy their own insurance rather than get it from an employer or the government — generally allow 60 days. Wait too long, and your baby may be left uninsured until the following year.
Michelle Critzer of Ventura, Calif., learned that lesson the hard way. She works as a sales rep and is the mother of a toddler and a newborn. Her second son, Hudson, was born in February, and Critzer missed the enrollment deadline for him. Ever since, she has been asking her insurer to make an exception — so far, without success.
"The way they set hard must-do's within 30 days of having a baby is actually insanity," she said.
The family was able to enroll Hudson in a health plan through Critzer's husband's workplace, which has a 60-day enrollment window. But that coverage is not nearly as robust as Critzer's insurance, she said. Still, she's grateful to have Hudson insured while she continues pressing her own plan to enroll him.
2. Ask about must-know numbers, like your MOOP
Budgeting for a pregnancy often begins with a tally of the expected expenses. The deductible is the amount you'll pay before much of your insurance coverage kicks in.
After that, you'll likely face copayments — fixed fees paid each time you receive service, regardless of the size of the bill.
Coinsurance is another expected expense, but as Grace discovered, it can be especially tricky to estimate. Coinsurance requires the patient to pay a percentage of the cost for each service received.
MOOP, which stands for "maximum out-of-pocket" expense, is another must-know number. Your plan's MOOP is the ceiling on what you'll pay each year for covered, in-network services (care that your health plan has contracted to pay at negotiated, lower rates).
Think of it as doomsday prepping. Some people get comfort from knowing and planning for the worst-case scenario. Under the Affordable Care Act, in 2026 the amount a person has to pay out of pocket for in-network care is capped at $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family. Your plan might set a lower maximum, but once your spending reaches your plan's limit, insurance pays 100% of all further in-network costs for that year.
One complication to be aware of: If your pregnancy overlaps two plan years, the tally of your out-of-pocket expenses resets to zero at the beginning of the second year, and you could find yourself maxing out your out-of-pocket expenses two years in a row.
Some plans have two MOOPs, one for in-network services and another for out-of-network benefits. Insurance plans usually track those expenses separately, and the out-of-network MOOP can be double the in-network limit. That's more incentive to meticulously seek out in-network care.
As a family, the Griffins had an $18,000 MOOP, and Grace's individual maximum was $9,000.
3. Choose in-network care, when you can
You picked an obstetrician in your plan, but don't assume others on the care team are in-network providers.
Ask about the hospital, labs and imaging facilities your doctor's office may use. Corlette, of Georgetown's Center on Health Insurance Reforms, suggests that patients explicitly tell the doctor's office to send tests to an in-network provider.
Federal law protects patients who go to an in-network hospital or other in-network facility from out-of-network "surprise bills" issued by out-of-network providers.
4. Check every bill — and don't be afraid to file an appeal
The Affordable Care Act requires certain recommended prenatal services to be covered without any additional cost to you. Among them: prenatal visits, folic acid, anxiety and depression screening, and breastfeeding and lactation counseling and supplies.
Still, these costs sometimes get mistakenly passed on to the patient.
To protect against billing errors, Corlette suggests patients become familiar with these pregnancy-related services and then check every bill.
If your insurer refuses to pay for a covered charge, consider filing an appeal.
5. Seek help before the bills pile up
Most hospitals offer financial assistance programs. Find out whether yours will work with you, either to reduce your bill or to offer a manageable payment plan. Your doctor or other providers might also offer assistance, if you ask.
Corlette said to make sure any arrangement is formally agreed upon in advance so the account isn't unexpectedly turned over to collections.
Also investigate other assistance.
Grace Griffin qualified for Michigan's Rx Kids program, which provides eligible families in certain communities with $1,500 during pregnancy and $500 a month for the baby's first six months or year of life.
That money has helped keep the medical bills from devouring the Griffins' emergency savings.
"It takes a lot of pressure off," she said.

France has released its Global Health Strategy for 2023-2027, in Lyon today, in the presence of three French Ministers, the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, the Minister of Health and Prevention, the Minister of Higher Education and Research, and WHO’s Director-General.
As a lead player for shaping global health policies, France has called on national and international stakeholders to support building a new global health architecture towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and in particular SDG3, focused on ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, at all ages.
The new Health Strategy aims to help reduce health inequalities and strengthen the One Health approach to better prevent and prepare for future global health emergencies. It urges the global community to address the health consequences of climate change and the environmental impact on health systems.
To underscore WHO’s and France strong collaboration and in recognition of France’s pivotal global health role, Dr Tedros travelled to France to join the launch event.
“France was a founding member of WHO in 1948 and has been a strong friend to WHO throughout the 75 years since then,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “As one of the world’s largest economies, France has a critical role to play in global health, and the new Global Health Strategy will enhance that role. It aligns well with WHO’s priorities to promote, provide, protect, empower and perform for health.”
France shares key health priorities with WHO, adopting a crosscutting approach and prioritizing universal health coverage (UHC) as part of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda. France also provides support for transformative initiatives at WHO such as the WHO Academy and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) which the Ministers visited today.
Dr Tedros addressed the audiences at the Academy and IARC together with Ms Catherine Colonna, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention, and Ms Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research.
"The World Health Organization, whose 74th anniversary we are celebrating today, must continue to play a central and driving role,” said Ms Catherine Colonna, the French Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “France will continue to support the WHO and its ambitious governance and financing reforms."
"France is also committed alongside the WHO Academy through several partnership with universities, research institutes, and public health institutions," remarked Sylvie Retailleau, Minister of Higher Education and Research. "Our goal is to enrich the learners' experience through a diversified training portfolio within the Academy."
"The launch of this Global Health Strategy is the perfect opportunity to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the WHO. The Organization plays a central role in global health, and we must continue to support it," said Mr Aurélien Rousseau, Minister of Health and Prevention. "This is why, I am announcing today, France is keen to host, in the first quarter of 2024, in partnership with the WHO, the first international financing conference for the fight against meningitis."
The 2023-2027 French Strategy for Global Health is the fruit of collaboration involving a wide range of French actors: public agencies, civil society organizations, higher education and research organizations, scientific institutions, foundations, organizations of human, animal and environmental health specialists, local government bodies and the private sector. They will all be represented within a monitoring committee to track the Strategy’s implementation and progress.
From left to right: Minister of Health and Prevention H.E. Aurélien Rousseau, WHO’s Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs H.E. Catherine Colonna, and Minister of Higher Education and Research, H.E. Sylvie Retailleau.

Trump White House aides have started to cast about for a scapegoat to offer the president in the event of bad midterm election losses, as Republicans stare down brutal predictions in key House and Senate races, sources familiar with the matter say.
Republican political operatives say privately that the real blame lies with Trump for starting the Iran war in an election year, causing higher prices across the board and prompting a nationwide voter backlash, the sources say.
“Clearly it's the president's fault,” one operative tells Inner Loop.
But Trump aides also know, for obvious reasons, they cannot say publicly or tell the president behind closed doors that his own policy decisions are at fault as they contemplate losing not just the House majority, but possibly the Senate.
The result has been an unusually early effort to find a scapegoat, and sources say eyes have fallen on deputy chief of staff and political strategist James Blair, who organized the Trump 2024 campaign's turnout strategy and returned to the role for this midterm cycle.
Blair's efforts included a marquee plan for certain states to redraw congressional maps early, which looked likely—though not certain—to yield favorable House seats for Republicans, so long as the coalition that Trump turned out in 2024 came out to support Republicans in 2026.
Even accounting for the Iran war, the redistricting gambit was supposed to bring roughly 10 to 15 pickups for Republicans in the House. After Virginia's top court blocked Democrats from redrawing maps to keep pace in the redistricting battle, wrote on X: “Lord grant me humility.”
But in a remarkable backfire five months later, election forecasters have found that some of the redistricted seats now favor Democrats.
The redrawn map for Florida's 25th congressional district just south of Fort Lauderdale, for instance, is now characterized as "Lean Democrat," and the outlook is so bad that the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republican–aligned group, has pulled money out of the race.
Maps that were drawn for Republicans in ruby-red Texas are suddenly also vulnerable, even in seats where the party has incumbents. In Texas' 15th congressional district, GOP candidate Monica De La Cruz's race is now rated a "tossup" by the Cook Political Report.
Blair's allies inside and outside the West Wing say the criticism directed at him is grossly unfair because he could not have foreseen the effects of the Iran war and scandals involving Trump officials undoing his planning.
Blair is also viewed as retaining the confidence of Trump and the White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and he traveled on Air Force One to two rallies within the past week, suggesting any blame that ultimately comes his way could be just symbolic.
After all, when Blair left the White House earlier this year to run Trump's midterm strategy from the outside, the president announced the move as only temporary and said that Blair would return after the election.
Responding to the reporting in this story, Blair said in a statement, “the President, our partners in the House and Senate, and I remain focused on winning in November. All Republicans should be spending themselves equally in our worthy cause.”
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle added in a statement: “These armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation to WIRED have no idea what they’re talking about. President Trump is laser-focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress this November.”
As for Wiles herself, despite reporting that she has been under fire, sources inside Trump's orbit are adamant that if Wiles leaves after the midterms, it will be purely of her own volition.
Trump aides acknowledge that much of the palace intrigue scapegoating is preemptive. Expectations are so low that if Republicans take some wins—like holding on to the Senate—Blair will be “seen as a savior,” one of the sources added.
But they also say that in many ways Blair has perhaps made it too easy for them to single him out. He explicitly owned the House midterm strategy, and now he may be walked to the gallows with that same rope.

Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
- Published
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.
Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.
Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.
Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.
The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.
But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.
Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.
The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.
Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.
"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.
Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.
We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.
Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.
"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.
The new rules have divided opinion.
Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.
One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.
''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''
In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.
"Get down, I say get down," he shouts.
But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.
Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.
"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.
Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.
"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.
"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.
For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.
"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.
Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.
But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.
Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.
The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.
He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.
"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.
For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.
