‘Don’t need permission to hoist Tricolour’: AISA chief tells Delhi High Court
NEW DELHI: All India Students' Association (AISA) president Neha Bora on Thursday told the Delhi high court that no permission was required to hoist the national flag, while challenging a police notice directing her to execute a bond to maintain peace.The Delhi police objected to the maintainability of Bora's petition challenging the notice, which asked her to execute a "peace" bond before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM).The Delhi High Court will pass an order on Friday evening on Neha Bora’s plea challenging a police notice directing her to execute a “peace” bond.Bora on Monday had moved the Delhi High Court challenging a police notice directing her to execute a bond before a Special Executive Magistrate for “keeping peace”.Bora, who has been at the forefront of recent protests against alleged irregularities in the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The notice, issued on October 17 under Section 126 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), directed Bora to appear before the magistrate on October 19 and explain why she should not execute a personal bond of Rs 10,000 with one surety “for keeping peace for a period of enquiry.”
Bora was taken into preventive detention on October 16 while on her way to participate in the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Central Park in Connaught Place. She was released the following day.In her petition, Bora has argued that the police notice is vague, factually incorrect and unsupported by any material establishing the likelihood of a breach of peace. It also fails to specify the “period, occasion or event in relation to which breach is apprehended”, the plea stated.She had described the proceedings as a “colourable exercise of preventive powers to suppress peaceful dissent, in violation of Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21 of Constitution”.According to the petition, the police initiated proceedings before the magistrate citing alleged sloganeering at Mandi House on October 16, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and alleged attempts to instigate people to join a protest at Connaught Place on the same day.“The impugned notice rests on a prima facie incorrect fact, namely that the petitioner instigated people to participate in the demonstration at Central Park, CP on Oct 16. The petitioner’s call and the incident alleged were different. The petitioner called for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5.00 pm on Oct 16, and it is a matter of record that she was detained from Mandi House,” Bora’s petition said.The development comes after the SEM court at Mandir Marg Police Station ordered the release of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 21, after they furnished personal bonds and surety bonds and gave written undertakings to maintain peace.SEM Ritu Raj directed the two activists to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the inquiry. The court noted that they had furnished the required bonds and that the sureties had been questioned before their release was ordered."In view of overall facts and circumstances, the respondents are directed to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds in the sum of Rs.50,000 until the conclusion of enquiry," the SEM court ordered.After verifying the sureties prima facie, the court directed their release and issued a warrant to the superintendent of Tihar Jail for compliance.The court also directed the investigating officer to submit a verification report on the sureties at the next hearing. Das, Ranka and their sureties were asked to remain present on the next date of hearing.Emphasising the conditions of their release, the court said, "Needless to mention, the respondents shall appear before this Court on every date of hearing and shall maintain law and order and will not breach peace / public tranquillity of the area and shall strictly adhere to the terms of their bonds and voluntary undertaking given today. The inquiry in the matter shall continue in accordance with law."The matter has been listed for further proceedings on October 23 at 3 pm.During the hearing, Das and Ranka voluntarily submitted written undertakings promising not to breach the peace. They also agreed not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law and said any protests they undertake would comply with the law.
The court observed that the immediate measures under Section 135(3) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) to prevent a breach of peace or disturbance of public tranquillity could be adequately ensured through the bonds and written undertakings."Hence, further judicial custody does not appear to be necessary at this stage, particularly after written undertakings before this Court," the court observed.Advocates Abhik Chimni and Abhisht Hela appeared for Das and Ranka.

US Army officials say the safety protocols for soldiers using lasers are surprisingly simple: don't stand too close to the target and don't look into the weapon.
Directed-energy weapons are seeing more operational use, particularly at the US southern border, where the Army has employed them against cartel-linked drones. The service envisions these systems operating on different vehicles and being easy for soldiers to learn and use safely.
At the Association of the United States Army, or AUSA, convention last week in Washington, DC, officials and industry partners spoke on developments in directed-energy weapons.
Asked about personal protective equipment, or PPE, and any concerns about specular reflection from lasers, Kirk Williams, chief engineer of the Army's directed energy project office, said the rules were similar in some respects to those for other weapons.
"Well, the short and sweet of that answer is: unless you're within ten feet of the target, a specular reflection is eye-safe, so the soldiers don't need the eye protection from the laser," he said, explaining that "it's like any other weapons system: don't look into it."
"We tell the soldiers the same thing about an M-16. Don't look down the barrel. Same thing with lasers, don't look down the barrel."
Specular reflections occur when light bounces off a surface. In the case of a laser weapon, reflected light can bounce off a targeted vehicle or drone. While the target absorbs most of the energy, some reflections might stray and cause eye or skin damage to soldiers near the target.
Williams said that part of the reason the Army likes these weapons is their relatively low risk to soldiers and the limited need for protective gear. "They are safe," he said, adding that "the great thing about a laser is we can also turn them off instantaneously."
The weapons also have safeguards that shut them down if there is a risk of hitting something other than the intended target.
During the panel, Williams and others also talked about the Army's priorities for deploying more laser weapons, an area of growing importance for the Army and the broader US military.
Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, the capability program executive for defensive fires, said the service wants to integrate high-energy lasers onto "any vehicle in the motorpool." He said the Army's Enduring High Energy Laser, or E-HEL, is mounted on a sled, allowing it to be integrated onto multiple types of vehicles.
The E-HEL is an Army directed-energy weapon program using AeroVironment's LOCUST laser system.
Yelverton said that making weapons compatible with different vehicles and usable by soldiers across military specialties will allow the Army to deploy them more widely.
The general said that this flexibility would allow the Army to deploy laser weapons "across all Army formations," giving commanders more options for where to put them and which soldiers should operate them.
"It's a great dilemma to have," he said.
Officials also said part of disseminating the weapons is making them easy to train on. "Most of our training sessions, we can train somebody in like, five minutes, to be able to use this system and start shooting things down," Williams said, adding that using standard controllers like those for an Xbox made it intuitive.
The Army's testing of laser weapons and other counter-drone systems at the southern border has reinforced the idea that the US will need layered defenses to counter a range of drone threats. Drug cartels are increasingly using drones to support operations, and the Army has already used lasers to shoot some down.

Nagaland United Sports Club (NUSC) has formally marked its entry into the Indian Football League (IFL), becoming the first club from Nagaland to compete in the country’s national second-tier league.
When the 2026-27 season gets underway on October 30, the Chümoukedima-based club will begin its debut campaign carrying Nagaland’s name, and its hopes, into national league football.
The Honourable Chief Minister of Nagaland, Dr Neiphiu Rio, attended the club’s opening programme at the Regional Centre for Sporting Excellence in Sovima on Thursday, where NUSC opened its club office and the Elevenses Cafe Lounge. His presence reflected the importance the state has attached to the club’s arrival in the IFL.

Addressing the gathering, Dr Neiphiu Rio, Chief Minister of Nagaland, said, “We are extremely happy and proud that Nagaland United Sports Club is playing in the Indian Football League for the first time. This is the beginning of a journey, and I hope the club will give its best and make this dream come true, inspiring the youth of Nagaland and Nagas wherever they are.”
NUSC was founded in 2024 by local leaders, sportspeople and supporters who wanted to give young footballers in the state a place to play, compete and be seen. It made its competitive debut in the inaugural Nagaland Super League in 2025, the state’s top-tier competition run by the Nagaland Football Association, and finished third.
Less than two years after its formation, the club now steps up to national league football. It will play its home matches at the Chümoukedima Football Stadium in Dimapur, bringing IFL fixtures to Nagaland.
The club enters the IFL by acquiring the league-playing rights of Mizo side Aizawl. Aizawl, nicknamed The People’s Club, was founded in 1984 and has been one of the most prominent teams in Indian football in the last few decades. It won the I-League 2 in 2015 before lifting the then-top-flight title, the I-League, the next season, under current India head coach Khalid Jamil.

“The intention behind building this club is to create a platform and opportunity for our talented youth, so that they can progress from playing in villages, districts and communities to the state and national levels. As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.
Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.
“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.
The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.
“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”
The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.
The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known as a “run time patch,” in this case a tool known as ClawGod, to add functionality on top of Claude Code and attempt to remove the “CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION” from the Claude Code system prompt, an instruction directing Claude Code to only participate in authorized security testing, not abusive or destructive hacking.
The actor that worked in Spanish and English targeted Argentine health care entities and successfully compromised at least 15 organizations. CrowdStrike researchers see evidence that the actor stole credentials and medical records from at least one of these victims. The actor special built a penetration testing harness, the kind an organization would use to test its own infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities. Using models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Deepseek V4 Pro, the group set up a full infrastructure for autonomous attacks involving a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent to direct the steps of an attack and an “Executor” agent to carry them out.
The attacker working in Chinese also built penetration testing harnesses to guide Claude Code in reconnaissance and then autonomously attack once a human had selected a course of action. The researchers found that the actor successfully compromised government targets in both Brazil and Colombia and also targeted private organizations in Brazil and the United States in a range of sectors that include biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.
According to the researchers, the Chinese-speaking actor primarily relied on Claude Opus 4.8, but also used other models including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Deepseek Chat. The actor accessed Claude through an AI proxy service based in China but set up multiple fallbacks to other AI tools if Claude was not available through the proxy.
Anthropic did not provide comment ahead of publication, and Deepseek did not immediately respond to WIRED's requests for comment.
The researchers say that both the Russian-speaking actor, which seems to have been focused on financially motivated “e-crime,” and the Indonesian-speaking actor (the least sophisticated of the four) used more basic, publicly available skills and harnesses to carry out their attacks. But both were still successful at compromising targets. This included multiple Indonesian government domains, a Bangladeshi government domain, and some private-sector targets, in the case of the Indonesian-speaking actor.
“What we are seeing is humans are doing some of the initial probing in these situations and then they’re engaging the AI for the hacking at scale,” CrowdStrike’s Meyers says. “I find it interesting that even with agentic attacks with all of these capabilities, we could still see that there’s a human behind it and what they’re up to.”

“Go woke, go broke” was a culture war rallying cry of the Biden years, with American conservatives waging battles against any corporate entity that dared to pay lip service to diversity or LGBTQ rights.
But customers of one successful anti-woke alternative brand later found their own wallets a bit lighter—with nothing to show for it.
In April 2023, at the height of a right-wing freakout over a sponsored Instagram post in which transgender actress and singer Dylan Mulvaney showed off a can of Bud Light with her face on it, a Georgia man named Seth Weathers smelled an opportunity to cash in. Conservatives were vowing to ditch the Budweiser brand and take their business elsewhere. (A tearful Kid Rock even filmed himself shooting up a few cases with a semiautomatic rifle.) It was an angry political demographic in need of a new low-ABV lager.
Weathers, a political consultant who briefly served as Georgia state director for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign in 2015 and went on to work with a county commissioner known for racist Facebook posts, swooped in to pitch a replacement beverage. Under his social brand “Conservative Dad,” he marketed a brew called Ultra Right Beer to the MAGA voters making a stink about trans inclusivity.
“America’s been drinking beer from a company that doesn’t even know what restroom to use,” Weathers said in a YouTube ad that included a clip of Mulvaney sipping Bud Light. “That’s why I created Conservative Dad’s Ultra Right 100 percent woke-free beer.” The commercial shows Weathers teeing up a can of Bud Light and walloping it with a baseball bat. “Stop giving money to woke corporations that hate our values,” he said, warning such companies to “stay the fuck away from our kids.”
The concept made a splash in right-wing media, which sent droves of readers and viewers to the Ultra Right Beer website to place orders—even though Weathers had yet to find a brewery to make the stuff. (He was also facing logistical hurdles to shipping the hypothetical beer, a process subject to heavy regulations that vary from one state to the next.) Within two weeks, Weathers had partnered with Big Kettle Brewing in Lawrenceville, Georgia, to produce the beer, and claimed he was closing in on $1 million in sales of six-packs priced at $19.99 apiece.
But while Fox News and similar outlets continued to tout Ultra Right as a stunning victory over Budweiser’s brewer, Anheuser-Busch, deliveries were slow to materialize. Weathers’ company, Ultra Right Beer LLC, would eventually receive an “F” rating from the Better Business Bureau, which notes that it has failed to respond to nearly 200 complaints over missing six-packs and virtually nonexistent customer service. The author of a one-star review of Ultra Right on the BBB website griped that its special edition “Revenge” cans of beer with Trump’s mugshot on them took a year and a half to arrive, while a “Fight”-themed six-pack (styled with the image of Trump raising his fist after surviving an assassination attempt at a July 2024 campaign rally) never arrived at all.
Weathers claimed in August 2024 that sales of the special edition Fight beer had reached the $1 million mark. It’s not clear how many orders of Fight beer ultimately shipped. On eBay, resellers have listed empty six-packs for as much as $115.
Two years later, around 400 people are members of a Facebook group called “People Still Waiting for Ultra Right Fight Beer,” with many claiming that they have received neither the limited-edition beer nor a refund after placing orders in 2024. “I no longer want the beer … just my money back!” reads a recent post on the page.
Enough of these customers have contacted Georgia attorney general Chris Carr to report on Ultra Right Beer LLC that the office has opened an investigation into the company, which has been unresponsive to compliance orders, according to court filings. Ironshield Brewing, the company that operated Big Kettle Brewing as a contract brewer, announced that it was shutting down in December 2023. Weathers did not respond to a request for comment and hasn’t posted to his Facebook or Instagram pages since late last year.
Many of the comments on Weathers’ dormant social media pages are from people demanding refunds or updates on beer orders. In response to a Facebook commenter who wrote that Weathers’ announcement of an Ultra Right restock in November was “plain bullshit” and called him a “thief,” Weathers wrote, “We do not want you as a customer,” adding that he had refunded the person’s order. “I cannot imagine how miserable someone must be to reach your age in life, to spend your time harassing small businesses who have made mistakes but is [sic] out here fighting for the causes you supposedly believe in,” he wrote.
Rich Alan, a police officer in New Jersey who spent more than $60 on two sixers of Fight beer that he says he never got, claims Weathers is a “fraud” and “scammer” who took advantage of Trump supporters. As his Conservative Dad character, Alan says, Weathers was “ stealing the hearts of these patriots and making you think that you're like you're one of them, basically. Like, ‘Hey, I'm just like you, I'm standing up to woke Bud Light.’ And then just taking their money and running with it.”
Paul Roberts, an employee of the Oregon department of transportation who shared a September 2024 receipt for three six-packs of Ultra Right Fight beer totaling $91.36, says he has tried in vain to get an update on the order. “Sent many emails, replies to texts, and on their Facebook page,” he says, and called a listed number as well. “No response.”
Both Roberts and Alan tell WIRED they only purchased the beers as collectible items and had no plans to actually drink them. They also say that their orders were not motivated by the Bud Light boycott. “I don't care what people drink,” Alan says. “You drink Bud Light, you drink Bud Light.” Roberts had previously bought the Revenge beer with Trump’s mugshot on it, which did arrive, although he says delivery was slow. “The mugshot had been used in a negative light, so I thought it was cool and collectible that they placed it on a beer can.”
Alan notes that as Weathers began running into difficulties with catching up on orders, he blamed these on legal wrangling with Anheuser-Busch. The company filed trademark opposition against Ultra Right Beer LLC in 2024, citing similarities to its own Michelob Ultra beer. Weathers called it an attempt at “corporate intimidation.” That litigation remains ongoing.
While Alan and Roberts have given up hope of getting their money back, they’d like to see justice served in some way or another. “I would like the state to enforce whatever laws apply to a business that takes your money and doesn't provide the product or service,” Roberts says. Alan adds that in his experience as a law enforcement officer, he’s used to seeing people get away with petty scams. “Accountability would be nice, whether it's seizing assets or seizing everything he has, some jail time,” he says.
“I'd like to cross paths with him one day,” Alan says of Weathers. “I'm sure a lot of people would.”

'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother
- Published
Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor of the US state of Ohio, has called an attack ad against her that features her estranged mother "despicable".
Acton commented on the campaign ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, on Wednesday, saying: "This is despicable, what he's done".
In the ad Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton "lied her entire life". But it does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child and that Acton and her brother were then removed from Arthur's custody.
The ad set off a storm of criticism from members of both parties. On Thursday, President Donald Trump sought to defend it and Ramaswamy on social media.
Acton and Ramaswamy are both running to replace outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, a Republican who endorsed Ramaswamy, in the 3 November midterm election.
In a sign that Ramaswamy may have hurt his chances at winning, DeWine has reportedly described the ad as deeply troubling and called for it to be taken down.
"I've never attacked his family. I would never do that," Acton said about Ramaswamy at the campaign stop on Wednesday evening.
"You can see that there are so many people who have experienced trauma and abuse in their lives," she continued, referring to the fallout from the ad.
The last time Acton saw her mother was in a courtroom in 1978 after her stepfather was indicted, according to Acton's campaign.
Arthur's husband fled the state before he could stand trial, was never prosecuted, and died in 2004. Arthur left with him.
In an ad that Acton released earlier this week, her brother recalled their abuse as children and chided Ramaswamy for using sexual assault as "a political talking point".
Trump, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, blamed the press for the negative reaction to the ad, in a long post where he also commended Arthur and Ramaswamy. Trump blasted DeWine, as well.
He urged Ramaswamy to keep up his attacks and "let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!"
"I only wish the mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse," Trump also posted.
In the ad, Arthur repeatedly says Acton lies and asserts she "needs help", but does not discuss anything related to cheating or stealing.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was reviewing complaints about Ramaswamy's ad, which may have initially aired without a legally required disclaimer to tell viewers who paid for it.
Ramaswamy claimed responsibility the day after the ad was released on social media and said his campaign would spend $4m (£3m) to air it across the state.
The editorial board of local Ohio news outlet The Columbus Dispatch endorsed Acton after the ad dropped, describing it as "revolting and unsettling".
On Thursday, former Republican Ohio Congressman Jim Renacci wrote on X: "The floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor.
"And any Republican who fails to distance themselves from this ad risks taking on water as well."
MK Pritzker, the wife of Illinois' Democratic governor, JB Pritzker, announced on Wednesday that she would donate $500,000 to help Acton in the election.
- Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad 
  - Published22 hours ago
Vice-President JD Vance has said he would like fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about the ad and that he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.
David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that attack ads are not new in US politics but said "they have become more intense".
He suggested Ramaswamy's ad could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour.
A poll by VoteHub, external released on Thursday suggested Acton was leading Ramaswamy by 1%, within the margin of error, and noted the surveys were done before the ad.
If Acton wins, she would be the first Democrat elected as Ohio governor in two decades.

Tesla plans to start selling Cybercabs by the end of the year
The automaker said it could start switching on Unsupervised Full Self-Driving on some vehicles by the second quarter of 2027.
Tesla is aiming to start selling Cybercabs to customers before the year ends. Lars Moravy, VP of engineering at the company, said that the automaker is "trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026," during its third quarter earnings calls.
Moravy added that Tesla is already manufacturing Cybercabs at its Gigafactory in Texas, but those are meant for its internal robotaxi fleet. If the company does succeed in getting the vehicles to customers this year, it will start small. As it learns about "ownership and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands," Moravy said, Tesla will scale up Cybercab's sales. Elon Musk admitted during the call, however, that "the vast majority" Cybercabs will be "essentially Tesla-owned" and will be under its ride service operations.
The company first unveiled the Cybercab back in 2024, but it wasn't until September this year that it started offering rides on it through its Robotaxi app in Austin, Texas. Tesla has also just started taking inquiries for those interested in buying units. Specifically, it's looking for entities who can help "build its robotaxi network," indicating that it'll initially sell them to companies that can purchase whole fleets.
Cybercabs, unlike Tesla's other vehicles, don't come with steering wheels and brake pedals. It cannot be driven by a human driver and relies on the company's Full Self-Driving software. Since the Unsupervised version of Tesla's Full Self-Driving suite isn't available to consumers yet, the first Cybercabs sold to customers can't be added to the Tesla's ride-hailing fleet yet. At the moment, Tesla owners can only get the Supervised version of the suite, which still requires a human driver behind the wheel. Ashok Elluswamy, Director of AI at Tesla, said during the call that the company believes it can start switching on Unsupervised Full Self-Driving on "some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the Robotaxi fleet" around the second quarter of 2027.
It's worth noting that shortly after Tesla started offering Cybercab rides in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) launched a probe into the vehicles. The agency said that the company self-certified that the vehicles are compliant with all relevant Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS). It plans to look into the process and data the automaker used to self-certify to determine whether the vehicles do indeed adhere to those standards.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say
- Published
Yemen's Houthi movement has said it carried out an attack on an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, which Saudi authorities said killed two people and injured eight others.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation identified those killed at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.
It did not say what type of attack occurred, but the Iran-backed Houthis said on Thursday that the airport was one of the sites they had targeted with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours.
Two more people were killed on Wednesday morning by debris from a drone that was intercepted elsewhere in Eastern Province, the Saudi energy ministry said.
The drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybah oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze, according to the ministry.
It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, did not claim the attack on the oil field.
In addition to Dammam's airport, he said they had targeted the Saudi defence ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis said four drones were intercepted over Eastern Province on Wednesday night, and that another four were intercepted over the provinces of Riyadh and Medina on Thursday.
At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.
One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
Houthi-run media reported on Wednesday night that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.
The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.
The fighting has also displaced more than 256,000 people.
The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces.

If you're still using the same password for everything, it might finally be time to get on that.
While the major cybersecurity vulnerabilities that OpenAI agents helped expose on Wednesday primarily impact the owners and operators of websites, it could also give hackers the opportunity to hijack your personal information, researchers said.
"Be extra careful visiting ANY web site in the next few days," Changpeng Zhao, the cofounder of cryptocurrency platform Binance, said on X.
OpenAI said on Wednesday that researchers using its AI models uncovered two "critical" flaws in the infrastructure of PHP, a popular open-source programming language used on about 70% of the world's websites.
Because digital commerce websites, for instance, can store personal shopper information in PHP systems, that information would be accessible to a bad actor exploiting the web provider's system if that provider hasn't updated it.
The National Security Administration warned that hackers using one of the PHP exploits could "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network."
"Even if you yourself are not building software and that's not where your core business is, a lot of your life does depend on companies that depend on those systems," Madeline Lawrence, cofounder of Aikido Security, an application security platform, told Business Insider on Thursday.
"And they could be deeply, deeply vulnerable," she added. She said that one day after the disclosure, cybersecurity platform Cloudflare reported millions of attempts to exploit the vulnerability.
If you do own a website, PHP has released updates it says will help shield websites from hackers. Instructions for applying those updates are available on PHP's homepage.
For everyone else, here are a few tips cybersecurity researchers say you can use to protect your info.
- Don't reuse passwords; use a password manager.
- Check for security advisories from your bank.
- Use two-factor authentication on your devices and accounts — especially for email, banking, and your password manager.
- If your data has been breached, expect more convincing scams and phishing emails.
- Turn auto-updates on and restart your computer weekly.
"You can ask your claude code to audit what on your laptop is out of date and needs updating," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, a bipartisan nonprofit that advocates for safety guardrails and federal oversight, added in a post on X.

* use two factor auth for everything important (not via sms!! Google Authenticator or better yet YubiKey)
* Auto-updates on,…

Omnichannel furniture and home furnishings brand Chapter Homes has raised ₹63 Cr ($6.6 Mn) in a strategic funding round through a mix of debt and equity. The fundraise valued the startup at nearly ₹1,000 Cr (around $106 Mn). The round saw participation from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, comedian Tanmay Bhat and a clutch of family offices. The brand claims to have also received further commitments from undisclosed backers for a future fundraise. In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen product development, expand into newer categories and invest in technology and brand building. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its omnichannel distribution network and set up its initial offline footprint. “... Consumers are increasingly looking for better-designed products, trusted quality, strong functionality and a superior overall experience – online and in store – and we see a meaningful opportunity to build for those needs. That is why we are building focused brands for each category across home and kitchen,” said Chapter Homes cofounder Nitin Chugh. Founded in 2025 by former PharmEasy executives Chugh, Akarsh Bharadwaj, Shrey Mittal, Dhiraj Jain and Dheeraj Goyal, Chapter Homes claims to be building multiple consumer brands across categories for home and kitchen needs of Indian consumers. It has already launched a home furnishing brand under HOKIPO. Going forward, it plans to leverage synergies across supply chain, content, technology and distribution to expand into adjacent categories such as cookware, home décor and small kitchen appliances. The startup also said that it plans to leverage AI across cataloguing and demand forecasting to product assortment and customer retention to launch faster and rein in costs. Notably, Chapter Homes is not the first home improvement startup to emerge from the PharmEasy stable. Earlier this year, AllHome, founded by PharmEasy cofounders, raised ₹200 Cr in its Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners. The fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in the home improvement and home decor segment. In August, home decor marketplace Vaaree raised ₹65 Cr in its Series A round co-led by Hero Enterprise and Cap Alpha Ventures. Hosps charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugs (Generative image)
NEW DELHI: Govt has admitted before Supreme Court the “malpractice” of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables, and said it was conscious of the problem, examining it and devising appropriate interventions in consultation with all stakeholders.In an affidavit filed in SC on the issue of capping prices of all medicines and medical consumables, chemicals and fertilisers ministry said that patients have a very low bargaining position with respect to hospitals, resulting in various malpractices. The affidavit noted the irony of India being home to companies making cheap drugs but patients here having to pay way above the manufacturing price, as well as patients being subjected to overcharging by hospitals.“The Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world. Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. However, by their very nature, health treatment and pharmaceutical products involve information and bargaining asymmetries between patients on the one hand, and retail pharmacies, hospital pharmacies, hospitals providing treatment and doctors on the other,” the affidavit said.
Hospitals charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugs
The govt affidavit said a patient has a “very low bargaining position vis-a-vis the hospital, and the patient’s knowledge of drugs, their substitutes and their prices is also very limited”. These bargaining and information asymmetries result in various malpractices in the system despite strong competition among manufacturers, leading to the need for regulation, it said.Enumerating the steps taken by it to control the pricing of drugs, govt said ceiling prices for 935 scheduled formulations and retail prices of 3,881 new drugs have been fixed. Govt filed the affidavit on a plea filed by Dr Sanjay Kulshrestha, who referred to a Niti Aayog report and a 2020 statement of the then health minister Harsh Vardhan that expenditure on health pushed an estimated six crore families below the poverty line each year.
The affidavit said hospitals buy medicines from manufacturers who provide highest trade margin and then sell those medicines to patients at MRP, with margins ranging from 170% to 700% or more in the case of anti-cancer drugs.“That another area of concern in the sector is the supply of consumables in hospitals, where margins of 100% to 1000% or more are prevalent, along with a tendency of hospitals to purchase consumables that have a high MRP and margin, with a low price to the distributor/hospital. Ordinarily, hospital supplies are included in the package cost for treatment of major diseases/procedures under govt schemes/insurance, and govt/insurance agencies negotiate and fix the lowest rate for such packages. However, for patients making direct payment to the hospital, hospital supplies are billed separately at MRP,” it said.

Egyptian editor faces trial after hours of questioning
Egyptian prosecutors referred Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of independent news outlet Mada Masr, to trial on a charge of operating a website without a license, after questioning her for more than six hours
The editor-in-chief of one of Egypt’s last independent news outlets, Mada Masr, will stand trial after prosecutors questioned her for more than six hours, her lawyer said early Thursday.
The Supreme State Prosecution referred Mada Masr’s Lina Attalah to trial on Thursday on a charge of establishing and managing a website without a license. She was also questioned on a charge of publishing false news, but that charge was not included in her court referral, according to Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari.
She was released Wednesday evening on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds ($1,800), but if convicted, she faces a fine of one to three million Egyptian pounds ($18,000 to $54,000), al-Azhari said.
Under Egyptian media law, the court may also order the outlet closed and its equipment confiscated. Al-Azhari called the speed of the referral, which came just hours after the questioning ended, “unjustified urgency.”
Attalah is due in court on Oct. 27.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, and its investigative reporting has made it a frequent target of authorities. The site has been blocked in Egypt since 2017. Time magazine named Attalah one of its 100 most influential people in 2020.
The case file included a Mada Masr report published earlier this month in which lawyers described a wave of protests at several prisons and a harsh security response, al-Azhari said. The protests followed parliament’s decision to delay Egypt’s new criminal procedures law by a year.
Mada Masr said it has applied for a license several times since 2018. It says the Supreme Media Regulatory Council never responded and that it learned of the council’s rejection from prosecutors in 2022. The outlet challenged that decision in court. Its latest application has been pending since 2023, Mada Masr said.
The case is the sixth against Mada Masr and its journalists in six years. It comes less than a month after security forces arrested the entire six-person newsroom of Matsadaash, an independent fact-checking and investigative platform, in raids across the country on Sept. 28 and 29. Their families and lawyers did not know where they were for days.
The six remain in pre-trial detention on charges including joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, which they deny. Their detention was renewed for 15 days on Oct. 13.
This week, Mada Masr and seven other Egyptian and Arab outlets launched a temporary joint fact-checking newsroom in solidarity with the detained journalists.
Egypt ranks 169th of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index.

Footballer Antoine Semenyo "froze" after he was allegedly racially abused by a Liverpool fan during a Premier League match at Anfield, a court has heard.
The Manchester City winger, who was playing for Bournemouth at the time, was preparing to take a throw-in when Mark Mogan, 47, allegedly shouted a racist insult at him on 15 August 2025.
Prosecutors said Semenyo was "clearly hurt and upset" and reported the incident to referee Anthony Taylor when the ball next went out of play.
Mogan, of Dovecot, Liverpool, denies racially aggravated behaviour.
Liverpool Magistrates' Court heard Mogan, who uses a wheelchair, shouted an offensive slur about 30 minutes into the opening match of the Premier League season.
Prosecutor Simon Jones said: "Mr Semenyo briefly froze as he couldn't believe what the male had said."
The court heard Mogan then shouted further abuse at Semenyo, who did not respond and went on to take the throw-in.
Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time, the court was told.
Two short video clips were shown to the court, with Jones describing Mogan as being in an "agitated and angry state".
He said witnesses saw Mogan throw chewing gum at Semenyo, hitting the right side of his shorts.
In a statement read to the court, Liverpool supporter Neil Sherratt, who sits next to Mogan at matches, said he saw him approach the pitch from the disabled section of the Main Stand.
Sherratt said he heard Mogan shout something along the lines of "hurry up" and saw Semenyo turn towards him.
He said the footballer had a shocked expression and he believed he replied: "you what".
Another Liverpool fan, Nicholas Collins, said Mogan became "very cocky and brazen" after the incident and threatened to assault police if they approached him.
Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police during an interview the following day that he had shouted at Semenyo to hurry up.
He claimed the footballer had called him "a cripple", which had upset him, and said he had thrown chewing gum on to the floor rather than at Semenyo.
Jones told the court the prosecution's case was that Mogan had lied during his police interview.
Semenyo, who was born in London to Ghanaian parents and has represented Ghana in the World Cup, is expected to give evidence over a videolink.
Mogan, of Templehill Close, Dovecot, denies racially aggravated behaviour.
The trial continues.

New Delhi: India is likely to import more edible oil next year despite an increase in early oilseed plantings, as inadequate rainfall clouds the production outlook for key crops such as soybean and groundnut, while consumption continues to rise, three trade executives said. Imports are likely to rise about 3% to 17 million tonnes in the oil year starting November, according to industry estimates. That would follow estimated imports of 16.5 million tonnes this oil year, and 16.01 million tonnes in 2024-25, they said. India annually consumes about 26 million tonnes of edible oil, which remains one of the largest agricultural import commodities for the country. “India needs an additional 8-10 lakh tonnes of edible oil every year to meet rising domestic demand. Producing this quantity would require an additional 25-30 lakh tonnes of oilseeds. Despite an increase in acreage in just concluded kharif season, we expect yields to decline because of less rainfall. The outlook for the rabi season is also uncertain due to the potential impact of El Niño. Given these factors, we expect edible oil imports to increase,” said B.V. Mehta, executive director, The Solvent Extractors' Association of India (SEA), the apex body for the vegetable oil industry and solvent extraction trade. India remains dependent on imports for around 60-65% of its edible oil requirements. Total oilseed area is estimated at 19.66 million hectares as on 2 October, compared with 19.63 million hectares a year ago, according to the agriculture ministry data. "However, gains in acreage may not translate into a commensurate increase in domestic output, leaving supplies vulnerable to fluctuations in crop yields and weather conditions," said Mehta. Soybean, India’s largest oilseed crop, covered 12.3 million hectares, with acreage declining by 14,000 hectares. Groundnut acreage, meanwhile, increased by 1,000 hectares to 5.1 million hectares. Among other oilseeds, sunflower recorded an increase of 59,000 hectares, taking its total area under cultivation to 129,000 hectares. Acreage trends for other crops, including sesamum and castorseed, also varied. According to experts, India's edible oil demand continues to climb, driven by population growth and rising income. "India's edible oil consumption increased from 22.8 million tonnes in FY22 to an estimated 25.7 MMT in FY26, representing a steady ~3% CAGR, in line with the industry's long-term structural growth trend. Consumption growth remains supported by favorable demographics and rising per-capita usage," said Rahul Guha, senior director, Crisil Ratings. Overall, India's edible oil consumption is projected to rise 3% to around 26.5 million tonnes in FY27, according to Crisil. "Despite inflationary pressures and commodity price volatility, demand has remained resilient, driven by population growth, urbanization, changing dietary patterns, higher consumption of processed foods, and expansion of the food-service sector. Consequently, the edible oil industry is expected to sustain stable volume growth of ~3% annually over the medium term, " Guha added. With consumption continuing to expand, boosting domestic oilseed production will remain key to reducing import dependence and exposure to fluctuations in global prices. Initiatives such as the National Mission on Edible Oils are expected to gradually boost domestic production and support growing demand. India's per capita edible oil consumption is estimated at 17.6 kg in FY26. While demand continues to rise, medical practitioners warn that excessive consumption can lead to health complications. "While healthy fats play a crucial role in cell structure, hormone production, and nutrient absorption, exceeding the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) recommendation of 20 to 30 grams of visible oil per day poses significant long-term risks to gastrointestinal and overall metabolic health," said Dr. Saurabh Bansal, a minimal access and gastrointestinal surgeon and founder-director of The Clinics and The Clinics Misc. Police are investigating the link between the sale and the case and whether the proceeds were used as bribes.
Police have registered seven cases of sexual assault under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act against Veeramani and recorded 11 statements of minors.
Veeramani’s drivers Lazer, Parthiban and Babu, who allegedly brought his victims to his home, were arrested on October 5 and remanded to judicial custody.
Police said searches were conducted at the residences of Veeramani in Chennai, his farmhouse and an office, and some incriminating documents were recovered.

The shortage of doctors in India, particularly in rural areas, is well documented. This shortage compounds the suffering of rural communities, where people must suffer not only with disease but also with the struggle to access care. Illness in rural India is therefore not merely a departure from good health. It can push entire families into generational poverty and, in some cases, drive people to take their own lives. It is no coincidence that illness is among the leading causes of suicide in India.
To address this disparity, doctors are routinely called upon to move to rural areas and serve those most in need. Instead of fixing an underfunded healthcare system, the responsibility is placed on individual doctors to be “good” and fill the void left by governments that have consistently failed to prioritise people’s health.
I define a good doctor as someone who is compassionate, competent, and courageous. However, I am increasingly realising how risky it is to be such a doctor in India.
Being a good doctor
A good doctor is not merely empathetic. Compassion goes beyond feeling another person’s pain; it demands action to alleviate it. Over time, doctors who take this responsibility seriously begin to recognise that a prescription or surgery may address a symptom without touching the larger suffering that produced it. They begin asking why a person fell sick in the first place. And that is what makes them risky.
In Indian medical colleges, disease is often taught as the consequence of an infection, a genetic predisposition, or an unhealthy lifestyle. But step outside these institutions and into the communities where disease takes root, and you begin to understand how inadequate this framework can be. The people living with illness often understand its causes very differently from the institutions tasked with treating it.
“What is your biggest problem in the village?” I asked 25 villagers in rural Assam who had gathered for a cancer screening camp.
“We don’t have a road here, which makes it difficult to travel to and from the village,” said the eldest man in the group. The others nodded. “Because of the poor road, it is difficult to bring water into the village. When somebody falls sick, we cannot take them to the hospital on time,” he continued.
The connections were obvious. The absence of a road restricted access to water and healthcare. Inadequate access to water exposed people to illness, while poor connectivity delayed treatment. These were not separate problems. They were interconnected consequences of deprivation.
Last year, in a village in rural Tamil Nadu, I learnt how health was tied to land rights. “The government took our land away and gave us land 20 km away. We cannot grow anything on that land. We do not have money to buy food every day. Whatever we grow is what we eat,” a group of Adivasis living in the hamlet told me.
When people cannot access adequate food, clean water, or timely healthcare, can the solution to their illness really end with a prescription?
Why a good doctor is risky
A good doctor begins to understand that a prescription cannot compensate for the denial of land rights, that surgery cannot undo displacement, and that no medicine can substitute for the basic infrastructure a government has failed to provide. They recognise that confronting corruption and demanding accountability for broken promises may do more to protect a community’s health than any individual clinical intervention.
Dr. Binayak Sen understood this. A paediatrician and public health specialist, he served rural communities in Chhattisgarh while questioning the structural conditions that shaped their health. “At present, the greatest violence is structural violence. Violence is not restricted to a few groups; it pervades the structure of our society. We need to break out of this structure of violence through a process of dialogue,” he said in an interview with The Hindu.
Anyone who has travelled through rural Chhattisgarh, or indeed much of rural India, will recognise the realities underlying this argument. People do not fall sick simply because of individual choices or personal failures. Poverty, malnutrition, displacement, hunger and illiteracy all shape health outcomes. So does a government that fails to address these conditions. To treat the resulting illnesses without confronting their causes is to leave the machinery of suffering intact.
In 2010, Dr. Sen was convicted on charges relating to his alleged links with Naxalites and sentenced to life imprisonment. His case became symbolic of the risks faced by those who challenge the political and economic structures governing people’s lives. In his acceptance speech for the Paul Harrison Award for Meritorious Service in Rural Areas in 2004, Sen had argued: “The first point that I would like to make is about the primacy of politics in any relevant programme for health and health care. By politics I do not mean the farcical electoral charades of political parties, but the matrix of power that determines control over resources at entry level of community.”
Nearly two decades later, the question of what happens to doctors who challenge these structures remains painfully relevant.
Randall Sequeira, a general medicine specialist and rural practitioner, was arrested on October 16 and, according to reports, remains in judicial custody. His work with Adivasi communities in Odisha has involved addressing health concerns linked to mining activities. He has also stood in solidarity with these communities in their resistance to mining projects.
The implications are chilling. When a doctor connects illness to the consequences of mining, displacement and the denial of rights, healthcare ceases to be a politically neutral exercise. It becomes a challenge to the interests that benefit from these conditions remaining unchanged; conditions that ideally the state should be preventing. A doctor working with marginalised communities should not have to fear incarceration for asking why those communities are being made sick.
What will it take to keep India healthy?
What, then, does India need to keep its people healthy? More evidence on the health consequences of mining? Or do we need yet another explanation of how dispossession, exploitation and crony capitalism devastate Adivasi communities?
Evidence matters, but evidence alone cannot protect people when the political will to act on it is absent, or when those who demand accountability are treated as threats.
India needs good doctors more than ever. Not merely competent clinicians who are up to date with the latest evidence, write appropriate prescriptions and perform complex surgeries, but doctors who have the courage to question the systems that repeatedly make their patients sick. Doctors who understand that health is inseparable from the distribution of land, wealth, power and public resources. Doctors who refuse to accept preventable suffering as an inevitable feature of life for the poor.
Healthcare workers have a moral responsibility that extends beyond the consulting room. They must challenge the forces that expose people to disease, deny them care and then blame them for their suffering. This does not mean that every doctor must become an activist or that clinical care is unimportant. It means recognising the limits of medicine when the conditions producing illness are left untouched.
But a doctor who speaks about these conditions risks being labelled a troublemaker, an agitator or a threat to the state. The experiences of Dr. Sen and Dr. Sequeira raise an urgent question: what kind of society punishes those who seek to protect the health of its most marginalised people?
If being a good doctor means treating the patient while remaining silent about the forces making that patient sick, then perhaps we need to reconsider what goodness in medicine means. And if questioning those forces is enough to put a doctor’s freedom at risk, the problem is not with the doctor.
It is time for healthcare workers to speak up, collectively and without fear. Silence is not neutrality when the suffering is preventable, and the forces responsible are identifiable. The longer we remain silent, the easier it becomes for those in power to keep the tap of suffering open.
(Dr. Parth Sharma is a community medicine physician and a public health palliative care researcher. parth.sharma25@gmail.com)

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.
The video campaign can also be downloaded here for editorial purposes.

Dawood Ibrahim living in Pakistan: New Delhi slams UN rapporteur over report calling D-Company ‘India-based’
Indian diplomat Raghoo Puri said that Dawood is a wanted criminal in India and, according to the UN's listing entry, was living in Pakistan.
India on Wednesday strongly hit out at UN rapporteur Ben Saul over a counter-terrorism report and called for high standards of impartiality after the document described underworld don Dawood Ibrahim as the leader of the “India-based” D-Company criminal gang with terrorist ties.
Raghoo Puri, India's First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN, expressed “serious concern” over the Special Rapporteur “releasing reports with factual inaccuracies while not being held accountable for them”.
ALSO READ | India slams UN over ‘selective targeting’ after experts flag crackdown on protests
“This presents Member States with a fait accompli, which is unfortunate for this organisation that is facing challenges of legitimacy,” he told the UN assembly.
India affirms Dawood Ibrahim residing in Pakistan
Puri said that Dawood is a wanted criminal in India and, according to the UN's listing entry, was living in Pakistan.
He said the report noted that the Security Council had listed the head of D-Company in 2003 over links to Al-Qaeda. However, he argued that “this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality”.
Puri said D-Company and its listed leader, Dawood Ibrahim, had been wanted in India over terror attacks since 1993. “This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons of listing under the 1267 sanctions regime.”
“Not mentioning this fact is regrettable, and such incompetence on the part of special mandate holders does this organisation tremendous harm,” Puri added.
He told the assembly that Dawood had been wanted in India well before the 2003 listing. He said Dawood was listed during this period for his links to Al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden while operating from outside India.
“To date, he remains a wanted criminal in my country, and as per the UN's listing entry, resides in the same country where Osama bin Laden was found and neutralised," the Indian diplomat said. Notably, he was referring to Pakistan, where bin Laden was found and killed.
India also criticised the bias in the report, arguing that human rights principles should not be used to shield those responsible for terrorism.
"It seems to have become fashionable for sponsors of terror to use human rights and the framework of counterterrorism to justify their misdeeds. The human rights framework cannot be the refuge of the perpetrators of terror and those who propagate radicalisation and extremism. Terrorism can never be justified," he said.
India slams Pakistan’s remarks on Kashmir
Puri also responded to remarks made by the Pakistani delegation and reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh were integral parts of India.
"Regarding the statement just made by the delegate of Pakistan, everyone in this room knows that what has been mentioned against my country, including about the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, is pure propaganda made for very narrow political gains. And these have been on account of the actual rulers of Pakistan, which is its military,” he said.
He added, “I would like to reiterate for the record that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are inalienable parts of India, have been so, and will always remain so.”
India hit out at UN over ‘selective targeting’ earlier
On Tuesday, India said that human rights should not be used to exert political pressure or to single out countries after more than 20 UN human rights experts in Geneva raised concerns over what they described as a "repeatedly heavy-handed police response" to youth-led protests in the national capital.
Barkha Tamrakar, deputy secretary in the ministry of external affairs, delivered India's statement at the UN General Assembly's Third Committee. “India engages with international human rights mechanisms, but such engagement must be based on dialogue, consultation, cooperation, with non-selectivity and transparency as guiding principles,” she said.
Tamrakar said India was ready to address specific cases backed by proper documentation through established channels. However, she opposed any "attempt to convert unverified allegations, incomplete statistics or a report that contains no India country observation into a negative characterisation of the world's largest democracy".
The response came after criticism from UN experts over the Indian police's “heavy-handed” handling of youth-led protests in Delhi and other areas over the past three months. They called on the authorities to protect peaceful demonstrations and ensure justice for alleged human rights violations during these and earlier protests.
Last week, India rejected as “hearsay” a report by a UN human rights expert that referred to a “satirical political movement” formed by young people in the country and alleged that its members had faced retaliation. New Delhi urged the expert to “verify” the claims before “vilifying issues based on unverified allegations.”
