Binny Bansal-backed AI startup ShopOS has launched Sloosh, a self-service platform that makes the image and video generation technology it uses for enterprise clients available to individual creators and small businesses. Speaking to Inc42, ShopOS cofounder Ajay PV said Sloosh targets creators, designers, photographers, video editors and small businesses who want to generate visual content using AI tools without engaging its enterprise creative team. “ShopOS owns the outcome for mid and large brands. Sloosh goes after a much bigger market: anyone who makes visual content needs creatives every day,” he said. The platform is being opened to users globally, with paid subscription plans starting at $19 per month. Launched today, the platform operates on a subscription model, with paid plans starting at $19 per month globally. Ajay said the decision to build a self-service product followed interest from smaller brands and individual creators who could not afford ShopOS’ enterprise retainers. “Some of our smaller brands couldn’t afford the retainers and asked us to turn the technology into a product they could use. The idea had been brewing for a while, and over the last three months, we worked on packaging the image and video orchestration engine we had built to generate millions of creative assets for our brands into a product called Sloosh,” the cofounder added. Sloosh brings third-party AI image and video models into a single platform, allowing users to generate content from prompts and templates. It also offers reusable workflows called Spaces and a visual canvas, Spacelab, for building or modifying these workflows. Spaces allow users to repeat a creative task with different inputs without rebuilding prompts and settings each time. The platform also supports batch generation, enabling users to produce multiple images and videos through the same workflow. Users can also access human creative experts for more complex projects, according to the startup. Sloosh supports connections with AI assistants through model context protocol (MCP), allowing users to request image and video generation from compatible tools. The startup said it is also launching an Adobe After Effects plugin and plans to add more integrations. To attract users, ShopOS plans to work with creators and build communities across markets. Users will also be able to publish and share their Spaces. Sloosh is currently part of ShopOS, but the team is open to exploring a restructuring depending on the platform’s growth, Ajay said. ShopOS Eyes Global Expansion Founded in 2025 by Sai Krishna V K and Ajay, ShopOS builds AI tools and services for ecommerce brands across catalogue operations, category management, pricing, promotions, recommendations, and marketing. The cofounders previously built augmented reality and AI commerce startup Scapic, which Flipkart acquired in 2020. ShopOS raised $20 Mn from Binny Bansal’s investment vehicle 3STATE Ventures in June last year to develop its products, onboard brand partners, and expand its team. Under its managed services model, ShopOS delivers finished creative assets, with its team reviewing and refining AI-generated content before handing it over to clients. Ajay said the startup currently serves around 30-40 brands in India and a few in the US. It has also secured US contracts worth around $500,000. Over the next year, ShopOS aims to expand its enterprise customer base to more than 100 brands in India and 40-50 brands in the US. Its clients include Kareena Kapoor-backed Fizzy Globlet, Van Heusen, among others. The startup claims its services have reduced clients’ production budgets by nearly 90%.

5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
If you feel tired and sluggish … go for a five-minute walk (every half hour)
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy.
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue.
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks.
If your back aches from slouching over your desk … rotate your spine
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
If your eyes hurt from staring at a screen … stretch your eye muscles
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
If you feel fidgety and restless … change your position (and don't worry too much about the "right" posture)
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman, a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters. Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough.
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek, a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
If sitting at your desk makes you feel uncomfortable … adjust your workspace
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.
For more ergonomic tips, read our story.

The Health Department has issued a circular directing the Director of Health Services and the Director of Medical Education to ensure uninterrupted treatment for patients in government hospitals.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan said that instructions have been given to ensure the availability of medicines and chemical reagents for laboratories and to monitor stocks accurately.
The circular directs that an updated list of the medicine stocks in hospitals be provided to doctors in the OP (outpatient) departments. This will help doctors have a clear idea about the medicines available in the hospital and to prescribe the same to patients.
The Minister also said that the generic names of medicines must be written on prescriptions issued by doctors.
A report on reagent stock and future requirements must be submitted once every two weeks, so that any shortage can be anticipated and supplies organised on time.
The circular also says that where materials needed for lab tests are unavailable, they can be purchased using Hospital Development Committee funds.

Bengaluru-based cybersecurity company eMudhra, which recently found itself at the centre of a security key issue, has announced plans to voluntarily wind down its global secure sockets layer and transport layer security (SSL/TLS) certificate business. In a filing, the company said that the decision followed a security incident in which a researcher discovered that the private keys of eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates were weak enough to be recovered. The discovery prompted browser root programmes, including Google and Mozilla, to distrust eMudhra’s certificates, affecting its global TLS business. eMudhra said it revoked the affected CAs within 14 hours of discovering the incident and disclosed it promptly. It added that no end-entity certificates had been issued by the affected CAs, its infrastructure remained uncompromised and no data was breached. “The impact has been quite severe over the last 24-48 hours. Given the risk to the rest of the business and our obligations as a publicly listed company, the board felt it was prudent to withdraw from this business,” Kaushik Srinivasan, cofounder, told Inc42. The company also cited rising compliance costs, declining returns and limited revenue contribution as the reason behind the move. The segment accounts for around 1% of its global revenue. The company reported revenues of ₹701.6 Cr in FY26. The segment’s future commercial prospects also triggered the closure. With Let's Encrypt offering free TLS certificates and Cloudflare planning to do the same, Srinivasan said the commercial return from the business looks limited, particularly as browser guidelines move towards 90-day certificates. “The board evaluated the social media reaction, but also took cognisance of the ROI, future potential and competitive landscape,” he said, adding that eMudhra would focus on more complex customer problems in areas such as AI and quantum computing. What Does This Mean For eMudhra’s Customers eMudhra said existing customers would be transitioned to alternative certificate providers free of charge over the next three to four weeks, with the company working with other certificate partners to avoid service disruptions. Srinivasan said the distrust of its G3 ECC root had already affected around 30,000 certificates in the US, which were transitioned to its G1 RSA root. To be sure, G1 and G3 are eMudhra’s root certificate hierarchies: G1 uses RSA cryptography, while G3 uses elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). Google and Mozilla distrusted G3 as a precaution following the security incident, while G1 continues to operate and issue certificates. All certificates in India and various adjoining markets were issued from the G1 root. However, the G3 root distrust impacted an undisclosed US client. “It resulted in around 30,000 certificates in the US market being affected because they were under ECC. We had to transition them to RSA. Following our announcement, we have to transition them to another provider. We are actively working on that,” Srinivasan said. The Incident That Shook The World On October 17, researcher Wayne notified browser root programmes and eMudhra that he had recovered the private keys corresponding to eight intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates. The keys had been generated with insufficient randomness, making them vulnerable to reconstruction. Such keys could potentially be used to issue fraudulent certificates for websites or software, although eMudhra said none of the eight intermediates had issued end-entity certificates. Six were intended for TLS and two for software signing. Browser root programmes from companies like Mozilla and Google moved to block the affected TLS intermediates. eMudhra, at the time, said the certificates were created on April 30, 2025, and had undergone independent audits, though it did not name the auditors or disclose the audit scope. The company said only one affected intermediate was deployed in production, none had issued end-entity certificates, and all eight had been revoked. The incident prompted a worldwide reaction, casting aspersions on eMudhra’s security controls and the reliability of its certificate issuance processes. Security experts were also unsatisfied with eMudhra’s clarification on the matter. Responding to this, Srinivasan said that it was a script error and a human oversight problem; no hardware problem was found. “We will share the facts in due course, and this will also be verified through independent research. It was a one-off, a bad day. That's exactly what happened.” Notably, the flaw went undetected for around 18 months, spanning two independent audit cycles. Srinivasan said eMudhra will now appoint an auditor to prepare the final report on the incident, which would take 2-3 weeks. Further, the company would strengthen internal accountability, maker-checker controls and independent reviews for critical processes such as key generation. The company is also exploring AI-based checks to detect weaknesses and flag potential errors.

Cong is fine when it wins, blames BJP and EC when it loses: Bhupender Yadav
Union minister Bhupender Yadav accuses the Opposition of trying to destabilise Indian democracy through its allegations against the Election Commission over SIR.
Union minister and senior Bharatiya Janata Party leader Bhupender Yadav on Thursday said the Opposition’s intent in raising questions about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls is not to correct irregularities in the poll process, but largely to destabilise Indian democracy.
In an interview to HT, he said the Opposition’s bid was to discredit constitutional bodies, and discussed why the Mamata Banerjee government was ousted from West Bengal after 15 years in power. Edited excerpts:
What is the government’s response to the Opposition’s serious charges of irregularities against the election commission over the conduct of SIR?
The Opposition is frustrated with repeated loses in state after state. The Congress doesn’t believe in EVMs, which was introduced by them. They don’t believe in Parliament, in the Supreme Court when the verdict is not to their liking. They don’t believe in EC if the poll result is not to their liking.
But the Congress has still not been able to invalidate the process of SIR.
It won in Kerala, and supported the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) that won in Tamil Nadu. It has not explained how, if the SIR is so wrong, did the party win the elections. If the SIR was flawed, then why accept the result and the victory? They accept victories, but blame EC and the BJP for defeats.
They have made several allegations of irregularities against the CEC over how SIR is being done?
They filed a case in the Supreme Court. The judgment clearly upheld and validated the proceedings of SIR, which is not being held for the first time. Between 1951 and 2004, it was conducted eight times and the current cycle which started in 2025 is the ninth. Of these eight-and-a-half cycles have been conducted during their tenure. Under Rule 25(2) of Registration of Electors Rules, during SIR, the electoral roll is to be prepared afresh for the correction of electoral rolls and the purpose is to update the voter list.
The Congress’s aim is to shoot and scoot. EC asked them to submit a signed affidavit with the complaints so that the cases could be investigated. Rahul Gandhi or their BLAs (block level agents) never signed any affidavit. The President of India asked them to submit proof. They are yet to do that.
The dynasts in the Congress believe they have a right to rule. Since they are unable to win fair and square, they want to discredit institutions and push people to take to the streets for a regime change. Indian democracy is far too strong and people are way too mature to fall for these gimmicks.
You were the election-in-charge in West Bengal, where the BJP swept to power with a huge mandate for the first time. Almost 2.2 million people were disenfranchised in the state and filed petitions. Opposition leaders alleged that the exercise was rushed and opaque and targeted minorities and the marginalised.
It was the so-called INDI alliance that asked for SIR, alleging voter rolls had issues. EC acted promptly and ordered SIR. In some states they won; in most states we won. They couldn’t digest this and started alleging foul play. It all started with blaming EVMs. In West Bengal, SIR was conducted by EC and monitored by the Supreme Court. And it was the TMC that won the 13 seats where the maximum number of voters were deleted.
Mamata Banerjee lost because of a huge anti-incumbency wave and people had faith in the leadership of PM Narendra Modi ji to provide good governance.
What about the voters who were barred from voting after EC marked them for discrepancies?
During SIR, EC first publishes a draft roll. It is bound to issue a notice to anyone whose name is deleted. The reasons for deletion are death, migration, duplication, or wrong information. The appeals of those who were excluded are pending before the appellate tribunal created by SC. If people come forward to give their documents, I am sure EC will take corrective measures.
Economist Surjit Bhalla in an analysis of SIR in Bengal said the 2004 electoral rolls had 2.8 crore more names than the estimated adult population-- an excess of 4.4% and in 2014, the roll was 3.1% higher than the adult population. We did not allege any electoral fraud, or question EC.
The TMC appointed BLAs in every booth and government machinery was there, but where is their complaint? You participated in the exercise, used the state machinery in your favour, used muscle power and even then when you failed, you are blaming the Election Commission and SIR.
It is not correct that only the minorities were left out; many Hindus who should have been protected by the provisions of the Citizenship Amendment Act were also excluded due to Mamata Banerji’s negligence.
The BJP believes every eligible citizen should be able to vote. EC is mandated to ensure every eligible citizen has the right to vote and to ensure the removal of those who aren’t. Our institutions must be empowered to discharge their duties, not discredited because someone did not get a poll result they desired.
What were the key factors for the TMC’s loss?
Mamata Banerjee lost the election because of arrogance, anti-incumbency, social unrest, and the politics of appeasement. If you fail in the eyes of the public because of your misgovernance, you cannot pin the blame on concocted reasons, especially those that imperil your Constitutional institutions.
The post-election scenario was intriguing. How did the 20 lawmakers reach out to the BJP and what were their concerns?
Mamata Banerjee lost the confidence of Bengal’s voters and her own party. The anti-incumbency was both within and outside of the party. She came to power in Bengal against the authoritarian rule of the Left. Over time, she became an authoritarian CM. People felt suffocated and so did the people in her party.
Adding to that the fact the TMC was not a party rooted in ideology, Mamata gave preference to family over senior party members. There was always disgruntlement in the party.
There is another set of assembly elections coming up. In UP, which is crucial for the BJP, the Opposition’s main planks are vote chori, chanda chori in Ayodhya and anti-incumbency.
The BJP is working hard on the ground, the organisational activities as decided by the national president, Nitin Nabin, are underway. The improved law and order situation in the state, the credibility of chief minister Yogi Adityanath and the leadership of PM Modi are there for all to see. There is no impact of the Opposition’s attempts to create any narrative. What matters is how in the last 12 years governance has become the main poll plank.
Look at states such as Telangana where the Congress and Chhattisgarh where the JMM also announced social welfare schemes but corruption hampered delivery. The NDA, on the other hand, has been successful in the delivery of pro-poor schemes.
In the past 12 years, the BJP-led NDA government announced and successfully implemented pro-poor policies. In the second term, major reforms through legislative action such as the GST rollout, Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, Direct Benefit Transfer happened. In the third term there is a more proactive push for reforms, the PM has called it the “reform express”. So, this is the core of Indian politics now. The issues raised by the Opposition are just to discredit constitutional bodies, which are highly respected worldwide.

Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.
It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.
Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.
Older but Still Capable
The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.
Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. However, for most users, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip (SoC) is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.
If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

China-made cancer drug to go on sale in US after Americans travel to buy it
AstraZeneca moves to make the lung cancer drug available in the US after lengthy delays raised concerns over patient access
Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca said on Thursday it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China.
In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease.
Developed by China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical, sunvozertinib is a targeted lung cancer drug designed to treat adults with an advanced form of the illness, offering another treatment option for patients.
“The drug was approved in China in 2023. The FDA approved it in July 2025,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, wrote on social media on Wednesday.

Motilal Oswal Financial Services and Calliope Capital Advisors have applied for a combined 2.39 Cr shares in Ola Electric’s ₹1,000 Cr rights issue against entitlements transferred by two promoter group entities. The electric two-wheeler maker said in an exchange filing that Motilal Oswal Financial Services applied for 1.28 Cr shares against rights entitlements renounced by ANI Technologies. Calliope Capital Advisors applied for another 1.10 Cr shares against entitlements transferred by Indus Trust. Calliope Capital Advisors LLP is an investment vehicle owned by Navin Agarwal, group MD of Motilal Oswal Financial Services. Both investors submitted their applications before 11:00 IST on the opening day of the issue, covering the full entitlements transferred to them. Renouncing a rights entitlement means transferring the right to subscribe to new shares to another investor. ANI Technologies, which operates the Ola Cabs business, and Indus Trust held 3.47% and 2.98% stake, respectively, in Ola Electric as of June 30, according to the company’s letter of offer. Ankush Aggarwal, brother of founder Bhavish Aggarwal, serves as the trustee of Indus Trust. Meanwhile, CMD Bhavish has committed to subscribing to his full rights entitlement. Promoter group members have also committed to subscribing to their entitlements or transferring them within the permitted categories, including to specified investors. Earlier this month, Aggarwal pledged a 4.32% stake in Ola Electric to fund his participation in the rights issue. Another Round Of Fundraising The rights issue, which closes on October 30, comprises up to 37.03 Cr partly paid-up shares priced at ₹27 apiece. Investors must pay ₹16.20 per share on application and the remaining ₹10.80 through a subsequent call. Ola Electric plans to allocate ₹350 Cr towards repaying or prepaying borrowings, including accrued interest and applicable prepayment penalties, and ₹400 Cr towards organic growth. The remaining net proceeds will fund general corporate purposes. The fundraise follows the company’s ₹780.24 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP) in June, with some proceeds from earlier capital raises yet to be deployed. As of September 20, 2026, ₹139.21 Cr of IPO proceeds allocated towards debt repayment, organic growth, and general corporate purposes remained unutilised. Another ₹190.77 Cr from the QIP remained unutilised across these common objects, according to the letter of offer. The fundraise comes at a time when Ola Electric is stepping up investments in its battery cell manufacturing and battery energy storage system businesses. On the financial front, its consolidated net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27. However, operating revenue plunged 45% YoY to ₹455 Cr. Sequentially, revenue rose 72% from ₹265 Cr, while loss narrowed from ₹500 Cr. Shares of Ola Electric ended today’s trading session 3.21% lower at ₹31.94 apiece on the BSE.

If you live anywhere on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong moths are back in a big way.
While we don’t yet have figures from ecologist-led surveys to compare with previous years, there is a wealth of data on the great moth revival being generated by citizen scientists across the eastern states.
In this animated map you can see bogong moth observations posted to the citizen science platform iNaturalist via the Bogong Watch project. Every dot is a sighting, which may include one or more moths.
While there are some caveats to keep in mind with citizen science data (observation numbers over time can be skewed because of differences in effort and participation, for example) it does clearly show how the moth population has exploded this year.
A rise from a great fall
Bogongs were once so common they numbered in the billions, according to researchers, with as many as 4 billion moths migrating to the Australian Alps in summer to aestivate in cool caves. The moths famously caused panic at the Sydney Olympics closing ceremony in 2000, and were known to invade Parliament House in Canberra each year.
But the bogong population declined slowly between 1980 and 2016, then crashed dramatically in the summer of 2017.
Moth numbers were so low the species was described as “undetectable” in the alpine regions.
Ken Green, an ecologist who has been monitoring bogong moths for more than 40 years, previously told the Guardian that Australia’s drought through 2017, 2018 and 2019 was probably the largest contributor to the population crash, with pesticides and urban light pollution contributing to the slower decline from the 80s.
After those years of catastrophic decline, the explosion of bogongs across the skies of eastern Australia this spring is great news for the plants the moths pollinate and the endangered species that rely on them for food, including the mountain pygmy possum.

Tom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien and Top Gun, has died at the age of 93.
His publicist confirmed to Variety that he died from natural causes.
“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” a family statement shared with People read.
In a career spanning more than 60 years, the actor had more than 170 big and small screen credits, winning an Emmy and receiving Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild award nominations.
After serving a four-year tour of duty in the US air force, Skerritt made his big-screen debut in the 1962 war film War Hunt alongside Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, but his breakout came in 1970 with a role in Robert Altman’s hit satire M*A*S*H. The film was a major box office hit and was nominated for the best picture Oscar.
The 1970s saw Skerritt follow the film with roles in the cult black comedy Harold and Maude, Altman’s crime drama Thieves Like Us, Roger Corman’s sexploitation comedy Big Bad Mama and the Oscar-nominated ballet drama The Turning Point.
The decade closed out with a role in Ridley Scott’s smash hit Alien, a film he had earlier turned down due to the low budget. “At two million bucks and with other actors that I don’t know about, this is a film that could have been directed by Ed Wood,” he said in a 2019 interview. “I was uncertain about it because my training with Altman and Ashby had proceeded me, so I had that approach that I had absorbed from watching those two guys going about their work.”
The following decade saw him feature in David Cronenberg’s The Dead Zone, the sci-fi adventure SpaceCamp, horror sequel Poltergeist III and female-led comedy drama Steel Magnolias.
Skerritt also worked with Tony Scott in the 1986 blockbuster Top Gun, a role he almost didn’t get. “There was some question about me playing that role because I was … I think they used the word, laconic,” he said in a 2021 interview with Vulture. “It pissed me off. I went into it with [producer] Don Simpson, who was still alive at that point … don’t tell me, as a producer, what you think I’m going to be doing. You’re going to get what you need.”
In the 1990s, he reunited with Robert Redford for A River Runs Through It and also starred with Jodie Foster in Contact, Drew Barrymore in Poison Ivy and Diane Keaton in The Other Sister.
Skerritt also received an Emmy for his role in David E Kelley’s family drama Picket Fences, a show that ran for four seasons.
The 2000s saw him star with Bruce Willis in Tears of the Sun, Kate Beckinsale in Whiteout and on the small screen he had roles in Will & Grace, The West Wing and Brothers & Sisters.
His last film role was in the western drama Broke in 2025 with Dennis Quaid.
In 2012, he also co-founded an initiative called the Red Badge Project, which aimed to help veterans process their PTSD through storytelling. “It starts with that wanting to help someone else rather than talking about it,” Skerritt said to CBS News. “I just got tired of talking about this if I could do something about it.”
“I’m just a lucky guy, man,” he said in 2021. “Strength is measured in how you confront your weaknesses. I have had a lot of weaknesses. I still have them.”

You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.
As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.
That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.
“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.
According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.
It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.
It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.
The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service. If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $799, and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.
The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.
Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”
OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.
It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.
“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”
The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.
Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.
Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.
“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”
Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.
“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”
When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.
“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”
Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.

Quick Answer
The Ai+ Nova 2 Power offers a massive 7000mAh battery, solid everyday performance, flashy design, and decent cameras for ₹16,999. However, its low-resolution HD+ display and poorly optimized software hold it back, especially against established rivals offering better displays and smoother software.
Because of ongoing RAM and component price increases, smartphone prices have risen significantly, and the budget segment is hit hardest. After price hikes, it is hard to find a recommended value-for-money phone.
At the same time, several new Indian smartphone brands have emerged, and some have launched their first phones with a focus on the budget segment.
Ai+ is one of the most talked-about names. It comes from former Realme India CEO Madhav Sheth, who led Realme during its rise in India. Later moved to Honor India, then went silent for a bit, and launched a new phone brand called AI Plus, which launched several phones in the budget and mid-range segments.
While the budget smartphone segment is most affected by rising component prices, plenty of established rivals remain, making it an easy pick for users who value brand and trust. However, this is also a segment where ordinary people are willing to live with modest specifications and generally not as choosy about every feature.
I recently reviewed the AI Plus Nova 2 Power, the company’s latest budget-focused smartphone priced starting at Rs 16,999 (6GB + 128 GB variant). This is our first time testing an AI Plus Nova phone. The smartphone packs a 7000 mAh battery and a Dimensity 7100 processor, on par with rivals, but it falls short in the display and other areas.
However, the biggest question is whether the new Ai+ Nova 2 Power matches established rivals or if the marketing outpaces the phone’s substance.
Table of Contents
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Review
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Looks and Appearance: Flashy, Solid, and a Little Bulky
Most budget-centric users, especially in this price segment, prefer flashy designs. AI Plus Nova 2 Power matches this by offering dual-tone finishes and a reflective design.
I received the dark blue variant, which looks minimal but still flashy thanks to the reflective back. I personally prefer having minimal designs.
It also comes in other variants for people who love flashy, colorful designs on the back. The dark blue variants, despite the reflective screen, also don’t register your fingerprint as badly as I expected.
With the camera in the top-left corner, the phone wobbles a little when you set it on the table. Big AI Plus branding sits in the center. Otherwise, the back of the smartphone follows the standard approach. You find both the volume and power buttons on the right, and the blue variant’s power button is painted red, which stands out.
When you hold the smartphone in your right hand, the volume and power buttons are easy to reach, and you can also access the fingerprint sensor to unlock your phone. The AI Plus Nova 2 Power also integrates a fingerprint sensor into the power button itself. If you have big hands, you might accidentally press the volume button instead of the power button because it feels positioned too low. But if you have shorter hands, this should be your ideal position.
At the top, you will find a second speaker in the stereo speaker setup. At the bottom, it houses a Type-C charging port and a speaker. The SIM ejector pin is placed on the left at the top.
The device is noticeably wide and also bulky because of the huge 7000 mAh battery inside. It also makes the smartphone quite a bit heavy at 222 grams. You feel that weight every time you hold it, and the included case makes the device even bulkier. The upside of all that bulk is that the device feels like a solid brick in your hand. This solid build might not appeal to users looking for a slim, lightweight phone.
The phone also has IP65 water and dust resistance, which isn’t top-of-the-line but is decent enough to keep dust off the reflective glass display and resist a small splash of water.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Display: HD+ Screen That Falls Short
The display is where the Ai+ Nova 2 Power falls short of the competition. The Ai+ Nova 2 Power comes with a 6.75-inch IPS HD+ display. This is especially noticeable in this segment, where AMOLED displays are increasingly common even at this price.
This lower-resolution display is easy to spot every time you look at the screen, so much so that a decent camera can pick out the individual pixels.
The display is perfectly usable for everyday tasks, including browsing and watching videos, especially if you are coming from an HD+ display on your previous phone. If you have used a Super AMOLED display or a higher-spec display, even a Full HD display, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power display can feel like a significant downgrade.
The panel also supports a 120Hz refresh rate. The refresh rate defaults to auto. Even when you bump it up to the max, you won’t get the smoothness you would expect at 120Hz because of poor software optimization.
It seems like animation scale has been intentionally reduced to make it appear faster. But it affects the smoothness. As a result, apps and windows open faster; however, they aren’t smoother.
Since it is an IPS panel, the display colors in the normal mode look washed out. Fortunately, the settings offer vivid options that boost display colors. I highly recommend enabling vivid colors if you want punchier colors.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Performance: Good Hardware, Held Back by Software
The Ai+ Nova 2 Power comes with a Dimensity 7100 processor. It is more powerful than most Unisoc processor-powered phones we usually see in that segment. But if you can stretch your budget a little, you can get phones that are noticeably more powerful than the Dimensity 7100.
My unit also comes with 8GB RAM and 128GB of internal storage. It also comes in a 6GB + 128GB variant. Both storage variants also come with expandable storage up to 1TB. The Dimensity 7100 and 8GB is a powerful combination at this price range, but the Ai+ Nova 2 Power’s poor software optimization doesn’t deliver a smooth experience as expected.
Don’t get me wrong, the smartphone handles everyday tasks well, whether it’s opening apps, browsing, switching between them, or gaming. The hardware isn’t an issue; it’s only the software that’s limiting.
The gaming performance is also decent. It can handle popular BGMI at smooth + ultra or smooth + extreme settings. I had no issues except some stuttering while playing BGMI, and Infinite Flight Simulator plays without any issues. Overall, the Nova 2 Power offers strong performance with its powerful combination. However, better software tuning could improve it.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Battery Life: The Big Reason To Buy
Battery life is where the Ai+ Nova 2 Power does really well. The phone can comfortably get you through a full day of both heavy and light use, and on light use alone, it can easily last two days.
But it could have been better considering its less power-hungry specs. Better software optimization could have improved battery life even further. Still, for everyday use involving browsing YouTube, watching videos, and a little gaming, this phone should last a full day.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power supports 33W fast charging, which can fully charge your device in 2.5 hours from zero to hundred. That could be slow in 2026, but it’s not much of a complaint at this price point, and most buyers are happy with these charging speeds. The company also includes a 33W fast-charging brick in the box, another plus since most smartphones skip the charger.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Software and UI: Plenty of Features, Not Enough Polish
Putting together the best hardware is perhaps the easiest part of building a phone. But the software experience is where the brand’s real strength matters. As a newcomer, AI Plus still needs to improve its software experience to match the rich experience established players offer.
The user interface looks clean, and in some areas it feels closer to stock Android, but that changes when you swipe down to access the control panel and settings, which closely resemble ColorOS from a few years ago.
The best part is that the software won’t miss any customization features. It offers plenty of home and lock screen customizations along with handy themes. It also supports Dynamic Island-like information, showing quick toggles in a pill similar to the Dynamic Island on most phones. Changing the theme also changes the entire appearance of the system UI.
There are also handy features like double-tap to wake and double-tap to sleep, which can be useful when using the smartphone one-handed, but these features are off by default.
The software also offers decent ambient light customization on the back. You can only enable it for a few apps to use it, which can be useful, especially if you want to use it only for important reminders. Another thing I noticed is that changing the theme makes the phone feel faster than the default out-of-the-box theme.
However, another new concern is the software; Ai+ only promises major Android updates, and there is no clear word on how long the phone will get security patches.
The phone also comes with stereo speakers, with one placed at the bottom and the other at the top. Both sound equally similar, with good stereo separation. The second speaker on the top also doubles as the earpiece. The phone is also 5G-compatible, and the network reception is decent.
Ai+ Nova 2 Power Cameras: Better Than Expected, but Inconsistent
The camera performance has turned out better than I expected. Daylight and indoor shots look decent, with good detail and solid color reproduction, leaving not much to complain about at this price point. The selfies also look good, with decent color and detail.
In low light, however, the cameras struggle, missing details and producing grainy textures. The same goes for video. The daylight samples are excellent, but performance drops in low light. Take a look at the camera samples below.
For camera hardware, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power has a 48-megapixel main camera. It also includes an 8-megapixel ultra-wide-angle camera, which is hard to find at this price, and a 13-megapixel front camera.
In daylight and under good lighting, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power 48MP main camera delivers natural colors, good detail, and solid exposure for the price. However, it won’t offer consistent performance even under similar lighting conditions.
As you can see in the images below, both were taken under similar lighting conditions, but the left image looks washed out, while the right image’s colors are punchier and have a more contrasty look.
Also, when pointing out and shooting directly into the sun, the main camera also performs decently while preserving shadows, but then it misses out on details because of high exposure and also adds a slight haze effect in the bright and backlit areas, which is again something most cameras, even the flagship cameras, struggle with in this particular situation.
In indoor lighting, if the subject is close, the Nova 2 Power’s main camera performs exceptionally well, preserving natural colors and adding a little contrast, which overall looks better. However, it loses color when you shoot from a distance.
In indoor lighting, Nova 2’s main camera also performs well, but it loses detail when you zoom in. The colors are somewhat natural, but it sometimes produces contrasty images.
The main camera is also decent for portraits, though it again smooths the skin slightly and adds a bit of natural blur when the subject is close, which works well. What surprised me was its low-light performance. Both the main and front cameras produced bright pictures with close-to-natural-looking colors.
I also shot videos with the selfie and rear cameras, and like the photos, the front camera produces decent, natural colors while keeping exposure in check, but it struggles again when the background changes. With the rear camera, the colors are natural; however, it again struggles in bright skies, which adds a haze-like effect to the video.
Overall, the main camera produces natural daylight photos with good detail, and the selfies look sharp and close to natural, with realistic skin tones, plus very good night and low-light photos. Low-light photos obviously introduce noise, especially when you zoom in. The ultrawide secondary camera is a nice addition at this price, but it’s not the best. It is useful for capturing decent wide shots, but the quality is not as good as the main camera.
Here are our detailed camera ratings based on our testing:

| Ultra-wide | 6 | Wider view, noticeably softer |

Ai+ Nova 2 Power Review Verdict: A Decent Newcomer With Tough Competition
Ai+ Nova 2 Power comes in two variants. The 6GB + 128 GB is priced at Rs 16,999/- and 8 GB + 128 GB is priced at 17,999/-. Overall, the Ai+ Nova 2 Power is a good package for people who prioritize battery life and performance for everyday use without spending too much. The Dimensity 7100 handles most everyday tasks and gaming well, although it can get even better with software optimization. The colorful reflective glass back will appeal to most users, and the huge 7000 mAh battery gets you through your day. Cameras also did a decent job of handling everyday photography and videos.
But the HD+ resolution display is a real letdown, especially when so much more is available; AMOLED displays and a more polished software experience could have been better. If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess three terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini-powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.
While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the last ten days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.
Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices, and that they've rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”
Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the last week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the last week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.
If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for what device could be at fault.
How to Check Your Device Usage
You have a couple of different options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app still lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.
There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router, and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:
- Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in.
- Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour).
- You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab.
- You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone.
Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:
- Open the Deco or Tether app.
- Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage.
- What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information.
Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter, you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface (it usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app). If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.
But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the last seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or my over the last three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home.
But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.
Why Should You Check?
It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the two terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a three-terabyte bug slowing down your whole network.

Ukrainian foreign minister slams Witkoff's 'appeasement' of Putin
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has become the latest figure to hit out at Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff for calling Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian”, contrasting the statement with fresh Russian strikes on Kyiv overnight.
Sybiha did not name Witkoff directly, but wrote on X: “Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like: a brutal attack with dozens of ballistic missiles striking energy infrastructure, medical facilities, shopping centres, and residential areas.
“Other cities across Ukraine came under attack as well,” he wrote.
“Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Russian strikes hit Kyiv as war intensifies
Russian ballistic missile attacks have struck several parts of Kyiv overnight on Thursday, injuring six people and damaging residential buildings, a car service station, a medical facility and a restaurant.
At least 13 explosions were reported in less than eight minutes during one wave of strikes around 3am local time, according to The Kyiv Independent.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said: "In the same district, debris also hit another private residential building. There may be people trapped under the rubble.”
Fires reportedly broke out and some areas experienced power and Wi-Fi outages.
Residents reported windows being blown out and houses catching fire. One resident said he and his neighbours rescued a couple from a burning home.
Witkoff faces criticism over Putin ‘humanitarian’ remarks
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has drawn criticism from Washington after describing Russian president Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” following Moscow’s release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis criticised Witkoff in a post on X: “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian’.”
Donald Trump declined to endorse or reject the envoy’s description, saying “I wouldn’t say anything one way or the other”.
Vice president JD Vance defended Witkoff, saying: “I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.”
Hubbard, 74, a former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian detention on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, was released as Witkoff met Putin. Hubbard has denied these accusations.
Trump said the release required no concessions from Washington. He wrote on social media: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard after over 4 years behind bars
Russia on Wednesday freed an American who had been jailed for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, a deal completed during a visit by a top US envoy and at a time when president Donald Trump has taken a series of actions meant to benefit Moscow.
Trump told reporters at the White House that he had asked Russian president Vladimir Putin during a recent call to free Stephen Hubbard and that, unlike previous releases, the US did not have to give up anyone in return.
“He is the happiest man around,” Trump said of Hubbard, describing the 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan as a “very high-quality, innocent man”.
Hubbard’s legal team denied the Russian accusations, saying he was not involved in any military activity.
The release occurred during a visit to St Petersburg by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who in a face-to-face interaction with Putin praised the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” as the men held talks about Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as Trump simultaneously pushes Kyiv to make a deal that stops the fighting.
Kremlin says peace proposals lack ‘substance’
The Kremlin has cast doubt on the peace proposals to end the war in Ukraine, saying proposals put forward by Kyiv and European leaders lack “substance”.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian president Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday after holding talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral talks in mid-November, but added that “there wasn’t really much substance in them”.
US president Donald Trump said the negotiations were “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war, while Zelensky backed an early resumption of three-way talks.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive”, but said “there is still important work left to do”.
Trump hails Putin for releasing US citizen Stephen Hubbard
Donald Trump has posted on Truth Social to celebrate Vladimir Putin’s decision to release Stephen Hubbard, a US citizen who was formally designated as wrongfully detained in Russia for four years.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia,” the post read.
Hubbard’s release comes after a number of US concessions towards Russia in recent weeks, including a deal signed by Trump to obtain diesel from Moscow.
Nonetheless, Trump claimed that “there was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release”.
“Welcome home Stephen, it’s great to have you back,” the statement quoted Trump as saying.
Kremlin says journalists from 'unfriendly' countries to be allowed to attend Putin's annual presser
Journalists from countries Russia considers “unfriendly” will be allowed to attend president Vladimir Putin’s annual year-end press conference in December, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
“They will attend. Yes, [we will invite them] – as we always do,” Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS when asked whether media outlets from countries deemed unfriendly by Moscow would be invited.
The annual press conference will once again be combined with Putin’s “Direct Line” call-in show, during which he answers questions from Russian citizens.
The combined event, known as “Direct Line with Vladimir Putin: Year in Review”, will be held for the fifth time this year. The format was first introduced in 2020 during the Covid pandemic and revived in 2023.
Russia designates countries including the US, UK and EU member states as “unfriendly”, largely in response to sanctions imposed on Moscow following its invasion of Ukraine.
The exact date for the press conference has not been announced yet
