Sixteen dead, 32 injured after strong 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s Tibet region late Thursday (October 22, 2026), and casualties have been reported, state news agency Xinhua said, citing local authorities.
The epicentre of the quake, which struck at 10:33 p.m. (1433 GMT), was located in a mountainous area about 190 kilometres (120 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, and 390 kilometres northeast of the regional capital Lhasa, the U.S. Geological Survey said.
It struck at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres.
A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, Xinhua said earlier.
The epicentre was located in Maru township in Baqen county. Township deputy head Lhawang Dagpo said the quake was clearly felt at the township office, which sustained cracks in the walls, according to Xinhua.
Houses were reported collapsed in the area, the agency said. Power and telecoms services were disrupted in the county seat.
Workers have been sent to the area to coordinate the response, and local officials were carrying out checks of nearby villages, the report said.
Earthquakes in China are relatively common. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in an earthquake in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

Zuckerberg gets new Meta shares to stay in California amid billionaire tax vote
The move is aimed at avoiding tax impact on the CEO’s company voting power ahead of next month’s ballot
Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg will get a new chunk of shares in the company he founded, and in return, he has agreed to stay in California, where the company is headquartered, for at least eight more years.
It is partly a financial carrot intended to keep Zuckerberg in California, where voters in November will decide whether to approve a temporary tax on wealth held by billionaires who live in the state.
Meta announced the deal on Wednesday in a securities filing that coincided with its quarterly earnings report, where it said it would offer a new class of non-voting shares and give all existing shareholders a one-time bump for every share they own.
That includes Zuckerberg, who owned more than 342 million Meta shares at the end of 2025, most of which are considered super-voting shares, effectively giving him more than 60 per cent control over the company, according to a filing related to its annual report.

'We don't really want to cancel': Singaporeans weigh France travel plans amid violent protests
Singaporeans in Paris last weekend recounted scenes of damaged storefronts, tear gas and transport disruptions, even as daily life carried on largely as normal away from protest areas.
SINGAPORE: A long-awaited birthday trip to Paris with her mother is something Rachel, 29, is reluctant to give up, even as violent protests in France have left her worried about their safety.
The pair are due to travel from Oct 28 to Nov 4, just days after another round of demonstrations planned for the coming weekend.
"I'm trying to still be a bit positive about this because I planned this for so long. It's supposed to be a birthday trip with my mum, so I don't really want to cancel," said Rachel, who only wanted to be known by her first name.
Rachel is among Singaporean travellers weighing their plans amid unrest in France, where protests over the rising cost of living and declining public services descended into violence last weekend.
Travel agency Dynasty Travel said it has received requests to amend itineraries because of safety concerns, although there have been no outright cancellations so far.
Meanwhile, Singaporeans who were in Paris during the weekend unrest described witnessing looting, encountering tear gas and having their plans disrupted by public transport closures.
With further protests planned for Saturday (Oct 24), French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has called for a "massive" police presence, while targeted nighttime curfews may also be imposed.
TRAVELLERS KEEP PLANS BUT PREPARE FOR DISRUPTIONS
For Rachel, who declined to give her surname, cancelling the trip remains a last resort.
Asked whether she feared for her physical safety, she said that she felt wary of potentially encountering rioters.
"I'm quite concerned, but I'll just take precautions. That's all I can do, really."
With accommodation booked in central Paris, Rachel is particularly worried about public transport disruptions that could affect her itinerary.
Although the metro services she intends to use were not closed during last weekend's protests, she fears that further demonstrations could lead to closures.
She is prepared to take taxis instead if necessary. "We are willing to pay more if it ensures our safety," she said.
Responding to CNA's queries, Dynasty Travel said fewer than 10 trips to France had been amended because of concerns over the protests.
The agency said it had received "some requests for changes in itineraries, not outright cancellations".
Other customers have indicated that they may seek changes if the situation does not improve closer to their departure dates, it added.
Dynasty Travel said it was also prepared to reschedule evening activities, change transport arrangements or move travellers away from affected areas if curfews were imposed.
Chan Brothers Travel said it had not received any cancellations related to the recent protests, with its upcoming tour groups departing in November and December proceeding as planned.
The agency said it was closely monitoring developments and would make itinerary changes or alternative arrangements if conditions changed.
“Traveller safety remains our priority,” it said.
Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) advises travellers to avoid large crowds and demonstration areas in France.
"Public demonstrations and strikes for political, social, or economic reasons occur regularly in France," it said under its travel page for France.
"They may sometimes affect traffic and public transportation. Singaporeans are advised to avoid large crowds and demonstration areas."
CNA has asked MFA about the upcoming protests, whether any Singaporeans have sought help and what assistance is being provided.
MASKED MEN, SMASHED SHOPS AND TEAR GAS
The concerns come after mass demonstrations across France on Saturday spiralled into some of the country's worst unrest in years.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets to protest against declining public services and the rising cost of living.
While many demonstrations were peaceful, violent groups attacked public buildings, looted shops and supermarkets, and clashed with police.
For Singaporeans caught up in the unrest, the disruption was immediate.
Ms Julie Haw, 54, was in Paris for a food exhibition when she encountered groups of masked men while walking to dinner on Saturday night.
She recalled seeing three men striking a shop's shutters and smashing its glass before another six or seven men joined them from across the road.
“We could hear boom, boom, boom, and we saw crowds just bursting into a run,” she told CNA.
Another Singaporean, who was in Paris for work and declined to be named, described being caught in tear gas near Place de la Republique.
The 33-year-old was meeting up with a friend who lived near the protest areas.
At the square, she saw police barricades but said people were still allowed to enter and leave.
The atmosphere initially appeared peaceful.
That changed when she heard screams and saw people suddenly running towards her.
“The next thing I saw was the tear gas was thrown towards our direction … The tear gas, when I first smelled it, it was choking on the throat and on the chest, and then slowly it affects the eyes,” she told CNA.
She said she and her friend tried to escape but were pushed back by police and directed from one side of the square to another before eventually being allowed out.
During the ordeal, strangers offered them eye drops, she recalled.
Mr Edwin Ho, 40, who has lived in Paris for four years, said the latest unrest felt different from previous demonstrations he had witnessed.
“I do feel like this time was a little bit different … I think people were much more affected this time round than past protests that I’ve seen,” he said.
Although his neighbourhood was spared from the worst of the unrest, metro closures forced him to cancel plans and stay home over the weekend.
Mr Ho felt that the destruction and chaos had overshadowed the causes that peaceful protesters were fighting for. “It wasn't what people expected it to be,” he added.
DAILY LIFE CONTINUES AMID THE UNREST
Despite the chaotic scenes, Singaporeans in Paris also described a striking contrast between scenes of chaos and everyday life continuing nearby.
Ms Haw recalled seeing diners remain seated at outdoor cafes and bistros even as masked men moved through the streets.
"You know how the Parisian cafes and bistros have outdoor seating … the people didn't move at all," she said.
“And you have groups, pockets of these masked guys, but the patrons are just sitting there looking ... they just carry on with their dinner, completely undisturbed.”
The 33-year-old Singaporean who encountered tear gas near Place de la Republique described a similarly surreal scene after leaving the square.
She came across a cafe still operating along a row of damaged and looted shops.
“It’s quite surreal … People are just going about their day. There were people exercising, and then people were walking their dogs, and it’s like just another day,” she said.
She added that the damaged and looted shops she saw were concentrated around parts of the city centre where demonstrations had taken place.
By Sunday morning, streets she walked through had already been cleaned up.
Ms Haw also observed cleanup efforts near her hotel in the days following the unrest, with workers already replacing damaged windows.
Fresh demonstrations are planned for Saturday.
The French government has pledged a heavy police deployment, with the possibility of targeted nighttime curfews in several cities.
For travellers such as Rachel, the hope is that the situation will improve before their departure - and that a long-planned holiday can still go ahead.
“I’ll just play by ear at this point because everything is so unpredictable,” she added.

North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un's sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign as tensions rise after land mine blasts injured three South Korean front-line soldiers.
Kim Yo Jong, her brother's top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul, made the announcement Wednesday after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. She renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work.
In a follow-up statement Thursday, she said the North would place "new counter means" on alert along the border and have its loudspeakers on "standby" within days.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what's already one of the world's most heavily armed borders as Kim Jong Un pushes a hard line toward Seoul.
Touring the area with Marshal Pak Jong Chon, one of her brother's top military officials, Kim Yo Jong called the fortification work a "sacred and great undertaking" supporting the leader's policy of permanently severing ties with South Korea, which he has declared his most hostile adversary amid a broader diplomatic stalemate with Washington.
"Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," Kim Yo Jong said, using the initials of South Korea's formal name, the Republic of Korea.
She warned that if South Korean warning shots — which Seoul says are meant to force North Korean soldiers doing fortification work back across the border — cause "actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons' safety," North Korean border guards "will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason."
Asked about Kim Yo Jong's threat to resume the loudspeaker broadcasts, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said Thursday that Seoul would need to take "proportionate measures" in response to the North's moves along the border, but did not elaborate on what steps are being considered.
North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency first reported Kim's border visit as Tuesday, but Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday in a separate statement.
Following an inspection with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, Seoul formally blamed North Korean-planted mines for the Sept. 21 border blasts and urged the North to apologize and clear its remaining mines. North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked.
"Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions," Kim told soldiers during her visit Wednesday, reminding them of her brother's order to make the border with the "enemy ... eternally impregnable."
South Korea's military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border's military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts. Kim has said South Korean's claims of border crossings are a "false pretext," and that its provocations have increased "beyond the red line" since the mine blasts.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, Jin Yong-Sung, called Kim's threats "intolerable" and ordered the military to "sternly respond" to potential provocations by the North.
During Tuesday's border inspection, Pak accused the South of making "deliberate, premeditated and absurd" claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an "overwhelming response" to South Korean provocations. He also denied that the North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying "our army knows where our borderline is better than any others," KCNA said.
Loudspeaker broadcasts are among the Cold War-era psychological warfare tactics the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other during times of tensions.
South Korea's liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted its broadcasts after taking office last year to improve ties with the North, which later stopped its own.
Kim Jong Un in recent years has cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and declared it a permanent enemy as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on.

Expectations among women for Japan’s first female prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, have turned into disappointment over the past year, Shin Ki-young, a professor at the Institute for Gender Studies at Ochanomizu University in Tokyo, said in a recent interview.
“Women and younger voters who were not traditional supporters of the Liberal Democratic Party had high expectations for Takaichi because she was a woman and appeared to represent a change in the party’s image,” Shin said of the Japanese ruling party. “Those expectations may now have given way to disappointment.”
The approval rating for Takaichi’s Cabinet among women dropped to 42.9% from 65.9% when she took office a year ago, according to a Jiji Press opinion poll.

A rumor that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance once compared the United States economy to the RMS Titanic, a purportedly unsinkable ship that famously sank after hitting an iceberg in 1912, circulated in October.
Users on social media shared the following alleged quote from Vance: "You don't turn the Titanic around overnight. It takes time to fix what was broken."
Some posts included a screenshot of Vance speaking at a lectern, suggesting he made the comment during a public address.
The rumor circulated as the 2026 U.S. midterm elections approached, with the Trump administration offering differing takes on the state of the economy and polls showing Americans' faith in the economy is at its lowest in over a decade.
VD Vance asks a crowd of people for patience with the economy. "You cannot turn the Titanic around overnight" he said. Well, you Should Not Drive the Ship Straight for the Iceberg Either !!! Trump is full speed ahead & going straight into the iceberg. #VoteBlue
— M Robeson🇺🇸🇺🇸 (@brooksidemb) October 21, 2026
The statement was correctly attributed to Vance, though some posts presenting it as a recent comment were mistaken.
The vice president made the statement during a speech in Toledo, Ohio, on Jan. 22, 2026.
The White House posted about Vance's appearance on its official website and hosted a video of the speech on its official YouTube channel.
The "Titanic" line in question occurs near the 19:51 mark in the White House's recording of the speech. In context, Vance was talking about the recently inaugurated second Trump administration attempting to address economic issues it blamed on former President Joe Biden.
The full context of the statement was (emphasis ours):
The Democrats talk a lot about the affordability crisis in the United States of America. And yes, there is an affordability crisis. One created by Joe Biden's policies. You don't turn the Titanic around overnight. It takes time to fix what was broken.
Some commentators pointed out and criticised Vance's turn of phrase at the time.
For instance, podcast host Brian Tyler Cohen made a social media joke wondering if Vance knew what actually happened to the Titanic. Media outlet The Daily Beast published an article that collected a sampling of criticisms of the Titanic comment and added, "Vance also seems to have missed the climax of the 1997 hit film of the same name, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet."
We reached out to the office of the vice president for further comment on comparing the economy to the Titanic and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading on things Vance has allegedly said, Snopes previously investigated claims that the vice president once said people born to noncitizens should be deported as well as rumors that he encouraged supporters to "vote against the crazy leadership" in Washington, D.C.

A female elephant died of anthrax in Periyanaickenpalayam forest range of the Coimbatore Forest Division, forcing the Forest and the Animal Husbandry Departments to step up vigil against the disease.
Forest Department staff spotted the carcass during a routine patrol within the Gopanari reserve forest of the Periyanaickenpalayam range around 4 p.m. on October 13.
According to the department, the carcass appeared to be about a day old. After reviewing the photographs of the carcass, veterinarians raised suspicion of a possible anthrax infection.
Blood smear sample collected from the carcass was sent to the Animal Husbandry Department on Wednesday. The department examined the sample and confirmed the presence of Bacillus anthracis, the bacterium that causes anthrax.
A senior official from the Forest Department said that the carcass was burnt on Thursday, without opening it, as per the protocol based on instructions from the Animal Husbandry Department.
Persons who handled the carcass wore personal protective equipment while carrying out the task.
