San Francisco-based enterprise AI startup AuxoAI has raised $20.7 Mn (over ₹195 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by NTTVC, a Silicon Valley VC firm backed by Japanese telco NTT. Industry executives including Norwest Venture Partners’ George Still Jr, ServiceNow CPO and COO Amit Zavery, and Charlesbank Capital Partners’ MD Giacomo Santina also joined the startup’s cap table. AuxoAI plans to utilise the fresh capital to deepen ecosystem partnerships, expand its talent pool of forward deployed engineers (FDEs), and invest in its proprietary technology and AI-native delivery capabilities, including its Damia platform. “Our vision is to build a new kind of AI company – one that combines human expertise, enterprise context and engineering to stay with the problem from the first idea through measurable outcomes in production. This investment gives us the opportunity to scale that model globally,” cofounders Avaneesh Tripathi, Avinder Pal Singh, and Kabir Singh said in a joint statement. Founded in 2023, AuxoAI offers an enterprise AI platform that pairs its AI strategists and engineers with enterprise client teams to build custom AI workflows. It helps enterprises accelerate AI deployment with Damia, a platform it describes as an “AI workbench for enterprise delivery”. It combines a pre-built skill catalogue with tools that capture institutional knowledge to build a context layer. AuxoAI says that it is an AI-native Google Gemini Enterprise Transformation partner and an AWS advanced-tier partner. The San Francisco-based startup operates engineering and operational hubs in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Over the past three years, the startup claims that it has worked with over 40 clients across manufacturing, healthcare, consumer goods, and telecom sectors to turn AI into measurable business outcomes. Early adopters, such as marketing firm Athlonearth and restaurant group Fogo de Chao, have deployed AuxoAI’s infrastructure to automate manual tasks, make better informed decisions, and shorten strategy-to-launch timelines. As enterprises increasingly turn to AI adoption to boost productivity, FDEs are becoming increasingly critical for customising AI deployments to the company’s needs. According to staffing firm TeamLease Digital, demand for FDEs has jumped nearly 800% over the past year. Startups such as Bolna use FDEs to accelerate enterprise onboarding and shape product development. While better automation could eventually reduce deployment complexity, fragmented enterprise systems make FDEs increasingly important to AI adoption.

A Kochi-based student of architecture won the 28th Charles Correa Gold Medal in architecture in Mumbai on Thursday (October 22, 2026). His project, ‘Energy Commons: Reimagining energy infrastructure as a place for civic engagement,’ reimagined essential energy infrastructure as a civic resource, transforming a conventionally restricted space into a place of shared public life. Radhakrishnan M.S. is a student of Seed APJ Abdul School of Environmental Design in Kochi.
The Charles Correa Gold Medal, initiated in 1998, recognises outstanding undergraduate architectural thesis projects that engage meaningfully with the challenges of the built environment. The award ceremony was held at Tarq Gallery in Mumbai ON Thursday (October 22) evening.
“Through this year’s theme of ‘Equitability through Design’, young architects explored questions of access to space, shelter, infrastructure, and the commons. We hope that this theme becomes a touchstone for the students to return to throughout their career and professional lives,” Nandita Correa Mehrotra, Director of the Charles Correa Foundation, said.
Book release
‘The State of Architecture — Practices and Processes in India, A Research Framework’, a book on inquiry into the practice of architecture in the Indian subcontinent, was also released at the event. It led to conversations around architectural pedagogy, public engagement, and complex issues affecting architecture. The book also looks into how large-scale economic, social, cultural, political and ecological changes impact architecture. It has been published by Architecture Foundation India.
Speaking about the theme of the book, co-author Ranjit Hoskote said that for architecture to be relevant, it has to correspond to the greatest good of the greatest number. “Equity and solidarity have been key themes for us in the book. There is no way to think about architecture without foregrounding these key questions of power, participation and possibility,” he said.
The State of Architecture process has looked into the issues of caste, gender, environment, and equity. It also looks at how architecture meets the urgencies of the changing times, changing the ground rules. Speaking about the changing nature of architecture, co-author Rahul Mehrotra said that liberalisation was a clear marker for architecture in India. He gave insights into how coalition politics and the strengthening of regional parties led to greater pluralism and diversity in architecture.
The event began with a panel discussion on the book, the thought process behind it, and its impact. It was moderated by cultural theorist Nancy Adajania. Rahul Mehrotra, Ranjit Hoskote, and Kaiwan Mehta provided a historical perspective on architecture, discussing the impact of architectural exhibitions on public engagement. This was followed by the Charles Correa Gold Medal award ceremony, where the winners presented their theses. Manu Viswam E from Trivandrum’s College of Architecture received an honourable mention for his project “Urban Scar to Social Commons.” It explored how urban fabric can be stitched together to create a more inclusive city. It grounded equality in the reclamation of a disused industrial landscape as shared civic ground.

Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low.
PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
Counterpoint Research says higher prices are tanking demand for new PCs.
Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes.
Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”

People with longCOVID, where symptoms persist after recovery from an acute Covid-19 infection, may have distinct differences in the mix of bacteria living in their mouths and lungs, research has shown.
The differences in the lung microbiome are linked to respiratory symptoms, as well as the cognitive and digestive problems known to occur in longCOVID, researchers said.
The findings, published in the European Respiratory Journal, may contribute towards understanding why some people develop long COVID and point to new ways to treat the condition, they said.
"Prior studies have shown some changes in the gut microbiome with long COVID, but Covid is a lung disease and so it makes sense to look to see if the lung microbiome is changed in long COVID," lead author Daniela Alferes de Lima Headley from the University of Dundee, UK, said.
"We know that millions of people worldwide are still affected by long COVID and its cause is still unknown. Long Covid affects multiple organs. The microbiome is important to maintain health throughout the body, so it is a strong candidate for something that may contribute to long COVID," she said.
The study examined 771 people treated for Covid-19 at one of 38 UK hospitals between February 2020 and March 2021.
The participants were divided into four groups based on how bad their symptoms were five months after being discharged from hospital, ranging from 'very severe' with serious physical, mental, and cognitive impairments to 'mild', with few symptoms and good recovery.
Six months after hospital discharge, samples were collected from patients' mouths through saliva and from their lungs through sputum. DNA sequencing was used to identify the microbes present.
By analysing the variety and quantities of microbes and comparing them with patients' symptoms, researchers found that people with very severe long COVID had marked differences in their oral and lung microbiomes compared with those who did not have severe long COVID.
The results also revealed differences linked to specific symptoms, including reduced lung function, in which the lungs cannot hold as much air as normal or air cannot flow in and out as easily.
The researchers also found differences in the mouth and lungs microbiome between people with varying neurocognitive symptoms -- including 'brain fog', difficulties with memory, attention and concentration -- and gut symptoms, including pain, nausea, diarrhoea and loss of appetite.
Among the changes associated with long-COVID symptoms, was an over-abundance of bacteria that produce lactic acid, which was also linked to signs of inflammation found in samples of patients' blood.
Lead researcher James Chalmers, chair of respiratory research at the University of Dundee, UK, said, "People who had the worst symptoms five to six months after COVID infection had big changes in the microbiome in their mouth and lungs."
"We also found that changes in the airway microbiome were linked not just to lung problems, but also to symptoms like brain fog and gut symptoms, suggesting the lung microbiome could have effects on health more broadly," he said.

Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.
Yemeni Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.
Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.
The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.
Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.
Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf.
However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.

Having a job doesn't always mean you have enough to cover daily living or savings goals.
A July survey of Americans by Goldman Sachs Asset Management and the behavioral economics firm Escalent found over 60% of respondents have worked outside their primary roles, largely because they needed to. Twenty-seven percent of respondents said work covers their expenses, but it's tough to get ahead.
"Employment remains essential for retirement security, but for many Americans, it is no longer sufficient," a Goldman Sachs Asset Management retirement report said.
Gen Zers were most likely to say they earn or have earned money outside their primary job; millennials followed closely behind. The report said that's despite most Gen Z and millennial workers reporting their jobs provide financial stability.
"Younger workers may feel stable in their main jobs while still seeing extra work as necessary," the report said.
Throughout the generations, a majority said they're doing gig or side work out of necessity or for financial security.
"The traditional full-time job may no longer be carrying the full weight of financial security," the report said. "For many, supplementing income appears to have become part of the baseline."
Some Americans are living paycheck to paycheck or adjusting their budgets to cope with rising gas prices and other everyday expenses. It can be hard to get ahead when wage growth has been consistently falling short of inflation, and it's tough to find a new job to try to earn more money.
Not feeling financially secure can lead to putting off savings goals. Eighty-three percent of Gen Z and 78% of millennials said they put major financial goals on hold. Forty-one percent of millennials have delayed emergency savings despite being employed, and 30% said they delayed housing or homebuying goals. For Gen Zers, the shares were 35% and 34%, respectively.
While some people may be working a part-time side job, others are "overemployed" and working multiple full-time jobs. One millennial has worked five full-time remote IT jobs, earning over $700,000 annually. As Business Insider's Jacob Zinkula reported, overemployed people use their extra earnings for different reasons, such as retiring early or paying down debt.
Having multiple income streams can also be considered a "portfolio career," where people piece together different kinds of work, such as writing a newsletter, doing a side gig, and holding an office job. It can be one way to try "stability stacking" to feel more secure about your career if, for example, you were laid off and lost an income stream.
"When you decentralize everything from one 9-to-5 and build a portfolio career, you protect yourself from the emotional and financial shock if and when business needs change at your 9-to-5," said career coach Janel Abrahami in a TikTok video.
And sometimes, working a side gig can become a complete career pivot. Harlan Rappaport, in his 20s, turned his email marketing side hustle into a full-time career after working as an investment analyst at a financial institution.
"I used to get really excited about the numbers, but over the last couple of years, I realized it's more about the freedom I've had in my life over the last couple of years as a freelancer," Rappaport said in an as-told-to essay. "I don't miss family events, can travel when I want, and can work from anywhere in the world."

A Chinese dissident falsely claims Kim Jong Un is dead - why is this rumour back?
- Published
Kim Jong Un has appeared in North Korean state media looking remarkably healthy for a man rumoured to have died from a brain haemorrhage.
Photographs published by state newspaper Rodong Sinmun show the 42-year-old dictator touring what the paper said was a clothing and footwear exhibition with his daughter.
The images emerged hours after a Chinese dissident who lives in the US claimed, without evidence, that Kim had been taken to a hospital in Beijing in a coma and had died.
For those who watch North Korea closely, this kind of rumour has become almost routine.
In one of the world's most secretive states, facts are often difficult to verify, creating fertile ground for speculation.
This latest claim originated with Wanjun Xie, who identifies himself as chairman of the Chinese Democratic Party, a group banned by Chinese authorities. He has previously circulated unverified claims, including speculation about the death of Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Xie alleged that Kim suffered a severe brain haemorrhage and was transferred to Beijing because North Korea lacked the medical facilities to treat him.
He claimed Kim later died and that his body had been secretly returned to North Korea, with the regime concealing his death.
Yet the photographs tell a different story.
Kim is seen examining displays, accompanied by Kim Ju Ae and his usual entourage of officials.
While there is no way to know exactly when the images were taken, there are other reasons to doubt the claim.
There would probably be signs beyond North Korea's borders if there were a sudden collapse in Kim's health.
China could tighten security along its frontier to prepare for potential instability or refugee flows. Activity around North Korean diplomatic missions might also increase. Defectors in South Korea often receive information through informal networks along the Chinese border. None of this has happened.
South Korean intelligence officials, meanwhile, told Yonhap they had heard nothing to support the reports.
The rumour also echoes previous false alarms.
In 2020, a high-profile North Korean defector claimed he was "99% certain" Kim had died following cardiovascular surgery. Not long afterwards, Kim appeared in public and the claim unravelled.
So why do these rumours keep resurfacing? The first reason is succession.
North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family for three generations, but what happens after Kim Jong Un remains less certain than it was for his predecessors.
Kim Il Sung spent decades preparing his son, Kim Jong Il, for power. By the time Kim Il Sung died in 1994, the succession plan was firmly established. Kim Jong Il's transition was relatively smooth.
Kim Jong Un's rise was faster and more precarious. After Kim Jong Il suffered a stroke in 2008, his youngest son was rapidly promoted through the ranks. By the time his father died in 2011, he had been publicly identified as the future leader.
Even so, Kim Jong Un spent years consolidating power, purging rivals and eliminating perceived threats.
Today, South Korea's intelligence agency believes he may be preparing his daughter as a successor. She has increasingly appeared at high-profile events and military displays.
But she is thought to be only 13 years old. North Korea has never been led by a woman, and she has not been formally designated as heir. Her youth would also leave her vulnerable in any power struggle.
All of this uncertainty helps explain why rumours about Kim's health attract so much attention.
The second reason is that the rumours are not entirely implausible.
Kim is overweight and a heavy smoker. South Korea's National Intelligence Service has repeatedly warned that his lifestyle puts him at higher risk of cardiovascular disease. Heart problems and strokes also run in the Kim family.
If anything were to happen to Kim, the stakes are high for neighbouring countries and the wider international community. Any sudden leadership crisis raises difficult questions about control of North Korea's nuclear weapons and the prospect of political instability.
Would a power struggle tempt hardliners to act aggressively? Could unrest trigger a refugee crisis along the Chinese border? These are questions that concern not only Beijing and Seoul but also Washington, which maintains around 28,000 troops in South Korea.
Intelligence agencies watch Kim Jong Un closely so they are prepared for any news.
Because North Korea remains an information black hole, it is also an easy target for false reports. Only a tiny circle has regular access to its leader. Even intelligence agencies struggle to obtain reliable information, and much of what emerges is heavily caveated as unverified or highly likely rather than confirmed fact.
The regime itself is also suspected of deliberately encouraging confusion, leaking misleading information to obscure what is really happening inside the country.
So it is hard to believe that Wanjun Xie had somehow stumbled across such significant news, when it had eluded those whose job it is to stay across it.
He may simply have been seeking attention. Or he may have wanted to embarrass Beijing by highlighting its ties to Pyongyang, although those are well-established for the world to see.
Whatever his motive, Xie is far from the first person to exploit the uncertainty surrounding North Korea's leadership.

There was a time when a patient simply asked, “Doctor, what should I do?” Consultations today, however, , sound remarkably different. Patients enquire if they should get surgery or take medication? Would a second opinion be recommended? What about side effects?
Modern medicine has handed us something extraordinary: choice. But it comes with a psychological paradox. Choosing an option becomes harder when there are more options. This heavy burden of choice now sits on both sides of the desk.
The patient’s dilemma
Illness already brings fear, anxiety, and uncertainty. Stack endless choices on top of that: which specialist, which test, which path, and decision fatigue sets in. It isn’t helpless collapse when an overwhelmed patient finally says, “Just tell me what to do.” It is pure emotional exhaustion.
Many people endlessly search for the ‘perfect’ choice, hoping to eliminate risk entirely. When there is a difficult outcome regardless, counterfactual thinking takes over: Did I choose wrong? But a crucial truth gets lost here: a good decision can still have a bad outcome. Choices should be judged by the information available at the time, not by what happens down the road.
The Doctor’s Burden
It is also important to consider what happens across the table. Modern healthcare asks doctors to be clinicians, risk managers, educators, and empathetic partners, often within a single 20-minute slot.
Doctors must navigate a delicate tightrope. Be too directive, and you strip the patient of autonomy. Offer every conceivable option without guidance, and you leave them abandoned in a maze. Add in the ‘second-opinion paradox’, where different clinicians legitimately weigh probabilities differently and doctors must explain not just the disease, but why medicine isn’t simple arithmetic.
Patients understandably crave certainty, but ethically, a doctor cannot promise it. Trust isn’t believing a physician knows the future; it’s knowing they will be honest about what is known, what is uncertain, and how to adapt if things change.
Carrying the weight together
More information doesn’t automatically empower. Raw data without interpretation only breeds distress. True empowerment happens through shared decision-making, a genuine psychological partnership where clinical evidence meets a patient’s personal values and priorities.
Sometimes, the most relieving words a doctor can say are: “Let us go through this together.”
To build a better healthcare system, we must support patients, but also support the doctors. The emotional labour of medicine is invisible on a prescription, yet physicians regularly carry one patient’s fear straight into the next room while remaining clinically precise.
Empowerment doesn’t mean offering the maximum number of choices; it means offering the right options, clearly explained, with enough support to make uncertainty bearable. The best healthcare never asks one person to carry the weight alone—it builds a partnership strong enough to carry it together.
(Dr. Sushma Gopalan is lead consultant – child life services (psychology), Manipal Hospital Yelahanka, sushma.gopalan@manipalhospitals.com)

The Delhi High Court has ruled that prospective adoptive parents with two or more children cannot be considered for adopting a child classified as “normal” under the Adoption Regulations, 2022. The ruling, delivered by Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma, clarifies the eligibility restrictions applicable to such couples and the circumstances in which they may be considered for adopting children with special needs or those classified as hard to place, Verdictum reported. The judgment came in a petition filed by an Indian-origin couple residing in Singapore, who challenged the withdrawal of an adoption referral for an infant girl identified as “Baby K”. The couple already had two biological sons when the referral was made. Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma, sitting as a single judge, held that the referral issued by the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), although accepted by the prospective adoptive parent, was contrary to Regulation 5(7) of the 2022 regulations. It therefore did not confer a vested right or legitimate expectation to adopt the child. The Court also held that a delay in issuing a No Objection Certificate (NOC) could not be treated as a deemed approval. It directed CARA to strengthen eligibility checks, audit profiles affected by a portal migration, process NOCs within prescribed timelines and ensure accurate application statuses and grievance responses. Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma is a judge of the Delhi High Court. In this case, she presided over a single-judge Bench that examined whether a couple with two biological children could challenge the withdrawal of an adoption referral under the Adoption Regulations, 2022. Her ruling addressed the application of Regulation 5(7), which restricts the eligibility of prospective adoptive parents with two or more children for adopting a child in the normal category, subject to specified exceptions. The judgment also examined whether an adoption referral that had already been issued and accepted could create an enforceable expectation of adoption when the prospective parents did not meet the applicable eligibility criteria. The Court held that the petitioner, who already had two biological children, was not eligible to be considered for adopting a child in the normal category under the 2022 regulations. Such prospective parents may be considered for children with special needs or those classified as hard to place, unless the adoption falls within the specified exceptions for relatives or step-children. The petitioner had argued that Baby K was not a normal child, or that her status had not been conclusively established, and that she could potentially fall within the hard-to-place category. “...it is clear that in view of Regulation 5(7) of the 2022 Regulations, the petitioner could have been considered only for adoption of a special needs child or a hard to place child. The petitioner, however, has also raised a contention that Baby K was, in fact, not a normal child, or at least that her status was not fixed, and that she could also fall within the category of hard to place children...this Court is of the considered opinion that the petitioner, having two biological children, was not eligible to be considered for adoption of a child of the normal category under the 2022 Regulations, and that Baby K, on the material placed on record, can neither be treated as a special needs child, nor as a hard to place child. The referral of Baby K to the petitioner was, therefore, contrary to Regulation 5(7) of the 2022 Regulations”. The Court held that a referral made contrary to the regulations could not override the statutory eligibility requirements. It also relied on Debarati Nandee v. Union of India, 2024 SCC OnLine Del 1075, and Union of India v. Ankur Gupta, (2019) 18 SCC 276. The couple registered for inter-country adoption in December 2020, when they had one biological child. Their second child was born in March 2022. Their Home Study Report expired in December 2023 and was revalidated only in 2025. In January 2026, CARA referred an infant girl, Baby K, to the petitioner, who accepted the referral within hours. CARA withdrew the referral on March 30, 2026, after the application status was reflected as “Application Rejected – Withdrawn”. The authority cited Regulation 5(7), under which couples with two or more children may be considered only for special-needs or hard-to-place children. The petitioner approached the Delhi High Court on April 12, 2026. On April 13, 2026, the Court granted a status quo order and directed a fresh medical examination of the child. The Court subsequently found that Baby K could not be classified as either a special-needs child or a hard-to-place child on the material presented before it. The latter category covers children for whom no eligible family comes forward after referral. The Bench also held that an NOC was not merely a procedural formality and that a court could not direct an authority to act contrary to the governing regulations. It further ruled that the principle of estoppel could not operate against a statute. The Court said that the principle of a child’s best interests could not be invoked to bypass the legal safeguards governing adoption and the placement of children with prospective families. “...the principle of the child‘s best interests cannot be invoked to circumvent the very safeguards designed to secure suitable and lawful adoptive placements. Accordingly, this Court is of the opinion that, notwithstanding the circumstances in which the referral was withdrawn by CARA and the emotions of the petitioner and his family, the best interests of Baby K do not call for grant of the reliefs sought in the present petition, as one of the paramount considerations remains the child‘s placement in a suitable family – through a process that conforms to the governing statutory framework, i.e. as per the 2022 Regulations”. The Court dismissed the petition and allowed the interim order to lapse. Alongside its ruling on adoption eligibility, the Court directed CARA to address administrative issues in the adoption process. Verify the eligibility of prospective adoptive parents before generating an adoption referral. The judgment clarifies that an adoption referral does not create an automatic right to adopt a child if the prospective parents do not meet the eligibility criteria under the governing regulations. For couples who already have two or more children, Regulation 5(7) limits consideration for adopting a child in the normal category, while providing for consideration of special-needs and hard-to-place children and specified exceptions. The ruling also underscores the importance of eligibility verification before referrals are issued and the need for adoption authorities to process applications and NOCs within prescribed timelines. The judgment does not impose a blanket ban on all further adoptions by parents with two or more children. Rather, it explains how the applicable eligibility restrictions operate and why the child’s best interests must be considered within the governing legal framework. When a schoolteacher in eastern Congo learned that five of her family members had been diagnosed with Ebola, she was “deeply shaken,” fearing the worst from a disease that carries stigma and is seen by some in her community as evil.
Two of her relatives — her brother and his wife — died of Ebola in July at a treatment center in Ituri province, the epicenter of the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history.
The 34-year-old teacher, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity for fear of being stigmatized, said grief and stress over the loss of her relatives led her to seek treatment at a mental health clinic.
After two months at the clinic, the teacher said she was feeling better but worried about her future. “Will these people still be there for me?” she said of her relatives in Bunia, capital of Ituri.
Her experience highlights a burden rarely talked about in the fast-moving Ebola outbreak: the psychological toll on relatives coping with loss, fear and rejection in communities already scarred by years of rebel violence.
The outbreak is spreading at an unprecedented rate under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, fueled by mass population movements, violence, mistrust and poor working conditions for frontline health workers. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there's no approved vaccine or drug, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people infected. The World Health Organization has said that it continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it.
Losing relatives to disease outbreaks is always difficult, but responders say grief can be especially severe with Ebola in a country where the disease is viewed by many as evil due to rumors and misconceptions. The risk of transmission also limits contact with the patients even after death, depriving families of closure and the opportunity to observe their preferred burial rites.
The psychological effects of past Ebola outbreaks can persist long after the immediate crisis, according to WHO, often taking the form of anxiety and mood disorders, exacerbated by prolonged grief and discrimination.
This is Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak and has spread to eight provinces, coinciding with an escalation of decades-long conflict in the east between government forces and rebels.
Experts say the outbreak has compounded the trauma for many across the region. The medical response has focused largely on treating and containing the disease, with little to no attention to the mental health of those affected.
“There are so many areas (in eastern Congo) already devastated by war, crisis and severe malnutrition" and Ebola has worsened the condition of vulnerable populations and their mental health conditions, said Mirella Riccardi, a mental health specialist with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French name Médecins Sans Frontières.
The Congolese teacher recalled that her family felt abandoned by neighbors when her relatives began showing symptoms consistent with Ebola, including fever, vomiting, diarrhea and muscle pain.
Neighbors stayed away until Ebola responders came to take the sick to a clinic and disinfect their house afterward.
“It felt as though we were living all alone because of the illness,” said the teacher, who did not contract the disease. “It has caused severe trauma within our family.”
She also lost someone she had regarded as a father and said many others in their Bunia neighborhood have also died.
“Many people initially assumed that their symptoms were due to poisoning or malaria. Only later did they realize that they could be Ebola,” she said.
The Samelo mental health facility in Bunia, where she was admitted, said it had received up to 350 patients, a surge it attributed to the Ebola outbreak.
“Grief, fear of infection, social isolation and a succession of deaths can leave families and communities lastingly vulnerable,” said Katembo Vyaluva Anicet, the head nurse at the facility.
Five months into the outbreak, health authorities remain alarmed. More than 70% of new cases involved people who were not among known contacts, while at least 60% of deaths occurred outside treatment centers as of early October, government data showed.
The teacher has been discharged from the mental health facility but returns often for follow-up checks. Her three other infected relatives survived, and her husband said she feels much better.
But fear of Ebola persists within her family and among her neighbors.
“This has reignited fear and tension within the community,” she said. “Now, everyone is wondering how this disease will end.”

In this debate, foreign policy and geopolitical analyst Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, Head of India Practice at Eurasia Group, joins Michael Kugelman, Senior Fellow at the Atlantic Council, to examine the strategic implications of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Reliance's Jamnagar refinery facility. The discussion outlines how India's surplus refining capacity and vast domestic consumption provide significant leverage in global hydrocarbon markets, prompting Washington to treat India as a crucial energy partner. Chaudhuri also addresses trade friction, potential punitive tariffs over Russian oil purchases, and the broader strategic and security considerations influencing foreign corporate players like Elon Musk in key domestic technology sectors including satellite communications and defense infrastructure.

The discussion also reviews global peace initiatives, including diplomatic efforts by India, proposals involving Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and an Egyptian plan. Foreign citizen killed during march in South Africa as anti-immigrant tensions flare
Police say a foreign citizen has been beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South Africa
CAPE TOWN, South Africa -- A foreign citizen was beaten to death by a group of around 50 people during a protest march in South Africa's east coast city of Durban, police said Thursday, as anti-immigrant tensions continue to flare in Africa's most advanced economy.
Police said the group approached the man, who was standing at the side of a road during a march through the streets of Durban's city center, and assaulted him.
Police did not immediately give the man's nationality or details on what the march was related to. They said the victim was in his 30s or early 40s, and they were still trying to identify suspects in the attack.
South Africa has struggled with months of anti-immigration tensions. Marches calling for government action against migrants in the country illegally have sometimes spilled over into violence.
Nigeria, Mozambique, Malawi and other countries have said some of their citizens have been killed in xenophobic attacks linked to the anti-immigration protests. South African authorities have disputed some of those claims and said some deaths were related to criminal activity and not the protests.
Tens of thousands of migrants have left South Africa in recent months in one of the biggest mass exoduses in years. Many cite the threat of violence from angry locals, though the government also said that many were deported for not having the proper documents to be in South Africa.
As Africa's biggest economy, South Africa attracts migrants from many nations on the continent, but that has sometimes brought tensions within communities because of the country's extremely high unemployment rate and overburdened public services.
Durban, South Africa's third biggest city of nearly four million people, has become a hotspot for the anti-immigrant tensions that have surged this year.
In June, thousands of migrants mainly from Malawi gathered at a park in the city seeking to be repatriated to their home country. They claimed they were fleeing threats of violence after a protest group demanded undocumented migrants leave South Africa by June 30.
The camp of migrants seeking to leave grew so quickly that authorities had to build more temporary accommodation centers to handle the numbers.

A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1?
- Published
Formula 1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the new deal to take the sport back to Africa - ending an absence of nearly 40 years - as a "landmark" achievement.
Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time.
But the sport's bosses already recognised the importance of the project. And this deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since it bought the sport at the start of 2017.
Rwanda, which has signed a 10-year deal to host an African Grand Prix from the "early 2030s", has succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, have failed.
That's because the east-central African country has managed to put together a single plan with the requisite financial backing and ambition to make the project work.
Morocco never found the requisite finances and South Africa has up to four separate projects ongoing with different promoters in three different locations, two in Cape Town.
For F1, with other countries also interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with.
The new Rwandan circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, is part of a wider development near a new international airport, currently under construction, that also includes facilities in sectors such as entertainment, residential, hotels, spas and sports science, as well as an innovation hub.
At the moment it is a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.
The race is likely to be controversial as Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing.
But for Domenicali the deal marks a key moment in the sport's development under his leadership.
"It is the legacy of all of us to be in this very special moment," he said as he took the stage at the announcement in Kigali with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.
He added that he was "very proud", and that F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision".
"Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories," he said. "A nation of extraordinary natural beauty and stunning landscapes, combined with resilience and courage to overcome and be reborn from challenges of its past.
"It is a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination. A nation that has become a destination for international investment, innovation and opportunity."
- Does Norris-Piastri crash show 'papaya rules' failing? - F1 Q&A 
  - Published8 hours ago
From a purely sporting point of view, it's easy to see why Domenicali is so chuffed.
He has brought F1 back to Africa, where the last grand prix was held in 1993 in South Africa, and opened up a potential market of 100 million people that is largely untapped.
And the track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, promises a great deal.
Wurz is passionate about creating circuits with natural flow that challenge drivers, and he has envisaged this one in the style of the classic Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello tracks, with its own unique character - and the renders released do bear some obvious similarities to the first part of Suzuka.
The track is not completely finalised - there will be further consultation with teams and drivers - but is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long, with 17 corners, and will use the undulating Rwandan landscape to help create a dramatic layout. It has nearly 200m of elevation change.
President Kagame has backed this project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa.
Kagame said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent", and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return.
"We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate. We have had many other big events."
Why is Rwanda a controversial choice?
Rwanda is fighting off any allegations that money that would be better directed elsewhere, in a country that receives international aid, by emphasising that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.
Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment to accelerate Rwanda's economic transformation and expansion.
The grand prix is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment, bringing more prospects to the country and further growing the overall GDP of the nation.
But Rwanda is not the first country to want to use F1 in this way. And the use of sport to build a country's image can, depending on context, be viewed in a less positive light, as sportswashing - the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.
The F1 calendar already contains a number of countries that fall into this category, not least Saudi Arabia.
Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
F1 is far from the only sport to face such accusations. They have been levelled at Premier League football clubs Arsenal and Aston Villa as a consequence of sponsorship deals with Rwanda.
Saudi Arabia will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034. Boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi Arabian finance. Golf came close to being torn apart by Saudi money and the establishment of the rival LIV tour.
F1 is not blind to such issues. Its own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders to address any issues that arise.
It also says it focuses its efforts "in relation to those areas which are within our own direct influence".
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
But Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, said: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.
"Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with.
"Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise."

Bolt comparisons a 'privilege' - Dambile
- Published
Commonwealth 200m champion Sinesipho Dambile says it is a "privilege" to be compared with Jamaican great Usain Bolt as he looks to establish himself among the world's leading sprinters.
The South African has enjoyed a breakthrough season, producing a string of impressive performances and underlining his credentials as one of Africa's emerging track stars.
Speaking to the Warm Up Track podcast, the 24-year-old revealed that he "enjoys the pressure" that comes with being mentioned alongside the fastest man in history.
"Pressure is a privilege," he said. "I love it because that's where I excel."
Dambile recalls meeting the eight-time Olympic champion at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, where the Jamaican offered him some advice.
"For Bolt, charisma naturally goes to him. Being able to meet him in person last year in Tokyo, he said: 'Please make sure you enjoy this thing'.
"That, until this day, still stuck with me."
Victory at last year's South African national championships secured Dambile's place in Tokyo, where he finished eighth in the 200m final, having set a new personal best of 19.97 seconds in the semi-finals.
That time was broken this season as Dambile accelerated his development.
June's Diamond League meeting in Doha saw him clock 19.74 seconds - the fourth-fastest time recorded by any athlete in 2026.
He went on to finish second behind the USA's Kenny Bednarek, but ahead of Botswana's 2024 Olympic champion Letsile Tebogo, in last month's Diamond League final in Brussels, while he was fourth in the inaugural Ultimate Championships.
However, the year's high point was undoubtedly the Commonwealth gold medal won in Birmingham in July, a result which made him the first South African to win the event.
While it is clear the 200m remains Dambile's principal event, he is "mentally willing to put in the work" to mimic Bolt, who likewise began his career specialising in the longer distance before going on to also dominate the 100m.
"He (Bolt) paved the way," Dambile said.
"I spoke to my team a couple of times and I was like, 'I want you guys to count me in on the 100m'.
"I want to do both. I know I'm going to be successful."
Akani Simbine's mentor role
A relaxed character, Dambile insists he will follow Bolt's advice to enjoy his time on the track, promising that fans will "get more of my personality" in future.
"I've never been a loud person, trying to bring attention to me," he said, contrasting his approach to the brash showmanship of Olympic 100m champion Noah Lyles.
"I'm always smiling out there, I'm always looking at the crowd, looking at the kids, and that's just me.
"I just want to go out there and do my thing, to make sure that everybody enjoys the show."
Dambile's success has coincided with a growing sense of belief within South African sprinting.
He was part of the quartet that won 4x100m gold at the World Relays in Guangzhou last year, running alongside team-mates Bayanda Walaza, Bradley Nkoana and Akani Simbine.
"We go as a squad, so we have that little bit of energy," Dambile said when explaining how the group's camaraderie has played an important role in their success.
"We pump each other up because we're going for the one thing - doing it for our country.
"The biggest sport in our country is rugby, so you get the Springboks going there winning the World Cup and we wanted to have the same feeling."
The influence of the experienced Simbine has been crucial.
The 2018 Commonwealth 100m champion finally landed an Olympic medal at Paris 2024, picking up silver in the 4x100m relay, having agonisingly finished fourth in the individual 100m finals in both the French capital and at the 2020 Games in Tokyo.
"He's made all the finals. He's been there. He's been the guy. He's been one of the best sprinters in the world," said Dambile.
"So when someone like that from home can do it, we also start to believe that it's actually possible to do it."
- How 'sub-10 king' Simbine shed his nearly man tag

- Luxolo Adams talks mental fitness and 'arrogant faces' 
  - Published5 July 2023
'I want to be the best'
Just like Simbine, Dambile is a product of the TuksSport team at the University of Pretoria, a breeding ground for South Africa's top talent, including fellow sprinter Gift Leotlela, who finished fourth in the 100m final at this year's Commonwealth Games, and 2025 world indoor 800m champion Prudence Sekgodiso.
"We all were scouted through different processes and we all ended up at the same school," said Dambile.
"Best place to train in as a sprinter."
All four Pretoria alumni competed in Birmingham this year, but only Dambile came away with a Commonwealth medal.
"It was so much relief because what I did was not just a small thing," he explained.
"It was huge, especially for myself [and] the country of South Africa. My emotions were all over the place.
"I just pushed through everything and when I was in that moment, I knew I deserved it because of the amount of work I've put in."
A double medallist at the 2021 Under-20 World Championships in Nairobi, Dambile's progression from promising junior to established senior athlete has not, however, been straightforward, with injury curtailing much of his 2024 season.
This year's success has changed things.
"It's easier to recognise me in the country now with me winning the Commonwealth," he explained.
"A bit of fame now - you can see people when they talk about you. It's like I've been experiencing beautiful things happening."
Things could get even better with plans already being made for next year's World Championships in Beijing and the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
"We've already set up a map towards that," he said.
"We definitely know how important it's going to be over the next two years.
"I want to be the best 200m athlete the sport has ever seen.
"I need to make sure that I have the World Championship [and] Olympic title. I want to do things that have never been done in my country."

As anti-government demonstrations spread across France in October, cities like Paris experienced riots and looting. Recent protests focused on rising costs of living and fuel after weeks of student demonstrations against poor school conditions. A purported aerial photograph claimed to show fires across Paris and around the Eiffel Tower.
The imagespread on X and Instagram and showed a red sky in the background, with numerous fires and plumes of smoke rising around the Eiffel Tower.
(Threads user @lionel_saal_)
The image is fake and has signs of being generated by artificial intelligence.
A reverse-image search directed us to Instagram accounts that credited the original poster as a pilot named Lionel Saal on Instagram. He posted the image on Instagram and his Threads account on Oct. 18, but claimed that it had been taken on Oct. 17. We have reached out to Lionel Saal on Instagram to learn more.
We ran the image through OpenAI's verification tool, which detected a SynthID, an invisible watermark that AI tools like ChatGPT embed in images they generate. The tool noted, "We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI." (We should note that OpenAI's service can only detect images generated with OpenAI's software and does not detect AI generation via other large-language models, such as Google's Gemini, which has its own SynthID detector.)
There are several other signs that the image is AI-generated. The cloud line appears unnaturally straight. The smoke from the fires is all moving in the exact same direction in an unnatural manner. In many aerial nightphotographs of Paris, the streets are visible because of streetlights and traffic, even in foggy weather. This image, however, has no discernible streets or roads.
Reputable photojournalism bank Getty Images has numerous authentic photographs from news outlets showing fires on the streets of Paris. Some of these fires occurred near the Eiffel Tower. Police fired tear gas at protesters around the Eiffel Tower as well.
For further reading, Snopes has been covering misinformation surrounding the protests in France.

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.
But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.
This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.
“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”
The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.
The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.
The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.
Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”
Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.
Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.
“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”
For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.
Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”
The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.
Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.
“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.
“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”
Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.
“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”
During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.
For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.
“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
Ugandan health officials say the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.
Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents’ attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying, his photography and videography brand.
It was Bielfeldt’s curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera’s shutter speed. Bielfeldt’s solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.

The Highways Department has called for consultants for preparing a detailed project report for the construction of a four-km elevated corridor from Lighthouse to Thiru. Vi. Ka. Bridge. This was one of the proposals announced in the Assembly Session to decongest city roads.
The Construction and Maintenance Wing has floated tenders for the corridor that is to run via Santhome High Road, Greenways Road, and Durgabai Deshmukh Road.
“Santhome High Road faces severe traffic congestion every day during rush hour as a number of VIP vehicles take it. The Marina Loop Road becomes a fresh fish market from 3 p.m. onwards daily. Though we need relief only till the the Thiru. Vi. Ka. Bridge is completed, one proposal is to extend the corridor across the river and connect it to the Adyar flyover, so that vehicles can remain elevated for another 700 m,” a source said.

The Santhome High Road, which has eight schools, Santhome Cathedral, various associations, and independent bungalows, apartment complexes, and commercial buildings, has not been touched by any widening project so far, the engineer added.
Circular corridor
A town planner suggested reviving an old proposal for an elevated circular corridor along the Adyar bund.
“It was proposed some 20 years ago. The corridor would help decongest city roads. It could run up to the airport and also connect the Outer Ring Road,” he added.

‘Flesh-eating’ screwworm confirmed in US wildlife as officials scramble to contain spread
The metallic, orange-eyed parasite uses mouth hooks to burrow into the flesh of mammals
