A case of New World screwworm has been detected in U.S. wildlife for the first time.
The flesh-eating parasitic fly was found in elk on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas, after being harvested by a hunter, the U.S. Department of Agriculture said Wednesday.
The state’s parks department is conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area and a previously-established “infested zone” will be updated following the detection, the department said.
“This detection highlights the critical role hunters, landowners, outdoor enthusiasts and wildlife professionals play in helping detect and stop the spread of NWS,” the department noted. “Early reporting is one of the most important tools we have to protect wildlife, livestock and pets in the United States.”
The detection comes as another new case was reported in a New Mexico cow in Otero County. Earlier this month, two cases were reported in a calf and a horse in the state’s Grant County, five hours West of Otero. In June, Texas also confirmed cases in calves, a goat and a dog in multiple counties.
The screwworms are often attracted to cattle after procedures such as dehorning, causing fatal infestations and costing millions in livestock losses, economic damage and eradication efforts. Related livestock losses in Mexico reached an estimated $2.8 billion since 2024, according to Bloomberg Law.
To stop the spread, the U.S. closed the southern border ports to livestock imports last year - sending beef prices soaring to a record near $7 per pound in August, according to Bloomberg Tax - and has since reopened the ports in phases.
“Every animal entering the United States through these ports will undergo a full USDA inspection to ensure it is free of any signs of New World screwworm,” the Department of Agriculture said in July.
While the orange-eyed New World Screwworm was eradicated from the U.S. decades ago, the pest has moved northward from South and Central America through Mexico since 2023.
Measures have been in place to combat the spread of the metallic-bodied maggots in Mexico - releasing sterile flies into areas where known populations were established - but the screwworm suddenly overtook the other insects.
It’s still not known exactly how this happened, but the American Society for Microbiology suggests interruptions in sterile fly production during the Covid-19 pandemic could have played a role.
Unfortunately, the New World Screwworm can infect any living mammal, including humans.
The female parasite uses mouth hooks to burrow into the flesh, causing severe wounds and complications that can lead to death.
There the small fly can lay up to 300 eggs at a time. The eggs hatch into larvae that burrow into the wound to feed on the living flesh. After a week of feeding, they drop to the ground, burrow into the soil, become a pupa, and emerge.
Secondary infections may occur in already-infected wounds.
Symptoms can include feeling or seeing maggots move in a skin wound or sore, worsening skin wounds, a foul-smelling odor from wounds and bleeding from open sores.
Bacterial infections may also occur in wounds where the maggots are present, leading to symptoms like fever or chills, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Some people are at greater risk of infection, including hunters, pet owners, people who work with livestock and people who have open wounds that can attract the flies. The best way to prevent infection is to avoid exposure - including sleeping outside - and be alert for symptoms in people with a history of recent travel to endemic regions.
The only way to treat an infection is to remove the larvae from the impacted tissue. People should contact their healthcare providers immediately if they believe they may have been infected and not try to remove any maggots or egg masses by themselves.
“If maggots or eggs fall out of the wound, place them in a leak-proof container with rubbing alcohol to kill them. Bring them with you to your healthcare provider,” the CDC instructs.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously thinks bots will drive us around.
On Wednesday, he took that long-running vision of autonomy a step further. During the automaker's earnings call, Musk predicted that Tesla itself would dominate how passengers get around — so long as pesky regulators don't get in the way.
"I think Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely," he said. "And you can come back and look at this prediction, but I feel confident about this prediction."
He said Tesla's biggest hurdle to world domination is foreign governments blocking autonomous tech "to protect a domestic industry."
That is a bolder statement than Musk's prior autonomy predictions.
During a January earnings call, he said the "vast majority of miles traveled" would eventually be autonomous and guessed that people would manually drive fewer than 5% of miles. That prediction left other autonomous competitors — Waymo, Zoox, Ford, GM, Rivian, etc. — in the fray.
Vehicle autonomy is core to Tesla's valuation story. The company says its future lineup will include only one vehicle that drivers can operate manually: the high-priced Roadster.
In September, the company started rolling out the steering-wheel-less Cybercab for ride-hailing in Texas.
That rollout has had its fits and starts. While Tesla says it's ramping production and preparing to launch Cybercab rides in Florida, the NHTSA issued an audit inquiry hours after the car's public release to probe the automaker's self-certification.
Musk, who has described his predictions as his "best guesses," has missed several recent timelines for Tesla's autonomy rollout — including a prediction that unsupervised autonomy would ramp across the US in 2025.
Now, Tesla has a new target date for the consumer launch of its full self-driving software. On Wednesday, Ashok Elluswamy, the company's VP of AI, said unsupervised FSD is coming "somewhere around Q2 next year."
Tesla didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

Spotify's Family plan QR code could cost you Premium access
Spotify is trying to make some Premium Family members prove they live at the same address.
Sharing accounts with family and friends is one way to bring down the cost of subscriptions. I've done it. You may have as well. Streaming companies are all too aware this is going on, and they've made moves over the last few years to prevent folks from sharing their accounts too easily. Those include introducing family plans (even Strava has one now) and extra fees for folks who don't live with the primary account holder. Now, Spotify is trying to tighten the screw on people who share a Premium Family plan and don't reside at the same address. It recently deployed a verification system that uses QR codes.
Spotify said on a support page that it might ask Premium Family members to verify they live with the plan's manager by scanning such a code. After Spotify makes that request via a notification, the user has seven days to complete their scan. Otherwise, they may be locked out and they can't join another Family or Duo plan for a year. Alternatively, they can sign up for their own Premium plan. An individual subscription costs $13 per month, compared with $22 for a family plan, which covers up to six accounts.
Spotify is ahead of the workarounds
The company has tried to prevent people from using screenshots as a workaround for QR code scans if family plan members aren't living close to each other. Reddit users claimed that Spotify refreshes the codes every few seconds, but suggested they were able to use video calls on additional devices to scan them remotely.
While some users are unsurprisingly not too happy about the QR code policy, it's really just Spotify enforcing existing rules, as Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström said on an earnings call on Thursday.
"This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base," Norström said, as to 9to5Google noted. "As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine."

Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
- Published
Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed?
The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has.
Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta.
The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce.
But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest.
Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule.
Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war.
That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs.
Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally.
But Min Aung Hlaing was delighted.
He replied immediately to express his "sincere appreciation for this encouraging invitation to continue participating in the extraordinary Economy of the United States, the Number One Market in the World", mimicking Trump's hyperbolic phrasing and eccentric capitalisation.
"It is with great esteem that I wish to acknowledge Your Excellency's strong leadership in guiding your country toward national prosperity with the spirit of a true patriot."
This was not just a dictator's hunch that flattery might be the best way to win favours from Trump. Min Aung Hlaing's coup, and the civil war it ignited, had turned him into an international pariah.
His regime was largely unrecognised. He was accused of being a war criminal, with cases lodged against him at the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Aside from Russia and, more recently, China, he was shunned by other governments.
Yet here was the US president addressing him just like any other president or prime minister, as "Your Excellency. There was no mention in Trump's letter of the appalling human cost of Min Aung Hlaing's power seizure; of a democracy crushed and leader Aung San Suu Kyi jailed.
That same month the regime signed a $3m (£2.3m) contract with DCI, a long-standing Washington lobbying firm which had been used by a previous Burmese military regime in 2002 to try to improve its image.
Since then the military government has also hired Roger Stone, a controversial lobbyist and confidant of President Trump, at a fee of $50,000 a month.
Also around the same time Adam Castillo, a former US marine and Trump supporter who had just stepped down as president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Yangon, was in Washington trying to persuade Vice President JD Vance's team that it was time to re-engage.
Castillo believed that the US reliance on sanctions to isolate the junta had failed.
"Myanmar mattered to America not only as a morality play but as a strategic interest," he wrote in his book Finding Our Voice: A Story of Leadership in Crisis and the American Spirit Abroad. He discussed with the vice-president's team how the US "could engage Myanmar without war or isolation, loosen China's grip on critical minerals, and align peace with American interests".
Castillo was pushing at an open door.
The US dependence on rare earths from China had been exposed when China blocked them in retaliation against Trump's tariffs in April. The administration began prioritising finding alternative sources. Myanmar happens to have large reserves of rare earths which are currently being exploited solely for China's use.
At almost exactly the same time, the state department issued new guidance to US embassies around the world on what to say about elections. From now on, it said, "messages should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question".
So, when Myanmar held its much-criticised general election in December and January, allowing Min Aung Hlaing to turn himself from coup leader into a notionally civilian president, the US did not, like most Western governments, condemn it as neither free nor fair.
For decades the US has consistently pronounced judgement on other countries' elections. Now the US had nothing to say.
Washington's decision to lift sanctions on some of those targeted by the Biden administration seemed only to confirm the new direction of US-Myanmar policy.
"For years, the US approach to Myanmar has been defined by isolation, sanctions, and distance," wrote the lobbyists DCI in a recent newsletter. "That era is over… thankfully, President Trump has the courage to try something different."
The tone is certainly different, but not so much the substance of US-Myanmar relations.
"In practice less has changed than the headlines suggest," says Richard Horsey, Myanmar adviser for the International Crisis Group, adding that Min Aung Hlaing is still sanctioned. "What is new is the level of contact and the location. Senior US officials have now been to Nay Pyi Taw, which is exactly what Min Aung Hlaing wanted. What he wants next is sanctions relief, and that will be harder."
It was another Trump initiative last year, though, which has arguably had a much greater impact on Myanmar: the dismantling of USAID, which slashed aid to opposition groups, dissident media and refugees by more than half.
There was also the decision, decried by human rights groups, to withdraw Temporary Protected Status from 4,000 Burmese who had sought sanctuary in the US. This has left them living in fear of being sent back, where many face being jailed, or worse.
As for the rare earths in Myanmar, few experts believe they will ever be of much use to the US. Most lie in areas contested by ethnic insurgent armies.
They are currently extracted by Chinese companies with long experience of operating in these lawless borderlands, and transported over the border to China for processing. It is difficult to see how the US could get access to them.
It is also doubtful that the US will get meaningful co-operation from the Myanmar government in combating the scam industry.
There have been a few highly-publicised actions against some of the larger scam compounds, but the syndicates running them have simply dispersed to smaller operations in more remote areas, and in any case most are run with the support of militia groups allied to the Myanmar military.
"Talking to Nay Pyi Taw is not wrong in itself," says Horsey.
"The question is what Washington asks for and what it gives away. It should use the channel for the things that matter most: humanitarian access, an end to airstrikes on civilians. It should keep talking to the opposition and the ethnic armed groups, who hold much of the country. And on scams, the most effective thing the US can do is to co-ordinate with other governments in the region, including China, to go after the money."
Perhaps the bigger question, though, is whether President Trump, distracted by domestic politics and the war on Iran, has the capacity to give any sustained attention to Myanmar, let alone enough to challenge the dominant influence of China.

Upper caste activists gherao HP Secretariat; demand UGC notification rollback, Swaran Aayog
Panchayat and Rural Development Minister Anirudh Singh was deputed to talk to the protesters on Thursday.
Hundreds of Swaran (upper caste) community activists demanding the rollback of the UGC notification in January and the enactment of a Swaran Aayog gheraoed the Himachal Pradesh Secretariat on Thursday, prompting the police to resort to mild use of force.
Protesters linked to the Rashtriya Devbhoomi Party and allied associations attempted to breach the state secretariat as the 21-day, 600-kilometre foot march 'Swarn Samaj Ashwamedh Nyay Yatra' reached the state capital Shimla.
As the traffic came to a standstill in Chota Shimla, police deployed water cannons and used mild force to disperse the demonstrators.
Panchayat and Rural Development Minister Anirudh Singh was deputed to talk to the protesters on Thursday. A meeting between the chief minister and the leaders spearheading the demonstration has also been scheduled for Friday.
Rumit Singh Thakur, president of Rashtriya Devbhoomi Party, which organised the foot march, said the yatra received an overwhelming response, and called it a "victory for the entire society".
He said they are grateful that no case was registered against the protesters.
Alleging that both the BJP and the Congress governments in Himachal Pradesh have failed to address the issues raised by his party, Thakur cautioned that no political party would be able to win the 2027 Assembly elections without the support of Swaran Samaj, as the community constitutes a huge section of the state's population and wields tremendous influence in the society.
He said Cabinet Minister Anirudh Singh was deputed to hold talks with the protesters, and this was no mean feat as he represents the government.
Mahipal Singh Makrana, president of Rajput Karni Sena, which is also associated with the agitation, said, "Our main demand is rollback of the University Grants Commission (UGC) notification and the enactment of a law for Swaran Aayog."
He said the provision of 15 per cent reservation for Scheduled Castes, 7.5 per cent for Scheduled Tribes, 27 per cent for Other Backward Classes and 4 per cent for Persons with Disabilities was a cruel joke on the Swaran Samaj and it will not be brooked.
The University Grants Commission notified the UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026 on January 13 this year to curb discrimination in Indian higher education. A Supreme Court bench stayed the operation of these regulations on January 29, 2026, observing that they appeared vague and were susceptible to misuse.
Swaran Aayog refers to the demand of the upper caste community to constitute a state-level commission to study and address the economic, educational, and social challenges faced by economically weaker sections among members of the general category.

iPhone Duo's next-gen prototypes are trying to cram in Face ID
For understandable reasons, the first generation returned to Touch ID.
You might have a hard time trying to get hold of one yourself for the foreseeable future, but the iPhone Duo has been in the hands of reviewers for a little while now. And while it is clearly a first-generation product, overall impressions of Apple's first foldable have been broadly very positive.
One potential annoyance for anyone coming from another modern iPhone, however, is the lack of Face ID, with Apple instead opting to go back to Touch ID for the first time since 2022's iPhone SE. Most iPhone users will have been using Face ID since the iPhone X. In our own review we said the Touch ID solution here works accurately, but can take a bit longer to unlock the phone than you might expect, and according to reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman, the company is already looking at how it can bring its newer technology to the iPhone Duo's inevitable follow-up.
Speaking on his new Power On podcast, Gurman said Apple is "actively working" on under-display Face ID, and that there are already iPhone Duo 2 prototypes that have the technology built into the phone's outer display. He also pointed to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with their shrunken down Dynamic Island hardware, as evidence that Apple is finding ways to move more components underneath its phones' displays. The first-gen iPhone Duo also features Apple's first under-display camera.
As for why Apple chose to outfit its $2,000 foldable with a feature it largely retired from iPhones almost a decade ago (although plenty of MacBook and lower-end iPad models still use Touch ID), it likely has a lot to do with the fact the iPhone Duo is designed to be used in a number of different orientations. Putting Face ID sensors on both the inner and outer displays might have been a bit of a stretch, and may have pushed up the price of an already enormously expensive device.
Gurman points out that the iPhone Duo's display is very thin, so squeezing even more components into it would have also been challenging. Apple wanted uniformity with both displays, so getting Face ID into one but not the other was unlikely to materialize this time. The Bloomberg reporter added that the action button, which Apple introduced on the iPhone 15 Pro, may also feature in an eventual iPhone Duo 2.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

John Mayer has had his hands full with what felt like a hundred projects over the past few years — with putting out new music not among them. It takes a stretch of the memory to even recall that he announced a parting of ways with Sony Music back in 2022, with no followup revelation about where, if anywhere, he planned to go next . Now, after hinting at the beginning of this year that new studio recordings were afoot, he’s finally publicly kicking the recording artist part of his career back into gear.
Mayer and associates announced Thursday that he has started up his own label, Sob Rock Records — which shares the name of the last album he put out for Sony, 2021’s “Sob Rock” — to be operated in partnership with Universal Music’s Mercury Records. No album has yet been announced, but his first single in five years, “Tom and Jerry,” is arriving under his new shingle Friday.
Popular on Variety
“Working with Tyler Arnold and the talented team at Mercury Records has already proven to be a great partnership,” Mayer said in a statement. “The path from creative vision to execution has never been easier or more rewarding. I feel very inspired, and I’m excited for what’s to come.”
	“John Mayer is one of the greatest artists of all time,” said Arnold, Mercury’s chairman-CEO, 
and I couldn’t be prouder to welcome him to Mercury Records. We’re excited to be part of his next chapter and to partner with his label, Sob Rock Records, to help bring his creative vision to life.”
The new single arrives at DSPs at the usual midnight hour as Thursday turns into Friday, but listeners to the artist’s SiriusXM channel, Life With John Mayer, will get a preview throughout the day Thursday. The song was produced by Blake Slatkin with Mayer and mixed by Serban Genhea.
It almost goes without saying that the credits acknowledge the song was recorded at Chaplin Studios. One of Mayer’s biggest endeavors in the past couple of years was joining forces with the film director McG to purchase the Hollywood lot that started as Charlie Chaplin’s studio and eventually became the home of A&M, then Henson Studios. Foster son accused of murdering mom who was battling cancer to get her money
Prosecutors say Cedric von Ferdinand carried out an elaborate scheme to take control of his foster mother’s real estate portfolio after she mysteriously disappeared during cancer treatment

A 34-year-old San Diego County man has been charged with murder after prosecutors said he fatally poisoned his foster mother with fentanyl and concealed her body on her Southern California property to steal her real estate assets.
Cedric von Ferdinand was arrested Tuesday in Los Angeles County and is scheduled for a Thursday arraignment on one count of murder and two special circumstance allegations — killing for financial gain and administering poison — in the death of 64-year-old Nadine Jett. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole or the death penalty.
The victim, a retired attorney who was undergoing treatment for pancreatic cancer, disappeared in January 2024, as reported by NBC 7 San Diego. According to prosecutors, Jett was last seen alive during a chemotherapy session on January 14, 2024. Investigators believe von Ferdinand killed her between January 14 and January 17.
Prosecutors said toxicology reports revealed a massive amount of acetylfentanyl, a compound found in illicit rather than pharmaceutical-grade fentanyl, in Jett’s system, prompting the medical examiner to rule her death a homicide caused by acute fentanyl toxicity.
In the days surrounding her death, he told her family and friends that her health was rapidly declining and claimed she wanted to travel to Mexico to be cremated without a funeral service, authorities said. He also dismissed Jett’s caretaker, telling her around January 17 that her services were no longer required because Jett had died.
Jett’s foster daughters reported her missing in June 2024 after becoming suspicious of von Ferdinand’s claims and after he repeatedly prevented them from visiting her in person.
Authorities later searched Jett’s 20-acre property on Oak Creek Road in Valley Center, where detectives uncovered her skeletal remains in July 2025. Prosecutors said that on January 16, 2024, von Ferdinand had hired someone to dig a six-by-six-foot hole on the property, where her body was eventually recovered roughly 30 yards from the home.
Investigators said the motive was financial. Following Jett's disappearance, von Ferdinand used documents bearing her forged signature to gain power of attorney, transfer control of her ranch and two Los Angeles County properties to himself and withdraw thousands of dollars from her bank accounts. He also used her funds to purchase another residence in Los Angeles County.
Two co-defendants have also been charged in connection with the fraud scheme.
Kimberley Pifer faces forgery and identity theft charges for allegedly impersonating Jett and marrying von Ferdinand under Jett’s name in May 2024.
Escondido-based notary public Raymond Joseph Alto, 46, is accused of notarizing documents with forged signatures, including a notary log where von Ferdinand allegedly submitted his own thumbprint in place of Jett’s.
An attempt to sell her primary home in Valley Center fell through when he was unable to produce a death certificate.
In April 2025, von Ferdinand was indicted on multiple counts of real estate fraud linked to the transactions.
“This is a case of deadly greed,” Summer Stephan, the San Diego County district attorney, said at a news conference announcing the homicide charges. “His deadly greed led to this horrific homicide. He preyed on her in her time of need when she was suffering from cancer. It is quite despicable.”
Bianca Lucci, one of Jett’s four foster daughters whom Jett took in after they had been in ten separate foster homes, expressed relief following the homicide charges.
“She was the mom we needed,” Lucci told NBC 7 San Diego. “She gave us a fair chance at life. I’m glad justice will finally be served. I do believe that this was all out of greed and money and it’s just sad.”

Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 200 people, sources say
- Published
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 200 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.
The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 73 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.
The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.
"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday, external.
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.
Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line 
  - Published25 February
The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.
A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.
Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.
Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.
Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.
The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) and had killed 73 people, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.
"We were surprised by bombing and thick smoke inside Amiet Common Market, which is located 10km [six miles] from Abyei town," he said.
BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.
It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.
Ngor told the Reuters news agency that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.
Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.

Muammar Gaddafi's 42-year rule over Libya ended violently near his hometown of Sirte on October 20, 2011, when opposition fighters captured and killed him.
His death marked the culmination of an uprising that began months earlier and was bolstered by a Nato-led military intervention. But the fall of one of Africa's longest-serving rulers did not bring the oil-rich North African country the stability many Libyans had hoped for.
Fifteen years later, Libya remains divided between rival political administrations and competing centres of military power. Although a unified national budget was approved in April 2026 and a United Nations-backed agreement in August set out steps towards long-delayed elections, the country continues to struggle with political fragmentation, armed groups and disputes over state resources.
The question, therefore, is not just how Gaddafi fell, but why his removal failed to bring stability to Libya.
Why Gaddafi's regime fell
The uprising against Muammar Gaddafi began in February 2011, amid the Arab Spring protests that had toppled long-serving rulers in Tunisia and Egypt.
Protests erupted in Benghazi on February 15, following the arrest of government critics, including a lawyer representing families of prisoners killed in the 1996 Abu Salim prison massacre. 
Libyan security forces responded with tear gas, batons and violence against demonstrators.
The crackdown escalated the protests into an armed rebellion, with opposition forces taking control of parts of eastern Libya. On February 26, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1970, imposing sanctions and referring the situation to the International Criminal Court.
On March 17, it adopted Resolution 1973, authorising member states to take “all necessary measures” to protect civilians. Nato took command of the military operation on March 31, enforcing an arms embargo and no-fly zone and conducting military operations.
Tripoli fell to opposition forces on August 21, 2011, forcing Gaddafi's regime out of the capital. Two months later, as rebels overran his hometown of Sirte, Gaddafi attempted to flee in a convoy that came under Nato air strikes.
He was captured alive by fighters from Misrata on October 20 and killed shortly afterwards. A subsequent Human Rights Watch investigation found evidence that he had been beaten and wounded after his capture, raising questions over a possible extrajudicial killing.
What happened to Libya after Gaddafi's death
Gaddafi's death in October 2011 left Libya facing the challenge of building a new political system while armed groups that had fought his regime retained their weapons and influence.
The National Transitional Council oversaw the transition before handing power to an elected General National Congress in August 2012. However, successive governments struggled to bring militias under state control, while political divisions and insecurity continued to deepen.
Libya's civil war deepens the divide
Libya descended into a full-scale civil war in 2014, as political divisions and rival armed groups fractured the country.
In May that year, military commander Khalifa Haftar launched Operation Dignity against Islamist militant groups and other opponents in eastern Libya, including Benghazi. Two months later, a separate campaign known as Libya Dawn emerged in western Libya, as Misrata-based armed groups and their allies fought rival factions, particularly over control of Tripoli International Airport.
The fighting left Libya divided between rival political and military camps in the east and west, each establishing its own institutions and command structures.
The security vacuum also allowed Islamic State (ISIS) to expand its presence. The group established a foothold in Derna before consolidating control over Sirte in 2015, turning Gaddafi's hometown into its main stronghold in Libya.
ISIS imposed its rule through public executions, kidnappings and intimidation, while recruiting local fighters and former regime personnel.
The United Nations Security Council warned in 2015 that the group's growing presence, alongside other extremist organisations, posed a serious threat to Libya and the wider region.
In December 2015, a UN-brokered political agreement paved the way for the Government of National Accord, intended to reunify Libya's institutions. But the arrangement struggled to establish authority across the country. However, forces aligned with the internationally recognised government, supported by US air strikes, drove ISIS from Sirte in December 2016.
Haftar's forces eventually launched an offensive against Tripoli in April 2019. The United Arab Emirates and Egypt supported Haftar's eastern camp, while Turkey provided crucial military support to Tripoli-aligned forces. Russia also backed Haftar's forces, including through personnel linked to the Wagner Group. These competing external interests reinforced Libya's internal divisions and complicated efforts to reach a political settlement.
A UN-backed ceasefire in October 2020 halted large-scale fighting between the principal camps, but rival administrations and competing security structures endured.
Libya after 2020
The ceasefire of October 2020 ended large-scale fighting between Libya's rival eastern and western camps, but failed to reunify the country's political and military institutions.
A UN-backed process installed Abdul Hamid Dbeibah as head of the Government of National Unity (GNU) in 2021, with elections intended to end the transitional period. The vote was postponed indefinitely amid disputes over electoral laws and candidate eligibility.
In 2022, the eastern-based House of Representatives appointed a rival administration, leaving Libya divided between competing governments.
The division remains central to Libya's current political and military landscape.
The GNU, led by Dbeibah, operates from Tripoli in the west, while an eastern-based administration led by Osama Hamad is backed by the House of Representatives and Khalifa Haftar's Libyan Arab Armed Forces, also known as the Libyan National Army.
Haftar's forces control much of eastern Libya and have expanded their influence and security presence in parts of the south.
Western Libya, meanwhile, remains divided among government-aligned and other armed formations.
Although the main east-west front has remained largely quiet since the ceasefire, rival military structures and local militia rivalries continue to pose security risks.
The US Congressional Research Service reported in July 2026 that Haftar's forces had expanded their influence in the south and strengthened their military capabilities, including through drones.
The political deadlock has also complicated efforts to organise national elections.
In August 2026, a UN-facilitated agreement set out steps to reform the High National Elections Commission and address outstanding issues in the legal framework for presidential and parliamentary elections. The parties committed to work towards holding the vote within 24 months, rather than agreeing on a fixed election date.
However, the process has encountered fresh resistance.
In an October 14 briefing to the UN Security Council, UN Special Representative Hanna S. Tetteh said the House of Representatives had endorsed the agreement, but the High State Council rejected it on October 5, citing concerns over constitutional, legal and consensual procedures.
The setback underlines how even a negotiated roadmap can become another point of contention between rival institutions.
Oil wealth, economic pressure and failing public services
Despite possessing Africa's largest proven oil reserves, Libya continues to face serious economic and fiscal vulnerabilities. Oil remains the backbone of its economy, accounting for 65 per cent of GDP, 93 per cent of exports and 72 per cent of government revenue in 2024, according to the World Bank.
Production recovery has supported economic growth, but dependence on hydrocarbons leaves public finances exposed to disruptions caused by political disputes, fluctuating oil output and weak fiscal management.
The International Monetary Fund warned in April 2026 that Libya's fiscal position had become increasingly vulnerable, estimating the budget deficit at around 30 per cent of GDP in 2025 and public debt at 146 per cent of GDP over the preceding two years. The IMF called for urgent fiscal adjustment to ease pressure on foreign exchange reserves, the dinar and inflation.
In April, representatives of Libya's House of Representatives and High Council of State agreed to a unified national budget worth 190 billion Libyan dinars, or about $29.95 billion. It was the first such agreement since 2013.
Central Bank Governor Naji Issa, who supervised the signing, described it as “a clear declaration that Libya is capable of overcoming its differences when a unified vision for its future is forged”.
The agreement was intended to improve financial coordination and support development spending across the country, although its implementation remains a separate test. The deal marked progress in financial coordination, but it did not resolve the political divisions underpinning the country's wider crisis.
The consequences of fragmentation are particularly visible in public services and infrastructure. The September 2023 floods that devastated Derna exposed failures in infrastructure maintenance, disaster preparedness and public accountability.
Public services remain weak despite the country's oil wealth. The World Bank has highlighted shortcomings in healthcare, education, water and electricity provision, alongside high unemployment, corruption concerns and an underdeveloped private sector.
These problems continue to constrain Libya's development, even as oil revenues offer the country significant financial resources.
Fragile peace, uncertain future
Although Libya has avoided a return to full-scale civil war since the 2020 ceasefire, rival military structures, powerful armed groups and foreign involvement continue to threaten stability.
Briefing the UN Security Council on October 14, Tetteh warned that “institutional and political fragmentation have continued to impact negatively on the economic and security situation in the country”.
She said many Libyans were seeing their purchasing power eroded by rising food prices, a weaker dinar and inflation above 14 per cent, while access to essential public services remained unreliable.
Tetteh also cautioned that the path to stability remained difficult, saying, “The path to a stable, unified, and prosperous Libya remains long, but our destination remains within reach.” She urged Libyan political actors to demonstrate the flexibility and political will needed to reach common ground.
Fifteen years after Gaddafi's death, Libya's challenge is no longer simply to prevent another civil war. It is to build a state capable of controlling armed groups, managing oil revenues transparently and delivering reliable public services.
The election roadmap and unified budget offer potential steps towards greater stability, but neither guarantees lasting peace. Libya's future will depend on whether rival leaders can turn these commitments into a functioning political settlement.
